Hands down, one of the best hidden objects games. Usually these Horror HOGs tend to go pretty dull and boring at some point throughout the game, leaving you with bad jumpscares, complicated storyline, minigames that don't make sense and no horror. This game though, is actually scary. It has one of the best horror atmospheres, intriguing story and exciting gameplay. Only thing that I find a bit extreme is the achievements, but nothing that is impossible to unlock. Still epic. I definitely recommend to horror lovers.

ARGHHH! ..I guess I just hate hidden object games or something.. but this game not only bored me to tears, but also tested my frustration.  There is NOTHING scary about this game at all, it's just walking around a house looking for hidden objects that you can use to open more objects to find more hidden objects.. only to open a door and find more hidden objects that help you open something else... over and over and over and over and over.
It's tedius, not fun at all.  And like I said, it's anything but scary.
Even the intitial sale price of $10.49 is about $10 too much for this game in my opinion, but again I just don't think I am a fan of these hidden object games.  I bought it because of the other positive reviews saying how great and different this game was from other hidden object games, but I was led astray.  ARGH. - No, wait that didn't help after playing this for over an hour... ARRRRGHHHHHHHHH!  Ahhh, better.
My Scoring:
VALUE: 2 out of 40: Because it's way too much money for such static simplistic hidden object solving, unless you perhaps tend to enjoy these sort of games.
FUN: 0 out of 30: Frustration 30 out of 30 equals 0 out of 30 fun for me!  ARGH (again)
CONTROLS & BUGS: 20 out of 20: Easily the highest part of my score because the controls work perfectly as intended, but this isn't exactly Mortal Kombat sort of controls we are talking about either.  - Still, I can't take points away here.  20 out of 20.
GRAPHICS & SOUND:  The graphics and sounds are pretty good for this kind of game to be honest, and the sounds are certainly convincing and creepy.  Add in pretty decent voice acting, and this aspect of my scoring is pretty high at an 8 out of 10.  ...Too bad graphics wasn't worth 80% of my score and more important then the value and fun eh?  Hehe.
MY TOTAL SCORE:  30% or a "3 out of 10".  Not recommended to anyone except maybe hidden object game fans.  My video above should give you enough information to decide if this game is worth it's price tag to you.

The Steam Controller is exactly why Steam reviews need a "Maybe" button.
If, and ONLY if, you are a person who for some reason wants to play Civ V or some other M+K only game on your couch with a controller should you buy this thing.  In almost any other situation an Xbox 360 or One controller will be more comforable and easier to use.
I played about 8 hours of Civ V from my couch and got so used to this controller I kind of forgot how I even used to play without it!
But on the other hand...trying to play a game with intricate mouse controls like MGSV, Just Cause 3, The Witcher 3, Bioshock Infinite and so on is EXTREMELY frustrating and diffuclt. The track pad just doesn't offer the same feel and smoothness of a joystick.
Even for 2D games like Oddworld, Ori and the Blind Forest, and Undertale I recommend a normal 360 pad because on the Steam Controller the A, B, X, and Y buttons are in an uncomfortable position.
I just can't recommend this thing unless you are DYING to play RTS games from your couch.

This is a great board game with lots of replayability, especially if you have all the expansions. Prior to the latest update, I played this game for well over a hundred hours both against strangers online and people on my buddy list. Screencheat puts a fun and intense spin on typical Competitive-Multiplayer FPS games by taking away a main element of typical FPS games and intensifying the use of another people rarely use efficiently. In this game, everyone is invisible, and it is really difficult to find them other than what the game title suggests you to do: Screen cheat, that being, looking at other players screens to determine where they are. Now by the sound of this it seems very difficult, but the intensely colorful environments and uinique areas of the maps make this far easy than as if this mechanic was in another game.
On top of this unique mechanic the developers make the game revolve around, the variety of gamemodes and customization are what make this game so much fun. From the classic deathmatch to capturing and running around with a pinata, playing this game with others is a true party (especially with 8 people at once!). Also, the customization, mutators, and silly announcers are sure to get a laugh out of you.
When I statrted out playing this game I had a hard time trying to kill ONE guy, let alone the other 3 at once (I started playing this right as soon as the game got out of Beta). Despite me failing hard at this game it was difficult to stay mad because the style of this game is just too damn funny. Instead of throwing my controller across the room I was too busy rolling around on the floor laughing. Of course eventually I got way too good at it and now people avoid me when I try to play, but that's another story.
So to sum it up: Screencheat is a funny spin on typical FPS multiplayer games that is sure to give you a good time with friends and just about anyone online.

Hell of a lot of fun. One of the few sandboxes that I've actually finished.
Bully takes place in the town of Bullworth in New England, possibly in 1970-1980s. That's never been made clear but nevermind. You're a boy that's basically dumped into this boarding school by your mother. You have to gain respect among your new mates while avoiding getting to trouble with the teachers. Basically GTA with criminals replaced by nerds, jocks, greasers and rich inbreds and police replaced by teachers, but there's more.
The town itself is also part of the game world and it offers the player lots of optional missions and some larger story missions also take partly place there. Every day you have lessons according to your curriculum and it's up to you if you are to attend those or just play hooky, go have fun and risk the punishment. The lessons provide you some nice bonuses upon completion (especially chemistry), so it pays to take the classes and if you're quick, you have time to go downtown at the end of the day anyway.
The game is heavily story-driven, but it's a fun experience and you do have all the time in the world to grind yourself silly before advancing the story if that's your idea of fun. Only the end felt a bit rushed and way too much of wish-fulfillment fantasy, but it isn't a deal-breaker. Bully is a very fun romp that feels like a game version Animal House, if Animal House took place in a boarding school instead of university. The game also reminded me somewhat of the old Jennings book series, if that is at all familiar.
Bully is frequently on sale and for a couple of bucks/euros you really can't go wrong if you like sandbox games at all. The game is a console port, but it works fairly well. The controls may seem weird at first if you're using keyboard, but they're easy and responsive once you get used to them.

Bit.Trip Void is the third entry in the Bit.Trip series, taking a much different gameplay approach not seen in many games. As with the other Bit.Trip games, it has its pixel based graphics and chiptune style music. However, this game's aesthetic is more chilled out with the backgrounds being mostly solid colors and gradients and the music having a more relaxed beat. The story brings Commander Video with other people who look like him and interacting some kind of aura or ball that makes them bigger or smaller. That brings us to the gameplay, which indeed revolves around a kind of ball.
On the screen is a black circle that can be controlled around. The goal is to get black blocks and avoid white ones. There are different patterns to react to with differing amounts of black and white blocks and some powerups that will be useful to finish some sections. The end bosses tend to reference other Arcade games from the 80s and fit in with the gameplay. In a way, this game feels like Katamari as the goal is to collect objects and in doing so, increases your circle's size. There is a button that allows you to reset your circle to the smallest, which is important to avoid white blocks or move faster. Hitting white blocks can make the ball smaller, but you do lose some points that way.
This game tends to be easier than the last 2 in the series, which is evident by the more relaxed style rather than the more energetic visual style of previous games. Simply controlling a black circle to collect other things and avoiding white lends some precise player control like in platformers or shoot em ups. The rhythm element is still in this game where collecting black squares make a sound, but the player has more control and can somewhat vary how each set of sounds play. Regardless, the unique gameplay makes this fun yet relaxing to play. That isn't to say this game is very easy, since the game does throw some challenging things that may cause a game over.
Bit.Trip Void is overall less energetic to give some relaxed gameplay with a slightly easier difficulty. The idea of collecting black while avoiding white is simple, yet lends itself to some complex patterns to tackle and has some difficult challenges that can appear. With a simple yet original gameplay idea and more mellow design, Void is both fun to play and not as taxing on reaction time while having some moments of difficulty to mix things up.

Void is possibly the oddest and hardest to classify of Gaijin Games Bit.Trip saga. Playing as what more or less amounts to an all consuming black hole, black and white blocks come at you from all sides of the screen in time with the beat of the track, and your job is to grab the former and dodge the latter. Every block you manage to catch increases your size a bit, which gives you more points but makes it harder to dodge obstacles and slower to move around, creating a game of give and take as you attempt to keep yourself as large as possible before having to shrink back down.
At its core, I think the ideas behind Void are really original and intriguing despite being incredible simple, but my issue with it is that Gaijin doesn't seem to have any idea what its doing with these mechanics. Through the games 3 levels I never felt particularly impressed with any of the patterns or sequences, they simply played out and I went through the motions to complete them, without so much as a small bit of satisfaction or enjoyment coming from it. Although it's a very short game (I finished it in under an hour), it drags its feet so much during levels that I found myself wishing it would end only halfway through a level. It fumbles over the line of acceptable repetition into monotony, and as a result I can't see myself wanting to ever replay it (which is definitely something the developers were hoping for, given its leaderboard centric design).
It's not that I think Bit.Trip Void is a bad game, it's just an unfocused one that attempts something neat but screws up the execution. The art design and soundtrack are as excellent as the series is known for, but where Gaijin's other games kept me glued to my screen for hours on end, this one made me want to abandon ship after only a handful of minutes with it. For as much as I love the rest of the series, there's no denying that that is a definite problem, and reason enough for me not to be able to recommend it.

As of writing this review I have just finished Episodes 1-5 (Not 6-8 included in the Adventure Pass).
Anyone who has played a Telltale game should know what to expect here. The game (although very linear) is all about making choices. This could be as simple as choosing a name for your team or as meaningful as choosing one of two characters to try and save from danger. Whatever your choices, the story will continue down the same path, with only minor branching parts determined by what you do. For me, the choices were about roleplaying who I wanted to be and how I wanted to present myself rather than what impact I had on the story.
The major difference between this game and the other Telltale games is the tone. The Minecraft theme is very light-hearted, which is a big change from a game like The Walking Dead. Even though the story involves overcoming dangers and saving the world, it feels like more of a grand adventure and less of a struggle for survival. Characters are constantly making jokes and everything has that family movie vibe to it. On one hand it was quite refreshing to play a character in a world like that but on the other hand it makes the most of the choices feel like they have less weight to them. The Walking Dead had tension hanging over every desicion you make but that just wasn't here for me this time.
Despite this I think the theme serves the game really well. The characters, culture, and world are based on the gameplay and weird quirky logic of Minecraft. The result of this is a living, breathing world that is completely new yet 100% familiar to Minecraft players. On top of that, you yourself are doing many Minecraft-y things in this game. You can tell without a doubt that the developers are big Minecraft fans and put a lot of thought into how best to use the setting.
One thing I should mention is that the game had a few minor bugs for me (some dialogue seemed to be cut short at times, and the game had some graphical glitches occasionally), but nothing that impacted my experience much.
On a more positive note another thing to mention is the fantastic voice acting!
Anyway, long story short I feel that the gameplay itself is good but nothing amazing but the use of the setting is extremely well done and that is what makes the game stand out for me. I would easily say this is worth a shot IF you already a fan of Minecraft.

I've been enjoying Ticket To Ride for so long on my mobile device I've decided it's time to write a few impressions here as well.
First of all, what is TTR? It's digital version of fun, strategic board game that lets you build your railways between the cities on the map. The goal of the game is to build as many railroads and 'clear' as many tickets as possible by combining train cards of different colors. It is one of those easy to learn, hard to master games which eventually turns out to be the main cause of complete mental breakdowns of its players while they scrape their last cards trying to clean their goals. It's a great board game and the rules are well balanced between luck and strategy, meaning you might be getting a great hands and still get completely destroyed by other players and their tactics.
Digital version of the game is pretty much polished. Lately, I've been encountering this 'authenticating' pop-up which ends with 'server error' message, but you can cancel it and go on playing. TTR offers solo, online, local and 'pass'n'play' options for up to five players, so no matter if you're able to sit down through the game or can spend only a few minutes each day - there's a mod for you.
Additional maps (boards) and rulesets are available as DLCs and currently you can get complete DLC pack for less than five bucks which is super cheap.
Where I live, base version of Ticket to Ride board game costs around 35 €. Expansions are either equally bloody expensive or unavailable. If you want to avoid mess and/or don't want to support greedy local stores, be sure to get digital version of Ticket to Ride and enjoy this fine, cross-platform mind boggling lunacy.

Playing FPS games with the Steam Controller wasn't as painful as I thought it would be. I first tested with the Serious Sam games and found it to be quite fun using the touchpad/gyro combo for accuracy. I'm still better with a keyboard and mouse, but if I'm gaming on the couch it's much more doable compared to an average controller. For example if I play Team Fortress 2 on the couch/in bed/in the bathroom my score isn't that far off from if I were sitting at my desk. It also handled hack n slashes like Devil May Cry and Metal Gear Rising, and stealth games like Dishonored and MGSV: The Phantom Pain like a feckin' baws.
If you play Skyrim or a similar RPG for example and you have lots of buttons and binds, another nice feature I like is the touch menu. You can set it so if you press a button a small screen will appear with options for you to click on. I have mine set to easily access my favorites, spells, inventory, etc.
Another nice feature: You can even use the Steam Controller with non-steam games. I own The Witcher 3 through GOG, and when I looked at the community configs I found a nice selection of presets to choose from. I didn't really care for playing The Witcher 3 with a keyboard and mouse, and aiming at your enemies with a controller was a pain for me. So for my own convenience it's nice to have the best of both worlds in one item.
If you play lots of games that are already pretty controller dependent you might not see this as a worthy investment, but if you're interested in a versatile controller for PC games of multiple kinds that'll work great with most of your library then I highly HIGHLY recommend this. Especially if you have an HTPC setup and want to be able to play almost any game from your collection from the comfort of your couch, bed, kitchen, bathroom, or wherever the hell you have your computer.

I rate the game Saints Row 2 (PC version of course) 3.5/5. Though essentially a rip-off of the Grand Theft Auto games, this still manages to be a pretty fun game in most respects.
(Of course, I played this using a graphics card and processor that wasn't even invented at the time this game first came out and used a version of the game that was probably completely patched and had most of its bugs worked out and so the game worked almost perfectly for me. It only kicked me out to the desktop once).
Controls: Certain controls cannot be re-mapped to other keys though most controls can. Specifically the controls required to allow you to make helicopters go up or down are permanently assigned to the arrow keys and cannot be changed. As certain missions absolutely require the use of the helicopter so figuring this out and then creating a control scheme that doesn't interfere with the arrow keys is crucial but frustrating as the game doesn't inform you if this situation. The game does not allow any controls to be mapped to the additional mouse buttons which most gaming mice have these days and as a result the controls were fairly clunky and even obtuse by modern standards.
Sound Effects: Adequate to mediocre sound effects in the classic tradition of Grand Theft Auto style games. Nothing sounds particularly realistic and the sounds can be fake sounding to the point of being funny. Movie scenes which advance the plot were always quite a bit louder than the main game.
Music: While not as good as the radio stations in most Grand Theft Auto games, this game has a bunch of fake radio stations to choose from, many of which sound almost too close to the truth. Unfortunately (and unrealistically) there are no talk-radio shows in this game though there are radio advertisements which are funny. This game caused me to buy two songs which I heard in this game however (Gangster ♥♥♥♥♥ by Apache and North American Scum by LCD Soundsystems). This rest of the music sounds like fairly trashy, standard music that it is common to hear on the radio in most large cities these days.
Graphics: The graphics were about as good as they were in Grand Theft Auto: Vice City except less colorful and sort of continually stained in a odd, faded sepia tone. The graphics could actually get quite ugly in a lot of places and got very boring and severely detracted from the game. Still, throngs of people, cars and lots of tall buildings and nifty city activity can be viewed throughout but expect some odd graphical bugs where people fly into and off of the screen and there is a terrible amount of graphical pop-in/pop-out effects (Like in Grand Theft Auto: Vice City).
Story/Plot: The story is the weak point of this game in that it is fairly boring. The story revolves around jump-starting a weak gang and then helping/running that gang and taking over the entire city by doing missions wherein you compete with other gangs (and eventually an evil corporation) for territory and for reputation. Mini-missions largely focus on causing various sorts of totally unrealistic mayhem to earn cash and respect for your gang. Mostly, the game is extremely unrealistic, doesn't take itself seriously and most events are played for sarcastic laughs but the game's cut-scenes are often not true to this spirit. The cut scenes tend to be extremely grimdark and feature pulp-fiction type situations that, if on film, would be completely R rated and would look like they are out of some sort of pulp-fiction/mafia/TheDarkKnight/John Wick hybrid movie if the graphics weren't so cartoony. This game is interesting in that, at best there are no heros in this game and at worst, you are playing as some sort of joker-type super villain in a city where there is no batman (and it really, really needs a batman) but beyond that aspect, the game's story is fairly uninteresting.
Other/Honorable Mention: The character creation abilities of this game are amazing and rival and in some ways, even surpass Skyrim's custom character creation abilities. I was fairly successful in my attempt to create an extremely unusual sci-fi character which I've dreamt up. The muscle mass/fat options can result in amazing changes. You can have a morbidly obese character or an extremely thin one. You can even do what I did and have an extremely thin, skinny character who somehow also has fairly well-toned and well developed muscles far beyond what such a skinny person would ever realistically have. You can have anything in-between. You can have a character with almost any major hair style or, like my character, no hair at all. You can make a character have any skin tone or color that is common in the USA. You can go to clothing stores in the game and buy custom clothing for your character (different stores sell different types of clothing so it can take a while to get your character's full wardrobe together) but whatever you decide to have your character wear, (anything from nothing but underwear to something as crazy as a hot-dog suit), whatever you wear will be what your character wears in the in-game cutscenes which can lead to a great deal of potential humor from start to finish. Or if you merely like your custom character's fairly unique style, at the very least it adds a great deal of interest to the game as your custom character strikes different poses while wearing whatever you want him/her to wear. For example, this would be an ideal game to play if you want to pretend to play as the Joker from Batman.

Hooray! A Xbox One Exclusive finally came to PC so I didn't have to spent money on a console that I don't see playing that much due to the fact that around 80% of Xbox One games are multiplatforms. I loved the Dead Rising series when I had my Xbox 360 and I did buy all three of them (Dead Rising, Dead Rising 2 and Dead Rising 2: Off the Record) including their DLC (Case: Zero and Case: West) but the problem with Dead Rising 3 that I had to buy the newest console to play it, which was a darn shame. But not anymore!
I'm still playing the game so I haven't reached the ending just yet. But it's not making me stop playing the thing. There is a lot of things to do to keep me engaged. Collectibles, side quests and challenges that are scattered all around Los Perdidos. Let's talk about that darn city!
Los Perdidos is huge. Definitely bigger than Willamette Mall and Fortune City and it includes no loading screens between these areas other than the loading screen when you first start up and small loading screens between cutscenes. There are four main areas (Districts) that you will be able to explore including small areas like labs and warehouses. Each connected by a freeway. These districts are quite filled. Stores, Garages, Clubs and more depending on which side of the city from the rich up-built homes of Sunset Hills to the Mills, Warehouses and strip clubs of South Almuda. Like I said before, looking around these places will reward you with collectibles and stranded survivors.
I loved Dead Rising 2's way of finding weapons to combine to create a pretty lethal assistant. But in that game you had to find workbenches to create them. Never more, you can now have the parts and create them where you are standing. The problem is, that it doesn't get used that much. Basically, there isn't one main safe room like the other games. There are a few that you'll need to clean out and claim it. After claiming it, you will have access to a weapons locker which will spawn combo weapons and firearms which removes the point of searching around for the parts and creating new combo weapons. Yeah, "Don't use them!" is one excuse but what's the point of them being there then?
The main story protagonist, Nick irritates me. He's very whiny and is always "so terrified" when wielding a sharp combo weapon and slicing around 13 zombies when he says those stupid lines. For example; Nick kills one of the biker leaders and he's breaking down that he "Didn't kill anyone who wasn't a zombie before" but he killed a Psychopath around 10 minutes before. I was pretty irritated about that line.. Some of the psychopaths start attacking him because of them saying something stupid to anger them.  If he didn't start blabbing, maybe those psychos won't be dead (But this game does need Psychopaths!). Nick is my least out of the three protagonist (Frank and Chuck) and he's pretty forgettable.  The other main story characters pretty much irritate me or are forgettable (Like Rhonda and♥♥♥♥♥♥(who is basically there to be Player Two). However, I did enjoy the lines of the not-so-important survivors and their quests. I love the neighbors bickering to each other and the meat dress lady's line.
Love them or hate them, I love survivors in the Dead Rising series. There could be really helpful on assisting you or an absolute pain on getting them in that room! (Curse you Snowflake!) But they are quite different on DR3. Instead of DR and DR2, you don't escort them back to the main safe house anymore which I..   ..enjoyed doing (even the irritating ones!) instead, they're split into three groups. Stranded Survivors who always need help on clearing zombies out of their area and they will run off giving you extra PP. The Side Event Survivors who needs errands doing (for example; "I need some guns" "I need to collect food") when completed, you will get PP and you will leave them to their everyday lives (I guess?). The last group are Posse Survivors which will accompany you when you finish their task. Each survivor have a stat. One could have excellent running speed but lacks in ranged attacks. The problem with these people that they are pretty overpowered if you give them something good. I had one survivor completely murder a psychopath without me helping her (Christine, you will always be my side gal). I might as well talk about the Psychopaths here too. They are pretty easy challenges which is a shame because some of the previous Psychos were pretty hard. (The Convicts, Brandon). You could easily whack a 2x2 planks and run off when they start attacking and they will be defeated. But I love their style and personality. For example, Darlene who represent the sin Gluttony will still give me the chills and shivers.
I read articles that this game is a bad PC port. I have mixed feelings about it. Yes, default settings is 30FPS which is horrible but I unlocked the Frame rate and I'll get around 60 - 90 Frames per second on my GTX 980/i7 4790k which is pretty fine for me. However, I have encountered random crashing and long startup times but this happened rarely. I still recommend that you unlock the 30 Frames-Per-Second lock. It looks horrible at 30FPS..
Would I recommend this game? I don't know.. The overworld and gameplay is fantastic. The ability to create even custom vehicles to drive around the large place and mowing down thousands of zombies is brilliant. It makes me want to explore the world even more than I did with Willamette and Fortune City. Lots of collectibles to find. Lots of side quest to do. I will also recommend listening to the soundtrack if you have any free time. I mean, I would listen to it when I write this but I haven't listened to the Super Smash Bros for Wii U yet. Sorry DR3, maybe next time. I don't recommend the story though (So far as I'm still playing). It's pretty forgettable and I highly recommend you playing Dead Rising 1 (If you have a Xbox..), Dead Rising 2 and even Dead Rising 2: Off the records. That reminds me. I haven't got them on PC yet. Might check it out and play them again.

ACTUAL REVIEW:
Keep in mind I'm viewing this from the prespective of someone who didn't grow up playing these games like many players did, and I actually began on FO3 before trying out the originals. As you can already see, this is not anything like Fallout 3, New Vegas, or 4. This is an entirely new game along the same story line, and if you enjoyed the Wasteland series, this is definitely the game for you. It utilizes seriously outdated graphics and controls are iffy, and support with higher-end PCs is minimal. However, it's still possible to play with a few adjustments and soon you'll be leaping through Navarro and experiencing so many pop culture references from the late 90s, your head will spin. In other words, this is a very nice game with a bit of a learning curve at first, but quickly gets easier and doesn't contain the short timelimit Fallout 1 did. This time, the timelimit is about 13 in-game years, which, even if you explore every inch of the map, do every sidequest, and find every special encounter, you should only be about 2-3 years in, allowing for lots of fun leveling afterwards.

There was a time when I would have recommended this game without question as an alternative to other PVP hero shooters such as Overwatch or TF2. There was a time when there were actually options in which hero shooters that you could play. And now, that’s all gone. So you are asking yourself, do I want to play Paladins since it’s the only modern alternative to Overwatch (TF2 feels a bit old at this point and all). I’ve loved this game, I’ve been a part of this community and suggested a lot of things to help this game over the year that I’ve been playing, and now I’m quitting and telling you why you shouldn’t play this game.
This game has been going downhill ever since Open Beta 44. Through its ups and downs, it maintained enough momentum to interest some people, which is why it has been the only PVP hero shooter to challenge the current Lord of the genre, Overwatch. Originally, Paladins in the Open Beta was regarded as a more skilled alternative to Overwatch. There was a higher time to kill, and there were no crutches like auto-aim abilities and one-shots which Overwatch of course has a lot of. Now of course we’ve got whole characters who are walking skill-less crutches and abilities and weapons that are braindead.
The Paladins team has made a lot of errors since the game went into Open Beta. When Essence was first introduced in OB44, it was extremely grindy and unfair to regular players compared to the easy card purchase before that. Even players like myself who wanted to initially see how the system played out rapidly came to despise it. Essence for those who don’t know was the currency required to get cards, and you could only get it by acquiring duplicate cards from lootboxes. What an absolutely horrible system that was a nightmare for new players. And what was the reaction of the dev team? They maintained complete radio silence on the issue for months, and didn’t bother answering any questions on the subject. This includes their alleged dev Q&As where they straight up ignored all of the most popular posts wanting answers on the issue of essence. Eventually they compromised a bit and lowered the essence prices while also giving people a few more ways to get the stuff (it still sucks btw).
The legendary card system introduced in that update has always contributed to a lower time to kill while almost never actually fulfilling its promise of bringing “different unique playstyles” to characters. You want to know what a unique playstyle looks like in the case of most legendary cards? Lets add 15% more damage onto an ability, because that’s apparently unique. Or, lets take something that a character had in their base kit (example, Ying’s Focusing Lens which in her original kit reward accuracy and shot placement by giving you bonus damage), and just make that a legendary. About 10% of legendary cards actually do something unique and viably interesting (and even then, its typically garbage like a flying super-mobile tank or get 90 damage reduction on a movement ability to compensate for flaws in the base kit of those characters), the rest are just boring and bland garbage. The new ones introduced in the current OB64 patch are broken, dumb down the characters, and are op to a hilarious point that its clear just how little testing is done for these things. Want to play a healer, but just want to do damage? Lets just give your weapon enough damage to out DPS most damage characters, or turn your primary healing ability into a damage ability, because that’s exactly what support characters should be doing instead of healing, dealing damage apparently. Yeah, that’s another thing about this dev team, they “fix” supports and tanks by making them deal more damage instead of reworking the actual flaws in their kits.

Now with OB64, they released the test version with an absolutely ridiculous amount of grind while also taking away substantial power from things that you already own. All card progression is based around random RNG lootboxes, so you can’t even get what you want by paying for it. All of the cards that you have grinded for and own are now only 3/5 as powerful as the new versions of those same cards . This is like walking into a bakery, ordering a cake, and just as you are leaving after having bought the cake, the staff come and chop 2/5 of the cake off and attempt to sell it back to you with random lootboxes containing tiny pieces of cake. I think we would call that fraud in most businesses, but in beta free-to play games, apparently you can just steal what people have without facing any consequences.
As the icing on the cake, you can now go into casual with power disparities. You see, before everyone who went into casual built a 12 point deck. Sure you might not have had every card to build the most “meta” decks, but you had enough to build something of similar power to other players. Now, they actually think that its fair in casuals to be a player with entirely level 1 cards and a level 1 legendary facing someone with level 5 cards and a level 5 legendary. Yes, this is entirely unbalanced and Pay-to-Win.
Lets assume the best case scenario for Paladins and say that the dev team doesn’t release OB64, they go and rework the OP legendaries, they don’t go through with the card system changes, and they make all cards available for Gold purchase. What does it tell you that they even thought these systems were fit for their players? Someone had to have done at least a bit of testing for this mass of stupidity to go public and hence know about this stupid grind and broken legendary system. That they have the gull to mock SWBFII when EA (frigging on my dirtbag corporation no-buy list EA) has less grind than this system is just unbelievable. Hi-Rez is getting added to my ever growing list of trashy big game publishers/devs to avoid.
As a few more gripes with the game:
- Tons of female characters are stupidly oversexualized to compensate for them being poorly written/having near 0 personality. This is just a case of cynical marketing using sexualisation to attempt to convince us to buy stuff. Guess what these geniuses thought would be a great thing to add in a cartoony kid game, a slaneshi demon-skin for a character that is constantly referencing sado-masochism. Slow claps all around for that one.
- They like releasing premium recolors for their skins which is just nonsense and then they stick them in costly event lootboxes.
- The themed lootboxes are designed to rip you off by cramming them full of things you don’t actually want like random emotes/taunts.
As far as suggestions for what to play instead goes, I think at this point you are limited to Overwatch or TF2 for PVP gameplay, and Warframe for PVE focused gameplay. Overwatch isn’t pay to win, so is fair from the perspective of gameplay, but has Activision’s typical scummy way of dealing with character skins by not letting you direct purchase them (they even nerfed getting duplicates, so you’ll now get sprays and icons instead of currency that you can actually buy stuff with), hence encouraging mass lootbox opening. Warframe is an amazing shooter with (mostly) excellent characters, but is marred by forcing you to do repetitive missions against boring and generic enemies for a grind that is basically a second job. I guess that leaves TF2, so why not stick with a classic game that is currently the best balanced of the bunch.

Bully holds a special place in my heart and having recently beaten it again, I would argue it manages to stand the test of time. But why should you still buy Bully years after its release? It's certainly not for its graphics. Or the clunky controls. I guess the game's lasting appeal rests mostly on the originality of the setting, story and characters.
Yes, it's goofy, but that's intentional, and rarely is the writing flat-out bad. There is a brilliance in the way the dialogues and characters embrace stereotypes, making fun of them at every turn but never in a mean way just for the sake of being mean. The problems the game tackles are serious and remain relevant to this day and I appreciate that it assumes players are smart enough to see the underlying messages. But fear not, Bully is still very much a Rockstar game, meaning it has no lofty aspiration of dragging you in an ethical debate as you play through its story. At its core, it's just pure fun.
Still unsure it might be worth your time? Fair enough. My only advice to you would be to 1. buy it when it's on sale (15 bucks is too much anyway), and 2. approach the game with an indie mindset. Forget the blockbuster AAA games you might be used of getting from Rockstar, this is a game from another time, and it should be enjoyed as such.

It's rare that a developer goes from making an adult game about crime with very adult themes, to making a game about a high school kid who moves to a school for child delinquents and socially challenged kids, but in a lot of ways Bully is like a GTA. For example, Bully is a open world with stuff to collect, bike races to do, arcade games to play and much more to just find and explorer. The mission structure is very similar to GTA, you do a bunch of work for one of the factions, like the Jocks or the Nerds, and the more you do with them, the more reputation you gain, which in turn effects how other people treat you around campus.
The combat is also very similar to GTA, but instead of machine guns and rocket lunches, you are playing with slingshots and stink bombs.
There are also lots of things different about Bully that really makes it feel like you are back in high school. It feels very structured, but that's not a bad thing at all. You have classes two times a day everyday until you pass the highest level of that class. All of the classes have their own perks, for instance, completing one class will show you where all of the collectibles are on the map.
Unlike the protagonists in GTA, Jimmy is 15 and needs his sleep, so if you are out past 2AM, you just pass out on the spot which can make some nigh missions feel a little too time restrictive but adds to the challenge.
I did't have any technical issues with Bully like a lot of people complain about on this port. Overall the game is well made but parts of it seem kind of repetitive, but I still think this is a fantastic game.

Ticket to Ride is a fun and great adaption of the Board game where you are a railroad tycoon, racing to connect the country with your own railroad company before your opponents do the same. You can play solo against suprisingly skilled bots or online against friends. The rules are simple and easy to get the hang off. The graphics are functional and simple although the menus are a bit clunky. The random draw of tickets and carriage cards means luck does play a part (especially when you need that last carriage or locomotive to finish a route!) but it means each game is different and the various maps available each provide their own quite different challenges. Fortunately the game keeps track of all the scoring (one of the more difficult tasks in the board game). Make sure you get all of the Maps in the bundle and you will have endless entertainment with a game that is ideal as a time filler in between other tasks or games or perfect for honing skills in-between tabletop sessions! Excellent value for money.

First and foremost, after playing this on games like Witcher 3 and Dying Light, I won't lie to you that it has indeed a learning curve as everyone mentioned. It requires some tinkering with the Steam app to get the settings you want unlike, say, the Xbox 360 controller which I rarely even need to remap.
The haptic vibration that is similar to cellphones is a nice feature for the pads.
There's also the ability to map buttons from the keyboard, mouse or an xbox controller reference. Multi-keys function is also supported for shortcuts.
A minor tip, though, the touchpads can be customized to mimic the function of analog sticks. By default, it's set to mouse joystick mode. This is easier for some games while harder on others. The analog stick setting is a little sensitive for me and is actually harder to get used to than the default. But just take comfort in the thought that if you wanted this function, you can.
Finally, I tested this controller in browser mode while chatting Facebook. The onscreen keyboard along with the two touchpads for selecting letters is surprisingly easy to get used to. Theoretically, you can type faster since you'll be entering two letters (like an amateur typist) at a time compared to other existing implementations of consoles.
My first gripe with it is that the ABXY buttons are a little too far into the middle for me. More often than not I find myself pressing the Y when I meant to press the X. I guess this happens when you're used to an Xbox controller? Again, it requires getting used to. But I'd imagine that the buttons aren't ideal for people with larger thumbs because the buttons are noticeably smaller than the Xbox controller.
My second gripe is that it somehow relies on the Steam app to work which I'd assume is where the drivers are also packaged. Most if not all my games are on steam so this isn't a deal breaker.
My third gripe is that games that normally have a rumble pad don't translate necessarily on this controller. So some movements like lock picking on Dying Light won't work here and the keyboard joystick default mode needs a few swipes for it to turn all the way. This, however, can be fixed by using the analog joystick mode for the pad's settings.
Some users here claim that the controller "feels cheap". I guess most people equate glossy black plastic to "cheap" but my first impression with the material is that it feels no different than a PS3 controller. I wouldn't call either cheap.
Finally, do note that this controller doesn't do USB charging.

The most versatile controller I have ever used.
Pros
- Wired and wireless capabilities.
- Amazing battery life
- It is fairly comfortable
- Able to customise your controller to how YOU want it along with try other peoples settings.
- Emulates a keyboard and mouse fairly well on games that require a mouse and keyboard (e.g cities skylines)
- Force feedback thingy feels great.
Cons
- Steam big picture is often buggy. Note: this is not really a fault on the controller, more of a fault on steams side but you're going to be usually using big picture mode with this controller.
- Normal batteries - no on board rechargable batteries.
- The placement of the ABYX buttons felt weird at first.
Do buy this controller if:
- You are looking for a slightly less efficient way of playing games that require a keyboard and mouse.
- You are willing to customise and play around with settings
Do not buy this controller if:
- You want something that is very easy to just plug and play - you need to spend time with this controller to use it correctly.
Games I have tried this with.
Rocket League - Felt great, forgot that I was using the steam controller as it felt as fluid as any other controller
Cities Skylines - Works as it should, it is a bit slow but there is no other controller on the market that can emulate a keyboard and mouse in this fashion.
Spelunky - Controlled great.
Next car game - Both the joystick and gyro felt great for steering - a very fun experience.
Binding of Isaac Rebirth - Felt even better than using a keyboard and mouse.
CSGO: I'm not going to lie, you do not want to use this controller with csgo or any first person shooter that requires some level of aim. - However it is still better than using a 360 controller.
My verdict 7/10 - Would be an 8 if steam big picture wasn't so buggy.

I like to think of the Steam Controller as "the God-Controller."
Here's why.
First of all, the package comes with both a wired and wireless adapter, which is great because I like wired so I don't have to change the batteries, but wireless is also cool.
Second, it's compatible with LOTS of games, even things like Legend of Grimrock, Portal, Team Fortress 2 (both Valve games, I know), and Wrack (you probably don't know that game, although if you do, good for you!).
Third, it added the G buttons, LG and RG. Those are the buttons on the back, and they can COMPLETELY change how you play a game. They give your ring fingers and pinkies a purpose for the controller. I've used all PlayStation controllers, and held every Xbox controller, studying them, and none of them utilize your back fingers like the Steam Controller does.
Fourth, the TrackPad. This thing is awesome, because it practically replicates a mouse. This can be very useful for playing first-person games.
However, despite there being a lot of good things about it, there are some things I don't like.
First, the D-Pad. The D-Pad works like any other one, but is SO LOUD. It is also a bit hard to click, or at least harder to than normal because the directions are all one flat thing.
Second, the fact that it doesn't function with normal Steam Overlay, only in Big Picture Mode Steam Overlay. This kind of gets on my nerves, although now whenever I want to play a game with the Steam Controller, I hit the big Steam Button in the middle and play the game in Big Picture Mode.
Well, that's my opinion on the Steam Controller. I hope you found this review helpful. Thanks!
P.S. Some people think this controller is too big. I beg to differ. Also apparently the XBox One Elite Controller has back buttons, but here's the thing (I actually looked on Amazon for this): the Elite Controller is $150, while the Steam Controller is $50. Do the math.

Honestly, I held off on this game for the longest time until it went on a "mid-week madness" sale, due to so many negative and harsh reviews.  (Though, would have honestly loved to have seen one of the extreme 70+ %-off sales!)
Now that I finally have the game, I'm not sure why there were so many harsh reviews... perhaps there's been decent patching done since to iron out a few of the hiccups.  But on a slightly-aged system, albeit a six-core, this game runs pretty great on mostly high settings, some customized to be more "medium"-ish.  Every once in a great while, like very rarily, there might be a subtle hiccup and that's it, while still looking breath-taking and beautiful; although, the sound tends to stutter from time to time, and can't seem to find the propper options to iron this out, even after tinkering under the hood with sound-card settings directly in the OS.  I also tried each of the quality ranges (720p, etc)... granted, sure, it looks crispier on the higher settings like "full", but I just run it on 720p and the difference isn't to over the top.
There are some tiny issues I've noticed, but moreso that just go to point out that it's a console-port... such as when you alt-tab out of the game, the music keeps going and you have to turn off your speakers when multi-tasking... be nice if there was a patch or fix for this.  Would also be nice to see a true sandbox mode as well (there is an "external work-around" for this, but I'd REALLY rather not have to go down that route if possible)... before buying the game, certain reviews had led me to believe that there'd be plenty of time for everything in plain "story mode", and since it seems the time-elapse is based on checkpoints in the story I believe, technically there is... but still semi-stinks to feel that there will be looming doom after a certain period of time that could blow up in your face (pun mildly intended).  Also, with the size of the city, which for the record is great... all the many side quests (which are also great)... sometimes there's an itching feel of doing lots of busy-work, or having to focus on everybody else more than your own character... which is a tad ironic considering it is a zombie apocalypse after all. xD
Only real reason I could see for the over critical-nature of most reviews, is probably because Dead Rising 3 remained a Microsoft-exclusive... would really have loved to see how this game runs on a PS4 myself... but at least on PC, thank goodness for the power of Linux! ^_^
PS - Only other minor issue I can think of is how the gamepad/joystick controls are hardcoded and not changeable as far as I can tell.  Used to having attack and power attack on the triggers along with the aim functionality... it's strange using face buttons for attack... of course, it is Capcom; it's like playing Street Fighter in Zombieland. xD

-Latest update lets you have a real world purchase related in-game heavy advantage over other players
-Constantly throws away everything unique about it
-Very biased balancing that focuses on a set selection of flankers being fun (Constant nerfs to DPS and tanks. Easily accessible way to reduce enemy healing by 90%)
-Prefers lootboxes with bigger than advertised filler to push new cosmetics that players would readily purchase outright if just put on sale individually
-Hides numerical data on characters they're biased about keeping strong where they are forthcoming about every other character's raw data. (Looking at you with your fourth consecutive buff despite already being strong, Lex.)
-Rapidly declining playerbase
This thing was an awesome and promising game when I picked it up. Extra emphasis is needed on "was". I wanted it to succeed, so I spent money on it, which I'm usually very picky about. I knew the risk, but I'm blown away on how wasted it is.
The game prides itself in having a wide character and gameplay variety.
This game used to have impressive balance for something that combines seemingly clashing shooter and RPG style characters in the same game with an RPG style class system. They have gradually nerfed tanks, healers, and DPS to the point to where they are practically just there to spectate the flankers. A good tank, DPS, or healer just won't win against one any more, not to mention the fact that they can hardly fill the roles in a team they used to. This game used to be something for everyone. Now it is just something for some people. Do you see a character you like? It may have mediocre damage with a tiny health pool and no redeeming qualities. (Most recent being poor Vivian, who was nerfed because of community memeing despite having inferior DPS compared to who she kept being compared to.) This was my biggest problem with the game until...
They pulled an EA on us. The previous character build system, which was completely unique to this game alone, was thrown out the window in favor of a Battlefront 2 style system where we have to buy lootboxes to get more copies of a same card to make it stronger with no limits on how many strong cards we can have on a character. Books can be written on why this is not okay.
Another problem with the Paladins community is how often the community discusses balance without knowing what they are talking about. This may seem like a glaring generalization, but please bear with me. Paladins uniquely gives you the statistics of exactly what kind of output a character has. With this information and middle school to high school level math, anyone can figure out anything about any characters in the game. (Barring Lex, who they intentional hide the data of.) This is the stuff you have to datamine and test for in most other games. For example, the game provides damage numbers in how much damage something does at what interval. One character may do 130 damage at 0.1 second intervals. The shots per second could be calculated by dividing one second over the interval of fire. The damage per second could then be calculated by multiplying the shots per second by the damage per shot. Though this was just an example, it is what you can expect with every other aspect of the game. I appreciate this as a math nerd, but this feature is very overlooked in the community. Despite the information readily provided, this has to be the single least aware community I've ever come across core game data wise. People will argue up and down in-game and on official forums about their viewpoints on balance based off of rumors, how things look, and what they're bad at playing against. A prime example to this would be Maeve getting a damage nerf because Lex players found it difficult to land the two to three shots they needed to land in order for their literal aimbot button to finish her off all because she can double jump not unlike Genji from Overwatch. As far as balance is concerned with blatantly underpowered characters, when buffs are brought up most of what you'll hear is "But then they'll be good like ____." Both the underpowered character and the character brought up for the sake of comparison are then promptly left untouched. Liking the aesthetics or playstyle of a character is taking a gamble with this game.
Speaking of gambling, this game reeks of lootboxes. Skins for characters used to be outright purchases, and still are to a minor degree, but now most of them are stuck in lootboxes that force you to end up paying around seven times more just to get what you want. What is worse is how they deceptively advertise the lootboxe's contents to have only a certain small pool of items, but upon inspection it actually contains four times that amount of item in useless filler that does not relate to the theme of that lootbox. You can earn free basic lootboxes at around the pace you can in Overwatch, but duplicates are far too common and there is way too much filler to hope to get something nice. I would give another paragraph about lootboxes being one of the only consistent ways to get essence, which is used for acquiring cards, but they got rid of our card system entirely for the EA tier garbage I've already covered.
This game was going to fill the void in my gaming that TF2 left and then some, but clinging to disasters with the hope they'll be good like they used to is unhealthy. TF2 taught me that one too. Dear lord Overwatch, please don't fail. You're pretty different, but you're all I've got left in this genre.

War remained the same when Fallout 2 was released a year after its predecessor. It was back in 1998 and it was a jolly good time to be a gamer. This game was the perfect example of "not fixing what isn't broken". So, game mechanics were pretty much the same while the game world became much, much larger.
Storywise we control a Vault Dweller once more - in fact, our protagonist is the descendant of the hero of the first game - who's tasked to save his establishment by acquiring the so-called G.E.C.K., a device with such a power that it can restore completely damaged environments to their default state.
Naturally, the "bigger the better" concept was followed by introducing a wider range of weapons and enemies and, of course, new environments. We also have more skills, perks and beside Karma we also have a Reputation. Something that is constantly changing along the way as we make progress by completing subquests. You can be attacked in a new town if you have a bad reputation -  settlements are not independent of one another; if you complete a deed somewhere it may very well be heard of elsewhere.
Finally, recruitable characters seem to be much, much better. We have total control over them by being able to issue orders, help them level up and provide equipment. Just make sure you have the necessary Karma to be able to recruit them - not that you don't have enough to get to know. With all the new stuff introduced Fallout 2 requires much more time to complete - if you're a completionist you can expect to spend 50-60 hours with the sequel. And, of course, like in case of all such RPGs you can start a new game, pick a different level-up method, solve quests in a different way and hire different people to be at your service.
I spent dozens of hours with this game when it came out. I remember being happy of having our own car (called Highwayman) which then could easily disappear (in fact, the game had a related bug which needed to be patched at the time). If you did not pay attention you could lost it forever. It was a shame as it made travelling between towns fast and easy.
Fallout 2 is a classic. And it comes patched on Steam which allows us to pick a higher resolution. If you have invested hundreds of hours into Fallout 3 et al you might as well check where it all started back in the '90s.

Fallout 2 does what Fallout 3 and Fallout 4 fail to do: Make you feel like your in the apocalypse.
Brilliant atmosphere? Large, non linear map to explore? 100% freedom to do whatever you want? Brutal difficulty? Shut up and take my money.

(In addition, I have hundreds of hours on the original retail version)
Where to begin?  This is one of my all-time favorite games, and I grew up with it along with the first game. It was part of my childhood and continues to be a part of my life all these years later, and it will always have a place in my heart.  Fallout 2 is excellent and anyone who likes RPGs who aren't afraid to play a game that isn't entirely welcoming should give it a shot; I admit I am somewhat biased because of my nostalgia but that doesn't explain the entirety of why I think this is an excellent game.  There is *much* more to this game than the references, humor and fourth wall breaking; that being said, the humor is a nice touch depending on your tastes.  This game deserves as much attention and recognition as the first in the series and I consider both games to be one in the same and part of the same collective experience.
This is game is punishing in certain ways, and is not that casual of an experience; and in some ways I would admit that this game isn't the most welcoming, but once you figure things out and start to progress there are numerous different possibilities and choices laid out before you, and you can play any type of character you choose and have any type of temperament you choose in this game world, which is rich and unique.
Fallout 1 and 2 haven't aged very well, although personally I can transcend that completely due to my nostalgia and attachment to the series; the game looks better now since we can change the screen resolution, and the game is even better with the Restoration Project mod.
You are the grandchild of the Vault Dweller from Fallout 1, the game takes place 80 years after the first game, and you are part of a primitive tribe which your ancestor founded.  You must save your tribe by finding the holy GECK.  Along the way in your quest, you can do many interesting things and talk to many interesting characters.
The gameplay is the same as in Fallout 1, aside from a few things like starting skills being calculated differently and starting at different levels. Fallout 2 is much longer and there is much more to do and see in Fallout 2 than the first (especially with the Restoration Project mod), although the first game is excellent for many of the same reasons this game is excellent.  Most people who enjoyed Fallout 1 (or similar titles) will probably enjoy this immensely also.  I would even recommend this game to people who don't normally play games like it, but are merely very interested in the Fallout lore.
There is an issue I have with the game but only due to playing it on newer, larger displays and playing it on a higher resolution than the game was initially intended for; certain scenes will look wrong if the resolution is set high.
In conclusion, this isn't for everyone and not everyone will be able to enjoy it in the same capacity as others might, for whatever reasons, whether it has to do with the age of the game or not.  But this is classic Fallout and deserves as much love as the first in the series.  This game is highly recommended for any fan of oldschool turn-based RPGs, this and its predecessor helped to redefine the genre. This game is old, but it's excellent and one of the best RPGs I've played, and is very well written.

Goodbye game... It was nice knowing you.
Paladins WAS a fun game that anyone could get into with relative ease. It was free to play. Its heroes were interesting (if a little unbalanced).
That has all changed in recent patches.
It started with the VIP system. A system that had an extremely low earn rate for some possible nice skins that were much more easily purchased alongside other xp boosts. This was all cosmetic though. And even though the game more incentivised spending it still wasn't necessary...
But now... Hirez has pulled a Battlefront 2. The old card system is gone. Yeah you get all cards for free now. But to get higher ranked, better versions of the cards you need boxes to get duplicates. You can earn these fairly quickly... But you need 18 duplicates of a card to get max rank. And so people who spend will most definitely get a quick and large boost over people who don't. This is further broken by the removed loadout point cap in quick play, where pay 2 win players can get a significant advantage over others for a long period of time.
Case in point. Bomb Kings new Legendary
Sticky bombs get increased radius by 50/75/100/125/150 percent range... People who pay can get up to an extra 100 percent range on the explosions of bomb...
All in all. Should these changes be reverted, Paladins is a good game behind this... But as it stands currently. Tread with caution, stand strong, and don't give in. Rest in peace my fellow community members.

Old review:
The games mechanics are good, and the music score complements it nicely. The voices are horrible, though, and my first step after installing the game is to turn them off.
The singleplayer games are challenging, especially if you increase the number of computer players, and the variety in playstyles found in the different (DLC) boards are enough to keep you busy for a while.
Hot Seat multiplayer is easy enough to set up, and runs about as fast as singleplayer.
The multiplayer lobby sometimes has a hard time logging you in, even with your login credentials saved, and may at times even kick players offline while they are in a game, replacing them by bots. This costs these players "karma", but it happens fairly infrequently.
One-on-one multiplayer with a friend goes through the same multiplayer lobby as all the other games, and setting up a successful game with a password lock will not always work.
Game lag is a problem with multiplayer games, no matter the amount of players. At times the game just doesn't recognize you clicked a card, or suddenly thinks you clicked the card stack twice when you only clicked it once, promptly ending your turn.
While it has its bugs, it is still an enjoyable game, and a decent digital version of the boardgame. I would recommend buying it if you enjoy playing digital boardgames with, or without, friends.

Greetings fellow gamers! This is Gamer Guy (In a Suit) from the Echo Army YouTube channel! Today I am bringing you a review of the indie Multiplayer, FPS ScreenCheat. ScreenCheat was released back on October 21, 2014 by Developer Samurai Punk and Publisher Surprise Attack.
(NOTE: This game was NOT reviewed using a key provided by the Developer and/or Publisher, it was a game I purchased for my own account)
Video Review:
The "Too Long, Didn't Watch" Review:
AWESOME throwback to old-school FPS (think Goldeneye). TONS of fun.
4/5 Definitley worth it.
The "Meat & Potatoes" Review:
Fantastic little throwback game, this game brought me way back to when I played Goldeneye on the 64 with my friends after work at my 1st job! SO MUCH FUN!!! See, the trick with this gem is to play like we used to play in those days. The Split-Screen exists in ALL modes, you can see where your enemies are...because you cannot see them at all! Each player is invisible and the ONLY way to track them down is by utilizing the "Screencheating" method of watching their screen to find them and shoot them. it is a VERY fun mechanic that will probably be familiar to those of you who have played the old console FPS w/split screen action. The unique variety of weapons also add some extra flavor into the mix. Trust me, they are quite unique. You MUST play to see them. All in all, this game is heavy on the pros if you dig FPS or just that Old School multiplayer feel. Good graphics, fun and easy gameplay, retro feel, TONS of customization. All positives. A big negative used to be that you had to play MP, there were no bots or single player mode....but that changed back in October! You can now play this game with bots, and they helped to enhance the game further by adding some extra ragdolls and a new level too. That used to be the single biggest gripe, but with that resolved the only issues are typical (occasional server issues and or finding people) and after a while you get used to the maps. However, with 9(!) game modes, you should be good for a while....pick this one up, get the 4-pack and have a blast with friends. I know I did. 4/5 and worth it to chip in with friends and get a pack.
Happy Gaming!

Would've been an alright port, if it weren't for the fact that it seems to crash every other cutscene. In my playtime so far, I've counted 13 crashes. This itself would probably not deter me from continuing to play it, but restarting missions from the beginning is really annoying.
The game itself is great, I loved it on PS3, and it feels a lot more fluid with a keyboard and mouse, maybe not as fluid for driving, but that seems to be the same on every open world driving game. You could use a gamepad, however the base game's support for it is awful, I couldn't figure out how to control the camera, even when changing up the binds from the options. I suppose you could use big picture mode, however setting up the controls is a pain, especially when nobody has posted any presets yet. (someone do that, please, I beg of you.)
Overall, it isn't as horrible a port to PC as perhaps, one very similar game, also released in 2008, you know the one. But nobody likes to restart missions all over again just because the game won't stop crashing. You might have fun just messing around in the map, blowing stuff up, which doesn't seem to crash the game. The character editor lets you create abominations, which can be pretty fun. However, seeing as how I played this game for countless hours on the PS3 already, I personally find that pretty lame now.
Anyway, it's well priced for what it is, and it seems to go on sale for $2.49 pretty often, however the same is true for Saints Row: The Third, a much more recent (and personally, more memorable) game.

This was one of my first MMORPGs, aside from Mabinogi, which was unique and different from other MMOs. And, of course, my newest computer had a sucky graphics card which couldn't - and still can't - run Mabinogi properly. So, I decided to search around and I found this game.
It's fun as hell.
I've gotten to lvl 21 in the timespan of five hours. Very fun times.
The quests are the usual 'Search for X and give it to Y' or 'Kill X amount of Y', but I honestly don't mind that. To me, those kinds of things don't bug me much. The storyline is the major portion of the game for me. And, from what I've seen so far, this storyline isn't half bad. The Eidolons are pretty kickass too.
The classes are unique and cool in their different ways - you have no idea how much I struggled to find the proper one that I really wanted to use. They all have different strengths and weaknesses and they provide the players with different playing styles a chance to succeed as well.
TL;DR - A pretty good MMORPG that I would recommend to my friends. Nothing too out of the ordinary, but still unique in it's own way.

The Steam Controller has allowed me to easily play games such as Europa Universalis 4, which are traditionally heavily dependent upon the use of a keyboard and mouse, on the T.V. That alone says a lot, in my opinion. In addition, I have found it to perform either as well or better than an Xbox 360 controller in every game I have tested the Steam controller with, and then there's the added bonus of huge amounts of control customization possibilities.
I recall hearing some complaints around the time of the Steam controller's release that it felt cheap. Personally, I do not agree. The Steam controller, for the most part, feels well-built and reasonably sturdy. The only issue I have noticed is that the back grip plate which covers the batteries jiggles slightly, but I suppose that is to be expected as it is removable.
At first, I found that the Steam controller caused my hands to cramp somewhat after a short amount of time. I quickly realized that this was because I had been holding the Steam controller with the sides of the controller resting close to the bases of my thumbs. I found that when I shifted my grip so that the controller rested closer to the center of my palms the discomfort ceased to be an issue, with the added bonus of making all the buttons feel more easily accessible.
The Steam controller offers a huge amount freedom in how you configure it for any given game. In fact, it offers so much customization over control configurations that some might actually find it rather daunting. For those who do find all the different options to be overwhelming, there are easily accessible templates as well as control configurations that have been made by other players. I would say, however, that an individual who does not want to try differing control configurations and/or create configurations of their own would likely be better served by sticking to a more traditional controller until more games have developer created default control configurations.
I bought the Steam controller in the hope that it would at least allow me to play keyboard and mouse heavy games on the T.V., which it does wonderfully. Using the trackpads on a grand strategy game such as Europa Universalis 4 feels natural and was easy to pick up.
I found that in third person games, such as the Dark Souls series, controlling the camera with trackball mode is quick and responsive, and those who find they do not enjoy the trackball mode can set the trackpad to emulate an analog stick. I did find that in third person shooters such as Grand Theft Auto V, aiming took some getting used to, but after using a combination of trackball mode and gyroscopic aiming for awhile, I am much more accurate than I could ever personally hope to be with a dual analog stick controller. It feels much more like you're aiming with a mouse, which anyone who primarily plays video games on PC will likely find much more natural feeling.
My use of the controller in first person shooters has been more limited. I have tested it in the game Tower of Guns and found that the combination of trackball mode and gyroscopic aiming is quite effective, as it was in third person shooters. Finer aiming is going to take some tweaking to make feel right, but it can be achieved.
In 2D games like Spelunky or The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth, I found the controller particularly easy to setup as it was pretty much ready to go immediately after selecting the gamepad template. In my experience the Steam controller does every bit as well with these types of games as an Xbox 360 controller.

While I originally had trouble getting to like it, it has grown on me tremendously. Discovering the gyro function and the on screen custom touch menus really made the difference.
For Xinput designed games, I originally had the urge to go back to the PS3 controller, but played through the whole Shantae series with the Steam controller and I adapted perfectly.
But then the true strenth of this controller is the ability to play on your couch, games that you wouldnt be able to play with an Xbox controller (or you would pretty poorly) with limitless tuning and customization options.
FPS games that require precision and a lot of buttons like Red Orchestra 2, I never imagined I would be playing in a couch, and yet I did and performed quite well thanks to gyro aiming.
More relaxed slow paced mouse only games like Xenonauts, visual novels or Darkest Dungeon, again, no problem.
The firmware gets constant updates that improves performance and functionality, so it gets even better with time.
The only two flaws I see now is that you can't use gyro as a joystick with 3 axis, so you can't make use of roll and yaw at the same time for games that would benefit from it like Elite: Dangerous. But this will hopefully get included in the future with firmware and patches.
The other flaw is that that the bumpers are in an awkward position and are a bit too hard to press for my liking, the back buttons are a bit too hard too, everything else is alright.
So yes, this is a recomendation. Just remember that it takes a little patience to get used to it at first.
Once you do and start to learn all you can do with it, you'll simply love it.

Bully was a game back in 2006 released for the PS2 that basically offered the gameplay of Grand Theft Auto to minors without penalty.
Bully is a game where you play as 15 year old Jimmy Hopkins as he attempts to survive his high school days after his mother and step father drop him off due to their honeymoon. While Jimmy attempts to fit in, he does various jobs for each of the cliques at the School to gain their favour. Whether its getting som D&D pages back for the Nerds, beating up the Jocks for the Preps, or roughing up the Preps for the Greasers, Jimmy does pretty much everything possible to just survive.
Gameplay wise, this is a text-book R* sandbox game with its own unique touches. You can go to class where you play mini-games to unlock new abilities, start fights with the various cliques of the school, or just be a delinquent and destroy everything.
Bully was one of the most unique R* games in it's gameplay feel. Sure it plays pretty close to the Renderware Grand Theft Auto games (GTA III, Vice City, San Andreas), it has its own unique feel with a pretty interesting plot, some great voice acting, and missions and activities that are fun to play. It's 14.99 and the game is pretty long, so you do get your money's worth.

Great and accurate translation of the board game to PC. And a great game whether or not you have played the board game. It's easy to learn, but hard to master. A big warning though: this is not a single player game. There is the option to play AI players, but those are mostly there for you to get to ropes. Once you understand what the game is about, you will win them every time. So this game is meant to be played against human players, whether those be your friends or fellow unknown gamers. If you create an open game, it will take 1-2 minutes for other players to join in, and then you can start. A game lasts for 10-30 minutes, depending on the number of players and how fast they play, however, it has to be played back-to-back, no saving and preferably no quitting. Ticket to Ride suits both those who want a little casual play every now and then, and those who like competitive gaming.
Some say it's simple, but I say even just the base game is complex. 2, 3, 4 and 5 player games all require different strategies. And apart from strategy, what is most required is adaptation. If your strategy is rigid, you will lose. You have to adapt it every turn.
In some way, I think this is a game where Chess meets Texas Hold'em. You have to anticipate the other players moves, you have to estimate the odds and you have to bluff and try not to give signs about where you are going. And you get better the more you play, until you reach a plateau. And then you realize something about your playing style, adjust and keep rising in the ranks. The game has a SELO ranking system, much like the one used by competitive Chess players. So you will see how you progress. You will know approximately how good your opponents are, whether or not you actually know them.
There are two distinguished playing styles. Cutthroat or friendly. Usually players accept that whatever you do, in the scope of the rules, and win, is OK. Some players however don't like blocking and screwing/getting screwed. These players will mark their games with words suchs as Fun, Fair or No blocking. Join these games if you want a friendly game. And don't if you're going to do whatever it takes to win.

Wonderful adaptation of the board game. In this game, you are a railroad tycoon, racing to connect the country with your own railroad company before your opponents do the same. The rules are fairly straightforward, and although scoring is one of the more difficult elements to track in the physical game fortunately this version takes care of all of the score tracking for you. It's a wonderful strategy game that's great for people who enjoy screwing over their friends, because that will happen a lot.
The interface is intuitive and easy to understand and it is a wonderful translation of the physical board into a digital enviroment. Highly recommended for people who like strategy games, but you definitely want to pick up a few friends to play this one with- it's best in multiplayer.
Edit: The main menu has gone through some changes that make creating and finding games nuch more frustrating than in the past- unclear symbols denote most settings and finding individual settings can be quite difficult. The main play interface is still fine, but I hope an update to the main menu is coming to help usability a bit.
