After quite some time, I finally managed to 100% Saints Row 2 and I must say, It was quite an adventure.
Saints Row 2 is one big and entertaining sandbox, where you can customize almost everything you want, from your gang to whether you want your shirt to be unbuttoned or not, or change any part of color on any clothes/car, anything. Not only that, if you finish the game, you still have a big couple of things to do, like activities: 15 mini-games that are level based, from 1 to 6, with a lot of unlockables and bonuses when you reach to the end; and Diversions, such as collecting 50 cds scattered all through out the city, Graffitis, secret areas, stunt jumps, etc., and Jobs, that are the usual like Taxi and Ambulance, and such.
The levels of detail are fun to find and satisfying, and It's a lot when we are talking about 2008, it (sometimes) makes GTA IV look incomplete, but they're different games and a different point of view, there's no "best" or "worse" on this. It also has a really great story, quite outdated but man, those cutscenes were really intense when it comes to drama, I definitely recommend NOT to ignore the storyline.
Now, I won't lie, It has its problems, but if we are reviewing this on Steam, I need to say that the PC port feels and looks like a really early Xbox 360 emulator. The controls are weird, the analogue stick will show up instead of WASD or Mouse, It was a really rushed port. But thanks to IdolNinja, former community developer of Volition Inc., It's fixed with the Gentlemen of the Row mod, which completes the PC version and fixes most of the big issues this version had, so this isn't optional, you really need to download that mod or else it'll be painful to play.
You can find it here
Aside from that, it has a lot of replayability, I've spent hours playing, with Coop as well, playing with your friend is fun as hell, especially with the activities, and I recommend this game a lot. Just make sure to fix the game or it won't have the same effect.

TLDR: Pixel Worlds is very similar in gameplay to Growtopia with frequent in-game purchases. Give both games a shot and whichever you like, you can play.
(I have very few hours on this game, most of it was on mobile.)
Pixel Worlds is a 2D Sandbox MMO game which involves trading, farming, a single in game currency-- wait, have I heard of a game like this before?
Yes, the game is nigh-identical to Growtopia, and while there are a few things that are different about this game than Growtopia, most of the content remains the same. The only thing I can compliment and appreciate is how much was put into how the game looks.
As far as visuals go, Pixel Worlds did a great job. The animations are pretty clean, the colors are fun and vibrant, and some of the *original* blocks and clothes are well-made.
Other than that, nothing (as far as I could see while playing on Mobile and Steam) is different from this game and Growtopia. Pixel Worlds has a handful of blocks and clothing items in that have almost identical looks and names to Growtopia-- a great example of this are the rainbow blocks, they only have little sparkle pixels and little curvy stripes that make them different.
They also share the same exact currencies, world locks, and gems, with gems being able to be collected via an in-game purchase or "farming". While Growtopia is more subtle with their in-game purchases, this game features V.I.P, which is essentially a paid subscription for bonuses in the game which many consider a "pay to win".
Overall, Pixel Worlds is an almost indistinguishable duplicate of Growtopia with a few sneaky in-game purchases in it to make a quick buck. I suggest you give Growtopia a try and then take a look at this game. Whichever you like; you can play. To each their own.

Ticket to ride began as an award winning board game made by Days of Wonder along with, Shadows over Camelot, Memoirs, Mystery Express, SmallWorld 1&2, and other titles. It is a casual turn-based strategy game, based upon the board game with the same name, and it is one of the best adaptations thus far.
is just about identical to the board game. You have two types of cards, colored train cars representing a type of cargo  such as black or pink, and destination cards which feature two city destinations, like Los Angeles and New York. Each player is dealt three destination cards, and must choose at least two of them.
Each of the players are also dealt six train cards and with that, the game begins. Each player takes turns in either drawing two face down cards from the top of the deck, two trains from the lineup (Not including rainbow carts as they account for your two), or place trains on the map and claim routes to your complete your destination cards and gain points. You also lose points for each route you don't complete, same per the board game.
2 to 5 players can face off, either as a single player game vs. the AI or online against human opponents. AI bots can also be added to online games to bolster the number of players.
reflects the charming old feel of the board game quite true to form and really brings out the atmosphere of it as a whole. The maps in which you can play on are always really well defined, easy to read, see were you were at and where you were going. I do however feel that your trains and your opponents trains on the map could have been slightly better defined to make them stand out more.
also holds well to the atmosphere and feel of the game, but after a while the same piano music track grates on your nerves and you tend to find yourself diving into the settings to shut it up and put some of your own music on.
This is where I delve into the biggest gripes I have with Ticket to Ride...
The layout of the menus are appalling. It honestly feels like they have taken a horrible old 90's layout and stuffed it in here. You have annoying and un-skippable voice acting as you go into every single menu and every cardboard cut-out of a character in the menus have something to say, which is the same infuriating audio each time you even so much put your cursor near them. This drove me insane.
Also, playing online with friends is made to be so obtuse, unclear and can be quite difficult to actually set up a game, because rather than being integrated with the steam interface, is goes through a backwards setup of making a profile on the Days of Wonder page to make your name easier to find, add the other person who has gone through the same process and try to let it ''find friends'' or if by some chance you can locate them yourself, adding them is just as tedious. This may just be me nitpicking, but it was something that bothered me intensely.
Regardless of it's flaws, it is by far the best adaptation of the board game. Whether you have played it physically or not, it can be enjoyed by anyone who enjoys a bit of strategy and board game adaptations.
If I had friends to play with it might be good. But I don't. 0/10

For all that hipsters and cynics love to mock it, we owe a lot to Go! Go! Nippon!. It was Monster Girl Quest 3 that set the benchmark for how visual kawaii novels looked and played in the HD era. It was Monster Girl Quest 2 that redefined the FPS as all-action blockbuster, while transforming PC single-player. So it’s a shame to report that Go! Go! Nippon! doesn’t set any new benchmarks or redefine anything. When OverDrive dropped Monster Girl Quest 3 to kick off a new series it could have given the franchise a brand new start. Instead we have something that’s less a reboot than a remake, giving us everything we expect from a Go! Go! Nippon! turned up to eleven, but nothing more.
The premise is interesting, albeit faintly ridiculous. In the near future a new power – The Toliet – rises the water from the bowl and swirls around.  Your character is shocked by the advancement that the Japanese aquired in their technology, For ten years your weeaboo habits have exceeded in a positive manner, allowing you a trip to Japan for quite some time. Aided by two girls who acompany you through your journeys. The single-player campaign charts the story of you showing up in Japan from a train, and after a short prolouge, are acompanied by two females. One with a large pair of brests that have obviously been over detailed to draw your eyes to, and a flat chested but unrealistic personality female.
In theory – and in OverDrive PR campaign – this sounds brilliant. You’re not fighting or doing anything interesting, but as a beta weeaboo who travels to Japan is hilarious. In practice, though, it’s all still business as usual, with access to the ladies, air support and high-tech gadgets, and missions covering all the usual infiltrate this, run to this point, visit this place tomfoolery.
What saves the game is its spectacle. OverDrive seems to have invested heavily in engine tech to make the scenery plants, intense sound effects, absolutely interesting dialouge and no level is complete without something big doing all of these things, often all at once when you’re running-and-gunning through it. When things aren’t getting wrecked, we get sudden erotica, This makes each mission like the climax of a blockbuster action movie, and while the effect is wearying spread out over the running time, it’s a great game to play one mission at a time. You know you’ve seen it all before, but you’ve never seen it quite this big.

The steam controller was nothing but trouble for me. When I first tried it out with a few games it hardly worked, the controlls I bound often overlapped during gameplay with what the default controls were, and trying to choose a community setting never worked either. The second thing I noticed was how weird it sounded from the haptic feedback; now this probably won't be a complaint for most, but I just found it odd how whenever you moved your thumb on the trackpad it sounded like a dying hard drive.
I didn't want to stop there and say I didn't like it so soon, though, so I continued using it with more games the next couple of days.
Any FPS that was not made with controller support worked HORRIBLY. While the frame rate for the game itself stayed steady, looking around seemed to lag, when trying to look around, the camera seemed to move at around 4 frames per second, while everything actually happening is running smoothly.
About 3 games out of the ~20 that I tried worked well with the steam controller, but even then my hands were very sore after about ten minutes of using it, because these games only used the analog stick and buttons, and trying to re map the controlls ended up layering the buttons (For example, if the default for A was jump, but i wanted it to shoot, it would do both).
I do not recommend the steam controller for these reasons, and I had returned it a little more than a week after I got it.

I am probably in the minority but I do not like the Steam Controller.
1. Buttons and Trackpad are reversed from a normal Xbox or PS controller, this forces you to reprogram your brain so you will constantly be fighting with all your controllers if you are switching between them a lot.
2. The ergonomics are terrible, my wrists and hands hurt after holding it for even a short time due to the way it angles my wrists.  I have mild carpal tunnel from programming so this is not good, it inflames it pretty quickly.
3. Cheap, Plastic feel to the components, the trigger buttons are AWFUL compared to a 360 or PS controller
4. Time, Time, Time - Expect to dedicate several hours learning about the controller before you even play for a second.  Then expect to spend several hours tweaking the controller for each game.  This is getting better as people upload profiles and the software gets better but compared to industry standard controllers, Xbox and PS, again this is a big negative.
TLDR: The Steam Controller has been collecting dust on a shelf for a while now.  I have no desire to ever pick it up again.

As stated in Article 93 of the UN Charter, all 193 UN members are automatically parties to the Court's statute.[11] Non-UN members may also become parties to the Court's statute under the Article 93(2) procedure. For example, before becoming a UN member state, Switzerland used this procedure in 1948 to become a party, and Nauru became a party in 1988.[12] Once a state is a party to the Court's statute, it is entitled to participate in cases before the Court. However, being a party to the statute does not automatically give the Court jurisdiction over disputes involving those parties. The issue of jurisdiction is considered in the two types of ICJ cases: contentious issues and advisory opinions.

TL:DR A Serviceable DR game with none of the charm or colour of its predecessors, only for someone fanatically inclined to the DR series or if you have a desperate need to downsize your amounts of fun that DR2 cursed you with
The first thing I noticed about this game is how brown it is (No racial undertones meant) Every sodding part of the city is drenched in either Brown or dark grey, I don't know what Triple A's Fetish is with Brown, Maybe it was his Highschool Girlfriend or something.
The Next Gen Transition seemed to have cost DR alot of its vibrancy, very few of the Bosses are "wacky" as opposed to just being disgusting and much too easy, the combo weapons have increased in number but are much more poorly implemented (I'll get to that)
Tangent aside, The visuals have that classic "LOOK HOW NEXT GEN WE ARE, DO YOU LOVE US NOW?!" Feeling of trying to show of the visuals as opposed to letting the visuals show off the game, When I am mowing through a horde of Zombies With a cone on my head, I am nto stopping to look at the visuals, Maybe I would have in DR2 where the casino's had life and vibrancy, as opposed to this rehashed Liberty City ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ we have here. The story is also a nice juicy target, in the second Game it had a feeling of retro camp with a grizzled one liner touting Chuck Greene, Who was not only adept at killing Zombies but also enjoyed it.
Nick Ramos on the other hand is a cookie cutter pretty boy who "jus wants ta help" (which is very inconsistent at the least) When I killed my first psychopath, Nick Ramos freaks out like he was caught in the girls locker room, in DR2 Chuck Green made a sassy and slightly Dark joke about my enemies Untimely Love Making with a chainsaw, The tone of DR3 is much too inconsistent as well, Capcom Writes Story the way a Child writes awkward fanfiction. That is to say very badly, If you have ever played a DR game before you will not be shocked to find out the zombie virus was started by some very short sighted villain (which I spoil with no remorse, as only a lobtomized chimpanzee couldn't see that coming if you have played a DR or any capcom game before) So the story is very flat, theres a big thing about people getting chipped or outlawed if they are bitten, but the characters are so stereotyped and over reliant on you for help, that any and all interest fades fast.
But no one comes to DR for a story in the same way no one solicits a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for an ethical debate. The gameplay of DR3 can be summed up as: It is DR2, but watered down and made insultingly easy. The combo weapons of DR2 were a brilliant method of providing countless experimentation attempts to combine weapons organically to create new and easy ways to break up the monoty of killing zombies, which worked very well. But in DR3 you cannot make any Weapon without blueprints as Nick is unsure of how taping knives to a pair of boxing gloves is in anyway an effective zombie killing tool. This terrible mistake means I have to scavenge out for blueprints scattered around the city as opposed to the fun of testing out which combinations work to create new weapons and a sense of satisfaction as you see what the game lets you get away with, makes me feel like I'm stealing someone elses creative dieas, not making them myself. In addition you can get a skill very early on to allow any weapon of any one category to subsitute as a replacement in a combo weapon, so two pistols can give you a combat shotgun/rifle Weapon which is already massively overpowered, and is now handed to you like candy.
Even worse is that now guns can be found in lockers, so you aren't enjoying a scavenger hunt to find the correct components to make your guilty pleasure Auto Turret Teddy bear or Twin MG Mounted Arm Chair, Nope instead you go to the Locker in a safehouse and it will just plop the bloody things out like a disinterested clerk at lost and found. Speaking of safehouses, the AI for humans is hilariously bad, Fighting AI soldiers makes me feel bad because I am worried I shot someones travelling Monkey Circus, The AI that "helps" is awful, inaccurately firing shotguns whenever the planets align or flailing a melee weapon like a weedy anime child, which is made worse by the fact that you now have to escort them over a much larger city to safehouses so they stop following you, because Boss battles and Story missions are blocked when you have companions, so they are only useful in Free Roam, and in Free Roam they are a pain and pointless if you have a friend or Dog that can pull Co-op duty for you, so the irritating escort mission that were survivors has made no improvements (Don't even get me started on trying to get them into cars).
There is one big improvement however: That is the ♥♥♥♥ing awesome Combo Vehicles, Having a steam roller taped to the edge of a Harley while my co-op partner throws molotovs off the back is defintely one way to make it enjoyable trekking round the city. BUT NO they ♥♥♥♥ that up too! everywhere you go, there are blockades, Rubble and barriers blocking your way down roads, so you end up building a vehicle in one area, and only being able to use it in that area, theres no way to get a good pace going in a vehicle so they only serve to make us feel nothing but contempt for this City and praise the Zombies for livening up the place.
The game is also buggier than a Mating Session between Watchdogs and Unity (Ok maybe not THAT bad) The Pc version was awkwardly capped at 30fps at release even on PC, and anything too long the game gets frightened and pisses itself, that is to say it crashes, Alot, I'm sure these things can and will be patched at sometime but when DR3 charges a full £40 then to have such glaring problems does show, especially now that there is no colour and vibrancy to allay the annoying niggles that plague DR games, like having to pick up an item under pressure or the irritating fetch quests.
So does DR3 do a few things better? Yes, the vehicles are tons of fun, I don't have to worry about running all the way back to Katie every time she needs her vitamins, and the customization is more varied (despite the fact dressing up Nick like a schoolgirl is no where near the levels of hilarity it was to put someone who was actually cool, like chuck greene into the costume.) It doesn't do anything to dynamically change the DR formula and as a DR experience,  you can get DR2 for cheaper and have more fun with it.
DR3 gets a 7.6 out of 10
I do not reccomend it as a DR game, but as a game on its own, it still manages to be a small cut above the rest (If only barely)

This game is fun to play, it`s a rockstar game so that means that is really good,Bully is an action-adventure open world video game set in a school environment. The player takes control of teenage rebel James "Jimmy" Hopkins, who from the opening cutscene is revealed to be a difficult student with a disruptive background. The game concerns the events that follow Jimmy being dropped off at Bullworth Academy, a New England boarding school. The player is free to explore the school campus in the beginning and, later on in the game, the town, or to complete the main missions. The game makes extensive use of minigames. Some are used to earn money, others to improve Jimmy's abilities or get new items.
School classes themselves are done in the form of minigames, broken into five levels of increasing difficulty. Each completed class brings a benefit to gameplay. English, as an example, is a word scramble minigame, and as Jimmy does well in this minigame, he learns various language-skills, such as the ability to apologize to police for small crimes. Chemistry is a button pushing minigame which rewards Jimmy with the ability to create firecrackers, stink bombs, and other items at his chemistry set in his room at the dorm. If you're looking for a game similar to Team Fortress 2, give this one a try. It is an energetic multiplayer shooter game, with goofy characters, comedic violence, and quirky scenery. Levels usually take place in dingy trailer parks, mining caverns, or space-like settings with odd machinery. While this isn’t a duck-and-cover kind of game, there are plenty of crevices you can try to hide in or platforms to snipe from. You just can’t stay there for too long! Nowhere is safe. You need to keep moving, help your teammates, and complete the objectives. It really keeps you on your toes.
This game is free-to-play, not pay-to-win. You have to earn better weapon parts and equipment. You can’t just buy your way to the top, which is nice. This helps to keep things level when you get matched up for battles with other players. What the developers really seem to push is the aspect of crafting your own weapons and testing out different kinds of ammo: laser beams, lightning balls, flamethrowers, missiles, etc. You can craft a few different guns and keep them in your locker, then pick which to use right before the start of battle. Honestly though, it’s better to find one kind of weapon you really like and put all your points toward upgrading the hell out of it. There are no classes, like medic or sniper, but you can easily take on these roles depending on your chosen weapons. Always try to craft one medic gun because it comes in handy and gives you extra points for helping out your team. It sucks when no one has a medic gun.
All in all, this is a really fun game to play. The competition is fierce, which makes victory all the more sweet. Though if and when you die, at least you can have a laugh too.

The hype is spot on for this classic, it actually is not blind nostalgia when it is said that this game allows for far more role-playing than every other video game in existence.
Fallout 2 is not bound by modern day game design limitations and rules, it does things modern games are afraid to do.  It was designed by the most talented game studio of all time, Black Isle Studios, with much of the excellence being on showcase in Planescape: Torment which was released the following year.  Largely a different kind of excellence, but both games are so much more original and limitless than anything today.  Everything you do in Fallout 2 leads to some reaction, big or small, but usually somewhat realistic.  When playing the game you have to think twice about what you say and how you act.
Keep talking to someone who doesn't want to be bothered, and there may actually be consequences.  Sneak around in the open and people will question you.  Walk around with a weapon equipped in certain places and you may find yourself being fired upon.  Throw away First Citizen Lynette's trust and say goodbye to Vault City forever.  Become a boxing champion in New Reno and you will be famous and respected in that area, with the townsfolk calling you "Champ" most of the time.  Play as a cold blooded, ruthless killer and you will be feared and certain quests will open up to you while others will become unavailable.  Finish the main quest in a positive way and you will be hailed a hero in most places.  Play as a low intelligence character and watch the whole game transform appropriately (look it up on YouTube if you must).  The list goes on, these are just some examples of the attention to detail in Fallout 2 that no other game exhibits.
Fallout 2 is also a very good satire, less serious than its modern counterparts.  If you've only played Fallout 3 and Fallout 4 then you've barely experienced Fallout.  New Vegas is an impressive sequel however, but still more "gamey" and with less role-playing.

'Deus Ex: Human Revolution' is your typical simplified reboot that doesn't hold a candle to the original. Except unlike the 'Thief' reboot, there is actually some effort in this one.
The game keeps enough of the originals spirit to make it fun. The levels are non-linear, and buildings have multiple entrances. The joy of carefully planning your entrance and the satisfaction of outwitting your enemy remains. It’s also great that the game gives a choice between lethal and non-lethal gameplay. The problem is that you’ll want to stick to non-lethal because the combat is quite bad.
Maybe its personal preference, but I dislike cover-based shooting. There is no energy to it because both you and the enemy end up stuck behind a conveniently placed piece of scenery randomly firing bullets waiting for someone to get up so they can be shot. It also doesn’t help that the health system is broken. Like the first game, you die very easily even on the easiest difficulty - but in the original game, headshots and body-shots were the only parts of the body where a person could be fatally wounded. In this game, you can die from someone shooting your exposed elbow, and you can kill someone by shooting them in the foot. It’s laughable that after dying from two bullet-wounds to the kneecap, the game suddenly throws you into a clichéd boss fight. Thank god the boss fights are fixed in the Directors Cut – although such incompetence should be fixed in a free update rather than making consumers pay for another edition.
To compensate for this, the non-lethal combat is far too easy. You get a load of useful augmentations like health regeneration right away, and there's no weapon specialisation - so you can pick up any weapon and use it. You can take someone down at the press of a button, meaning there isn’t the risk that knocking someone out might backfire. After about the second mission, I was comfortably settled with a dart gun, a stun gun, and a couple of useful stealth-related upgrades that unfortunately removed most of the challenge from the game. I deliberately avoided upgrades like the one that makes you sprint silently and the ability to take down two enemies at once because then I would be playing the game in God Mode.

It’s becoming an unsettling trend for Action/RPG games to be at their best when you’re exploring the enviroment and interacting with NPC’s – or just doing anything that avoids the lacklustre combat. But, like ‘Bioshock’ and ‘Mass Effect,’ this aspect redeems the experience. Give the level-designers a medal, and send whoever designed the combat back to play the original some more.

- Quests completely re-roll on startup. For better or worse, restart your game for a different quest!
- Edit : One of my trees are cutting itself down now... What. Invisible Wood Cutter?
- You can't click off screen or alt tab
- The sound settings don't actually work
- The one song there is cuts out after plying and doen't loop.
- For an idle/ cl;icker style game, there is no idle. Period. Unless open (with an issue)
- If you do idle for even a few minutes, plants will break, they are highlighted with various numbers of fruits ready to pluck, because the game bugged out. I have a stalk of corn I never clicked myself, I let my wood cutters harvest it, and now it's ready to harvest, but only has 1 corn on it and it can not be interacted with, along with a few other crops... Unless I restart. This happens every 10 minutes are so, for no reason.
For $1.99 USD, you get your moneys worth. I could spend $2 on far more worthless things, and it's got its own charm. I really don't know where to begin. This controller is just straight away amazing. It can be anything you want it to be. If you prefer a x-box style control over the trackpad, you can set it to act like an x-box controller.
Build quality: Its a pretty solid and good feeling contoller, although there are most certainly ones with a lot higher quality. Yet for the price of 55€ it is absolutly fine.
Gaming: You can play almost any game with this (pretty much anything except from CoD WaW and CS:GO). FPS games all feel very good with the trackpad, specially if they have controller support. Aiming feels after a bit of practice and adjustment of sensitivity very natural. Same goes for third person shooters. Both genres can be played very good with the steam controller, but where it really shines is in my opinion RPG games. They just feel so good and easy when played with the steam controller. What suprised me was how well the gamepad works with strategy games though. Although they usually dont have support for controllers, you can usually donwload a preset for it, which will work just fine most of the time. Now I didn't test how this works on platformers, top-down shooters or sidescrollers, but I believe it would also be an awesome experience.
As a conlcusion: the steam contoller can handle basically any type of game very well, there should not be any problems.
Software: I can only say that the software is very well done and it works perfectly fine. For any game you can use recommended, preset, community or your own custom controlls. It always works.
The bad: theres not much bad to say about this controller really. Yes it does take a while to get used to, and yes it looks a bit awkward, bur overall the contoller is amazing.
The only problems were minor ones and could easily be fixed.
But you still shouldnt play CS:GO with it, the controls are awefull.
Also I experienced some games crashing at launch when using the steam controller, but I think that might have been a problem with my system, not the actual controller.
Summary: the steam controller is an amazing device, making gaming extremely comfortable. It is extremly fast and has a long battery life (about 1-2 weeks). If you are looking for a controller which does exactly what you want, and which can adapt to almost ang situation, then this is what you should go with.
I give this 10/10 points, for being better than any of my expectations.

As Rockstar's only T rated game, it's also one of their most unique for the setting, mini "class" games, advancement through society and character development. Obviously, the game is about bullying and fighting your way through the ranks only to try and bring peace to the school. While the plot may not be as strong as other Rockstar titles, it's certainly more fun than others for the exploration of the school and outside areas, including the town, carnival, and industrial park. Overall, it's an exceptional game.
You are Jimmy Hopkins, all around average teen that is sent to a private school in the New England area. Jimmy eventually befriends the idealist Gary Smith, and Pete Kowalski, the resident dweeb. Jimmy is able to attend classes, make friends, have a relationship, and fight bullies. The main enemies are the preps and jocks, but there's an underlying story here as the game takes place throughout the school year.
I have to say, watching Bully's story unfold was exciting and exhilerating as I was fondly reminded of Harry Potter.
9.0/10

Bully. It's GTA, but without blood and deadly weapons, and instead of playing as an adult man, you play as Jimmy Hopkins. A 15 year old kid who's aggressive and a fighter, but not truly malicious. He only gives people what they have coming to them.
Bully takes place in Bullworth, a town in New England. Your mom, well, Jimmy's mom, drops you off at Bullworth Academy. A boarding school. The school is full of bullies and corrupt teachers and it's up to you to put a stop to it.
The game's storyline will guide you through six chapters (There are 65 missions, the sixth chapter is an endless free-roam chapter, giving you the chance to complete non-storyline missions and to collect collectables.) Each of them takes place in a different weather season. The missions vary, it's never the same. One time you're cleaning a rat infested library and the next time you're helping a teacher escape from a psychiatric hospital. As Jimmy, your main goal is to bring peace to the school by helping and befriending the four school cliques: the Nerds, the Jocks, the Bullies, the Preppies and the Greasers.
Of course you'll have to go to class. These classes are: English, gym, geography, math (ew), music, shop, art, photography and biology. They are simple mini-games which become noticeably harder every time you attend them and make progress. You'll also have to deal with a time schedule. You can skip class, but you won't get any rewards if you do so and prefects will chase you down and send you back to class if they catch you.
Jimmy, your character, is highly customizable. You can buy clothes, change your hairstyle and more. You can even buy a bike, a go-kart or a scooter if you save up enough cash. Money can be earned by either taking a paper route, doing missions for townies or students or by completing storyline missions.
You've got weapons. No, they are not guns and no you can't kill people. There's a super slingshot, you can use firecrackers, stink bombs, eggs, a bag of marbles, a bottle rocket launcher and so much more. You can also pick up one of the many objects around you (umbrella's, vases, bottles) and use them as a weapon.
Interacting with your fellow students is fun too. You can talk to them, give cute presents, put them in trash bins or lockers, steal their books, take their pictures for the yearbook, punch them in their faces (aka bully them) and if you feel like it you can make out with a girl or a guy.
The game has a very impressive map size. You can explore the entire school, the school grounds, the town, a fully functional theme park, an industrial park and a few more awesome places. There are many collectables scattered around the map too.
Bully may be pretty good, but it's not perfect. The graphics are rather outdated, the sound isn't that amazing, the controls are a bit clunky at first and there are some bugs. But don't worry! It doesn't kill the fun. Bully is an amazing game and there's much to do. And for only $14.99 - £9.99 - €9.99, it's certainly worth it.

Unlike its followup SRIII which was a much more goofy entry that was trying to go balls out with its humor, SRII is much more grounded whilst retaining alot of over the top elements, striking a very good balance.
You have many more ways to customize your character, being able to pick two different sock types or stack multiple hats if you so choose.  The layered clothes system allows for remarkably crazy levels of personalization. On top of that, unlike SRIII which had you tackle the various gangs in a linear fashion, SRII has you tackle them in any order that you choose. The writing also fits the tone, a great blend of comedy, over the top drama, even dramatic moments that tug at your heart strings.
If you want to get involved in an entertaining experience and can bear with the aged mechanics, then SRII is definetely worth the purchase.

Fast. Brutal. Gory. Fun as hell. Looks gorgeous, runs well. An amazing game, start to finish. The game is split into three modes, so I will review each one:
SINGLE PLAYER:
Easily one of the best FPS campaigns I have ever played. The weapons feel powerful, but so do many of the demons. The fights are action packed, bloody, and feel high-stakes. The levels are beautifully crafted and are generally non-linear, encouraging some exploration. The single player perfectly combines old-school and new-school mechanics that flow really well. Doom 2016 feels like a classic arena shooter with the same mechanics you loved back in the 90s, blended with newer mechanics that fit just right. There are secrets and Easter eggs everywhere too. In addition to the main campaign, there is also an Arcade mode, which really pushes players to be even faster and to compete against their friends. There is no real deep story aside from picking up data logs, but this game proves that all you need for a fun single player experience is blood, action, and kickass weapons. 9.5/10
MULTIPLAYER:
Okay, so this game's multiplayer has been catching a lot of flak ever since the beta. Nowadays, I think a lot of the negativity towards the multiplayer is entirely unjustified. The weapons have been balanced well, and several different combos of weapons are viable. A lot of bugs have been ironed out, and a lot of features have been improved (hack modules, spawning, etc.) If you come into it expecting a clone of Quake 3, you will be disappointed. But if you come into the multiplayer expecting a decent, fun, action-filled frag fest, you will be more than satisfied. The maps are well designed, the weapons are awesome, and it still feels like a quality arena shooter. There are a multitude of clever game modes and a large enough player base to be able to find games consistently (on the NA servers, anyway, can't speak for others). I have put hundreds of hours into multiplayer on both Xbox and PC and don't plan on stopping soon. 9/10
SNAPMAP:
For those of you who don't know, Snapmap is a map editting tool that allows players to create a near-infinite number of levels and game modes. It's kind of like Halo Forge to a certain degree. Snapmap features a wide array of level modules, props, decals, environmental effects, weapons, enemies, hazards, you name it. If its in Doom, then its likely in Snapmap for you to play around with. In general, Snapmap is an excellent tool to scratch your creative itch, though I will say its sharing mechanics are not great. Its difficult to get your map noticed, and its also difficult to play other player's multipalyer maps unless you have friends. Overall a decent creative outlet that I would defintiely recommend exploring. 8/10
Overall, a fantastic entry into the FPS genre. Doom 2016 is probably one of my favorite games. I have put many, many hours into each of its game modes and have enjoyed each one thoroughly. The game has beautiful graphics and a badass soundtrack to boot. Definitely worth picking up at $30 bucks, and a must-buy for anything less than that.

Ignore the hours. I didn't play the game on Steam, but I've spent quite a bunch of hours on the game downloading it through their launcher (60-70 hours or so). Only downloaded it to write a review.
Now let's get to the review:
Aura Kingdom is nothing fancy. If you search for innovation you won't find it here (and anywhere to be fair, sadly the last game that really changed the genre was WoW).
It's a solid and fun, WoW inspired, MMORPG with nice graphics.
It's Free-mium, which means you CAN spend money on the game for cosmetics, but you don't have to. It doesn't give you an advantage but makes the game more attractive I suppose? (Never understood paying for cosmetics but some people really like it, look at LoL)
It's no MMORPG were you'll spend 2k-3k hours like some others *cough* WoW *cough* (dark times, guys) but it's a really fun way to pass the time. You have lots of different classes to try out and re-try the game with. Every class is different and, thus, the way you experience the game is different. With some you tank and spank, with others you really have to position intelligently if you want to make things right.
The game isn't frustrating by making you Grind the same monster for +50h but you can't really rush through it without grinding either (it mantains a good equilibrium with that).
You can solo the game in case your friends dont play MMORPG's (♥♥♥♥ you, guys) or play it with a couple friends you'll be able to finish the game without mayor problems in either way.
Of course it has some flaws. A few little bugs here and there (nothing game-breaking, really) and some people don't like that the game is rather short for a MMORPG as they normally require at least a few hundred hours to complete. Let's just say it isn't a deep MMORG but a little game to have fun with when you have nothing to do and/or want to relax a bit.
Overall a really nice game and I recommend it to every fan of the genre. Polished, fun and Free2Win. Seems good enough, right?

War. War never changes.
The end of the world occurred pretty much as we had predicted. Too many humans, not enough space or resources to go around. The details are trivial and pointless, the reasons, as always, purely human ones.
The earth was nearly wiped clean of life. A great cleansing, an atomic spark struck by human hands, quickly raged out of control. Spears of nuclear fire rained from the skies. Continents were swallowed in flames and fell beneath the boiling oceans. Humanity was almost extinguished, their spirits becoming part of the background radiation that blanketed the earth.
A quiet darkness fell across the planet, lasting many years. Few survived the devastation. Some had been fortunate enough to reach safety, taking shelter in great underground vaults. When the great darkness passed, these vaults opened, and their inhabitants emerged to begin their lives again.
One of the northern tribes claims they are descended from one such Vault. They hold that their founder and ancestor, one known as the "Vault Dweller," once saved the world from a great evil. According to their legend, this evil arose in the far south. It corrupted all it touched, twisting men inside, turning them into beasts. Only through the bravery of this Vault Dweller was the evil destroyed. But in so doing, he lost many of his friends and suffered greatly, sacrificing much of himself to save the world.
When at last he returned to the home he had fought so hard to protect, he was cast out. Exiled. In confronting that which they feared, he had become something else in their eyes...and no longer their champion.
Forsaken by his people, he strode into the wasteland. He traveled far to the north, until he came to the great canyons. There, he founded a small village, Arroyo, where he lived out the rest of his years. And so, for a generation since its founding, Arroyo has lived in peace, its canyons sheltering it from the outside world. It is home. Your home.
But the scars left by the war have not yet healed. And the Earth has not forgotten.

So... where should I start...
Well, the first thing you should know about Go! Go! Nippon! is that it's a pretty basic visual novel, which is a game genre that is very plot heavy and very light on gameplay, which is usually limited to choosing one option out of a given set of choices. In Go! Go! Nippon's case, there's next to no gameplay as there's about five points where you are given a choice, which doesn't give you much replayability.
Plotwise... well... if you picture a generic rom-com anime, this will come very close. And yes, that means there are some ecchi (perverted) scenes (they're unavoidable and totally irrelevant, but at least they are very brief).
So, why am I recommending this game? There's one thing that this game is good at: it gives you plenty of tidbits of Japanese culture and history. Makoto or Akira brings up a slew of facts in each area as you "explore" each area which makes up a good portion of the game. Although the game has a extras section which contains the same facts, the entries are not unlocked until you get there in the game. It may not be much, but the game provides some facts about Japanese culture and history in a more entertaining way.

After seeing all the reviews in store page, I was baffled with the sarcasm so imma give a proper review for this visual novel.
First thing first, this is not AAA VN; with all the content in this game, $9.95 is reasonable enough. This VN is more focused on being a tourist guide and it did a good job for that.
For story, it has 2 routes, 1 for each heroines. It is divided into two part, Common Route and Heroine Route:
The Common Route is focused on providing tourist information on the location that you selected in the game. There are 5 destinations to choose, in which you choose one location per day. The information that are given by the heroine is simple yet very useful if you're going to Japan. It provides background information on the location, the adaptation of the area as time progress, and you get to know what's what in that location. You can go to 3 location max. The destination that you chose determine whose route you gonna take.
The Heroine Route is focused on romantic development for the heroine that you progressed. THIS IS WHERE I GOT FRUSTRATED BECAUSE OF THE CLIFFHANGER ENDING... ehm, ignore my fanrage. As a person that plays countless of eroges, visual novels and galge, I can say that the romantic part of this VN is under-developed but it has a lot of potential. The romantic development is fast-paced but it leaves you wanting for more. It might be a quick romantic trip, but the characterization is very good for this size of VN so I guess I can't complain about that.
The gameplay itself is pretty simple, you just read-click-read. A feature worth noting for this VN is the option to show Japanese text alongside English text, a very useful feature if you're planning on learning Japanese. The currency conversion is a pretty neat feature of this game as it allows you to set the rate of $/€ to ¥ and vice versa, it gives you an estimate of how many dough you might spend on the trip there (train fare can vary depending on which location you might stayed if you really come to Japan).
The art of this VN is quite good for its size, with the feature of upscaling to HD I can't even ask for more. Then again this is not AAA VN, the amount of CGs and sprite quality is decent enough.
All in all, I gave this game rating 7.4/10. It did a good job for being a tour guide, but then again, I DEMAND A SEQUEL FOR THIS GAME KMON WTF GIB ME A SEQUEL WITH MOAR H/E-SCENE AND PROPER ROMANCE + DEEP LOVE RELATIONSHIP WITH THE HEROINE !!!

In relation to the other Deus Ex games, HR is a perfect prequel.  It creates a realistic world that leads organically to the events in Deus Ex.  It’s very cool to see the era when the ‘old’ augs in Deus Ex came from.  I remember seeing Gunther in the first game and thinking “damn, must suck to have all that metal when I can do the same with microscopic robots.”  If you choose one of the endings it will actually hint at the birth of the Dentons.
The only real negative I can point out in Deus Ex: Human Revolution is actually it’s ending.  I won’t spoil it with any details, but the problem is that exactly like Fallout 3, this game ends with a “pick one of three pre-rendered slideshows.”  That’s right, all of those decisions you made don’t matter for crap in the end because you get one of three boring montages with narrated monologue.  I was thinking to myself “WTF Square, did CG suddenly get too expensive in the last 5 minutes of the game?”  The most frustrating part is that just like the aforementioned Fallout 3, the game strings you along for hours on the belief that you are shaping your own story with all these choices you make.  Then, after it’s all over and you’ve kicked everything’s♥♥♥♥♥ you get some grainy slideshow that does nothing to tie up the plot and instead features some morality prose that’s pretty weak.  Especially since the loose ends that needed tying up by the end of this game were substantial, especially if you saved everyone and did every quest.  Boo Eidos Montreal.
Overall Deus Ex: Human Revolution is an amazing game.  None of the gameplay design is original, but every part functions better than in the game it was borrowed from and it creates a game that is a Jack of All Trades, master of all.  The people who made about 20 other games over the last few years must be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that Eidos Montreal just came along and made them all look like amateurs in one fell swoop.

Two quick things to note before you purchase Bully: Scholarship Edition:
1. The game runs at 30fps natively (Whoop de doo, but apparently this is an issue for some people.)
2.  An XBox 360 pad or 360 pad emulating software is highly recommended to play this game properly. Other configurations can work, but it works best with 360-styled controls.
Anyway...Bully: Scholarship Edition is a 2008 upgrade of the 2006 PS2 game, so don't expect a lot of the bells and whistles that open world games of today have, and even in scale it's much smaller than Rockstar's other PS2 offerings. The smaller scale works in Bully's favor however, as the world is much easier to navigate and able to breathe a bit more.
In the game you'll spend your time juggling your school studies alongside completing various missions to advance the story and curry favor with the various cliques around campus. Mission structures are fairly simple and easy to execute and have a certain charm to them given the high school setting. Blowing up toilets with firecrackers, dropping stink bombs in lockers, and rolling teachers down a hill an a locked porta potty are a lot more charming than the typical Rockstar fare of "Go here, shoot dudes, now go here." There's still a bit of open-world repetition to the process, but the story missions are varied enough and the scholastic mini-games fun enough that tedium rarely sets in.
Narratively, Bully is more a comedy than most open-world games. There are quite a few genuine laugh oud loud lines and moments that make seeing the story through a worthwhile endeavor. Though the story and characters are brilliantly acted, they're unfortunately not written quite as well as they should be and the overall narrative and anti-bullying messages end up muddled. The main antagonist only appears in the opening and final chapters and the climax feels very slapdash and out of nowhere. With as strong as the Grand Theft Auto PS2 games were in this department, it's a bit of a bummer that Bully ended up getting a bit of a short stick.
All that said, if you missed Bully the first time around, it's certainly worth a look. There's enough charm, comedy, fun things to get into, and great acting to keep the tedium of an overworld game from creeping up too often, just be aware that the payoff might not be exactly what you were hoping for.

I'm not too keen on third-person competitive shooters. At first I was skeptical about Loadout. But after giving it a try I have warmed a bit towards it.
The greatest feature it has to offer is customizable weapons. You get a basic kit (rifle, launcher etc.) that you can turn into anything you like (Assault Rifle, Sniper Rifle, Machinegun; Rocket Launcher, Grenade Launcher, Missile Launcher). This gives a new dimension to grinding, as it allows you to upgrade your weapon gradually until you finally make that perfect gun you've dreamt about while playing other games.
This game also has a coop mode, where you can practice against AI (which is pretty dumb but compensates for it with terrific aiming accuracy). And once you're done with your loadout and are confident enough you can slowly transition into PvP.
I'm still fighting bots because I'd like to test out various weapon combinations and learn the 3 maps they have in the game. And to tell you the truth, it's a lot of fun. Partly due to the game's fairly high production values. Partly due to the fact that you don't get owned by bots unless your team really sucks.
All in all, for a free-to-play title it's a very solid game taht definitely deserves a chance.

The first NieR is a game that holds a special place to me due to where I was in my life when it came out and I played it, and what was going on at the time, as well as just how unique and strange it was in a lot of ways. So going in to Automata I simultaneously wasn't quite sure what to expect, but was also expecting quite a lot.
I got all 4 endings of the original, and I thought it was really something unique, and as it turns out, Yoko Taro did it again. This time with one of my favorite studios on board, Platinum. Without saying too much, it's just as WEIRD as the original, and subverts your expectations in similar ways. Playing the tropes in a very self aware manner that makes you smile and wonder just what it's really doing until it finally reveals its cards. It's only sort of related to the first NieR, but I won't go in to exactly how all that intertwines.
The combat is the biggest improvement, with Platinum at the helm you would expect it to be fantastic, and they nail it down pretty well, it's a great mix between Action RPG and Spectacle Fighter combat, lots of weapon and move variety with some other shinies like your pods and their skills. There are also chips which augment your stats and add new passive abilites in various aspects, and these are actually involved in a sort of Dark Souls-esque death system of body recovery to retrieve your things.
Of course, the game also changes on subsequent plays, just as you would hope, and it changes pretty immediately and importantly too, going so far as to show you familiar events from other perspectives and to let you play as other characters. Overall, it's a definite must-experience for me, I love it and need to finish all the routes, because it's really something special. The soundtrack is phenomenal as well, as you would expect if you played the first NieR.
One caveat, for some people, it does have crashing problems and resolution issues, I can't comment on these because I never had them on the machines I can test it on, but apparently their is a community patch called FAR that fixes basically everything quite handily for most people. Unacceptable that a proper official patch hasn't been made, but like I said, that's all I can really say seeing as it works flawlessly on everything I can throw at it.

This "game" (more like graphic novel) sort of came out of nowhere (in terms of advertisement and in my gift inbox), I never would of suspected this game to be as entertaining as it was, now let me type a crappy review on it. (SPOILERS BELOW!)
Story:
There isn't much of a story to go over, You're a socially inept eyeless male (<-insert name of choice here) who's dream is to go to Japan, At some point in time you met two people in a chat room named Makoto and Akira who happen to live in Japan, after a discussion you decided visit them for one week.
Upon your arrival you discover that Makoto and Akira are both girls (sisters to be exact) and not the big burly Japanese guys you thought they were, thus making a new standard that in Japan the gender trap can work both ways.
So for one week both girls take you to different locations of your choosing while providing facts about its culture and history (Your location choice determines which girl you go with).
Characters:
In my honest opinion, I didn't like the main character you play as, he comes off as a clutz while attempting to converse with the sisters, It gets really awkward towards the end when you get romantically involved with one of them and your character just stutters a lot as he admits his feelings. (Locations you choose determine which sister you fall in love with)
Makoto and Akira on the other hand, I thought were pretty interesting, Both had solid personality traits different from one another, Makoto being the polite and sweet older sister who's good at English, but she can't cook to save her life, Akira being the sassy yet bashful younger sister who's horrible at English, but she's a master of culinary arts and clothing design.
My one complaint, their personalities’ could of been fleshed out a bit more, considering the fact you end up dating one of them at the end of the game, It just felt like you confessed deep feelings for someone you barely know outside of being a good host/travel guide.
Performance:
This game had a few minor performance issues on my pc, Mainly with the steam in-game interface which succumbed to a lot of latency or flat-out froze forcing me to ctrl+alt+delete the game exe, Adding more fuel to the fire the skip button glitches out sometimes, forcing me to power click my way through sections I already read.
Scenery/Graphics:
The game included some nice artwork for the characters along with some cool tourism sites to explore; however, I feel they didn't provide enough sprites for the characters or sites of interest for each location, which made things a tad repetitive in the visual department.
Summary:
This game is a unique experience, many games out there have tried to be educational while being fun but ended up being very boring, this game is spared of the boring factor by keeping you interested with soft-core hentai while dumping facts about Japans history on you, Feeling like spending money and hate going to Wikipedia? This game is your calling card.

The best way to describe Skara would be as a raw gem.
Skara is a fantastic concept of a game which still needs to be polished in order for it to shine as it trully deserves. Skara is a fighting game which is based in attacking and dodging. However, as you invest time into the game, you start realizing it is much more complicated.
Every attack can be outspaced and punished, every ability can be used in original ways to throw off your opponent, the same combo is never guaranteed to work twice, therefore being unpredictable is important to achieve victory against skilled enemies. Every character is inherently different, Shinse is fast but frail, Kharn is slow but beefy, etc. Every matchup is very different and has no clear winner so everything comes from the players behind the characters.The involvement of the developers with the community is outstanding, they are very close and personal as long as you are polite.
Finally, Skara is a game without a main already written story behind it. In Skara the events are the ones that decide how the worl changes and which outstanding figures show up. As a player, you can affect the lore just by playing, ans if you are dedicated enough, you can become a main character in the lore. However, Skara does have some problems.
First of all ( of course, this game is at its alpha state, so many of my issues with it will be solved sooner or later), there is a clear lack of content, when it comes to gamemodes and, from my pov, characters.
Secondly, the playerbase is quite small at the moment, and without a constant reward system players tend to leave the game until the next event arrives.
Finally, most new players do not stick for long, they come into the game, skip the tutorial, go into online pvp (which is the only gamemode atm) and die constantly for 1hour because they do not even know how to dodge, then, this people go ahead and write a review in which they crap all over the game because they did not understand anything about it.
As a conclusion I would reccomend this game to everyone. Since it is F2P there is no drawback for trying it, if you do not enjoy it you can always stop playing, if you do, then you can slowly build your way up into a game with fantastic promises towards its future

First, some reviewers on here did not recommend this title because they claimed it was buggy. I did not experience a single bug from my 30 hour playthrough so I am not quite sure as to what they were referring to.
As far as the DLC that comes with this title: the DLC mission is integrated so seamlessly into the main story that I didn't even realize it was the DLC until after I had completed the game.
I think the best part about Deus Ex: Human Revolution is it literally allows you to play the game however you wish. Do you enjoy complete stealth missions and sneaking around? You can do that and there are weapons designed specifically for stealth (tranquilizers and stun guns for example). Do you enjoy running in and blowing up everyone you see with a rocket launcher? You can do that too. You have special augmentations that you choose to unlock in order to play the game to your style. For example you can unlock short bursts of invisibility in order to avoid being seen; or if you choose to fight you can augment hand to hand combat and weapon abilities. The game is designed so that you, the player, are given the ability to choose exactly how you play the game.
As far as the story goes, it was good/above average but not amazing. It felt extremely rabbit holey. The rabbit hole went down so far that I just kept thinking to myself "welp, I guess I'll find the bottom around 50 hours in." The story has a lot of twists and turns, but none of them are particularly interesting. It was just like, ok, you found out something new, better go check it out.. and down the rabbit hole you go. Rinse and repeat. But it was never an overly interesting rabbit hole. On the flipside, the ending is simply one of the best endings I have experienced. It reminds you of just how empowering, yet brutally dangerous technology can be to society. To quote Einstein: "Technological progress is like an axe in the hands of a pathological criminal."
Overall, the gameplay is one of the best I've experienced. The story mixes technology and the choices it forces on human morality. This title is close to perfection in both terms of gameplay and story, and I can't give the developers enough praise. Deus Ex: Human Revolution takes about 20 hours playtime to finish, and about 30 hours if you do all the side missions.

Pros:

I have been a fan of this developer and their interactive story games for a qhile, not including this (Zombie Exodus) I think I own 3 or four of their previous games and despite the short-comings these sort of games may or may-not have they've been really good.  And then I bought this one.
You see first I downloaded the demo, it was ok, short, naturally as you dont wantt o give the entire thing away but enough to make me sure that this like the others was well written and structured to be worth buying.  However after playing to it's conclusion all  I can say is that I feel conned.
Previous interactive games by this creator have been full stories, a beginning, middle, and end of sorts, and they've been great, sure some may be split across separate volumes but overall they have been worth the money because they have had been long-enought o keep you satisfired.
This however is a travesty, you get PART of the entire story, a chunk of it that is very short, and leaves you in the position of having buy the next part in the story if you want to continue. It feel like the remaining parts were locked behind a paywall, and nominal fee or not, the developers are still holding the remaining parts of the story to ransom, with an attitude of pay up otherwise you don't get to continue the game through to it's conclusion like you've been able to in numerous other intactive story games this publisher has released in the past.
In it's current state and given that you pretty much only get a small fragment of the game for the price, and it most definateyly isn't worth it, I WOULD NOT recommend this game.

This controller is absolutely intriguing. When I removed it from the box, I thought it felt light and a little chintzy. However, after plugging it in and trying it across a few varied genres, I'm convinced of the Steam controller's genius. I've even tried it in a game where the dev specifically tells you not to use a controller, and it's phenomenal. My biggest fear was that the face button placement would be too far out of the way for my lazy thumbs, and really — at least for fighting games  — they are. One community configuration for the controller changed my mind. For Mortal Kombat X, some sharp cookie set up the left pad as a touch "stick" and the right one as simulated face buttons with touch input. The fluidity and fast action of this setup was jaw-dropping. Incidentally, that's another positive for this thing beyond it's mechanical delight. The community support  for this controller is superb. I normally don't like tweaking that much on my controllers, and the massive amount of player-made custom configurations makes finding the best bindings a cinch. Furthermore, it actually encouraged me to play around with it. The♥♥♥♥♥♥you can customize on this thing, including the connect/disconnect chime, is staggering.
I just recently picked up one of the new MacBook Pros with that force-touch trackpad which tricks your fingers into thinking you're actually pressing a button when you're totally not. The Steam controller does this, granted, with a little less finesse. If you configure the left pad to behave as a d-pad, it will definitely feel like a d-pad. You actually feel the buttons that aren't there just by the haptic feedback. When the pads are acting like scroll wheels or arcade trackballs, it actually feels like you're rotating a wheel or a ball.
One of my favorite uses for this, aside from being a convenient cross-platform controller, is simply using it as a wireless remote for media. I can easily control my music and movies from across the room and map common commands to the myriad of programmable inputs on this thing. It's a joy.
For more intense FPSs or RTSs, I don't think I'll ever shirk the mouse, but the Steam Controller is definitely my new fallback. I love it.

Lots of run'n'gunning, satisfying gore/explosions/melee attacks, plenty of secrets and easter eggs, gorgeous open worlds and fantastically detailed indoor realms. Adventure Capitalist, stylized as AdVenture Capitali$t!, and abbreviated as AdCap[1] is an incremental video game developed by Hyper Hippo Productions and published by Kongregate for Windows and on March 30, 2015, for iOS,[2] Android,[3] OS X, Linux and Adobe Flash,[4] and on August 16, 2016 in North America for PlayStation 4. Adventure Capitalist allows players to live like a capitalist, and invest funds into certain products to generate revenue, by starting out with a single lemonade stand. The more revenue generated, the higher the player's cash is. A player can receive an angel bonus when resetting their progress, which provides a boost in all products' revenue for the next progress timeline.[5] A spin-off, AdVenture Communist, was released on Steam on May 2016.[6] It is also made by Hyper Hippo, and is currently in open beta.

Saints Row 2 is definitely not a new game, but it's quality says otherwise. While I'm aware that the PC port was not that great and that people may encounter issues, the only problem I had was with the fps, but other than that my experience was fine. Skip to the end for the summary.
Considering this game was released in 2009, the graphics aren't all that bad. Sure, it's not good, but it isn't something that will distract you from the gameplay
. The only glaring issue with the graphics is the attempt to add in weather effects. I appreciate Volition trying to make the world dynamic, but it just doesn't work out. Whenever it is raining or there is gloomy weather the game just looks awful. All the textures look smudged and blurry. Also, if you run this game at above 30 fps you will have a problem with the cutscenes where the objects will be bugged(i.e someone will be holding a pistol but it will floating in the air a few feet away from him) Other than that, the graphical part of this game is ok.
SCORE 7/10
The gameplay is really what makes Saints Row 2 stand out. If I could describe it in a few words it would be fluid and fun. Gunplay is satisfying and really makes you feel like a badass. Cars are smooth to control, in fact the driving is perfect. There are also a lot of cars to choose from and almost every one of them feels unique in the way they control. The gang system in the game is also really good. Capturing "hoods" and removing the hostile presence in the area makes it feel like you really are taking over Stillwater. Every gang also has their own cars and they have a radio station they listen to, for example the Sons Of Samedi, a drug cartel, will usually be playing "420 radio" whenever you get into one of their cars. There is also a "respect" system in the game, and while I like the idea, I think it was poorly executed. When I first heard of this system I thought you would unlock things like new guns in the stores or more clothes when you got enough respect, sadly this was not the case. In order to get respect you either do random things like drift, drive in the other lane, or kill gang members (you get very little respect this way) or do the activities, which I admit are pretty good(you get a lot of respect). So how this system works is when you fill up your respect bar you level it up and what do you do with these levels you ask? Well, for every time you fill up your respect bar, you get to play 1 mission. So if you fill it up 5 times, you get to play 5 missions. It wouldn't be so bad if it didn't feel forced, you do a certain amount of missions and then you have to go do the activies for however long in order to play more. Speaking of the activities, they are actually very good and I would've probably played them a lot more if I wasn't forced to by the game's main story. Missions are designed well, but there is a problem with them. Since there are around 50ish missions in the game they get repetitive. Some of them are designed so well, with fun cinematic moments and twists in gameplay. The problem is that the same unique idea that made the mission great gets used again in another mission. One that comes to mind is in one you get to fight someone with a sword while he also has one. That mission was probably the best in the game but when you sword fight someone later on in the game it just feels unoriginal and boring. The final flaw in the gameplay would be the open world. Stillwater isn't poorly made, it's just empty. The world is just made for you to get from point A to B. Nothing is done with the world, even the activities don't utilize the open world. Even if the open world is just a placeholder, it isn't a terrible one.
SCORE 9/10
For a shooter game, the story isn't all that bad. The game mostly focuses on taking back the city that you and your gang used to own. There is that Saints Row humor that everyone talks about, and it really is quite funny at times, the best part of it is that it isn't forced *cough*Saints Row 3*cough*. Even though the game usually has a pretty bright mood, the game does delve into some serious topics such as loss, revenge, and murder. While the story is good, the thing that really makes it good are the characters. Every character, whether in your gang or not, has a great personality and feels very unique. There is not a single character that feels like another character, and I loved that.
SCORE 8/10
After the main story ends, there are some activities to do. These activites are pretty fun but as I had mentioned beforehand, you get pretty tired of them after being forced to play them. There isn't a real point in replaying the main story other than it's fun.
SCORE 7/10
For the most part things like cars, guns, and voice acting sound pretty good. It's nothing special, but it works. The only really good thing about the audio is the radio in the cars. There is a great choice of radio station, ranging from classical music, to Jamaican music, to 80's music. Every radio station contains some great songs of the genre. However, I was disappointed that the developers didn't include any music in the missions. Think of something like Make it Bun Dem and Far Cry 3. Heck, even some classical music to blowing up helicopters would've been great. That is probably the only thing off with the audio, something that they didn't even add.
SCORE 9/10
Looking past the pretty bad PC port, Saints Row 2 can be most easily described by the phrase "old but gold".

What an amazing game. TLDR below
At this time, I feel obliged to write down a big recommendation to pick this up if you haven't since Bethesda/Id comepensated for their mistake to release MP-only DLCs and patched them in for free.
I mainly bought the game for the campaign, which didn't disappoint and gave me that same special feel that the other Doom titles also conveyed. The gameplay is super fast, g(l)ory kills super fun, the mission areas are cleverly designed, there are alot of extra content elements and achievements to unlock for hunters and gatherers and the graphics run smooth and stable even on my old graphics card. Especially worth mentioning is the exquisite soundtrack, which supports the bloodrush feel of this gorefest perfectly and adapts to situations. Ingame videos are a bit bland and I didn't wholly like the main villain in retrospect, but I guess Doom was never really about the storyline but more about murdering demons, right?
The multiplayer is not as bad as I read in many reviews. I feel pretty comfortable in it, but that probably is due to that I played alot of UT and Quake back in the days. I don't know if the MP gets stale after the free weekend, which I enjoyed (no empty servers etc), but so far I had a blast (literally). I'm not sure if the whole loadout and unlock system makes sense for a Doom title tbh, they could have just stuck to cosmetic unlocks for those who need it, but the Rocket Launcher is avaiable at start, so there's no real downside to it. ;) In one Lobby I had a few lag stutters, but that only occured in one of the 10-15 matches I played so far.
All in all, this game is a 9/10 to me.

Fallout 2 is the pinnacle of the Fallout experience (in my opinion). This game presents a truly open world with hundreds of choices for any style of character to truly live in. Besides a slow start, increase in comic references, more complex story, and a few bugs here and there; Fallout 2 truly exceeds the accomplishments of its first installment here. Skills are much more useful, weapons and choices are abundant, and companions take on a life of their own here. Although most prefer the 3D titles in the Fallout series, this one truly feels the most imaginative and true to style in the series. If you haven't played it and are inclined to play 2D isometric RPG’s, this one is a real treat.

I will start with saying that this game is far better then Fallout 3 (ps3), Fallout 4 (pc) and i probably enjoyed it more then new Vegas (ps3) too and tactics ( only played 2 hrs).
Onto the review.
Gameplay: This game is a turn based rpg , set in a post apoclyptic world. You have huge map to explorer and you can if you want to go straight to the last locations. The game has tons of various cool character you can talk to. And quests you can do. With multiple factions all with they own agendas, and if you don`t like any of them you can either kill them or skip doing those quests all together.  Also every companion can be order to be offensive, use melee weapons or ranged, carry stuff or to wait or move if they stand in you way , witch may happens sometimes. It might no be the best gameplay but it still works just fine. And the game is neither to hard nor to unforgiving.
Character development / leveling/skills and quest: How your develop you character is entirely up to you. Do you want to fist you way trough the game you can do that.  Do you wanna be a sniper and let your companions if you want to have companions do the fight for you , you can do just that. Do you want to play the game alone you can do that. For every four level you reach you can choose a skill and some of this skills is pretty good and actually has a meaning. Do you want to be a sweet talker and try to talk your way trough most of the quests you can do that. Compared to the later fallout especially fallout 4 at least in a large extent you have more freedom in how you do your quests and how you accomplish them all with multiple solutions and your choices also has  consequences. All the character you meet have their own personalities and perhaps even problems or a reason they need your help or a reason  why the want to join you and lastly those character especially on the companion side is plentiful and enough of them but not to many and neither to few. All skills have they own usefulness. Almost every character you meet has something to tell about the world. Plus if you really want to you can be a made - man/woman.  And lastly you earn exp by doing quests and killing or even picking up a special items or using seeing special encounters.  So yeah the game is pretty violent. Like shooting the groin of someone or the head of someone.
Factions: A short note on factions. Every factions as previously said have they own agendas. Some are evil som are good some are somewhere in between. Some want to make prostitution and gambling legal. Some want to focus on something else.
Setting: Perhaps most important of all is the setting. The setting is great. It feels very mush like an a post-apocalyptic game. All of the locations feel different in a good way. Different cultures. Different rules in the different places. Every places has it own mini-stories of side quests to tell. And with the wonderful music it could nt be any/much better. And the game has tons of Charm and Humor.
Music: the soundtrack is very good. And a lot of the tracks if not all you will remember.It really helps you immerse yourself into the setting
Bonus: I would put it here. The humor is very good. There is a lot of times you will laugh. Like missing a 95% hit or hitting a target with 20% hit for that matter.  You will laugh by the funny and witty and good written dialogue. A lot of cool Easter eggs that even i understood or laughed and thought was funny, i am not the best at finding Easter eggs, but i could in this game.
And the ending is more then good enough to and so is the voice acting at least for that time. And  despite some few crashes the game is still utterly fantascic. Give it a shot , even if you disliked fallout 3/4. Hugely different.
Score : highly recommended 10/10 if you enjoy turn based rpg set in a wonderful and brilliant rpg setting

Bleeding from several wounds, I thrust my spear once more toward my enemy, this time connecting, finally. I'm poisoned, bleary eyed and have six hitpoints remaining.
I just survived the first dungeon with a charismatic character. I killed some Giant Ants.
This is what Fallout was. A sprawling, tough RPG that actually required some amount of planning toward your character and your decisions. Even to this day the dialogue is great and the story gripping yet allows a sense of freedom. If you want a fighting character you better make a fighting character. When I played Fallout 4 I made an incredibly charismatic, intelligent character with poor stats in fighting. I still managed to kill everything. In Fallout 2 I barely survived the first dungeon, getting mauled by Lesser Scorpions and Giant Ants, all because I wanted my character to be a talker, not a fighter.
Obviously it's aged; three mousepointers need to be alternated between; combat, movement and interaction. There's a panel that brings up skills and not everything is made immediately clear.
But if those main 'problems' with the game don't scare you away then this is a great game. It's worth a try, even if just to see how Fallout was and to experience a true gaming classic; one that will remain for countless years as a great game in the history of gaming.
