Sigh. I really wanted to love this controller. I did. The features are amazing, it's comfortable, it's well built, it can be tweaked out the wazoo to do almost anything you could imagine with it. And yet... there's a problem. A really, really big problem. A game breaking problem in a literal sense.
There are plenty of reviews that will tell you everything else, but I didn't get this information until I actually tried to use it so this review will focus entirely on the problem: the GUI/software is absolute garbage.
The problem here is that you absolutely have to enter into big picture mode for most of the controller's features to work at all. If you aren't in BPM, you can't even so much as program the buttons and the defaults it will go to are for a mouse/keyboard setup instead of an actual controller. There is no way to change this.
It gets worse.
Any game which can't bring up the steam overlay, such as most very old games or emulators, will be completely unable to use the steam controller. It will be locked in the default mode and will not be changed no matter what. It doesn't matter if you tell it to change to a different button setup, it doesn't care. I even went in and manually edited the config file to force the default to use a sane button setup, but no, that doesn't work either because every time it tries to access the controller it "fixes" the config file and rewrites it back to the default mouse/keyboard setup.
I mostly got the controller to play old games like tie fighter, mechwarrior or my emulators so I wouldn't have to play console roulette on my TV. Virtually every game I wanted to use the steam controller for it will not work with. There are workarounds, and after 7 hours of troubleshooting, I have managed to get two emulators to vaguely sort of work, but nothing else.
So long as the controller is forcibly tied to the steam overlay, it's a paperweight to me because the vast majority of the games I wanted to use it on will not work. The frustrating part of this is that the games themselves do in fact recognize the controller and will accept the inputs the controller provides - the problem is that steam doesn't recognize the games as being games so it never exits the generic desktop mode and absolutely refuses all efforts to change that horrifically awful functionality.
Now, if you want to use your controller to play modern games? No problem, it works great! It's an amazing controller when it recognizes that you're playing a game. It's by far the best controller I've ever had when it works. But so long as it's completely incapable of changing its default control scheme and continues to have severe issues with detecting games, it simply has lower functionality than a $5 piece of junk controller from China.
If you want to play older games or emulators, DO NOT UNDER ANY CIRCUMSTANCE BUY THIS CONTROLLER. It will not work, and it's tied directly into how it interfaces with steam and the games themselves. It's purely a software/programing issue, so it may be fixed at some point in the future however. Given valve's strong track record in updating their stuff to provide better functionality, I figure within the next few months to a year it'll probably have the capacity to set the default button setup while in desktop mode, but until then, avoid the steam controller like the plague if you want to play older games.

Never had a chance to play the original Deus Ex, as I was in elementary school when it released, but a couple of years after Deus Ex Invisible War came out, I played through it.  To this day it still stands as one of the greatest single player games I have ever played, even surpassing the KOTOR series by a small margin.
Deus Ex:  Human Revolution surpasses even Invisible War.  With a stronger emphasis on stealth and espionage, it realy feels like you are a futuristic mechanically augmented assassin detective, with nearly any weapon at your disposal -- from silenced pistols and arm-blades, to rocket launchers and chain guns.
The story is potentially even better than that of Invisible War, and lets face it, Deus Ex is always heavy on the story.  Where it really excels, I think, is that the side quests that are available do a good job of uncovering the backstory of the main character and of the game as a whole, which is a detail that a lot of current RPG's fail to deliver.  It makes the side quests feel just as important as the main story line -- which makes for a much more immersive game.
I would give this a 100/100.  Best single player game I have played in the past 25 years.

Overall, recommended!

Bleeding from several wounds, I thrust my spear once more toward my enemy, this time connecting, finally. I'm poisoned, bleary eyed and have six hitpoints remaining.
I just survived the first dungeon with a charismatic character. I killed some Giant Ants.
This is what Fallout was. A sprawling, tough RPG that actually required some amount of planning toward your character and your decisions. Even to this day the dialogue is great and the story gripping yet allows a sense of freedom. If you want a fighting character you better make a fighting character. When I played Fallout 4 I made an incredibly charismatic, intelligent character with poor stats in fighting. I still managed to kill everything. In Fallout 2 I barely survived the first dungeon, getting mauled by Lesser Scorpions and Giant Ants, all because I wanted my character to be a talker, not a fighter.
Obviously it's aged; three mousepointers need to be alternated between; combat, movement and interaction. There's a panel that brings up skills and not everything is made immediately clear.
But if those main 'problems' with the game don't scare you away then this is a great game. It's worth a try, even if just to see how Fallout was and to experience a true gaming classic; one that will remain for countless years as a great game in the history of gaming.

A lot better than I expected, especially since this game had many mixed reviews early on. Enjoyed it more than the recent Walking Dead seasons. In fact I consider it one of TellTale's best games.
Story-wise, it reminds me of those early Saturday Morning Cartoons, especially Duck Tales. A group of friends go on lots of amazing adventures, exploring new cities (and other dimensions), meeting wacky villains and saving the day. My favourite episode is definitely Episode 6, where you are trapped with a group of strangers in a creepy mansion, being hunted down by a serial killer.
People complain about the price a lot, but games cost a lot of money to make and I feel the price is fair for both the main game and DLC. The 1st episode is also free now, so you can test it before deciding to buy the rest.

Sigh. I really wanted to love this controller. I did. The features are amazing, it's comfortable, it's well built, it can be tweaked out the wazoo to do almost anything you could imagine with it. And yet... there's a problem. A really, really big problem. A game breaking problem in a literal sense.
There are plenty of reviews that will tell you everything else, but I didn't get this information until I actually tried to use it so this review will focus entirely on the problem: the GUI/software is absolute garbage.
The problem here is that you absolutely have to enter into big picture mode for most of the controller's features to work at all. If you aren't in BPM, you can't even so much as program the buttons and the defaults it will go to are for a mouse/keyboard setup instead of an actual controller. There is no way to change this.
It gets worse.
Any game which can't bring up the steam overlay, such as most very old games or emulators, will be completely unable to use the steam controller. It will be locked in the default mode and will not be changed no matter what. It doesn't matter if you tell it to change to a different button setup, it doesn't care. I even went in and manually edited the config file to force the default to use a sane button setup, but no, that doesn't work either because every time it tries to access the controller it "fixes" the config file and rewrites it back to the default mouse/keyboard setup.
I mostly got the controller to play old games like tie fighter, mechwarrior or my emulators so I wouldn't have to play console roulette on my TV. Virtually every game I wanted to use the steam controller for it will not work with. There are workarounds, and after 7 hours of troubleshooting, I have managed to get two emulators to vaguely sort of work, but nothing else.
So long as the controller is forcibly tied to the steam overlay, it's a paperweight to me because the vast majority of the games I wanted to use it on will not work. The frustrating part of this is that the games themselves do in fact recognize the controller and will accept the inputs the controller provides - the problem is that steam doesn't recognize the games as being games so it never exits the generic desktop mode and absolutely refuses all efforts to change that horrifically awful functionality.
Now, if you want to use your controller to play modern games? No problem, it works great! It's an amazing controller when it recognizes that you're playing a game. It's by far the best controller I've ever had when it works. But so long as it's completely incapable of changing its default control scheme and continues to have severe issues with detecting games, it simply has lower functionality than a $5 piece of junk controller from China.
If you want to play older games or emulators, DO NOT UNDER ANY CIRCUMSTANCE BUY THIS CONTROLLER. It will not work, and it's tied directly into how it interfaces with steam and the games themselves. It's purely a software/programing issue, so it may be fixed at some point in the future however. Given valve's strong track record in updating their stuff to provide better functionality, I figure within the next few months to a year it'll probably have the capacity to set the default button setup while in desktop mode, but until then, avoid the steam controller like the plague if you want to play older games.

This game truely falls into the Visual Novel category, those looking for more "interaction" or choices that affect the outcome are going to be very disappointed. The lack of voice acting also put a damper on the experince. Its basically a well illustrated "E-book"
That being said this game does exactly what it says it would do, give you a "guided tour" of certain parts in Japan. However I must throw in that just a quick look on google will get you more images of the sites mentioned in this game. They could have done much more, there are many scenes in the game where you are looking at clouds, when they could be showing you just what is being talked about, or what is happening.

I'm a pretty die-hard mouse-and-keyboard guy, but credit where credit is due: this is the best gamepad I've ever owned.  Now, I haven't owned many, to be honest, so maybe take what I have to say with a grain of salt, but I'd be very surprised if you were disappointed.  I like that it can operate in wireless or wired mode.  I'm terrible about buying batteries (it needs 2 AAs) and I'm glad to know that if I forget, I can just tether this thing, and still be in the game.
However, it does take some getting used to.  My first night with it was a bit frustrating, and some games needed some tweaking, but once you get used to it, it's very natural to use, either with gamepad-oriented games, or just as a mouse/keyboard substitute.
The D-Pad is a bit clunky, and I do wish it had less travel on the button press.  You may want to unbind the grip buttons, as it's hard to hold the controller with one hand and *not* press the grip, so reaching for your drink can cause unintentional input.  If you have calloused thumbs, the trackpads aren't as accurate or responsive as they need to be; so much so that I strongly suggest trying one out for yourself before buying.  I tilt my thumb to the side a bit, and I'm fine, but YMMV.
In conclusion, this is a very impressive piece of hardware, reasonably priced.  I recommend it.

My favorite thing about it, though, is how unique you can make your character with the skill points and tree. I also really love being able to get a secondary class. Basically, to enjoy this game you have to level up. You have to get past like, level 45-50ish to really start getting to the meat of the game. Getting to that point will require some serious patience. It is boring and dulls the mind but if you get past that, it's a pretty okay game.

Loved Zombie Exodus and it was the Gateway game that got me into COGs. The game does have some bugs and is a what I can best describe as a slow start.
-Cons-
-Skill system locks you into just your prime and secondary skills when you try to start game with extra starting skills.(as lots of others have touched on. I have talked to to the email support and good news there is a patch. Bad news its just not updated on steam yet. Mary who I talked to did say it should be fixed soon tho so here's hoping.
-The game is linear. While you can choice between several different characters that only effects intro.(I do think in later parts it will play a huge part but as far as the this game goes bit of a let down.) Its not the worst thing ever but does get repetitive after several play throughs. This is the starting point though and the game has to start somewhere so in the end it is understandable.
-Pros-
-Everything else
I say that but I'm not really kidding
-the story and the writing is great. You can feel that the plot is leading you to something epic and the journey is just getting started.
-the NPC are written wonderfully and feel real. The interactions feel life like and the choice they make can shock you as well as play right into what you expect from them. I love the diversity so far.
-Romance in the the apocalypse? Please and thank you. It might seem odd to think about dating while zombies are trying to eat you but when the world is ending you find comfort where you can. I've always  loved loved loved this aspect in games and ZESH it looks like is setting up to be might impressive in the area. I can see spending way to many hours of my life playing with this mechanic and loving every one of them. So many choices and I will find them all.
-skill system is flexible. When they get it working you will be able to be any type of person you wont really. Be a soldier with great weapon training or a hacker thats terrified and allergic to everything.
-Extra bonuses for beating Zombie Exodus was a nice touch as well. You can buy another 25 extra starting skill points for .99 which while I usually hate dlc I'm dealing with this one.
Overall its a great game with a lot more to come. I'm looking forward to the next and the next and the all the parts of the game. This game is very much worth a look as well as his other Zombie Exodus one. If you've never tried one before give this one a try.
-Personal Note-
I would love to see a God mode at the end of the game or something. After completing the game say 5, 10 or even 20 times. You can start the game over with the Char's stat's you finished the game with. New game plus but with hopefully near maxed stats. Then you can play through and just see what would happen with the higher stats. Not something you'd have to use if you want to play normally but a gift for completing the game so many times. Would be nice and spice the game back up after putting in what at that point would have to be 100's of hrs.

I'm a huge fan of the first Zombie Exodus game and enjoyed the beta for this one.
Cons (as of 10/31/16):
+ this is only the first part of the game; part 2 is due out sometime in 2017
+ dying means you need to start over again from the very beginning, which gets repetitive
+ some bugs, most notably not being able to invest in more than your two career-related skills if you use bonus points from owning the first ZE game, which basically defeats the purpose of using them and actually makes gameplay more difficult. Also, using the bonus points seems to lock you in as a male character, which is irritating.
Pros:
+ stellar writing and storytelling
+ a patch for major bugs is coming soon
+ different prologues for different careers adds to replayability
+ your efforts making noticeable differences
+ the disadvantage choices at character creation add to the plot, not just the difficulty level
+ character creation allows for entertaining combinations of characteristics (my favourite playthroughs so far have been a gay bank robber with a heart of gold, and a chain-smoking teenager caring for her newly-orphaned nephew)
Overall, the pros definitely outweighed the cons for me, especially knowing a bug patch is on the way. I think this game is more than worth the money.

(NOTE: STEAM may say that this is review, but keep in mind that this is my first impression. I will edit this with a finalized review and thoughts about this game when I get around to buy the full version and actually play it.)
I downloaded DOOM for the free weekend and started playing it, although my laptop is already old and it did significantly slow said laptop down even with my video and graphics settings being at the lowest possible.
This game has a lot intuitive design thought and applied to it for my first few minutes of gameplay-- The levels are easy to navigate through (although being someone who has problems with sense of direction or focus, I got confused with part of the first few missions), there are tutorials that are simple to follow to newcomers, which by the way, only apply to both "I'm too young to die" and "Hurt me plenty" skill levels, the gameplay has interesting flavor with the introduction of glory kills, and the music (and some ambient sounds) actually responds to both where I am and what I do.
The one downside to this though is that the Free Weekend download of this game is a demo rather than the full game itself, though it is understandable in some cases, this being the fact that this game underwent so much development and I did hear that it went into several difficulties trying to pull through with the final product. As I said before, my laptop is too old to run DOOM on and I'm better off with a desktop computer for when I finish my course studies in the university which is only one year left.
I have not touched multiplayer so far, so I have no words for it as of the writing of this impression. Not many things can be pulled off perfectly, but when I get the chance to, I'll grab this game in the future and give it a full run for me to tell my experiences with it. Whether you're new to the franchise or otherwise-- If you're into kicking some demon guts and a fan of first person shooters, I cannot stress this enough that you should give this game a try.

I'll admit, part of the appeal of Screencheat is feeling justified for past games. Taking the occasional glance at my friends' screens during Goldeneye and it's kind. I wasn't cheating, I was practicing for this!
But Screencheat doesn't rely on peoples' nostalgia. The core gameplay is fun. It takes the basic concept of a local split-screen shooter and expands on it. The mechanic of using other players' screens to determine their location takes getting used to. A good use of colors helps make locations easily identifiable. There's a good selection of levels to choose from, as well as different weapons to help mix gameplay up. Do you want to use the Blunderbuss's range of fire at the cost of slow shooting? Or maybe charge people with a stick horse?
While the game is based on one of the keys from local play, the split screen, online is also an option. Now you can peak at your friends' screens through a series of tubes! And you don't have to listen to them complain when you shoot them through a wall!

There are a lot of things to be said for the game. It offers a huge nostalgia kick for those who remember playing splitscreen shooters, and goes there with a light-hearted approach. It also offers a unique take on the genre. Invisible avatars creates entirely new tactical decisions. Where you are standing matters less than what you are looking at. A precision weapon with a narrow line of effect is a bit weaker when you can't see the target. Delayed weapons become a bit more difficult to aim when you can't trace their movement as easily.
Pros never come without their cons though. As someone who isn't the best at shooters - especially fast paced ones - having to watch numerous 'screens' and then play around with multiple perspectives can be a bit rough. The game also greatly rewards knowing the map, as you can more quickly grasp where another player is in relation to you.
All in all, I definitely enjoy the game when I'm with people I can voice chat with. I've yet to play it in a local setting, but I imagine that would just make the experience even better.

The overall game itself remains what it is. A coherent story and solid stealth and FPS gameplay. Don't fix it if it ain't broke. Although there are still prevaling bugs that were not addressed. While the boss fights are still shoot n' scoot, they improved upon it by giving you more options. No longer are you left doging bullets and grenades from everywhere scrambling to find a weapon and ammo becuase you decked yourself out for hacking, stealth, and/or non-leathal. If you are keen enough to go around the boss rooms, you'll find areas that can help you defeat the boss regardless of how you upgrade yourself or what weapons you have on you.
Gameplay wise, The Missing Link DLC was seamlessly integrated into the flow of the game. Story wise it kind of fit in very loosely.
It is sort of daughting to suddenly not have everything you collected (including praxis upgrades) at your disposal, but it does present a certain challenge. There's even an achievement for getting through the entire DLC portion with only your "armour" and what you collect through out rhe level and use no praxis upgrades. But when you complete the Missing Link, you ultimately get everything you had before you were KO'd and strapped in plus what ever you collected in the level.
The New Game+ option after completeing the game once overall is probably my favorite addition. When playing though the story a second time through the vanilla Human Revolution, I kept wishing in the back of my mind I had more augements and how that would affect how I would approach a certain part of the game. Now I don't have to! New Game+ carries over all the augmentations you aquired through your first playthrough, eventually gaining enough Praxis to max out everything. All in all DXHR Director's Cut is a solid game.

P2Win? No.
All gear currency is earned through playing. gear can be "fortified" up to +20. In many MMO's the higher ranks have a chance of breaking the item if you fail. This game is the exact opposite, if you fail enough the item gets upgraded instead of breaking.
Now that that's out of the way, I wanted to share how the game works.
You quest (same old kill mobs/collect style thats been around forever). There are dungeons, both group and solo content.
PROS:
Cash shop: As mentioned earlier, no cash shop advantages. If you want to argue that being able to buy things like xp boosts and whatnot is pay2win, you have no idea what youre talking about. You can advance your characters faster with cash shop, but they wont provide you with an ADVANTAGE over anybody else. Basically the fortification system is not a pay2win system like it is in so many of these asian MMOs. There are no "real money stat boosts" to speak of either.
Visuals: The game looks great and runs well on my semi-modern 700$ PC (gtx 950, i5 6500, 8gb ram, 850 PRO SSD). The art is very anime style and the effects are well done.
Story: Despite the bland gameplay of the quests, the story and setting are quite interesting IMO.
Classes: Lots of classes.
Loyalty Points: An Alternative currency you acquire by playing the game that can be used in place of cash shop money to use in the cash shop.
_____________
Cons
The chat window: Settings for the chat window do not save on client restart. The default "general" tab is mostly trade chat spam. Sellers and buyers completely dominate the window most new players will see as well as gold spammers. If I wasnt actively fiddlng with the chat window I wouldnt have ever known someone even whispered me or seen guild chat.
Sound design: For the most part all skills sound almost exactly the same. If you pay attention to games such as WoW or Guild Wars 2, youll notice skills have such an iconic sound you can tell whats happening with your eyes closed half the time. In Aura Kingdom the sound design does not contribute to your awareness whatsoever. The music is pretty generic Asian MMO as well.
Questing: Bland and generic quest system thats in a thousand games. Kill these, collect these. Over and over and over and over. A lot of people like my self have no problem tolerating that sort of thing though.
Eidolons (youll learn what they are) and new loot kept popping up over my quest tracker and blocking the button you can click to autopath. Pretty annoying, especially since the Eidolon that pops up cant be closed quickly and you need to wait for it to go away/ Might just be my resolution though.
_____
Pro/con depending on who you ask
Autopathing: Game has autopathing and you will be doing a lot of it.
Character design: Premade faces with no "slider" customization. You can however acquire many costumes, hats and weapon skins and dye your armor. Personally I felt I was able to customize character so its pretty unique.
Grind level: not so bad in the beginning, but getting and upgrading the end game items to max is extremely grindy.
Battlefield: Havnt tried all the pvp types, but the one I tried involved putting players in 2 groups regardless of their level and making them fight. At lvl 53 with full pvp gear, People could blow air at me and id drop dead right then and there. Like honestly, I had 20k hp with -50% crit dmg from players and about -20% total damage from players on top of that due to my pvp gear, someone hit me for over 800k with one ability, when my max hp was just barely over 20k. So yeah. Dueling people around your level is fun though.

So if the devs could slightly change steam versions of this game, would be cool.
Overall: For standalone game It's not that good, considering that you have to wait presumably another year for next part of the story. But I can see that when next parts of the story will come out, It could be the best text game on steam.

If you didn't like the last one, this one is better. It's your choice now whether you have to deal with family members, pets, handicaps, and addictions. Better yet, your family member now consists of a terrified eight year nephew you can leave with strangers, instead of a scantily clad, ghoul-possessed sister. It's nice not to have the cure in your hand, and have to play exorcist.
It almost feels like you're making the decisions. There's so many choices, that I honestly went back, and reselected the traits in a manner to experience it, rather than game it. The joy of a real choose your own adventure, where you actually are the reader in the story is there. You have true diverging starts. Your career choice affects the start of the opening scene. The location affects the story proper.
I almost believed. Except for programming. Hacking  is apparently Swordfish, by the power of 812th episode of the Grassy Knoll on the History Channel, with the literacy of the /b/ boards. Fortunately, the other professions (at least doctor and engineer) were more believable. You may be on a bad episode of ER, but you aren't getting coffee and bragging about your super skillz.
Suspension of disbelief is especially important to survival stories. In many ways, Safe Haven surpasses its predecessor. The apocalypse doesn't reduce the city to zombies in two seconds. People are relatively smart. They don't insist on fortifying churches built out of asbestos and black mold. They don't worship zombies. They survive without your constant nannying and intervention.
Unfortunately, depending on and in spite of your choices, there isn't much to do. Of course, you can research for the cure. You can communicates with your peers - military hardmen, hacker blofeld, your neighbors. You wire camera modules in your house. (Does zombie drool make sudo apt-get install libopencv-dev run faster?) Ultimately everything in this story of any overreaching consequence is without resolution.
In fact, when it really comes down to it, this is a daring tale of YOU (Dr. Neville?), your dog Max, and your nephew Frodo drawing bath tub water (possibly bath tub gin) and boarding up your house till you got to save the noble princess from the elementary school of doom.
To be continu-
Maybe. But the real question is, should you play it? If you like this type of game, yes. Even incomplete, Safe Haven is longer, more immersive and better written than many other instances of the same genre. And in distinct contrast to it's linear predecessor, Safe Haven is an incredible, if inconsistent, exercise into the power of RPG choice.

Zombie Exodus was quite enjoyable, so imagine my excitement when I learned about Zombie Exodus: Safe Haven.
Without mentioning any spoilers, if you played the demo, you know exactly what to expect. Zombie Exodus: Safe Haven ends very close to the ending of the demo.
That being said, it was worth reading the end to that scenario. I must admit the last demo I played was not the last revealed one, so I can't say anything based on those changes, but from what I did play, it was interesting to see the differences in drafts. I was able to prevent different events from happening, and while I'm not sure if this was just due to me playing awfully beforehand, I'm going to write it up as an improvement done by Dattilo.
For those who did not play the demo, Zombie Exodus: Safe Haven is good. It's a Choice of Games/Hosted Games story, meaning this isn't really a, "game." It's a novel where you are able to make choices for the main character. No visuals, no sound. For someone who needs high visual or auditory stimulation to enjoy something, this definitely is not for you.
It's worth mentioning that this game is short compared to its predecessor, Zombie Exodus, but it is worth mentioning that this is only part one of the story.
The story is creative and the different options that range from occupation, living factors, etc. are fun to test out for different results.
I'd highly recommend this, as well as Zombie Exodus, as they are fine editions to the Choice of Games/Hosted Games selection. Dattilo has done a fine job in writing these and I am happy to support his work.

This is a case of learning from past mistakes and implementing fixes that are fun and fair. The improvements in gameplay are spectacular and make this a must own for nearly any gamer, both new and old. Then the beautiful mixture of story and world building. One of the best old school RPG's I've played.
So like I said in my Fallout review this game fixes nearly every gameplay issue I had from the first one. The VATS hit calculations seem far more logical and correct, though it suffers a few times in a playthrough. I did not feel like rage quitting because of it at any point like the original did so many times. Thank you for this improvement.
Criticals, another point from my Fallout review, vastly improved. So now enemies will actually do damage to you throughout the game, and criticals won't drain you in a single shot usually. Once again I found the new system of critcals to be fair and appropriate.
So the story takes a step backward but then takes two more forward. The stepbackward is the depth of the NPC's. That has left, unfortunately, but has been replaced with greater variety. These enhance the world quite a bit, while giving you a little wish that some NPC's were used a little more. It's a better trade off in the end, because not only does it build story within The Chosen One's life but it also creates world depth. So this could go either way depending on your preference.
Add onto all of this more weapons and items. Then a Highwayman to boot. This is a monumental increase in gameplay making this a fun game and a great story.

Also, I did not see an option (possible I missed it) to change gameplay options (ie, give each player more or less trains, set a round limit instead of train limit, etc.) which could have made games more interesting and allowed for variants, although I certainly understand you can't really program an AI to handle all the options.
The games don't take very long to complete (I usually get 15-20 mins / game offline), a perfect amount of time for a board game, although online play obviously runs longer as people are making decisions, but typically they don't go much longer.
If you've played the board game you know what it's about, nothing has changed apart from new map variants. If you've never played ticket to ride I do recommend it if you enjoy other board games.

Okay so a lot of people might have mixed feeings about these japanease dateing sims, but hear me out on this one.
Short intro: The game is about you going to Japan and visiting it's locations with one of the 2 girls: Makoto and Akira. You can choose where you go every day and you can choose some other minior things.
So, to start off. This was my first dateing sim (if you don't count the random ones i played on Newground when i was 10) and i wasn't really expecting much honestly. The artstyle looked decent, but other than that i really didn't think there was gonna be much interaction or anything (since it isn't on a PSP or other handhelds)
And as i assumed i was right! There were not many things you could influence! It was basicaly just a story with some pictures.
So why am recommending this?
Because for some reason it was interesting. The player didn't have much choice, other than where he wants to go visit and what food he wants to eat, but it was really interestign to learn about Japan with this game. Maby it's just because i love Japan already and that's why i could enjoy this so much, but non the less it was really a fun trip to Japan in a way. You could learn a lot about Japanease culture, the citys and ofcourse FOOD! Th game also didn't have any nudity and only had two shots with the girls half-naked. (which is a good thing, or a bad thing, depending on the person ofcourse)
The end would basicaly depend on how many times you went to visit with one of the girls and that girl fell in love with you (much like in anime and manga).
The endings weren't anything spectacular but they did have some inpact on me at the end.
Overall here are my +/- about the game:
++++
~Really good english translations (if it was translated atall. Don't really know this)
~Works as a actual tour guide for someone who wants to know more about japan
~Almoast no perversity (good thing for me, maby not so good for you other perverts out there ;) )
~Has nice relaxing music
------
~Not much choice or inpact on the games ending
~Not much replayability (basicaly it just takes 2 times to get all the pictures and info about towns, and the two endings)
~I might be a cheep♥♥♥♥♥ but 9.00 Euro for this is way too high in my opinion.
Overall verdict:
Buy this game if you want to relax from your daily life, learn a bit about japan, it's history and culture, without wikipedia and with two cute anime girls as your guides.
But i do suggest you get it on a sale since i don't think it's worth 9.00 Euro honestly.

So here's the deal: I'm a stickler for the original Deus Ex, and Human Revolution is simply not as good as the original in many ways.  The story here is passable, but doesn't come close to the original.  Additionally, the "variable" approaches in Human Revolution are, very frequently, just a matter of being able to unlock a door or take a short vent trip instead of always shooting your way in; compared to the original, where there are big secret sections you may not even HEAR about if you aren't attentive, HR falls pretty short.
However, that's all pretty okay, especially in the Director's Cut, which pretty much everybody should get.  Sure, HR isn't as good as the original in many ways, but it's definitely a great game on its own, especially now that the boss fights have been altered to something other than completely idiotic (like the original version of HR) and the DLC missions have been properly inserted into the game rather than being standalone.
Basically, the only reason to not get this, especially on sale, is if you plain just don't like FPS games in any shape or form.  Otherwise, just about anybody should be able to get more than their money's worth here.

Perhaps one of the best games I have ever played, not only for the gameplay, but for the exceptional story. I found myself amazed at all the little details and touches that were put into this game. The ending left me speechless as I watched the credits, mouth agape. 10/10

In short: wow! What a phenomenal game, and it sure did not disapoint my expectations either! Keep in mind, I have have only played the director's cut edition, so I will be basing my review on that version alone.
Let's begin:
Aesthetics 8.25/10
The game looks very good, and the unique orangeish-hue scifi color is obviously present as well. The soundtrack was composed by a person that has receieved great appraisal, Micheal McCann. The music fits a very diverse set of locations, ranging from the iconic chinese jingles in Shanghai to futuristic stealthpumping action music. The game knows it's setting well, and shows it. The voice acting is great, but the lip-sync is kind of awkward and the animations for various npc's are reused over and over again, if you can overlook the usual shrugs by the females, then you'll be dandy.
Controls 9/10
The controls are near perfect for Deus Ex. Besides the usual flip flaps and glitchy control support, the game on keyboard and mouse is perfection.
Story/Characters 9/10
Words cannot describe the masterpiece that is the story, however the characters are somewhat bland, excluding Jensen. The story revolves around an augmented spec that works for a tech-company. As the game progresses, we see the various changes that have effected the world due to human augmentation. The game plays with the minds of the scientific illititerate, so as long as you have some standing knownledge of the original sequel to the game, you might get slightly lost.
Gameplay 8.50/10
The game is around 35-50 hours of gameplay. Not too long and not too short, a perfect margin. The game will try to force you to stick to stealth, however. As it does not condone nor reward you for killing people, you don't want to be a bad apple. The stealth system is so much fun, it's actually better than most stealth games actually! The hacking mini games are unique in the start of the game, but if you max out the hacking skill early on, it get's boring late-game. Lastly, the RPG system is a bit flawed, but  it does reward exploration. If you like to explore, you'll be treated to some augpoints.
Final Verdict 9.30/10
The game deserves the praise it is recieved. Buy the game, it's cheap and if you're into scifi and dystopian-esque societities, this is for you.

I downloaded DOOM for the free weekend and started playing it, although my laptop is already old and it did significantly slow said laptop down even with my video and graphics settings being at the lowest possible.
This game has a lot intuitive design thought and applied to it for my first few minutes of gameplay-- The levels are easy to navigate through (although being someone who has problems with sense of direction or focus, I got confused with part of the first few missions), there are tutorials that are simple to follow to newcomers, which by the way, only apply to both "I'm too young to die" and "Hurt me plenty" skill levels, the gameplay has interesting flavor with the introduction of glory kills, and the music (and some ambient sounds) actually responds to both where I am and what I do.
The one downside to this though is that the Free Weekend download of this game is a demo rather than the full game itself, though it is understandable in some cases, this being the fact that this game underwent so much development and I did hear that it went into several difficulties trying to pull through with the final product. As I said before, my laptop is too old to run DOOM on and I'm better off with a desktop computer for when I finish my course studies in the university which is only one year left.
I have not touched multiplayer so far, so I have no words for it as of the writing of this impression. Not many things can be pulled off perfectly, but when I get the chance to, I'll grab this game in the future and give it a full run for me to tell my experiences with it. Whether you're new to the franchise or otherwise-- If you're into kicking some demon guts and a fan of first person shooters, I cannot stress this enough that you should give this game a try.

The Steam Controller is just more work for about the same outcome of a regular controller but worse than a regular controller. It took me several days just to change all the buttons to correctly work for GTA V and even then it just felt worse overall. It costs 20 dollars more than a logitech controller from walmart which is already ready for non-steam games. the joystick is way too loose, the mousepad doesn't sense movement properly, the d-pad broke after just a few clicks, forcing me to use touch controls on the d-pad as well which usually either doesn't sense that i touched it, or thinks i touched 2 of them at the same time despite how small my thumbs are and how big the d-pad is. When trying to be precise with aiming, aka having your thumb completely still on the touch pad, your reticle will fly everywhere. When trying to move your reticle, however, it decides to barely notice you trying to move it and does next to nothing. The "grip" buttons or whatever they're called are hard to press, which kinda makes sense because of they're placement, but make very loud noises when they are pressed. The bumper buttons are way too big, causing you to have to shift you're entire hand just to get your finger to it, and are even harder to press down compared to the grip buttons. The gyro whatever-its-called is impractical for as obvious as the same reasons why any gyro effect on any controller would be (for games that normally don't use it anyhow).
The only things I do like about it is the right and left trigger buttons which can be set to soft pull to be a button and full pull to be a button (good for guns in games where you can set soft pull to aim and full pull to fire) and the ability to fly a helicopter regularly in gta v, but the latter doesn't matter since any controller can do that.
I give the SC a 4/10.
I'm sure I'd grow to like it and tweak it just right to get it to work correctly, but it's just way too much work for an outcome thats worse than just going to walmart and buying a regular controller for 20 bucks cheaper. It's not worth the effort. If you get this controller you're going to be spending more time getting it to work correctly than actually playing games, at least for a little while.

In some ways, this is a direct improvement over the first. There is more stuff to do, more stuff to unlock, bigger map, etc. The character customization is deeper. That's all fine.
However, what I appreciated about the first game were its simple objectives with various free-form solutions. Fallout 2 seems to strip these away in favor of increasingly complex and awkward quests. Often, they will require speaking with specific characters who are almost indistinguishable from other, less important NPCs, and doing so in a specific procedure. The Gecko Power Plant quest is a good example of how this, combined with a lot of tedious running around, results in a tiresome game of "who's who". Of course, the player usually has a choice in these sorts of situations to take a moral shortcut for negative karma, but the rewards for pursuing a "good" outcome pretty much always outweigh the rewards for "bad" behavior. I prefer to finish quests in as complete a fashion as I can, but their weird, constricted structure here bores and angers me.
Other times, logic is sacrificed for the sake of creating gameplay. I understand that Vault 13, literally a hole in the side of a mountain, could be easily ignored, but if this Pipboy is the same one that belonged to the Vault Dweller, wouldn't it make sense for the locations canonically visited in the previous game to be on it already? At least the military base should be on there, if not the vault, but at least it's not hidden to the point of requiring a quest for exploration; Speaking of bases, what about the Sierra Army Depot? It sounds and looks like it would be big enough to be noticed just by going near it, but nope, it only appears when a certain quest is activated. There's also the Enclave power armor that's good at fooling Enclave soldiers in every situation save for the map's random events, but whatever, I'm sure someone with nothing better to do has come up with an explanation for all this. Bottom line is, the first game did not do this sort of thing. It let the player reap the full benefits of accidental discovery.
A large map is good, but the random events happen WAY too often. I breathe less often than I encounter something on the map screen. Almost every time, the enemies appearing in these events are too hard (instant death), too plentiful (slow, agonizing death), or easily outrun (waste of time). Save scumming becomes a necessity for travelling through particularly brutal areas, such as the region around Navarro, where movement needs to be taken an inch at a time, lest I come across a patrol and get a one-way ticket to the game over screen. Get the car, because that♥♥♥♥♥♥happens a lot less often, although there is still the occasional stop made involuntary for whatever reason.
Overall, the game is representative of living in modern day California; It's buggy (frame drops, some crashing), very disorganized, and constantly frustrating, but it has its moments, and it gets more fun after the first few hours. Bigger? Yes. Better? Maybe. It's still worth playing.

This is really a case where a mixed option would be nice, because while the game isn't bad, it's not excellent either.
What's great about this game is the characters, story, and music. Making a story from minecraft couldn't have been easy, and they exceeded my expectations in this. They also include adaptations from the og mc in this game that are a nice touch. You can tell they really put a lot of work into the story, characters, and details. Music and sound are also done really well, with it being similar to the music used in og mc.
However there are some glaring issues that hold this game back from being great. Tech wise this game is a mess. During gameplay and cutscenes I have experienced random fps drops (I think my 1080ti should be able to handle this game...). I've had too many times where my input wasn't recognized during a quick time event that would screw me over, during almost every dialogue the lines are cut off too soon, lip syncing is off, and characters awkwardly teleport, or move around wrongly taking you out of the experience. It would be ok if this happened every once in a while but every time someone has a conversation?! ( which is 80% of telltale games). Music will also cut off, play the same song too often, or be put in a certain part where it doesn't fit. The graphics can sometimes look good, but it's mostly just ok. Animations for characters is also meh. When a minecraft youtuber can make better animations than an entire dev team, there's something wrong. The characters will also have some cringy, cheesy dialogue to probably to appeal to younger gamers. Also you have to have your gamepad turned on before starting the game (not really an issue but still notable). Can any of you tell me if other new telltale games have this many issues or similar ones? I'm considering getting the Batman Telltale, but not if its as buggy as this.
Despite all of the glaring issues, none of them made me want to stop playing when the story and characters are done this well; it's just a shame they didn't touch up the game a bit after releasing every episode.
Don't ignore this one just because it's based on minecraft. You might be just as surprised as I was.

Even from the preview I saw, I knew I would love this game, and was extremely excited for it (which I haven't been THAT excited for a game in a long time). Bascially, if you want to know some stuff about Japan, and want to be taught about it by some cute girls that you can forge a relationship with, then this is right up your alley!
You play the role of a guy who's trying to learn Japanese, so he decided to go to Japan to be mentored by two brothers he met in an internet chat room. But, lo-&-behold, these two guys were actually sisters! You get to pick 3 of 6 places to take tours around before your time in Japan is up. Now, if you wanted to just learn about Japan, this is awesome enough as it is. BUT. Depending on which places you choose to tour, you develop a relationship with one of the two girls! TOO MUCH AWESOME. Not to mention, the endings are simply adorable. If you're someone like me who enjoys cute and innocent romances like "Ai Yori Aoshi" or "Clannad," I can just about guarantee you'll fall in love with this game! ...And one of the two girls! ;D
The soundtrack is amazing (I would have the game on in the background just to listen to the tunes), the visuals are great, and if you're actually trying to learn Japanese, it's great because in the dialogue, you can view the Japanese right above the English! The info they give you is fantastic, and the romance storylines are really nice!
All in all, I highly recommend this game! I sure had a blast playing it, and now I kind of want to learn Japanese so I can play through it while reading the top text. Not only that, I also have the goal of going to Japan in real-life to get firsthand experience. This game is a great way to get introduced to a new culture, and I surely hope they expand on this game in the future! Maybe a sequel or add-ons...? I hope so!

Full review:
Hey, look! A VN on Steam! Although a rare sight, it's always a welcome one. Especially considering that this is from MangaGamer, their first game on Steam. Props to them for bringing the title to Steam, hope to see more in the future.
Anyways, Go! Go! Nippon! is a semi-educational VN in which two beautiful girls give you a tour of some of Japan's popular sightseeing spots. A lot of the game is about Japanese history, with the other half being the development of a relationship with either of the two girls giving you the tour. I know little about Japanese history (I do, however, know a lot about its culture), making this game quite the enlightening experience. Now if only I could get the rest of my education taught through this format...
Aside from the game's educational aspect, there's also the relationship aspect. It may not be as large of an aspect as I had wanted, but it was enough for me to sit through the game's lecturing. The game opens with the protagonist landing in Japan and meeting up with two friends he had met online. Unknown to him, both friends are girls. Sisters, actually, who you'll be staying with for the duration of your visit. Coincidentally, their parents are gone on some trip and won't be back until your stay is over, one week.
You'll end up building a relationship with one of them, depending on the locations you choose to visit while staying in Japan. That aspect was a bit annoying, as I didn't know which of the two I'd be spending more time with. You're given no info about which girl corresponds to each location. I ended up going down a route I did not particularly want to. Well, that just adds to the replayability of the game, right? I'd say that 99% of VNs are developed with replayability in mind, as is Go! Go! Nippon! Playing through the game multiple times finally netted me the result I had wanted.
The game's art is fantastic. The characters and backdrops are great. There was no voice acting, which was a bit disappointing at first. Even if it was in Japanese (which I was originally expecting), I'd still prefer for it to be added. Instead, all dialogue is shown in both Japanese and English, which was quite cool. I've never seen a VN do that before. The game's music sounded rather generic, like it had been recycled from elsewhere. That said, I'd still like a soundtrack download, even if the tracks are recycled.
Overall, I can highly recommend Go! Go! Nippon! I'd love to see more VNs on Steam, especially some of those already available from MangaGamer (Shuffle! anyone?). Maybe we'll see more MangaGamer titles in the future. I'd personally love to see Shuffle! and its sequels, although I'm certain that Steam wouldn't allow it. :(
Anyways, be sure to check out the game. Give it a few plays for the full experience, one well had!

From the very short amount of time playing the game here's what I must say about it. It's a great concept and has a lot of potential. The combat is slightly clunky, but what else do you expect from an early access F2P game. The characters are pretty cool looking and customization looks like it'll be great later on. It has very poor optimization, even for someone like me who can play most games on their highest setting with no issues, I had to play on the lowest graphic setting just to be sure I wouldn't lag, I didn't attempt a match on Medium due to how Low, when loading in had some lag issues. There is no further graphical settings other than the basic "Low, Medium, High" type of deal. I hope to see that in the future these issues are addressed and that the game is better optimized for at least computers of my standpoint, which is a relatively good one. The community is quite small, I tried to get int a Duel and waited for roughly 4 minutes before giving up to come write this review. I played three matches of 3v3 last man standing, and two of the three only had one player on the opposing team, and only two total in the match(myself and the enemy player), with four filler bots. My last match was just me, my two bot teammates vs three bots. Now some people might not see this as a terrible thing, lets you get used to the game early on without playing against players that have more time into the game than you. If you have a good PC, give it a try and check in every once in awhile(after updates), to see what they've added, or stick around in the community to further increase it's rather small population. If you have a lower end computer, at this point in time, don't even waste your time downloading the game, as you won't even be able to play the tutorial, or look at the menu screen without lagging(I have a friend who checked it out and thats his experience with the game).
In the end, if you have a good computer, check it out and maybe write a review like I have. If you have a low end, check back in the future to see if the game has been optimized and see what people in the review section are saying about the game, if and when the time comes that it's better optimized, I'll be sure to edit this review.

So, call this game a rip-off if you'd like, but this fact alone does not subtract from the fun factor at all- it's actually completely irrelevent.  If you like Growtopia, then you should enjoy a game that's 99% similar to it.  To hate it for being like Growtopia, it is only logical for you to also dislike Growtopia.  I mean, imagine if Growtopia never existed.  Would this game suddenly be stellar to those who hate that it copied so much?
If you're going to dislike PW, dislike it for the game itself.  For example, there are some items like Lava Lamps which have an incredibly low seed drop chance and one quest calls for 100 of them.  Then there are also rare decorative props that, when hit, are permanently deleted.  Now these are reasons to dislike a game- actual problems in it.  Judge a game by the game itself, independent of others before it.
I fully understand why someone may not enjoy this game.  It can be incredibly tedious.  I still find my own way to have my fun though, but if you really are unable to find anything thrilling in the game, and if it's just not for you, that's fine.  I can respect not liking it for that.  But to hate it for being a near copy of a game you DO like, doesn't make an iota of sense to me.  That's hating the act of copying, which is separate from whether the game is fun or not.  I can understand the disturbing feeling of a game so closely copied, but to not recommend it for that alone is misleading and does a disservice to those who might actually enjoy the game, but be turned away by how many unwarranted negative reviews there are.  I'm seeing so many one line "it sux, copy of gt" reviews being upvoted as a "helpful" review while other positive reviews that actually go in depth about why the game is enjoyable to them are being tanked down with downvotes.  C'mon everyone.. let's be better than this.
Anyway, definitely expecting to be hit with dislikes for this, even if I am speaking the truth.  I do think a lot of GT fans should give this game a shot.  If you go into a game wanting to hate it, you'll probably hate it.  Try going in neutral and you might have more fun than you thought you'd ever have!

The Steam Controller is amazingly comfortable to hold, the trackpads are smooth like a baby's bottom, and the amount of customization allows you to easily personalize games to fit your preference on controls. Sure, it may take a few minutes to get the precise settings, but I don't think it's much of an inconvenience to get the perfect configuration (hell, there are some games on the xbox 360 controller or the keyboard and mouse where the developer controls were weird and I've had to spend the time rebinding key after key. It's all about whether you want to take the time to get used to developer controls or take the time to make your own). I've found that I am always turning off trackball mode. It seems every developer controls want to make use of that, but it doesn't really work for most games IMO. I suppose if you got used to it that would be a different thing, but a lot of times it just feels like the controls are trying to be too intelligent. I just turn on low acceleration and make the trackpad work like that of a trackpad on a laptop. The buttons on the back of the handles are a godsend. It's awkward in, for example, FPS games to be navigating with the trackpad while running with the joystick and have to jump and needing to take your thumb off the trackpad and find the "A" button. This is where the buttons on the back save your life so much. There was a lot of thought into the design of this controller, and it really pays off. I love it, and taking screenshots with it is easier than trying to reach "f12" on your keyboard when a split-second picture worthy moment passes. (to screenshot with the controller you hold the middle "steam" button and then hit right trigger). In my experience so far, I've tried it out on a select few games and have found that Borderlands 2 on the steam controller is amazing with little configuration tweaks (i just turned off trackball mode and tweaked the haptics and sensitivity). In fact, call me weird if you want, but I like Borderlands 2 better on the Steam controller than keyboard and mouse. I don't know why, it just feels so right. Left 4 Dead 2 took a lot of tweaking, but with the right configuration, it's really nice of the steam controller as well. Killing Floor 2 also took quite a bit of tweaking on the trackpad settings but I've got it so it's really fun on the steam controller. Synergy (Half-Life 2) is a lot like Left 4 Dead 2 on the Steam controller, and it's fine. The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth is literally the same as on an xbox 360 controller, except you need to use the A B X Y buttons to shoot instead of the right joystick. Batman: Arkham Asylum has this weird camera configuration where the camera pans in the direction based on where your thumb is on the trackpad and I can't seem to get to change to a regular trackpad configuration in a way that's functional enough. For the most part, the Steam Controller works well with Arkham Asylum, but if you need to make a quick escape, I can't get it to turn the camera around effiecient enough. So I'll stick to 360 controller or keyboard on that game. Tony Hawk's Pro Skater HD is unplayable. Not just because that's how the game was made in general (lol) but also on the Steam Controller, it's not very functional because directional buttons are pretty much necessary. But who cares about that game anyway. And the last game I've tried with the Steam Controller (unless I'm missing some) is Resident Evil 4, which is very awkard because of the way you steer Leon Kennedy. I can't even remember how I was able to play that on the playstation 2 with that controller. That's definitely a game that's best for keyboard IMO. That was my first impressions of this controller. I use it daily, and I've started to use it every time I'm playing a game it works decent with. It does take a little bit to get used to, but if you're a PC gamer exclusively, it pretty much takes the same amount of time to get used to ANY controller. It's just one of those things, you know? I recommend this controller a lot. I LOVE it!

I will try to keep this recommendation short, but whatever I put here know there is still much more awesome to this game.
The game is huge and can take anywhere from 15 hours if you rush through it, to 30 hours if you take the time to read all the lore and details that is everywhere in the game. Said lore is expansive and actually very interesting to read. So is all the dialog, with very well done voice acting especially by the protagonist. The sounds are great too, including the weapons.
The game is first person and seamlessly moves to third person whenever you hug a wall or climb a ladder. You can use a variety of weapons from pistols to shotguns, rifles and crossbows, even rocket launchers. There are non-lethal weapons too like tazers and a tranq rifle. You have an inventory you have to manage which holds your weapons, ammo, and everything else you might want. There are plenty of lootable objects, including your enemies.
The game works like this: you are given a goal and are free to get to it how you wish. And I mean really free. Not like some other games which try to make you believe their attempt at stealth actually counts, because in the end you just kill the guys anyway. No, here you actually do have a choice. It is quite possible to avoid contact with any enemy in the game (except bosses), and doing so actually earns you more rewards than if you killed everybody. And if you're real good you can silently take everyone out and earn the ghost rewards. You do this by utilizing alternate routes, many of which can only be accessed if you take non-combat perks. You can also talk your way through certain areas, or hack certain things so you can slip by. This is far from a linear game.
Perks you can get include higher jumping, more strength (to pick up that vending machine revealing the vent behind it, or use it to access a high ledge, or even as a shield from gunfire or to throw at your enemies for lots of damage), poison resistant lungs (to move through contaminated areas), hacking, stealth perks, and more. And of course there are perks to aid in combat like less recoil, damage resistance, ability to see through walls and mark targets too.
Yes there most definitely is replayability. You are given choices throughout the game which does have a minor impact on what happens along that avenue, including what some people will say to you. If you choose to go in guns blazing your first time, you should probably try it a second time as a stealth person; you will learn things about the game you never would otherwise. There is also a new game plus so you can keep your perks from last game and eventually have everything unlocked during your second, if you so wish. Some people don't like achievements, but if this game didn't have one for beating it without killing anyone and another for never setting off an alarm, I most likely never would have bothered and therefore would have missed out on some fun and challenge.
Closing remark I would like to say that this game is a very worthy successor to the original masterpiece of Deus Ex. If you enjoyed that classic then you are all but guaranteed to enjoy this too.
If you want a very in depth game filled with many hours of memorable gameplay, then do yourself a favor and buy this. At 20 bucks it's a great deal, on sale you have no excuse to pass it up. Buy now!

Go! Go! Nippon is a visual novel game that has a lot going for it, but there are some things buyers might need to know before you buy it.
One- The price
At this current time the game is selling for 3.49 on steam, which is not bad for a visual novel game which takes around three to four hours to complete. However any  higher than this and I would suggest you wait for it to go on sale again.
Two- The story
The story of the game is a love story hidden within facts about Japan. It's not a bad story and if really do read all the text you do start to feel what the main character is going through. However don't expect to reply this game over and over. The story has two girls and two endings where you fall in love with one of them. That's it. Nothing more. A third play through might be in order if you would like to go to every location you can. But after that you might not play again.
Three-  Scene error
All visual novels have them, but here it's a little weird. At the very beginning of the story you land at the airport and are you can see your inside the airport lobby but then your main character says, "That land mass below us  must be Japan!" A little weird. But after this most scenes are ok and you accept them for what they are. (At the price of £3.49 that is. Otherwise you can find better looking images on web created visual novels)
Four- Enjoyment
Go Go Nippon certainly is  an experience and  an education if you don't know a thing about japan.(Like me) Sure it's got the scenes where you walk in on the girls changing. But I guess if you're not really interested in learning about japan then you've got to get your enjoyment somewhere right? But don't be fooled by thinking love gets in the way of your learning. It doesn't. In fact you do learn a lot before the love story part begins.
So to end this review I would recommend Go! Go! Nippon! to anyone wanting to have a bit of fun while learning facts about japan. However if your just going to race through it to find the love scenes then perhaps it's not for you. The joy of this game i found is taking your time and ignoring the skip button. Because if you do, you'll feel and understand the special moments between the main character and the two girls. And that's not just from a love view-point, but from a friends on a trip view-point too.
All in all, give it a try if your visual novel fan. It's not something you see everyday here on steam. Plus I think games like this focusing on other countries are entertaining and help give the player some history about the country.  I hope overdrive make more games like this about other countries as it's fun and interesting. But I also hope they think again about their pricing. Seven pounds for a game like this is a little steep. When there are visual novels out there that are free and give their player a little more to do.

Mystery of Neuschwanstein is a classic Hidden Object Scenes game, with casual puzzles and mini-games.
The plot isn't very exciting, nor sophisticated, as most games of the genre. At least it's not full of monsters, beasts or other unrealistic creatures and fantastic events. And it refers to real historical figures (mainly Ludwig II of Bavaria who commissioned the construction of the splendid Neuschwanstein castle) and some true facts about them, which is a good informative and educational attempt.
Even though most unlikely, the events of the story remain credible. The storyline and the characters are pleasant enough to peacefully travel from mini-games to HOS and kill several hours of time till the end of the game.
Some HOS may require you to use some of your inventory items, which adds something to a classic HOS.
Achievements unlock easily and can be obtained with a unique playthrough.
The voice acting (English version) is fine by me. All the documents you're supposed to read can be listened to by clicking on them, which is nice if you're playing after a hard day's work or if you're lazy when it comes to reading.
I regretted the lack of music. Well, there was some but it was either very slow, somewhat sad and almost unnoticeable or either too loud (action cutscenes).
You can skip all cutscenes and dialogues. Important facts are still available in your phone and no achievement depends on watching them.
I wouldn't recommend it at full price because as most games of the genre it has a low replayability value and this one is quite short to finish (don't take my shown hours of playing time into consideration : I've let the game running on the start menu for hours while i was at something else and it took me 3 playthrough to write some guides since I had forgotten to take screenshots etc..).
On sale it's a good acquisition.

A game that executes on its core idea very well.  It's a very good party game, as my brother and I found out, although it wasn't quite as frantic because it was just the two of us.  If we had another 2 players for the full 4 I think it would have been even better.  The maps seem to be sized for 4 players as well, though that can be remedied with a couple of settings, or playing King of the Hill, forcing both players into a small space.
Speaking of gamemodes and settings, there are plenty of them.  There is standard deathmatch, one shot (every player has one shot, and cannot reload until everyone else has shot), coin battle, capture the fun (a flag with a visible trail left in the map), juggernaut (only one player can get points, and whoever kills them is the new juggernaut), and more.  Nearly every mechanic in the game can be tweaked; from weapon selection to point scoring to campers becoming visible to adding mutators like low gravity and flappy jump.  All settings can be saved with a custom name, which is a nice touch.
I am not the person to comment on the quality of the gunplay; I don't play many shooters.  I find that if it is lacking, it's made up for with the weapon variety.  It's not like you are going to get AAA-shooter-franchise level gunplay from such a company.
There are no gamebreaking bugs, but there is an issue I found with naming settings.  If I pressed the "r" key (which was bound to "use" in-game, it would save the incomplete name and return me to the previous screen.  The devs have been pushing updates fairly constantly, so that issue may not exist by the next build.
There is a lot of ridiculous things in the game, including references to other games and even MLG montage parodies, but I'll let you find that on your own.  Because if you have IRL friends, you are going to buy this game now.  So that you can play with them and so that they will no longer be your friends.

Open world action adventure about gang wars in the city of Stillwater. Third person shooter with fun activities and good music.
PROS:
- City design is really cool with variety of districts like University, Marina, Chinatown. Each is distinct.
- Nice feel of daytime/nighttime - colors, lights, visuals.
- Lots of fun activities including hitman contracts, street racing, stealing cars, insurance fraud and total mayhem.
- Graphics is kinda oldish today, but I liked it anyway.
- The main story plotline isn't bad.
- Music is awesome: multiple radio stations with good songs.
- Radio commercials are HILARIOUS. I loved these.
- Multitude of vehicles with awesome engine sounds.
- Certain comedy elements in plot (Troy vs. Shaundi) are quite funny.
- Distinct evil bosses and gang.
MEH:
- Flying vehicles are kind of difficult to operate.
- Some choices by characters in the story seemed stupid, but I understand that to have a lot of fun shooting and destruction, there have to be poor choices ;-)
CONS:
- Bugs and glitches. Even with "Gentlemen of the Row" mod pack installed (recommended) there are many glitches with parts of map disappearing, characters falling below ground and vehicles crashing into invisible walls.
- Crashes. The game crashes on a quite regular basis. The worst part: in some missions checkpoints were set somewhat apart and after a difficult part, there was a glitchy point before checkpoint. The game crashed at the worst moment. Had to try it a few times.
So... If you are prepared for a glitchy and somewhat aged game, but with nice visuals, engaging story and good music, give it a try! For me it was 33 hours of fun.

I have recently purchased a steam controller for myself and depite the learning curve have enjoyed the product emensely.  The only complaint I have about this product is that while for some games it is plug and play for others there is a lot of trial and error when it comes to setting up the controls. however, with the ability for users to share their own controller set up helps to mitigate this problem. Over all I really do enjoy my steam controller.

If you're willing to put in the time to master this controller and set up configurations for the games you play, then it might be the best controller ever made outside of a mouse and keyboard. This is not a pick up and play device. You need to play around with what works and what doesn't work for you personally. After about 20 hours with this controller in CS:GO, I have a configuration that is absolutely perfect for me and I can play competively while lounging on my couch. Most community configurations are pretty solid so you just have to experiment.
I use a combination of the built in gyro and touch pad in most games to simulate the precision of a mouse and keyboard. Some games like Cities Skylines have pre-made developer configurations that work really well. I love this thing although I'll admit the learning curve is steep.
In conclusion, you'll get out of the Steam Controller what you put into it. If you're willing to figure out what works best for you then it works as advertised. I love the fact that I can play games like CS:GO, Dota 2 and other keyboard mouse intensive games while laying in my recliner in my living room and keep up with players using a mouse for precise movement. It's the ultimate tool for the lazy PC gamer, but only after you set it up for the games you play.
Pros:
-TouchPad gyro combo works super well, feels great
-Super long battery life
-Tons and tons of customization options for any genre
Cons:
-Takes time to wrap your head around it
-Can only be configured in Big Picture mode
-Some games take a long time to figure out a comfortable configuration

(NOTE: STEAM may say that this is review, but keep in mind that this is my first impression. I will edit this with a finalized review and thoughts about this game when I get around to buy the full version and actually play it.)
I downloaded DOOM for the free weekend and started playing it, although my laptop is already old and it did significantly slow said laptop down even with my video and graphics settings being at the lowest possible.
This game has a lot intuitive design thought and applied to it for my first few minutes of gameplay-- The levels are easy to navigate through (although being someone who has problems with sense of direction or focus, I got confused with part of the first few missions), there are tutorials that are simple to follow to newcomers, which by the way, only apply to both "I'm too young to die" and "Hurt me plenty" skill levels, the gameplay has interesting flavor with the introduction of glory kills, and the music (and some ambient sounds) actually responds to both where I am and what I do.
The one downside to this though is that the Free Weekend download of this game is a demo rather than the full game itself, though it is understandable in some cases, this being the fact that this game underwent so much development and I did hear that it went into several difficulties trying to pull through with the final product. As I said before, my laptop is too old to run DOOM on and I'm better off with a desktop computer for when I finish my course studies in the university which is only one year left.
I have not touched multiplayer so far, so I have no words for it as of the writing of this impression. Not many things can be pulled off perfectly, but when I get the chance to, I'll grab this game in the future and give it a full run for me to tell my experiences with it. Whether you're new to the franchise or otherwise-- If you're into kicking some demon guts and a fan of first person shooters, I cannot stress this enough that you should give this game a try.
