A great adaptation of a fun board game to computer, and which comes with the added benefit of being decent fun when you don't have anyone to play it with.
Most of the pluses of course come from the well designed nature of the underlying board game it is based off. Essentially each turn you get to do one of a few different actions - draw a couple of carriage cards which come in various different colours (or an engine that effectively works as a joker) - either face up ones (so both you and your opponents know what you are getting) or from the face down pile. If you have enough carrriages in a single colour you can use them to build a section of track, or you can pull out three extra route cards (each having two cities you have to connect up, and how many extra points it is worth if you do so - also the penalty if you don't connect them by the end of the game) each of which you can keep or not.
From this relatively simple seeming set of options, the strategic options get very deep and complicated if you want to take the time to study what is going on, or the game can just be played as a fun family game, it works either way. Should you try to get more route cards early so you know everywhere you need to connect up from the start, or should you wait until the ones you start with are completed routes and then see if you can get some quick and easy expansions near the end of the game? Should you play your carriages early to avoid being blocked on that section of track, or risk waiting to avoid giving clues to where you are planning to move next? Should you block that opponents obvious route attempt knowing that might decide to retaliate and make one of your route cards difficult or impossible to complete? Should you pick up a couple of same colour face up cards that you don't really at the need all that much to make it look like you are planning to go down a different route than you really need to head?

This version is much better than the board game version - the computer does a better job of keeping tabs on everything (drawing cards, scoring, keeping trains on the board, etc.).  That really helps keep down the amount fighting the family usually gets into when we play the board game.
Can't take much more of the background music though...

OB64 (the december 2017 update) is bringing heavy p2w lootbox mechanics. Basically, before this patch players would grind to get more diversity/adaptability in gameplay while remaining equally powerful against any other player no matter what money or time they had sink into the game. This was the main feature that made Paladins unique and fair and also stand out from its competitors. But now, with the new "cards unbound" system, players grind for pure power (or levels) just like in any other mmo or pay to win mobile game. Someone who has played longer or paid more has clearly full advantage against someone who hasn't. (inb4: casual mode also affects competitive as you need it when dealing with new heroes or patches or just plain training).
But this is nothing new. They're basically killing the game in order to focus on their next big project: Tribes Royale (a PUBG knockoff). It's not the first time this company (Hi-Rez, and more specifically its CEO, Erez Goren - a shady guy according to many reviews on glassdoor) has done this. Global Agenda and Tribes: Ascend got the same treatment before Paladins.
Play Hi-Rez games, they are good. But dont ever give them money. I have around 250 hours of Paladins playtime and dont regret a single second of it. I also don't regret the fact that I never spent a single dime on crystals or any other microtransaction. Now that OB64 is confirmed, I feel good for doing so.
If you remove the management team, the developers and the artists of this company are awesome and doing an excellent job, it is very important to point that out and show them our support as they are the ones who made this game so great.
For the rest, if you want some constructive criticism on how to tweak OB64 (altough I'd rather cancel the update), here's a link providing some very solid points.
But I think it's too late now, I'm out of this game.
If you want to play a good alternative to Paladins and are put off by Overwatch's pricetag and/or toxic community, check out Gigantic by Motiga, a great "hero shooter" with MOBA elements and beautiful graphics. Definitelly deserves more attention than it got.
Battleborn is still out there too and might get a second chance now that Hi-Rez is commiting suicide.
And finally the one I'll be definitelly moving on to is Battlerite by Stunlock Studios, not really FPS but still a hero based battle arena, sort of middle point between DOTA and Overwatch. Great fun, short matches and nice community and only weights something like 1.7 Gb on your hard drive, highly recommended.
And the best part is that these three games are completelly free so there's no excuse for you not to try them ;)

Please read this whole paragraph before to think something wrong:
I give this game a thumb down for a PERSONAL taste because i enjoy more to play Overwatch, i won't deny it but despite that i still wanted to give this game a shot after hearing it does some stuff "better" than it's Blizzard counterpart, and while i think this is not really a ripoff is undenyable that HiRez most definitely took some heavy inspiration from it.
First i gotta admit there are some things this game does better than Overwatch.
For example i like a lot the fact that there are no real healers. Most of the healing abilities are put on characters that are not marked as "canonic healers", and if you don't take damage for a certain amount of time you regenerate health by yourself. THAT is amazing because it's like the game says "you don't wanna play medik ? ok, you don't have to". I wish more team games would do that instead of forcbly trying to shove certain roles into the team composition.
And another thing i like is the level of customization of the characters, both with skins pieces and "cards" you can craft in the game to change stats and abilities.
Sayd this, maybe it's because i played Overwatch first, but i feel this game kinda "disappointing" on an actual gameplay and mechanical level.
I don't know how to explain it because you might have to try both games to understand it but let me try with a couple of examples:
- while Drogoz seems to be mechanically almost identical to Pharah from Overwatch, it's "flight" doesen't feel as satisfying because it doesen't have the same potential. With pharah you can reach higher spots just by holding down the hover button, Drogoz seems to can't do that without using the boosters. With pharah you can stay up in the air for a potentially unlimited amount of time, but with Drogoz you are forced to land at somepoint no matter how hard you try to carefully manage your jetpack "fuel".
- Fernando is almost identical to Rheinhardt from Overwatch, except he doesen't feel as "mighty" nor doesen't give the same feeling of "strenght". Rheinhardt has a hudge rocket hammer to smash on people's faces, Fernando has... a flametrower... sorry for the joke but does he think to be Pyro from TF2 ? Isn't he a knight ? So what's the flametrower about ? Other than that, when Rheinhardt charges he can go on until he either slams on a wall (and squashes anybody he happens to pin in his way) or falls off a cliff, Fernando boosts for a few meters and stops.
Besides the mechanical feeling, HiRez also seems to have a fetish for "limited edition" skins, which seems to be getting potentially worse with this game compared to the previous ones, and while some people might come and say "aw com'on, it's just cosmetics" i'm still gonna say that if i'm going to potentially miss a hudge chunk of content of any kind at least for the characters i like, i'm just not even gonna bother.
Sure, Overwatch also has the "blizzcon" skins but so far it's 2 in two years, This game has already exceeded that and is still in beta, and it's not a good sign on the matter for me.
Bottom line: Paladins is not a bad game, but not even a really good one. While it does take some really heavy inspiration from Overwatch is not really a ripoff, and there are SOME things it does better than Overwatch too. However Overwatch still has a better mechanical and gameplay feeling to it, and while Paladins has a lot more customizations, most of those are gated behind the HiRez fetish for "limited edition" tags, while Overwatch has a strict limit to those items and event ones can be obtained every year.
Get this game IF you cannot or do not want to play Overwatch. Otherwise you may just better off spending 45$ for the "other" game.

This is a very hasty recommendation.
Doom or 'New Doom' as I'll call it, is an excellent shooter- one of the best on the market today as of Q2 2017.
It looks gorgeous and the gun audio is on point, everything looks and sounds even better than you'd expect.
Doom gets nothing wrong when it comes to shooting demons with every different kind of upgradeable weapon
you can think of- plus the glory kills are rad.
Saying that, going into this game I expected the glory kill system to get old quite quickly, yet it was the game itself which
did that for me. Glory kills switch up most of the time so you don't see the same repetitive animation too much, the developers understood this and made it a great compromise. Why didn't they understand that about the game itself?
DOOM is an excellent and mechanically brilliant FPS in a Groundhog Day style loop. Every mission is fairly similar
-cutscene
-shoot minions
-destroy gross demon thing which spawns boss demons
-destroy all demons
-progress
The only break in this rule tends to be when the game gives you a new weapon or sends you on an obligatory platforming mission which well and truly breaks whatever pace the game had left.
Overall, this is a great callback to the original DOOM- repetitive slaughter of demon after demon for self mastibatory satisfaction of the player.
John Romero, creator of DOOM once famously said that people did not buy video games for story or substance, simply for the experience of the game itself- something I profoundly disagree with, but if we adhere to his maxim 'New Doom' entirely fails in being a worthwhile experience. If you want to scratch that ID Software itch, maybe return to Wolfenstein the New Order or wait for Quake later down the line. However, if you're only interested in repetitvely shooting demons- this is the game for you.

The original changed my life back in 94. It got me into modding which eventually led me to software engineering. It's difficult for me to be objective about DOOM but I'll try.
This 2016 remake is a worthy successor in the series. It takes the strengths of the original (spooky atmosphere, rooms full of demons, power fantasy) and wraps them in a beautiful engine with modern gameplay traits. These modern traits, like a progression system, FPS movement changes, never feel tacked on mind you. Instead they add extra depth we've come to expect nowadays.
The campaign is not overly long but the skill challenges and (with a later patch) the arcade mode give you plenty to do. The story is pulpy as you'd want in a DOOM game. The characters take themselves seriously but the protagonist goes through it as we, as players, should: fast and unconcerned.
A true come back from id Software, focusing on gameplay while not losing sight of a beautiful presentation.

Capcom landed themselves a slam dunk hit with the original Dead Rising on Xbox 360. At the time, the next generation of gaming had no real open world style games. Not only that, but an original zombies franchise hadn't been created in quite some time. The year before saw the release of Resident Evil 4, but that was a sequel in a well established franchise.
Taking cues from nearly every game in their past, Dead Rising paved the way for a new style of sandbox that focused on story, mission direction and nearly endless interaction. A lot of people still consider that game the pinnacle of the series, even with a successful sequel and spin-offs.
Dead Rising 3, at surface level, is entirely different from it's predecessors. Darker, more violent and seemingly devoid of color, one could be forgiven for assuming that Capcom decided to take Dead Rising into far darker territory than it's light-hearted and goofy roots.
While a lot of the zany attitude still permeates the experience, Dead Rising 3 is a bit more bleak in tone. The change in tone is matched with the story, which makes the tale a bit more personal and a lot more open-ended. You are seemingly dropped into a GTA style world and given free reign over how to explore, all without loadtimes to break up the areas.
It allows for a city literally filled with tens of thousands of zombies. At any one moment, a player can be faced with upwards of 1,000 zombies running towards them. It can be unnerving at times to see such a menace prancing towards you. It's also quite frightening how unstable the framerate can be.
For all of the positives that this experience might bring. Capcom pretty much phoned in the PC port. It definitely looks sharper than it's Xbox One cousin, but it seems to have inherited all of the performance hiccups that plagued the original release. Cutscenes are practically slideshows at points and turning too fast will often bring the framerate to a crawl.
It's very distracting and unfortunate for a game that is, honestly, very good. I don't know if I prefer this over Dead Rising 2, but the extra weapons, combo weapons and inclusion of combo vehicles make for a game that holds delight around every corner.
It's refreshingly chaotic in how much destruction one can reap on the undead. You never feel outnumbered, despite always going up against a threat with odds in their favor. Co-op makes the game a lot more enjoyable by giving players the ability to heal when downed, preventing frustrating deaths due to sometimes clunky controls.
For as much has changed with Dead Rising 3, your character still performs weird pauses during some actions. Jumping prevents you from shooting immediately, getting knocked down leaves you open for a lot of damage (or to get knocked down again), weapons and vehicles break quickly; sometimes the past just creeps into the present.
Psychopaths return, but their difficulty is dramatically decreased. Since you can now quick fire with an auto lock-on, all of the boss fights amount to running and gunning with wreckless abandon. Since the bosses are pretty much resistant to all form of combo weapons, they end up being mindless.
As far as plotline goes, the game isn't anything special, but still reveals some nice tidbits and developments for fans of the series. There are a lot of throwbacks to the previous entries (Dead Rising 2, especially) and even some characters return. Nick is a decent hero, but he's the weakest in terms of development of the main character (Frank and Chuck).
Nick is pretty much a pretty boy with a heart of gold. Aside from that, he doesn't emote much. He has the hots for a girl, helps everyone and gets scared a lot. It's nice to see a protagonist who isn't gungho or overly confident, but Nick doesn't ooze any kind of charisma. He's just afraid of everything.
Summing this up, I would recommend Dead Rising 3 to a bunch of people. It's fun, creative and a little bit silly. It's also riddled with issues in this port that a patch should have corrected at this point. Even with some flaws, the game is well worth your time. Just make sure to ignore the included DLC packs. Those are terrible.

While many good horror/scifi games use this sort of setting (Black Snow, Penumbra, The Thing), Antarctica doesn’t need monsters or a horror tone to be interesting and dangerous.
In Near Death, the elements are your only adversary, and they are formidable enough. The cold will kill you in a minute or two. It’s conveyed with flair and immersive atmosphere. See if you can play this game without shivering at the sound of the wind howling through broken windows while you scavenge for meagre resources or huddle beside an oil heater for warmth. Or try to walk a short distance between two stations in the middle of a blizzard, the gale-force winds blowing you off-course. It’s a great game to play in winter, or in summer if you want to forget about the heat.
With streamlined survival and scavenging mechanics, the game slowly raises the challenge, although it never gets terribly complex. You’ll need to set up light beacons and rope guides to get between some of the more distant buildings, and you’ll need to prioritise resources to enable you greatest mobility through the base. It’s simple and absorbing.
The story is basic but compelling, offering likeable characters who try to cope with challenges in a practical way. The writing builds a plausible world and situation without encumbering it with melodrama or complicated backstory. There is enough inherent drama in the basic scenario, and it was better that the game kept it simple.
It’s neither very difficult (on normal) nor very lengthy, but it’s probably the right length to not outstay its welcome. I enjoyed the 3-6 hours I spent shivering through it.

I love Near Death because it offers something different. It's a man vs. nature conflict. Weather is the only enemy, and it's a deadly one. Your plane crashes in the late Antarctic winter near an abandoned base on the continent. You have to get yourself to McMurdo Station where there is help, but it's a long way from where you are.
You run around the abandoned base, which has many different buildings on a large campus, looking for supplies that will help you. Meanwhile you try not to get lost in a nasty blizzard that gets worse with time. You're trying to avoid freezing to death so time outside or in unheated buildings is very limited. Oh, and it's pitch black outside, except for the snow. Your map is helpful, but you need to use your compass because the map, by design, does not give your "live" location. The wind builds and your trek between buildings slows to a crawl, you realize you were off on your map reading just a bit and are now lost (this rock wall isn't supposed to be here!!), you're shivering, the screen is getting blurry -- death is imminent. Good times!
You do low level crafting, making items that help combat the elements, but you rarely feel safe. I died several times on the normal difficulty. There are two levels of difficulty above that, for those who want more than a tourist experience. Ha!  Very enjoyable. The only thing I didn't like was that it ended. That said, the game doesn't overstay it's welcome. Highly recommended.

Ah, Minecraft, the LEGO kit of the 21st century, and with it comes a little something called branding. Skins, mods, toys, posters, everyone wants a piece of the blocky building game. And that includes none other than TellTale Games, the company famous for making choice based games. Most of these games come with an innate sense of humor, and are good at mixing that with the heavy feelings that some of the choices can inspire.
Truly I feel that TellTale Games are instead 'diamond games', where one can alter which facet you travel upon, but you will always end up at the same angles. There's nothing wrong with this, and I actually find it fascinating how many different ways the same scenes can play out depending on who you befriend, and who you choose to save. It's just a simple note before I move on to the 'review' itself.
In Minecraft Story Mode you play as Jesse, a person who's looks and gender you decide upon when you start up the game, They're best friends with Axl, a tough as nails simple fellow with a few tendencies called 'griefing' in the Minecraft community; Olivia, an engineering genius with the material known as Redstone, and Rueben, simply a pig with a birthmark that is ironically one of the most expressive characters, and who can interact with anyone as if he's speaking English/Whatever language you've set the dub too.
Currently it is 8 episodes long (With about 6 'Chapters' within each Episode), with 1 (The Order of the Stone) through 4 (Between A Block and a Hard Place) focusing on gathering an ancient order of heroes as well as new friends and allies to save the world from a threat that could very well consume it if it isn't destroyed, while 5 (Order Up!) through 8 (A Journey's End?) focus on Jesse and three of their teammates from the first Episodes trying to find their way back to their home realm after going through a mysterious portal.
The graphics are about what to be expected when everything is built cubic and blocky like Minecraft, and while at times they can be kind of clunky, they certainly have impressive moments of size, scope, and smoothness, like the opening of Episode 3 (The Last Place You'll Look), where Jesse and their friends fight their way through a massive monster infested area.
The gameplay, as is normal with TellTale Games, involves use of choice bubbles when it comes to conversations, with one option almost always being silence. QTEs, or Quick Time Events, is what makes up the majority of the combat within the game, though Minecraft Story Mode also offers a 'fencing' type of combat that comes up occasionally, where Jesse must step forward and back in order to get close enough to strike or evade an enemy's blows themselves.
The plot is surprisingly well structured considering how it seems at first to be a simple cash in, and flows rather well in my opinion, keeping the player interested in the consequences of each decision in the hopes that any one choice could impact the rest of what happens. Some things could change, others couldn't, but it maintains replay value by offering different locales and sometimes entire scenes based on different choices, such as the choice at the end of Episode 1 which completely alters the locale Jesse and a friend (The specific friend is decided by this choice as well, Rueben tags along nevertheless) travel to and explore come the start of Episode 2 (Some Assembly Required).
The characters are where I think the game shines however. In Minecraft nothing at all has a set personality, other than behaviors that are specific to the MOB race as a whole. Despite this, Minecraft Story Mode has a huge cast of interesting characters, and that isn't even including Jesse, who can act anywhere from the strong silent type to a Paragon of the world to an opportunistic cutthroat. Every character has a specific personality that is their own, and the ways they interact with Jesse and the choices they make (*Insert name here* Will remember that...) can change almost drastically based on how you treat them and their ideas. However, thanks to 'The Diamond Story' there is only so much that can be done, but sometimes actions will have reactions that reach into the distant future and can make or break a plan.
Final Decision: Buy It!
Minecraft Story Mode has its flaws, as all games do. The writing can be stiff, the character models even stiffer, and some things can be wonky simply because they used Minecraft's style rather than a normal animation technique like cel-shading (A technique used in many of the other TellTale Games), but it has a lot of heart, plenty of laughs, choices that will make you think, characters you can sympathize with, and the promise of more to come in the future thanks to the game not yet 'ending' with a summary of who you chose to make Jesse be throughout it. When Episode 9 and possibly more come out, you can be sure that I'll be jumping right back into the Portal of Adventure that is: Minecraft Story Mode: A TellTale Game!

, stylized as AdVenture Capitali$t!, and abbreviated as AdCap is an incremental video game developed by Hyper Hippo Productions and published by Kongregate for Windows and on March 30, 2015, for iOS, Android, OS X, Linux and Adobe Flash, and on August 16, 2016 in North America for PlayStation 4. Adventure Capitalist allows players to live like a capitalist, and invest funds into certain products to generate revenue, by starting out with a single lemonade stand. The more revenue generated, the higher the player's cash is. A player can receive an angel bonus when resetting their progress, which provides a boost in all products' revenue for the next progress timeline. A spin-off, AdVenture Communist, was released on Steam on May 2016. It is also made by Hyper Hippo, and is currently in open beta.
There are three areas: Earth, Moon, and Mars. The player starts out on Earth. You start with a single investment: a lemonade stand. Tapping it gives you money overtime. When you earn enough money, you can buy another stand, or a different investment at the cost of more time until the payout. Once the player has purchased the manager for said investment, it will run automatically, which means you can successfully idle, even offline. Upgrades can be spent to add multipliers to any investment.
When the player reaches 1 trillion dollars on Earth, they can start investing in an area. Once invested, said area will unlock in 200 hours, but can be sped up using video advertisements, angel investors/mega bucks, or gold. Gold can be bought via in-app purchase with real money, and can be used for things such as a non-reset way to gain angel investors, instantly earn money for a day's worth of idling, and more. Mega Bucks are bought starting at 1 decillion of an area's currency, and will be multiplied every time by a fixed increment (the game describes this as 'inflation'). When one player has at least 10 Mega Bucks, they can purchase a golden ticket, which when used on a single investment boosts its profits permanently by ×7.77. After one has boosted a whole planet, they will gain an additional ×10 boost, which adds (not multiplied) to ×17.77 multiplier. This multiplier can be upgraded using Mega Bucks.
Since October 2015, players can also play a limited time special event, which usually are around holidays and other annual events, such as Halloween or Black Friday, and occur once every month for several days. These events are like the three main areas, but are only available during that correlated event. If a player reaches at least one of the objectives of that event, they will get a badge shown in the 'Swag & Stats' page. As the player progresses in some events, they may acquire free gold or Mega Bucks based on unlocks, and even a special badge that when equipped can provide investment specific boosts.
Since The Love of Money event update, the 'Swag&Stats' section is now renamed 'Career', with a revamped stats page, support, swag, and news section. Along with this, there now is an option to make your capitalist a female. The Adventure Capitalist update notes for 4.2 state the monthly events will re-occur, with the same past events being in random(?) months of the year. (Specifically, The Love of Money event will reoccur in October, with more gold and Mega Buck rewards for unlocks.)

A nice action sandbox game, although in my inexperience with the genre I don't have anything else to compare it to.
Fair warning is that it is a poor PC port, no windowed mode or advanced graphics settings, mouse has some sort of analog dead zone which exaggerates large movements and totally ignores small ones, mini games designed for analog sticks but using the mouse can be frustrating to get used to.
There is quite a lot to do between missions, collectibles, and mini games. I was able to get 97% completion within 50 hours so it's a fairly long experience, probably longer if you feel like messing around in it instead of going straight from one objective to the next.
Combat is clunky, only hit and grapple, and most bosses are invulnerable to grapple. So it's button mashing hit most of the time. You do get combat upgrades that are just holding down hit after x amounts of button mashing it, but it's all largely irrelevant.
For me it was enjoyable up until end game, then all that was left was reoccurring boring mini games, and directionless mischief in the sandbox. There isn't anything branching story so there is also no reason to replay it as well.
TL;DR: Do you like sandbox games?

With the Director's Cut, you get the Missing Link DLC integrated right into the game, and you also get NG+ which allows you to carry over your character with PRAXIS upgrades into a second playthrough. I found myself at numerous points quicksaving and trying something else just to see the different outcomes. If there's a downside here, I'd say that the story itself doesn't resolve itself in a way I found satisfactory, and I really felt that the ending(s) were forced. Overall, I highly recommend, and I hope that the developers build on the successful factors of the gameplay formula here...but maybe next time weave together a more cohesive narrative to go with it.

tl;dr
Skara is a medieval PvP RPG action game. There are 3 game modes free for all, deathmatch (which is actually a hard-point type mode) and a duel mode. I played with the Kharn class which was very fun to play, the more you play and level the mode abilities you unlock such as the charge etc. Skara is a strategic game where hits and dodges must be planned before hand, so do not depend on button mashing.. It won't get you very far in this game. The game is stunning to look at, since it was made with Unreal engine - that isn't that hard to believe. There are a few cons with this game but I will get into that later. I feel like this game has a good base, it just needs a push in the right direction.

The board game is a better experience, obviously, but in a pinch this game is one of those fine idle fillers that doesn't require a vast amount of attention.  The music, an eternally looping midi of Red River Valley, will induce suicide if you don't disable it, but I strangely find myself slavishly enduring it in a masochistic fashion.

As an indie game, I think they're going in the right direction.
But, as an indie game and of early stage of development, a lot of things currently are questionable. One thing that really stood out for me is the free-for-all arena with a boss battle. The mode lacked direction as I had no idea what to kill. Hitting the boss gave me some points, but it wasn't as rewarding as killing off the characters who were getting damaged by the boss. In conclusion of this, I felt that the boss was more like an obstacle for people to avoid instead of trying to defeat.
Regardless, I'm happy that this game was able to go through testing and I was part of it. I see great potential in the game and I hope the devs continue their best to keep it going!

[h2]Early review:[/h2]
First impression when openning the box was of cheap plastic. But seeing it had batteries included I said ok, fine.
The one stick has a nice rubber texture and provides a lot of grip and control. I agree that the 4 action buttons are a bit small, but it's a thing of getting used to.
The right trackpad is really easy to get used to and I immediately liked it. The left one on the other hand needed a bit of time spent in order to find the settings that worked best for the purpose I use it for.
The buttons in the back are nice as well, but i feel that the upper ones are too big and proeminent, and for me it feels they are not too comfortable to use.
The gyro function seems nice and can be used for steering in racing games, it feels quite reactive to movements.
For the games I tried it with, there have been preset settings to choose from, which was perfect.
The one thing I didn't like was that in order to reach the presets, you had to be in the Big Picture interface, and I hope Steam will include options to change controller settings in the regular overlay as well.
Also, you can use the controller in windows to move your mouse and for basic commands like click, back, scroll, etc. which is nice. What is not nice is that you cannot move the mouse when you go into the Regular Steam Overlay in-game (not Big Picture). So basically, if you don't use Big Picture it's like you're using a regular Xbox controller, which I don't feel it's right, and hope some improvements.

The Steam Controller is actually fairly good. It's strength is it's customizability, and it's haptic feedback touch pads, they are very well designed and the software is spot on.
Pros:
= customizable
= easy to configure, easy to use
= wireless, with no latency issues
= good build quality, plenty of buttons
= downloadable profiles
Cons:
= must be running the game through steam to get it to detect the controller
= a/b/x/y buttons are too small, and too close together
= a/b/x/y buttons are _slightly_ too far away to be comfortable. I don't have this issue with the xbox360 controller, which sits perfectly.
Overall:
4 out of 5 stars.

Let me start off by saying in this review that I REALLY wanted to like this controller.  Steam has done great things for computer gaming so I had absolutely no problem supporting their company and buying their hardware (I also purchased Steam Link).
When I got the controller right out of the box I was dissapointed, it felt very cheaply made, the left joystick was pretty horrible, but I will get to that later.  Every review that I read on this did come with a disclaimer that the controller did have a learning curve, but I was assured once over the hump it was the best controller ever.
The Trackpad on the right, while it feels nice, I'm sorry to say but plays like crap.  The trackball feels nothing like a trackball, the mouse and keyboard setting is worse than just using an actual mouse and keyboard, and having it on joystick setting was a nightmare, because there is no way to tell where the center of it is.  I actually ended up taking a knife and etching into the center so I could find it while I was playing (that helped some but not much).
The left joystick is a joke....feels cheaper than a PS4 controller (I always plays Xbox controllers because I think they are made better).  When you would hold it down to sprint in a game, if you tried to move left or right while springting it would "pop out" and take you out of the sprint.  So if you wanted to sprint it had better be in a straight line or you are SOL.  The buttons feel extremelly cheap and are made smaller....for what purpose I have no idea because larger buttons wouldnt have gotten in the way of anything.  The Left D-Pad is garbage as well, if you don't hit it at the very right spot (the absolute outer edge of the D-Pad) it will bring up the wrong in game selection, and this D-Pad is HUGE so it is very akward trying to use it, I have no idea why Steam felt the need to make it so huge other than purely looks, but I can assure you it does not function well.
Overall: I spent 2 weeks playing games with NOTHING but the stream controller, tried all different sorts of settings, after the two weeks I couldn't take anymore and went back to my X-Box controller, as I said I know the controller has a "learning curve" but I'm not about to spend longer than 2 weeks trying to force myself to like a controller when my X-Box controller works just fine.  The customization options on the controller are nice, I will admit that, but sadly it is the ONLY redeeming factor of this controller.  Steam tried to reinvent the wheel, and they failed.
3/10: Good customization, horrible controller overall, extremelly cheap build.

Stonekeep is a 90's tile-based dungeon crawler and is also probably the most memorable game of my childhood. While there were certainly far better games of the kind around that time, some of which I consider to be the best games of all time, Stonekeep is a solid entry into the genre. The plot is centered around the character Drake, who as a boy witnessed  the people of Stonekeep being destroyed by an evil God named Khull-Khuum and is saved just in time by a Goddess named Thera. Drake returns to the ruins of Stonekeep 10 years after these events took place to defeat Khull-Khuum. There was a novella released with the game back in the day which goes into detail about the lore of Stonekeep and is also quite a good read.
Stonekeep features large dungeons in which you fight monsters, find keys to access new areas and uncover secrets. The combat is pretty average and often requires you to cheese fights but functional and very solid nonetheless. The difficulty the game presents is mixed, it can be insanely hard if you go into combat trying to chop your foes down head on but much easier if you mix melee attacks along with throwing items such as arrows and rocks at the enemies.
The dungeons themselves can get pretty monotonous which is why this game is probably best played in shorter doses if you get bored easily, they do vary through progression though. The art direction is superb and one of this games strengths, the 2D sprites are easily some of the best of that era and the environments are extremely well presented, though as said before, dungeons can get very samey after a while until you progress to the next.
The voice acting is also pretty amusing, although some may find the high fantasy stuff pretty cringey and a weird contrast to this games dark atmosphere.
Despite being very good for the most part, the game has a lot of flaws, one of them being the inventory system, requiring that you scroll down a list to select which items you want to use or equip each time you open it, it's time consuming and clunky and the amount of potential this game had to be more than a decent dungeon crawler is painful, you can see this had a very complicated development cycle and they didn't implement all that they had on paper, what started out as being a 50K project ended up costing over 5 million dollars to develop.
All in all a solid dungeon crawler, I'd recommend this to people who may have fond memories of this game from back in the day and those willing to try something new, although with caution, it's reasonably accessible but some may find it a bit monotonous for their liking.

Stonekeep is a game created by Brian Fargo of Wasteland and Fallout fame. It's a dungeon crawler in the style of Ultima Underworld and Eye of the Beholder and other similar games.
What set Stonekeep apart at least at the time was how the game mostly conveyed it's environments through fmv. This is the part of the game that aged the least gracefully, and you can always tell what you're fighting is a 2D sprite. It's also grid based so it doesn't control like something like Doom. The entire game is however in real time so it is relatively easy to get into compared to other games of a similar style.
The story to Stonekeep is a little confusing and much of the backstory to the game was told in a novel that shipped with the physical release. Which went into great depth about the different deities in the game's universe, the backstory of them and so forth. The basic gist of it is one day one of the gods goes insane and destroys the protagonist's home. So he journeys into the ruins of where his home once stood to vanquish him. The plot is fairly basic and the story is only really saved by the presence of some fairly entertaining characters and somewhat redeemable fmv sequences.
Unfortunately as ambitious of a project Stonekeep was at the time it's not exactly a game i'd recommend easily to people. Unless you're curious, or you're a fan of old school dungeon crawlers and 2.5D games in general.

One of the best entries in a classic genre that has only recently seen a revival thanks to titles like Legend of Grimrock, and a piece of PC gaming history as one of the first titles to offer support for Windows '95.
Stonekeep offers everything one expects from a classic first-person, grid-based action RPG and more. The setting is interesting and well-fleshed out. The cast is full of wonderful and diverse characters -- fully voice-acted, quite possibly a first for the genre. There's even a nice recipe for muffins hidden in the game's data files.
Some parts of the game have not aged as well as others. Most notably, inventory management leaves a lot to be desired. And the fact that the ending is only about four seconds long is somewhat disappointing.
But if you're looking to immerse yourself in a classic fantasy world, befriending dwarves and dragons, fighting grotesque tentacle monsters, and listening to faeries singing about how stupid dwarves are, Stonekeep is an absolute must-have.

Played through the game, unlocked like 8 endings or so, including the joke endings. Looks like it's gonna be a grindfest to go through all of it, which I don't mind too much.
The first thing is that the controls for PC are♥♥♥♥♥♥ Get a controller if you can, it's a PC port of a PS4 game.
Dashing is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥- having to double-tap a key is pretty bad when you're trying to react to enemy attacks. You have to either predict or memorize enemy attack patterns. Playing in the various 2D modes is hella awkward - it's impossible to shoot properly without relying completely on your auto-targeting. It's playable, but don't expect to have a good time until you get used to it. 3/10
Visually, I thought the game was pretty good. Granted, the world is pretty drab, and the color schemes of various areas are extremely limited, but it looks nice for what it's trying to be. I'd give it a 7/10, but I think there's something about it all that adds to the story in a very specific way. 8/10
Very nice soundtrack. I wasn't really wowed though, there's an endless list of epic soundtracks out there in the world. Also, there's a few tracks that are recycled throughout the game - not necessarily a bad thing, but I wasn't impressed. There wasn't anything that stood out to me, other than maybe the track that plays when you enter the Resistance Camp. 7/10
Combat is really nice. The game is incredibly forgiving when it comes to the dodge mechanic, it doesn't actually matter what direction you're dashing in as long as you're dashing when attacks make contact with your character model (or at least, that's how I'm assuming it works). The plug-in chips, or the upgrade system, is fun to tinker with. You can set up 3 chipsets and switch between them in the menu for various situations - I have one set up for bosses and one for pretty much everything else, and also one to screw around.
I never did much experimenting with different weapon types, but there's various combos you can use depending on what weapon types you have set up for your light/heavy attacks.
Combat feels super good. When you dodge, the game goes slo-mo for a split second, and you can see your character performing the dodge animation. It also just feels good to hit things and watch them explode afterwards. It's also a nice challenge to try and fight bosses when you're underleveled, because the game allows for you to still beat them as long as you're good enough.
Overall 9/10. We're gonna ignore the problems with playing on a mouse/keyboard.
After the regular combat, there's the various 'game modes' that the game forces you through. There's the sequences where you have to fly and shoot hostile aircraft (shoot 'em up), fly and shoot hostile aircraft but where you can free aim (shoot 'em up?), 2D sidescroller, 2D top-down fighter/shooter, and the arcade shooter-esque hacking sequences. The shmup sequences are terrible, I hated them until I got a plug-in chip that healed me for every enemy killed because it's impossible to tell exactly what direction and how quickly the arrow keys will take you because they keep moving the ♥♥♥♥ing camera angle. The 2D sidescrollers are okay until your pod shoots into outer space because it's shooting in a straight line while enemies are coming at you along the spiral. The 2D top-down wouldn't be too bad if I didn't have to move my hand from my mouse to my arrow keys to aim. The arcade shooter is the only thing I liked - they provided a unique challenge throughout the game that was both fun and challenging for the reason that they were meant to be challenging.
shmup is 3/10, 2D sidescroller portions are 6/10, 2D top-down is 4/10 and arcade shooter portions are 10/10 because I feel bad, and also because 10/10 might be a legitimate score.
Overall 5.2/10
Also including gameplay in general - there's actually a very large portion of the game where you just run around collecting crap for quests or whatever. This wouldn't be too bad if it weren't for the fact that you have to both be near an object and also facing it in order to pick it up, which I hated because I would always end up running past things or running in circles trying to pick up these friggin objects which would inevitably turn out to be mundane junk.
Thank god they give you a plug-in chip later for auto-pickup.
There's also a bunch of side quests you can do if you want for gold/items/xp/moral reconciliation with yourself. They're kind of annoying to track if you start a bunch of them at once - the quest menu is a bit too deep into the main menu for my liking. Overall, the side quests aren't that meaningful. Oh well.
6/10

Honestly this game is a spreadsheet.
The goal (at least the only one I can think of) is to maximize the rate at which you acquire money.
There are a set of timers, click to start one, when that timer reaches zero you get money.
Timers are enabled by purchasing them, and the cost of an additional 'payout' in a particular category of timers appears to increase 10% over the previous cost - ie:
#1 = $10.00
#2 = $11.00
#3 = $12.10
Total cost for 3 = $33.10
The astute player might decide to do maths to choose what to spend money on, however the game doesn't display the time required or payout for timers you haven't bought... actually the game doesn't display the total time required for any timer.  Instead you have to pay attention to the moment the countdown starts and record the first value.
You can buy (one time cost) managers to click on the timers for you, and the accrual continues when you quit the game, so if you log back in a week later I imagine you can buy everything... (well one of everything...)
The game keeps track of the total amount of money you've made, but somehow doesn't calculate the rate or give you a profitability breakdown... or any meaningful feedback.  I didn't even see a way to compare my progress against other players or time limited leaderboards or anything.
Frankly this 'game' can be completely experienced in 20 minutes, and the experience isn't good.

Bully is an action open world game released by Rockstar originally for the consoles and later the game was also released for the PC.
This game reminds me a lot of other games made by Rockstar such as the Grand Theft Auto games, mostly because of the open world and the huge variety of things you can do in the game. I would describe the game as GTA: School Edition.
We play as teenager named Jimmy Hopkins, a bad student who was expelled from all his previous schools. You start as the school underdog (being the new kid in school sucks) and eventually rise to the top, after being bullied by all the groups in the school (the Nerds, the Jocks and more). In the beginning of the game, the player can only explore the school campus, but later you can explore the entire city, the beach and even hangout in the carnival.
Gameplay: Missions - There are a variety of different missions in the game, side quests that give you money or items (such as new clothes) and the main plot quests. There are also missions in the city described as jobs that help you earn money. Money in the game is used for buying different cloths, tickets in the carnival, bicycles and more. In the school you are obviously meant also to learn something, which is why Rockstar created the classes in the game. Basically there are two classes each day, one in the morning and another one in the afternoon. Most of the classes are based on mini-games, for example in the Geography class you see part of the globe and you have to drag the correct country flags to their correct place in the globe. The last type of missions is the "conquer" missions, where you have the option to obtain a new saving place, by beating the head master of the place. For example, if you want to have the beach house you need to beat up the guys that rule the place. Like in other open world games, there are a lot of ways to fail, including getting busted by the police or the prefects (In the school campus area).
Weapons - In the game there are different kinds of weapons you can pick up, such as the baseball bat, the plank and more. These kind of weapons break after few uses. There are also your own weapons such as stink bombs, bottle rocket cannon, spud cannon and more. The fight mechanic is really funny in the game, and you also have an option to learn new moves. You can't kill other students in the game.
Vehicles - There are a few different vehicles in the game to help you move from one place to another. The skateboard, bicycles, motor scooter, go-kart and a lawn mower (Only available in certain missions).
Graphics: The game graphics aren't bad at all, considering its a game from 2008. The artstyle is really good, and all the cutscenes are not bad either. There are few bugs here and there, but nothing worth mentioning. The animation of the characters are well done, but sometimes they are silly.
Audio: The music in the game is great. The dubbing of the characters is not bad at all either. There are even many funny moments in the game.
Performance: The game runs really smoothly, and it doesn't require the best modern of PCs to run the game. I would suggest using a controller but thats just me. Keyboard and mouse are also a good option.
In conclusion, the game is really different from other games and thats why I really liked it.
Gameplay: 9/10, It's really great but it isn't perfect.
Plot: 7/10, It is well done, but there are many stupid quests that make the plot a little bit silly.
Graphics: 8/10, You can't complain, it looks really really good and runs pretty well.
Audio: 9/10.

Long♥♥♥♥♥review inbound, brace your bums.
Holy sh*t would you look at the hours. Didn't think this game would be any good, turns out it is quite f*cking good. My second most played game on Steam turned out to be another F2P. Let's get down and dirty into why this Anime MMORPG isn't as bad as you might think it is.
Aura Kingdom, i'll summarize it for you, the gameplay that is, I don't... Pay attention to the story too much until I reached the "ending" in the games current state (meaning i'll have to wait for the next story update). The gameplay is basically... A more simplistic WoW or TERA, however you would describe that cooldown, button mashing gameplay. Your abilities have special effects such as self buffs, debuffs to enemies, and I believe there was a team buff or so. The stats are the basic bread and butter of anything you can expect from an MMO: ATK, DEF, HP, etc. There is a a class specific tree you build through to get bonus buffs to abilities. You have a selection of many "eidolons" or what you would call "pets that give stat boosts when you level them up." You start out with 2 eidolons given to you for free, the rest you collect their key frags and create their entire key to unlock them. You can have a maximum of 3 eidolons that suit your classes playstyle. There are around, I want to say, 9-10 classes in the game in which you can select. You can select another class once you reach a specific level as a "subclass." You gain the subclass' abilities and a percentage of the subclasses stats. The gear in this game also has %-tage such as 100% or the desired 140%+ as it gives better stats (RNG BASED). There probably is a lot more gameplay added into new updates that I didn't check out yet, so don't think this is the entirety of the gameplay.
Now that the long summary is over, pros and cons:
Pros:
- FREE DLC! (It's meh - good, depending on how much you like being a reindeer) But hey, free DLC, no harm done.
- PvP, ah yes, this community is... nice or jerkwads depending on who they are as a person. I've had my share of nice people and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s in PvP. This community isn't necessarily... dead. It's just not very active. Overall community is generally friendly unless you reach a high world ranking without paying to diss all the P2W people.
- Guilds are usually open and quite friendly from what i've seen, but there can't be an online game without a few bad weeds. You could gather a bunch of irl friends to play, makes it all the better.
- There are pages and pages of costumes in the catalog and paragon table (the wheel of fortune in this game) and you can cosplay your favorite waifu or husbando or w.e. the hell else you want to be, like a streaker with a rainbow afro.
- All the classes are actually fun to play and reach a point of "OP" when it is built statistically and geared a certain way. And you can reset skill trees with in-game gold compared to other games in which you need some stupid scroll that costs irl $$$.
- You can lone wolf the entire game. Yes, you can go solo without a guild the entire game for all you solo players out there. Be warned, it takes a lot longer as joining a guild gives you an XP and loot drop boost and this % increases as your guild levels up (Max level 5).
- The daily rewards give you what you need to improve your gear, get better drops, etc.
- The raid bosses are really well done imo, managed to reach the final hall of a raid boss (Zaahir) with my guild and it was quite intense, an actually fun raid boss that gets harder as you progress. The time limit is a good factor I feel as it makes you try harder.
- The crafting in this game isn't as awkward as i'd expect, it's simply once you get used to it, like many parts of this game.
- Mounts aren't garbage, they actually make you move faster. WOW! And as a bonus, some of them look quite good. Most of their gold value is in the rarity and looks. Same goes to costumes and accessories.
- IF YOU SPEND MONEY, check the website for look crates instead, those usually hold a lot better value in their price.
- I quite like how you can choose whether to place items in the auction house or in your own stall to sell. Manipulating the economy might be looked down upon, but I make money off it. ;P
Cons:
- Now i'll admit, there is huge incentive to just sink your cash into this game if you're desperate for the loot or cool costumes and whatnot. However, the paragon table doesn't have good loot on it, and when it does, based god RNG doesn't allow it.
- I won't lie. It is very difficult to get into the game's higher tier as it has an economy barrier with how much gold or grinding it takes to get the good items. Basically, if you don't have gold or good luck, you spend ages trying to reach higher tiers of gear once you hit around level 60.
- Sky Tower, this is what some people would call similar to how the entire SAO anime operates. Multiple floors and each floor has a boss and sometimes along with a  puzzle you have to beat/solve. Without extreme guild coodination, you can't really rely on the pubbies who go in there randomly. They stand in there randomly waiting for someone else to finish the floor.
- It gets harder to solo the game when it comes to raid bosses, yes this game has raid bosses. It takes groups of specifically geared guild members (pubbies usually can't do it, not trying to trash them as bad, you just can't trust some of them).
- Making huge money is boatloads easier if you spend cash to sell Ruby Coins, an in-game premium currency.
- BOTS, THERE ARE BOTS. Not as much as before, but they still exist, sending you random messages to buy gold from their websites. Report, delete mail, move on. That's all you can do.
Overall: Game isn't bad for an F2P, there is literally nothing a P2W can do that an F2P can't. P2W just progresses faster if they're smart and don't spend all their cash on looks. Like an old friend said to me, "don't be that guy with a weapon that costs 100 gold and wear a costume that costs 10 million gold." All dungeons are open and only restricted by level. Dungeons are well balanced in terms of party mode or solo mode. Dungeons do get harder, gives sense of progression. This game can get very grindy after reaching level 50 or so. Making it to level 70+, I commend you, welcome to our realm of hardcore grind. The xp bar in some sense, disappears from the game as you barely see it fill up, but rejoice once you see even a sliver of it rise. Final note, costumes have slight stat bonuses and you can re-color them with in-game dye, all cost in-game gold.

Overall its a great buy, especially if you like splitscreen fps games.

Pros and Cons, here we go!
Pros
1. Quite intense
2. Started on normal and you really do feel like you have to fight to survive.
3. The music at times knew how to take everything from intense to unsettling. Always quiet but disturbing
4. The price tag is really great.
5. Games like this continue to erode my confidence in huge titles and companies and now favor more Indie games(this being indie of course)
6. The story line while simple made sense.
Cons
1. The game felt like it set you up perfectly for a second stage but instead ended. I don't mean it felt like a forced ending because it didn't. I'm just saying it easily could have gone further. DLC could very easily be added to this game and not feel forced in the least bit. DLC e.g. you have to make your way home of course but have your radar direct you to different outposts to gain much needed supplies. A different station, different requirements and so on.
2. Crappy batteries made sense and was spot on. Batteries sitting to long lose charge and therefore it easily stands to reason that you would chew through them quite quickly (as is the case) Kerosene did not make sense. It burns slowly so it made no sense that you burn through your fuel as fast as a drag racer goes through fuel. At the same time it's a semi con to the game because its understood that your fighting to gain body heat. If your fuel went on forever, half the strain of staying alive would be eliminated. That being the case I hold that con with a very light hand.
And that's it on the cons. All I can say is I really wish they would add DLC and new areas so you have to fight your way back home.
Also, for there not being a single monster in the game the intensity, darkness and soundtrack really freaked me out at times and I wondered if something was going to step out of the shadows. Even when I knew that there were no other creatures in the game the feeling was always there. If anything had stepped out I would have♥♥♥♥♥♥myself. I know horror games that try to instill this level of fear and don't even come close to what they achieved here, maybe by accident.

Stopped playing this after Level two or three. This game is so far from anything good or a DOOM game, keep your hands off it.
Gameplay
If you like fast or gory shooters, play Titanfall 1&2 (TF2 had an awesome SP Campaign) or Brutal Doom. This games pacing is more towards an aborted quake arena singleplayer. It forces you from one boring arena to another. Same enemys, same enemys. You can spam the execution for easy rewards, if you can endure watching the same 2 or 3 bad killmoves over and over again. Really gets old fast. The movement system also is an abomination. Why the player sometimes doesn't grab ledges, I can't say. What I can say, that it just eliminates the fun of vaulting objects, finding secrets to climbs or any juump and run section that would untwist the shooter sections of former games. The enemys themselves have ven become dumber. If you had 3 basic types of enemys in D3, Zombies (slugging towards you, with melee in mind), Zombie guards (using tactics and weapons, with skill dodges for higher tier enemys) and demons (using a mix of mellee and ranged combat, while advancing towards you, often very mobile), DOOM just manages to give you canon fodder jumping from one highpoint to the next. I can sit in a bottleneck passage of the current arena and just wait any enemy out. Very, very boring.
Story
The story never was a mayor point in Doom games, but Doom 3 still managed to get you into the game with setting the games tone, the enviorment and its characters. All that is gone. You just wake up and start smahing things, with a pistol lying near you.
Video/Atmo
Doom 3 worked with its strong contrast of Darkness vs. Light, where shadows often have sharp edges and there are moments of fear when you can't really see what is lurking in the dark. All that is gone. Enemys announce their presence long before you seem them, there is no more Horror or disturbing feelings in this game. The enviorments are neat, but very bright, again Doom 3 had a more unsettling and dark tone, making Mars look like an all time hazard enviorment, not like a playground.
Soundtracks
The soundtracks go along this. Most tracks just kick up when you are in an arena but won't get me up or anything, just dull heavy metal. D3 themes work more into the grim and demonic theme of the Doom games, while Doom 1&2 sounds are iconic. The weapons and enemys don't really sound that great, an the kill moves often feel like you beat someone with a foam sword. Blood splatting is good though.
Unlocks
Kinda feel forced and unnecassry. They seem to matter so little, only acting as another device to get me playing towards the next level. Weapon progression also is a nightmare. While you worked your way up in former Doom games, I found the pistol, then the shotgun, then the chainsaw and then the plasmarifle, just after finding the assault rifle. All that in just 2 Levels. Makes me shrug and scratch my head, what the devs were thinking. I have seen most weapons already, why even continue playing, there are no weapon specific killmoves anyway.
Conclusion:
If a Quake game had a child with an Arena style SP game and you would abort it, while the abortion still cried:" Killl me, KILL ME!" Behtesda would come around the alley and would publish it. If you want a good Singleplayer FPS then play Titanfall 2, if you want a good horror shooter play Doom3, if you want some old-school demon♥♥♥♥♥kicking play Brutal Doom. This game dropped in price rapidly, what is always a good sigh of how bad it is. Stay away from it. If you play this for multiplayer there is a boatload of better games, and you should be ashamed of yourself.

That's something a lot of people heard about this game, and what more even experienced. And it is an experience that changed a lot of them, me included, for this game is truly a masterpiece :
One word : fluidity. Combats are fast-paced and allow great mobility at no expense, attacks connect easily on targets, combos get running flawlessly, for a pleasant, if classic, hack'n'slash experience. But that's only the tip of the iceberg. Throughout the game, you'll switch from 3D Hack'n'Slash to 2D Brawler, Shoot'en Up, and Dual-Stick Shooter seamlessly. Never the game feels slow, and that's something few games can brag about. Also, you will never see a loading screen in the entire game. Know that the game is split into 3 "routes", the first 2 ones being the same story seen from different perspectives. Don't stop after ending A, you'll have seen nothing.
Now to the most interessant part, the story of Nier: Automata is a heart-breaking tale of androids and machines, at war for millenias, searching for the meaning of life. At a complete opposite to most mainstream games and movies nowadays, where you have an epic story of a group of people fighting the greater evil and winning triumphantly, the story of Nier: Automata lays more in its characters' developpement through the events of the game, and is more of a psychological thriller than anything else. It forces the player to think about its own humanity, and never provides clear answers to existancial questions : at the end of the game, you'll know yourself better than ever, and that's not something that happens often in modern media.
"Yet another open-world". The map itself is not immensely big like more known recent open-worlds, but it get straight to the point. All zones are very distinct, and no place feels useless. It also changes dinamically following the events of the game, so some zones are entirely different depending on when you cross them. Though you mostly play the same game a second time in route B, a lot of secondary content only unlocks there, and while the main story is the same, the new informations you possess makes it a very different experience. Don't go rushing it because "you've done it already", you would miss on a lot of developpement.
Graphics : Well, the game looks like it could have been released 5 years ago, though by all means, games were already pretty at the time. Just don't expect photorealistic textures everywhere.
Controls : You should play it with a controller, not only all genres this game falls into play better with a controller, but the poor port make M+KB really painful. Every movement is extremely fluid, for a smooth and pleasant gameplay.
Performance : The port is awful, and Square isn't willing to do anything, so you will have to download and install FAR, a fan-made patch to basically every problem the game has. With it installed, I never experienced a crash, or anything looking like a bug during my playtime.
The soundtrack is a true masterpiece, in and out of the game. Nothing more to say.
If you play games for their stories, make yourself a favor and buy this game. If you like hacking and slashing through hordes of robots, buy this game. If you're a perv and want to watch some android butts, buy this game. All in all, buy this game

Holy sh*t would you look at the hours. Didn't think this game would be any good, turns out it is quite f*cking good. My second most played game on Steam turned out to be another F2P. Let's get down and dirty into why this Anime MMORPG isn't as bad as you might think it is.
Aura Kingdom, i'll summarize it for you, the gameplay that is, I don't... Pay attention to the story too much until I reached the "ending" in the games current state (meaning i'll have to wait for the next story update). The gameplay is basically... A more simplistic WoW or TERA, however you would describe that cooldown, button mashing gameplay. Your abilities have special effects such as self buffs, debuffs to enemies, and I believe there was a team buff or so. The stats are the basic bread and butter of anything you can expect from an MMO: ATK, DEF, HP, etc. There is a a class specific tree you build through to get bonus buffs to abilities. You have a selection of many "eidolons" or what you would call "pets that give stat boosts when you level them up." You start out with 2 eidolons given to you for free, the rest you collect their key frags and create their entire key to unlock them. You can have a maximum of 3 eidolons that suit your classes playstyle. There are around, I want to say, 9-10 classes in the game in which you can select. You can select another class once you reach a specific level as a "subclass." You gain the subclass' abilities and a percentage of the subclasses stats. The gear in this game also has %-tage such as 100% or the desired 140%+ as it gives better stats (RNG BASED). There probably is a lot more gameplay added into new updates that I didn't check out yet, so don't think this is the entirety of the gameplay.
Now that the long summary is over, pros and cons:
Pros:
- FREE DLC! (It's meh - good, depending on how much you like being a reindeer) But hey, free DLC, no harm done.
- PvP, ah yes, this community is... nice or jerkwads depending on who they are as a person. I've had my share of nice people and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s in PvP. This community isn't necessarily... dead. It's just not very active. Overall community is generally friendly unless you reach a high world ranking without paying to diss all the P2W people.
- Guilds are usually open and quite friendly from what i've seen, but there can't be an online game without a few bad weeds. You could gather a bunch of irl friends to play, makes it all the better.
- There are pages and pages of costumes in the catalog and paragon table (the wheel of fortune in this game) and you can cosplay your favorite waifu or husbando or w.e. the hell else you want to be, like a streaker with a rainbow afro.
- All the classes are actually fun to play and reach a point of "OP" when it is built statistically and geared a certain way. And you can reset skill trees with in-game gold compared to other games in which you need some stupid scroll that costs irl $$$.
- You can lone wolf the entire game. Yes, you can go solo without a guild the entire game for all you solo players out there. Be warned, it takes a lot longer as joining a guild gives you an XP and loot drop boost and this % increases as your guild levels up (Max level 5).
- The daily rewards give you what you need to improve your gear, get better drops, etc.
- The raid bosses are really well done imo, managed to reach the final hall of a raid boss (Zaahir) with my guild and it was quite intense, an actually fun raid boss that gets harder as you progress. The time limit is a good factor I feel as it makes you try harder.
- The crafting in this game isn't as awkward as i'd expect, it's simply once you get used to it, like many parts of this game.
- Mounts aren't garbage, they actually make you move faster. WOW! And as a bonus, some of them look quite good. Most of their gold value is in the rarity and looks. Same goes to costumes and accessories.
- IF YOU SPEND MONEY, check the website for look crates instead, those usually hold a lot better value in their price.
- I quite like how you can choose whether to place items in the auction house or in your own stall to sell. Manipulating the economy might be looked down upon, but I make money off it. ;P
Cons:
- Now i'll admit, there is huge incentive to just sink your cash into this game if you're desperate for the loot or cool costumes and whatnot. However, the paragon table doesn't have good loot on it, and when it does, based god RNG doesn't allow it.
- I won't lie. It is very difficult to get into the game's higher tier as it has an economy barrier with how much gold or grinding it takes to get the good items. Basically, if you don't have gold or good luck, you spend ages trying to reach higher tiers of gear once you hit around level 60.
- Sky Tower, this is what some people would call similar to how the entire SAO anime operates. Multiple floors and each floor has a boss and sometimes along with a  puzzle you have to beat/solve. Without extreme guild coodination, you can't really rely on the pubbies who go in there randomly. They stand in there randomly waiting for someone else to finish the floor.
- It gets harder to solo the game when it comes to raid bosses, yes this game has raid bosses. It takes groups of specifically geared guild members (pubbies usually can't do it, not trying to trash them as bad, you just can't trust some of them).
- Making huge money is boatloads easier if you spend cash to sell Ruby Coins, an in-game premium currency.
- BOTS, THERE ARE BOTS. Not as much as before, but they still exist, sending you random messages to buy gold from their websites. Report, delete mail, move on. That's all you can do.
Overall: Game isn't bad for an F2P, there is literally nothing a P2W can do that an F2P can't. P2W just progresses faster if they're smart and don't spend all their cash on looks. Like an old friend said to me, "don't be that guy with a weapon that costs 100 gold and wear a costume that costs 10 million gold." All dungeons are open and only restricted by level. Dungeons are well balanced in terms of party mode or solo mode. Dungeons do get harder, gives sense of progression. This game can get very grindy after reaching level 50 or so. Making it to level 70+, I commend you, welcome to our realm of hardcore grind. The xp bar in some sense, disappears from the game as you barely see it fill up, but rejoice once you see even a sliver of it rise. Final note, costumes have slight stat bonuses and you can re-color them with in-game dye, all cost in-game gold.

So let me clear a few things up first. I have been playing AK for about a year now. I have 6 characters on the Chimera server(all of my characters are ranging from lvl50 to lvl 80). Aura Kingdom is not a new game but it has a very active and large community. The story line is good and the fighting mechanics are superb aswell.
CLASSES:
As in any MMO RPG when you first create a new character you will be able to pick between a couple classes. You can chose between Guardian, Duelist, Ravager, Wizard, Sorcerer, Bard, Grenadier, Gunslinger, Katar, Battle Bow, Tachi, Scythe or Holy Sword. Depending on your liking you will chose the class that suits your game style the most (Although  I have seen a lot of new players chose Duelist as their first class I have to say that if you are just starting to play the game make a Holy Sword it is a easy to play class and it has a lot of dmg, while Duelist is one of the hardest to play classes(Hardest to play and be GOOD at it).
CHARACTER CUSTOMIZATION:
There is not a lot to talk about when it comes to the basic character customization that you get at the start of the game, however this isnt all you can do to customize your character. In game you get different costumes (body, head, weapon, back, face,..) With these costumes you can completely change your characters apperance to your liking (you can even change color of CUSTOM Costumes).
LEVELING:
The leveling process is as in a lot of MMO RPGs. Leveling from 1-40 is not that hard you can get 1-45 within a day if you get really into it. The next stage in leveling is at 45-60 you will notice that you need enourmos ammounts of xp for a lvl. And this just continues the ammount of xp you need to get to lvl 80 in insane but once u do its worth it. I also think its worth mentioning that the level cap is now 90!!! So there is a lot to do to reach endgame.
PVP:
The pvp aspect of the game is as in any other MMO RPG. You have arenas and Battlefields. While arenas will match you up with players around your level lvl 50-59, lvl 60-69 and lvl70+, Battlefields on the other hand match everyone togeather no matter the level. For PVP you will need pvp gear which isnt that hard to get (although pvp weapons are a bit trickier to get). Now I would not recommend pvp to new players since you will most likely get killed instantly. Since for pvp it is important to have your gear fortified and starred (This gives you bonus def and HP in armor and DMG in weapons).
PVE:
In the case of PVE there is not really one bad thing I have to say about it. You have a large veriety of dungeons (solo and party to chose from). Dungeons are locked to different levels so as you level up you will unlock more dungeons. Also PVE gear can be crafted but I would recommend crafting PVE gear after you reached lvl 60 since green gear for your normal solo dungeons until lvl 60 is fine.
All in all a very good Anime MMO RPG game with a great community and good mechanics.

A rare find in the survival genre, Near Death is a tighly packaged experience that proves that you don't need monsters to make being trapped in the Antarctic horrifying. Playing a pilot whose plane went down over a decommissioned research station during polar night, the infeasability of rescue means you need to scour every inch of the station to put together what you need to make your own way to safety, all while the dark and cold do their level best to make you as miserable as possible.
This game is fairly short - I beat it in around four hours - but any longer would've just dragged on as the game sends you into a desperate survival situation at a fairly breakneck pace. Near Death presents a lonely, isolated setting where the air itself is such an oppressive, omnipresent threat that spending more than a minute outside of a sealed room will kill you, and such havens can feel few and far between as every other window is blown in and even a number of the walls have collapsed from the incessant siege of wind and snow.
Outside of the mere challenge of having to exist in such extreme conditions, the game is fairly straightforward and isn't much more than a series of fetch quests, but when the basic logistics of getting from point A to point B without freezing - or worse, getting lost when visiblity is next to zero - are so mounting such basic tasks are anything but trivial.
All in all I find very little to criticize about this game, and while the premise may not be for everyone, if what I've described here sounds like your cup of tea I suggest giving it a try.
