I bought this on sale, and I can say it was worth it.
Near Death has no zombies, vampires, plagues, robots, ninjas, trolls, elves, etc etc.  There are no enemies at all, and you have no weapons ether.  The whole story feels very realistic--I imagine that wandering around while stranded in Antarctica in 1982 would probably be very much as depicted in Near Death.  I kept wondering if there might be some jump scares, if I would find some creature lurking in the cold darkness of some room in the base.  Or, perhaps I would uncover pieces of some twisted military plot, some terrible research going on at the Sutro base.  But in fact, there's basically no one to interact with in the game, except some people you communicate with via a teletype (like a typewriter and a telephone together), hundreds of miles away, as they provide you guidance and warm wishes to help keep you, and the story, moving forward.  Apart from that, and the bit of humor that comes through at times in your communications, there is really only one main thing that drives the game forward--and that's the gameplay itself.
In a much larger and much broader game, perhaps a Mass Effect or Elder Scrolls or even Half Life, the gameplay of Near Death might make up a chapter or two.  But in this game, the creators have chosen to focus in on a few very specific gameplay elements.
The challenge is to survive the worst nature can throw at you: the wind, the snow, the darkness, and the freezing temperatures of Antarctica.  You do this with a few pieces of equipment, such as a flashlight, and later light rods you can plant in the snow; a heater you carry around to warm you up inside closed rooms; a blowtorch, to melt snow and ice and gain access to new rooms and supplies; and even your character's clothing is important, as you realize you can find ways to upgrade your clothing (and other items) to stay warmer for longer.  The game actually reminds me some of Neo Scavenger, another game in which it's important to manage the cold, stay warm with good clothes and scavenge stuff to stay alive--though Neo Scavenger also features food and sleep, and combat with sci-fi enemies.
If you manage to survive the earliest and most disorienting stages of the game, you will begin to get fetch quests, essentially, as you are sent off to the different parts of the base to retrieve pieces of equipment to aid your in your survival and escape.  Along the way you must properly manage your equipment and supplies, and avoid getting turned around too much when you're in the heavy wind and snow outside, and be certain you can get to heat sources in time.
Do that, and you should have a good chance of surviving and ultimately escaping Sutro.
If that sounds fun to you--a game where you're pitted against Mother Nature herself, rather than any kinds of enemies--you may find Near Death to be a wonderful little game, as I did.
Now, with all this said, there were some issues I had with Near Death.
Firstly, my laptop moved at a crawl much of the time while my character was outdoors.  Having some options to turn down the detail of the snow falling, and other such things, would have been nice.
I fell through a catwalk next to the power station--this was a clipping issue, not a piece of catwalk that broke (though there were a few catwalks that broke in scripted events).
And a few more gameplay-oriented annoyances:
It would have been nice to jump a little higher, and be able to climb up short objects.  There were several times where I would have just climbed up the side of a building, rather than being forced to find some way to go around.  And the duck-jump feature, by which I was able to gain access to certain areas, felt very clumsy compared to in Valve's FPS's, often requiring me to make several attempts.
The main character gets cold and dies too quickly in my view.  Even with all my clothes fully upgraded, I think it would only take one or two minutes to die.  Perhaps this was a deliberate decision to keep up a sense of urgency, but I think it could have been handled better.  Also consider that, in addition to dying too quickly from cold, I think the character also warms up too quickly once in the presence of heat.  You can go from being right on the point of death--wobbling around with your vision and hearing badly blurred from being too cold, literally ready to fall down dead--to being 100% OK and ready to go out into the cold once more, all in less than a minute, so long as you enter the presence of heat.  No frostbite, no numb limbs, almost no recovery time.  It's fun and scary to deal with, but it's also a kind of simplistic system that I think could do to be revamped.
Every single door in a room must be closed, and all of the broken windows must be sealed--no matter the size of the room or how closed off certain parts of it may seem--before your personal heater is able to warm you up.  I was bothered that I couldn't just move into a secluded corner, turn on the heater and get warm.
On a similar note, I kept on waiting for one of the generators to fail or run out of fuel, taking my best heat sources and forcing me to go on a hunt for more gasoline.  I was kind of disappointed that never happened.
I would have preferred if the locations, shapes, and sizes of the buildings, and their rooms, and the supplies available within them, were randomized.  Near Death kind of suffers from convenientitis.  Of course the very first building you find has the personal heater.  And of course that is the sole building that possesses the only personal heater, of the ~15 buildings in the game.  I think it's pretty clear that the game is meant to be played in a linear fashion, moving from one particular building to another in a particular order.  Early on I didn't realize that I was supposed to activate a generator, and instead ended up moving to another building.  Only after getting there and spending some time there did I realize I didn't have enough propane to stay warm with the personal heater.  I kept searching for propane but didn't find enough to last long.  Realizing I was probably going to freeze to death, I checked my inventory and objectives and such, and only then discovered that I had skipped an objective earlier, so I had to restart from the beginning.  Personally I think that randomizing building locations and supplies would really have added a whole new level of fun and difficulty to the game.
Overall, I enjoyed Near Death a lot.  It doesn't take too long to finish, even on the highest difficulty, which I've now completed as well.
***Minor spoiler alert***
Other than that, the only I have to say is that, on Normal difficulty anyway, the game ends with what is basically a sandbox mode.  After completing what was basically the last objective, the temperature suddenly went up from about -100 C to -5 C, and the wind and snow and darkness cleared.  It was the perfect time for this to happen, as I was up on top of the radar tower at a high elevation, and thus able to look down on all the other buildings below, able to see their lights and the green lights I'd placed around on the snow.  It was quite a beautiful moment, perhaps equally as memorable as all the chaos and peril of the game up to then.  Under those conditions, with virtually no fear of death, I happily went back to every building I could, exploring all around inside and out.
***End spoiler***
7.5/10  Near Death is nothing amazing, but it's certainly a lot of fun to play around with for a little while.

Near Death is a very linear survival game. You have set goals with set locations. The only thing between you and survival is the harsh weather of Antartica. Through my own observations, it appears that the weather and temperature are dependant on which "checkpoint" you are at. When you first start, the temperature is well below 0 degrees Celcius. As you progress further in the game, the winds pick up and temperatures reach nearly -100 degress celcius. Im not saying that this is a bad thing, however, when the game is as short as it is (about 2 hours + if you understand what youre doing), RNG with the weather might be a nice touch.
The game itself isn't very dependant on the map and compass (default button is M). You'll notice the compass in the top left hand corner, and the blue dial is the direction you are facing. While early game this is useful, towards the end, you should have rope poles and light poles set up so that you can run from building to building without much problem (rope poles allow you to sprint, even in the heavy winds).
Now, since this game is linear, there isnt much "re-playability". Yes, there are 4 different difficulties, but you are essentially doing the same thing over again, just on a different difficulty. (And a lot worse weather)
It is a wonderful game for what it is, and if you are looking for a nice survival game with a wonderful atmosphere, then Near Death is a good bet for you.

Outstanding PC adaptation of a classic board game.
Each turn a player takes a couple of train cards or spends those cards in order to place trains on pre-defined routes.  Completing some objectives like a continuous route between two particular cities earns the player more points.
So the game is both about strategy of choosing what routes to use and how to achieve that, while also denying your opponents from achieving their targets.
The game is well balanced and the DLC additions while far from necessary certainly add to the longevity of the game if you find yourself enjoying the mechanics.  Surprisingly for a game like this, the AI is decent.  However in most cases it is not difficult to win if you have even a modicum of strategy.
If you've always wanted to try a board game on PC then this is a good place to start.

itsy bitsy review(more of a note about the progress really):
the game has come quite far over its development(i've had it for approx. a year now if my memory serves me right, i can check if it really matters to anyone).
the game currently has 4 different classes, which players can unlock for free(just need levels)
each class currently has 3 skills which you can mix and match to suit your style, in addition to ranged abillities and talents.
the game itself is an arena fighting game which plays very well.
you have all the lovely basics- light attacks which stagger the foe and do most of the work,
heavy attacks which add their own special touch to the mix, combination attacks, and lastly, dodging and blocking
(all in the flavor of dark souls- to those of us who need a reference).
things get a little different thanks to the different races(whose roles ill try not to go too far into because the game is still in development and things change but on the surface):
-khan, the tanky giant axe carrying folks with a bit of a super armor and a slow attack to go with it(super armor as in doesnt stagger not the "i dont take damage")
-shinse, nimble, agile, dextrous, more words that show accuracy and quickness. these guys are the friendly neighborhood assassins with their set of skills to get past armored foes and keep them guessing while they do it
-tamvasa, the newly introduced ice folk with their dual axes who can either support their teammates by weakening foes or unleash a barrage of blows on their own
-celean, the veteran humans(humans, right?) who use their spear and shield to keep enemies in check before they charge them down.
(currently things are mostly balanced btw and ive used all classes to defeat all classes with fair ammount of ease but not lacking depth)
the game also has different game modes, which will change how you can use your classes a little:
a duel 1v1 mode, simple as it sounds
a colloseum free for all PVPVE mode with a giant boss monster(named "the groth")
a team versus team conquest mode.
tldr;
the game plays well. its taking its shape well and and came a long way over the time,
the dev team is nice and communicative(very active on their steam forums)
the fighting is the easy to get into hard to master kind of thing.
the bad parts:
fps drops come to visit at times, lags in multiplayer and crashes(inevitable for a beta build)

This is possibly one of the worst games I have ever played. On its own, the game consists of farming and trading with other players. The catch is, unlike many other games that involve pixel blocks, the only way you can get ANYTHING AT ALL is by breaking as much as possible, with the  VERY SMALL CHANCE that they will drop their specific seed, allowing you to get the material by planting the seed. You can also combine seeds to make more things. This would be somewhat unique if you had large worlds and actual challenges, but the worlds are small and their is nothing to stop you, other than long and painful processes. The game is online, and anyone can join any world at any time. This leads the game to round down to mostly worlds focused on recipes and trading. Any form of challenge only exists in the worlds focusing on platforming, but the controls were designed for a mobile device, so platforming is just pressing the same group of 3 buttons, and by default w is the jump key, condensing the controls in a way that is pointless. The only thing they did when they ported it over to steam, is put the controls onto the keyboard and mouse. They didn't even hide the original control scheme, which can be put on a overlay on top of the game with the press of a few buttons. The seeds system ruins any form of quality the game once had, for certain items that are "RARE" or "VALUABLE" cannot be recovered if they are missplaced, forcing the player to restart the long and boring process of shoving seeds into the same hole.
The system of daily quests is the only reason anyone would want to continue playing, by giving almost pointless and boring missions to complete.
EDIT: I've been thinking it through, and I think I know why this game left such a sour patch on me. The concept of only being able to gather materials by planting seeds is common in farming games, but in those games the rewards are aparrent, there are goals that are more interesting than "GET MOAR STUFF", and interesting areas as well. But those games also have things that can challenge you more than a simple wait. With no enemies nothing can kill you unless you are a dunce, and other players cannot kill you as well.
As I said, this is one of the worst games I have ever played. Do not get this game, unless you like to annoy 8 year olds like me. Even though this game is free, it sucks from you as a person, your life, fun, and emotion. This game is not free, even if it claims so. It sucks your "soul" with its infinitely slow gameplay, and your wallet with countless microtransactions.
NEVER THINK OF EVEN GETTING THIS GAME.

Played the free weekend and I kept going AFK. Boring. Nothing groundbreaking nor particularly nostalgic save for the obligatory tribute nods inserted here and there. The controls are ok, some stuff is neat and the quality is decent but didn't capture the mood of the original dooms, I and II. It is better than doom 3, but that's not saying much as that was extra boring and felt unfinished.
Of course the graphics and overall functions surpass I and II, but I would imagine a title that attempts to have the nerve to reboot the franchise with just calling it DOOM with no sequel number would try to bring the mood of the originals to life. But there goes silly me, being idealist again.
I want to see Doom have a breath of fresh air but there's not much style here that doesn't make it feel stale and holding back, while it tries to shine you on with upgrades and extra dialog.
The scenery is decent but feels a bit rehashed from other games. Some of it works, but it feels generic and otherwise a bit try-hard with very little in terms of truly wacky and dreadful like the originals. I mean I've felt more evil locations in Elder Scrolls games than this. The music feels like it was ripped off of DmC which itself is OK, but is nowhere near an improvement on the original Doom tunes. It almost has a rainbow six seige vibe as well, trying to sound all cutting edge with cliche style of excessive bass and digitized distortions.
The demons aren't as bad as doom 3 had but not much better either. They just feel like futurized, alien like monsters for the most part (though the summoner does look cool). The originals, even in their crappy graphics, just felt more authentic to what one would naturally consider evil and scary. Not because of pixelated sprites that I first experienced but because the basic style they were based on did the trick and it seems only the Revenant is a direct improvement in my opinion.
Besides the graphics, the sound, which is really where the originals shine, for the demons sounded extremely scary with their unique hissing, snorting and growling. Now I can barely hear them and they sound dime a dozen? zzzzzz.
Tired of these so-called reboots 'fixing' stuff that isn't broke.
It does excel at making more fast paced mayhem than 3, which is great, except for the fact that there are already countless games that provide this with just as good graphics. What should set DOOM apart is the mood and atmosphere created, and I didn't really get the creepy vibes I was expecting. Of course I only played the first 2 levels, but I've seen the rest of the game on youtube and not much stood out.
Overall, I feel it is mainly a fanboy cashcow with some superficial fluff, but maybe that's a good thing as some doors should probably remain closed. There's nothing special here beyond the level of bandwagon hype it has received.
MULTIPLAYER: seems to play ok, but just that. it's matchmaking, no server browser, no ping (just cellphone bars). zzzzzzz.

I have owned this controller for some time now and I had no expectations for it. To make something clear, people compare this to other console controllers and it is different from those yet the same in a way, so people have negative thoughts about this controller. If you take away the comparison of console controllers until after you mess with this controller then you will have a better experience than a snappy judgement.
I see where Steam was going for with this controller. This controller is meant to be for a living room setting and to replace the mouse and keyboard with the feel of it. They got that right except for the keyboard. There is more of a mouse and controller feel to it than a mouse and keyboard.
You have to use Big Picture for this controller from what I have experienced because that is where the interface is to customize it.
It fits in your hand like an xbox controller and the location of the ABXY buttons are a bit odd but a little time will make you get used to it. The buttons on the back are conveniently placed so that you can press them without moving much. The triggers have the ability to have a hair trigger press or a hard press that can be customized to whatever you want. The buttons are buttons nothing new there. The left and right trackpads can have many customizations being touch or physical. The left analog stick is like on many controllers and is placed comfortably. There is a built in gyroscope that can be helpful for aiming in games or as a wheel for racing games like your phones gyroscope. The battery lasts awhile and can be plugged in at any time or wireless with AA batteries.
The two trackpads are nice to use when it comes to games that don't require you to aim much like first person shooters. Although there are some customizations I have found on the workshop from others that have helped me aim better in an fps with this controller than a mouse because of the use of the built in gyro. The trackpads can be very precise when customized correctly to your playstyle.
All buttons on this controller can be customized to your desires. I was overwhelmed with the amount of customizations that could be made with a single button or trackpad. It takes time to get used to all this depending on the person. So if you buy it, take your time and don't rush it. It takes time to customize the controller before you play a game.
I recommend this controller to people who want to experiment with controllers and who are open minded. I prefer this controller over an xbox controller because of the super customization that you can't do in any other. A mouse and keyboard will always be better than this controller, but I think that this controller is better than a console controller mainly because the trackpad is more precise than a joystick.
This controller requires an open mind, practice, time, and patience.
I don't recommend this controller to people who want to just play games without that hassle.

I hope we get some way to just plug it like a normal controller and the option to configure it outside big picture.

Purchased the controller a couple of months ago as an alternative to my wired xbox 360 controller so I could couch game.
I've had some fun playing titles that require little skill, such as Kingdoms of Amalur and Torchlight II. However, for games that have required a more dexterous input, like any FPS - even some third-person games such as the Batman Arkham series - the touchpad lacks the familiar comfort of a joystick.
Whilst playing games I've found myself paying more attention to not messing up the haphazard touchpad input than any actual gameplay, ruining immersion completely. I've also found that some games crash (Saints Row IV) when using a custom configuration, which you will almost certainly have to do as the defaut one will be unusable.
The controller configuration options are nice but also a necessity. Community-driven configs are awesome, but way too reliant on Big Picture mode.
Ergonomically, the Steam Controller is bigger than I anticipated. Whilst the triggers and bumpers are tactile, the touchpad material and buttons are coarse and I haven't enjoyed sanding my thumbs every time I turn my camera. I've also found myself clutching the controller and pressing the rear buttons accidentally. The A, X, B and Y buttons are nice to press but quite small and far away from the right touchpad considering the size of the controller.
I'm tempted to say that the price is fair compared to other console controllers out there, but the lack of quality doesn't justify a £40 pricetag.
8/10 for people who have no prior experience in controllers, playing low-skill titles.
2/10 for people who have controller experience and are playing any first-person shooter or camera-driven third-person title. I'll be going back to my 360 controller.

This controller is amazing! It beats every other controller on the market for every kind of game. Im not overstating this. It can do everything your dualstick controllers can do, and more, and better.
Can it replace your mouse? Yes and No. It can replace your mouse and keyboard in cases where your input reaction time isnt comeptitive. In other words, it doesnt beat a mouse for multiplayer FPS at top tier levels. BUT it does perform well enough to play in casual FPS. And, I would argue, that with enough time and effort, it could even work for competitive FPS (for some people). But that you shouldnt get it for that purpose alone.
The other thing to note, is that if a game has hundreds of controls, it may be hard to map them all. That said, it still works well enough to justify using it and only occasionally having to press an obscure keyboard button in a game such as Arma 3.  But you can certainly fit 99% of use cases on the controller.
It is perfect for puzzle games, platformers, arcade games, driving games (better than mouse and keyboard, but wont replace 500 dollar steering wheel and pedals), Sports games, RTS, RPGs, FPS, and pretty much anything else.
Downsides? It still needs a lot of software and UI management help. At time of writing I cant pull up an onscreen keyboard OUTSIDE of steam. But thats coming I hear. Oh, didnt I mention? It also replaced your mouse if you are using this at a range from your computer as I do. And with the keyboard addition, it will be great for PC use at any range.

Near Death is a great well structured game that tasks you with surviving against the cold with limited resources fighting against time to secure your way out of the abandoned research site. What separates this game from other survival games is it always has a task and goal for you to work toward rather than most games where the only goal is to aimlessly survive.

Overall, I liked it... Despite the bugs, the game was enjoyable enough for me to keep playing. The game itself is a set of simple fetch quests. However, in order to sucessfully travel around the map and complete these fetch quests, you will need to craft various items and manage your resources. The difficulty slowly ramps up as you complete each task: visibility decreases and the wind becomes stronger, making travelling between locations increasingly difficult.
Bugs... there are a lot of bugs. You can jump-crouch through some of the windows (intact, non-broken windows), and you can also use/pickup items through windows. The collision with the terrain is sometimes glitchy as well. Worst of all is that whenever I'm within approximately 100 metres of the garage, my game starts intermittently freezing up for approximately 20 seconds at a time (nobody else seems to be experiencing this, so maybe it's just my setup?). I also experienced a total crash at one point. Regardless of the bugs, the game was still enjoyable.
Many people are complaining that the game is too short (about 3 hours), but I would argue the mechanics would get boring if the game was much longer. The game is bite-sized, but it's also quite tasty. That said, I don't think it's worth buying at its non-discounted price.

*For this game I will pretty much copy and paste my Fallout 1 review with a few changes, such as this game's world being larger and more content as well as the reputation system and Karma, other than that the game is pretty much the same as the first Fallout.*
For those of you who got this game after playing 3, New Vegas and/or 4, prepare for a whole different cup of tea.
This game is a isometric top down RPG(in case you didnt see the screenshots) and is a game that does not hold your hand whatsoever.
And this being an older Fallout game means.....
1) No tutorials and you are just thrown into the game straight.
2) No quest markers meaning you might bang your head trying to find the correct location.
3) You have to figure things out on your own.
4) You have to save frequently lest you lose progress.
5) Combat is significantly different that what you are used in future Fallouts, being slow and tactical.
6) Inventory management and bartering is more cumbersome.
7) Movement and exploration is slow with random encounters of random difficulty.
If any of those turn you off then I suggest you rethink your purchase. Other than that, the game has a compelling story, great characters and quests to take on, its pretty much what you expect from the Fallout games, you are tasked with a huge responsibility and you set out to explore the wasteland. Its a very good game for its time and if you can get over the old game tropes I listed above, you are gonna have a good time.

Storms were difficult, and honestly terrifying at times, and I perished many times while thinkng I could make a trek when I couldn't. I had to navigate a map without a marker, making me

Over all, the game is fantastic. It was short, and took me just under three hours to complete with all but one of the blueprints found. Despite being on the shorter end of the spectrum, the game was beautifully crafted in that I was rather psyched out every time I hear the storm, every time I frantically tried to patch a window or repair circuitry. The game doesn't need monsters or animals of any kind: the true enemy is nature itself.

This game is a breath of fresh air. Pure adventure survival against the elements, no zombies, mutants or robots. Basically you are trapped on an arctic station, in the middle of a storm. As the storm gets worse, you need to find and fix items to survive and ultimatley escape. There is also limited crafting of items to aid your survival.
Graphically it is pretty good, and the environments really feel isolated and bleak. Controls are smooth and the game is well put together. There is only a little voice acting but it is well done.
The only real issue is it is somewhat short, but there are several difficulty modes to up the challenge. Well worth the cost if you want a more pure adventure driven survival game.

Deus Ex. A lot of people like this series because of the nostalgia. Well, for me thats not the case. This is my first Deus Ex game, and it is beautiful. Sure, it may be just a dumbed down version of the first, but I've played the first and found it too dated to enjoy. But this game is really well done.
Story:
You play as Adam Jenson. He is a security guard for Sarif Industries in the year 2027. Sarif specializes in nanoaugmentation. They are kind of like prostetics, but they make you stronger than human. nanoaugmentation is a very controversial field, and it shows. In the game you can even see riots and attacks on Sarif.
At the beginning of the game, Sarif was attacked, and Dr Reed's (Adam's Girlfriend) team of scientists were killed, and Adam's attempt to save theme, he becomes wounded by one of the attacker. They throw him through a pane of glass, causing him to lose his limbs, eyes, and most of his torso.
6 months later, you are off of sick leave, and on call to defend the manufactoring plant of pro human purists, the ones against augmentation. One of them is actually neuroaugmented, and when they scan his neuroaugments for data, Adam gets tangled up in a quest to find his attackers, and a conspiracy thats been going on for twenty years.
If you are a fan of conspiracies like internment camps, FEMA camps, the Illuminati and human enslavement, this game is right up your alley.
Graphics:
The original style of Human Revolution was a very oranged-hued, yet somewhat realistic style. Things looked a bit too futuristic, in my opinion. It looked more like it was 50 years in the future, because everything kind of has this cyberpunk design, and the cities look radically different, comparing 2027 Detroit and Monteal to modern day is kind of jolting, but it looks good nonetheless. If you enjoy that Blade Runner aesthetic, than you'll love this.
Howefer, that orange look just isn't there is the Directors Cut, which I think is a bad moove. Everything looks bland, but it is bearable. It is jarring to see a transition from gameplay to pre rendered cutscenes, however, because they kept the filter for the cutscenes.
Music:
What a treat. The score is so good. You have ambient music in cities and buildings, really good music on the radios, interesting techno in clubs, and a mix of almost cyber and orchastral for cutscenes. The mucic goes well, and it was so good I had to download it to listen to all the time.
DLC:
The DLC in this game is boring, and you lose all your augments at the beginning. The game forces you to play their stupid DLC, which drags on for 5 hours.
Gameplay:
This game is meant to be a stealth game, of course. But, it really didn't play out that way for me. I didn't have the patience. So, I played through the game killing everything that shot at me. And boy, was it satisfying. At first it feels like your average action shooter, but then I got my augments up, and it was great. The feeling of punching down a wall and killing someone directly behind it at the same time feel awesome. Jumping from above onto a group of enemies and launching missiles from your chest feels great. But one augment that you have to get for this game is invisibility. That is when the game really just feels like a breeze, yet it still feels good to play through. It feels so good to confuse enemies while invisible. I absolutely love the augmentation system.
Hacking is boring, but I recommend it. It's free EXP.
Overall, with the DLC and filter removal, I give it a 9/10. I put 40 hours into this game and I do not regret one minute of it.

I finally finished this game at approximately 4am in the morning and wanted to get down a few words while it's fresh. Firstly though I should mention I've owned DE:HR since it first came out and have never managed to finish it through the years until now, purely because I always chose to play stealth and the game always punished me for that with it's redundant boss-fights that force you into a FPS combat game. So this time I played as an armed to the teeth psycopath and managed to create fun enough to get myself through the game. I'm left feeling though that the few chuckles I managed to summon by building box forts or comically placing explosives or dragging an entire apartment building's contents to the roof and throwing it into an alley rather than follow a quest marker, are some very brief bright spots of fun totally outside of what the games normal behaviour and everything else was a frustrating chore.
To put it simply, DE:HR is like sex without ♥♥♥♥♥♥. It's still kind of fun for a while but in the end it just leaves you tired and frustrated. About half way through I was looking at the clock ever five minutes and begging for the next terribly written boss encounter to be the end, but it just never came. Eventually I only finished the game due to my apparently masochistic completionist tendencies.
DE:HR is not a "bad" game. It is however a game that falls just short of being a good game. A sentiment that was only reinforced the few times I enabled developer commentary. So many small parts of the game could have been taken just a little further, or focused on a little more, and they would have come together to make a wonderful whole of a game, but instead they lay about as individual parts that frustrate the player by how obviously "almost" they are in nature, and I feel this way about almost every aspect of the game... giving it a few minutes thought just now I can't think of a single aspect, audio, story, animation, models, scenery, layout, ai, etc, that didn't severely disappoint me at least once.
In summary, DE:HR is a dissapointment and now that I've justified my purchase of it by putting in the work to complete it I'll happily never play it again.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution!! Awesome Game!! Love The Stealth On The Game And The Stealth Killing. Hacking Devices Is Fun Too '-' I Recommend This Game To Anyone Who Is A Fan Of FPS Games Or Simply Just Deus Ex Games, Go Buy It!

Deus Ex (pronounced day-us ex, not due sex) is a game set in the mid 21st century where humanity stands on The Techno-Social Brink: where technological advancements have caught up with, and threaten to surpass, social advancements. You play as Adam Jensen, the Chief of Security for Sarif Industries, the leading corporation for Human Augmentations.
The plot line is bloody brilliant, if a bit hard to keep up with. All the characters are strikingly independent in mannerism, look, and behavior. Dialogue has left you to want for nothing, and the voice actors are top-notch. What's interesting is that, while the plot will always remain the same, small branches will appear in the form of secondary missions which, while optional, are interesting in themselves. You have a choice in how you complete most of them; several you can just gung-ho murder spree everyone, but most there's always a second, and sometime's third, approach in how you solve the mission. In the end, morality does matter.
This game isn't so much a shooter, and should not be viewed that way. Nearly every encounter can be solved through stealth, which is way more interesting, and usually easier, as well as challenging. It also allows for a more realistic experience. Exploration of the enviroment will reveal multiple ways to approach a situation, as well as reveal thousands of lines of extra text; some are entertainingly random and unecessary, some are lore and extra plot, others will reveal codes and other such alternate routes or easy ways of access, and still others reval the secrets of the game itself.
To be honest, I was slightly dissapointed by the ending, but that's just my opinion. It's possible they left it open to a sequal. I haven't yet played, but have purchased, the Missing Link Expansion, so perhaps that will answer a lot of unsolved questions. I'm also sure a second play-through will reveal a lot of plot which I missed the first go-round.
Several of my lady-friends have a man-crush on Jensen. He's quite the masculine fellow. I myself fancy the fashion of the 2050's; a futuristic approach to Renaissance style.
In the end, it's definitely worth the $20.00.

I just finished Episode 4 and figured this was as good a place as any to leave my thoughts on this game.
When this game was first announced by Telltale, I was actually sorta disppointed.  At the time, there were plenty of other Telltale games that could use sequels or that I thought warranted attention other than something about Minecraft.  I mean, who would want to hear a story about Minecraft?  That would be stupid.  There was no way I was going to buy this.
Then, one day while I was suffering a weak will and may have possibly even been drunk, I ended up buying this game.  But I'm here to tell you right now it was probably one of the best mistakes I've made in a while.
To explain a bit about the game, like a lot of other Telltale games, it plays like a "choose your own adventure movie" of sorts.  It probably won't appeal to everyone... if you're looking for extreme action or something like a FPS or platformer, look elsewhere.  You spend a lot of your time watching scripted game sequences that are mixed together with interactive scenes that require you to make choices, perform actions, or navigate and interact with a game world scene.  It's basically an interactive story.
But what a story it is!  It's got excitement, comedy, love, betrayal, triumph, failure, happiness, and sadness all mixed in.  It's actually a rather brilliant piece of writing that kept even a skeptic like me thoroughly entranced through at least these first 4 episodes (the first major arc).
All in all, if you're into Minecraft at all, you'll probably get the most out of this game and it is well worth it.  I suppose the concept is simple enough that even though those who haven't experienced Minecraft may like this as well, but it may help with understandability to have at least a passing familiarity with it.
I'm definitely looking forward to continuing the series with episode 5 (and beyond), but I think before I do that, I'm going to take a little break.  If there's one other thing this game has done, it has also made me want to play Minecraft again.

Below you'll find a written and video impression on the game.
Remember back in the day, when people played multiplayer FPS on the same screen locally and on split screen? Remember how there's always that one person who's looking at your screen to find where you are? Well Screencheat is made for that one person! Except this time around, the game promotes each player to screen cheat and every one is on equal grounds!
The gimmick behind Screencheat is that every player is invisible with only each other's screen as indicators to where s/he might be. As a player, you must manage your own screen so you know where you're going and shooting, while paying attention to every one elses, so you know where to aim. It's a very simple idea that's executed very well.
Graphically the game isn't much to look at. It's more functional than it is pretty. Luckily for most, this is not the type of game that people will care too much about the aesthetics, rather the mechanics. As mentioned above, mechanically this game pulls off it's goal with success. It is a pretty basic FPS when you strip away the multiscreen / invisible player gimmick, but in a game like this, simplicity is probably for the best.
The game is very fun, especially if you have a soft spot for old time local play FPS feel, even if it does support online as well as local. It's nothing too special to look at, but it is something special to play with friends!

This review is a first impression of the controller. (Used it for one day in a variety of games)
Payed $80 with shipping to get it (I'm from EU, so in USA it might be cheaper). But I'm not regretting any penny of it. I have to say that I also have a Xbox 360 wired controller and I've used a lot a PS3 controller. So I have some experience with controllers.
I am fully recommending this Controller. Why:
1) The customization you can do with it is incredible. Additional to that, you already have mappings done by other people. This essentially means that you can play ANY game on Steam with it. EU4/CK2/you-name-it from the couch - no problem. No other controller on the market has this capability.
2) It's comfortable (for me). Almost on par with Xbox.
3) Uses 2 AA batteries, which means that you don't have to order a special accumulator in case the controller one dies or other charger bs. AA batteries are cheap and easy to acquire.
4) Almost 80 hours charge. (I haven't tested it yet, but people say it's pretty accurate)
5) Dual work mode: wired/wireless. Although in the description it is said that you don't get the USB cable, I had it in my box. Maybe they forgot to update the description?
Now I'm gonna list some negative things about the controller:
1) If you've never used a laptop touchpad, it'll take a bit of time to get used to the touchpad. But no big deal.
2) If you're transitioning from the Xbox/PS controller, it'll take some time to get used to the buttons' size and location. The Xbox guys will get used easier.
Basically, if you get used to things fast and are interested to get a controller that will offer you the power to customize everything you want - get this. (Like, it's not even that expensive, considering an AAA game costs about the same.)
Definitely buy it if:
- you don't have any controller and would like to get one for Steam

Near Death is an excellent game, in a minimalist sort of way. The only enemy is the environment: a freeze-to-death system which players of Cryostasis will find familiar, with the remarkably frightening addition that it is easy—and deadly—to lose one's way in the dark. The map is only that, and it's on the player to figure out where they are on it. This, combined with the darkness and whiteout conditions, makes placing guide ropes and beacon poles a very important (and actually rather enjoyable) mechanic. The crafting system works well, too. If I had one quibble, it would be that the final objective at the radar facility is not nearly so difficult as one might expect. (Or that the downed plane really should have been carrying survival gear.) Anyway, it's fun, it's atmospheric, and it's short enough that the limited mechanics don't get old.

No aliens, no enemy soldiers, just you and the weather.  The main thing to be aware of is that this is a short game, and does not encourage open exploration of the site.  That said, I felt tense when I was freezing, relief when I found a sealed room, and joy when I found a wiring box to fix.  Overall I greatly enjoyed the game, but would probably wait for a sale only because of the time to completion.  I hope at some point they consider making an expanded sequel.

This, is a very neat little game.
It's short, but there's not much else like it out there. Beat the game in just under 3 hours, so I would recommend grabbing in on sale somewhere in the $7-$10 range- you'll probably at most get double that hourage if you're looking to grab all the trophies.
The game does a great job of creating a constant sense of urgency, without being overwhelming brutal (on the normal difficulty), and there's a scene at the end of the game that's almost literal magic. It's one of those experiential things that is less about what occurs on paper, but how it impacts you directly as a player, how it makes YOU feel, and that alone makes me recommend this to ANYONE who enjoys good storytelling.

Not a horror game in the traditional sense, but a great "walking simulator" survival game where the only monster is the desolate terror and frigid cold of a very real place on Earth. Thoroughly enjoyed this short gaming experience.

You feel the pressure this game puts on you.
Things I didn't like:
- There is no way to easily return to
if you didn't clear it out the first time around.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution!! Awesome Game!! Love The Stealth On The Game And The Stealth Killing. Hacking Devices Is Fun Too '-' I Recommend This Game To Anyone Who Is A Fan Of FPS Games Or Simply Just Deus Ex Games, Go Buy It!

Deus Ex (pronounced day-us ex, not due sex) is a game set in the mid 21st century where humanity stands on The Techno-Social Brink: where technological advancements have caught up with, and threaten to surpass, social advancements. You play as Adam Jensen, the Chief of Security for Sarif Industries, the leading corporation for Human Augmentations.
The plot line is bloody brilliant, if a bit hard to keep up with. All the characters are strikingly independent in mannerism, look, and behavior. Dialogue has left you to want for nothing, and the voice actors are top-notch. What's interesting is that, while the plot will always remain the same, small branches will appear in the form of secondary missions which, while optional, are interesting in themselves. You have a choice in how you complete most of them; several you can just gung-ho murder spree everyone, but most there's always a second, and sometime's third, approach in how you solve the mission. In the end, morality does matter.
This game isn't so much a shooter, and should not be viewed that way. Nearly every encounter can be solved through stealth, which is way more interesting, and usually easier, as well as challenging. It also allows for a more realistic experience. Exploration of the enviroment will reveal multiple ways to approach a situation, as well as reveal thousands of lines of extra text; some are entertainingly random and unecessary, some are lore and extra plot, others will reveal codes and other such alternate routes or easy ways of access, and still others reval the secrets of the game itself.
To be honest, I was slightly dissapointed by the ending, but that's just my opinion. It's possible they left it open to a sequal. I haven't yet played, but have purchased, the Missing Link Expansion, so perhaps that will answer a lot of unsolved questions. I'm also sure a second play-through will reveal a lot of plot which I missed the first go-round.
Several of my lady-friends have a man-crush on Jensen. He's quite the masculine fellow. I myself fancy the fashion of the 2050's; a futuristic approach to Renaissance style.
In the end, it's definitely worth the $20.00.

I love this game's storyline, the way it plays and the way it looks! This "Director's Cut" addresses some valid concerns about the game's infamous "boss fights" (making stealth and/or hacking useful in those scenes). I particularly like the augmentation that provides more options in social interaction.
I love the writing, and interactions between Jensen and other characters (Malik, Haas, Zeke, and especially Pritchard). Jensen's interactions with Sarif really *feel* like having tense conversations at work with your boss.
So why am I uninstalling it, while I'm still so far from completion? Here's why
1) While the game carries on the tradition of multiple solutions to problems on many levels, it doesn't seem to recognize that the save function needs to be a little friendlier to actually implement these solutions. If I come to some sort of "fork in the road" involving mutually exclusive choices, I want to be able to access that crossroads again to try "the road less travelled". Having only this year discovered new dialogue choices in Deus Ex 1, despite frequent searches for them, you can see how much that fascinates me and other DX fanatics. Unfortunately, the save function doesn't allow for the naming of save games. This makes keeping track of where to find the road left unchosen, to explore the other option, a real pain in the sack.
2) Starting the game from scratch involves many scenes you can't avoid every time you restart. The most frustrating one is a walk over the factory floor with Megan that seems to take about half an hour every time you are forced to go through it --- you can't even bypass the identical conversations that she has on the way! Next time I install it, I'll be sure and keep a save near the beginning of the game when choices appear (i.e., when Jensen returns to Sarif Industries for the first time after his surgery).
3) The game crashes. A LOT. It also sometimes crashes my laptop. A LOT. I'll have to try installing this on one of my older laptops, one that doesn't also hold currently critical information about my professional life. (In other words, one that wouldn't rock my world if I lost the data on it).
Don't get me wrong, I still love the game and I'm sure I'll get around to starting it over and finishing it eventually. As frustrating as my objections are, I still think the game's worth playing. But I can't help but think that these frustrating problems were not unavoidable by the game designers, who (judging from the opening credits and the retooling of the boss fights, may have suffered from a case of too many cooks spoiling the broth).

This game is fantastic. There is no two ways about it. Well, mostly. The combat is solid. The level design is good with plenty of detail and believable clutter. The enemies are varied and they in themselves are also varied without looking like palette swaps. Imps can rush in for melee or hurl fire balls or giant fireballs, zombies get in the way as they should and big, ugly monsters scream and roar at you with the kind of hatred the game's narrative evokes. The weapons feel weighty in sound and action. The guns don't feel like your throwing pebbles (except for the pistol but you should never, ever be using the pistol). The mods you get for the weapons allow you to vary your attack style and everything in this is geared towards producing flying by the seat of your pants combat, often fast, brutal and ending messily for either for you or the demons. The game's speed and mechanics are a beautifully crafted and polished hybrid of modern FPS and old school twitch shooters.
The campaign is nicely long (no four and a half hour nonsense here) with varied rooms and environments to fight in. Discovering how to glory kill demons by positions, facing and how they are located around the environment can vary the mechanic enough and it's also quick enough that you're not going to spend an annoying amount of time watching the sequences.
The bosses are varied and entertaining, very interestingly constructed.
Playing on the hardest difficulty is the only way to play this as it makes everything frantic and all the more thrilling because of it so I will happily recommend this.
For the only negative, the multiplayer. It's done by some other team and you can tell. There's no heart, it's bland, by the numbers, console multiplayer pap. It feels slow and lethargic with gimped weapons and plays in a singularly uninspired fashion. Consider the multiplayer to be the ugly tumour festering on the face of a singularly beautiful game that honestly deserves far better.
[Edit] The ♥♥♥♥ing music, man! It'll have you pumping weights, punching through walls and making you feel pumped and angry, the exact mindset of the protagonist who gives not one♥♥♥♥♥♥for the story happening around him, only for the death of the demons.

I loved how cute this game looked and I'm really easily entertained when it comes to video games, so I was very excited to give this a shot! However, I've gathered my 'hours on record'' over the first 2-3 days of playing Aura Kingdom, and literally haven't touched it since.
The most appealing aspects of Aura Kingdom are the cute outfits, cool fighting partners, and relaxing environments. It's very easy to chill out and have a calm MMO experience with this game. I'm a huge fan of just, mindlessly farming for things in MMOs, and it had a great balance of being engaging, but also relaxing. At least, at first.
Once I got to around level 40 (which took me less than a day) the quest progression came to a screeching halt. When leveling up from 1-30, there was a good variety of quests. Of course, the most common quest type was the "go kill 8 mobs, then report back to me!" but it didn't feel too overwhelmingly prominent until I hit level 40. As I progressed through each zone, the variety of quests all just became the same "go kill 14 of this mob, and report back to me" back to back. Increasing with the number of mobs to kill as the zones levels became higher. I stopped once it had reached '16' as the norm for quests.
An example of a quest area would go as such...
NPC: "Hi! I'm in trouble, can you go kill 16 of those [insert mob here]?"
NPC: "Hey! Thanks for killing them. Now, can you kill 8 of [mob A] and 8 of [mob B] for me?"
NPC: "Yo! Awesome man! Alright, go collect 16 of this material around mobs you have yet to see! You'll have to kill some to get to the stuff I want you to collect, but that's fine!"
NPC: "Oh hey! You got the stuff I wanted... but those mobs you just killed a bunch of are scary! Kill 16 of them even though you've already killed quite a few"
NPC: "Thanks! Okay, now go kill 16 of [Another mob]"
NPC: "Oh wow! Kill 16 of the SAME MOB again! Why? I dunno they're like REALLY scary"
And this repeats for literally every single quest area. The questing is just, absolutely atrocious. I understand that some people love kill quests, it's the standard for MMOs, but this games way of doing it really just begins to feel like a chore at the later levels. It also doesn't help that the EXP you get from completing quests is nerfed significantly. Once you reach around lvl 45-55, it expects you to start the daily dungeon grind to gain the remaining levels to reach level cap. (which has been raised to 90 recently) So instead of completing a super tedious task and receiving around 10% - 15% of your current level, you only receive 2% at most. Which is a bit discouraging when each enemy takes a good 15-30 seconds to kill, and you have to kill 16 of them.
All in all, this game was very fun from the start. I played with some friends, browsed the item mall and contemplated sinking some cash into it once I reached max level. But I was never able to. Even if the added content from levels 60+ makes the questing better (even though I've read that quests full on STOP at lvl 55) I cannot recommend this game. Questing from 40-55 was such a low point that I have given up on it completely. :(

I just finished Episode 4 and figured this was as good a place as any to leave my thoughts on this game.
When this game was first announced by Telltale, I was actually sorta disppointed.  At the time, there were plenty of other Telltale games that could use sequels or that I thought warranted attention other than something about Minecraft.  I mean, who would want to hear a story about Minecraft?  That would be stupid.  There was no way I was going to buy this.
Then, one day while I was suffering a weak will and may have possibly even been drunk, I ended up buying this game.  But I'm here to tell you right now it was probably one of the best mistakes I've made in a while.
To explain a bit about the game, like a lot of other Telltale games, it plays like a "choose your own adventure movie" of sorts.  It probably won't appeal to everyone... if you're looking for extreme action or something like a FPS or platformer, look elsewhere.  You spend a lot of your time watching scripted game sequences that are mixed together with interactive scenes that require you to make choices, perform actions, or navigate and interact with a game world scene.  It's basically an interactive story.
But what a story it is!  It's got excitement, comedy, love, betrayal, triumph, failure, happiness, and sadness all mixed in.  It's actually a rather brilliant piece of writing that kept even a skeptic like me thoroughly entranced through at least these first 4 episodes (the first major arc).
All in all, if you're into Minecraft at all, you'll probably get the most out of this game and it is well worth it.  I suppose the concept is simple enough that even though those who haven't experienced Minecraft may like this as well, but it may help with understandability to have at least a passing familiarity with it.
I'm definitely looking forward to continuing the series with episode 5 (and beyond), but I think before I do that, I'm going to take a little break.  If there's one other thing this game has done, it has also made me want to play Minecraft again.

Summary
The Steam Controller offers gamers a new and intuitive way with which to play games through the use of touchpads with haptic feedback, gyro capability and deep customization. As a person familiar with typical game controllers and keyboard/mouse scenarios, it was difficult to wrap my mind around using the touchpads. An example of my early confusion is where you use the right touch pad in place of the right stick. If you tilt the right stick on a game controller all the way left or right, the camera would circle your player, however with the normal setup of the touch pad it just reached the end of your finger slide (on the touch pad) and stopped. By going into the Steam controller settings for the right touchpad and utilising the Edge Spin Radius and Edge Spin Speed I was able to emulate and fine tune this feature to my liking. The gyro sensor came in handy for FPS games. Enabling and configuring this feature allows me to press (think RS stick press) the right touch pad and tilt the controller in any direction to position of the weapon's crosshairs for a more precise shot. The haptic feedback tracks your finger movement on the touchpad. This can be extremely useful in letting you know exactly where you are touching and which direction your finger is travelling when panning a map for example. You can also assign mode shifting to buttons which allows additional buttons to be mapped or settings to be changed when pressing the button and each trigger also has a soft pull and full pull action (think weapon melee on soft, weapon fire on full). The customization possibilities are really awesome.
Aside from all these neat tricks and customization, there is a definite learning curve associated with the Steam controller. Because the layout is similar to, yet very different from an Xbox controller it's taking some time to memorize the layout of the buttons in addition to their functions when customizing. As I use it though, I am getting more proficient at the games I play. Would I recommend it as a replacement for other game controllers? That depends on what you want to do. If you just want to plug and play, then use the tried and true and get a standard controller. However, if you want to customize your layout and achieve a finer degree of control then yes, do give the Steam controller a try.
I haven't tried any keyboard/mouse games yet (e.g. the Witcher and so on) but it's good to know that I won't be confined to playing them in only that manner. The Steam controller brings user customization to the table, along with the ability to use it to actually play most PC games out there. In addition, the customizations can be saved as profiles and shared/ downloaded among other users. Final rating 8/10.

Near Death is, for all intents and purposes, a survival game. Unlike the sandbox survival titles that are usually associated with "survival", however, this game is story-driven, hand crafted with little to no random elements and, while it doesn't avoid the concept of "crafting", it has more in common with the permanent upgrades you'd see in a metroidvania here than collecting random junk to created another random junk. In fact, despite one open map, the game is very much linear.
Which is, probably, the biggest gripe I have with it. With the way the story progresses and the map is set up, I'm genuinely surprised the developers locked down exploration as much as they did with outright not giving you tools necessary to progress before they want you to by just making them unpickable. Which, unlike other key stuff the character would really have no reason to pick up until it becomes important, looks extremely stupid and also introduces the ugly "okay, now what" problem, when you have explored a location before you had to and have no clue that now you have to go back to it again.
All that said, this is quite a unique and amazing experience with you stumbling in extreme conditions from building to building, from room to room, searching for a warm place and something helpful to scavenge. To fix the rooms, to make navigation between buildings easier. It's a unique concept, which, while looking less beautiful and impressive as in Cryostasis, works really well and shows how exploration games can be made and how many themes, locales and ideas are still left unexplored for truly engaging experience. I would highly recommend checking Near Death for while it is deeply flawed, it is also very fun. Also, a great game to play during hot summer.

Near Death, a game about surviving alone in Antarctica after your plane crashes near an abandoned research facility, is a treat of smart and unique game design.  It's a short but sweet experience, with a simple premise elevated by its attention to detail and valuable sense of progression.
You start things off out in the open, facing down the chill and inky darkness of the derelict facility with only a flashlight to help peer through the night and a kerosene lantern for warmth.  The flashlight has limited life unless supplied with fresh batteries, and the lantern will warm you in sealed spaces, but only when fueled with vital kerosene; both of which can be found in precious scarcity throughout the facility.  Some parts of the facility interior have busted windows letting in the cold or doors held open by the wind which need to be patched up and shut respectively.  This is where some light crafting comes into play as the remains of canvases and duct tape allow for makeshift seals, letting you break out your lantern to ward off death once a room is closed off from the elements.  These mechanics never feel cumbersome though, as progress is saved regularly and you learn to think in small goals; taking baby steps to ensure survival rather than making a mad dash from one end of the map to the other, freezing to death in the process.  Immersion is a big part of the experience as well, as the only indicators that you're getting too cold or have fully warmed up is through convincing voice acting; shivering in the cold growing more and more panicked or a quick "much better" after huddling with your lantern.
The key to survival then, is braving the outdoors in hopes of making it alive to the next sealed facility space to warm up and look for supplies, then continuing on to the next major goal.  It's easy to get disoriented when out in the elements however, as the few, sparse lights of the barely functioning facility act as dim beacons in the dark and the wind rages against your progress.  It very accurately captures the feeling of struggling to find safety as your head bobs violently, exhausting yourself before barely reaching respite.  Yet narrowly escaping death and warming yourself in a new space, filled with supplies, is a feeling of pure joy and quickly becomes a highlight of the game.  It never feels unfair when you die, but rather, an error in calculation.  Perhaps you tried to go too far in a single trek and had the misfortune of coming upon a door that's been frozen shut with no more time to look elsewhere before you freeze.  You quickly learn from these mistakes, and learn the facility bit by bit, so you reload your last save and try to be smarter next time.
In short time, you come into contact with help via a teletype 2-way messaging system, and from there are given some hope for rescue and instructions as to how to survive long enough to be saved and bring some of the facility back online.  Turning a part of the facility from a barren deathtrap into a self-heating haven is elating, and offers a welcome break from the survival aspects of the game; allowing you to save on batteries and kerosene.  Rescue is still a long ways off however thanks to the turbulent weather, so basking in your small victory must give way to soldiering on and securing more long-term means of survival.  It keeps you engaged with realistic survival objectives to achieve, and rewards you for your efforts in tangible and surprising ways.
Ultimately, Near Death sets out to do one thing right, and it accomplishes it in spades.  Simulating a no-frills survival experience in a lonely, unforgiving place.  There's no monster besides nature itself, no magic to learn or shelters to construct from wood and earth, just you, some hobbled-together necessities of life, and the punishing cold and darkness.  It feels simple, but intuitive and engaging because of it.  It doesn't need to be more, and what it is is done with exceptional thought and care.  Near Death is a hidden gem in the survival genre, and it frames its own identity with a well-earned confidence.

Remember the good old days of local split-screen multiplayer? Remember how you could just look at your friend's screen to see where they were at any given time, even if they had an invisibility power-up? Well, this game was designed around that type of strategy and as far as I know is the only retail game in existence to have online split-screen multiplayer in an FPS. It's invisible screen-peeking instagib madness, and it's the most fun I've had in an FPS in a long time.
Many people argue that "screen peeking" is cheating, but in this game it's the only way to win since everyone is invisible until gibbed... or fragged... or eliminated... or slammed... or unfriended... or corrupted... or #PWN'd... or any verb the kill feed decides to use. And then you find out your ragdoll is a humanoid chicken, or a man with the head of a horse, or even just a good old fashioned skeleton. The game is very silly and doesn't take itself too seriously, which only adds to the fun. Even the weapons are silly, including a remote detonated bouncing bear bomb, a stick horse that allows you to charge at your opponents, and a candelabra that acts as a standard melee attack, as well as a more traditional blunderbuss (shotgun) and revolver.
Every stage is split into 4 colored areas, and for the most part they all have some kind of symmetry to them, but they still manage to be unique and some are almost just as maze-like as the old Goldeneye 64 maps. Overall, I'd say this is an excellent game to mess around with friends in, and the 4-pack is definitely worth it if you can afford it or get your friends to chip in.

I really wanted to like this game, but i just simply cannot.
I can't really mention any real pros, and cons, because everything would be a pro in this game, but fails at some point, so it becomes a con.
Let's start with the length. I have completed the game in about 35 hours, and after 15 i was really hoping for all this to end.
That's because the game fails at so much point, that it just couldn't keep me entertained for that long time. It was fun in the first hours, i got the feeling, i really got, but then it all passed. Let's see why.
*missions (no spoiler) - the skeleton of the mission-lines looks like this: you get an important mission. you go to a place, you find someone that could help, but he doesnt. instead, he wants you to do something for him, then go back, then talk again, then get on your important mission. Now. yeah, this is cool, if it gets played once. But not in the case of every damn mission. Seriously? I facepalmed myself so much during this game, that i just cant count it.
*world design - You will spend a lot of time on the streets, at a part of a city. You will have to navigate in it, go to places, find alternate ways, explore etc. But this aspect of the game becomes a mess, when you realize, that the design of the streets is so bad, that you would rather bang your head to the wall, than walk through the city again.
*loading screens, walking time - (let me mention, that i beat the system requirements by a lot at this game, so thats not the problem) I'll come up with an example again. You get a mission at x point of the city. You gotta go to y, but thats on the other damn part of the city. you go to one loading screen, go past a city hub, an other loading screen, and at the end of that hub, you will finally find the palce that you have to go to. This time gets doubled, by the fact that you cant navigate in the streets. After that, you have to go back to x, which is also a whole lot of time. This one also really annoyed me.
*AI - the AI is either too good, or too bad. Sometimes, they walk on a corridor, you sneak behind them, and all of the sudden, they hear you breathing, or something, and they turn to you, and shoot. But sometimes, you can just keep jumping behind them, or even sneak in front of their legs (!), they wont notice.
*boss fights - they are really bad. i cant really say much without spoilering anything, but they really are. They are buggy. They are bad. For example in one of them, you can climb up to a place on an open ladder (!), to a place to which the boss just cant follow you, even though he is a human being too, with a little bit of metal in his body. now, when you are there, the boss will go under you, will start throwing grenades, will hit himself, get confused, start walking confused, and then when you shoot him, he will notice you, and repeat. I get that in almost all of the games, there are bossfights, that you can, y'know, 'bypass the system', but this is just hilarious.
*story (no spoilers) - the story is kinda OK-ish too. It could have been good, but it just gets ruined by my first point. Only the basic situation, is what i can come up with as a pro, but that's not a thing to save a game.
*voice acting, gestures - An other example: the main character is squatting next to a dieing women, and he is like: 'stay with me. stay with me.' and does absolutely nothing else. I dont expect him crying, but cmon. at least touch her or something.
The voice acting is incredible good at some characters, or just annoying at the others. The last is the case at the main character. It's like he has a cold or something.
I played trough this game, just because i didnt want to leave it unfinished. Overall: this game could have been really good, but fails at decent points, which ruins the game. If you loved the original game, you cant be disappointed with this, but if you are new to the series, you will either pass these problems, because you will manage to enjoy the gameplay, or wish to get back the time, that you wasted on this game.

Bully is one of my favorite Rockstar games, and it comes highly recommended from me. It is well worth the price of admission.

This product fails both as an interactive movie and as a Minecraft spin-off.
I love the original Minecraft, I played it for more than 1,500 hours. What I love most there is the freedom of creativity, and for that, I was willing to accept the lack of refined graphics and roleplay in NPC dialogues. This so-called "Story Mode" keeps the blocky graphics (not in a game engine, that could have been spectacular - it is all drawn), but it takes away your freedom of movement and interaction with the environment completely, you folllow strictly limited corridors and obediently press buttons that are prompted to you on the screen or execute very obvious point-and-click set-ups. Building tasks are just recorded sequences that you go through by repeatedly hammering the same button a few times. Occasional puzzles and crafting tasks are so simple that a six-year-old could solve them with ease.
The dialogues are voice acted in decent quality. That said, they are slow, dumb and predictable, just like the story itself. Telltale is allegedly specialized on interactive movies like that, but they did not even get the technical basics right: The time to make your choice in a dialogue is limited, and the NPC keeps on talking while your time runs out, which means you have to listen to what he or she says, read what you could respond and think about which option would fit best with your character at the same time - really distracting! From time to time, the last word of the player character gets cut off; no idea wether this was bad audio editing or a performance issue. Anyway, neither the story itself nor the presentation made me happy. Is this supposed to be a cartoon for little children? That would explain a lot, but it was not advertised as such.
I will not get into that widely discussed issue with the final chapters of the story coming out as paid DLC - I could not even play beyond the second chapter (of eight in total) anyway because it was so painfully boring.
3.5/10 - not only is this not a good game, this is not a game at all. It is an overpriced and dull animated movie with Minecraft assets, constantly interrupted by short interactive sequences that are neither exciting nor fun. (For example, in more than one case you have to walk around 10 steps between two scripted scenes - this is not immersively interactive, this is just annoying.)
If you want a real Minecraft story mode, get one of those adventures written by modders, who set some parts of the environment as indestructible, but otherwise tell a story while still letting you play an actual game. If you are interested in the story that is told here, save your money and watch a walkthrough or LP online, but even if you won't: You do not miss out on much.
