I would like to start this review by commending the Development Team for being extraordinarily involved with the community and quite friendly. I asked a question before purchasing the game and the creator of Skara The Blade Remains, cromlech_, responded in a detailed and helpful manner. He then proceeded to invite me to his friend list and took the time to chat with me about my opinion regarding the game. This Dev team seems to be trying really hard to engage the community, be transparent, and take all of our suggestions to heart, and it's wonderful. For anyone interested in Q&A about the game etc., I recommend asking on the forums about when there will be Dev streams on Twitch. After the Q&A they will also be playing the game, so you can watch live footage straight from the Devs. See the TL;DR at the bottom for a short summary of my review.
Now, for the actual review- which I will likely edit as I play more of the game, play more characters, and as the game evolves:
As you would have likely noted, this game just released in a true Alpha state rather recently(about 3-4 months ago). Currently, since the announcement of true alpha, there has been at least one update a month; the last two updates added a playable tutorial, some new skills, bug fixes, implementation of suggestions by the community such as keybinding etc., This game is still in early Alpha - and I repeat, IT IS EARLY ALPHA. Do not expect a fully fleshed out game yet. The framework is there, and it looks quite promising. It will be free to play in the future, so if you would like to wait until its full release to play, then by all means, please do so. That being said, right now your job if you purchase this game is to test current balance between characters, test maps and game systems, and make suggestions on how to improve the game - because the Devs will listen and almost always respond.
General Gameplay - This game has a ton of potential and will be ludicrously fun once all the features are implemented. Right now there are 3 maps, one for each game mode, with plans for more. Some have lava(fall in it and you die) and levers that activate certain map effects. For example, in one map there's a ring in the center that gives way if you hit the lever and this leads to you, or your enemy, tumbling down into a pit of lava. There's also a huge boss-like monster that arises from within the depths of an arena. Currently this monster is an NPC and will attack every player that comes near it - players get extra points for hitting and killing it. A clever player could just stand back as his/her feeble opponents attempt to battle it..and pick them off as they back away in horror. Alas, you will respawn after perishing..so find solace in that.
There are 3 game modes. Team deathmatch, free for all, and duel. They are fairly self-explanatory. - I will update this section further the more I play, if I notice any notable deviations.
Each character, as you level up, has a set of skills the player can pick. Hold down RT or RB on the gamepad to execute said skills. Shinse has a skill that makes her invisible for a short period of time, and a teleportation ability that switches the player's position with that of his/her target. Also, the devs recently added an ability called, "forest wind," basically you can dash forward in a straight line, damaging any opponents in your path. They also added 1 new skill for the other two currently playable characters, which you can unlock through progressing(leveling up). There are plans to add passive skills and more primary skills.
There will be a store where you can buy costumes and weapons with in-game currency as well. These costumes will modify stats.
There will be daily quests/missions, factions, gems to modify stats and more in the future. There are placeholders available for them in game already, but they haven't been implemented yet.
For new players - There is a playable tutorial right after you create your first character. It explains basic attack, movement, and how to utilize your special attacks. You'll also be able to test out your skills at the end of the tutorial against a few AI opponents.
Most of the above systems are fairly barebones at the moment, because, well, it's an early alpha. Once they become more fleshed out, the game will have far more depth. I say that to warn the people expecting some kind of fully fleshed out product, in the hopes that the people purchasing the game will do so knowing that they are helping develop it with their suggestions et al.,
Combat Gameplay - Each character utilizes a string based on heavy/light attacks. I use an Xbox 360 gamepad so this would be RB and RT. I have played Shinse, thus far. She is a quick assassin-like character.  Her attacks feel appropriately light and heavy depending on what combination of attacks utilized, and they also look nice. Each character can also throw projectiles, a limited number, per life using the A button. Blocking is here too, but blocking attacks drains stamina - and you do NOT want your stamina drained or your block broken as you will be brutally punished by the AI or other players. That being said, the AI so far is kind of placeholder - For example, if you stealth as Shinse the AI will just stand there until you appear again. The last of the controls I will mention here is the "dodge" ability(B on the gamepad), which effectively...dodges. How effective the dodge is depends on your character - some of the heavy characters are a bit slower to dodge.
The devs also added 3 new abilities - one for each class, so far I have tried Shinse's out and it is mapped to the X button(again, using a 360 gamepad) by default.
Graphics - The game is optimized fairly well for an early alpha, though with recent updates the optimization seems to have gotten a bit worse. That being said, I experienced no notable system lag with all settings maxed. It looks really nice too. I realize "nice" is a vague descriptor, but it's the best I have. To put it another way- this game pleases my ocular orbs.
Controls - They are quite responsive. There doesn't seem to be any noticeable input lag. This game does have gamepad (360/Xbox) support as well as keyboard support. The developer has implemented keybindings with update 0.5.3.
Community/Online - You'll likely match up against the creative developer and creator of the game if you try out the online. Sadly, the community is fairly small at the moment and you may fight exclusively bots a majority of the time. I hope this changes in the future because these guys deserve both your support and your input as both will help make this game great.
So if the game is so early, why do I recommend it? Well, because I really like how involved the Developer is with the community, it shows supreme potential that I have no doubt will be met, and as a barebones early alpha, it's actually pretty fun!
TL;DR - Right now you're buying into an early alpha, with an established framework(meaning there's stuff there, like characters, some maps to fight on etc., but it's basic at the moment. Many features still have to be implemented), to help test out balance, make suggestions for improvements, and support the developer. That being said, it's only a $5 buy-in, and it is indeed fun even at this early stage of development. ^_^

Nier: Automata is a a beautiful game of rare depth and idiosyncrasies. While not the most technically accomplished--it sometimes looks like a much older game in terms of low quality art assets--it's washed out color pallet, sun drenched ruins and choir based sound track establish a world of echoes, one in tandem with the faded past it's narrative explores.
The story purports to be about a distant future when humanity is on the verge of extinction and has created andriods to protect its future. The games main protagonists (2B and 9S) are andriods tasked with this mission, but in actuality that is only the set up and not at all what the actual narrative is about. The game continually pulls the rug out from under the player in terms of what they think they know, but it does so in a way that gives new insight and meaning into what has come before, shifting perspectives--both literally and metaphorically--in a way that enriches and complicates rather than erases the knowledge the player has previously gained. If that sounds incredibly vague it is because I'm hesitant to spoil or telegraph the reveals.
At times it's anime stylizings almost overwhelm it's narrative, but they are kept in check by the understated themes it inhabits. It explores weighty topics of consciousness, the search for the definition and purpose of God, what it means to be human, and the struggle to find and/or make meaning. But more importantly its take aways on these topics aren't cheap or cliche, or even always uplifting or complete, but they are well earned.  At times the game seems very self serious steeped in it's own lore.  At other times it is playfully flippant or engages in meta-humor, but it all works together to create what is one of the most thought provoking and original JRPGs I have ever played.  Highest recommendation. 5/5

Near Death creates a fantastic narrative around two major gameplay mechanics: temperature management and orienteering through incredibly an harsh/disorienting environment. The game gives you a visceral feeling of urgency, dread, and with nothing more than the conditions and your situation, can cause the hair on your neck to stand up.  The environments are well done, the difficulty is well-balanced, and the story/portrayal of events is engaging.  I'll be honest, It's roughly 3 hours of gameplay while moving at a relatively casual speed, and thus falls out of my normal $1/hr of entertainment guideline I typically stay to, but this was a very unique and enjoyable experience that left me happy with my investment based on what I got out of the game.  The psychological and physiological effects this game has on the player without any monsters, jumpscares, or anything of the sort was thoroughly enjoyable.

: I mean, in the middle of the Finnish summer, short as it is, I was
while in-game I was freezing at below 80 degrees C temperatures and fighting for my life.
is a convoluted experience. It's a survival story about not freezing to death. It's also got simple crafting mechanics and some exploration aspects.
However, the emphasis is really on the story and the desperate atmosphere. The limited resources demand action and constantly pushing forward. It is
despite its gloomy looks and rather obvious sources of inspiration, although the situation presented would be considered horrendous in most scales. Yet the atmosphere is intense and keeps you on your toes.
Story begins as you crash-land to Antarctica in the middle of the (polar) night. Alone in the dark, the only spark of hope is the nearby research station. Alas, it is abandoned. You have to get out of here before lack of heat, hunger and shear exhaustion bring you down!
The story is simple, yet powerful. You set out to gather various resources and find shelter. Not only are the supplies extremely limited, there's also what would be considered the blizzard of the century coming up if it were experienced way up here in the squishy latitudes. Your only solace: a contact in another station. But the news are always bad.
Atmosphere in
is immense: darkness engulfs the landscape and only dim storm lights lead the way to a shelter. And the storm is getting stronger.
Fairly intuitive, you will die of hypothermia if you stay too long in the cold. A main game resource is heat and how to retain it long enough to complete all your tasks. Fortunately you've got a heater that can be used in-doors, as long as the room is sealed.
However, heater takes fuel. Your meagre flash-light requires batteries and it keeps running out. Good thing the protagonist has a knack for tinkering and can craft all kinds of nifty tools and upgrades. No silly combining is required, you just click on the craftable item in the inventory and she creates it if there's enough parts at hand.
The constant rush forward is relaxed only after you get the power up and may think about your slim options.
The whole game only takes a few hours to complete but it is intense. There are four difficulty options, from
to
, the latter a reference to the classification of the most extreme weather conditions on Antarctica. Difficulty affects the amount of resources, the resilience of the protagonist and the duration of the flashlight batteries/heater fuel.
Almost bug-free, only once I got stuck in some snow bank and promptly died of cold. I experienced no crashes during any of my playthroughs. I played it once on Normal (I took ~4 hours) before playing it through thrice on Condition 1 (~2 hours per new game).
The experience was so cool (pardon the pun) that I feel
has great re-playability (hence my extra playthroughs), even after grabbing all the achievements. I feel that a great part of the reason was the intense ending that only feels stronger at higher difficulties.
The game is unfortunately quite short so maybe the €15 ask-price is a bit steep, but on a sale, I think it's well worth at least €10. It surely made me appreciate our double-paned windows in a new light.

When I first got the steam controller, I was fairly impressed. After less than 40 hours of use, the battery capability of the controller is completely broken. Refreshed with brand new batteries, it just plain doesn't work and requires the cord to function. Very poor and disappointing performence based on that.

At first, this controller was difficult to use due to the strange layout of the buttons and analog stick. Later on, I got used to it, and I prefer it as my main controller for all games. The mouse pad on it is very useful and the haptic feedback is spectacular. I started to use the paddles on the back more than I ever thought I would, and they are great! The battery life on this controller is untouchable. I have been using it for almost a month and still haven't switched from the batteries it came with! This controller is a must-have for any PC gamers out there looking for a gamepad.

So after using the controller for a while, I think it's okay to write a review.
I only ever used an Xbox controller and a ps1 controller before in my life, but the steam controller felt something very different from any of those. And not in a bad way. The controller feels good in your hands, it handles inputs very, VERY well, you can basically configure the inputs to any games you want, and the extra two buttons on the back really help with so many games out there. The only sort of negative experience I had with it is the software part of the controller. Some games, like Warframe, just cannot be played with the steam controller because every time I try to config the controller while in-game, set the sensitivity right and such, steam randomly decide to reset my whole configs to the default one i've been editing for some reason. As soon as valve fix this issue, I'm happy.
Overall I can't find a reason not to buy a steam controller, it's fun to use and after getting used to it, you just can't put it down.

The analog stick feels great, as do the XYAB buttons, but everything else feels like it's got a limited number of presses before something's going to crack. This may sound nit-picky but a controller's button feel is something fundamental that needs to be right.
On the usability side, the conventional layout is jarring initially but it doesn't take long to adapt. I haven't had any software/compatibility issues yet and using Big Picture to configure the controller is less painful than it sounds.
If the build quality of the Steam Controller was on-par with Xbox and PlayStation controllers it would be much easier to recommend, ideally there would be a middle-ground between a Yes/No recommendation. As is, it's a decent attempt by Valve but the cheap feel really lets down what could be a fantastic product.

It's hard for me to review this controller and not rate it based on the potential I see for it. A lot of reviewers are going to tell you that this controller "might not be there yet." I've had this controller for about a month now and I think I'm ready to give my verdict on it. But first...
I'm a tinkerer. I love getting gadgets that do new things and learning how to use them and how to tweek them to make them work better. Getting new kinds of periferals is one of my favorite things, from the Hydra Motion Controller to the Rift and now to the Steam PC Controller. I'm no stranger to working with xml files and spending the time to learn how to use every feature one of these "toys" has to offer. I think this is important to understand about me when I tell you this:
I think that this controller is very much a success at what it has set out to do. I'm loving playing games with the controller from my couch and I feel very competant at them 90% of the time. I have played games like Total War, Street Fighter, Dark Souls 2, modded Skyrim, etc, and I've put the controller through it's paces. At first, it was easier to play the RTS games than the action adventure ones, but with a little exploration and practice I found a configuration for the trackpads that makes camera controller and movement nearly flawless. And the grip buttons are LEGENDARY! I honestly can't complain, and every firmware update releases new fixes and potential posibilities for this controller.
Sadly, the only genres that I don't have a lot of experience playing with this controller on is the Action RPG and MOBA genres. My short brushes with the genres and this controller have left me a little troubled... I'll need to play around with it more before I can say for sure that these genres aren't well suited to this controller. I do believe, however, that with time and practice I can change this part of my review.
That being said, I do highly recommend this controller to anyone, under the condition that you don't just pick it up, try it once, and throw it down in frustration. You will have to play around with the track pad configurations to find the perfect fit for you. The payoff? You'll finally be able to enjoy gaming on your computer while reclining in your favorite couch/chair. If that doesn't appeal to you, then just stick to what you know and wait for the next big thing to come around.
I look forward to watching this controller evolve and it's player base grow more experienced!

I got the Steam Controller because I like revelational technology and interesting new ways to experience the entertainment we call "Gaming". I'm a programmer and everything I do has a PC component: TV, social media, calls, work, and gaming. For the longest time I have considered every aspect of a computer better than a console.
PCs are easily updatable and upgradable, they perform many more functions than a console, they are more portable, personalizable, and their gaming potential has always been--to me--more purposeful and accurate.
So obviously I don't often game on consoles and when I do I always have trouble with the poor accuracy of the basic console controllers. But the Steam Controller intrigued me for its potential and open-minded design. When I finally got a Steam Controller I specifically bought some games that would pair well with a controller as opposed to the PC so I could measure how it performed compared to the industry standard for consoles. I was happily surprised.
The Steam Controller takes some time to get used to because it really is a blend of a controller and a mouse; and it is a very good blend at that. It can easily play any controller based game without issue and work just as expected, but where it excells above and beyond a standard controller is in its PC-minded customization.
The Steam Controller can be rebound to your hearts desire, but it goes even further than that. Just as you can alter the hardware and software of your computer, you can do the same with the Steam Controller. You can set and name the buttons, adjust dead-zones on the touch pads, you can even rebind the left touch pad to be a second set of four buttons.  You can set each button as a Macro to perform several button presses at once and have buttons change the purpose of other buttons while held down.
The dramatic customization options not only improve and personalize a gamer's experience, but inhance its tactile effect as well as performance. I have yet to investigate it myself, but from simply checking out the customization menues I have become quite excited about the possibilties of customizing the motion-gyro as well: flying a piloting game by actually moving the controller for example.
All of that is simply the Steam Controller's use and versatility in controller-based gaming.
The Steam Controller really shines when you realize you can make a PC exclusive, non-controller supported game into a controller game. With some customization you can perfect and create your own controller commands for any mouse and keyboard title. This kind of versatillity has yet to be matched and I am happy to say it will be hard to exceed the current power and potential of the Steam Controller in this aspect.
On top of everything else, Valve has made the Steam Controller with the community in mind. Control schemes are available for download and upload as part of the community which makes finding the best control scheme for you without having to do it yourself easy. On top of that, having the same controls as friends or simply on multiple controllers is a breeze. What I salute Valve for, however, is examining community contributions and including the best as actual features in software updates. This means that improvements to the software are able to come sooner rather than later because Valve has a whole modding community assisting them at times or simply coming up with better improvements.
If it's not obvious enough yet I give the Steam Controller 9/10. It works wonderfully and functionally now, but not only can it be improved with software advancements, but it will be improved because if Valve doesn't do it, there is a programmer out there who will.
The Steam Controller also works as a mouse when you are outside of steam, allowing you to stay on the couch to quickly find something on the internet or close out an alert. The Steam Controller also has a great built in keyboard function that mimics texting and is WAY better to use than standard controller-based keyboards of the thumb-to-and-enter-each-letter variety.
Comes with batteries and can be wireless or corded and the cord doubles as a wireless extender.
The price is a bit high for a PC controller, but when you consider the XBOX 360 Elite Controller is $150 and the Steam Controller is just as accurate and even an improvement on functionality it is a steal.

I had reservations regarding the new paradigm that Valve is pushing with this controller layout, but my wired 360 controller started shorting out, so I was looking for a new controller (possibly just hooking up one of my Dualshock 4's).
Being a Linux gamer, and having looked at the work-arounds for getting either the DS4 or Xbone controller to properly function, I became pretty discouraged and decided that I should go with hardware that had native support.
Initially it's a bit a odd, and does take some time to get used to, but after only a couple of hours I became a huge fan.  It works really well with games that already have controller support, and does an excellent job at emulating a mouse and keyboard setup.
I highly recommend owning one of these if you prefer a controller for most games; OR you've done like I have, and you have your Linux/SteamOS box connected to your TV to play your Steam games.

I cannot recommend his contoller enough!
If you love micromanaging your controls schemes and making them perfect for your playstyle, this controller is for you. I've played first person shooters, platformers, adventure games, and even pinball, and this controller has never let me down. I prefer it to a mouse and keyboard in almost every scenario. Even games I've played for years like TF2 I now enjoy using the Steam Controller.
I have almost no background in consoles. Other than owning a few Nintendo consoles, I've always been a PC guy, and I certainly never enjoyed having to play an FPS woth the dual stick setup. The track pads work like little mousepads for your thumbs, but are even better than that odd description I just gave them. And as if that weren't enough, there's also gyro controls, programmable for whatever you like, whether it's extra precise aiming, the tilt on a pinball table, or anthing else you can think of.
One last thing on the level of customization: you can change just about any setting for the controller. Want the triggers to activate sooner with a lighter push? You got it. Want to make a button into a turbo-button for super-mashing-action? Sure thing. Would you rather your control stick act like a group of buttons, rather than a stick? Why not? And with the ability to change your preferences on the fly, you can make modifications even once your game has started.
All in all, throw out your Xbox controller and check your mouse and keyboard at the door, 'cause where we're going, we don't need traditional peripherals.

Very impressed with this game! Not your typical survival game, as it's not open ended, has a storyline, and is rather short, but a masterpiece nonetheless. I'll try to keep this review spoiler free, as giving away details will ruin the experience.
You play as a pilot who's plane crashes in Antartica. Heading for a nearby research outpost, you discover it abandoned, and must find a way to survive and escape.
Graphics aren't top of the line, but are decent enough. The game makes liberal use of the snow effects, using it to obscure far away distances, but does so in a realistic manner. Most of the interiors were fairly generic, but given that it's supposed to be an Antartic rescearch facility, it didn't need to be unique, in my opinion. Exteriors were better, but that may be because I didn't take too much time to examine them, as you're almost never safe outside, and can rarely see very far in front of you.
Lighting was well done, not too bright not too dark, enough to make me have to make use of my flashlight, but not so much to where I was leaving it on all the time.
The game offers a few filters in the options, which I thought was a nice touch, however, I don't recommend them for your first playthrough. It's hard enough to get your bearings in the storm without extra filters.
One of the high points of the game. From the foreboding music, to the near constant howl of the wind, to every creaking metal door you open, even the crunch of snow as you walk, the sound design of this game did an amazing job of setting the mood. There wasn't much in the way of voice acting, but the little there was sounded realistic and well placed. The deep gasps of warm air after trudging through the snow and nearly freezing to death are incredibly satsfying to hear.
The story wasn't deep, but served it purpose of driving the game foward. It consists of your character's correspondence with home base, which is where you get your objectives and information on where to find suppiles. The teletype machines, reminicent of old spy movies, made the choice of minimal voice acting interesting. Still, I felt connected to the character. Her sarcastic wit, to her reassuring herself she can make it, and even her sighs of relief when she finally gets warm, really helped put me in her shoes- er, snow boots.
Controls were simple and intuitive, consisting of WASD keys for movement, C to crouch, space to jump,  1-5 for selecting items and left clicking to interact or use your equipped item. The game did a good job of making me feel like I was stumbling and having trouble walkng in a straight line during strong winds, afraid that I wasn't heading in the direction I thought I was, just like a real storm.
Another high point of the game, arguably the best point. Sound and graphical design did a good job of immersing me in this game, and gameplay mechanics did a good job of keeping me there.
The heat/cold system was well done, rather than giving you a temperature gauge, gave you audible cues from your character to let you know when it was time to stop and get warm and if you were warm enough to continue. I usualy see games like this trying to add monsters or creatures creeping around in the shadows trying to kill you, instead this game decided to make nature itself the antagonist of the story. As the game goes on, the storm gets stronger, and you start to wonder if you're going to make it.
The crafting system was simple, but interesting. Supplies were just sparse enough to force you to manage your inventory carefully, lest you run out of something important like kerosene for your portable heater or batteries for your flashlight. New recipes were unlocked by finding folders stamped with the research facility logo, or a couple of times by finding a new item. There were even a few upgrades for your gear, such as a manual that details how to make your parka warmer so you can last longer in the cold.
This game had me so sucked in that even though it was 70 degrees in my house, I was getting chills, and when I paused to take my dogs out, I was fully expecting a blast of cold air to hit me when I opened the back door. At points, I'd recieve another objective and would just stop and stare at the door for a few seconds, mentally preparing myself for the storm raging outside. The sense of dread that you might not make it to the next safe space to get warm hangs over you right up until the end. The thought of "Did I get everything?" that crosses your mind right before you step out into the snow to trek to the next building, because you REALLY don't want to have to come back because you missed something. The thoughts of, "Will I make it?""Should I use my meager supplies now or save them?""Oh God, I hope the next building is close" all cross your mind as you focus on trying to stay alive, and trying to escape.
This was probably one of my favorite purchases in a long time, and my only regret is I waited so long to pick it up.
This game nailed the atmosphere, and it's a great survival challenge.

Cold, dark, tense, and fun as heck! There are no jump scares and there are no monsters. Just our protagonist and the elements. An intensely compact game that can be finished within a few hours at most, but packs an incredible amount of tension and palpable fear of the cold. The immense struggle to compare this to more famous survival games is hard to let go, but I'll instead wish to point out that there is no amount lacking in conveying the unforgiving nature of being alone in the cold hoping to just make it to the next building to warm up.
The environmental detail is sparse - but then again this is a land of ice and snow. The game succintly develops a sense of tension as the weather whips up and the cold drops down further and further around you. There is an amazing soundtrack that creates an oppressive feeling in your ears when you wander into the darkness. It's a pulsing sound like that of a heartbeat. Which leaves you feeling paranoid, alone, and as if something is hunting you. The Artic has thrilled the minds of explorers and scientists since it was first recorded. And has taken it's fair share of lives of the brave, unfortunate, and unlucky. When the very elements of the land are so hostile and dangerous to people that is the greatest threat and it's fascinating that this game was able to re-create this feeling.
I greatly enjoyed this game and recommend it to anyone who wants a short but great game. I highly recommend playing this in the dark with headphones. I hope the developers of this game will create something akin to it in the near future with the same nuanced fear inducing feeling.

A short but sweet game.  I put nearly 4 hours into it, but I was taking my time and thoroughly exploring everything I could.  It's probably no more than a 3-hour game for most people.  Although it bills itself as "survival" and "action", there is not much of either, except in a broad sense - you just have to stay warm! - so if you are expecting mechanics that focus on either of those things then maybe think twice.  It is more of an exploration game, with a series of quests to find your way to specified building (which are all marked on your map) and scour the place to find some item or perform some action.  Along the way you can collect various odds and ends for some simple crafting to create useful items or upgrades.   It reminded me a bit of the beginning of Kona, where you explore the icy village.  All in all I enjoyed it.

"In the face of overwhelming odds, I'm left with only one option. I'm going to have to science the s**t out of this."
I've described Near Death to some people as an excellent video game adaptation of The Martian; a story of a scientist alone in an incredibly lethal environment, fighting against all odds and incredibly poor luck to stay alive. It's definitely scary, in fact many other readers have tagged it as a Horror Game. But for once, it's really really cool to have a horror game in which camp-enthusiasts are not encouraged to laugh in jest at the weirdness of the tentacle-faced monsters you face. Near Death's only opponent is the cold - temperatures below 100 degrees celcius, and winds that have the power to turn a sprint into a 1-foot-per-second crawl.
Progress in the game involves a long series of fetch quests through the facility's many buildings. Any room without a total vacuum seal against the outside is freezing cold, meaning that sometimes your progress through buildings may have to be taken in steps, and some rooms have such large breaches that you'll need to rush your looting to avoid freezing.
The game is actually quite brutal just in the challenge of getting between buildings. Mercifully, you have a compass, but even with that, it's very easy to lose your bearings in such total darkness, and even high winds reducing your speed. You can redeem yourself by planning ahead and crafting light / rope poles to make return trips easier, but even these can go wrong. More than once I made a stupendous trek through the snow, found the building, got inside, only to find out that through my desperate run, I ended up at the wrong building (or, even, the back door of the building I had left from).
Sometimes, I thought "
. The doors here are frozen over?? This turnout feels unfair. I want to give up. Kill me so I can go back to my last quicksave." But...something about the theming of the situation made me reconsider. I thought about moments in The Martian where Mark exhibits just about the same feelings. It made me want to turn those situations around. I knew I wouldn't reach the building I was aiming for, but I kept going, kept trying to recover my goals, because a person in this real situation wouldn't get a second chance. I certainly did die a few times, even playing on Easy Mode (
)
Near Death is very short, so buy it if you tend to not have enough spare time to finish off most games in your Steam backlog, since you could very likely easily binge through it in one gaming session. I felt like it was unique enough and well-executed enough to be worth my time either way.

This is a game that provides a true feeling of survival without being annoying. There are no monsters or enemies, just an agressive weather which requires you to move quickly between safe areas.
The game is well balanced because, while you cannot explore everything at first because of the limited time you can stay outside, you'll be required to come back to certain areas, with better gear and your memory will help you to avoid getting lost, which is the true danger.
The graphics aren't amazing but they're good enough and give a certain mood to the game. I played at normal difficulty, died a few times and finished it in around 3 hours, which seems short but the immersion was great and for the price it's right.

The words ‘indie survival game’ might rightly encourage a degree of nausea in many of Steam’s users, after the horrific flood of terrible titles allowed onto the marketplace through Greenlight and the like poisoned the well for so many genuinely competent works. But every once in a while you find that diamond in the rough that bucks the trend and actually manages to deliver everything that indie games promise – a unique experience that doesn’t have the market clout necessary to see it given attention or funding from a major studio, often an experimental or left-of-centre concept, perhaps something personal, or simply something with a single, focused ambition.
Near Death is absolutely that diamond. Built with a loving nod to John Carpenter’s The Thing, you play a pilot and engineer whose plane is downed in a storm whilst on-route to her base in Antarctica. You crash-land near a decommissioned station, and with the temperature plummeting and visibility decreasing by the minute, you must find your way to the nearest building and contact your colleague via teletype, who gives you what little assistance he can. From then on, the situation becomes more and more bleak as you find supplies and reactivate the power to the various parts of the station, braving the storm to venture between different buildings and build your plan of escape. Spending any more than half a minute outside will kill you, and your movement and vision is impeded as you freeze to death. You aren’t much safer indoors, as rooms with broken windows or walls offer no respite from the cold, and you have nothing to warm you but a small portable heater that will only work in sealed rooms. You can improve certain items such as your torch and parka, and these will make survival marginally more likely, but despite my initial overestimation of my abilities, you can and will get lost outside if you’re not careful, which will spell certain death under most circumstances.
The game saves frequently, thankfully, so even if you die, it won’t likely set you back very far, but there is a certain degree of anxiety that hits every time you have to trek to another building, especially as the game progresses and the storm gets worse. The wind picks up and can make walking almost impossible unless you have fashioned or manage to find or build a rope line, which mitigates the movement penalty of high winds, and gives you a trail to follow to the nearest building. These are few and far between, and absolutely necessary in the later stages of the game, and there’s no worse feeling than knowing you’ve left underprepared when the wind is stopping you from moving forward, and you’re too cold and tired to move back, and you just know that you’ve doomed yourself.
The games visual assets are simple, but suitable. We’re not looking at the Unreal 4 engine here, but there’s enough of a degree of detail in the environments to give an immediate feeling of familiarity to anyone that’s…y’know…been to a science base in the Antarctic, and the lighting effects are extremely well-implemented; darkness feels suffocating, the buildings are creepy in their dark, unexplored corners, and the eerie green pulsing glow of light poles will fill you with dread as they appear and disappear from view. Similarly, the script is simple but tight, and the small amount of voice acting on hand is believable and helps immerse you in the world. As your character starts shivering uncontrollably and your movement lurches and slows, you might feel a genuine chill within yourself as you know that you’re killing her. But in that way, every light in the distance becomes a beacon of hope, and closing the door on a sealed room leaves you with a palpable sense of relief.
Near Death is not an epic affair, but in a market that has been flooded with games that oversaturate themselves with gimmicks and vast but empty worlds, it’s always refreshing to come across a game that performs a single premise very, very well. And Near Death absolutely nails it. I recall that when pondering whether or not to buy this game I was unsure from the reviews as to whether it was just a ‘walking simulator’ or something similar, but I can assure you that it’s not. It is a survival game, and a bit of an adventure, and the degree to which you scavenge and prepare ahead of venturing into the cold, especially in the later game, will absolutely make the difference between life and death. As your supplies dwindle (maybe you’ve been a bit too frivolous with your flashlight or your heater), you will find yourself praying to find a single item in one of the desks or lockers, and if you can’t, you will steel yourself to make do and hope for the best. Or perhaps you’ll do as I did and run out of the equipment to make rope poles, be forced to venture blind into the height of the storm and pray you make it to the nearest building, get disorientated, nearly die, and make it inside just in time to save yourself from the brink, all in order to retrieve and reuse some poles from elsewhere. This game is harrowing, and after I was finished I felt like I watched a great survival movie. It’s a class act, and I frankly can’t believe I haven’t heard of it before.

Starting from presupposition that I'm a fan of the Metal Gear Solid's saga since the first chapter, I have found that this chapter's gameplay, above all if it's played in a stealthy way, is as deep as the older games like MGS that I played years ago making so my game experience even more exciting.
The plot is intriguing and quite twisted, It pushes the player to complete It, intriguing him even in doing side quests in order to understand better the game's world and the issues addressed such as, for example, transhumanism and the ethical and moral implications of progress scientific.
The story is about a man, Adam Jensen, who found himself involved in a terrorist attack facing the Sarif Industries for which he works as a security guard. He is mortally wounded and converted later into an enhanced cyborg.
There's a high graphic detail, which allowed me to admire some beautiful landscapes. Among them one in particular is still in my memories. The secondary characters are poorly characterized, and this is a shame, but the choice that is given to us to respond to the various dialogues on the basis of what we want allows us to give some peculiar personality to the protagonist.
Furthermore, the possibility to choose the skills of the protagonist based on the type of game you want to play (ranging from the action to stealth) is quite guessed, so we can complete the game several times in different ways, although not influencing the ending, unfortunately.
The only flaw? The difficulty! Do not get me wrong, it is quite high in the general gameplay, especially if played in stealth mode, but I personally found the boss a bit too easy to overcome!
I loved to play this game from the beginning, so I recommend it to everyone.

Partendo dal presupposto che sono una fan sfegatata della saga di Metal Gear Solid fin dal primo capitolo, ritrovare un gameplay che se giocato in maniera stealth sia profondo quanto quello evocatomi anni fa da MGS ha reso la mia esperienza di gioco più emozionante.
La trama è intrigante e parecchio intrecciata, cosa che spinge il giocatore sia a completarlo sia ad incuriosirsi anche nel compiere sidequest per capire al meglio il mondo di gioco e le tematiche trattate quali, ad esempio, il transumanesimo e le implicazioni etico-morali del progresso scientifico.
Racconta di un uomo, Adam Jensen, che ritrovatosi coinvolto in un attacco terroristico rivolto verso le industrie per cui lavora come addetto alla sicurezza, le Sarif Industries, viene ferito mortalmente e trasformato, successivamente, in un cyborg potenziato.
Il dettaglio grafico è elevato, il che mi ha regalato alcune splendide panoramiche da ammirare, delle quali ne ho conservato una in particolare. I personaggi secondari sono poco caratterizzati, e questo è un peccato, ma la scelta che ci vien data di rispondere ai vari dialoghi in base a ciò che vogliamo ci permette di dare una personalità nostra, al protagonista.
Inoltre la possibilità di scegliere le abilità del protagonista in base al tipo di gioco che vuoi effettuare (dall'action allo stealth) è parecchio azzeccata, così da poter completar il gioco più volte in modo diverso, nonostante non influisca nel finale, purtroppo.
Unica pecca? La difficoltà! Non fraintendetemi, è abbastanza elevata nel gameplay generale, specie se giocato in modo stealth, ma ho trovato personalmente i boss un po' troppo facili da superare!
Ho adorato giocarci fin dal primo momento, per cui lo consiglio a tutti.
Worth every penny.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is set in one of my favourite universe: the Cyberpunk universe, set in a near future where all is black and there is no more hope. Even if a lot of games use that universe, Deus Ex: Human revolution makes it look fresh and new. And this time you play as an overpowered Cyborg ex SWAT with bionic arms with bombs and swords in them!
The story is set before the original Deus Ex, and just like his predecessor, Deus Ex: Human Revolution has an addicting story and you will immerse yourself in after only a few minutes of gameplay (at least for me). The game also has really good soundtracks that perfectly fits in the game.
There are a multitude of lethal and non-lethal guns, rifle, shotguns, pistols etc.. that looks unique and different, and almost all the weapons can be upgraded with weapon mods. there is also a multitude of explosive weaponry such as RPGs, grenade launchers, grenades and remote explosives. Or you can go with the takedowns, which allows you to kill or knock out an enemy when close to them. And you can also hide their bodies afterwards.
There is also a small hacking mini-game which allows the character to hack multiple electronic items such as keypads and computers. There is also a persuasion mini-game which allows the character to persuade other characters to do special favors which can unlock other side missions. The mini-game are fun to do and are not overused.
The game is an action based game mixed with stealth with multiple choices of mission completion. The game takes about 20h to complete and there are multiple side quest at certain points in the game. The missions are all unique and mixed with multiple choices of gameplay which adds variation to the game.
There are multiple augmentations for the character to acquire, almost all of them are varied and creative. per example, you have one that allows your character to see through walls, or another one that allows you to deploy multiple small bombs that instantly kills all the enemies around you which make you feel like a total badass.
The game also has a lot of Unique NPCs, bosses and enemies to encounter all included with Robots and Cyborgs.
With the Director's Cut, the game now has a New Game+, Which allows the character to carry over his augmentations in a new game, which is really awesome. The Director's Cut also added the DLC: The Missing Link in the game instead of making a separate game like in the original Deus Ex: Human Revolution, which makes it feel more natural. There is also multiple small additions and tweaks added in the game.
However the game has its flaws, first of all, the character isn't that powerful at the beginning of the game. The new body of the character uses energy, so some equipment that the character has such as the invisibility cloak, the advance vision or the sound suppressor will use energy, which makes sense, and the character can regain energy over time or by eating food or vitamins, but the thing is that energy is also used when doing a takedown, so your going to end up waiting 30 second for your energy to fill up just because you punched a guy in the face to knock him out, which is kind of pathetic for a Cyborg ex SWAT. But the character can acquire augmentations that will give him more energy and that will make the energy fill up faster, which allows him to do multiple takedowns before using all of the energy available.
The game has no Multiplayer, which would have been awesome, but the game makes it up with its awesome Singleplayer.
Also, any save of the original Deus Ex: Human Revolution won't carry to the director's Cut version. Forcing you to start alll over again.
You will need to buy the game again if you already bought the original Deus Ex: Human Revolution once in order to have all the bonuses that the Director's Cut offers, so you are going to end up with the original game, the separate DLC, and the Director's Cut version with the game and the DLC combined, which is kind of pointless.
The Goods:
+ You're a Cyborg, nothing more to say!
+ Unique and creative augmentations for your character.
+ Now with New Game plus, which allows the character to carry his augmentations to a new game.
+ Improved textures over the original Deus Ex: Human Revolution
+ Now with the developer commentaries.
+ Reworked bosses over the original Deus Ex: Human Revolution.
+ Addictive storyline.
+ Good soundtrack
+ Fun and varied missions.
+ Unique and different NPCs and enemies.
The bads:
- Loses energy when doing takedowns.
- End up with three games if you already bought the original one and the separated DLC.
- No multiplayer.
- Any save of the original Deus Ex: Human Revolution won't carry to the director's Cut version.
I recommend it if you're a fan of the Cyberpunk universe, and the action stealth type of game if you haven't already bought the original one with the separated DLC, or if you simply want the small additions and tweaks that the Director's Cut version offers.
Final Verdict:
9/10.
Must Own!

With a whole lot of mythology and some admirably detailed science fiction on top of core gameplay emulating a 90's PC game with modern polish, it's hard for me not to recommend this game. It's incredibly immersive, with the HUD explained in-game, and most importantly (especially in this version), you get to play through it the way you want to, be it stealth or guns blazing, item-hoarding or bare-minimum speedrunning. There's a lot of flexibility.
The Director's Cut in particular fixes up the boss battles quite nicely. I gave up on the original after getting stuck on one for hours, but this adds some new features to the boss arenas so non-lethal, stealth, and/or hacking players actually have a chance at not being swiss-cheesed in ten seconds. However, the drawback to using this version of the game over the original is that The Missing Link is now integrated into the main story. This may not sound like a problem, but it is integrated very, very awkwardly. You will know exactly when it begins because it cuts to a flashback of a scene that happened several seconds ago and then strips you of all your upgrades and weaponry, a♥♥♥♥♥♥move I haven't seen since Tomb Raider III. You get this all back, but only after a long while, and while it's nice they included this chapter (which gets better as it goes on), it could've used some tweaks so as to fit in a bit better.
I'm gonna be straight with you, I haven't played the original Deus Ex yet. I will soon. But I can vouch for those concerned about picking this up without knowing the original that you don't have to. It's a prequel, and contains foreshadowing to sometimes heavy-handed levels, but it generally doesn't effect much. The story is generally intriguing, and the locations it brings you to are quite fantastic. I loved exploring the streets of Detroit, but as soon as you see Hengsha, you're probably not going to believe it.
Augmentations are fun. There are useful ones like being able to track enemies and hack higher level machinery, but then there are ones that (while still useful in the right situation) are just fun to use, like being able to jump 9 feet high in the air, or punch through walls. There's generally enough Praxis points to go around for whatever it is you want to use eventually, but it's tight enough that you'll want to budget it. (Especially on The Missing Link, where you have to start from scratch until you get them back at the very end. Prepare to grind for XP. Hard.)
Gunplay is never really my favorite thing, but works well enough for me here. Cover is a bit awkward, but serviceable. The control scheme in general takes a little while to get used to if you're using a controller. If you're using a keyboard, well, more power (and menus) to you. Upgrading weapons is a thrilling process, though there's really not much you can do for non-lethal weaponry. Keep a pistol on hand just in case.
The inventory system is a bit restrictive, but as many players of many adventure games know, that little bit of restriction can really make you think about what it is you really have to carry. It adds a lot of thought to the process, though some items don't stack that seem like they should. All in all, it works out in the end, and you can use augmentations for a little more space if you need to. (Prepare to not have your stuff fit in The Missing Link until you re-upgrade, BTW.)
Now, the ending really kinda disappointed me. Not because it's bad, but... because it was a 24 hour long game, for goodness sake, that's a full day of my life for a clip show and some philosophy out of nowhere. I find that the multiple-choice ending only really has one choice that's satisfactory at all, but even then, there's still the question of why. I didn't fully understand why I had to make any of these choices, and the game just went to monologue and then credits. I still don't know why it has to end like it does, and I'm underwhelmed by it pretty heavily. Still, the game's worth playing, just don't get your hopes up for a satisfying resolution.
In short, a fine version of a great game, with an expansion pack oddly wedged in there and repairs only to gameplay, not story. (Also, the orange tint on the screen is gone, if that bothered you. If you liked it, liked the boss fights, and don't like the DLC, don't bother with this version, I guess.)

I give this a highly-conditional thumbs-up.  This is not a 'game' as such.  There are no game mechanics in play.  What this IS, is a tourist's introduction to Tokyo, with some anime-style story-fluff built around it.  There are no meaningful choices to be made, just picking what order you do things in.  The rest of your time will be spent reading.  It could just as easily have been made into a TV spot, and you wouldn't have to click as much.
That said, the art is decent, the summaries of various districts are made relatable, and I had fun learning things.  So I'm recommending it.  It's one of the better edutainment products I've tried and worth the five bucks in prep-work for an upcoming overseas trip.  But..

Stopped playing this after Level two or three. This game is so far from anything good or a DOOM game, keep your hands off it.
Gameplay
If you like fast or gory shooters, play Titanfall 1&2 (TF2 had an awesome SP Campaign) or Brutal Doom. This games pacing is more towards an aborted quake arena singleplayer. It forces you from one boring arena to another. Same enemys, same enemys. You can spam the execution for easy rewards, if you can endure watching the same 2 or 3 bad killmoves over and over again. Really gets old fast. The movement system also is an abomination. Why the player sometimes doesn't grab ledges, I can't say. What I can say, that it just eliminates the fun of vaulting objects, finding secrets to climbs or any juump and run section that would untwist the shooter sections of former games. The enemys themselves have ven become dumber. If you had 3 basic types of enemys in D3, Zombies (slugging towards you, with melee in mind), Zombie guards (using tactics and weapons, with skill dodges for higher tier enemys) and demons (using a mix of mellee and ranged combat, while advancing towards you, often very mobile), DOOM just manages to give you canon fodder jumping from one highpoint to the next. I can sit in a bottleneck passage of the current arena and just wait any enemy out. Very, very boring.
Story
The story never was a mayor point in Doom games, but Doom 3 still managed to get you into the game with setting the games tone, the enviorment and its characters. All that is gone. You just wake up and start smahing things, with a pistol lying near you.
Video/Atmo
Doom 3 worked with its strong contrast of Darkness vs. Light, where shadows often have sharp edges and there are moments of fear when you can't really see what is lurking in the dark. All that is gone. Enemys announce their presence long before you seem them, there is no more Horror or disturbing feelings in this game. The enviorments are neat, but very bright, again Doom 3 had a more unsettling and dark tone, making Mars look like an all time hazard enviorment, not like a playground.
Soundtracks
The soundtracks go along this. Most tracks just kick up when you are in an arena but won't get me up or anything, just dull heavy metal. D3 themes work more into the grim and demonic theme of the Doom games, while Doom 1&2 sounds are iconic. The weapons and enemys don't really sound that great, an the kill moves often feel like you beat someone with a foam sword. Blood splatting is good though.
Unlocks
Kinda feel forced and unnecassry. They seem to matter so little, only acting as another device to get me playing towards the next level. Weapon progression also is a nightmare. While you worked your way up in former Doom games, I found the pistol, then the shotgun, then the chainsaw and then the plasmarifle, just after finding the assault rifle. All that in just 2 Levels. Makes me shrug and scratch my head, what the devs were thinking. I have seen most weapons already, why even continue playing, there are no weapon specific killmoves anyway.
Conclusion:
If a Quake game had a child with an Arena style SP game and you would abort it, while the abortion still cried:" Killl me, KILL ME!" Behtesda would come around the alley and would publish it. If you want a good Singleplayer FPS then play Titanfall 2, if you want a good horror shooter play Doom3, if you want some old-school demon♥♥♥♥♥kicking play Brutal Doom. This game dropped in price rapidly, what is always a good sigh of how bad it is. Stay away from it. If you play this for multiplayer there is a boatload of better games, and you should be ashamed of yourself.

The game is mainly a hex-based, turn-based combat system with "Action points" determining what you can and can't do.  The "S.P.E.C.I.A.L" leveling system is there and will also determine what you can and can't do in game. ( Playing with Intelligence less than 4 you can't even speak properly and NPC's will even ignore you or not give you quests )
Just like most RPG's of the era the beginning game is a hard survival but as it gets to approx mid-game money becomes so plentiful and your skills advance so quickly that most challenges are cleared easily.

This game features a car for you to drive around the wasteland quicker than normal and can be upgraded slightly for better fuel consumption, etc. It does, however run on the same ammunition as energy pistols / rifles.  It can also be used as a storage container but beware a bug where too many things are inside it, you'll get locked out of the menu. It also seats all your followers which is a nice added feature. Speaking of followers, they're still the same stupid things that block every-bloody-entranceway when you walk into a room. However they've put a helpful "Shove" Icon in which pushes the follower one hex away, they've also added extra combat controls ( Although default is usually best for pretty much all situations ) that come in Beserker, aggressive, defensive and custom. The ability to choose which armour they wear, although there is no visable change and the ability to get them to use a selection of weapons ( Although they can only use certain weapons, not any weapon as Followers are only "loaded" with certain animations )
However I cannot recommend this game solely on the basis that it is so buggy and frustraiting. Walk into the wrong part of town at the wrong time of day and all the guards shoot at you. Enemies ignore you if you wear a certain armour type but if you have a follower in the same armour only 1 type of enemy will shoot you, yet if you walk into a town with your parties weapons drawn everyone will shoot you.
It's highly inconsistant and irritaiting, saving everytime you do something successfully becomes regular. The game only received one patch in it's life and like many others have said, you have to mod the game for it to become bareable. So likening this over Fallout 4 but then telling people you need mods to enjoy Fallout 1 or 2 is hypocritical.
It's a shame because I got it as part of the Fallout Anthology and I haven't enjoyed either game and I cannot really see why it has such a cult following. Even other RPG's of the time period this was launched fare better and I think being the one of the only post-apocolyptic and non-fantasy based RPG got it where it is.

- Storage lockers undermine the need to learn the layout of the city and locations of crafting items.
- Survivors and psychos are automatically marked on your map, making exploration less rewarding.
- Increased travel time means you rarely have enough time to do any side missions or exploration when playing in Nightmare mode.
- Poorly optimized with highly variable framerates.

Conclusion: While not as good as its predecessors, Dead Rising 3 is still an enjoyable romp if you like killing zombies in creative ways.

I love this thing! It's a KB+Mouse user's perfect transition to controller gaming. The best thing about it is that it's completely customizable and customizing it is pretty easy, especially with the explanations written for each option. The trackpad/mousepad thingy on the right is incredibly useful and can be made to feel like 1) a thumb mouse, 2) a trackball, 3) an imaginary analog stick, and 4) pretty much anything in between since the advanced settings are pretty detailed. There are even more options than those 3 but those are the ones I've tried so far so I can't vouch for the rest.
And btw, the customization can be done mid-game. Just press the Steam button, edit the controller config and then go back to your game to try the new settings. Don't like them, just repeat. No need to leave the game and play with some external config file.
And if you're worried about having to customize every single game, have no fear. The community's got you covered. You can choose from several configurations that other users have submitted, and the different ratings for each config show you how popular it is. Not to mention the generic templates that are available in case you run into that game that no one else plays with the controller.
The only only thing that's missing from this controller is that it has no audio jack so you won't be able to connect any headphones to it.
Just as a side note, I have zero experience with the xbox controller so I can't compare to it. But I imagine it lacks this kind of customization. For games that inherently support the xbox controller, you can map the steam controller buttons to the xbox controller buttons. This is actually pretty much the default and they're even named the same (A,B,X,Y).

If Nintendo and Valve have anything in common, it's their confidence in outlandish innovation.

I personally feel they're the most outstanding feature. Having the pin-point control of a mouse in a controller is unheard of.
Possibly the least discussed feature, the keybinding tool, is incredibly well rounded. If you've spent any time with JoytoKey or MotioninJoy, this keybinder will have you drooling. The only complaint imaginable would be that it only works with Steam controllers.
So if you have a controller for games that support them, and are fine using a keyboard and mouse for ones that don't, then you'll be happy without a steam controller. But if you're like me, and wish more games had controller support, this was built to fill that gap.

Near Death is a survival sandbox indie title similar to The Long Dark or Stranded Deep. It is a bare-bones, but delightful experience overall.
The game is set in 1980's Antarctica, and it is all about surviving cold temperatures. The player is placed in the boots of an unnamed female pilot who crashes (because helicopters in video games) and has to survive in an abandoned base.
The only real mechanic to worry about is body heat. The player gets colder and colder until she dies, and can only warm up by sealing the doors and using a portable heater (or turning the generators on.) Hazards include storms, broken windows, pitch black conditions, and other fun things.
The game is easy to get a hold of, looks very nice, and is very well polished. There were a few clipping issues where I phased through closing doors, but ultimately, nothing was confusing, and the game's two characters (Miss Pilot and a man she talks to on what passes for 1980's texting) have loads of charm.
If you're into survival games, pick this up. It's easy to play and understand. Fairly short (I beat it in an afternoon).

Let's get this out of the way.  Near Death is an indie game and it is short.  It is *very* short.  I took my time, wandered about at the end, reloaded the ending a few times, toyed around Sutro station after campaign end and sat back and soaked in the menu imagery/soundtrack before I uninstalled.  The game is probably closer to 2 hours in length than 3.
I still recommend it.
Why?  The engine runs well, the game experienced minimal glitching during the three hours I played it.  The game was serviceably attractive and brutally atmospheric.  It's not often that you encounter a survival horror title that doesn't revolve around aliens, or zombies, or monsters, or evil people.  Near Death pits one determined woman against the most dangerous and inhospitable place on Earth: night-cloaked, winter-ridden Antarctica.  The game has minor crafting, some minimal puzzling and solemly ominous script.  However, the star of the game is the intense environments, coupled with an almost frenetic need to regulate your body warmth.
Jaunts, however temporary, between structures in Sutro station become an all-out fight for survival.  Visibility declines.  Temperatures plummet and the wind gusts can easily move you/point you in different directions.  It is exceptionally easy to get lost or pointed in the wrong direction, where a short trek into the snowy wilderness means certain death.  Players must carefully ration batteries, kerosene and other equipment for maximum efficiency.  Light/rope poles become your greatest friends when caught outside during a blizzard.
I initially started the game on basic Easy mode to finish it one quick go-through (I didn't think dying would support the premise of the game).  However, after finishing the game in about an hour and 45 minutes with no deaths, I can honestly recommend that Normal difficulty would probably be a better fit for most.  With careful gameplay, deaths can still be avoided and the game would probably lengthen to 2 hours +.  The game provides a satisfying, if not exactly flamboyant ending and the Antarctic landscape offers a glorious surprise while you descend from your final fetch quest/mission.
The game isn't exceptionally complex.  It lacks a wide array of features.  It doesn't have a hyper advanced graphics engine or massive multiplayer longevity.  What the game *does* have are atmosphere and tension in spades.  You will struggle to keep cool as you stumble towards your destination, as your labored breathing and chilled feet continue to plod slowly forward in knife-like blizzard winds.  You will care for the protagonist and most of all, you will appreciate the opportunity to play a game where your task isn't to kill, maim or destroy but, instead to survive against mother nature, in the face of overwhelming odds.
Near Death can be had on sale for five dollars and for a 3 hour jaunt unlike anything you've likely ever experienced before...it's worth it.
Recommended.

OK, It is Early Access game and so its still work in progress. There are some tech issues in joining a match lobby and Devs are working on it and on keyboard controls and further customization. Now is the game good at basic? I think yes. It has potential to be very good and is even now quite fun and I fear addictive. Its Combat arcade meets RPG Fantasy. A Mortal Kombat or Street Fighter in fiery pits of hell and fighters from fantasy epics meets survival. Its simply a fun multiplayer combat game set in RPG mould. I found it simply fun and addictive. Even at early stage its deeply satisfying. Menu is simple and easy to follow. Graphics is quite good. Its a dog eat dog ruthless world. The environment, the players everyone or everything is your enemy. You don't just have to beat the enemy players in rapid deathmatches or the Bosses that jump in simply to kill all, you have to survive also the hostile environment while trying to stay alive and thats both challenging and fun. There are no friends here or even temporary allies to face bigger enemies. You are on your own all the time and anything that can move will certainly kill you. Between friends this will be a kind of extremely fun vs mode, if you are bored of shooting folks down or sniping them in normal vs games. Have fun guys! I look forward to playing this more in coming days.

Now, I first saw this game when Two Best Friends played and and they did nothing but talk trash and not give it a single chance. Honestly, I can't blame them. This is game making a story out of a sandbox builder that has become incredibly popular among children and if I remember right, they have never actually played it. But I decided to give it a chance and I'm glad I did. It's not a pinnacle of story telling or anything but if you give it a shot, you'll find a nice, comfy story that can surprise you.
To start off, if you've never played Mine Craft, it's probably not for you. Similar to how people would not recommend you play Tales from the Borderland or Game of Thrones before playing/watching their respective franchises. Also if you think you're to macho to enjoy a story that isn't filled with grim, gore, and dark undertones it's also probably not for you. I would not say this is a kid's only game but it is certainly a family friendly game. No cursing and you don't get to bang your love interest in the end (There's really not any romance plot at all).
I've heard people complain about the dialogue being "cringy" and I'd have to disagree. I personally feel that it just has fun with itself and it's helped along by a great factor of the game and that is that pretty much every single voice actor is phenomenal. Every single one puts so much character and charm into all of their roles, the main character (male anyways, can't speak for the female VA) especially carried his role to the next level.
Most of the choices change dialogue or have character be there or don't, very much like most Tell Tale games. If no incredibly drastic changes bother you Tell Tale games in general probably aren't for you. I've always hated this complaint as I've felt it's more about enjoying your journey while also making it your own. I can't really speak for replay value but there may be some.
As for the story telling itself, it's no revolutionary story but it does fine and where it shines is how well it develops the cast of characters and how well you get to like and know them. I wasn't expecting much but I actually ended up caring about the cast by the end and was happy to see the grow in the story. There's some moments
that really are rather touching that I wasn't expecting.
A few small thing I think that are worth mentioning is that the game had surprisingly nice animations, they did some great things with Mine Craft character models and they overall had some really nice designs for things not original to Mine Craft.
As for cons there aren't many except that the game does have those usual Tell Tale bugs like some desynch and such and I wish it wasn't there but some things can't be helped and it didn't hurt the experience to much.
The base game is 5 episodes and then there's an "adventure pass" DLC that is another 3 episodes. The adventure pass adds the final episodes and wraps up the story so I would also recommend that. A little warning to something that might put some people off, one episode does feature Mine Craft You Tubers but it's really not that bad. Honestly, if I hadn't recognized one from seeing a video years ago I wouldn't have even known, just thought they were some character with weird names. I don't know if knowing them all would make the experience any better since I barely knew one but not knowing them was fine. They actually delivered their lines fairly well and made fine characters even though they were just playing themselves.
All in all, I've very glad I played this. It made a nice, wrapped up adventure. Nothing ground breaking but still fun and worth the time if you're willing to give it a chance. Honestly, if they made a season 2 or more episodes, they'd be on my wishlist in an instant.

One of the most surprising of Telltale's recent game releases. Stellar Voice Acting, Animation and a surprisingly good Story (For a game trying to add lore to Minecraft that is). The only negative is the fact Telltale stretched the game out to 8 Episodes instead of the traditional 5, Episodes 6-8 feel tacked on and they basically made you basically buy 2 Season Passes.

This is not a game for the average Telltale player. It is much more basic and when compared to something like their 'The Wolf Among Us' or 'The Walking Dead'. It is oriented primarily towards young children, around the age of 10. Older players may find the story to be too childish and predictable for their liking. That being said, 'Minecraft: Story Mode' isn't
. But it is far from being decent.
I bought this game to play with my five year-old sister, since she loves playing 'Minecraft'. After playing the first two episodes with her, I ended up going back and playing through the original five episodes by myself. I am 20. I went through the game, really examining each aspect of it to see if there was anything in it for me. There wasn't. I found that when playing through the game with a critical eye, it was a very shallow experience. The story and characters were incredibly cliche and none of the decisions I had made really mattered. It felt more like I had just sat down to watch a cartoon show that I had no control over, rather than a video game whose story is "tailored by how I play". The dialogue of the characters isn't anything impressive either, with a few cringe inducing lines and delivery sprinkled around for good measure. On the plus side, the voice acting wasn't abysmal, but wasn't memorable.
Each episode has their self-contained goal that adds up to the overarching goal, but what ends up happening is that your Mary Sue character and friends are constantly being introduced to the new mcguffin of the episode because "plot". Character development is a far off myth and any relationships you might have damaged go quickly back to being good in a scene change.
I also experienced consistent bugs that irritated the hell out of me. I was playing with an Xbox One controller, which was working perfectly fine for the most part. The points it wouldn't work confused me at first, because what was happening, was that the game was telling me the incorrect prompts during action sequences. The primary action button during these sequences is the left trigger, yet the game
gave me the right trigger prompt. After a few failed prompts, I went into the options to discover what had happened. Of course, there was no way to remap the buttons so I spent the rest of the game having to associate the RT prompt with the LT button.
If that wasn't enough, during the exploration sequences, another bug persisted, though this bug only came up from episode 3 onwards. RT is the button used to make your character walk faster. In my case, pressing RT did nothing. Instead, LT was used to make the character go faster, but the walk cycle did not seem natural at all. My character was moving far too fast and once I had pressed LT to go faster, I was stuck at that speed until I interacted with something.
Other bugs that popped up occassionally yet far too frequently were audio cutouts (making me miss over half a sentence) and prompts just straight up missing from the game (only in episode 5 so far). All of these bugs left me with the impression that the game was rushed and left unfinished.
Look, this is hard for me to say, since I had a poor time with this but my five year-old sister seemed to enjoy it. Anyone over the age of... let's say 14, I would strongly suggest you either play the first episode for free if that's still an option, or watch the first episode online to get a feel for the game. Because once you've seen the first episode, you've seen everything that this series has to offer; Dialogue choices, exploration sequences, action sequences, and very, very minimal crafting. However, if you're a young child around the age of 10 or you're looking after a young child, 'Minecraft: Story Mode' provides a nice, light-hearted adventury distraction from the oncoming existential dread. I'm not sure what people expected from this game initially to give it a bad rap in the technical Minecraft community.
What on earth is this?
- It is a movie in a Choose Your Own Adventure style set in the world of Minecraft, but marketed as a game.
So, not Minecraft?
- No. That is just the setting of the story. Though a knowledge of crafting recipies can improve play experience slightly. Not everything in this is canon with vanilla Minecraft. It is simply using Minecraft as a base for a story.
Is it worth the cost?
- That depends. Playing through the game has a certain charm to it that you won't get from watching the Youtube LPs. If you like story driven games, you might consider this fun.
It has DLC?
- Yes! That is one thing everyone should know going into it. The story branches off starting at episode 5, and continues in the DLC pack for episodes 6, 7, and 8, WHICH COSTS ADDITIONAL MONEY.
Does it have replay value?
- Not as much as you might think for a story-based game. Again, I consider this an interactive movie marketed as a game, so if you enjoy watching some of the same things over again while you make different choices, then you might enjoy playing through again.
How long does it take to play through an episode?
- Anywhere from 45 min. to 2 Hours depending on the episode and how quickly you play it.
Do you reccomend it?
- Yes. It is a quality "game". Well put together, with an engaging story. It is expensive for my tastes, but it gives a clean experience I have yet to find elsewhere.
