First off, this game is short. Like Two-Three Hours short, mind you, this is only if you do one of the two paths.
When it comes to visual novels this game really isn't doing anything new when it comes to plot or story. Though what it does nicely is introduce you to Japanese Culture.
In a nutshell, you are going to Japan for the first time to meet up with two online friends, and from there your adventure starts! You get to tour all of Tokyo and bond with your two friends. Of course this can also lead to romance.
At first, the plot and the character interaction seemed rather shallow, and I didn't really care what was happening. But as the story goes on you start to get connected with the characters. (Even if the game is rather short.) You'll start caring about them and want to know even more.
To be honest, the game ended just when I was really starting to enjoy it.
I don't think we'll see a follow up and that is a shame. Mind you, the game has been out for a few years. Overall though I did enjoy the game! If you like visual novels then I would recommend giving this one a shot, even if it is on the shorter side.
If anything support these types of games so we can see more of them on Steam!

A truely wonderful piece of equipment. I've handled xbox and playstation controllers, but this is by far the most comfortable, responsive, customizable, and takes the cake.
I have used the controller for incredibly complicated games such as Guild Wars 2. The customizability of the controller is fantastic. The complexity of a 10 skill game, dodge, jump, camera, and a series of F skills means that any controller has to be flexible enough to accomodate all of these keys. The steam controller does just that. With the ability to set different controller configurations for each of your games, this controller is sure to put all others to rest. Not to mention the flawless communication with the Steam link. Now, nothing is going to beat a good old-fashioned keyboard and mouse, but if you're looking to just casually play your favorite game without the intention of being number 1, this will work out perfectly for you.
Useful information:

There's really no way you can go wrong with Ticket to Ride.
Firstly, the game is brilliant in it's simplicity. There's only three types of moves you can make (alright, a couple others in additional maps, but the point is pretty much the same) and yet it's endlessly fun to play. It's a brilliant adaptation of the board game that, for once, does the original justice.
Multiplayer adds great depth and infinite replayability. While the lobby and game set up could use some polishing, it doesn't /need/ it. They work! Plus, you can use the pass-and-play to practice against yourself from as many players as you add to the game. You can play bots. Still so much replayability, just as always the AI will never live up to the fun of playing other people, most likely. I found something oddly dulling about it, even before I tried multiplayer, and I'm usually not a multiplayer person.
This is one board game you do not want to pass up, and this rendition of it is just as worthwhile, plus cheaper and easier to get a game going!

Yes, it's a children's game, but it's a children's game that defined my childhood!

The PC adaption (and iPad/iPhone versions too, for that matter) of Ticket to Ride is a very faithful recreation of the classic board game, where the only gameplay differences between it and the physical version are fast and accurate scoring and the fact that enraged board-flipping is no longer a possibility. (Not to mention the bonus of the game + DLC being cheaper than their physical counterparts, and is significantly easier to play with people on the other side of the world!) So, for people who have played the board game before, I think this should be a no-brainer.
However, I wrote this review for those who aren't aware of the greatness that is Ticket to Ride and are seeing this from a bystander's point of view. You might be thinking that this is just some boring train game played only by weird people who smell funny, as a diversion from their regular riveting pastime of watching grass grow. However, I can assure you that this is most certainly the opposite of the truth.
Ticket to Ride is, in actual fact, quite a tense game that can quite easily take you from absolute confidence in your position to having all your hopes and dreams shattered, as you realise that you didn't take that vital Los Angeles > Las Vegas track yet due to over-confidence, that you had multiple 20+ point routes hinging on! Not to mention the level of back-stabbing and collaboration that can come into play (especially with the Steam overlay making this oh so easy), that can easily create bitter feuds between two rival rail barons, which can last across a series of games.
Overall, I strongly recommend this game to anyone who wants an enjoyable, classic example of a game that's easy to learn, but difficult to master. It's always a good game to play with friends, strangers or alone with bots, especially as each game tends to only go for 45 minutes at most. (Although you can quite easily find that time has flown, as you wind up having rematch after rematch, without noticing the time passing by!)

This is one of Mojang's sad attempts to revive their signature game, Minecraft. The storyline actually had a bit of interest, but it was way too much of a storybook rather than actual gameplay. Having made one of the most impressive sandbox creations to date, I would expect much more from Mojang to promote their dying franchise.
Not only has this game been priced inappropriately, but after a few episodes they've continued asking for more money. Minecraft, which is 26.95 USD, provides so much more for the player to do rather than sit back, click a few buttons, and get almost no excitement except for the way each story turns for 24.99 USD.
Each company has had a very low point during certain times. Mojang is executing this very poorly. Shortening the time between updates, creating minigames that were once meant to be made by players who had huge imaginations, and the EULA that completely destroyed the business aspect of Minecraft servers. This is yet another terrible decision to try and revive a dying franchise. The developers need to look back at the peak of the franchise, what they had done to make it so successful, and go back to that.
Overall, this game... well... story wasn't THAT bad, but this game overdid what Minecraft was actually about, trying to lure the player into the entire franchise with mysticism that is foreign to the game that started it all, thus resulting in a very choppy execution of the storyline and what Minecraft is meant to be, that being a game for the player to explore, not a player to be forced to explore.

However, there is one major issue: The touchpad concept. It detects where exactly your finger is pointing by looking at the whole area you touch. If you're just using the tip of your thumb, all is good. However, if, in the heat of the moment, you push down some more, the aim goes way off target. I can't possibly keep my thumb bent like required all the time. It's very straining.
I feel I can manipulate a regular gamepad's mini stick much more precisely. If need be, I could even grip the stick to be even more precise.
But then again, maybe I'm just holding it wrong. :D
There are some other issues like missing gamepad emulation on OS X. It would also be nice to have a fallback mode that works without having Steam running, to control HTPCs and whatnot.

The Steam Controller does just as it says, it allows you to play your steam games from your couch. In addition, it has a software keyboard (using the touchpads) that can be used to control your desktop (so long as Big Picutre Mode is on and minimized). There is some very limited desktop control capability without big picture mode (but no keyboard functionality). The two touchpads (as well as the other inputs) have a ridiculous amount of customizablity and each can be used as a mouse, joystick, directional buttons or some combination thereof (and of course the sensititivy and many other settings can be adjusted to fit your liking). I just discovered yesterday that in addition to these features there is a tilt feature built into the controller, which makes aiming in FPS-type games much easier (its actually been very difficult for me to aim using the touchpads). There are also a myriad of custome controls set by others in the Steam Community so you dont have to spend the ridiculous amount of time to make your own. I wish the controller had more lighting so that I could see it when I use it in a dark room or at night. Keep in mind that the device is powered by two AA batteries (included). There is also an included extender for the USB reciever. Overall, I'd give the device an 8/10, I love it, I can kick back on my couch and play any game from my steam library. I also love that it provides enough desktop functionality that I don't have to leave my couch if I want to quicky look something up on the internet or change a setting on my computer. Ive had some difficulty trying to get the steam controller to work with non-steam games, but I believe it is possible if you play them through Steam (as a non-steam game).

Human Revolution was actually the first of the Deus Ex games that I've played. I've heard a lot of good things about the series as a whole (or at least the original and this one, Invisible War was another story) so I figured I'd give it a shot. The developers did a good job setting the tone of the game between the established world, characters and style. The golden hue the game has (prior to the Director's Cut release) gave the game a strange sense of personality, I actually like that so when I started playing the Director's Cut I was a little saddened by this missing element.
The RPG elements found in Human Revolution primarily revolve around enhancing Jensen's augmentations, allow him to be stronger, faster, become invisible or even drop from the roof of a ten story building and land softly. Upgrading these augmentations come in two forms, through experience gained by doing quests, taking out enemies and by being as sneaky as possible. The second form is through Praxis kits, some of which can be found, others are rewards while some you can buy.
How a player progresses through the game is up to them. The game doesn't force players into being a killing machine nor does it force stealth (however prior to the Director's Cut, the boss fights kind of pushed the straight up fight approach, but the stages were redesigned to allow more options), so you're free to choose how you want to go through the game. Players are also given the option between lethal and non-lethal. The non-lethal approach tends to be a bit more fun since just about every game out there already does lethal.
The Director's Cut (which is the only version Steam offers) has some issues though, last played (by the time you read this maybe it's changed) a few graphic options didn't work as they were suppose to, Smart Glass support wasn't functioning right and I even noticed some reflection's not have their textures come up, just random patterns that looked like bad data. The developers are suppose to be working on it, but still waiting for things to get sorted. On the plus side though, The Missing Link DLC is integrated into the game for a more seamless transition, revamped the boss stages, added in a few new gadgets as well as new game plus, which was a major complaint before since you always had to invest your points in a certain fashion if you want to take advantage of certain approaches.
If you were a huge fan of the original Deus Ex, you may have some complaints about Human Revolution as some aspects were removed, but that doesn't mean the game was bad, just a difference in generations, so it's still worth checking out.

Near Death was a game I picked up on sale with mild expectations but was actually blown away by. The premise is very simple but the devs manage to do a lot with it. The game reminded me a lot of Penumbra, with a monsterless metroidvania twist. The puzzles are all believable scenarios as you try and find your way across an ambandoned base and slowly bring enough systems back online to keep yourself from freezing to death while also forming a plan to get back to humanity.
It all comes together to make a very immersive story that is surprisingly tense for your only enemy being nature itself. When I started the game I pretty much ignored using rope poles and light beacons since everything seemed easy enough to find just using the map and compass. But as the weather worsened and took a huge toll on visiblity and mobility those simple tools became life savers for traveling between the longer streches between some parts of the base.
All in all I'd highly recommend Near Death to anyone who enjoys a unique immersive experience. Destroys everything, one of the greatest pieces of art ever created, Fallout 2 is an RPG in which you play a tribesman who is tasked to find and return a device to his village known as the G.E.C.K (which is a piece of technology that is able to revitalize areas of a post-nuclear wasteland, transforming dead, irradiated soil into viable land suitable for farming) to save his people from famine. The plot is subtle and a great break from all the melodramatic, save the universe type♥♥♥♥♥♥most games consist of.
Fallout 2, like the first, gives you a large, brutal and unforgiving world to traverse at your own risk, full of genuinely fascinating locations and extremely interesting characters to interact with; from scientists who give mutated scorpions chems to their increase intelligence, talking plants and a highly intelligent and articulate Deathclaw, there are tons of geniusly fantastic, memorable characters to interact with through-out and even though Fallout 2 doesn't always take itself too seriously and is sometimes outright comical the game still portrays a grim, cruel and extremely immersive world like no other.
Fallout 2 features some of the finest role playing out there, with tons of meaningful choices and consequences through-out which question your ethics and morality on a far deeper scale than just simply being the good / bad guy. The quests you recieve in Fallout 2 are diverse and often offer multiple ways in which you can complete them, some ways which were not even intended by the developers, there is just so much freedom of choice here that is completely non-existent in 'RPGs' today.
The character building is brilliant and has a ton of depth, every little stat directly affects how your game plays out, being highly intelligent with the personality of a brick or being a knucklehead with the charisma of a dictator will deeply affect how NPCs interact with you. There are so many choices to make in character building that have huge, meaningful impacts on the world around you that multiple playthroughs are essential to experience what this masterpiece has to offer.
The visuals at first glance may seem bland and out-dated but the art direction is beyond brilliant and is complimented by believable, excellent world design and an insanely thick atmosphere - this doesn't feel like videogame world nor like it was designed to be one, rather an actual post-apocalyptic place.
The sound effects are absolutely spot on. The ambient, non-intrusive music through-out is fantastic and adds a lot to the atmosphere and the voiced dialogue is pretty well done.
Fallout 2's combat is turn-based and offers a ton of depth, giving you the opportunity to use a tactical approach rather than just mindlessly clicking away like in many of todays so-called RPG's - I do however encounter frustration with not being able to control friendly AI in combat and as a result get shot in the back and watching friendly AI running at an isolated enemy instead of backing up your character who then gets outnumbered and killed is rage-inducing to say the least, these flaws only occur right in the beginning until you get used to pathing and such but rather big flaws non-the-less.
Overall Fallout 2, along with Baldur's Gate, Darklands and Planescape Torment are the pinnacle of RPGs in every regard and will probably remain that way until the end of time judging by how far the genre has declined since. You can't call yourself a fan of RPGs until you have experienced these absolute masterpieces, if you're interested in playing Fallout 1 or 2 for the first time and haven't played anything of the sort before I'd advise a lot of patience in the early stages which by judging from some of the negative reviews is too much to ask for some.
This is a mandatory experience for anyone who loves videogames, experiences like this simply don't exist anymore.

Skara - The Blade Remains is a very interesting project, I am one of the original Kickstarter backers. You can really tell that the developers have a passion for the game and do their best to improve it. They are eager to hear what the community thinks and love to hear feedback of how to improve the game. They’re really putting that feedback to use by implementing and changing things suggested by the community. It’s one of the things that I can highly appreciate.
The design of the characters, environment and the concept art  is phenomenal. They definitely have talented people working on the project. The characters are all very unique and diverse which is pretty nice. Currently they have implemented two out of the five characters that they have announced. The environments have changed over-time quite a bit and are beautiful. You currently can play in three different maps and they’re pretty diverse. I like the fact that they keep things minimalistic yet diverse.
The game is in early access still so the game is far from being completed. If you’re looking for a well-polished and functional game I wouldn’t recommend the game in its current state. The combat, user interface and some technical issues are the biggest problem right now and they still need a lot of work. Because there’s still quite a bit of work that has to be done before the game will become “good” there’s also a low population.
If you’re willing to see the project grow larger, test new builds and give feedback to the developers then I would definitely support the project.

This controller is amazing. Like many games that receive updates, this controller is designed to have more enhanced capabilities added far outside the initial launch. This means that you don't have to buy a Steam Controller V2 in a year to get more features...barring any major breakthroughs or alternative designed controllers.
Loved it since I received the first batch in Oct'15, but the only issue is lack of desktop support for configs and stuck with big  picture to config.

tldr: Buy it if you are looking for something more than just plain XBox 360 compatible controls
We use 2 of the steam controllers together with our Steam link to play games on our TV, streamed from my gaming pc - or even to browse the internet using a proper browser (chromium) on the tv, rather than our Wii U or something.
First of all: I would not recommend the Steam Controller for People who just search for a "normal" gamepad, comparable to the XBOX 360 ones - dont missunderstand me, Steam Controllers are awesome, but they are far more than a normal gamepad.
Secondly: Quality of the Controller is just great. I was really surprised by the well produced controller, and some nice ideas like hiding the batterys in the handles where the controller needs weight and thickness non-the-less - especially as SteamController and Steam Link are the first peaces of Hardware published by Valve. My most used Controller is still running on its first pack of batteries, even though we easily have played / browsed like 60 Hours with it. I still would have liked an rechargable battery with the possiblity to load it via Mini-USB, similar to other controllers, but as changing the batteries isnt necessary that often this is acceptable.
I love the configurability and beeing able to emulate a vast amount of controlls - ranging from simple stuff like Minecraft (mapped the quickbar icons 1-8, as well as wasd, shift, control, f3, left klick, right klick, mousewheel, and much more) - to more complex configurations like Witcher 1 (i.e. circle clockwise on the left pad to open map, circle counter clockwise to open questlog, press left pad to open inventory, etc) to really complex configurations that mimmick mouse behaviour while simulating an Xbox controller (used that for Fallout 3, as it either supports Xbox OR Mouse controls). You can map so many different controlls, its really awesome! But you need to take your time to configure the controller - even though there are many community templates already available, most of the time you pick one, and modify that one to your liking, to maybe share it with the community again. So, if you just want to play Xbox 360 controller compatible games, rather buy a normal Xbox 360 controller, or an elite controller if you like the "grab" controlls - but if you want to play games or do stuff similar to a touchpad etc, and are willing to get used to this new gadget - definitly worth a pickup!
So far my only negative is, that it is somehow really hard to use the pads as an joystick substitute, esp. as there is only one physical joystick and so in general for Xbox 360 games you have to use the right joystick for camera controls. This seriously isnt that easy as the distance you need to travel on the pad is far greater for the same effect as on a normal stick, and the configuration options so far (for example, using the profile "agressive") still do not cover this completely. also the lack of physical resistance compared to a normal "spring" based joystick takes some time getting used to.
Basically i would say 8/10: But there is still lots of potential given the multitude of ways how to use touch controls, so improvement potential via software updates is still great (as a positive point)!

I don't remember if i wrote a review of this thing or not, so here, have (another) one.
Things I like:
- I like the Linux-from-the-ground-up design. It makes configurability kind of a dream.  I like the programmability a lot.
- I like the glidepads, but they take some getting used to. (I don't like glidepads on notebooks, but these make sense).
- I like the weight, and the feel, and the size, and the construction. It feels industrial strength, and doesn't feel like a cheap knock off. This is a huge accomplishment IMHO, because it's easy to feel like a cheap piece of hardware.
- I like the underneath buttons, and the gyro. those are neat and work like you'd imagine.. Like the Wiimote but not shaped like a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
- I like that I can use a regular microusb cable if i don't want to be wireless for some reason.
- I like the noises it makes, and the way chicks dig it.
- I really like how well the haptic feedback works under your fingers, and all around the controller. Well thought out, well designed. I like little details, like how the feedback follows the cursor when mousing, not just your finger. And the way the gyro feedback feels when turning the steering wheel in GRID..
Things I miss/don't like:
- I miss the second thumbstick. The glidepad is nice, and a cool design, but there's something about that second thumbstick which makes me SO MUCH BETTER at Assault Android Cactus than i'll ever be at the glidepad.
- i miss bluetooth. I don't like having little dongles I can lose.
- I don't like that I MUST use Big Picture Mode™ to configure/manage the configuration of the device. I get it?? I just don't like it. There needs to be 1) a non-BPM way to configure it (that doesn't involve a command line), and ideally 2) a separate utility to manage the controller as its own input device (under linux, i don't care about windows), so I can use it without Steam running.
- it's too attractive to my children, who take it from me to play Goat Simulator (a game that i didn't realize is A LOT MORE FUN with a controller)
- the top two shoulder buttons are juuuuust a bit too hard to hit sometimes.
- So awesome, it convinced me to buy a Steam Machine, and now I somehow have to explain this to the wife.
- I DO NOT LIKE HOW IT DOESN'T VIBRATE. So many games have a vibrate option! This is not a dealbreaker? But, it needs to vibrate moar.
TL;DR?? BUY A COUPLE OF THEM, you will like them lots.

Go! Go! Nippon is a very cute, all ages visual novel in which you take your first trip to Japan. It does a good job of introducing you to certain elements of Japan, and even has Japanese text along with the English so you can hone your skills at the same time. It features two sisters, that are members of your host family, that show you around Japan, and at the same time you are able to woo whichever one you desire. You will want to play through this game at least twice to enjoy all of the content.
The game was created by Overdrive, the company behind such eroge titles as Kira*Kira, DearDrops, and others. So even though it is short compared to those titles, Go! Go! Nippon! features the quality they are known for.
I highly recommend this game having played through it entirely prior to being on Steam, and will now be replaying it again. My only hope is they add trading cards and achievements one day.

So I recently purchased a steam controller, to test it out.
First, I have large hands, so some of this may not aply to you.
Next, I'll start with my likes then move to my dislikes, then provide some feedback with each point.
- I love the haptic touch pad on the right side.  I wish all controllers did that instead of using a thumbstick.
- I love the buttons on the bottom, especially using them as shifters in racing games like Project Cars and The Crew.
- I love that there are gyroscopic sensors - this can certainly help in the future if games program for them.
- i love the way the two buttons at the bottom are configured. they are PERFECTLY placed. I wish all controllers did this.
- I dislike the haptic dpad on the left. I think it is a touch too big for its clicky function, but perfectly sized for its haptic functionality. The depressed crosshairs on the NSWE sides are tough to sense with your thumb when in the middle of a game where you can't look down. and it is practically impossible to use as a thumbstick in a driving game. i'd like to see it smaller but more sensitive, and maybe swapped with the left thumbstick, for comfort, as my hand cramps in driving games.
- I dislike the yaxb button placement, but I believe I will get used to it with more playtime, so the awkwardness will go away. Sadly, the placement also cramps the hand a little bit. The concession for the placement is clear, to make way for the haptic pad above it, though, and it is a compromise i'm willing to make, if something can be done for the cramping and fatigue.
- I dislike the gyroscopic lack-of-sensitivity, and the inability to have a hardware toggle to turn them off, on the controller itself. The sensors themselves are innovative and once balanced properly will hopefully become the norm on controllers. Keep them but work on them a bit more in the coming revisions, please.
- I dislike the controller casing. It feels flimsy and brittle. It is too light, which is a big part of the 'flimsy' feel too. it isn't textured enough, and it isn't ergonomic enough. lots of the cramping and fatigue could be remedied with ergonomic curves ridges and valleys for optimal placement of the fingers, alongside a more rigid texture, and maybe a touch thicker plastic casing.
For a first-run controller that is attempting to change gaming as we know it, they have done a great job with the innovation. Now do another run in QA and fix a few minor things here and there...Then I believe this controller will absolutely take the gaming world by storm.
For folks who plan on playing for hours on end, I'd recommend something else. For a casual gamer who usually has an hour or less to play at any given time, I'd recommend this controller hands-down.

This Controller has been a strange trip. At first I didn't like it much, but after a couple of hours in borderlands and skyrim this controller has really grown on me in a huge way.

First, it's 100% re configurable on the fly. You get the sort of customization that you never could with a 360 controller and joy2key. If you don't like how one aspect of the controller works you can change it and tweak it until you have the perfect setup.
The right trackpad for aiming feels like a trackball if that makes any sense. You can even flick it like a trackball and do a full 360 spin in game. It has options for mouse (works like a trackpad on a laptop, or the apple magic mouse), joystick, or mouse like joystick (mouse style control, but it sends the game joystick input. Good for games that don't have real mouse support). I've found that each game is different and you have to test and tweak a bit to get the right feel.
The controller feels solid. I'd say it has a similar weight to a 360 controller although it has a better more ergonomic feel in the hands, and I often forget I'm holding it at all while playing.
The buttons all give nice satisfying clicks when pressed, especially the two-stage L+R triggers which you can customize to an insane degree. I often have a half-press pull up iron-sights and a full press to fire in FPS games. The L+R shoulder buttons are slightly larger than I'd like and take a bit too much pressure to fully actuate but this is a minor annoyance and far from a deal-breaker.
I was also concerned that the ABXY face buttons being placed below the right trackpad would be a distraction, but fortunately they aren't and after a few days of use my thumbs naturally move to the correct buttons from muscle memory.
Another annoyence is that you can't reconfigure the controller outside of big picture mode. I don't really understand the reason for this decision. Again, it's not a deal breaker by any means,. but it does make customization harder for games that use 3rd party launchers or mod managers like Skyrim. I've found to change my skyrim settings I have to launch BPM, change my skyrim controller preferences, exit BPM, then launch my mod manager and run SKSE. Not the worst thing, but slightly annoying because I then can't rebind keys in-game.
My only real hardware complaint is the exclusion of a proper d-pad. the left trackpad with the indented "+" pattern simply doesn't feel as good as a real d-pad with solid buttons. If you want to play retro platformers you'll want to get yourself a proper arcade stick or at least a controller with a good d-pad.
Overall I'm quite impressed with this controller. The amount of customization and control you get is amazing, and the trackpads feel quite good in game once you get used to them. If you're in the market for a new controller it's definitely worth checking out.

The Steam Controller does exactly what it adverises (plus one thing it doesn't - it has motion sensors comparable to those in the Playstation 3's SIXAXIS  technology), and does it pretty well. One of my favorite tricks with it, is that I can have it connected to one device wirelessly, but when it's wired into a different one, it acts as a controller for that one - but switches back once you disconnect it.

There are but two things that irk me.
1) you have to launch any game you want to use it with through Steam. This is a minor thing, because, meh, I'm okay with this, because it allows for some crazy ninjary with directinput or whatever that crazy microsoft specific input method is, allowing you to have keyboard AND controller AND mouse AND joystick inputs all simultaneously bound to a single controller. This is great.
2) to modify your controller mappings you must be running in big picture mode. This is irksome. Very Very irksome. I get it, this is being marketed as something to use as a controller with a steam machine and attached to your tv, fine. that's great. But.. what about those of us who don't want to use big picture (because, for example, it acts really bizzare and eats resources for no real reason) on our desktops?
I would hope that this particular shortcoming is corrected in the future, because holy mother of deities of your choice. I picked this up on a whim for myself for christmas, just to try it out and see if it would replace my x360 controller for games that play better with a controller on my desktop (the answer is yes. a thousand times yes.), and the Big Picture mandate is just absurd.

---Short: This is a great piece of hardware, but don't buy if you wish to have a smooth experience---
Just to clear the air: this controller is not meant to 'reinvent the wheel' as many are complaining about, but rather it is an experiment and should be treated like one. By buying this you are risking the possibility of it not being a fleshed out design, like the traditional Xbox or Playstation controller. You are not being forced to purchase the controller as if it was hardware standard, like a console, so keep that in mind.
In terms of physical ware: It is fantastic. It feels nice, plenty of buttons like: the back paddles, dual stage triggers, ect. The touchpad is nice and I personally don't have any issues about them wearing my finger pads down. The gyro is eehhh so far, very nice in concept, although in practice it could take some getting used to.
However, the negatives and jankyness are mostly with the software. First of all: the software is tied directly into Big Picture Mode, which is an issue. BPM is made for couch play, and highly favors that. Trying to use the software on the computer feels unnecessarily clunky and generally annoying. Why do I have to load this software just to use the controller instead of the option to plug-and-play, with an independent controller configuration?
The customization is great, however the interface needs a lot of work. For example: Why are there multiple joystick modes for the touch pad, instead of just one? You can map the 'Movement' joystick mode to emulate the right or left stick, as well as the 'Aiming' joystick mode, so what is the difference? Why are some setting present in one mode but not the other? Why not have both of them just labeled as Joystick and put their differences in as options and presets?

IF YOU PLAY THE FALLOUT OR ELDER SCROLLS SERIES: Just buy this thing right now. The touchpad all but God-mods lockpicking in both series. The sheer precision you can use while turning the pick/bobby pin is ridiculously good. I don't know if Bethesda will fix this fact in a later Fallout 4 patch but it will always be the case in the older games, I suspect.
Now, on to the general review:
ABOUT ME: I am a longtime console gamer (PS2, 3, and 4, primarily) who primarily plays sports games and RPGs. I had always played some computer games but they were mostly ROMs of classic games, and I had a cheapo Gamestop XBox controller knockoff I used. I recently built a gaming PC and started replacing some of my old console games with Steam equivalents (and quickly wished I had never bothered spending so much on console stuff in the first place). Right around the time I decided the fake XBox controller was not hacking it anymore, here came the Steam Controller.
The most general thing I will say about the Steam Controller is this: it is definitely optimized for FPS games/games with an FPS element. The trigger buttons are generous large and precise, and the right touchpad, which is indeed TOUCH-CONTROLLED, allows for extreme precision in camera changes and change-of-direction. The left control stick is similarly subtle and tracks very nicely for general character movement.
On the flip side, the XABY buttons are much smaller and much lower than you will be used to if you have used other controllers. This is by far the largest adjustment to using the Steam Controller if, like me, you have logged a lot of hours in games that were XABY-centric or make heavy use of the XABY functions in live-action situations. There is no simple fix to this: this is retraining very precise muscle memory and it WILL take time. But if you use controllers alot you already know that the trend in many games is moving toward a trigger-centric functionality. The Steam Controller is thus designed for today's games and tomorrow's, but you may find it less than ideal for your classics unless you tweak the controls.
For a slightly lower price tag than the PS4 controller you get a controller with superior functionality including the right touchpad, which is a significant upgrade.
The only knock I have: it needs batteries? Really?
Overall 8.5/10. Recommended if you are a controller person.

Fallout 2, like it's predecessor and sequels, stands to date as one of the greatest roleplaying games ever devised. First introduced to the original game in the series as a youth, I quickly became addicted to both the setting and the story being told; I loved the choices you were asked to make, and the customisation options that were available to you; I adored the pre-war 50s feel that inhabited the wasteland, even as you carried plasma rifles and power armour into battle.
In a word, Fallout 2, like the other games in the series, is sublime. As a fan of roleplaying games in general, I recognise that the post-apocalyptic genre is harder than others to make enticing - and yet Fallout somehow manages to nail it. Gore and mature themes meet head on with quirky humour, memorable locations and characters (Dogmeat and Harold the Ghoul being just two), and an expansive world to explore.
Unlike the first game in the series, Fallout 2 has you taking on the role of a tribal youth who is sent out into the wasteland in order to secure a G.E.C.K. - a Garden of Eden Creation Kit - which will help your primitive people make the land furtile and liveable again. Who your character is - what gender, what they're good at, what their quirks are - is entirely up to you, as are the dialogue and moral decisions you make, and the route you take across the wasteland. With side quests all over the place, you can spend hours after hours trudging through the Fallout world, making your mark as either a sentinel of justice, or a madman with a shotgun. Good or evil, hero or villian - it's entirely up to you.
The latter games might be controversial to a select few - after all, not everyone liked Bethesda's treatment of a classic game, and it's their perogative to think that way. However, it's almost unanimous fact that Fallout 2, like it's predecessor, stands as one of the greatest RPGs ever made.

tldr:  Detailed open world w/ lots to do vs. uneven tone and poor controls.
Full Review:
This is one of the best open world games out there, but it's not perfect.  There are problems with this game.
PRO
Huge, detailed open world.   You can go into lots of stores, and there are a lot of different stores.  There's full airport, a shopping mall, caverns, a prison, a nuclear power plant and a lot more.  There are islands you can visit.  There are secrets and easter eggs all over.  If you're only doing the missions, you're missing out on half the fun of the game.
There are a LOT of activities:  be a firefighter, police officer, paramedic ... run drugs, escort ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, do insurance fraud (play in traffic), use helicopters to protect your drug dealers, and a lot more.
There are a lot of different missions, and they're not JUST "go there and kill that".  There are also stronghold missions.
It has a detailed plot that holds together, and each gang has a different story to it, so you're really playing five different stories in one game.
The characters are fun, and the voice acting is great.  The radio is also fun to listen to.
The pedestrians are more "alive" than in almost any other game.  You feel like you're in a living, breathing world, because people aren't just walking around the block.  They're actually doing things, and their conversations are fun to listen in on, and sometimes those conversations are relevant to what's going on in the game.
SR2 also has one of the best character customization systems in any game ever.  You can be male, female, or in between.  You choose, within limits, how you want your character to look.  Clothes have a LOT of options for customization.  There are also customizations for "cribs" (safe houses) and cars.
CONS
The graphics don't hold up well.  They're dated, and while it's not that bad (I mean, I've been playing video games for over 35 years), they're looking their age.
The control, especially vehicle controls are awful.  If you need to walk precisely, be prepared to fall down.  If you have to drive, be prepared for your cars to rag-doll if you hit something.  Character rag-doll is set too high for my taste, and the vehicles bounce around like beach ball.s
SR2 has a very unstable tone.  It's like a teenager:  part of the time, it's goofy and a bit childish, and part of the time it's trying to puff out its chest, flex its muscles and screech "Lookit me!  I'm a badass!"  The enemies are cartoonish, stereotyped caricatures ... but not in the deliberately over-the-top parodying of the sequels.  There are poop jokes and dumb sex jokes ... and then you have the major character maiming and murder that goes on.
Don't get me wrong:  the deaths in this game are some of the most inventive, brutal and memorable in gaming history, but juxtaposed with the humor, and the game's tone bounces around, well, like the vehicles in this game:  like a beach ball.
So while this game is awesome, and I love it.  It's a classic.  It's not perfect.
I highly recommend playing this with Gentlemen of the Row mod.

Screencheat is damned clever. It is a fast-paced first person arena shooter in colorful  maps where you are always watching the screen of every player, to find their position and murder them. There are several game modes, including death match, king of the hill, murder mystery, and others. Murder Mystery is like death match, except you are given a weapon to pick up and a target to kill -- and you only score if you accomplish killing that selected target with that specific weapon. The weapons are clever, too. Rifle revolver, exploding bear bomb, blunderbuss, brave knight charging on a children's makeshift horse-on-a-stick.
The only downside is the limited player-base. As of this writing, you can find a game, but it will take awhile and you will probably be the one who has to host it. This would be improved, if the developers didn't require you to leave the game and go back to a lobby in order to pick up new players (including those who are actively spectating you and may want to join). A smarter move would be to just fill the empty slots with new players as old players drop off. If not during a game or round, then in-between rounds. This oversight is frustrating.
As of this writing, Humble Bundle store has this game on sale for four copies for ten bucks. It is absolutely worth that. Even if you have to find a few people to play locally on a LAN with. This is a unique experience that should be tried.

IF YOU PLAY THE FALLOUT OR ELDER SCROLLS SERIES: Just buy this thing right now. The touchpad all but God-mods lockpicking in both series. The sheer precision you can use while turning the pick/bobby pin is ridiculously good. I don't know if Bethesda will fix this fact in a later Fallout 4 patch but it will always be the case in the older games, I suspect.
Now, on to the general review:
ABOUT ME: I am a longtime console gamer (PS2, 3, and 4, primarily) who primarily plays sports games and RPGs. I had always played some computer games but they were mostly ROMs of classic games, and I had a cheapo Gamestop XBox controller knockoff I used. I recently built a gaming PC and started replacing some of my old console games with Steam equivalents (and quickly wished I had never bothered spending so much on console stuff in the first place). Right around the time I decided the fake XBox controller was not hacking it anymore, here came the Steam Controller.
The most general thing I will say about the Steam Controller is this: it is definitely optimized for FPS games/games with an FPS element. The trigger buttons are generous large and precise, and the right touchpad, which is indeed TOUCH-CONTROLLED, allows for extreme precision in camera changes and change-of-direction. The left control stick is similarly subtle and tracks very nicely for general character movement.
On the flip side, the XABY buttons are much smaller and much lower than you will be used to if you have used other controllers. This is by far the largest adjustment to using the Steam Controller if, like me, you have logged a lot of hours in games that were XABY-centric or make heavy use of the XABY functions in live-action situations. There is no simple fix to this: this is retraining very precise muscle memory and it WILL take time. But if you use controllers alot you already know that the trend in many games is moving toward a trigger-centric functionality. The Steam Controller is thus designed for today's games and tomorrow's, but you may find it less than ideal for your classics unless you tweak the controls.
For a slightly lower price tag than the PS4 controller you get a controller with superior functionality including the right touchpad, which is a significant upgrade.
The only knock I have: it needs batteries? Really?
Overall 8.5/10. Recommended if you are a controller person.

Dead Rising 3 is a poorly optimized console to PC ported game, however If you have similar or better PC than below example; then you should enjoy a trouble free game:
i7 2600k CPU (Games very drawcall heavy so needs high end CPU)
16GB DDR 3 System Memory (8GB might be OK)
Nvidia GTX 780 3GB (Or AMD equivalent)
SSD Hard Drive (Or at least a decent 7200rpm Hard Drive)
Game worked fine for me using spec above with graphics options maximum at 1920x1080; always stayed between 50 - 85fps (With 30fps enforced cap removed & vsync turned off via options). However Dead Rising 3 is a major resource hog due to the sheer number of Zombies on screen at once. But if it runs smoothly for you; then games a blast to play through 2 player Co-Op whilst using the built in voice communication.
As expected with this franchise; story is more of a side show to the very funny costumes, over the top weapons, and slicing up of zombie hordes. Zombie game Co-Op fans should enjoy Dead Rising 3 big time, if your PC can handle it. Whilst many of the games negative performance reviews are more than justified; cant leave a negative review as i enjoyed playing through the game Co-Op, and we had no peformance issues on either PC.
>Go to your deadrising3 folder. Default should be (C: Program Files (x86) \ Steam \ Steam Apps \ Common \ deadrising3
>create new text file in the folder
>name it "user.ini" (make sure you change the file type from txt to ini)
>open the new text file and type in “gmpcr_unlock_frame_rate = True”
>save the document
>start the game
>enjoy!!
Edit: Tested the game out via my newer GTX980Ti 6GB with rest of PC spec still same as above; and FPS was almost identical to old review (Between 61 - 87fps). So the game is clearly becomes CPU restricted if you own a GTX780 3GB or better.

This game does aboslutely everything right (aside from one thing).
FIRST: You make weapons the way you want them to be. This adds an interesting feature that allows players to conform and get ideas.
SECOND: Unlike TF2, you can't pay real money to get items. Microtransactions are used for cosmetics. Many games don't do this, while the developers of Loadout did it right. More games should learn from this.
THIRD: The actual gameplay itself is fun, and always has you on your toes. You have to be sneaky so someone doesn't spam a rocket launcher towards you.
FOURTH: No voice chat
FIFTH: The graphics and physics of this game are fun. Shoot someone in the chest and a huge hole appears in it. This game has massive amounts of blood, making it fun for everyone (over the age of 15). The game also has a cartoony style, which very few games can capture these days. The graphics aren't REALISTIC, so if that's a dealbreaker, don't get it.
SIXTH: This is the one con of the game. As stated in the second point, they did microtransactions right. They also did them wrong. They made everything way too pricy. This, however, is not an important gameplay aspect and should be overlooked.
SEVENTH: It's a free game! How can you have THIS much fun and pay not a dime? By getting Loadout.
All in all, 9/10 game. I do recommend it.

I've only been playing this game for a small time now, but from the moment I actually got into the game I noticed a few things that I want to note about this game. Of course this is a limited view as of right now, and I'll probably right more on this game in the future, but there are just things from a new player that I'd like to discuss that are appealing and absolutely not.
1. CAMERA DIRECTION. The camera is fixed, and not on the direction that your character is running, which is common in practically 99% of RPG games you and I could probably think of off the top of our heads. You have to hold down the right mouse button and manually steer around where your view is. This can be considered an infuriating experience at first. It also completely ruins the flow of the game, adventure, and just kinda sticks it more into your head that this is a program instead of your own cool anime adventure.
Even when it feels like I've gotten used to it, I end up in situations where this absolute design flaw sticks out like a sore thumb.
2. QUESTS OBJECTIVE TRACKING. While we're on the topic of that feeling of adventure that a lot of people would consider crucial for an RPG, myself included, the game has a function that can completely destroy the sense of adventure and exploration in quests. How? Well I'll start off by saying that any good RPG has a way to track the general destination or area that you have to go to for your quest, through just a little symbol that appears on the map or a symbol that appears generally on the top of the screen that points you where to go (note: in some games this can be executed poorly, however there are also games that can do this while still giving a lot of sense of adventure, Skyrim is a good example).
This game, however, has a pop-up screen that displays the goals of the quest, and if you click on the sentences of these obective (e.g you have to kill 5 of a certain enemy), the game will not only lay out a sparkly trail on the ground that not only leads to your goal, but also automatically starts taking you there. If you needed to find people that you can tell are supposed to be hard to find, you can just click this and you'll just be taken to them. More hidden resources that needed to be found? No worry, you'll be taken to it instantly.
For some, this is quite the positive, since a lot of people would find having to always look for the quest's objectives manually each time tedious and tiring; and it's a completely optional too. Honestly it's a pretty convenient function for people that just wanna blast through to get to the higher levels.
Although the bad thing I'll have to say about it is that the icon on the mini-map in the top right-hand of the screen the icons were absolutely confusing. There is a lot going on, and the icon that displays the direction of the quest does not stand out as much as the other symbols. The good thing is, however, that if you go into the regional map there is a list of icons on the side that not only tell you what each is for, but also has an option to not display them! Very handy.
I'd say these functions are honestly up to interpretation for whether they're good or bad. Personally, I find that it's very hard and not as clear as other RPG games in the showing of a more general direction and in frustration, can push you more to the option of just letting the game take you everywhere. I'm all about immersion and for me, even having that option takes away from the potential of the experience of adventure.
3. THE DESIGNS AND ITEMS. My god, everything is cool in this game. As an artist, aesthetics and the way colours and design catch the eye are very important to me for just about everything; especially in anything that's definitely more visual-based like games. But I've caught myself thinking quite a few times that it's overwhelming in this game, and even a bit 'too cool'.
Generally when we start to play a new fantasy MMORPG we start off with these kinda mediocre and mundane gear. In some you can see how it's kinda cool, but it's definitely not awe-inspiring. Especially compared to high-level players that you see running around mounted on something crazy like a lion with a fire mane, and gear on them that is radiating with some awesome aura, with wings coming out the goddamn back. We look to these players and start to idolize them in a sense for looking so rad. And when you start to reach up closer to the top, and start to collect your own cooler items, you definitely start to get a sense of pride and accomplishment in the hard work you've put into developing your character so much, especially if you paid money for it.
This game off the bat gives you awesome items. For exmaple I choose the Scythe class for my first character, at a very early level I can summon not one, but THREE beautifully designed demons to accompany me; and the choice is out of six demons in total. Even if you didn't choose the Scythe class, under level 10 you are given a mount, which personally I've never witnessed in a fantasy MMORPG before.
And to top it all off, the game itself is actually based around the lore of it's world that there are these people chosen by destiny, that are given little creature companions (which is a very stereotypical thing to see in anime) that help you fight with their special abilities. While in character creation you get to choose out of four which one you want.
This trait in the game is also really up to interpretation just like the last one, too. On one hand, it's very rad that we all can have so many magnificent items, and can just look so fine. But on the other hand, it personally gives me less of an urgent want to progress fastly to be able to look good since I already am satisfied with my gear. Also on the more negative side, town centers were lots of players congregate can look completely ridiculous; like a hub for really over the top, overpowered original characters from deviantArt. And despite actually loving all the designs in this game, I still feel more neutral about it all.
4. LAG. The bane of all gamers out there, the insufferable force which destroys the natural flow and order in your gaming session - yes, ladies, gentlemen, and honoured guests - this game has so, so much lag. I don't believe I have to go into such extensive detail for this section, but it's so much that it DOES need to be noted. It's not so bad that it crashes my game or makes me lag for more then 10 seconds, but I do have a good laptop and internet.
Why so much lag though? Honestly, blame the dirty weabs. All there for the designs, I swear.
5. POP-UP CONVERSATION SCENES. In this game when you talk to anyone that isn't a background character a pop-up screen with your character's and the npc's top half of the body show up. Dialogue, actions each character makes shown in text, intervention from not only your first mount, but also your little companion that's always given to you... it's all just like a visual novel. And it's very appealing, and even refreshing and unique to see in a fantasy MMORGP.
It wouldn't be too much of a stretch that they put this in to appeal to those that are loyal anime fans, seeing as a lot of very popular games in Japan have these kinds of cut scenes that are very iconic in visual novels. They even give your character very over-exaggerated reactions that intergrate into the 'weaboo sub-popculture'.
I can imagine some people would find this cringe-worthy, but I doubt anyone that would see it like that would be interested in a blantantly obvious anime-inspired game in the first place.
6. CLASSES. I was going to write about this extensively, but I ran out of space, so here's the basics. There are a wide range of classes, up to 13 classes in total.
I'd recommend this game since most features that I see as note-worthy are more postive or up to interpretation, and therefore, worth giving a go and seeing if it's for yourself!

In the event that the world ever ends, be it zombie apocalypse, nuclear armageddon, or any other fun kind of catastrophe, I feel like humanity definitely will live on. We're a stubborn race of beings. Like cockroaches. We're everywhere, we just won't go away, and we seem to find a way to procreate everywhere.
Out of every possible way that the human race could near extinction, I think being mostly annihilated by an atomic bomb or so would be the best way to go. Especially if Fallout is something we could go on.
In Fallout 2 specifically, one of the great tactical CRPG classics, an atomic post-apocalyptic wasteland is a pretty fun place. You can pretty much do whatever you want.
Fallout 2 takes place after the events of Fallout 1, with your character from the first game starting their own village outside the Vault to live out the rest of their days. Your new character is a descendant of them, and has grown up outside the Vault. Their village has had a horrible drought, and it's up to you as The Chosen One to set off and save the world.
Fallout 2 is near identical to the first game in terms of gameplay, polished and upgraded to make it the definitive classic Fallout experience. If you're looking for the very best in terms of isometric, tactical CRPG action, Fallout 2 is probably your game.
The time limit is gone. You're free to explore Fallout 2's vast, open world to your heart's content. There's all sorts of side-quests, missions, and just random nonsense to get yourself into. You can join the mafia, become a pornstar, or just slaughter every human being you see. It's all free game.
To start, you just need to create your character. There is a selection of pre-made ones, but the real fun of the game is creating your own character to fully immerse yourself in the world of Fallout.
From there, you just need to play through what could be called a crude tutorial dungeon. After that, the world opens up. Slowly at first, as your stats will not allow much exploration when the wasteland is crawling with giant scorpions and freaks. But with time, you'll be able to do as you please.
Mechanically, it's better than the original Fallout. It plays better, it controls better, and it has more depth than the original in terms of what the world offers. The gameplay has been balanced to make all character skills viable, which was an issue with the first Fallout game. As a sequel, it definitely has at least improved upon the original.
However, I personally still prefer the first one. Fallout 2, I felt took a lot of what made Fallout special out of the equation. The time limit, while brutal, was part of giving that sensation of hopelessness and urgency. And having your character born outside of a Vault, it took some of the impact away of having stepped out into the wasteland for the first time.
The story was not as compelling, and it didn't really feel like Fallout at first to me. The early game is particularly slow, and it takes a while to really capture that Fallout vibe.
As an older game, it is still a little bit dated. Especially in the graphics department. But still completely enjoyable as a game. I always did have a thing for older games. I like them a little mature, you know?
Regardless, Fallout 2 is still a very special game. There aren't very many other games where you can blow up small children with powerful explosives, become a slaver, or have sex with a mutant. Fallout 2 really is something special, and it's an essential part of any PC game collection. The sheer depth of the game constantly gives off the feeling that there's still more to do and more to see.
In the event of a real nuclear apocalypse, I call dibs on leader of the pornstar mafia. No, I already got dibs, it's official. Too bad. You can be something else.

I recommend this game WITH SOME RESERVATIONS.
If you are interested in Near Death because, like me, you crave first-person adventure/exploration scenarios and you saw the Near Death trailer and thought it seemed pretty original and rad, well then good news! You'll be pleased with that part.
If you are interested in Near Death because you like survival, then you need to know something. Near Death is not a survival game in the way that "Don't Starve" is a survival game, where you are merely fighting hunger (plus whatever other stats) using resources that are infinite if you are careful, economic, and smart. Near Death is survival in that more "survival horror" way where there are some finite and predetermined resources available to help you get from A to B, and if you squander them or dawdle too much then you're basically outta luck and dead.
Near death is also a game where the objective is not just to keep putting food in your mouth and warmth on your body for the purpose of staying alive forever. There are specific story goals that must be completed in a specific sequence, and you have to keep moving, moving, moving. There are finite resources, which by extension means there is finite TIME. And trust me when I say that this creates a harrowing situation for you that is quite interesting.
BUT.
It also creates a kind of frustrating scenario that you, depending on what kind of player you are, may find awesome or frustating. And I will explain via analogy. Imagine if I presented you with a game that was just a maze. All you have to do is get to the end. But you only have ten seconds to solve it or you die and have to start over. If you already know the way through the maze, it's easy. If you don't know the way through the maze, it's incredibly frustrating. And Near Death is extremely close to being this exact scenario. (Did I mention the maze has incredible atmosphere, though?)
So I will recommend the game, yes, bearing in mind the above reservations.

Orthogonal Games' grim survival tale Near Death was the gaming surprise of the year for me. Neither focused too too much on crafting but utilizing light elements of item construction along with plenty of survival strategy; in the form of conquering the game's starring blizzard, the experience of dealing with isolation, how to avoid hypothermia, making successful desperate dashes to light up the next part of abandoned Arctic facility to avoid frostbite and the game's sparse narrative...Near Death is a success across the board. It actually gave me the experience that I hoped to take away from Firewatch (even if it too was a good game), by not falling into the trap of being simply another walking simulator.
The story begins with the lead character crashing his/her (not sure on that voice, honestly) plane in Antarctica, thusly beginning the first in a grueling series of mad dashes to the communications building to reestablish comms with the McMurdo H.Q via teletype. Dialogue is in short order and I fond that to work to the game's advantage personally. You will cherish your few comminques with Jack back at basecamp as he tries to formulate an ever more complex plan to keep you freezing in the tundra's icy blight. Thanks to a recent update you can play the game on the ruthless Condition 1 difficulty where movement is difficult, the wind is against you, blizzard snowfall limits your visiblity to zero and time is generally not on your side. The story itself is a simple one...similar to other stranded feature films from The Edge to The Martian to Gravity and beyond. In my opinion, the stakes felt much higher in this game because there's just enough interactivity provided to make you feel that you are in total control of the pilot's fate. While the plot doesn't change necessarily from difficulty to difficulty, the way you must plan your moves ahead is altered dramatically on the hardest setting. Learning the map and your surroundings will be key.
Although the graphics are slightly dark and muddy it doesn't hurt the game but in fact enhances it. Nobody expects a derelict research facility in the Arctic to be in tip-top shape and things are appropriately rusted, broken down and blown asunder from the whipping gale force winds. There's enough detail and signs of where life once existed (like in the haunting biology and science sectors) that you can get mental pictures of the once hustling, bustling enviroment the compound gave purpose to. I also found the sound to be a highlight with the ever intensifying quiver of your character's breath giving you much needed clues as to when you need to seek shelter with heat/light or find a place to set up your portable heater. Winds howl like the last cries of the dead, eerie teletype keys echo the halls and the overall atmosphere is somewhere between the 1950s version of the Thing, Carpenter's version, Cryostasis and even The Long Dark.
Gameplay in this case is refreshingly devoid of monster combat. Some reviewers question the choice but I found it quite pleasing. If you choose to jump into the Condition 1 difficulty the storm has a personality all of its own hellbent on burying you beneath the permafrost and even on normal the wintry mix ranges from manageable to pounding, so each difficulty lends the snowstorm its own dangerous and wholly ominous vibe.
Thankfully, you are not helpless to just freeze, die and hope the nearest generator that you encounter will turn on with a flip of a switch and offer instant respite. Oh no, it's not that easy bub! You're going to need to scavenge for supplies to create much needed protective items along the way with each crafting requiring a certain number of excavated supplies. You can insulate your pants and parka for more defense against the elements (adding precious seconds to your outside forays), bypass electrical boxes with tool kits, marks your travelled paths with rope lifelines and glowing light markets and even wield a blowtorch that can melt your way into much needed supply rooms and pantries. With the grim situation at your feet and a number of useful tools at your disposale, you can fight back against the cold and buy yourself time whenever you're on the verge of totally freezing.
As you progress through the game you'll be provided with numerous different tasks and objectives, discovering snippets of information along the way. The narrative isn't in depth but the discoveries that you make and lonely conversations with McMurdo make you feel for the character that you play and hope there is some bright light at the end of the tunnel to get him home. Getting lost will happen from time to time, especially moreso in the harder blizzard conditions, so it's important to keep an eye on your completely realistic map/compass system that leaves navigation in your hands. Visibility can quickly go to a total whiteout and it's a frequent challenge to move heavy pieces of gear back to certain locations whenever the wind is blowing you left, right, back and taking down bridges beneath your feet. Some scenes are scripted, yet there's enough moments of white-knuckle gameplay alone to keep you playing for the duration. I immediately soldier through a normal playthrough and subsequently bumped up to Condition 1 since I knew the lay of the land. With the tougher conditions this didn't always end up easier than it sounds and I both froze death and was reaching for restart in sevral instances. Progression isn't beyond frustrating, just fairly challenging and it always feels good to fail miserably at a mission the first time only to think your way to a successful solution further down the line.
There are plenty of tools to help you along and the game never suffers from excluding a more in-depth crafting system. What's there is exactly what you need and yields multiple options for keepng the heat in. Two full-playthrough and earning every achievement but one ensured that I got my $14.99's worth and then some. Walking simulators can be fun in the right circumstances, though the team that coded and created Near Death came up with something far more unique than a simplistic "walk here, okay walk there, okay back track there to see one minute thing" style of walk-sim gameplay. Near Death might not be for horror fans into the stranded aspect looking to build camps, go hunting and stave off piles of foes but it offers a formidable foe in the blizzard and the ever hopeless conundrum of just how in the hell you're going to beat Shackleton at his own game.
Pros:
-Chilling, desolate atmosphere with a fairly immersive map to explore.
-Appropriately dark, downtrodden graphic style that really pushes the isolation aspect to the breaking point.
-Rewarding exploration that yields supplies, clues and creepy locales that you must power up.
-Several optional questions for powering up generators that will tip the light/heat dynamic in your favor.
-Condition 1 difficulty is a really authentic blast of fun with a decent challenge.
-Solid crafting system; never too deep for the game's style but provides multiple options for progression/protection.
-Simple story told through teletype machines furthers the trippy descent into arctic insanity.
-Ability to save anywhere besides simply checkpoints which helps cut some time out of trial and error dashes.
-Authentic navigation system.
-Elements naturally have effects on control which makes for an engrossing, immersive expedition.
Cons:
-The game's short length of 4-5 hours or less makes one long for an expansion pack. It doesn't HAVE to be as the game stands on its own but the quality here definitely makes me want more.
-The ending while marginally satisfying could have been better or perhaps lead to another run of problems to solve.
-Controls/interactivity can be wonky.
Overall: 8.5/10

Very cool and seems to resemble the game Grand Theft Auto San Andreas, or at least that's how I see it as. Get this if you liked that game!
Ok, so this game takes place before Saints Row The Third, which is sequel to this game and after the first Saints Row game, which unfortunately isn't on PC so I will need to watch a full gameplay moive of it or something to see what that was like...
Much of the gameplay is still very silimar to the sequel, though of course there are some changes....um, apparently this is a badly done console port to PC and I guess I will find out later why....as I've not yet understand what's so bad about this *port*....
The graphics is, yeah pretty dated compared to 2017 visuals, but if you just put your mindset in the year of 2008, it actually looks pretty cool.....with everything maxed out of course.... Resolution limit appears to be capped to a 4:3 aspect ratio one and that is the 2048x1536, you can't play the game on anything higher......but I'm sure there are mods that can enable 2560x1440 play or even 3840x2160...... However, 1920x1080 is available as an option if you ahve a 1080p display so that's not forgotten. I am not sure why it's capped at 2048x1536 for a 2008 game, usually those caps are for games from 2004 and 2005......but not 2008 released ones...
SLi support is NOT very well done here, I run two GTX 770s in SLi and neither of them hit 99% or more in GPU utlization, even on its highest resolution setting with everything maxed out. I have tried forcing "Alternative frame rendering 1 and 2" but they don't seem to help at all to get them working their butts off which is rather ironic because they're supposed to force *any* game to work with any SLi setup, but it would appear this game is an exception to that.... Well anyways, everything maxed out @ 1080p, I get around 30 to 90 - yes it drops down to 30 and sometimes even utlization of my graphics isn't maxed out either......which means this game isn't well optimized.
Game appears to run all 6 discrete channels, ie 5.1 (I think, could be 7.1, but will edit this if I'm wrong on my next playtthrough, but I'm just pulling this from the top of my head), BUT the channels are used in their correct way - for example, the center speaker should be where all the voices should be coming from, the front speakers having taking most of the brunt of the sound, rear speakers for the surround effect and sub channel for the LFE; in this game, it takes all of them, and just spits them all out in the exact same way, so all speakers get the brunt of the audio, there is no one speaker that is specifically dedicated to voice, specifically dedicated to LFE, etc. It looks like they either ⓕⓤⓒⓚed this up but kept it as is anyways and hope no one finds out about it OR I have some sort of issue with my system that is making SR2 spitting sound to all channels the exact same way where all speakers mirror each other...... I will need to dwell into this some more...
So far I like it enough to thumb up this game so yeah...
> There *is* an option for coop mode but that requires gamespy.....I'm not sure why they haven't fixed it up for the steam version.....so that it's done through steam, since it's released on steam anyways, so might as well.....lazy ⓑⓐⓢⓣⓐⓡⓓⓢ! haha
There were other issues I wanted to point out, but I forgot what they were.......oh yes now I remember what one of those issues were; sometimes, or after a while driving, the movement keys become unresponsive and you need to lift off and press the key again for the game to register that you want to go forward or turn left.
No mouse support for the main menu, so you need to use your keyboard....or if you have a gaming mouse and software to control that, you can bind those mouse buttons to actual keyboard buttons on the keyboard and work it that way - that's what I'm doing with my Razer Ourobororus. ☺

Amazing game. It's very reminiscent of old N64 screen splitting games and definitely has a Goldeneye 64 feel to it, which I consider a huge plus. You have up to 4 screen and all the player models are invisible, and the only way to kill someone is by watching their screen and estimating their movement.
It's hilarious how when you build a game around what most people go to such big efforts to cheat into normal games, even big FPS games like Counter Strike and Call of Duty, you realize how hard it is to kill someone even with all the knowledge in the world when it comes to raw skill and reflexes.
The art is very pleasing and makes finding people cake, dividing each map into multiple color sections to easily screenpeak and figure out where to go to hunt down your quarry. The game looks great, honestly, and plays very well even on an old laptop. Optimized well, quite hilarious, and a lot of "pure fun" vibes going for this game. The music can be a bit repetitive after you've played so much of the game with so little tracks, but you'll be killing too many invisible men to care.
The weapons are insanely balanced and despite the small selection of maps and, there are 5 game modes that turn Screencheat into a hilarious and fun party game for you and your friends. Good luck on finding anyone in the random matchmaking, there are pretty much no public lobbies.
I would buy this game again for myself even knowing there was no real community for it yet, but honestly trying to get a 4 pack and some like minded friends is your best bet for this hilarious retro-feeling game.

This is a fantastic game made out of a simple concept
GRAPHICS:
The graphics may not look AAA, but the game has a lot of charm in it's colorful art style, plus the maps are color coded, which really does help when you are looking for other players.
STORY:
There is absolutely no story to speak of, if you're looking for a story based game, why are you even reading this review?
GAMEPLAY:
Incredibly innovative concept and it plays out perfectly, the weapons feel right and killing someone is incredibly satisfying, I reccomend playing this game with friends though because servers are very limited and there are no dedicated servers to speak of, if there were i would play this game much more often.
SOUND DESIGN:
The background music is pretty charming and the weapons feel powerful enough to make it even more satisfying to kill someone in this game than it already was.
HUMOR:
This game is quite funny, as it has some of the greatest kill messages i've ever seen in  a game (e.g. 'you got #YOLO'D by [player name]', 'you Google Translated [player rame]' and '[player name] [player name] [player name] [player name] [player name] [player name]'. Also there are 3 announcers tochoose from, a silly one a brutal one reminiscent of games like quake, and an australian one, this isn't relevant at all but i figured i should mention it.
OVERALL:
I like this game a lot, although the lack of servers is a problem, this game is well worth your money, (I reccomend the 4 pack though otherwise you will only be able to play on weekends at certain times)
