Minecraft Story Mode is made to tell a tale in the Minecraft Unviverse, this is Telltale's first big project aimed at a child demographic, so the dialouge can be a big dumb and cringy at times, but this remains to tell a decent story where you can choose what happens (although 90 percent of the choices do nothing but change no more than one setence of dialouge)
8/10

I have written a review for each episode right after I played each one of them. As a final notice, I've never played Minecraft more than a couple of minutes (a demo on xbox live) and never really enjoyed it, so I had no fan bias while reviewing this game.
Episode 1:
Grade: 10/10
No great technical problems, long enough and entertaning. The characters are well fleshed out, the voice actors do a great job and the whole Minecraft aesthetic looked pretty nice in the Telltale format. Chioces do matter, giving me different pahts (I made some choices in the demo and different ones in the actual game) and, despite being an older gamer (39 next month), I found the whole family-friendly story to be actually fun, not so childish. It's certainly a light-hearted game, but if you play games and forgot about your inner child, there's certainly something wrong with you, buddy :)
Episodes 2:
Grade: 6/10
Comments: This episode is half the size of the first episode, lasting only about 1 hour. It plays out differently depending on a your last choice from episode 1, with a different beginning part depending our your choice. I picked the girl's path and, while it was entertaining, it was too short to be called a full episode. In addition, there was a huge glitch that made Jesse walk on thin air while trying to escape (you press a button, then jumps on nothing and runs away) and one of the achievements glitched (I'll probably have to replay the first part of this episode to unlock it). All things considered, I still recommend this game and I'm curious to see what's next on episode 3.
Episode 3:
Grade: 10/10
Comments: Episode 3 brings our heroes back in a 2-hour episode. The only bug encountered was the lack of subtitles in some parts. The story comes to a climax and I had a lot of fun playing this episode. I'm curious to see what's next.
Episode 4:
Grade: 10/10
Comments: This is not the last episode, but it finishes the first part of the story. Why, you ask? That's because they wanted people to get the rest of the story through DLC, of course. That's a lame move from Telltales, but I'll just discuss the episode's quality here. I had no issues whatsoever, and had lots of fun with the game. This episode took me 2.3 hours to finish, and it takes longer because there is a labyrynth and a puzzle to solve. I don't want to spoil anything, but I must say the story, even if very simple, works really well. The actors are perfect, and they really make you care for the characters. Havint just finished this episode, I can say this game has been totally worth my money and time until now.
Episodes 5:
Grade: 10/10
Comments: This episode begins a totally new adventure, in a new world, and it lasts 2 hours. The story flows pretty well and the gameplay is still fun. It's impossible not to be in love with Jesse and the other main characters. You get to a new place in the end and you need to buy dlc to play it, and this was a bad move from Telltale, but that's obvious when you think that they'd never finish the first season without cliffhanger, so people would pay more for a second season or - as it turned out - for DLC.
Conclusion: This game deserves a 9/10 for being a light-hearted, fun adventure in the Telltale format. Choices do change something in story, characters are well fleshed out and voice actors do a great job, and crafting is made simple and fun, even if you never played the original Minecraft game. Considering the game requires DLC to be finished (I'll review it in the DLC page after playing it), though, I only recommend this game when you can get it in a sale (I bought it 50% off).

While my play time for this game on Steam is limited, I've played for some time on mobile.
The game seems as if there is something shady going on, it's so very close to an older Growtopia engine in every way (with the old flaws they had back then too and without any changes or improvements).  It seems as if someone took apart the Growtopia code and just replaced the graphics, I doubt they copied it this close without getting the code but I guess there is a slight possibility that they copied it so very exactly that they copied the flaws as well and simply couldn't come up with any new design or interface element changes on their own.
The main difference is this is far more expensive.  You get the option to change to rare and cool skin colors in Growtopia pretty early on without spending much.  Here it costs $44 just to change to blue.  See that cool looking jet pack in the game video?  I hope you have about $120 to spend on it otherwise you won't be using it.
The pricing started out okay when the game launched, but it has crept up with each update to the silly amounts that exist for the new cooler items now.  Without them the game is pretty boring.  Spending money on farming you mostly get the same objects over and over.
Play Growtopia instead, yeah, the graphics are a generation below this but it's a far more advanced game with far better pricing and it's actually original, not a direct copy of a game like this one is.
I'm someone who likes both Free to Play games and Mobile ports too - but I just don't find much to like here.  Possibly if it was original and had better pricing, but it isn't and it doesn't.
It's small in size to download and doesn't really hurt to check out really quick but if you like it even a little bit I'd suggest going to search out Growtopia instead.  What little fun there is to be had here is done better in every way except for graphics over at Growtopia.  There really is far more to do at a far cheaper price over there.

You take on the role of James Hopkins, a new kid in a private school that is full of juvenile delinquents. You can run around and explore or complete side quests to advance the game. You can even go to classes during the day and play mini-games that unlock extra abilities. If you're late for class and the guards catch you in the hallway they will chase you down unless you outsmart them and hide in a locker.
The graphics are outdated and the controls are awkward due to it being a console port, but that shouldn't prevent you from having a lot of fun with this game. It literally has everything. Near Death is a brutal first-person survival game - you versus the viscious elements of the Antartic.  There is no micro meter-management as found in many survival games, and your role is to escape rather than remain.  The story starts with you surviving a plane crash at abandoned Antartic station Sutro, and you must gather enough supplies to plan your escape/rescue while not becoming victim to the hostile minus 100-degree temperatures and storm blizzards.  Resources such as batteries for your torch are scant and you must use these VERY carefully, as is your only source of heat: a portable kerosine heater.  Make these last because they've all you've got!
The game also involves a small amount of resource gathering and crafting to make rooms of the shelter tolerable and functional.  These steps are optional objectives but your survival experience will be much easier if you do this.
The totally believable atmosphere and difficulty scale.  Although the game is short, it is INCREDIBLY atmospheric - perhaps one of the most atmospheric survival games I've yet played (and I've played quite a lot of them).  Nothing feels unreal or silly.  Everything feels urgent and not at all easy - as it should!  There is very little hand-holding.  The difficulty curve seems spot-on: hard without being frustrating.
One of the complaints people have about this otherwise-excellent game is that it's short, but it's only a quarter of a full AAA game price, so I would expect a quarter the amount of playtime, and I exceeded that easily with 7-8 hours (others have reported less, so this might rather depend on how fast you speed through games). I would have liked to have had a little further playtime at the end of the game
but that wasn't to be.  There were a couple of minor world glitches such as being sometimes a little too easy to fall into impossible-to-escape crevaces and I did accidentally drop a piece of vital equipment a few feet ahead of me, only to find there was an invisible barrier prevanting me from walking towards picking it up (presumably I had reached the edge of the map but objects were able to sail over that same edge).  Still, save-games weren't spaced too far apart, so no huge deal there.  It wouldn't stop me recommending this game.
For those "challenged" by video games like, er, me, the 'normal' difficulty is difficult enough!  You WILL die, you will become lost (and die), you will freeze (and die).  There will be times when you're groping around in the dark because you didn't listen to yourself when you said "be sparing with those batteries!" and you will absolutely run out of necessities.  I haven't tried the higher difficulty modes (ho ho - I'm no mug!) but at 'normal' difficulty you will be returned to the point of your last save following death - which will usually be the last moment you managed to use your kerosine heater to generate warmth succesfully (you can also quick-save).
It will be eminently replayable for me, but I'm the kind of person who can read a good book several times over.  Some reviewers don't feel the same replayability, but for me it's a definite and I intend replaying at a harder difficulty level immediately.
Despite its somewhat short length, this game is currently carrying a 91% positive feedback score for good reason.  It's a must-have for every escape/survival fan.

I held off on getting this game for a while. My experience of indie FPS' has been mostly negative, some have been OK but really havn't been able to offer anything unique at the cost of smooth play, graphics and content. The concept of this game looked funny and original but I was sceptical about how fun it would actually be.
Boy was I wrong. The basic concept of invisible players and having to "screencheat" to find them is really something you need to experience for yourself. Level design colors rooms differently to make it easier to screencheat - thus familiarity with the map is not everything. Games are intense and involve split second choices such as firing in the enemies general direction or glancing over at their screen one last time to determine their location more precisely.
The game offers more than this concept though. The game offers tradition kill mode, king of the hill, capture the flag. It also has a "one shot mode" where you cant fire again until 15 seconds elapse or all other players fire. As well as a cluedo inspired game mode, where you have to kill a particular player with a particular weapon.
The weapon system is also in my opinion far superior to other FPS'. Instead of being aware of weapon spawn points on maps being the key to winning, each time you respawn you pick your weapon, ANY weapon, and you cannot change it until you respawn again. The weapons are all balanced, unique in concept, and offer different strategies, advantages and weaknesses.
Graphics are suitable for the purposes of the game but quite poor. If you're overly concerned with graphics in your FPS' then this game might not be for you. Otherwise there are no drawbacks.
Thrilling game. Best FPS I have ever played.

The steam controller.  Long awaited, much debated.  Despite some people not being fans of this, I have nothing but praise for it.
First thing I noticed was how easy it was to use.  I plugged the usb dongle into my computer, turned on the controller, and steam instantly detected it and it was ready to play.
It works for any game.  You can configure it completely from scratch for any game, or choose from some preset templates or community created layouts.  I prefer to make my own complete layout.
I have greatly enjoyed playing with the steam controller an RTS (wargame red dragon), a third person shooter (star wars battlefront 2), a turn based strategy (civ 5), a top down shooter (running with rifles), and a brawling game (brawlhalla).  For most genres you will have no issues at all playing with the same proficiency of a mouse and keyboard, after about 15 minutes of getting used to it (for each game).
The steam controller also has many buttons.  The triggers have a half and full pull function which can each be set to different actions, paddles on the back,
A good hint for aiming precision, the controller has motion controls.  They are high quality, and can be set as if it controls the mouse, alongside the touchpad.  For example, playing a shooter game, you can make larger motions such as turning around and seeking targets with your touchpad, but for precision aiming where you need to land headshots you can make small movements with the controller to get the reticule right where you want it.  It works very well and is pretty neat.
The only caveat is multiplayer fps games.  For competitive FPS playing, nothing is better than the good old keyboard mouse combination, however, for single player or relaxed experiences such as cod zombies or wolfenstien, it works just fine.
If you folks have any questions please ask in the comments I am happy to answer to the best of my knowledge.

Hey, I'm LStarr01, otherwise known as PaRappa in-game, on the forum, in the official Discord, etc. I felt like it would be best to introduce myself like this, so people who were to see the reviews could really know who was behind this all. This review isn't centered around me, but rather my insight though. Let me carry on.
Pixel Worlds, a game many have known to be as "a massively social sandbox game for mobile" (and PC) "platforms." A game stemming from the roots of other games, those being names you may know, such as Growtopia, Terraria, Minecraft, and a few others. Being a long-time Pixel Worlds player, since global release for mobile platforms in fact, I've grown to love and appreciate this game. Before this, I had played the game Growtopia for over four years, but after being told of Pixel Worlds, I was instantly swept away. I love this game, and I always will, for the future of this game holds such an immense amount of greatness... it is beyond me. Just because I love this game doesn't mean that I'm going to be biased, however... I am going to be weighing in on many factors of Pixel Worlds, giving my perspective through everything I truly know.
I downloaded Pixel Worlds on January 28, 2017, creating an in-game and forum account. I instantly became known as PaRappa. The welcome to the community was very nice. The mobile version was under beta for around two months before I joined, so I was welcomed by some experts of the game. I was given some tips on how to start, but I, being a Growtopia player, knew much about how to start in an online game, such as this, already. Overall, I have loved the community of Pixel Worlds dearly. I have some great friends among the buttload of players out there, some who I know would stick by me through thick and thin, even through an online game. The community, from my point of view so far, gets a rating of 9/10.
The game functionality is great. I would say that is quite similar to Growtopia, but it still manages to be unique in its own ways. You are given a variety of options at the current menu screen, being:
- You have the world selection tab, where you can choose whatever world you'd like to visit, look at current active worlds, view your recently visited worlds, the top rated worlds, and your favorited worlds. With the favorite option, you can favorite a world that you enjoy visiting, so you are not to forget the name. Along with all this, you are given two buttons that will instantly warp to you worlds classed as "Dynamic", these being the Daily Bonus and Daily Quest worlds. These worlds are for you to explore and gaze alore, but I will say that they reward you, both in different ways. Continuing with the menu screen, we also have the "Rules" and "Help" buttons that can basically show you what you can/cannot do and guide you if you're ever troubled in-game. These buttons are there mainly because of the effort that our admins will put in to help and show players what's right fro wrong. Super awesome to see that.
- You have the News section of the menu, showing the many announcements by the staff at Kukouri, which if you didn't know, Kukouri is the founder of this game. Our current news consists of many sections, including the Steam release for Pixel Worlds, the current Influencer Program, a tutorial video for Pixel Worlds, recent patch notes, a summary of the game, a tab talking about life as a VIP, and a button that links you directly to the Pixel Worlds forum. (I'll be getting into some of these later on.)
- You have the account tab, where you can view your basic profile info, including your username, recovery email (if your account were to be lost), and your Player ID.
- There's also the Social tab, where you can view Pixel Worlds videos created by the community of players in-game, as well as the videos created by Pixel Worlds' official YouTube. There are also buttons that link you to Pixel Worlds' Instagram, Facebook, and Twitter. Along with this, you're given another option to join the forum.
- Finally, there's the Shop tab, where you can view the many boosters, blueprints, wearables, special items, etc. that Pixel Worlds has to offer. All of these items cost Gems which you can earn by playing in-game or through IAPs. The shop also allows you to purchase a VIP membership as well, which will cost real-life currency.
All in all, the main menu has a lot to show, but some room to grow as well. The announcements need to be updated more often. This also goes for the Social section as well, with some videos being there for a while before being replaced. Other than that, I would say that the menu has some awesome, unique features to it, which will get better in the future. 8/10 for the menu.
Going into more detail with the store, I'd like to discuss the VIP Membership and Gem Purchases in the store. I'll start with the gems.
- Gems: Gems are expensive, and seeing as a couple of gem purchase options were removed recently, I don't know what to think. You are given 3 options, and as the price of each gem pack doubles, so does the amount of gems you get. With US dollars, you can choose to spend $4.99 for 10,000 gems, $9.99 for 25,000 gems, and $19.99 for 75,000 gems. This may seem like a lot of gems, but the items in the shop cost a lot as well. This will drain the amount of gems you have really quickly or cost you a lot more to get the item you really want. The most expensive item in the shop is the Flame Sword Blueprint, at 725,000 gems. This would cost you roughly $200 US dollars in order to purchase the item, if you were to gem your way to the item. I would never be one to perform this action, but there are some players that can't imagine saving up gems in-game in order to purchase this through the game instead of through a credit card or cash. Needs to be some sort of rebalance there though.
- VIP: VIP Memberships can be bought in the store, which gives you a chance to spin for the grand prize at DAILYBONUS, one of those dynamic worlds I was talking about earlier. There is always the option to spin for the normal prizes, but the grand prize takes the cake. You can purchase a Bronze Membership (10 Days) for $1.99, a Silver Membership (22 Days) for $3.99, a Gold Membership (50 Days) for $8.99, a Ruby Membership (150 Days) for $18.99, and a Diamond Membership (1 Year; 365 Days) for $44.99. The chance at actually striking big on the grand prize haven't proven to be the best for me personally, but there are some players that have definitely lucked out with this, winning 5+ grand prizes already. Though VIP is available in the store, you can also earn it in-game by completing achievements.
The Influencer program in Pixel Worlds allows popular YouTubers or people centered around social media to partner together. This will give players a green name in combination with bars around that player's name, sort of a way to stand out. As an influencer, you just need to post Pixel Worlds related content every once in a while. Overall, I find it super cool that Pixel Worlds does this type of stuff with players on social media.
Now that I've gotten through the menu, I'll go into gameplay.
- Locks: The lock system in Pixel Worlds is extremely similar to that of Growtopia, but I understand because it is very hard to find a similar type of item to describe what you're doing with a world. Locks are used in-game to protect your world, in a sense. When you first start, you place a Small Lock on the entrance portal to a world, then block the sides, that way no one is able to bust their way through, keeping your items safe beyond a distance of 1 block out. When you save up gems, you're able to expand the areas you have locked with Medium and Large Locks, covering a larger area than that of the Small Lock. Eventually, you'll even reach the World Lock, which protects the entirety of the world, also serving as a currency in-game.

Near Death is an indie survival adventure game that has been developed by Orthogonal Games. The game places you in Antarctica after the plane that you were traveling in has crash-landed. You are stranded and alone. Thankfully, the plane crashed near an abandoned research facility. Unfortunately, however, you have crashed in the midst of a deadly blizzard. It is blindingly dark outside and obviously frigid. In order to survive, you must explore Sutro Station.
There are so many survival games on Steam that rely on resource management. They have almost become a clone of one another. If you throw a different skin and setting on it a developer may assume that they have a new game. But it’s certainly not true because there is little to separate them from one another.
If I were to compare Near Death to any genre on Steam it would be the Unity engine horror games. This is strictly because of how the game plays and controls are. However, because of the genre differences and the associated quirks that come as a result the similarities end there.
Therefore, because of the lack of resource management, I feel that this may prove to be a major positive selling point for the game. That doesn’t mean you don’t need to look for tools to aid your survival. You’ll need things such as kerosene to fuel your heating device (and the heating device, of course). Consequently, your focus is not on finding X amount of an object but rather where it should be – on the adventuring itself.
The game isn’t a particularly simple game to play… at least in the beginning. It certainly controls well but it is difficult. I died several times very early in the game. Your body can only sustain the Antarctic conditions for a short period of time. Consequently, you must constantly search for the next safe zone. This is a place where you can set your heater down on the floor in an enclosed area and generate warmth.
The game makes superb utilization of the realities of Antarctic conditions. If you ever wanted to understand what it was like without experiencing it yourself then this game does a very good job of simulating it. One of the highlights of the game is the dynamic weather system. It utilizes snow, wind, temperature and lighting to create a realistic setting. It feels as though you are in a genuine blizzard where there are genuine moments of calm weather interspersed with craziness.
Further, the temperature simulation takes into consideration each room and area of the map. This is an outstanding feature of the game as it realistically calculates what each area of the map you are in and what the conditions would be like.
For all of the plaudits that I can willingly throw towards the game the biggest negative is arguably its brevity. For a $14.99 game, I was expecting to be glued to my seat for a number of hours. I am not sure where players are claiming to get more than several hours out of a single playthrough. I clocked in my first playthrough at about three hours and twenty minutes. For the amount of content – albeit much of it is quality – that you are getting I would claim that the asking price is too high. As others have recommended a $9.99 price point would be more reflective of the title.
Another complaint about the game that I have is that the difficulty appears to be front-ended. The game starts out difficult and becomes easier the longer you play. I personally favor games that offer a consistent level of challenge across a game or an increased level of challenge. The problem is that the availability of life-sustaining items becomes too frequent the longer that you play. You can almost guarantee that if you survive the beginning parts of the game that you’ll be able to complete the game.
Another issue that I have with the game is that because of the way that it is programmed it doesn’t allow for an exploratory playthrough. I readily admit that it was in reading GameSpew’s Christian Mincks’ review of the game that this truly dawned on me. While I appreciate that that is not the intention of the developer having the ability to have a game in this setting that you can explore would have been nice.
Near Death has a set of Steam trading cards and 18 Steam achievements. You’ll have to complete the game on each of the levels in order to unlock all of them. This may be a sore point for players who would like to perfect the game with only one playthrough.
I love the way in which the weather systems have been implemented. I’m never going to be able to travel to Antarctica and explore it. Therefore, I have to commend the developers on creating a game that was able to take me there as well as any documentary that I have ever watched. On that basis, I recommend the game but perhaps you would be best served to wait for a lower price point just because of the lack of content will disturb some patient gamers.

Near Death puts you into the position of a pilot who has crash landed in an abandoned station and must scour the decrepit remains to find a way home. The core mechanic of the game is that you are in an ever-increasingly-dangerous cold climate. To survive, you must seek shelter from the cold in one of the many buildings scattered about Sutro Station and either heat up via a powered room or your gas-powered lamp. There is also a crafting system in place to make the suvival aspect even better. This game will really make you feel like your in the protagonist's position, fighting the cold and the strong winds, testing your sense of direction and determination to live, and ultimately provides an experience to behold as you encounter some things you might not expect to find in the harsh cold.
If you want a game with good survival elements and writing, then pick this up.

This review may start off a bit odd, but stick with me...
I'm a massive Dark Souls fan. I've played every version of DS 1, 2, and 3 on every system it's available on. Hordes of hours of my existence. I enjoy the Souls series so much that, as others have claimed as well, it's practically ruined other games for me. I find it extraordinarily hard to really get invested in other games. I have tons of partially or barely completed games on both PC and consoles that I just flat out lose interest in, oftentimes very easily.
Then there's Near Death. One of those rare games that truly captured my attention and held me firmly in place for the entire journey.
You have one enemy: the weather. You're trying to survive against the cold and the wind. That's it.
But it's so beautifully done. The items you scavenge are used to craft realistically useful items that have true purpose in helping you to survive. The key items you'll need to collect make sense as well and are scattered brilliantly, having you make use of the full game world without ever feeling like a slog for the player but definitely an arduous task for the player character. Even little things, like kneeling becoming more useful than you would initially think, work favorably to immerse the player.
And another big deal for me: I generally cannot stand games that force you along, fighting a timer in whatever form that takes. Timed missions you fail when the clock hits zero. But it just plain works here. I felt a definite sense of urgency, but looting is done so well that I never felt overwhelmed by some insane quantity of containers to check before I froze to death. And you're actually given multiple ways to bring your body temperature back up, which was a welcome and thoughtful addition.
Also, the little bit of writing throughout the game was informative when it needed to be, and both clever and witty at other times that made me smile.

Orthogonal Games and all those involved in the creation of Near Death, ultra running super jumping electric exploding high fives to all of you!
P.S. Not everyone will care about this point (some may even roll their eyes at it), but THANK YOU SO MUCH for including full controller support. I can use a mouse and keyboard with the best of them, but I just plain prefer controllers. My PC is hooked to my main TV, and I play most games from my couch. In fact, had Near Death not had full controller support, I may never have seen it. I was specifically looking for a new, not-so-expensive game to play under the "Full controller support" category. And it's not half-baked support, either. It works for everything you do, including navigating menus. All prompts appear as controller buttons as well. You people rock ^_^

This now brings me to the addtional DLC episodes (costing around $12.99 USD when I purchased it), which I believe killed the good feeling vibe I had for this game. Episode Five begins with you killing monsters as any hero would, diving into some ruins for some obscure treasure which so happens to be the key to a set of new adventures. These adventures however dont seem to satisfy the story any longer, or expand on it other than you going on these said adventures, helping people solely because you are a good person. At this point your character goes from generic hero who vanquished evil to full blown savior of worlds which seems kinda over the top for my tastes. Nevertheless you always come out on top and save people left and right in the process. These DLC's are filled with diolouge options that seem to good for your character, even if you were trying to be a selfish self centered piece of crap. Like the first four episodes, all your choices lead to the same endings, but it just feels more artifical and it feels like you are a unstoppable force.
Overall I dont think you should buy the game in its entirety, as I belive the base game itself (Episodes 1-4) are the best part of this game, whereas the DLC's are just there for the cash grab..

There's a bit of stuff I consider uneccessary. New Reno as a whole is... Well really designed for fan service. There's a brothel and a porn studio here.
When you have entire PERKS centered around sex, you know something is wrong.
Progression in the beginning is slow
Geckos. Screw these things. Especially at the start.
Missing content that's easily replaced with Fallout 2 Restoration mods.
Getting a gun that isn't a pea shooter takes FOREVER. Prices are INSANELY high after Fallout 1. I mean, REALLY high. At the start, it cost me my entire supply of money, a gun I previously had (which was an EVEN WORSE pea shooter) and whatever I could scrounge up from the houses near by to get a 10MM pistol. Still a pea shooter, but it dealt more damage.
Random encounters are FAR too frequent. It's frustrating when the second you leave the city you're attacked by tweleve dogs, and it takes a few minutes for them to end their turn. And you can't run because they've trapped you.

On the whole, Fallout 2 is a game everyone who can think should own. This isn't a game for people that played 3 and New Vegas and enjoyed the shooter aspects: This is a bare knuckle, hard core RPG, and you WILL die. Many many times.

Hoo boy. I have mixed feelings on this one.
Fallout 2 is more or less the same as Fallout in terms of gameplay, but with improvements, which is certainly a plus. There is one minor gameplay quibble I have, and that's that they slightly nerfed the Turbo Plasma Rifle for no good reason. Why, besides trying to make the Pulse Rifle seem better by comparison? That seems like the completely wrong way to go about it, making and trying to balance new content by changing the old. It was fine! On the subject of equipment changes, they also reduced the weight of the Power Armor by about half with no explanation. I'd accept that if you at least acknowledged it, but now it just seems kind of silly. Just one offhand remark about removing unnecessary systems in there! THAT'S IT!
Anyway, the story issue is a bit more complex. The focus in Fallout 2, I've noticed, is more based on the moment-to-moment or area-to-area experience, rather than Fallout 1's cohesive whole. As a result, the whole thing seems more scattered, muddier, and overall less entertaining and less absorbing, as they'll do anything to make sure that you're never not entertained, while Fallout made sure that there was a single, easy-to-follow narrative, leading to a better and more consistent atmosphere.
One other really annoying thing: the game takes forever to get going, especially for gun-oriented characters. The Temple of Trials and the majority of Klamath have nothing but scorn for your desire to find a single ranged weapon that doesn't have a 1-bullet clip, and even then you're still on shaky ground until maybe the Den. For a while, I even tried to just play a hand-to-hand character for this game simply because the beginning is so stupidly unhelpful! In contrast, take a look at Fallout 1's beginning. You're kicked out the door. You have a gun, a knife, and ammo to spare (and a definite and straightforward goal). Boom. All playstyles are go. Even with the gameplay sorting itself out, the whole Fallout 2 package doesn't really get engaging until Gecko. After that, though, it really does pick up steam, and by the Enclave you realize that just now you're getting the experience and thrills that Fallout 1 was delivering from square one. (I should probably mention that eventually I was so desperate for some fun way forward that I looked up Per Jorner's excellent guide. That was what truly rekindled my interest, and I urge everyone to check it out. It contains levels of love and research of and for a game that I haven't seen since Everything You Wanted to Know About Headcrabs and More. Check that out too, actually.)
Overall, I like Fallout 1 more. Fallout 2 is huge, much bigger than its predecessor, and has its share of wonderous delights (don't get me wrong on that), but more often than not for me they're hidden behind some sort of obtuse non-engaging..sloppiness? Design oversight? Overreaching? that the first game rarely if ever had. I guess I'd still recommend it -mostly for the story connectivity- but really, Fallout 1 is the better of the two, in my opinion.
TL;DR I like Fallout 1 more, it seems to me that they got sloppy with this one. Too big to ignore, though.
Also, some of the canonical and best endings are hidden behind lazy bugs? WHAT?
EDIT: Just recently, I've been replaying the Fallout games in preparation for Fallout 2. When it came time for Fallout 2, I used Per Jorner's guide to speedrun through the thing in the course of a night. Playing through the entire thing once was enough for me.

Loadout - A FPS that goes against the tradition of most FPS traditions of Pay To Win(DLC Weapons and extras) and instead have the much more enjoyable Play To Win concept, By this you need only to play the game and pick your weapons choices wisely. With Loadout you rely on your skills with the mouse/keyboard or controller and not on the boosts of purchasable content. What you can purchase is almost only for cosmetics, Granted there are blutes/xp boosters but even these still require you to play the game. I have immensely enjoyed playing Loadout and have purchased the Steam Starter Kit (During The Holy Summer Steam Sale) and have edited the character I use for fighting. And for those who would rather not pay for anything on this game you still have the chance to aquire random clothing from the Daily Rewards.
The last item I want to bring up is the unique type of characters you get to play as: Axl, T-Bone, and Helga. These three characters are probably what makes this game so great, From the hilarious character models to the outfits you can have on them, Fighting the bots and seeing their unique outfits is probably the best part about this game, And if You really want to spend the money for Spacebucks you can get some hilarious outfits for your character (Axl's Rod is perhaps the most hilarious)

you can choose between 6 gamemodes, deathmatch, hillcampers, one shot, murder mystery capture the fun and Party mode. Instead of talking about the facts about being invisible and screencheating i will explain these gamemodes
Deathmatch: your average deathmatch, by default 5 kills to win, fast paced
hillcampers: King of the hill, stay in the area indicated by a box and hold it for 40 seconds (by default) be warned, the areas move and people may spam the area with explosives
one shot: everyone has the same weapon, blunderbust (by default) and must get a cirtain amount of kills. the twist is that once you shoot you can't reload until the timer runs out or everyone has shot
Murder mystery: each weapon is scattered around the map, you start with no weapon and are given cards, they show you what coloured are your victim resides in, the weapon you must kill them with, and the amount of points you must aquire to win, you must hunt while being hunted. be warned that sometimes your victim may have you as their target aswell.
capture the fun: much like one flag ctf, the fun (flag) will spawn randomly in the map, its marker will appear on your map, you must collect it and hold it for 80 seconds in total (default) whilst you have the fun you are unable to shoot, whilst you can gain around 10 points for each kill you get with using the fun as a melee weapon.
party: a collection of every gamemode that will randomly be selected each round, by default it has every gamemode in the random selection but they may be changed to your prefrences

Screencheat. The multiplayer topic not many of us have said about since N64 day's of GoldenEye. But now, Aussie (yes!) studio's; Samurai Punk and Surprise Attack! Games have made a game where the only way to win, is to screencheat, and this game is called... Screencheat (not a very original name, I know). In this multiplayer only shooter that can be played locally or online (or a bit of both) has you and up to three friends battle it out in the five arena's that have been made, where you must only do one thing, KILL EVERYONE! But it's not that simple because, everyone is invisible so you must screencheat to know where they are. Obsiously, many of you will go; "But wouldn't you only see your screen on an online match?" Well the answer that wheather you are playing online or not, you will see everyone's screen's. I really enjoyed this game, I played mostly with my brother and... it ruin's your LIFE! (ish). It's just so fun, knowing that your enemy is somehwere, but you don't really know where he/she is. My only real problem is that there isn't exactly enough content here, as I said, there are currently only 5 maps, FIVE. And while the six or so game modes including "Murder Mystery", which is basically Cluedo: The Videogame. Maybe having Workshop support would fix this problem. I also found a few bugs here and there, but I'm sure they will be patched out. Overall, I really enjoyed this game and hope it is constanly updated. Not many maps and qutie a few bugs do ruin it a little bit, but the funny things that pop up after killing someone are just funny. For a game that recently came out, I enjoyed it, just make sure you have lots of friends. I'm giving it 8/10 Times I slamed my hand on the table because I got killed. (GO AUSTRALIA!!!)
A fun party game, Screencheat is best played with three of your friends. It is the sort of game that rewards knowledge of the maps more than playing skill.
It's alright if you ever actually manage to find a lobby.
Screencheat is a completely amazing multiplayer experience - you're missing out if you don't buy this right now!  I can finally screencheat with pride instead of guilt ;)

I was gifted this game by the friend of a guy who plays TF2 with me. In retrospect, I'd buy it twice over.
This is a one of a kind, unique indie game that takes a bit of getting used to.
Regardless of whether you are playing local or online, the game plays in splitscreen (meaning you can see the point of view of the other players), much like local console shooters.
In this game, there are no world models. You are all invisible except for the occasional smoke trail.
This means to locate your opponents, you have to
. Look at their window to see where they are, and fire accordingly.
You aren't stuck with just guns either, you also get candles, hobby horses, crossbows, exploding teddy bears, and more of that wacky stuff. There are various gamemodes, ragdoll skins and such. Also, ragdolls don't disappear. You can play 10 rounds in a row and be drowning in ragdolls.
It supports local and online multiplayer and has controller support.
The only problem is that you will most likely need friends with the game to play it. I've yet to find a public server to play on, but this isn't a game fault.
tl;dr: unique game where everyone is invisible and you ride a hobby horse into them to win

I've felt a vareity of emotions while playing Near Death: annoyance, relief, joy, frustration, curosity, accomplishment and many others. This stems from the game throwing you in a very hostile environment that's indifferent to how your character, or even you as the player behind the screen, are handling issues like dealing with -100C weather (great feeling) or physics bugs (not so great).
In the end, despite its flaws, Near Death has what I look for in games these days: an experience I will likely never feel IRL or even in another game and for it to treat my time with respect by keeping that experience short but sweet.

Deus Ex is a cyberpunk-themed, action-adventure sci-fi game developed by Eidos. It is an FPS but shows our character from the third-person perspective once behind a cover. The game, thus, puts a lot of emphasis on stealth-based approach taking down enemies one by one without allowing them to see us. The more silent approach you pick the more experience point you obtain after a successful takedown, therefore, the easier to level up. Once at a new level you can spent your hard-earned Praxis points on various skills further enhancing your capabilities: you can learn taking down enemies by smashing through walls, you can run and jump almost silently or if you want you can just become invisible for a short period of time.
There are two areas where Deux Ex shines:
1) Story: You need to find out why Sarif Industries, the world's leading nanotechnology firm was attacked by an unknown group of mercenaries. You look for clues in Detroit and overseas in China, Singapore and even Australia. Each city offers a lot of side missions for you to further develop your skills and to get to know more of the story or just the world Deux Ex takes place in. It is common that you can make a decision as to how you want to accomplish a mission: if the requests are coming from more people you can decide who you'll favour eventually. There are collectibles in the form of e-books providing you with further background of the year 2027.
2) Gameplay: As mentioned, while running and gunning is also an option the game is best played by picking the silent approach: each section offers extra bonus if you do not eliminate anyone and if nobody sees you coming. I also liked the hacking sequences - I hacked each and every panel in the game even when Jensen was in possession of the code to unlock a specific door or to turn off the turrets aimed to protect a certain area.
Now, the Director's Cut is a newer version and has been available for a while instead of the vanilla edition. It comes bundled with the game's DLC and offers some graphics and AI improvements. As you can see from the store page patches were released as the DR version suffered from some pretty annoying bugs. Personally, I did not encounter any of these and I liked how they changed the boss battles in favour of those who decided to remain silent assassins throughout the game. The Director's Cut employs more vivid colours - I can understand this irritates some people. We have some documentary videos, audio commentaries and the good old new game plus mode which is so famous nowadays.
Overall, I was satisfied with Deus Ex and with the Director's Cut I completed the game 3 times. That's 3 times 30-35 hours if you complete all side-missions and talk to everybody and explore every corner just to see if there are some extra equipment or Praxis Kits lying around. What's more is that the game offers 4 endings but in order to be able to see all of them you need to complete a lot of missions in the last segment of the game.
If you want a story-oriented, long-lasting cyberpunk experience then Deux Ex is for you. With the Director's Cut coupled with a discounted price you cannot make the wrong decision by purchasing Human Revolution.

(Pixel Worlds) is a Mobile Game that started off as just that. June comes along as we are now filled with joy that Pixel Worlds is now a cross-platform PC game. Starting off with comparing it to the Early Days of Pixel Worlds. So much as changed, and many of these changes have been shaped by the Pixel Worlds Community. If there's something you dislike about Pixel Worlds- just remind yourself that the community had a say in that feature. They may have influenced it to the Staff Team, and the Pixel Worlds Community also may have supported it.
- More In Depth -

Block Variety - 85/100 (Rating)
Clothing Variety - 95/100 (Rating)
Creativity Allowance - 100/100 (Rating)
Item Variety - 75/100 (Rating)​
Tutorial (Early 2017) - Pixel Worlds tutorial was aimed at Mobile Users as it was the only platform the game was on. The tutorial section started off with an NPC telling you what to do. Teaching you the basic controls, and not really going into much depth about what you should do in order to understand what type of game this is. Break blocks, and that's about it. I mean it does go into a few short details on why you need to break. But it doesn't explain what to do in enough detail to new users.
3/5
Tutorial (June 2017) - Pixel Worlds tutorial has been scrapped with the replacement of PC Controls showing up instead of Android / IOS device controls. This is a very nice touch, and adds to the depth of PC Release. However, nothing has changed besides that. And this is one of the biggest reasons why Negative Reviews are appearing so commonly.
3/5
Style / Clothing - The fact that can't wear some items with other items is one of the most saddest features. It's something that drives back the Creativity, it stops us from getting real creative with our unique looks. We are all having to wear our own Sets, but can never go above & beyond due to the way the game has been coded. Maybe a change in the future where we can wear Neck Items with other items, and we can wear Hats & Masks together. Plague Mask would have probably been more popular if you could wear it underneath a hood. So, now you can see why some items go down in price due to their customization ability.
2/5
Farming - Farming has always been something that becomes tedious quickly. But the Staff Team did promise us new ways to earn Gems. And so far they have kept to that promise, and are giving us a few hints towards what we can expect. However, farming is more fun when you are farming for an individual block or set of blocks that you need to create your world. When it comes to farming for Gems? It's not as fun . . . and I also believe that there should be wayyyy more farmables included as it deserves its own update title: Farmable Update.
3/5
Locks - Everything is fine with these Locks. Not really going to complain about anything about the Locks. Maybe more ability to possibly stop players from placing blocks in some of your Public Locks? That would be cool as it would allow many to function better.
.5 / 10 (Not really important)

If you want something a little more realistic and a lot more terrifying from your survival horror, this is a great game.  You're not fighting anything except the cold.  No monsters and no jump scares, just frigid Antarctic weather.
It's atmospheric enough that I was bracing myself before I had to open up the door and brave going outside into the cold, and there's nothing quite so terrifying as losing your guide rope in the middle of a blizzard 50 feet from safety.
There's several complaints about the shortness of the game, but I appreciate having a tight and well-composed game over the usual sprawling mess.  It was the right length for the story it was trying to tell.

I like survival mechanics, but generally don't enjoy how most games put them into practice.  Perma-death is mostly, though not always, a barrier to entry for me.  I enjoyed this more survival light experience.  Still some crafting and resource scrounging involved, which I like, but all in the name of not freezing to death.  And NOT permanent.  Can save anytime you wish.  A nice compact game that picks up intensity the further you get.  Trying to run against the wind to get to another building to warm up could prove quite tense.
There were some bugs during my playthrough.  I went to this one area before the story told me to, and found I could just jump off a cliff and not die. The original Xbox controller came out in 2003 (Not the Giant "Duke" model which originally shipped out with the OG Xbox). There are some ergonomic changes going from the orginal to the 360/Xbone, but not significantly enough that it takes much time to re-adjust. Thats a little over 12 years using the same controller, so its not exactly easy to pick up something new.  I never got into playstation consoles simpl It definitely brings something new to the table, but it doesn't quite bridge the gap between mouse and keyboard vs controller inputs.  The trackpads allow for more precision in some cases; playing Civ5 or Simcity was far easier, but racing games were pretty difficult. Using the trackpads to control cameras also was frustrating, I always overshot and ended up getting the camera at a weird angle, this can be crtical in games like Dark Souls.  Using an Xbox controller for CSGO is the worst experience I have ever had, The Steam contoller was pretty on par with this, The trackpads have a bit of acceleration to them, so you tend to over track with them.
I realize that it is a very user customizable device, so I am sure that most of the tracking issues I was having can be mitigated by adjusting some settings. I'm just used to the defaults of a plug and play controller.  I think it does somethings better than a controller, but still can't quite match a mouse and keyboard.
For sitting on the couch and being able to navigate the entire desktop and not just games, its a pretty sweet device. I'm not sure I would pay 50$, luckily you can get gently used ones for 30$ online.

I purchased both the Steam Link and the Steam Controller together.  I did a review on the Steam Link already (I liked it, just need to find the right settings for your tv/pc)
I bought the Controller with reservations as to its ability to play games as well as other controllers.  Also, I wanted to try playing League of Legends with it.
As compared to other controllers (Xbox one and 360) I believe the xbox one is definitely better as far as feel and responsiveness.  Compared to keyboard and mouse it is not as good.  However, it does do both of those things well enough.
I use the Steam Controller to play games with my steam link AND to use it to do things on my desktop from my couch using the steam link.  It is great for a mouse when you want to do stuff on a couch.  If you have windows 10 then you can turn your desktop into tablet mode so you always have a keyboard on had with it.   Steam is also developing more things for the controller such as settings for it to be used on your desktop (not in big picture mode, or during minimized big picture mode)  This way you can pull up the keyboard that comes up in big picture mode (which is awesome and intuitive surprisingly)  I am excited for that feature to come out.
I tried making settings for it to play League of Legends.  I found a decent setup that works pretty well.  There are a lot of different ways you can set it up which is fun and neat if you are into that kind of thing.  I was able to play LOL with it.  Playing against bots I could go toe to toe with them on my first try using the controller in the right settings.  However playing pvp would require a lot more practice but it seems reasonable to be able to learn it well enough to be somewhat competitive with it.
There are a ton of things you can do with the steam controller with the settings!  I was really surprised at all the options and tweaking you could do.  I have been planning on making my own "arcade" with old arcade games and the steam controller could be a one size fits all controller for everything you would want to do with any arcade game (unless you want an actually roller ball or gun or joystick and arcade buttons) But with it you can have it setup so whatever game you go to play it automatically chages to the settings for that game which is great.  You can load any game or program into Steam so that you can make an individual steam controller setup for it.  Sometimes there are some issues with that just because there are bound to be programs that just don't jive with Steam but overall you can (I did it with LOL and Google Chrome).
As a competitive piece of equipment is it the best thing on the market? No.  Does it have potential to actually replace a mouse a keyboard? I think so with enough time and practice on it (probably A LOT of time).  Will you be the one to change over to it?  Most likely not, I am not either but someone out there might.  But overall for my couch style pc controller it does everything both an xbox controller and a keyboard and mouse can and more as long as you set it up that way.
I hope it helps! Again I made a review for the Steam Link.  I am one of those that actually got it to work nicely and talk about how I did it in the review there.

*I have included some tips at the end to help newcomers to the early Fallouts*
I remember the hundreds of hours I've spent on the console version of Fallout 3 back in 2011. Fast forward to early 2015, I've decided to try out the older Fallouts, starting with Fallout 2. This being my first "true" RPG experience, all of the info and stats, along with the fact that it was a turn based isometric game, made it look intimidating from the surface, but after some researching, the game starts to look less daunting.
Just like the Bethesda Fallouts, the game uses the S.P.E.C.I.A.L system and the familiar stats, along with traits. Fallout 2 really does gives you a lot of options on how you can adjust your character. Naturally, I (stupidly) chose to have a really buff gunman with perception and agility as my dump stats. I went through the Temple of Trials (the tutorial dungeon) and got demolished. My stats made playing through the game a nightmare.
See, unlike Fallout 3, the stats you choose matter a great deal more. Some of stats in Fallout 2 function the same as Fallout 3 (Strength judges carry weight and ability to use weapons, Intelligence increases skill points, Endurance increases HP and resistance, Agility affects Action Ponts, Luck increases stats slightly and influences random encounters). However, some act differently. Perception affects how acurate you are at longer ranges, every single action requires Action Points meaning that high Agility builds are better for combat, Charisma affects the number of companions you can have, and low Intelligence can effectively deny you from a large amount of quests and activities.
With this information, I remade my character and went back into the Temple of Trials. It must be said, however, that the Temple is a very poor representation of the game. The game forces you to use melee and barely gives you enough healing items to get past the darn thing if you don't use hit and run tactics with high agility. Fallout 2 gives you no information regarding mechanics, and it's clear that the devs were forced to phone in a tutorial segment (if you can call it that).
Fortunately, the game starts to show its magic after you exit the Temple and rejoin the villagers of Arroyo, the home of the decendants of the protagonist of the first Fallout. The village is dying and you are tasked to gind the G.E.C.K, a device that can help bring life back to the village. From there, you find a multitude of interesting characters and locations, such as New Reno and its many gangs, to the Broken Hills with its super mutants. Although there is a small amount of quests compared to the later games, the quality of the dialogue and the world you are thrown into makes it easy to forgive. The game also includes some returning characters from the first Fallout, which give some background to the protagonist and the events of the first game. Unfortunately, the humor of this game is something that may not be appealing to some, however. Fallout 2 does include many pop culture references and fourth wall breaks, which does get tiring admittedly.
Combat in this game is very enjoyable and has a satisfying punch to it, with gory animations accompanying sounds of limbs being blown off. The amount of weapons in this game is fairly reasonable, but this is mainly towards the end where you have gained large amounts of money and can handle the tougher enemies with better loot.
Overall, Fallout 2 is a real classic of a game. It may be hard to adjust as a newcomer, but the game is very much worth it.
*Some tips*
- You have four types of cursors in the game (switch by using M2), a yellow arrow (click on items to interact, hold M1 to get a list of interactions), a red hexagon (decides where you go), a hand (decides what you pick up in the inventory screen), and a red crosshair (decides what you shoot, only accessable when you are in combat).
- You can break wooden doors by using melee on them or using a grenade.
- To use Skilldex skills, click on the skilldex button, choose the skill and then the item you want to use the skill on.
Examples: Click on Doctor and yourself to heal. Click on Lockpick and a door to lockpick. Click on Steal and a person to steal.
- Before exiting towns or talking to important characters, save.
- To change the action done to a weapon you are holding, press M2 on the weapon box. For guns, this can change them to Single Fire, Aimed, Burst (If the gun has it), or Reload. The green ticks on the side of the weapon represent the ammo level.
- When bartering, make sure to get change from transactions. For example, if I bought a gun that costs $1000 and gave a gun that costs $950, I need to bring the vendor's money into the transaction area to get money. In this case, I would ask for $50.
- The red button above the inventory button helps switch weapons.
- To enter combat with friendlies (or unaware enemies), click on your weapon. To end combat, press the CMBT on the bottom right. To end your turn, press Turn. (Also on the bottom right).
- Rest by clicking the Pipboy button and clicking on the yellow button on the top of its menu. This can only be done after finishing the Temple of Trials.
-  You can scavenge extra ammo from dead NPCs by using the yellow cursor and choosing the "unload gun" icon (picture of a gun and magazine) from the interation list.

lets get this out of the way right now, if you need a hand to hold you the whole entire game or are a graphics ♥♥♥♥♥, you will not enjoy this game. There is next to nothing in terms of a tutorial, and it is much different in how it handles quests compared to NV and 3. It does not throw them into your face and say "DO THIS♥♥♥♥♥♥OR NOT FINISH GAME!" Instead, it leaves you on your own the moment you leave the temple. The character creation is something that we are all familiar with, but matters alot more in this game than it did in fallout, 3, and NV. You have your standard S.P.E.C.I.A.L. selection, and lots of things to specialize in. Unlike in NV and 3, the game doesn't force you to go through primm, and do vault missions. You just get thrown out into the wasteland with one overall quest. It puts one place on your map and it is entirely up to you on whether you go there or not. Also, the wasteland encounters are completely random, and unlike in NV and 3, you cannot take out a group of 5 bandits fresh out of the gate. Also this game is a roleplayer unlike 3 and NV (I havent sunk alot of time into fallout yet, only 3 hours). The choices you make leave a huge lasting impact on the world, you can be a truly evil sonofa♥♥♥♥♥ and kill all the kids in the den, or you can be a nice guy and help torr take care of the "moo-moo's." Hell, you can be a pornstar. This game also has alot of pop culture references. Arnold swollenmember being a pornstar name. It knows when to be serious and when to be funny. It has a rich amount of lore, and you feel like this world is alive. In fallout 3 and new vegas, never once did I feel like the world was living and breathing. Every random encounter felt perfectly timed, and it has put me on the highest of high's and the lowest of lows. This game is one of my top 5 games of all time. I love everything in this game. You can feel your character get stronger. The combat can make your heart pulse rapidly, making you question on whether or not you did the right thing. Every choice you make has a consequence. I got the steam controller for christmas.  There's one thing you need to understand about this product right off the bat: it's not made as a controller replacer, it's made to allow mouse-level detail and keyboard-level control without the need for a bulky keyboard and mouse.  Your best bet is to set the device up so you never need to use either the joystick or the a,b,x and y buttons.  The buttons are in an arkward position and the left haptic pad is oversized, making the joystick awkardly placed as well, however, most of the controlls are available from a single hand position.  You have the two triggers, two bumpers, two pad buttons, and two additional bumpers for the fingers that rest under the controller to use.  That makes akk but two controller buttons (and the d-pad) accessible.  At first I thought the under-controller bumpers would be odd and always be clicked, but they aren't and don't.  While it will take you a while to get a feel for the controller and how to use it, it has the potential to be a great addition to any PC gamer's arsenal.  All this needs is a thumbpad keyboard attachment like the xbox 360 controller and headset jacks and it would be perfect.

Overall, the Steam controller is probably the best controller I've ever used. Controls are somewhat finicky at first; if you buy one of these, you'll probably find yourself rebinding controls for every other game, fiddling with sensitivity and going back and forth between controls for the first couple of weeks. Hand pain is also common at first. However, these all subside with continued use, and once you've gotten used to it, it works beautifully. It can handle just about any game with any balance of controls you could ask for, at a lower price point than the console competitors, with an accuracy and stability of control nearing what you might expect from a standard keyboard and mouse. The trackpads are actually very intuitive - the built-in haptics make it so you can feel the controls working in a way that you can't with, say, a touchscreen. The addition of grip buttons compared to console controllers is also pretty nice. It's also a necessity at some points, as the trackpads are sensitive, and pressing them in can screw with your aim. My only complaint is the lack of rechargeable batteries - the controller takes AAs, and coming from a DS3 user who's used to charging from USB, that's kinda offputting. But as I said, probably the best controller I've ever used.
tl;dr: Amazing controller. Definitely worth the buy. Hard to get used to at first, but works like you wouldn't believe when it does. Rechargeable batteries and initial hand strain may be offputting to some users, but I assure you it's worth it.

I personally am a gamer who has learned from past experience to never pre-order games, but sometimes I let my guard down and do it, even if I know the possibility to get disappointed again is nearly 90%
Until a few weeks before its release I saw a small “Lets Play” from Outside Xtra where they played “NieR: Automata” a game I never heard of or have seen screenshots (I don’t read gaming sites anymore) but I knew “NieR” (which never really interested me). What I saw really surprised me and I had this feeling I wanted to play this game, something I didn’t had for a long time. So, I threw every warning in the wind and ordered it and was looking forward to it release.
I played it, and I am really honest with you, this has the chance to be my personal best game of 2017.
I won’t go to much into detail, just what I thought worked and what not, so don’t expect a professional review of some kind – I try to keep it short…
If you are a fan of Hack and Slash games with exploration, partly open world, interesting characters and story, different playstyles and love twists then please check it out, it has its flaws, I won’t deny that, but the rest is absolute strong to let you overlook them – you will be invested in the world and what is going on.
I won’t deny, this game took me by surprise in so many ways. I bought it because I thought the fighting parts looked very well designed and executed in the video, I loved the presentation of the big intro battle against this giant machine – it just looked fun. And after starting the game and having the controller in my hand, I was really surprised how good the controls really are. They are fluid, never had the feeling that they don’t react to what I do and ever hit was satisfying and had weight, something I miss a lot from many games out there.
Something else that surprised me was, that you don’t start with the 3rd person view but in an top down shooter (which will come back more times). But it didn’t feel like this was just there to put something in there but that it belonged in this game and this part. And even the later stages never felt tacked on, it enjoyable to have this mechanic also used in the boss fights to change them up a little bit and it works really well. I know some players will have problems with these bullet-hell parts but believe me they look extreme, but I think everyone is able to finish them except on special stage that isn’t necessary to finish but to really see the end game you have to play it (and it even gives you help – so in the end everyone can finish the game.
I know how the last part sounds, but believe me, when I say, the way the story is told is amazing and telling you about specific parts would take away a lot of its impact and fun. So I wont tell you anything about what our heroes A2, B2 and 9S go through. But let me just say one thing because I know a lot of people didn’t realize this: If you finish the game the first time, keep on playing, just start a new game from the last save, where it says start new game with all you experience and equipment. I just did it because after the game ended I was so flashed and I wanted to find more of the side quests I missed and maybe do some a little better, and what then happened I didn’t see coming, so do yourself the favor and at least start it once again – without spoiling to much it will answer the question why the playtimes are so different between a lot of players who said they finished the game.
From the gameplay elements I really enjoyed the weapon and equipment part. Yes a lot is already well known from all these jrpg titles out there, like gathering items, buying stuff, creating things etc. but again I never felt like it was just a tacked on part. It could have been done a little bit deeper, but in the end, It served its purpose. The part I loved was the way you could customize your character: You have different kind of chips you could insert in some of your slots where you are limited, so you have to think about what do you want to use. This goes from just more weapon damage to have more speed or to jump higher, but you are also able to configure your HUD, removing everything so you have no interface and feedback and also bring up one specific ending of the game. It’s a really neat system that brings a lot of fun to experiment with.
The weapons are upgradeable, and because you can always carry two weapons with you, you are able to change your playstyle on the fly but also experiment what you think suits your playstyle best, it doesn’t put you into one spot which I really like.
There is a lot more I really enjoyed, the changing world after specific fights, the different kind of regions you could travel to, the enemies (even if there are just a few), the characters are amazing, the voice actors did a great job and a lot more and the sound designs is fantastic.
Some things I had some problems with, but that didn’t kill the fun for me.
The open world aspect. Yes, it was fun to run around it with these different styles and regions, but at the end it was just a bunch of corridors you walked through like every jrpg. Some people will hate this, and I can totally understand this. What was more problematic for me were all these invisible walls. There where places you just couldn’t go even if it looked like it (and they used different techniques to cover some up (like in the desert the wind) but I don’t understand why the developers didn’t think of a solution for some parts in the city – it can get very frustrating if you want to explore and think you can reach a specific point which isn’t reachable.
Another thing that frustrated me a little bit – as fun as the story missions can be, some of the side quest where just boring and too long or too hard (gathering items on the other side of the map or a specific race which I wasn’t able to finish) – don’t get me wrong these are only a handful, and some are of them have a really great end to them in many ways, but come on, there were so many possibilities – and you had a lot of ideas (just throwing out robot knights, people who played it know what I mean).
And the third bigger problem I had, was the map system. Its great to have a map, but if you need it and it only shows basic stuff but not some more details it gets nerve wrecking if  try to enter a specific part of the map and just cant find the entry to it, even if the map says its in front of you.
But all in all even this more bigger problems didn’t made me quit and always continue to find out what happened in this world an what is the ultimate goal of the people behind it.
Is it for everyone, definitive no, I think you have to be a fan of jrpgs and more extreme hack and slay titles (like Bayonetta) but then you will have a lot of fun.
On the technical side I can’t tell you much, I played the game on a notebook with an Intel i7-6700HQ, 16 GB RAM and Geforce 970GTX with 3 GB graphic memory. Never had any problems with it in high settings or any slowdowns. The graphics of the characters look good, but the world is not as detailed as it might be, so I think you are able to play it on slower machines with higher details, but I cant really check this out.

Deus Ex Human Revolution is the third chapter in a legendary series that innovated genres such as stealth and rpg, and gave great freedom to the player's choices.
Unlike Invisible Wars, HR, imo, is a great continuation to the series and delivers an experience on par with the original Deus Ex.
To begin with, all the mechanisms of the game, from shooting to stealth and interactions, works great.Stealth is particularly important in the game and such approach is greatly rewarded by the game (as in Deus Ex).Of course, shooting is still there and is viable too.The rpg elements are well done with things like exp bonuses ,upgrading and the many different choices beign well implemented.Augmentation in HR, imo, works the best in the whole series with, at last, passive augs and a few meaningful active.
Story-wise the concept is of course...CONSPIRACIES! For a few hours the player will see a corporate warfare unfold but later the story begins to broaden and eventually getting the player to choose his road.Take note that HR is a prequel to the first DE but whoever played the first 2 will get a nice treat, through easter eggs.
Graphics and sound are well done too (NOTHING beats DE main theme ofc).
The characters are well-written and Adam Jensen comes VERY close behind JC (maybe more in-depth than JC).
All in all, DE HR is worthy of the Deus Ex title, and succeeds to do all that which IW couldn't.So I recommend this great game, especially the Director's Cut version with the redesigned bosses, for all those people who want to taste a bit of gaming history and either remember the fond times of DE or get initiated in this great universe.

What makes a person a person? At what point does someone stop being a person and start being a machine? Will the human being ever be 'upgradable' and what happens when those upgrades are rendered obsolete? Deus Ex 3 puts these questions to the player all whilst providing a roller-coaster of a gaming experience.
Deus Ex 3: Human Revolution is a Cyberpunk First-Person Shooter / Role Playing Game with a heavy emphasis on Stealth, thinking through problems and giving the player enough different ways to solve those problems.
The year is 2027. You play as Adam Jensen, Chief of Security at one of the largest biotechnology corporations in the United States. On the evening your girlfriend is about to make a speech that will change the face of biotechnology forever, your headquarters comes under attack from an unknown force. From here on, Adam will be, in traditional Deus Ex fashion, thrown into a world of secret dealings, sinister plots and corporate espionage.
For a first game from a new studio, what they have done here is absolutely amazing. Eidos Montreal took a look at what made Deus Ex such a phenomenal game, what made Deus Ex 2 a controversial game for the fans of the original, and they've managed to create a game that not only feels like a Deus Ex game down to its core, but also modernizes the mechanics with amazing polish and care.
The story is very nicely written and well paced. Since the game is set in the year 2027 and the way our technology is progressing, the story has a very real and 'close to home' feeling that the human race could well have to deal with some of the issues that Human Revolution portrays regarding biotechnology and the ability for humans to control their own evolutionary path. It's very clear that the team behind the game have been researching heavily on where biotechnology currently is and where it is going, they use terminology that you may have never heard of before but it just helps to add to this amazingly built world which they have created.
The game also has a visually unique art style. The settings and costume design for characters is like nothing anyone has really seen in a game before. Don't think however that Eidos Montreal have sacrificed game play over aesthetics, this game is amazing to play.
The only way to Game Over in this game is, like all Deus Ex games, when you die. There is no wrong path to take and your decisions will stay with you throughout your entire experience. This has been a staple through the series and Deus Ex 3 does it no differently.
The stealth in the game is cover based. I've never been much of a fan of cover-based stealth games but Deus Ex 3 does the mechanic so well, I had no problems adapting. All the levels and the AI are so well thought and planned out, you'll be ducking and rolling between guard paths with ease in no time. Every level has enough chest-high walls, ventilation shafts and general cover that stealth is a viable option throughout the entire game.
The levels are huge in size with lots of hidden elements to find and lots of areas to explore. Finding most of them is rewarded with Experience Points which don't contribute to a 'level' but a Praxis Kit instead. Praxis Kits can be used to upgrade and switch on your augmentations. Augmentations that will allow you to take down multiple enemies at once, turn invisible, drop from any height without taking damage and even punch through walls!
The Director's Cut also includes the Missing Link Downloadable Content which is at least an extra 6 hours of game play. It is nicely woven into the original experience and will force you to make some very tough decisions. The outcome of the DLC doesn't really affect the outcome of the overall game but it is still quite entertaining to play.
For all the things Deus Ex 3 gets right, its fault are largely centred around its boss battles. For the Director's Cut, they have been opened up to allow people with different play styles to have a better chance of beating them. Unfortunately, they seem to suffer from being inconsistent; one boss battle took me 5 attempts to beat in which I only won because the boss ended up killing themselves with a badly thrown grenade. One boss I killed with the Stun Gun of all things and one boss even conveniently managed to kill themselves when I was running in the opposite direction and not even firing at it.
Don't let the boss battles put you off playing though. This is a smart and powerful game with powerful messages behind it. I was hooked right until the very end and seeing a world crafted with such love and attention to detail made me all the more sad when the experience was over. Oh well.. there is always 'New Game +' to play!
Get this game and play it your way! You won't regret it!

Awesome game, huge improvement on many of the problems that plagued the dead rising series.

Dead RIsing 2, the canadian studio took over and upped the anti some but remained almost too faithful to the original game and failed to advance on the basic gameplay problems that really hindered the first e.g. clunky combat, crappy checkpointing; less novel weirdness and disappointing while fun for a good while.
Dead Rising 3, finally seems to wake up to this problem and fix it as well as ramp up the graphics, traversibility of the game and the fluidness, had a lot of fun wiht this, and still crave more zombie murder. Needs more than 2player co-op modes.

The Good the Bad and the OKAY
Loudout is a regular 3rd person shooter. Moving your charecter is easy as pie and you will get the hang of it in seconds and will be running around killing guys in no time.
