Overall, the Steam controller is probably the best controller I've ever used. Controls are somewhat finicky at first; if you buy one of these, you'll probably find yourself rebinding controls for every other game, fiddling with sensitivity and going back and forth between controls for the first couple of weeks. Hand pain is also common at first. However, these all subside with continued use, and once you've gotten used to it, it works beautifully. It can handle just about any game with any balance of controls you could ask for, at a lower price point than the console competitors, with an accuracy and stability of control nearing what you might expect from a standard keyboard and mouse. The trackpads are actually very intuitive - the built-in haptics make it so you can feel the controls working in a way that you can't with, say, a touchscreen. The addition of grip buttons compared to console controllers is also pretty nice. It's also a necessity at some points, as the trackpads are sensitive, and pressing them in can screw with your aim. My only complaint is the lack of rechargeable batteries - the controller takes AAs, and coming from a DS3 user who's used to charging from USB, that's kinda offputting. But as I said, probably the best controller I've ever used.
tl;dr: Amazing controller. Definitely worth the buy. Hard to get used to at first, but works like you wouldn't believe when it does. Rechargeable batteries and initial hand strain may be offputting to some users, but I assure you it's worth it.

I own a lot of different periperhals from an X-55 HOTAS, a G600 Mouse, a G13 Keypad, and an X360 controller, all for use on my computer. And after 3 weeks on the Steam Controller, it's replaced all of them.
I won't lie to you; this controller is going to take time to get used to. It is going to require some tweaking to get it to exactly where you want it. But that's part of the draw; it's so extremely customizable, you can make this controller do almost anything! It is, hands down, my favorite peripheral that I own, and is going to replace my keyboard and mouse in 99% of the games that I play.
If you're looking for a pick-up-and-play sort of controller, the Steam Controller might not fit that as well as other controllers. But if you're looking for something that will let you play any of your games anywhere in your house? This is definitely the controller for you.
Highly recommended.

It is way better than it has any right to be. The precision is insane for a controller, and UT and Quake are fully playable on it (even instagib!). It is, however, still much inferiour to mouse aiming, so if you're going to use it for multiplayer, get more than one so you'll be equally equipped. In that respect, it's sort of a downside that it is so much better than a "normal" controller, because it really necessitates other Steam controller(s) to even things out if you're intenting to play with friends.
Another sweet feature is how the Steam community ties into the Steam controller. By a press of the middle button, you bring up the Steam overlay, where you can switch between lots of controller layouts and settings. If you're in-game, you can bring up the most popular controller settings provided by the community for that particular title, and simply click one to use it. It couldn't be more practical.
That said, the "haptic feedback" is pretty much just a buzzword. The weak "clicking" the pads make when you turn it on can make aiming a tiny bit easier (it makes it somewhat easier to orientate your thumb), but Valve strongly suggested that the haptic feedback would make the pads feel like buttons if you wanted it, and thus be a great substitute for a D-pad. That is VERY far from the truth, which renders the left pad almost completely useless (unless you're left-handed, I suppose), and platformers and fighting games are almost unplayable on this thing because of that.
Racing games, action games and TPS games work just fine, although FPS games and first person RPGs are where the controller trully shines. It also works very well as a substitute for a mouse, if you're browsing the internet from your sofa.
EDIT: Also forgot to mention one thing, and thatis Big Picture mode. You HAVE to use it to get the full functionality out of the controller, which can be a bit annoying, because Big Picture is slow, BIG and lacks many basic Steam features (for example, you can't easily turn on the FPS view from the overlay). Outside Big Picture, you don't even have access to the basic controller settings page.
EDIT 2: Also, although it has more buttons than a conventional controller (the flaps on the underside are particularly useful for jumping and crouching, I find), I'd really like to have a few more. PC games often make use of a lot of keys because the keyboard is jammed with them, so it can feel a bit hampered to work with the limited set the Steam controller provides. The ABXY-buttons are also placed so that you have to let go of the track pad to access them, so they're nowhere near as useful as the 6 triggers/flaps. I would've loved to see more small buttons placed on the upper edge or on the underside of the controller.
A quick-switch mini-trigger for swapping templates would be particularly welcome.
And finally, the ergonomics are quite good, in my opinion, although the ABXY buttons could be a little bigger. The build feels a little bit thin and light, but it's solid enough. I definitely reccomend having batteries inserted, simply to give it some weight and balance.
I love that it's a bit big, because some standard controllers can feel a bit small and cramped in my hands, but I suppose someone with very small hands might dislike the huge grip lumps.
All in all, it's a very big step in the right direction, good fun, and it works well - but I really hope they put a proper D-pad on the next iteration.
EDIT 3: Well, I'll be damned. I just found out that the controller has a gyro for motion control too, as well as two-stage triggers which can be mapped to different functionalities. Looks like I'm going to have to do a  lot more experimenting with this thing.

The pure customizability, and versatility of this device makes it the best choice for a couch gamer, hands down. At first the trakpads may be daunting, but with some adjustments, and with the addition of motion controls, I was back to getting headshots in no time. While it does rely on Big Picture Mode, additional features and support is being added regularly.

(Post Fallout 1 Review) Fallout 2 continues 70-80 years after Fallout 1, playing as the ancestor of your previous character, the "Vault Dweller" or also called the "Chosen One". You are sent off into the wastes to help your tribe "Arroyo" and uncover the legacy The Vault Dweller left behind within California/Nevada and introducing a new grand threat who origins are from those whom governed before, the "ENCLAVE". Remnants of the United States.
The core gameplay mechanics never really changed when transitioning between Fallout 1 and 2 (Isometric turned based combat). The most noticable differences is the amount of new perks, and the way you begin the game. Fallout 2 entices you to create a close-quarters heavy build, over Fallout 1's small guns since you are a tribal. This game also introduces a boatload of new companions (12-13), which smothers Fallout 1's four followers. Fallout 2 has plenty of new quests that all intertwine nicely together, as multiple factions and cities effect one another.
Tons of Fallout cameos, pop-culture references, and tons of new content.
Such a lovely addition to my Fallout experience!
(Did one playthrough, with around 90% of the sidequests complete. Time clocked: Around 50 hours)

I would like to begin my review by saying I started the Fallout series with 3 (I know shameful right?) But soon learned about the first two games and how different they were from Bethesda's Fallout 3. At first, I thought they looked horrible with their dated graphics and gameplay. But after reading hours upon hours of lore and story tidbits on the Fallout Gamepedia, I just knew I had to play them. I was on Xbox 360 at the time so I couldn't play them yet, so I figured I would play New Vegas in the meantime.
Anyways, eventually I got my PC, and one of the first games I got on their was the entire Classic Fallout Collection. I played through 1 first, I loved it. Then, after a long break, I started Fallout 2. I was blown away by it's atmosphere and compelling story. Even though I am not used to turn-based gameplay, I have come to enjoy it because of Fallout and Fallout 2. The game makes you think about your moral desicions and the consequences they bring, something Bethesda games could never really do. For example, if you kill a child bounty hunters will chase you down and everybody will hate you, discouraging you from doing such evil things. I highly recommend this game to any Fallout fan, even the new ones like me. This is definitely my favorite RPG game, and maybe even my favorite game. 10/10

+ Combat is for the most part, satisfying. It may get repetitive sometimes, especially if your in power armor running into little Golden Geckos, but when you defeat a squad of the Enclave, it is very satisfactory
+ Cities have more of a 40s-50s vibe than Fallout 1
+ Again, a few different endings depending on your choices
+ Explains what happened to the Vault Dweller after Fallout 1

I really enjoyed this game playing through it in 2 sittings (darn work). The antarctic base feels authentic, run down but still offering some shelter from the relentless weather.
The weather is your enemy every journey outside is taken with steeling yourself first and planning your route. As the weather worsens it gets trickier and trickier and that moment when you lose your bearings in a blizzard and stumble in the wrong direction really gets the tension rising.
The game also convey the sense of isolation partly because there is just enough evidence of the former inhabitants to really reinforce this and due to some clever decisions on communications.
Overall much like in a story like the Martian it is being in a terrible, life threatening situation and trying to survive.
It's not the longest game but it is a fantastic experience and one I would greatly recommend, especially if you are a fan of games like Dear Esther, Firewatch and to some extend Soma.

In a day and age where 'horror' ends up being, for the most part, a game filled with laughing children and cheap jump scares - it can be hard to find a title that insilts dread and fear in someone without resorting to startling them and causing a heart attack.
I think I can safely say that 'Near Death' is at it's heart a narrative-driven survival game, but it goes deeper; and in a game where you never once run into a crazed maniac, supernatural monster or ghost driven to kill you - it's pretty damn scary.
Antarctica is not a place most people would want to be in - and it seems like for the most part, it doesn't want us.  I've never been, myself, but I feel like the devs really captured that feeling of unwelcomness in Near Death.  From the minute you step off the plane, it's clear you're in trouble.  Visibility is poor, you can hear your character chattering her teeth and the only thing you can clearly see (albeit barely) are some lights obscured by the snow in the distance.
The game's systems are all designed around the idea of 'dont freeze' and they support it well.  This isn't a quick A to B to C game, you're going to spend time in each area you expore trying to find every useful scrap for crafting; though even on Normal difficulty, I found by the end of the game I had more than enough of everything.  You can repair holes in windows to seal rooms and make them safe, but you can't repair EVERY room - so a large part of the game involves managing where to make your 'safe spots'.  Places you can duck into as you make your way around the base (and you will backtrack quite a bit) to quickly warm up before continuing on.
The heat mechanic is especially harrowing - on more than one occassion, my sight began to fade and sounds drowned out (warnings you're about to die) only a dozen feet from a door.  The dread comes when you open it only to find a single window is broken - this spot is not as safe.  If you're about to die, the game gives you a quick 'second wind' before you hit the game over screen.  If you can patch that window in time and drop down your heater, you'll be fine.
The score really adds to the experience as well - adding to the already sense of loneliness, although as the night goes on and the storm gets worse, you can only really hear it when inside.
The only negative I would probably say is Normal felt a bit too Easy, however it always felt tense which I think for this sort of a game is probably more important than difficulty.

Near Death is an immersive walking adventure where your goal is to survive the frigid climate in Antarctica.
After your helicopter crashes, you’re stranded, and completely alone in temperatures well below freezing. The entire story is a tale of survival, as you battle the elements, searching for warmth, and a way home. Your only contact is with someone on the other end of the teletype.
You get cold very quickly, especially if you are outside or in unsealed rooms. It adds a sense of urgency, which I did enjoy, but some people might feel too rushed. As you get colder your vision gets blurry, and then turns into black and white. If you don’t get to heat quickly, you die. The greatest foe you encounter is the frigid temperature, and you need to scavenge supplies and components, and restore the power whenever you can to stay warm.
The components you find are used to craft various items to aide you on your quest for survival. Crafting items takes a short time, and recipes are found as you explore. Accessing the inventory or crafting menu doesn’t pause the game while in it, so make sure you’re somewhere warm. There are quests you need to accomplish, and most of them are straightforward fetch quests. I didn’t mind the questing, but expect to do a lot of walking, and stopping to warm up.
The game took me about 2.5 hours to complete, which I feel is a bit short for full price. I still liked the game though, and I really enjoyed the atmosphere a lot. If you’re interested in an immersive walking adventure in the Antarctic, with crafting, and a heavy focus on survival, Near Death might interest you.

This is one of those Why hasnt this been done before? games. Everyone who has ever played a multiscreened first person shooter with their friends knows about screen cheating. We've all blamed our friends for doing it, while simultaneously snuck a quick peek at their screens to gain an advantage. It's part of the experience. The guys at Samurai Punk have taken that simple Idea, and ♥♥♥♥ing ran with it. In this game one is forced to screen cheat. All the characters are invisible, so the only way to findout where someone is, is to look at their screen. and It's hard work. There is a lot of information you have to keep track of in a match. But, there are so much going on to help you. First off the level design is brilliant. Each of the levels, for now there are only three, and laid out and colored to let you know roughly where someone is just by quickly glancing at their screen. A quick peripheral look will tell you everything you need to know. Each shot you make also reveals your location with various particle effects. If someone tries to shoot at you, you will know where the shot came from. It's simple and intuitive. you are outfitted with a number of various weapons to actually do the killing, and these weapons are all ♥♥♥♥ing fantastic. There is a simple shotgun, but incredible effective. There are weirder things with the Giant bouncy ball launcher, and the "Chargey Horse." and some more standard stuff like a melee weapon (although this happens to be a giant candle stick), a rifle, and a grenade launcher. They are all Beautifuly designed and no one weapon feels more useful than the others. they each have their pros and cons and all have their idle situations. The trick is that you only get one per life, so choose wisely. There are a few bugs that need fixing, while we were playing there was an awful lot of simultaneous kills, and a few other random glitches. Nothing game breaking though. You guys, this game is incredibly fun. It reminds me of my time playing old fps games like Golden Eye, or Perfect Dark with a group of friends. but with such a new and refreshing take on the genre. Plus, It's an absolute delight to look at.

This controller, if you couldn't tell by the way it looks, is very different from the usual Playstation/Xbox controller. Namely, it comes with two trackpads that replace a directional pad and right thumbstick.
Due to this, you're not going to be able to use this as easily as the current Playstation/Xbox styled controller you own. In a way, it's a lot like learning how to ride a bike after you've been riding a tricycle: You're not going to get it immediately, and you're definitely going to stumble and fall and get mad while trying to learn how to use it. But if you take the time to get used to it, you're not going to want to go back to using a standard controller.
As the demonstration video shows with Cities: Skylines, games that typically require a keyboard/mouse can be played to a surprisingly fluid degree due to the aforementioned trackpads. In order to compensate for the lack of buttons, it is possible to use "mode shifts," where you hold down a button (for example, one of the bumpers on the bottom of the controller). Then, while the button is held down, the button functions of the button pad/analog stick/trackpads change until the button is released. Because of this, a surprising amount of hotkeys can be bound to the Steam Controller, not to mention the ability to bind multiple keypresses to a single button.
However, while it is entirely possible to play these games with the Steam Controller, don't try to play a game of Dota with this; you will never be able to play to the same level as you can with a keyboard and mouse. For slower-paced and/or turn-based games, such as Civilization or The Sims, this is almost a non-issue (According to Steam, I've played more than 20 hours of The Sims 3; all of it was with the Steam Controller and, after some adjustments to the highest-rated community config, I never felt as if I were compensating. Along with the Steam Link, this has made relaxing on the couch and playing The Sims an actual, feasible thing, which is nothing short of amazing to me.
Of course, it is more than possible to play first-person shooters, such as Fallout 4 or even CS:GO, and, in my opinion, offer a much greater degree of accuracy in aiming compared to standard controllers not only due to the trackpad for aiming, but also the built-in gyroscope. When I bought the controller, I didn't even know about the gyroscope functionality. But now that I've played Just Cause 3 and some Warframe with it, I'm amazed at how I played FPSes with a controller before. The gyroscope makes tiny aim adjustments very feasible, and at times I find myself aiming almost as well as with a mouse.
Overall, for $50 USD, this is probably the best controller for the price it's offered at. While it won't be replacing your keyboard and mouse, it definitely provides many advantages in comparison to regular twin-stick controllers. If the idea of playing games on the couch appeals to you, this, along with the Steam Link, are well worth the asking price of $50 USD each.

So I recently turned 30 and decided to splurge on a $1500 (CAD) gaming PC. I was always interested in some of the innovative/massively multiplayer stuff that only comes to PC, but was forever secluded to the console world. I could never justify spending enough to end up with something high end. After finally researching and building the rig, and going giddy over my first Steam Sale, I ended up with tons of games and the ability to play them maxed out...
Then...  nothing...
I just couldn't get excited about playing these games with a keyboard and mouse. No offense to those who prefer this - it's just not my cup of tea, and there isn't much space to maneuver the mouse on the chair in my gaming room.
Enter the Steam Controller... suddenly all of these games became super playable. I am having FUN on the $1500 purchase which, until then, was beginning to feel like the product of a mid-life crisis. Customizing the controller is honestly a lot of fun in itself. When you learn new tricks like the gyro aiming* or touch menu* so much playability suddenly opens up in front of you. Movement and aiming feel super smooth, and if you don't like anything about the controller you can basically customize it with the massive list of settings.
So here I am, revisiting Skyrim (which I hadn't touched since the PS3 days) with the input method I grew up with - on STEROIDS - flawless 60fps gameplay, tons of community-created content and so on.
**About the gyro aiming and touch menu:
Gyro aiming: I'm still getting the hang of it, but can target things 5-10x more efficiently than with the Dualshock 4 joystick. With the joystick I found the camera would madly flail about, even after years of practice, before landing roughly where I needed it. The gyro aiming basically lets you use the muscles in your wrists to precisely aim the controller exactly where you need it. People are saying this is still a bit less effective than mouse-aiming, but I disagree. I was actually a total mess when I first used  a mouse, but way more competent when I started using gyro aiming. I do have some transferably skills after many years of PC activity, but still - I bet someone with years of experience using this functionality could get as good or better than mouse users. (Hides in a bunker.)
Touch menu: Using the left touch pad, you can basically put your thumb on it and a touch menu of up to 12 items pops up. You can assign these to keys on a keyboard or your own button mappings from the game. Basically this shuts up a lot of the people who dumped on gamepads for games like MMOs. And I've been desperate to play some good open-world PVP on a gamepad. (Message me with recommendations!)
Last but not least, it seems Valve is really serious about supporting this peripheral. I do have fond feelings of Sony after many years of great gaming experiences, but have to admit Valve has really impressed with the amount of updates and serious commitment to making this new tool work really well.
The one negative at this point: It seems smart to customize the controller for each game, but I'm wondering how adaptable my mind and muscle memory are to remember all of these settings. There's something to be said for the prescribed, consistent expeirence of console gaming - you know the same keys generally do the same things every time, so you can use these transferable skills to go from game to game without much adaptation. With the Steam controller, it might pay off to focus on one game at a time and really get in the groove of things before switching to a totally different configuration. This is easier said than done on a platform like Steam, which has a seemingly endless list of interesting games, but potentially a smart move for 30-year-olds like myself who have limited agility.
Hope you found this useful. I wholeheartedly recommend this controller. Try it out and have fun!

The Steam Controller is a tinkerer’s dream, the most configurable PC input device I have ever used, however it is designed for larger hands than mine so I don't use it.
Pros: Community profiles available on Steam provide good starting points for personal customizations. The Steam controller works especially well in turn-based PC games not designed for couch play like as Civilization and Bejeweled. The analog stick feels more precise than the Xbox360 and the track pads are far more sensitive than the average laptop.  The fine level of control would make this my favorite controller for the PC if it fit my small hands comfortably.
Cons: As a first generation device, the Steam Controller software is still maturing. Expect to spend a lot of time tinkering with the dazzling array of settings and options and community bindings, and to encounter some bugs and crashes. Finding the right bindings may involve also adjusting in-game settings like mouse sensitivity.  The Steam Controller fits an average man's hand size, but I have very small hands so I stopped using it and I went back to the Xbox 360 controller.
Conclusion: If you play PC games on your couch, have average man sized hands, and a lot of patience it's a great accessory.

I think that after so many time spent on this game I'll drop by for an eval, I'll try to be as precise as possible with the pros and cons of this game, but be aware that my eval will be negative in the end.
I really loved and got hooked by the game at first, the graphics arent ultra shiny but the game works on lower ends pc and I think the game is globaly nice to watch and play, the art team is doing a great job at making new skins (at the exception of the many recolors skins that are a real plague)
Lets start by the cons shall we?
1 : Monetization of the game
The game is lately becoming more and more grindy, I dont know if the feel that they have a loss in revenue from the game, but the system is being more and more locked up behind rng chests (aka lootboxes) and this is a real problem, especially for newcomers. They are actually trying to push a new deckbuilding and card system that will create even more difference between veterans and new players, because you'll have to grind the hell out (but no worries, you'll be able to pay 2 win soon enough) in order to havemaxed cards for your champions in order to play at the same level of "bonus" that the veterans who already have all the cards maxed out. Even the skins are no more in direct access and are locked behind rng chests, so basically if you want that particular skin you have to gamble to obtain it, period. They are also pushing hard the ViP system which basically will give you bonus in xp / gold etc the more you grind it, resulting in total bs when it comes to levels and cards levels access.
2 : The matchmaker is horrible since the beginning of the game
We had like 1000 threads over the last year asking for a total rework of the matchmaker on the paladins forums, including a 95 pages one with exemples of silly matchups that should never happen in the first place. Still nothing and soon (tm) being told at our faces for too many times now. Basically, you can be a diamond or master and play with people still qualifying in ranked, being a team game, and acknowledging the fact that only your win/loss ratio determine your progression in ranked, you can quickly understand why playing with potatoes have a negative impact for you (because you are dragged down) and for the newbies (because they are destroyed). In casual its even worse, you'll get owned by pro team 5 men partying for pubstomp fun night, or you'll play with and against totally bad team composition with no chance at all to win, because some people still cant move and shoot at the same time, and they are placed in games with players either playing pro or just veterans players who knows the in and out of the game. It is not possible to carry and entire team of nutbags and your gaming frustration will drasticaly increase if you (like me) like to play in a serious environment where you try to win and progress. The feeling of progression is utterly destroyed by these random games where you have literally no chance to win the match, even before it started.
3 : Recurrent bugs
The game is still filled with bugs, because "they are hard to fix", I'm not a dev and cannot speak too loud about this, but if something is rampant for a year, maybe its time you dedicate your time and effort to fix it instead or reintroducing new contents every two weeks... introducing more bugs in the process! Champions like PIP, Evie, Bombking have recurrent bugs that are simply game breaker for so long I stopped counting. And instead of fixing them, what Hirez do is frenetically  pushing new (broken) champions and new mecanics into an already broken game... The game is a big ball of ducktape at this point.
4 : New content agenda >> balance
The game is becoming a noobfest lately, with new uncreative champions (vivian, the turret, or the "hold M1 to win", champion) being pushed without any balance testing upon release, totally destroying casual games because OP. Their agenda is a priority, so we have new broken♥♥♥♥♥content every two weeks / every month, with a dire need for a hotfix the week later, it only shows amateurism because they constantly release broken things, without proper testing, resulting in unbalance between champions skill floor and ceiling, resulting in more ♥♥♥♥♥♥ matches. The ttk is getting lower and lower each patch, and from a strategical fast paced shooter I loved at first sight, they are turning it to a CSGO clone where you die even before you have a chance to turn around and counter the champion with 2k dps on your face. Lately they want to push a 4th legendary card for every whampion, and 90% of these are... more dps! Its becoming a hurr durr who deals more damage fest and I dislike it from all my guts.
5 : Toxic kiddos and trolls
Being a team game and being evaluated solely as a team (winloss ratio only, not personal performance), the amount of frustration generated by trolls is over 9000! You can report them (usually results in nothing) ingame or use a pretty heavy ticket reports where you have to waste some of your time in order to provide evidence against a player who will probably never get banned or temp banned anyway.
6 : Bad UI and options
We asked for crosshair optimisation for ages, and they finally delivered a broken thing, half of the crosshair still blends too much in the background so you lose it, there are no decimal sensitivity so you cant create custom sens you feel confortable with. These are two of the majors UI / HUD / customisation problems on a very long list of problems we should never have in the first place in a FPS, this shows again that they are trying to push a FPS without any knowledge of the genre, resulting in major problems for fps veterans like myself and many others.
As for the pros, well, the game was (still is to some extent) fun, relatively fast paced even if mobility is reduced patch after patch, easy to grasp if you have played fps before and can be balanced if you play the meta champions exclusively. As said, the art team is doing a great job (sadly only the art team at this point)
Sadly, I wouldnt recommend this game anymore due to the amateurism Hirez is showing lately, like, they have no roadmap for the game and I'm under the impression that the dev themselves doesnt have a clue about where their own game is going... The inexistant matchmaker being the major problem to me, because after some time played and getting stuck with low elo teammates for some "forced loss", you lose the feeling of progression I like to have in any game I play, and I dont want to be judged by a rng system, but by my performance as a player. I still play this game, but I fear that the next 2 or 3 patches will be the major nails in the coffin.

I have to say that this game is surprisingly fun.  By that, I mean that I purchased this game for my son to play because he really enjoyed the single-player game
.  Figured it would be his first MMORPG.  But I found myself playing this game together with him to do the puzzles and then kept on playing after he went to bed "so I could help him out better" the next day.
How is the game?  It's an educational game!  Designed to be fun!  And it succeeds in both.  My son was so busy collecting pets
, outfits, and stuff for his in-game home that he really got into all of the puzzles and learning quests.  We're talking simple things like which animals eat what food to complex things like heredity and behavior.
How is the Early Access?  I haven't seen any bugs or had the game crash at all.  There is new content and improvements added on a regular basis and regular (31 as of this review) communication from the developers here on Steam.  Basically, everything you should expect from Early Access.

Honestly, I would seriously recommend investing into this game if you're the kind of person looking for a little bit of fun. So far I've completed around 12 quests all of which have taught me something about science I never knew.
There is much more that can be said but until I finish what the game has to offer right now I think i'll keep it short.
Overall: 8/10

Oh, where to begin?  Deux Ex is a decent game, blending concepts of stealth, shooting, and social engineering.  Unfortunately, it doesn't really excel in any area.  The stealth sequences are very old-fashioned, in that they work well enough if you choose to stay concealed but fall apart badly if you prefer to kill quietly.  The shooting mechanics are hindered by poor controls - left trigger dives for cover instead of aiming down sights, etc - and by guns that just don't feel good.  It's great that the weapons can be upgraded in all manner of ways, but it's all for naught if they don't feel good to shoot.  Case in point: the round from a sniper rifle shouldn't drop in flight by 18 inches during a 25 yard shot.  Also, a guy that gets hit in the head with a finger-long projectile traveling at roughly 700 mph shouldn't immediately snap to attention and try to figure out who shot him just because he's wearing a helmet.  Finally, the parts of the game that attempt to challenge players by way of dialogue choices feels like LA Noire - the clues and responses that you're given don't correspond very tightly to the desired outcomes; two players making the same choices won't necessarily get the same result - it's stupid.
All that said, the game features an intriguing story and is good enough (barely) at what it does to be worth playing.  The director's cut (poorly) incorporates the Missing Link DLC into the main campaign and adds some optional DVD-style commentary.  Unfortunately, because the upgrade exists as a separate title in the Steam library no saved games or achievements carry over into the new game.  I'd say that it's worth grabbing, but only if you don't already own The Missing Link.

is a satire about the modern world and capitalism. Here, you just need invest your money. Click and click, nothing more.
You start with a lemonade stand, tap to make some money and then earn enough to buy either more lemonade stands or a newspaper stand. Your lemonade stand will get you a small return in seconds.
As your coffers swell, you spend virtual money on further virtual businesses. The bigger the business, the more it costs, and the longer its progress bar takes to clear. Cheaper ones are simple fare involving newspaper delivery and car washes. Banks and oil companies lurk at the high end. An oil company nets millions per tap, but that might take ten hours.
Businesses can be upgraded, each bump costing more than the last. You must therefore figure out the best balance of investment/return before heading on to a more expensive option.
You can also buy upgrades to increase your profits, hire managers to tap on your behalf (including when you're away - the app then tells you how much you earned while sleeping), and rolls in the concept of angel investors if you reset and start from scratch.
There's little reward for progress, and zero imagination regarding achievements. Furthermore, it lacks the satirical sharpness.

is a survival game, in which you’re stuck in the Antarctic, and you have only one issue to worry about: cold. Every part of your journey through Sutro Station will have you contending with an increasing cold and heavier wind.
The game is similar to
in its concept, but
takes it a bit further and adds an active story. You are a pilot who has crash landed near Sutro Station, a research facility in the Antarctic. Your first objective is to find warmth. Once you’re temporarily heated up, you need to make contact with another base. As the game takes place in the early 1980’s, you do this by interacting with teletype machines, which is where the bulk of the story is told from. You’ll need to restore power to buildings for warmth, find parts, and rebuild a vehicle, all while battling the elements.
As you progress in the game, it gets colder and the wind gets more harsh, meaning that’s less time you’re able to spend outside before needing to warm up. It’ll eventually be -100, making traversal quite difficult. The wind plays an active role against you, and slows your progress down; if you’re walking against the wind, you’ll move extremely slow, making crouching the faster bet, and if you’re walking with the wind, you’ll move pretty much unhindered.
To help you navigate when you can’t see more than ten feet ahead of you, you can craft light poles and rope poles. Lights can be planted anywhere to mark something of interest (perhaps a shed you can duck into to place your heater), and rope poles can be used to help navigate so you don’t get lost. Walking next to a rope will help your movement, even in heavy wind.
The game contains a fairly basic crafting system, and components are pretty easy to come by. You can make window patches to block off broken windows, allowing you to warm up inside that room. You can craft lights and ropes (as mentioned above), repair kits to restore power, a liner for your jacket and pants, which reduces the frequency of your body heat loss, and a few other items.
looks pretty good. You’re on a research base, so the buildings all have a pretty similar style, but the environment itself is great to look at, and all the objects in the world have a distinct 80’s look to them, from the old computers to the teletypes to even the filing cabinets and equipment.
There is an awesome soundtrack accompanying the game, and the sound effects really make you feel like you’re stuck there. Having the wind howl in your face while your feet crunch the snow underneath is a pretty terrific experience.
Unfortunately, there’s not much replayability to the game. There are two difficulties, normal and easy. I’m not sure what the exact differences are, but I assume on easy you can spend more time outside before needing heat, and perhaps crafting items costs less materials. I finished the game in about 2.5 hours, on the normal difficulty. I missed some item blueprint somewhere, so I’ll go back and find that, but otherwise, there isn’t much of a reason to revisit the game. The world is the same, the story is the same, and the game will always follow the same outcome.
Well worth the cost,
is a fantastic survival game that makes it somewhat easier on you by giving you only one stat to manage: warmth. Exploring the frigid Antarctic makes for a tense experience, and one you will enjoy if you like survival games.

Near Death is a narrative survival game in a dark, cold environment. You are stranded in a research station in Antarctica. It's cold, it's dark outside and you are alone.
'The Martian' in Antarctica. A clear, simple, straight forward mission: survive the cold till rescue!
If you like Firewatch, Kona and TLD, this game could be something for you.
edit:
It's also worth mentioning, that the soundtrack nicely accompanies the different stages of the game and emphasize the feeling of being stranded.

The good:
1.	The game is a well-designed maze (instead of a sandbox that is dominating the survival genre right now) which means you can left no stone unturned and feel good about it.
2.	The game has a plot; it is nothing out of the ordinary but it is just interesting enough to keep you going and already more than many early access games could ever dream of (looking at you, The Long Dark).
3.	The game has a replay value (though you would probably never play it more than five hours).
4.	Good performance & minimum requirement: I was running this game 720P on an Intel i7-6500U and its on-board HD520 graphics card yet the game was still playable.
The bad:
1.	The price tag is a bit aggressive; $9.99 would be a fair price and give the game more attention.
My Conclusion:
Near Death is the exact kind of game I was looking for: a short survival maze that is driven by a plot not mindless resource gathering.

The Steam Controller. One thing: Haptic trackpads are to analog sticks what analog sticks are to d-pads. They are far superior and can do a million things analog sticks wish they could do. Since I got these, my xbox controllers have been sitting in a corner gathering dust (I think my cat knocked them around somewhere. I don't care, cat gets more fun out of the xbox controllers now than I do anyway.) These feel like a major upgrade over xbox controllers. The downside is you can literally feel everything the controller is capable of, and almost nothing is living up to its potential, and that aspect is frustrating (please steam big picture mode, use the haptic pads!) Basically, right now, it feels like it's only a medium upgrade from xbox controllers, but it *feels* like it has the potential to be an insanely huge upgrade from xbox controllers. Almost nothing I do makes full use of all its buttons and capabilities.
Pros -
--- Customizable confuguration in everything
--- Haptic pads are freakin' awesome.
--- Back buttons are another new addition to classic-style controllers that give you more options.
--- Despite its size, lightweight controller reduces less fatigue.
--- After you adapt, much faster response time than a traditional controller.
--- Two keyboard layouts overlays. Haptic Keyboard tap keyboard is good for when you don't know what you're doing. Daisy layout is significantly superior once you learn it. Your choice, slow with no learning curve, or decent learning curve with almost physical-keyboard typing speed.
--- Battery slots instead of battery packs. Means you don't have the replace the controller when batteries go bad, just grab new ones. I suggest grabbing rechargables. That said, the controller doesn't even need batteries, it'll run off USB power just fine (which, if I understand correctly, it also communicates via USB if the option is there, meaning no wireless lag if you go that route.)
Cons -
--- Definately not at full potential yet, and it shows. Most games don't have good layouts built by the community yet. Despite the fact you'll never want to pick up the xbox controller again, you'll constantly feel, "This has the potential to be so much better..."
--- Steam Big Picture mode doesn't make good use of haptic pads yet.
--- May make you to change some gaming habits and slow down your response time until you adapt.
--- Lack of weight makes it "feel" less impressive when you first pick it up (lack of fatigue later makes up for it later.)
Seriously, most innovative controller in years.

At the time of this reveiew, it has been less than two months since the release of this hardware, so thing may have changed since this review.
Interestingly, the Steam Controller does not appear to have a lot of *official* developer support at this time. However, the fact that the user can map functionality to any of the multitude of buttons and control axes, along with the availibiliy of community mappings, makes this less of a problem. Furthermore, games that were built with the Xbox 360 or Xbox One controller in mind support the Steam controller as one of those controllers. In addition, the gyroscopes and accelerometers inside the controller provide something on par with the current console generation controllers. You'd be hardpressed to find a game pad for its price that has this level of control.
Now for the quality of the controller. It feels like a $50 controller. The controller feels sturdy, well built, and is kind of heavy, as though they worked to cram as much hardware inside the controller without leaving much space left over inside it. What I'm trying to say is that the Steam controller does not feel like a cheap controller at all. Don't be fooled by it only having one analog stick on it; it has two trackpads that have similar range of movement to an analog stick.
Overall, I love the hardware, as you'd be hardpressed to find a similar controller of similar quality at this price. Even my mainstay for periphrial hardware, Logitech, does not offer anything remotely like this. It takes some getting used to if you're coming at it from a Xbox360 / PS3 / Xbox One / PS4 controller scheme, but it'll grow on you after a few hours and then you'll figure out how to remap the controls to be more to your liking. Point is, I highly recommend this controller and hope to see more of it in the future.

After about 1000+ hours there's a lot to say about this game I cant fit into a small review. The greatest thing that makes me recommend Paladins Game are within 2 aspects of the game and its communtiy.
1. The card & Item system: The loadout system implimented within paladins gives a wide variety of playstyles for each champion. Each champion has 3 legendary cards (soon to be 4) that can change the playstyle you want to play as with your character, the 12 point based card loadout system allows you to reinforce those playstyles and these playstyles can go a long way to help your team succeed and win a game. Along with the loadouts your choice of item selection can weigh a game in your favor, with 16 items in the game many can give your team an advantage in a fight if executed correctly One thing to keep in mind is this is a team game so buying items that help with you team rather then yourself can make a big difference between a win and a loss.
Many people have related this game to overwatch and this is my #1 argument that makes me feel Paladins is more unique and supperior in comparison. Overwatch and Paladins both take influence from the FPS and MOBA genres, Overwatch seems to lean more towards the FPS side while Paladins takes more of a MOBA side with its loadout and itemization.
2. It's community. Never have I seen a community so welcoming especually to its competitive (esports) side. Its very easy to connect with pro players by either meeting them in-game, or connecting with them through there twitch. This makes it easier to learn from these pro players and the current strategies and meta shifts that may take place. Along with this the community can seem fairly small dispite the large amount of players playing daily, you begin to recognize players names you've seen around and its really easy to create brand new friendships of them. Its easy to get into the competitve scene as there are many tournaments for all levels of players and its really easy to connect with a team and participate in these tournements with players around your skill level.
Pros:
-Free to play and the developers really respect this aspect.
-Consistant updates, they continue to polish there game, add new champions monthly along with various bug fixes and champion balancing.
-Overall beautiful community, Everyone knows eachother by name. Easy connections with pro players, helps you learn the mechanics and strategies of the game.
-Thriving competitive eSports scene, Very easy as a newer player to meet other players and build a team in open tournements with real rewards.
-large number of cosmetics, new ones added bi-weekly all unique and themed for that weeks patch.
-Developers listen to players comments and concerns at every level from New to Pro and try their best to implement and fix what players are bringing to them.
-A strong competitive scene with dedicated players for all you hardcore gamers out there.
-Drafting system for ranked games is fun and unique you don't get stuck with duplicate champions on the opposing team
-Fun for both new and expeirienced users within the genre of Team Based Shooters, FPS & MOBA games.
Cons:
-Developers like to experiment, so don't get too attatched to some items, champions or playstyles within in the game. The meta can shift dramaticly. (this is the biggest "con" within this game and causes a bit of tention between the developers and the players. In my oppion I believe this is because the players truely care about this game and this community and they want to see it succeed.)
-New champions always seem to arrive unbalanced and it takes 2 weeks to a month for them to be balanced to the point where they are no longer seen as overpowered.
-The community can get fairly competitive at times causing a bit of toxicity (this happens in most competitive games anyways, no suprise here).
-Microtransactions can get a bit pricey, but there's always opportinites for sales and other events making it cheaper and easier to get cosmetics. Developers also offer opportunities to free cosmetics.
-Matchmaking system seems unabalanced at times, hidden elo can affect your matchmaking with other players. Developers have taken steps to try to fix this but it still seems to come out balanced and mismatched.

I see a lot of people comparing Paladins to Overwatch. I'll be one of the many people in the other reviews saying, Paladins is NOT an Overwatch clone. Play it yourself before you try to compare this game to another one. I got into Paladins in Closed Beta via a promotion link, and as a fan of Hi-Rez's other game, Smite, I was eager to give it a shot before I ever heard of Overwatch. Keep in mind when taking into consideration my hours played that I've played outside of Steam as well.
For a newer game, I find Paladins rather enjoyable. There are still bugs and some issues with matchmaking, but that's going to happen. It's not happening so often that it makes the game unfun; Paladins is still listed as Early Access and these things should be taken with the consideration that they will be fixed once Paladins is out of Early Access. The developers allow you to review maps and beta test things before they're released and give feedback on everything, should you so choose. That's more than a lot of devs do these days.
The champions come out at a decent rate, about the rate as they would in most other games of the genre. The thing I really enjoy about Hi-Rez is that they give you access to a pack that gives you all current and future champions for one price, so all your in-game currency can go towards skins and other cosmetics, which yes, you can buy with in-game currency instead of real money, which is a big plus in my book. If you find yourself invested in the game, by all means pick that DLC up. It's very much worth it.
The gameplay feels smooth and easy to pick up for all skill levels, so don't feel discouraged if you can't keep up at the start. When I first started, I'd never played a game like Paladins before, nor had I ever heard of anything like it. After a few games I got the basics and found myself struggling less and less with every match. I personally play with a controller after having played with a keyboard in the past and both are easy to learn and pick up for veterans and newbies alike. So long as you have some decent aim, you can play most of the characters in this game. If not, there are still a few characters that are little more newbie-friendly (Ying comes to mind, for me), that don't require you to heavily aim your things to do well.
If you find yourself getting lost in all the information, there are many presets available for both cards and items, or you can always make your own once you get the hang of it. At no point should you feel lost in what you're doing, because the game does help you out quite a lot along the way should you need it. Speaking of cards, there's no one right way to build them. I find myself making multiple different card sets for my mains based on how aggressive I feel like playing, and that's what makes Paladins so fun compared to other games of its kind.
For those of you worried about pay to win, Paladins is not that. Loot boxes drop upon level up, or upon champion mastery (last I knew of, at least) so you get them often. When they do drop you're able to open them immediately. Granted, you can always buy special keys that make the drops a little better, but it's never absolutely needed. Loot boxes give you cards, or essence if you already have that card, along with the rare chance for a cosmetic item. Essence is used to buy cards, so you can pick and choose what cards you want. As far as I know, loot boxes that are bought with real money do not give cards, just skins and cosmetic items, which is the exact opposite of a pay to win system.
If you're looking for a new free to play game, and/or you enjoy this genre of game most definately give Paladins a try.

Pros and cons put into thoughts;
I knew what I was getting into. I was sinking $40 into the dreaded "number 3." As we all know, in the triple A game industry, the number 3 is rarely a good thing. In this case, it wasn't a BAD thing but it wasn't what I personally dreamed of. I'm going to try and lay out why I really just couldn't get into this game.
I hated the characters. It was a tough pill to swallow going from Frank West, the every man's man and one of gaming's most memorable characters, to Jawline McNievel (Chuck Green) a badass with an endearing story, to No Neck Nick. A goofy and somewhat dim-witted hero, but he's always on the side of good. Honestly, he just doesn't fit. His character is obsenely cartoonish at best and I just couldn't get behind it. There's a particular lack of maturity in a character that says "s###balls" and other weird things while the world is falling apart around him. Maybe I'm just nitpicking, but his dialogues are just so awkward especially with Rhonda, leading to my next point.
I couldn't stand the dialogues. It feels like the scripts were written up at 3am of the due date and were never edited or looked over or even questioned by the VAs (I would know, I've written 3am essays and read over them in the morning, It's not pretty). The majority of conversations are just awkward and disconnected from the world around them. The characters are generally (but not all of them) tasteless or cookie cut. The psychos are the most disappointing. In the previous titles the psychos had their own agenda, sometimes philosophies, their own drive, or they were just plain crazy. The psychos in this... Are just psychos. They're just psychos and all they want is to snap and kill people. Not mention, you can't take a single one of them seriously. They're all just jokes with health bars.
Lastly the world design. In an outdoor world that has a mild focus on vehicles, normally you expect to be able to drive around from point A to point B, usually for a "collect 5" fetch quest. Instead, there's random unecessary roadblocks EVERYWHERE denying your ability to travel by wheel unless you either, A, find a ridiculous way around, or B, take it on foot until the next vehicle. It's such an awful gameplay mistake and creates frustration. In the previous installments, everything was connected and had shortcuts or other ways around. In DR3, have fun going from one corner of the map to the other to do a fetch quest.
Side note, I never liked "challenges" in free roam games. That's just a bias though.
Also, I don't know the conditions but it feels like the 'S' ending was just the default ending and there wasn't much you could do to screw it up. At least in DR1/2 I didn't get 'S' until the second playthrough and the 'S' endings were great and not just slammed in your face.
So now that I've hated on it and fanboy'd the crap out of DR1/2 some positives. It still has a certain charm to it and corely, it is a Dead Rising game. It's fairly fun, I enjoyed the playthrough, and there's a decent amount to do if you're willing to sacrifice some time to do it. Will you get $40 out of it? Maybe if you play through a few times and collect everything. It has its issues, but it's still a decent game. I just couldn't rate it fairly because it's following up in DR1/2 which were both very great games.

I've been playing the board game for about 6 years now.  This digital version has a good interface, though I find the AI to be relatively ineffective.  I would prefer if it had the ability to alter the difficulty level of the AI, but that might be asking a bit much for the price point.

I got the TTR Europe and USA 1910 DLC as a part of a Humble Bundle, which included copies of the game on Android in addition to Steam.
If you've played the board game, there are absolutely no surprises here. As a game, it is well designed, but fairly dependent on random chance e.g. your missions, the colors of trains you get (there should be a rule where you have to brag every time you draw two locomotives). Regardless, it's an entertaining game, but it will most definitely ruin friendships if you play with people you know. The game for PC and Mac have pass-and-play local multiplayer, but it's a little iffy, since your hand of cards is supposed to be hidden.
The electronic edition is nice, because you don't have to keep track of pieces and points by hand, and you don't have to clean up or set up either. Additionally, you can play with other people online, making getting stressed out by board games even easier. However, I think that half the fun of playing a board game is having a physical copy. With the electronic version, you miss out on nervously fumbling around while placing down cars, accidentally knocking over other people's cars, proclaiming your masculinity by taking a route with eight locomotives, trying to figure out where the hell your cities are, trying to figure out where the hell your friends' cities are, pleading for mercy from your friends, yelling at your friends, getting yelled at by your friends, putting your friends in headlocks for blocking your long mission, and overturning the board in rage.
Don't have any friends? I'd pass on this game then.

Long ago I used to play a board game called Rail Baron, based on the buying of train routes and getting paid for destinations.  So it was easy getting into Ticket To Ride, a far simpler and less agressive game that's also much faster and relaxed.  This game is simply fun, and quick enough to play during a break in most cases.
At the start of the game, you choose up to three destinations (more depending on DLC), and spend your turn either building routes, drawing cards, or choosing new destinations.  The goal is to score the most points in the end by having the most completed destinations, the most trains on the board, and the longest routes.
There are several DLC packs for the game, and I have several of them.  I especially enjoy the Europe DLC, and these provide alternate ways to play the game.  These include new maps and rule variants for use in the game.  These are not essential, but can enhance the game if the classic USA map and rules aren't interesting anymore.
The Steam version of this game also runs very well on Ubuntu.

Ticket to Ride is an easy game to understand, but impossible to master.  You could play this game for centuries and you still would never be able to win every game.  It's a game of luck and skill combined in perfect unison.  Whether you're a fan of board games, strategy games, or trains, you will enjoy this game.  I guarentee that anyone at any age can sit down and enjoy this game.

Last Hope may not be the deepest or most well-balanced tower defence game, and it may have the annoying vestiges of a freemium mobile title, but it nevertheless exudes a certain charm that is hard to deny. Furthermore, the RPG-lite aspects of the game will probably appeal to a fairly large slice of the gaming population, and some levels and game mechanics are pretty clever even if not truly ground-breaking.
Despite my frustrations with the game - some levels are quite painful to play through and grinding for XP and coins can be a bit of a chore - I have enjoyed it enough to have obtained all campaign stars in Nightmare difficulty.
There is one quite unfortunate design decision in the game that I simply cannot accept, however: while the devs have given us three (!) separate endless levels, towers in these levels get wrecked every few waves. While we do get a visual indicator of which 10 or 15 towers are about to get smashed by meteors (yea, meteors; because why not, I guess?), there is not quite enough time for us to sell all of these towers off. A large part of the satisfaction in playing tower defence games is building up a solid defensive matrix, and having our towers arbitrarily broken every so often is not very fun at all. For this reason, I cannot find the motivation to play the endless levels more than once. Pity. I would have much preferred throttled action point income to this.
Anyway, that one grouse aside, Last Hope is certainly worth every penny I spent on it and should be an instant purchase for anyone with an interest in tower defence games.

This game is not fun. It's not visually appealing and just plain bland. Rather than try to make enemies more varied, the game just randomly makes paths for enemies beyond chokepoints(which you've built at).

It has its moments, but its roots in mobile are obvious at every step: in-game menu selections are obtuse with mouse and are clearly engineered for touch screen, ridiculous timers on "upgrades" ala pay to play mechanics, double-click select function to avoid "accidental" pressing, and visuals and tinny sound echo mobile-quality asset use.  If playing a mobile game doesn't bother you it is an inoffensive fun time.  However, if you expect basic menu additions like editable scroll & mouse speed then this game pales in comparison to other available tower defense games that are much more suitable to PC gaming.
As others have noted, pathing by the horde is NOT in the game.  As a game mechanic it is laudable in theory but frustratingly obtuse in execution: you will have to re-play levels not out of any oversight on your part but because the game decides some previous routing barriers need to go away.  There is no innate logic to said deployment of these "disappearing" barriers; you simply find that your best tactical work is for naught and hopefully make do ... or just do over.  The end result of this is the game dispenses cheap defeats.  You don't lose because you are a bad player.  You lose because the game wants you to grind some more.  Minus any in-game purchasing this is simply bizarre game design.
The story is cute and the environments - although limited in their asset use, lighting, and depth - are vivid and reinforce the story well.  I enjoy TD games and there are good roots here that are, perhaps, not maximized fully for total enjoyment of the game.  Menus are clear, albeit limited, and there is a quite significant amount of levels to complete, so there is little argument that you cannot get your moneys worth.  The primary issue is how balanced the fun vs. frustration battle is.  So far it is even for me.  Consider this a tepid recommendation.

This game had a lot going for it. The first 5-10 hours, it was a fairly enjoyable Tower Defense game. As you are leveling, and buying new things, everything feels OK. Challenging levels, many different variants of levels including several "arenas" where you can try your luck on a single map where other variables will change.
The story is pretty decent as far as games go. They aren't going to win any pulitzer prizes, but it's serviceable and progresses the game.
Towers, the heart & sole of Tower Defense, come in many varieties, but you'll find yourself using such a low number of these, because of the upgrade costs,  that all the spots they give you maps will go empty.
Pathing is a big problem in this game. You aren't told the paths that enemies will take, and you will constantly be starting over levels because of a new path that the zombies will take around your defenses. I hate games where I have to play several times just to memorize the paths. So many TD games give you the paths they will take with a simple key that I'm surprised they didn't include this. I guess they consider this a game mechanic. Oh, and levels will change on you from one try to the next.
Where the game falls apart is the end-game and the leveling mechanic for the heroes. It's quite obvious this game started out as a Free / low cost with a store to buy yourself credits for additional $$. The problem is when they ported this to Steam, while they removed the store, they didn't adjust any of the exponential cost / experience required for leveling heroes.
So I went through all levels on Normal, then again on Hard, and I've done about 15 levels on nightmare. I have 2 heroes leveled all the way to 25, and two more that are level 23.
I just don't see the point of continuing. I'm close to getting to level 25, but the repetition is absolutely killing me. It's not fun.
With the upgrade paths for both towers and heros, you can just grind yourself through the game. You don't have to try any new strategy, you just need to level up your hero and towers. This is a flaw IMO because lack of repeatability means I'm not sure I'm doing good or not. Also, it's impossible to give any specific advice to people because of the variation of heroes and towers with the leveling mechanic means that you and someone else will not have the same things, so any advice on levels is just not going to work.
Another negative is the implementation of the endless levels - if I could pick a game with the absolute worst endless mode, Last Hope would be that game. Every 5 levels the game wipes half your towers. It's absolutely not recoverable from and the randomness of it really is super frustrating - I never did play any more levels after the first few forays.
If this game is on sale for $1.99 or cheaper during a steam sale, go for it, but don't get hung up on the hero leveling or upgrading towers. Just pick a few towers (poison, sniper, farmer & air defense) and that's all you really need.

I just finished the game. 3.4 hours logged with a few quickloads (if I had to guess, maybe around 12) and restarts in the beginning and I have to say I really enjoyed the game. It was brief, obviously. The game felt as though it should have been an episode of a larger game, so for the money, I'm not sure your average consumer would say it was worth it. But, for me it was worth it - much better than plopping $25 to sit through another mindless Avengers movie.
The game's atmosphere is superb. I felt physically frozen for most of the game. The lack of light, blinding snow, and the destroyed, almost post apocalyptic setting was marvelous. Right from the jump, your situation feels completely hopeless. After dying the first few times so easily, I wondered how long my persistence would hold up. But, after figuring out a couple critical mechanics, I was off and running. The feeling of isolation saturates the game's feeling of hopelessness. The crafting system is simple and absolutely necessary regarding a few items. Some items you may disregard, as YMMV, but each item can have a significant impact on your situation. It was an intense, brutal 3 hours of gameplay.
Now, I simply have to point out how much this game resembles The Long Dark. Audio clues, the protagonist's voice, even certain sections of the soundtrack were ripped directly from The Long Dark. These things were really easy to recognize, as I have probably put in a couple hundred  hours in TLD. The similarities were so much that after 15 minutes into the game I began wondering if this game is merely a pilot for an episode the creators for TLD were planning to include in their game. So, I suppose that should say a lot about how well Near Death was done, since TLD is probably the greatest Indie survival game currently available.

Never felt like it was trying to make more of itself than was actually there and each step I took felt like an accomplishment.
Hope to see more like it!

I will be finishing the game tonight and will update this review to include more information. As it stands, I still, and will almost certainly, recommend this game upon completion. <3
*FINAL UPDATE*
In this game, you're essentially Matt Damon in The Martian - except you're a lady in Antarctica. Same principal.
You've crash landed and you've got to scour an abandoned research facility to search for supplies, craft items to aid with puzzle solving, and eventually - get the hell outta there.
This can be beaten in a 3-5 hour span, and because of that, some would say it's not worth it. I would argue that - if you're gonna go spend $12 on a movie ticket, spend the extra couple bucks to experience this game. It's a great little story-driven, puzzle solver, survival game developed by 4 or 5 people, and it fills a void that other games in the genre don't. It gives you an experience that's intense, and only meant to last a few hours. It's crafted that way to deliver a story that you see from start to finish, rather  than feeding your addiction to scavenge day after day, getting little achievements here and there to string you along. (It's worth pointing out that I love those games too, I just want to clarify that it isn't that type of experience.)
I thoroughly enjoyed the game, and would recommend that you try it. :)

At the time of this reveiew, it has been less than two months since the release of this hardware, so thing may have changed since this review.
Interestingly, the Steam Controller does not appear to have a lot of *official* developer support at this time. However, the fact that the user can map functionality to any of the multitude of buttons and control axes, along with the availibiliy of community mappings, makes this less of a problem. Furthermore, games that were built with the Xbox 360 or Xbox One controller in mind support the Steam controller as one of those controllers. In addition, the gyroscopes and accelerometers inside the controller provide something on par with the current console generation controllers. You'd be hardpressed to find a game pad for its price that has this level of control.
Now for the quality of the controller. It feels like a $50 controller. The controller feels sturdy, well built, and is kind of heavy, as though they worked to cram as much hardware inside the controller without leaving much space left over inside it. What I'm trying to say is that the Steam controller does not feel like a cheap controller at all. Don't be fooled by it only having one analog stick on it; it has two trackpads that have similar range of movement to an analog stick.
Overall, I love the hardware, as you'd be hardpressed to find a similar controller of similar quality at this price. Even my mainstay for periphrial hardware, Logitech, does not offer anything remotely like this. It takes some getting used to if you're coming at it from a Xbox360 / PS3 / Xbox One / PS4 controller scheme, but it'll grow on you after a few hours and then you'll figure out how to remap the controls to be more to your liking. Point is, I highly recommend this controller and hope to see more of it in the future.

Used a Dualshock 4 before getting this. Once I got used to the Steam controller, there was no going back for me.

Normally a mouse/keyboard user. I don't think the Steam Controller trumps mouse/keyboard for FPS multiplayer, but it's good for singleplayer FPS games and any game that you would ordinarily use a controller for. The customization feature that's part of Big Picture mode is quite nice, no remapping keys for every single game (unless you really want to of course). I'd consider it the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of a mouse/keyboard and a controller. You have a bit more precision aiming than you would if you were using a controller, but not as much percision as you would have with a keyboard and mouse. I'd like a few other steam controllers for LAN parties, but can't justify spending that much on controllers friends will probably use for 30 minutes and they'd find clunky. It takes some getting used too, but once you use it for an hour or two you can see what's good about it. My biggest complaint is that the shape of the controller isn't very ergonomic and sometimes it feels awkward when you're using the touchpad in the upper right along with the analog stick in the lower left in order to move while only really holding onto the controller with your ring and pinky fingers, it's a bit of a strain, but perhaps it's because I don't hold controllers that often anymore? But I don't remember ever feeling that way about 360 controllers back when I used those a bunch. Overall it's a good piece of hardware.

This is a really great game for introducing non-gamers to Steam and to online versions of boardgames.  The interface is a little clunky and old-fashioned, but gameplay is stable, and the atmospheric sounds and voice-overs are cute and add to the train theme.

For those who have never played Ticket to Ride: it's a fantastic entry into the world of board games. The rules are simple enough that anyone can understand them in a few turns: draw colored train cards to save up enough of them to claim routes between cities on the board and make longer connections using multiple routes between destinations to score more points. Turns happen quickly and competition for routes is fierce, making for an exciting experience.
While the best way to enjoy the game is to pick up a non-digital copy and invite some friends over to play, sometimes a quick game is preferable (or the thought of spending $50 on a board game sounds a bit risky). That's where the digital version comes into play.
For this game to not earn a recommendation, Days of Wonder would have had to totally drop the ball. While this isn't a perfect adaptation, the PC port available on Steam is a pretty good one. The game menus are ideal for newcomers, but a little less direct for veteran players. The graphics and sound are appealing, the interface inside the game is intuitive, and online play is a breeze (well, except for the occasional player who takes way too long to take a turn - and sorry if that ends up being me). While I did run into a bug that prevented me from making a valid move once, that is out of dozens of games. Several of the expansions and maps are also available for purchase at a lesser price than the physical versions, making it an ideal way of trying out new ways of playing Ticket to Ride before investing in them.
The only legitimate knock on this version is the lack of local multiplayer. While the PC might not be the most popular platform for this feature, it is a bit puzzling given that it exists on other platforms, such as the Xbox 360 and iPad.
Overall, Ticket to Ride is a great board game and this is an above-average implementation of it recommended for fans of the game and anyone curious about board games in general.

The game looked good in my opinion.
-----The story wasn’t particularly remarkable. But it didn’t really matter, I didn’t pay close attention to it and it wasn’t an important factor in my enjoyment of the game.
-----I found some of the characters amusing including the hotdog masterchef and the transvestite NPC companion you can eventually recruit.
-----But I disliked half the main characters in this game. Characters tended to be superficial stereotypes. A lot of the dialogue was cheesy and action in some scenes was unconvincing.I only really like early dialogue of a single main character.
-----I think a troubled expression of concern was overused on many characters’ facial animations.I personally hate seeing that look on faces all the time in games.
-----I didn’t have a problem with the games actual graphics.
What I liked was slaughtering Zombies. I completed the previous two Dead Rising games and I like the series.
-----The gameplay is very sandbox you can just spend your time mucking around having fun. It’s really cool to play this game through with a friend.
What I didn’t like was having to wade endlessly through hordes of Zombies. It didn’t feel quite as bad as in previous Dead Rising games. You don’t have to guide every survivor through them in order to save them anymore. But on the other hand, that took away that challenge.
-----Unfortunately the game isn’t challenging in general. Virtually the only time survivors in distress that I came across died was because I ignored them or missed them and they died instantly when I travelled a certain distance away.
-----I completed the entire main storyline, every side mission and killed all the psycho side bosses. I didn’t really have any trouble achieving success in any of this. I never had to repeat anything. The closest way this game came to being challenging was that some tasks and travelling long distances through masses of Zombies could be tedious.
-----I felt like I’d done the whole get through 1000’s of Zombies to get from one place to another thing enough times. It’s not something I want to spend so much time doing.
-----I think the game could really do with fast travel. Players could be penalized with a loss in time remaining in keeping with the whole constantly against the clock premise.
-----A lot of weapons in the game were a novelty. None of the combo weapons really stood out in terms of effectiveness.
-----DLC weapons made high tier combo weapons somewhat pointless, because it’s easy to get them in great quantity instead.
-----A problem with this game was aiming weapons. Not only because of the problem with aiming in general using analogue sticks. But because aiming would face you in the direction the character is turned, not where you are looking with the camera. It’s counter-intuitive.
-----You can even end up aiming your weapon in the completely opposite direction than intended. If you're using a gamepad like I did you must then slowly turn around. Unfortunately Zombies don’t wait while you do this so they are right on top of you by the time you’re facing them. Having to face the character in the right direction first was frustrating, it can’t really be done in a precise manner.
-----The other problem I had with this game was NPC A.I. Mainly in relation to travelling in vehicles. It can be hard to get them on board and take them with you when you want to move on. Mission NPCs will only get in the host player’s vehicle. Additional NPC companions would not get into a vehicle until after Mission NPCs are onboard.
-----This could be problematic especially because most of the vehicles I wanted to use couldn’t carry more than one passenger and I had to abandon my companions. If an NPC or player can hang on one side of my Steam Roller, why can’t another one hang on the other side?
Unlike previous Dead Rising games you are not confined to a shopping centre. There are lot more vehicles in this game
-----I didn’t like most of the custom vehicles. But probably the best thing in this game was the Rollerhawg. It’s a steamrolling motorbike with flamethrowers. You gain access to it early on But it’s the best vehicle in the game. Regular Steamrollers are also cool and forklifts are arguably better than the Rollerhawg.
-----Being able to craft on the spot without having to find a workbench was a convenient change from Dead Rising 2. Also being able to access supplies of any item you have found or crafted from safehouses was also a very welcome feature. This saves you the hassle of having to find or craft items when you need them.
-----With all the silly weapons, vehicles and costumes at your disposal this game has some pretty hilarious moments.
Early on I was sceptical that it’s just another Dead Rising game. But actually the more I played it, the more I wanted to keep going until I finished the game.
-----Overall I enjoyed the game. It’s introduced some good features to the series. I was not disappointed.
