whilst there are many who claim this game is a 'poor port', i found that it ran very nicely (even above nvidia recoomended settings). the only issues i had where pop ins when for examplel i drove at top speed into a building, as well as pretty long load times (at least 30 seconds). other then that, the game ran pretty sommthly and looked pretty good :)
if you enjoy slaughtering a freak amount of mindless zombies with cool looking weapons (and vehicles), then this is for you. the game is a big step up from DR2 and doesnt feel as cheap *cough*psychos*cough*. movement is also pretty tight this time around, letting you vault over rails, climb on top of vehicles and objects (though climbing on top of useable vehicles is buggy) and commando roll out of harms way.
the upgrade system is really neat and skill points are handed out generously (you can hit level cap and max out almost everything if you complete side missions and challenges). the game has a time limit (just like previous DR games), but i never felt in a rush to complete the main story (hence why i got to level cap and collected majority of blue prints and other collectibles before finishing the game).
combat is really smooth (though sometimes there is input lag for heavy attacks), weapons last quite a while (weapon life is based on kill count, so you have to be somewhat strategic when going out on massacres) and on the fly crafting means the action is always constant. the item wheel is fast and more or less responsive (i found it sometimes jumped to a weapon next to the one i wanted to select) and again, makes things fast and smooth.
vehicles are also a nice addition, though i found the health on vehicles to be a little too short... but i suppose it balances things out considering they can plough through hundreds of zombies like a warm knife through butter :D
the sound design is pretty good and makes slicing zombies down the middle very satisfying and bad a** :D, the soundtrack also does a nice job at building tension and making the player feel cool when mincing through hundreds of zombies at any given time.
i would give the game a solid 7/10. it could have done with more zombie types, better ranged weapons and ranged combat (guns are good but no where near as effective and melee weapons), tighter movement and more mission variety (everything is pretty much a fetch quest).
worth checking out if you can get it on special (i only paid $30 and got almost 30 hours out of it (including DLC)).

I've been gaming for quite some time now and have played on most gaming systems at one time or another, and personally owned more than a few. One system that I did not own was the Nintendo64. I was rather lucky though, because a mate of mine did. I would often go over to his house and we'd play for hours. The one game that we couldn't get enough of was GoldenEye, now a gaming classic (which is more than I can say for the Pierce Brosnan movie). The split screen local multiplayer game was heaps of fun as we ran around shooting each other, trying to get bragging rights with the most kills. As we played, we often worked out where the other was by looking at their screen. Some would call it cheating, others would say it was tactical.
Screencheat plays out much like GoldenEye or games like Quake Arena in that you run around the location attempting to dispose of your opponent(s). The thing that sets Screencheat apart from those others, is that looking at other players position on the split-screen is encouraged. In fact, it is absolutely necessary because... all the players are invisible.
Yes, that's right, invisible
So, in order to make a kill, you are required to look at their screen to ascertain their position. It may seem difficult, but once you get the hang of looking at both where you're going and where your enemy is going, it becomes quite easy. And although the opposition players are invisible, there are often some telltale signs of where they are. Whenever someone discharges one of their weapons, their position becomes apparent by the vapour trail of the rifle shot, the smoke trail of the grenade launcher, the shell casings of the blunderbuss, or the flames of the candlestick.
Games can be played either via a split screen local multiplayer, or, for those without friends, online with up to four players. Both play identically. At present, the weapons mentioned above are the only ones available (during the early beta), but the developers have eight lined up for the finished product. Each weapon has both its advantages and disadvantages. The grenade launcher, for example, has a large blast area, but its shots are easier to see, giving away your position. Also, you can accidentally harm yourself if you run into the grenade zone. The rifle allows four quick accurate shots and leaves a minimal trail, making it a great weapon to keep you invisible. But it takes longer to reload than the other weapons.
Beta limitations
There are only two maps at this point, and they are fairly small, but with two to four players in a game, they feel about right in scope. The Museum map is probably my favourite of the two, with its layered rooms, the quick getaway zones and the dinosaur display in the middle. The other is an outdoor area known as the Garden. It feels slightly larger than the Museum with its four colour areas that merge together at a central statue. Hedges, large plant pots and park benches are scattered throughout the area. There are three more maps in development, and I'm certainly looking forward to exploring them at a later stage.
There are six different game modes, of which only two are playable during the beta. I did, however, have the chance to play a third, which is probably my favourite. The two playable modes during the initial phase of the beta are Deathmatch and King of the Hill. Deathmatch is self explanatory, requiring gamers to be the first to score the allotted amount of kills. King of the Hill requires competitors to stand in the hill area for forty seconds, all the while being attacked by the other competitors. The third mode that I played, which is not yet playable in the beta, is Murder Mystery. It is a rather cool mode that plays out like a game of Cluedo (or Clue, depending on where you come from). In it, the game sets a particular task to each of the combatants. Each player is required to kill a certain opponent with a particular weapon in a particular room (or coloured zone). Completing all three sections of the task gives maximum points. Other points are awarded for partial completion and for killing other players as per the traditional Deathmatch.
Nostalgic two to four player fun
Visually, Screencheat matches the nostalgic feel of playing GoldenEye. But with the nature of the game it works remarkably well. The bright colours for each of the areas make it simpler to work out where other opponents are located. The controls are simple as well, with both the keyboard/mouse combination and gamepad controller supported. As primarily a PC gamer, I found the keyboard and mouse combination easier to use, but I trust players with a console flavour would prefer the gamepad controls. With its simple controls, simplistic visuals and fun gameplay, Screencheat is well worth getting into, even with the two maps and two modes during the initial beta. And, if you get in during the beta, it's free.

Just bought the controller a few hours ago and I LOVE IT! (I got it at GS didn't order from Steam). One of my favorite aspects is that the mouse pad (right touch pad) defaults to a trackball setting and as a track ball user it just felt right. The haptic feedback on the touch pads helps them feel a lot better than one would expect. I have had very little issue going from a standard 360 controller to the Steam Controller...
HOWEVER.
The placement of the face buttons (ABXY) is HORRIBLE. It is incredibly to far from the Right touch pad and the buttons are WAY to small. I find myself hitting the B button when I mean to hit A and it's going to take a quite a bit of getting used to, especially if you have larger hands like me. Secondly, the ONLY way to configure the controller is in Big Picture Mode. That too is slightly annoying, especially if you are trying to use the controller in a non-Steam game. It means you must configure the controller before you start playing or Alt-Tab back and forth to set things up how you want them.
I also think the configuration list could be set up better. As of now there are three options and you can actually on select and edit one, that being Desktop Mode (or whatever it's called) and if you change that one at all, if Steam gets closed completely, it resets to the default settings. If you do change and save the Desktop Mode, EVERY time Steam gets restarted you have to go to the settings, select it, import your saved settings and THEN you can finally be on your way. I do believe you can however set up a different config per game from your library but like I said, you HAVE to be in Big Picture Mode to do that.
Overall, I really do like the controller. It does take some getting used to and can be a hassle at times but I already believe it's one of the best gaming investments I've made. Hell, it's even replaced my mouse.

TL:DR Everything is customizable. If you are able to buy it, buy it. It's a want not a need, though.
+ CUSTOMIZABLE

+Now I can lay down and play videogames, make music, draw, whatever I want... on the computer.
+My right thumb doesn't hurt at the back joint for two days after excessive usage like most controllers did to me in the past because I don't have to bend my thumbs anymore and instead can choose to make the left pad the joystick (for some reason it's always the right thumb).
+Starcraft 2 hotkeys and maneuverability was pretty awesome, but I need to practice more.
- If you're on a Mac and you want to play games on Steam that's available for Windows via Windows Parallel, the controller will not be recognized in Big Screen mode on the windows side (That means no rivals of aether/Dark Souls II/Game Maker: Studio). I'm hoping it will be patched and I already can expect the update to not be some kind of DLC, because Steam is awesome like that.

As a game, it's pretty decent. None of the maneuvering seems particularly bad so it's controllable. Meleeing has a bit of a dash animation to it, which takes some getting used to, since sometimes the camera goes haywire depending on the situation. Beyond that the game is rather interesting. The ridiculous art style perfectly compliments the disgusting nature of the injury system (and of the character model animation). In terms of gameplay, Loadout seems to try to blend a few Retro elements like Pickups and more modern concepts like a recovery system (healing guns). The multiple game-types prevent Loadout from getting too monotonous, and the endless ammunition actually compliments the gun-construction theme rather well. You notice the difference when you modify certain aspects of your gun and will have to pay the consequences for a gun that does not suit the game-type or situation. Though the downtime between reloads is still an issue, you have unlimited ammunition, you can't blame anyone but yourself when you craft a gun that has large ammunition deposits but a heartbreaking reload time. As it is, Loadout is okay. I would've liked to see them do more ridiculous things with their gun designs to compliment the art style a tad more--make the guns larger and more ridiculous looking, but that isn't much of a fault as it is something to work towards. We'll see what hap[pens with the coming patches.

Siralim 2 is essentially a monster rancher style game meets Magic the Gathering level of interesting abilities for each creature that a practically infinite array of synergies, combinations, and ideas available for teams. The one downside of the game is this same upside. You can create some absurdly strong teams that can pretty much face smash any enemy team, but getting there takes a while and the journey is great fun.
The mechanics in this game, and especially their diversity, are the best I've ever seen in the monster raiser genre. More than 600 creatures and relatively few are just throw aways.

Dont be fooled by the artstyle (which is btw beautiful), this is a deeply strategic team based rpg style game. There are infinite options for a team, you can give artifacts for your creatures, artifacts can have several different abilities, similar to spells so when six creatures fight against another six it can be hard to follow what is happening. You can get creatures in fights by extracting cores or by doing small favors for all the gods in the game (and boy there are a lots of them!). The game fortunately isn't really punishing, you dont lose items or creatures when you lose a fight but this doesnt mean that the game isnt extremely grindy! The levels sometimes will feel unbalanced; certain random groups of enemies are much stronger than others, so it can happen that on the same level you win a fight without casting a spell or thinking about which enemy to attack first while you die against the next group of enemies. To sum it up, there is a lot of content here, you can probably play this for hundreds of hours and you will find new creatures etc, meaning this is a proper game for killing time. Also the devs seem really nice and will help you out in the discussions.

From there, the game walks you through the base mechanics and sets you off on your own to grind awy for hours on end. With over 600 unique creatures there is a ridiculous amount of diversity at the player's fingertips. It is important to note that this game has some crazy balancing, by that I mean that pretty much everything is capable of being OP if used in a correct combination. So, the game never forces you to go down one path in order to succeed. The choice is always yours. The story is very simple and straightforward. It personally doesn't bother me, but I definitely consider Siralim 2 to be plot driven. As for the graphics, I love them. I think they fit the game perfectly. They just add to the nostalgia while also not being sloppy. In terms of difficulty, most of the challenges you'll encounter in your adventure come from a need to level up to beat bosses or perhaps find a new team composition to clear realms quicker. As I stated before, anything can become OP when used correctly, so it is extremely fun to experiment with different creature combinations and team compositions.
For anyone that enjoys monster taming/catching games, I would definitely recommend that you buy this game.
Important Note: The devs actively respond and adapt to feedback from their community (via forums and discord as far as I know).

Short review: I got this for free... and I still want a refund. Feels clunky, unfinished, heard there was a hoo-haa between dev & publisher. Either way my advice is to avoid.
Indepth: I got thie game for free for kickstarting another project by the devs.  I'm not sure if it's possible but I'd like to give it back. I would have prefer a thank email instead of this game because this game gave me hope of reliving my days playing Freelancer, Privateer and heck even Solar Winds (if you're old enough to remember that) but sadly it didn't appeal at all.
Ignore my hours as I also played this on a friend's laptop while on holidays recently to see if my first review was unjustified... sadly it wasn't.
Graphics: The graphics are extremely dated. They would have looked stunning... late 90s, early 2000... maybe. But I remember a game called Freelancer (Chris Roberts of Wing Commander/Star Citizen) and it's graphics were/are far superior and that was made back in 2002. It says HD... but it's not. The screen shots provided make it look so much better than it is. Which is a real let down during the golden age of retro gaming you'd think if they(Dev/Pub) were more honest, I would be far more forgiving esp. since I'm from the older generations that played Wing Commander back in the day.
The opening cinematic was so bad(graphics/plot/audio) I can't help but think it was a test and they just went with it.
Audio: The Sound design=Horrible. The voice acting is the worst I've heard in a long time. I would have preferred none but it seems you get half and half. The brief tutorial you get are silent with your "Cortana" telling you to press the 'Dock' key or the 'Teleport' key... you'd think since they are doing text their allow user-defined but nope.
The music is barely noticable, the sound effects for collision and fire of your laser cannons (pew pew) is just bad. I would have preferred the silence in space than what was provided.
Gameplay/Story: This is the worst part of the game. The controls are unintuitive, all over the keyboard, make no sense and the only decent thing is allowing joystick control (who has one of those there days?).
The menus are annoying to navigate as they do a 5 second slow fade to black and back again. There is NO tutorial. None. just go fly... good luck. You accidently shoot friendlies so many times in the early stages of the game you may as well just be a pirate to start with.
The starting packages do include pirate as well as soldier, scientist, adventurer, hunter, spy, the third nut of the pop and don't forget your mum. They don't do much except give you a slight advantage in a few minor things otherwise there is no customising your character.
The story is simple: You are Ace McPretty-Boy-with-Dead-Eyes in search of your lost sister.
Beyond that I have no idea. I tried to sink in an entire day playing this but it just didn't appeal in any way and I didn't like it.
Don't buy this. If you like space sims. Like really love them. As in you sneak off for quick space hyper jumps whenever you can... still do not buy this game. I really wish it was good... seems like it could have been a new Privateer style game... but it isn't.

Dead Rising 3, the latest in the costuming zombie killing franchise comes as a port of the XB1 with some mixed feelings due to porting issues.  While the performance isn't ideal, it deosn't hurt the gameplay significantly, and if you can run it it's a fun time.
I've played: Story mode through the 'S' ending, some of the DLC, level 40 character, ~25,000 zombies.
My rig (all stock)
CPU: Intel i5-2300
GPU: Gigabyte GTX 770 Windforce
Ram: 16GB
HDD: 5400 rpm green drive (recycled from a NAS box)
I set up the game to run at an internal 1080p resolution since I game on my living room TV.  I'm a late purchaser, so all 5 paches are applied.  I had no crashes, bugs, glitches, or other graphical issues.  The framerate is locked at 30FPS, but it was consistent, and as a converted X360 gamer that's around what I'm used to, especially for this series.  I had one startup where things were chugging and dropping frames, but a quick restart fixed that, and I attribute it to the plethora of other software running rather than anything DR3 specific.
The story is basic Capcom style, where the game's lore is just kinda slapped on top of the previous iterations and connected where it makes the least sense.  It gets pretty self-referential near the end, but if you're buying this for the story, you're picking the wrong game.
Compared to previous DR games the gameplay itself is far less restrictive.  Combo weapons crafting can happen anywhere, saving can happen anywhere, survivors and psychos are almost all optional, and you can make super combos and combo cars.  The super combos get really fun and greatly aid the survival challenges scattered throughout the game, and the combo cars are a requirement if you're going to travel from Pt. A to Pt. B with any reference to the game's internal clock.
Speaking of the clock, it's not hard to beat it.  I restarted once, somewhere in Chapter 3, about a day and a half into the game's internal time system.  In previous DR games this would be the first of many restarts, as the time ticked away quickly and often accelerated based on how you were doing.  Not so in DR3.  My second "start" saw me getting all the way through Overtime, beating all psychos, finding about 70% of the collectibles, and rescuing about 15 other survivors.  I finished the main portion of the game with a little over 3 days time remaining, which was a bit surprising.
The bosses aren't too bad, if you have some combo guns where you need them.  The weapons lockers help restock before hand, a couple of bosses have handy blueprints nearby, and the police sergeant was really thy only one that gave me much trouble.  Most of the time, go in with your rocket punch and you'll finish anyone off easily.  Same story for the seven deadly Psychopaths, and while their attacks were somewhat varied, the dodge roll keeps you out of trouble pretty easily.
The zombie slaughtering remains fun, the weapons are more plentiful, and the optional crafting upgrades (use any blung weapon instead of just a crowbar) make combo weapons as pletiful as you want them.  The addition of the combo cars (especially the forkwork or the party slapper) add to the fun.
There's plenty to complete for the completionists, plenty to do for the casual, and enough of a horde everywhere you go to add tension even for a higher level character.   If you've got the hardware to run it, it's a fun fun game.  Now if you'll excuse me, I've got a sledghammer that needs to find a fire axe.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a prequel to the original Deus Ex game and follows the story of Adam Jensen, a security chief at an augmentation (cybernetic implantation) industry, who finds himself augmented against his will and put against a myterious conspiracy he must discover and twhart in time.
The story of Human Revolution keeps itself interesting for the whole game, with a very clever portrait of technology advancements debates, few cameos from characters of Deus Ex and a good bunch of original protagonists. As with every Deus Ex title there is a lot of reading and exploring to do for players who really want to dig further in the game's setting: doing so even awards you nice chunks of experience every time.
Gameplay-wise, one must say that Human Revolution offers less freedom of action than its predecessor. While in the original Deus Ex you could go around destroying anyone and anything or decide to either incapacitate or plain evade both regular enemies without any consequence, truly allowing you to slowly build your own way to overcome the game's challenges, this sequel still gives you the same amount of freedom, but turns the table more in favor of an action-packed approach. Each boss encounter requires you to kill your enemy and every one of them are very durable augmented agents that will torn apart a player that relayed only on stealth and evasion up to that point. You can't run away either. There are also several instances in the game where going full killing mode against your enemies is required to achieve certain results.
The Director's Cut DLC tried to fix such design choices by adding to the bosses arenas more way to eliminate them with indirect means. However, it's worth mentioning that you still HAVE to kill them and they have been severly buffed up from the first version of the game, to the point that even trying to off them with hacking or unconventional means is very hard without some protective or straight combat augs.
The Missing Link DLC is a four hours worthy new content that was fully integrated in the main story of Human Revolution with the Director's Cut. The DLC takes place on a Belltower cargo ship, the Hei Zhen Zhu, and requires you to find and neutralize the local mercenary leader in order to continue your main story to Singapore. Whyle the ship features very crampy environments, the whole DLC still feels like a Deus Ex game, with plenty of alternative options to choose from. The final boss of the Missing Link is also much more Deus-Ex-esque than the ones from the vanilla game.
I would totally reccomend Deus Ex: Human Revolution due to its outsanding story and gameplay united with a huge replay value that allows you to experience a different kind of game every time you decide how to deal with the enemies and the other NPCS your own special way differently

Let me tell you why you need to get this game RIGHT NOW.
Did you do that? Yes? Good. No? Fine, but you're MISSING OUT!
So, everyone has played a First-Person-Shooter, the concept is easy: Run around with a weapon, find the enemy, and shoot them. It's easy! Gamers have been doing this for years. Now, grab a drink and listen closely, this is where it gets juicy!
Back in the old days of FPS' on consoles (N64, PS1, ect. ect.) when you wanted to play a game with a friend, you grabbed your extra controllers, went to a friends house, and all sat down in front of the same TV. When playing multiplayer, you all shared a "chunk" of the screen, and the "rule" was to keep your eyes on YOUR "chunk" of the TV, and no one elses.
Not everyone followed that rule.
People would look at the other players "chunks" and found out where their friends were hiding, what they were doing, and pretty much knew everything that was needed to be known to find that player, destroy them.
But what they didn't realize is that they were destroying friendships, and honorable play.
This technique of looking at the other players "chunks" was soon named "Screenpeeking", or "Screenlooking". It was a technique that was hated by everyone, and it was a general rule not to do it.
That was the old days, and due to advancements in technology, you don't have to worry about it anymore.
Now, imagine if there was a game where the only way to win was Screenlooking?
WELCOME TO SCREEN CHEAT!
In this game, everyone in invisible, but, you can see everyones screen, no matter where they are playing from! You literally have to look at everyone elses screen to find out where they are at, and to see where you must aim to kill them.
It's a simple concept, but it is the most nostolgic fun I've had in forever.

The remappability and versatility of this controller are phenomenal. It is NOT perfect for all games - emulators especially hve issues when using it, and may be better off with an XBOX controller. However, for most games, and especially for disabled gamers, this may be the ultimate controller.
It's important to note that as of now, many games will not work perfectly out of the box. You are required to lean heavily on the community configs, or on taking the time to learn to engineer your own. Given time though, this will be the best controller on the market.
NB: I am comparing to the XB360, XB, PS2 and PS3 controllers. I have not yet tried the DS4 or the XB1 controllers. Since those are evolutions rather than redesigns I suspect the main benefit of this controller, seamless remapping, is not present. For those controllers hardware mods are required for diabled users. No such mod is required for the Steam Controller.

This Christmas was like any other Christmas, we were all waiting downstairs while our father dozed away all morning long. We waited and waited until we heard the not so jolly man walk down the stairs. At this point we knew that it was time. We dug through the stockings with smiles seen plastered on all of our faces. After a few breakfast sandwhiches we made our way to the tree with presents marked for one and all from the great Santa Claus! One by one we took turns opening presents and then from below the wrapping paper emerges a Steam Controller (which my brother originally thought was a ps4 controller and he was excited) I took it out of the box and immeditaly felt the touch pads. "It feels like nothing" I said as I looked to my brother concered.
After presents were done we all split our ways playing with our new toys and thingamajigs. Straight away I stuffed the batteries into my Steam Controller and plugged the wild adapter into my usb port. I was pleasently surprised by the haptic feedback and all the customizable aspects. As I started playing with it more and more it started to feel more natural and I started to really enjoy using it until it felt no more difficult than the controllers I have used before in my life.
Overall the Steam Controller is a worthy investment that will enhance your controller experience on PC.

UPDATE: I can confirm that you can use the controller on other games - as long as Steam is running in the background.  The other thing to note is that this controller is only useful if the game you're playing does not support gamepad - for example Mass Effect 1-3.  In this case, using the steam controller works great.  If you own games that support gamepads, then don't bother buying the Steam Controller. This thing is only useful if you play games that only wants to work with mouse/keyboard.  It is still not a comfortable controller if you use the XABY buttons a lot.
Original review:
Users of the Xbox or PS4 controllers, there is really no reason for you to get the Steam Controller.  The Steam controller is terrible at shooters (the right-touch-pad is not a good replacement for the rightstick).
The four button placement (left center) forces your thumb to bend in the center to cover the left stick and finger over the buttons.  It is very close and cramps your hand.  I don't understand why Steam didn't look to the Xbox or PS controllers for inspiration or just comfort design?
Games that doesn't require the rightstick for movement works great with the Steam controller.  Unfortunately, any games that uses the rightstick (like any shooters), you're going to have a problem.
I think for now, I'll just stick to the Xbox controller....
Pros:
- Wireless
- Came with two AA batteries
Cons:
- Only really works in Steam's Big Picture Mode (I think it will work if you have Steam running in the background)
- The two pads are confusing, not great controller in shooters
- 4 buttons placement is awkward and too close to the center to be useful

When I first got the Steam controller, I assumed it would be like a laptop's touch-pad on both of the circular touch-pads. That is to say, not very sensitive, and difficult to control in games especially. I have had no such experience with the Steam Controller, although it does have a fairly steep learning curve (~4 hours to comfort)
The first game I played with my new steam controller was my other Christmas present, Rainbow Six: Siege. Out of the box it felt different than mouse and keyboard, but easier to make precision movements than an xbox 360 controller, ESPECIALLY with the gyro controlls, and I can comfortably say that with the steam controller I can play that game about as well as I can with mouse and keyboard.
I think that's enough nariative, here's some pros and cons.
PROS
+ Very sensitive aiming touchpad, similar to high-DPI gaming mice (in that you have to turn your in-game sensitivity down.)
+ Haptic responses on touchpads to give texture and quantitative judgments of movements (think texting with an android phone.)
+ Comfortable left thumbstick.
+ Trigger layout similar to XBOX 360 controller.
+ Detailed binding customization.
CONS
- Counter-intuitive setup; the computer does not see it as a gamepad by default and as such this only works with games that you have imported to steam (initially). That's not to say it won't work with non-steam games, look up how to import games to the steam overlay.
- Can start to feel oily to the touch after hours of play.
- Does not work very well with some games outside of Big Picture Mode.

Amazingly different from Microsoft's Xbox and Sony's PlayStation controllers, even though the Steam Controller is definitely harder to get a hang of; however, it was definitely worth it as I now can flick, switch, use emotes, jump, crouch, move, aim, and an extraordinary amount of other features that can be binded to all the buttons and grips on the Steam controller.

Well I can't hit "NO" on bloody Fallout 2 can I? It's a cult classic.
That said, I'm sure you've heard all the good stuff about it from everyone else. Maybe you remember playing it as a kid (and remember all the good stuff). All that good stuff is true. This game is awesome.
That said... there are some things that really grate on me...
Combats are painfully, hair-tearingly slow. Sometimes you have to wait minutes for some scorpions to crawl ahead a few hexes each, only to fire at one and find out that you missed. Again some minutes of crawly-crawly. Until they surround you and tear you to pieces within a single round.
Your weapons don't really improve all that much. Later in the game, around San Francisco, even though you can upgrade your arsenal, it feels like a downgrade with the ridiculously overpowered (and numerous) enemies.
Merchants run out of cash, and you run out of storage space. You'll end up lugging around dozens of extremely valuable guns you can't use, and can't barter in for an upgrade, because, say, the gun you'd want to buy costs 10000, each of the old guns cost 1000, but you can't carry 10 of them at the same time.
Party members are bloody idiots. They are a liability 50% of the time. They are very good at two things - getting themselves killed, or killing you and each other. If you give them powerful weapons, they will try to shoot a full cartridge into some enemy right through a party member standing inbetween. If you give them crappy weapons, or tell them to run away, you can't win most of the fights late in the game.
The NPC control dialog is incredibly hard to navigate.
Did I mention how slow combat is? On a computer maybe a 100 times more powerful than the one this game was written for.
Anyway... of course it's recommended. It's Fallout 2. But it will frustrate you to no end.

Siralim 2 is a combination monster catcher, castle management, and semi-roguelike RPG. You begin by selecting from one of five types of mages: Life, Nature, Chaos, Sorcery, and Death. After a short introduction, you find yourself at your castle with lots of stuff to do.
You can teleport to a realm, which is a contained random map with enemies, treasures, and one of 15 gods with whom to gain favor. Gaining favor with the various gods gives various perks and access to new cores.
Cores can be extracted from most creatures, though there are some (such as those gained by earning favor with the gods) can only be purchased. From the beginning, you can only extract cores from the base creatures. Once you have bred or summoned a creature, you will be able to extract cores from creatures like it that you find in the wild. The creature count (with the expansion) is somewhere around 700 different creatures you can have (with no limits on how many of each).
Breeding is done one of two ways. You can pick the parents yourself, or you can use recipes you have found while exploring realms. Breeding creatures gives them an increase in power, so even breeding two of the same creature together can be beneficial as they become more and more powerful. The only drawback to breeding is that you are limited by your Power Level, which is increased through combat and has a maximum of 200%, minimum of 20% (there are also fairies you can use to give you a boost to Power Level). Since breeding costs 50%, you can only breed three creatures before needing to increase your Power Level again. Still, it is lots of fun to breed new creatures and see them show up in the game world (where you can now capture their cores).
There are many more things to do, and with 40 hours in the game, I have only scratched the surface. You can craft artifacts to equip on your creatures and give them special boosts. There are many spell gems that can be equipped and modified with special bonuses (such as automatically being cast when your creature is hit). You can cook different foods to give special bonuses. Recruit villagers into your castle who give you various quests, along with a tailor who can craft costumes for you. Plus more.
Combat is not just about dealing a lot of damage. Each creature has a trait which can greatly change the course of battle, so you will need to prepare for anything. I had to forfeit battle against a much weaker creature because my party could only deal physical damage, and this particular creature casts Shell on itself each time it takes damage. Shell prevents all damage from the next attack against it. If I had equipped a single damage spell, I would have been able to defeat it, but even my much stronger creatures were useless against it.
The bosses are also difficult and unique. I have only fought through to the 19th-level boss, which is difficult because it requires your party to be able to survive for a long time (unless you just happen to guess the correct combination). My "all-powerful" team of level 30+ struggled against this boss.

There's something about open-world space simulators that is inherently appealing to me.  That's why I think I was more forgiving of Spaceforce Rogue Universe HD from Dreamatrix Game Studios despite having a number of issues with it when it came to stability and execution.
The game itself may be showing its age, but the transformation to HD has helped considerably.  While the cut-scenes look dated and pixelated, the in flight models are attractive, and the backgrounds are just filled with interesting things to look at.  Ship and creature design are both intriguing and weapons look powerful, if not exotic.  What really impressed me were the explosions, with cool looking shock waves and flying debris, and the incredible reflections and distorted images in the cockpit view.  The visuals were aided by a good soundtrack and sound effects.  Unfortunately, the already weak cut-scenes were hampered further by absolutely dreadful voice acting.  It's actually hard to fully fault the acting, however, because so much of the dialogue was ham-fisted or downright schlocky.  It's a shame because it's clear the team was trying to tell a heart-wrenching story about family and the horrors of war, but I found myself wanting to skip over it and just continue flying around performing tasks.
Flying around in Spaceforce Rogue Universe HD is fun, but it takes FAR too much setup to get everything working properly, and the game has bugs aplenty.  First off there is only partial joystick/controller support, which is frankly unacceptable for a spaceflight game.  It's annoying watching enemy craft pull off maneuvers you can only dream of because you need one hand on a joystick for pitch and yaw and one on the keyboard to handle roll, which makes dogfighting more awkward than it should be.  Sure, once you get the hang of things, it becomes easier, but flight never feels second nature the way it does is something like the Evochron games.  Couple this awkwardness with a glitch that prevented me from firing weapons with my first craft (which later solved itself-  I don't know whether the Logitech profiler was acting up or if the game itself was glitchy), and I nearly stopped playing right out of the gate.  It also doesn't help that the tutorial is inadequate, and there are no button prompts for actions.  I like that the game used context sensitive icons to denote things like docking and initiating trade with various crafts, but it would have been nice for it to also tell me in flight that I needed to hit Enter to perform those actions, or which buttons I needed to jump to a station or wormhole rather than making me consult a guide.
There's a LOT to do in this universe, and I liked the freedom the game gave me to explore/fight/trade/pursue the story as I went along.  Unfortunately, that freedom came with a price.  While trading itself was fairly straightforward, equipping weapons/upgrading my ship's systems was more problematic.  I was able to figure it out, and the system is fairly intuitive once you know what you're doing, but again, it would be nice to have the basics covered in-game.  It also would have been nice to know what weapons/systems I could install immediately on my ship and which ones required me to upgrade my systems first.  I could always sell back items for full credit, but it wasted time when a simple heads-up display of usable items could have been implemented.
Missions themselves are plentiful and easy to find, but it wasn't always easy to determine just how difficult a mission was.  It was nice to see that enemies had a level ascribed to them and that missions were apparently color-coded for ease of completion, but I often found myself hopelessly outclassed by enemies I thought I could defeat.  Between not being able to remember (or properly execute) commands due to the incomplete controller support, and the ability of my enemy to absorb simply ludicrous amounts of damage, it made flying missions seem like something I should wait on.  I'd rather have the choice of whether I want to be a soldier or a trader, and not have the game feel like it's making me perform actions I don't want (mining, etc.) just so I can level up.
The weird thing is, despite everything I said above, I'm still somehow enamored with Spaceforce Rogue Universe HD.  The universe is immense, there's a lot of bang for the buck, and flying can be enjoyable once you work out the quirks.  Do I think it's worth the full price?  Potentially, if the team is able to patch the rough edges.  The game is still charming in its own right, and worth playing, but you will want to either wait for a sale (or patches) and bring plenty of patience.

I played a good 8 hours of this game before I finally put the game down and I've come to the conclusion that it's simply not worth anyone's time.
Story - It's honestly not worth your time. But that's not really a big deal. The game offers freeplay mode and it is much prefered. With all the exploration the game gives you, you don't really care to follow the generic naive-hero plot. Another problem the story presents is that the difficulty ramps up immensely. The first mission isn't so bad but I had to grind out ship upgrades and weapons for a solid 3 hours before attempting the second mission.
Graphics - It was made in 2007 so I can't say much here. Honestly it doesn't bother me and since you're in space 99% of the time anyway, the only graphics you should be focused on is the background. Fights are usually so chaotic that you don't notice the dated textures anyway. For 2007 not bad though by today's standards it certainly is dated... Which is strange considering "HD" is in the title
Audio - Laughably bad. The voice acting is cheesy and not in a good way. Characters constantly repeat the same damn lines over and over and over and over and over and over and there is no button to turn them off from what I've seen. Surely the devs would have come to their senses and said to themselves - "Man, our audio is abyssmal, lets add in a feature that turns off voices". But surprisingly they didn't. The rest of the audio sounds like stock sound effects and random pew-pews etc. It sounds very 1998 Starcraft-like. The only Voice acting that is cheesy in a good way is the Ord.
Gameplay - Boring. I spent 7 out of my 8 hours just mining asteroids because the game starts you off in such a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ state that you have no option but to grind out upgrades and wepons just to find a single lowly ship (Which, by the way even with many missiles takes up to 10 minutes to kill). Don't bother fighting more than 1 enemy, you'll die, a lot. Because of this, you're stuck in the first two or three sectors going back and forth mining asteroids and doing the crappy fetch-quest missions of 'repair the satellite' because you can't fight in your tincan ship. Whatever more advanced combat in this game exists, I don't care. It's not worth spending another 10 hours getting to level 3. Yeah, I spent 8 hours going from level 1 to level 2... and most of the enemies start off at level 4. Enjoy your MMO grinding.
Over-all - I see the potential, I really do. It has some interesting civilizations, but they never interact beyond a random dogfight here and there (Don't rely on your allies to help you kill bad guys). The exploration is fun, but you aren't allowed to explore a whole lot because of the grind etc. Over all not even worth the 3 dollars I spent on it and I was excited at first. I thought it was amazing but the deeper I dug the more I noticed the smell....

Every game in the Deus Ex series is great, but each one has its faults. The first one (my favorite) is so open and engaging, but the clunky controls and dated graphics (even for its time) have kept many people from experiencing it to the end. The second one has good graphics and a good story, but its buggy and streamlined to the point of ludicrousness.
Deus Ex: Human Revolution is probably the best game in the series, but I place it just a notch below the first one. The story is interesting, but it never reaches the suspense I felt in DX1.
That being said, what a game it is! This game has probably the best cover system I've ever seen. It's so satisfying to sneak past the guards. I'm half-way through a new game plus playthrough where I'm not killing anybody or setting off any alarms, and this is truly the best way to play.
The graphics are artistically astounding, but look pretty bad technically. The character models are strange and inexpressive. However, the warm golds that permeate every frame of the game distract you from the characters' tiny heads, odd faces, and huge shoulders.
I love the Mass Effect games, but I felt that they could have been so much more. People praised the dialogue circle as feeling like a real conversation. But if you've ever tried to have a conversation like you do in Mass Effect (for example, abruptly changing the topic immediately instead of letting it flow naturally), people look at you funny. Here, there's so much depth, and using your augs to persuade someone feels so satisfying. In my opinion, Deus Ex: Human Revolution achieves every goal Mass Effect almost accomplished with flying colors.
The sound is incredible. The soundtrack oozes atmosphere.
The game is quite lengthy, and multiple playthroughs still feel rewarding.
I didn't care as much for the Missing Link portion, but maybe I will when I go for completion on that, too.
I recommend everyone play this. It controls as smooth as butter, so the clunky excuse won't apply to this one.

For you to know if your game preferences aligns with mine: I play a lot of TD and I love hunting that last 100% achievements. I like strategy over clickfest. I like unique td mechanics and difficulty that forces you to try many strategies before succeeding.
After 50+ hours (sounds like a lot, I might have left it on running during night or something) and 100% steam achievements (which are different from the in-game achievments of which I have 94/154).
The dev(s?) seems to be very active and you can feel there is heart in the game. Artstyle is nice and stylish and the theme is consistent.
But even if I really want to like this game, I feel it's a very dull and average tower defense.
It's a progression fest with "go back and level up your hero and come back when you are ready". I think that can work very well, but in TD's it generally means that "none of those levels were balanced for you, we just used a steadily increasing algorithm to control the pace".
So I gambled and leveled my poison towers first, and then the advanced 2x2 tower, and later the anti-air. And most of the time I just pressed fast forward and watched the game fly by. The first 80%-90% of the game was just so incredibly easy. Did I get lucky with my tower picks? I'm more inclined to believe this is some futile attempt to reward the achievement-hunter in me. And trust me, I love that kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥ but there has to be
challenge! I never changed my tower setup all game through. Not once. And I never used any of the "defensive" towers/tents.
I randomly looked at some monster stats and found one saying "This monster is immune to stun.".This sure sounds like an attempt to force a situation where the player should switch up his towers.Instead the reaction you get is "Oh, there is a stunning tower? Good thing I never used it!".
And I believe that really defines this game. The lack of strategy. If you can go whatever random tower loadout and still breeze through the game I think there is a problem. I think you need more situational towers. Yes that could gimp people who invest too much in the wrong towers, but I still feel it would be more fun than this.
So what if there is 50+ monsters? If all I can even remember afterwards was a fast monster and a fat exploding one, what does it matter? Oh yeah there was flying one as well. My bad. And how many levels was that? About 50 x 2 modes x 3 difficulties? I would take 10 good levels over the 140 bad ones any day.
It's not all bad though. I really liked hunting the last "graveyard something something" achievement.I found joy in controlling four heroes, swapping them around at different spots and then going back and leveling upthose heroes up to meet the next difficult challenge. But to be honest, those levels were WITHOUT towers!! So don't come and tell me there was any tower strategy involved.
So for what it's worth I think this game works best when it does it's own no-towers hero-defense-kinda-thing. I also enjoyed the two "mini-MOBA" maps quite a lot.
But the actual tower defense maps? Meh. Sorry. Not for me.

After a good 2-3hrs of playing on one server, I'd had a base up and running, collected a couple guns, worked up some blueprints from random barrels and such, and made a couple friends along the way. I've also noticed a couple improvements to be made to the game, but I'll get into those later.
Firstly, I know people are saying the game is a blatant copy of other indie games, for example Unturned, another free-to-play post-apocalyptic game. At first, I could see where they were coming from, considering the preview videos and pictures but after playing the game and getting used to the mechanics, I found this game was actually more in-depth and different in comparison to other games alike.
Bare in mind; game designed on the same genre are bound to be similar.
Now for the improvements I formentioned;
- A "favourite" button for servers.
- Voice chat (I'm sure it's already work in progress)
- A group system.
- More base customisation - tables, counters, more stuff to spice up the look of a base.
- Last but not least; singleplayer! A world where you can just make a base and not worry about being raided over night! One man versus the world. (This is my one pet pieve about most survival games.)
Good work with the game and keep it up.

Despite the many games I play at a single time, I still always find time to play Saints Row 2. Even though it is dated to a certain extent, SR2 to this day still packs hours of fun and loads of content. Many current open-world games even lack the amount of enjoyment this game has to offer. This pro is accentuated by the fact that you could pick-up this masterpiece for only $10 on Steam. However, it must be said how problematic the PC version of this game could be. Many players including myself have a rough time running this title without it's FPS dropping dramatically at points. To repel this, definitely download IdolNinja's wonderful Gentlemen of the Row mod for this port. It still does not fix the FPS problem completely, but there is an obvious difference plus there is a behemoth of new content within this mod.
Pros:
+Tremendous character, vehicle, and safehouse customization
+A memorable story with dramatic moments mixed in with great humor
+Huge arsenal of weapons including assault rifles, RPGs, satchel charges, and katanas
+Vast array of vehicles including supercars, airplanes, rocket-launching choppers, and APCs
+Stilwater - This is the gigantic open-world city in the game. The city is extremely varied and well-put-together, especially for the time it came out. Seriously, you could spend hours-upon-hours exploring and still find new things
+Fantastic soundtrack
+Enjoyably unique activities
+Interesting boss fights
+The main character models, buildings, and water still look quite good
+Destructible environments add an extra layer of fun when going on rampages
Cons:
-Admittedly visually outdated in certain areas
-Both DLC stories on console are not available on PC if you were looking for them (But they are not great anyway)
-Frame-rate is still not perfect even with GOTR
-Multiplayer is offline but can work with 3rd party servers to my understanding
Overall:
Saints Row 2 is a fantastic open-world game, however be prepared to tinker with it in order for it to run adequately on your PC. Do recommend.

A fun, chaotic TF2-esque game. Everyone's invisible, and you have to look at the other player's screens to know where to shoot. Requires more brainpower and focus than generic first person shooters like CoD. You can sign up and play the beta for free starting August 4th
: Beta has ended.

An enjoyable game for those who think CoD matches are too slow.
Screencheat requires you to be on the move constantly whereas games like CoD, BF, and the likes all have their campers.  In this game, other players can see exactly where you are(at least from your/their point of view) so camping is useless since they can see what you are seeing and kill you from behind. Because of that, you have to be moving non-stop while also glancing at the other three screens to see where the opponents are. It's a lot harder than it sounds because glancing at the other screens is a near requirement to survive however the intensity of the game makes it hard for one to glance away from your little quadrant on the screen. The maps are quite small so there is little to no moments for reprieve during a match lest you be blown away by a well aimed grenade. Certain map functions like air vents increase your mobility and allows you to do sneak attacks but be prepared to be shot out of the air due to the predictability of the air vents.
There are only two gamemodes at this time: A free for all Deathmatch and a King of the Hill match. A King of the Hill match is basically camping(if you can even call it that) at a specific location to gather points while waiting for the inevitable death to claim you in the form of a blunderbuss or a grenade. Deathmatch currently only supporst to 10 points per game so a player has to get to 10 kills max.
Currently, there are two maps available. The first is a Museum map with a huge fossil in the middle. There is a ramp that leads to the top, an elevator that leads you to the top floor, and an air vent that drags you to the floor below it. It's quite easy to score points on this map (IMO) because the ramp makes enemy movements extremely predictable. The second map is a garden with air vents on the bottom of the floor that can boost you to around the middle of the map or even farther. The map is slightly symmetrical in it's shape and is a lot harder to get kills on(for me at least). One positive note about this map is that in a 4 player server or 2 player server, the map's color changes so you can easily locate the enemy. In a two player server, one half of the map is blue while the other is red. In a 4 player server, the map is split into quadrants with a different color in each. Despite this, I still failed at this map compared to the Museum :p
A small thing to note is the kill feed which is EXTREMELY satisfying. More often than not, it gives a small line at the top of the screen that says "_____ creamed ____" or something that basically says that you got owned. A few times, the entire screen would be filled with the text in CAPS basically rubbing it into your face that you were killed or that you killed someone. It's hilarious but causes you to screw up because you can't see where you're going and you cam be killed by another player in the few short seconds the message stays on the screen. But it is satisfying XD

It's an interesting take on a controller, and does what it's supposed to do; emulate a mouse and keyboard for games that don't have controller support.
The haptic feedback on the touchpads works quite well, allowing you to know the positioning of of your thumbs when playing.
That being said, I did experience thumb fatigue after extensive playing, and for games that support a traditional controller I was far more adept with a Xbone controller than the Steam controller.  For traditional mouse and keyboard games (RTS, diablo-like), the SC is no where near as good (but still functional).
Other games such as FF7 and FF8 didn't really make a difference due to their nature.
This makes the SC sit in a somewhat awkward position between a traditional controller and a mouse/keyboard setup, becoming somewhat a jack of all trades and a master of none.  The product does work, and the customisations are very thorough, but you will have to "learn" a whole new set of controls depending on the game you're playing or if you choose to use a community made configuration.
I want to like this product, I really do, but I don't feel it's quite there yet. Perhaps the next revision will be something to look forward to.

I love Dragon Quest Monsters so I wanted to like this game. Monster trait interactions can lead to complex, Magic the Gathering-like combos but none of the other pieces fit together.
The grind is extremely heavy and is exacerbated by the large number of resources that require grinding (among them experience, four basic resources, and favor with twelve different gods). Basic quality-of-life features such as non-sluggish map movement speed is gated behind ~10 hours of gameplay, and even then the speedup only applies in certain areas.
Experimental breeding is discouraged as it costs power balance (the precious resource that makes grinding faster) and introduces wild monsters which may have annoying traits. In addition, breeding matters far less than in the DQM games as monster traits and spells (the important bits) aren't inherited and the stat increases aren't important.
Overall the largest problem is that it substitutes RNG for game design. Apart from a few set bosses all team compositions, enemy artifacts, and drops are randomly generated. Whether you get access to resurrection and healing spells is entirely up to the RNG.
The effect interactions are interesting and might make a good card game but the core gameplay loop is fundamentally unpleasant to interact with and for every 10 minutes of figuring out clever combos you can expect 10 hours of using it to one shot endless waves of randomly generated trash enemies.

It's alright. A fair and honestly developed indie game. I normally concentrate on basic to-and-fro combat stats in RPGs, but this game proves combat based entirely on obscure/minor special abilities interacting with each other can work.
I didn't find it all that much fun though personally - and I can't put my finger on what I'd change. There is much here that is underdeveloped or even lazy - the ancient JRPG game engine makes looting, breeding and creature management tedious. The casual, mini-roguelike dungeons are a good idea - but it's too basic IMO. In a true roguelike, like Moria or Angband, the randomly generated corridors are a) tactically important and affect how you tackle the enemies, and b) much more random. In Siralim 2 you get a sequence of JRPG fights one after the other - the layout of the corridors doesn't matter, there is no sneaking, cover, or terrain bonuses - the procedural corridors are a time sink. Making the dungeons small though was a good move, as it means you can play this in 10-minute bursts.
The game world, music and atmosphere is completely lacking. 15 zones, each with a few lines of dialogue and a small selection of map tiles - they could have simplified them right down. The 5 creature classes are almost identical to Magic the Gathering (Life=White, Chaos=Red, Death=Black, Nature=Green, Sorcery=Blue), a bit lazy perhaps, and the game might be better without them.
Other games have achieved more with the ancient JRPG format: through good graphic design and engaging writing. These things won't be of core interest to Siralim's players, but the lack of them, for me, highlighted problems with the "bare bones" mechanics of the combat. Two sets of six creatures face off - they have (probably) two special abilities each plus an assortment of spell gems that mostly auto-trigger. Fights can be really interesting when these abilities happen to connect up into long chains of effects all triggering each other. But the game doesn't actually show what hidden abilities the enemies have (which I suspected is due to the limitations of the engine more than a design choice) - so although the abilities are ingenious, and there are loads of them, and they are really well balanced, the actual experience of sitting playing this is like an early Final Fantasy game. Hold down the attack button, wake up if health is low or enemies' abilities seem to be linking up.
The developer is active. They have managed to balance hundreds of special abilities better than many professional games, so it deserves a recommendation. It might appeal to fans of Dominions IV. Hopefully they can find a way to make it multiplayer - the drawbacks wouldn't matter then, and it would make use of the truly colossal range of possible builds.

I've been playing Ticket to Ride quite a bit lately. Essentially its a bit like a fast version of Monopoly, with trains, except that instead of building hotels and collecting rents you're using train carriages to claim routes between cities. You start out with a choice of cards depicting routes to aim for. On each turn you can draw two coloured carriages, one loco (which you may use in place of a carriage of any colour), or another route to complete. You cannot discard any route cards - if you don't manage to claim them all, unfinished ones count against you. To claim a route between two cities all the carriages you place must be the same colour as each other, and often need to match a particular colour (or one of two alternatives) shown on the route itself.
There can be many ways to complete a long-distance route - but other players may be looking to claim segments you require. You can really spoil someone's day by blocking them at an opportune moment.
Single player mode vs the game's AI is not great (though it does allow you to learn the game at your own pace), but playing online against one or more human competitors can get quite tense and challenging. The game is simple to learn, quick to play, but is well constructed and has an interesting balance of conflicting strategies. Its absorbing entertainment and good value considering that the boxed game costs £40.
The DLC isn't essential. The base USA game is the most balanced of the boards available, but the alternatives do provide some variety - if you can find other people to play against, which isn't always easy on the non-US boards. If there's a bundled offer to pick up all the DLC's for cheap I'd recommend you go for it, otherwise check out just the main game first.

The Director's Cut edition fixes the few minor issues that were in the regular edition. There's now a stealthy approach to every boss battle, the yellow filter can be removed, and the DLC is included seamlessly within the story.
Now, onto the gameplay.
In this game, you can play however you want. You can be a stealth pro who uses tranquilizers, invisibility and other methods to remain undetected. But you can also be an edgy augmented guy who uses augmentations and big guns to kill everyone. That's fun too. Or you can be a mix of both. For example, you can kill people while remaining completely undetected, using silenced pistols and silenced sniper rifles.
A bunch of cool features: You can choose your augmentations. You can hack terminals to disable cameras and use enemy turrets and robots to your advantage. You can read NPC e-mails on every computer in the game (which makes the world even more believable). You can persuade NPCs through dialogue options.
All of this stuff is put together in a way that always feels wonderfully fluid and intuitive. You play the game the way you want, at your own pace, and no one will tell you how you should be playing. The flow is great.
The music isn't particularly "catchy", but it really adds a lot to the game's atmosphere, as it fits the vibe of the universe at all times.
The story is incredibly thought-provoking and touches many actual, real subjects, like human evolution, the media, freedom, power, society, etc. It really makes you think about what it means to be human, and makes you wonder how far technology can go before we lose our identity. Where do we draw the line between human and machine? It puts you in a position where you feel like your opinion actually matters. It's always interesting and it really pulls you in. Not to mention, the voice acting is excellent and every important character is memorable.
I'd give this game a very solid 9 out of 10.

Far more enjoyable than one might imagine and clearly the work of a caring designer.  Though the marriage of zombie genre and tower defense might sound ridiculous (and it most definitely is) Last Hope is a surprisingly well done and fleshed out tower defense game with a theme that works better than you might initially suspect.
RPG elements are added to the standard tower defense structure by including heroes that are fully controllable on the map.  These heroes level in traditional ways, vary in gameplay, and have their own tech trees complete with upgrades.  Last Hope may not be the first game to do this sort of thing, but this is clearly an example of the sum of its parts being better than the individual components.  That's important, because the plot is (intentionally?) silly and not the least bit compelling.
There's about 20 hours worth of game time in earning all of the steam achievements, but if you're so inclined you can spend a great deal more time in earning in-game achievements and unlockables.  At a very modest price tag, this is a complete and enjoyable package that rises well above the concept of a "Zombie Tower Defense" game.

Spaceforce: Rogue Universe HD is exactly what it seems to be, a HD re-hash of a 2007 twitch space shooter for Windows, it is also far more. As ever with games of this ilk it derives a lot of its gameplay from a rather popular and famous space combat and trading game, namely, Elite. This, in my opinion, is where the game may fall down to those who do not give it enough of a chance. Back in 2007 there was no new Elite game, there were Elite ‘clones’ dropping like flies and have been and no doubt will continue to be for many years to come. Spaceforce appears at first to be yet another one of those clones destined to drop by the wayside of its bigger and arguably better brother, Elite Dangerous. With that said there is something to offer here for those with and without the new Elite experience.
Let me deal with the HD in the title before I go any further. This is a pretty game in the sense that it is a eight year old game with sharper resolutions. It runs smoothly on older systems and as the title implies it will happily run at 1080p with everything turned on. Now, no, it does not look as good as Elite Dangerous, nor should we ever expect it too but for those interested in the game this will matter less than you think.
Spaceforce: Rogue Universe HD is about missions, in this it has more in common with another staple classic of the genre, Wing Commander. You choose a mission, you head to the jumpgate and jump through, complete the mission and head back or dock and repeat to fade. Elite was always more about exploration and trade and whilst you can do those things in Spaceforce it feels as if you are not really meant to.
As it stands, Spaceforce: Rogue Universe HD is a very competent, combat heavy, mission based RPG that, if you are a fan of this genre, you would be silly to ignore. It is priced perfectly, as a game that whilst never intended to be a triple A title or compete with its more complete brethren will give you many hours, weeks and months of fun. Yes, it can be repetitive but then again the same can be said of Elite Dangerous and some of us enjoy that repetition because it is safe, because we can master it and then beat it.

I've heard about this game some time ago, but apparently the publisher screwed the dev over, or something like that, so the dev re-released the game on their own in May 2015. So, what it is about? In short, it's an old-school homage to Elite-style of titles, where you can play in two game modes: Story or Free. In Story mode you have to follow the main quests, but honestly I didn't play much of that. I sticked with the Free mode, because in this mode you can go wherever you want, trade, fight, explore and generally do whatever you want. But, it has a steep learning curve, so you'll have to learn the basics. The lack of the official tutorial might be a minus for some folks, but there is a beginner's guide available.
I'll try to break it down with "pluses" and "minuses":
+ Open-ended Elite-like space sim
+ Two game modes (Story Mode and Free Mode)
+ Crapload of sidequests
+ Good gameplay mechanics
+ Solid graphics
+ Awesome music
+ If you like Elite, you'll dig this
- Lack of tutorial (there is a beginner's guide available)
- Just a partial gamepad support, but you can configure the buttons
I liked it and I'm still playing it.

This review is mainly based on the terrible port that Square Enix has released and has not resolved for over half a year now, not the game itself.
Sadly what I have heard is an amazing game still contains a broken resolution and shoddy framerates after being on Steam for a little over eight months. It seems the game has gotten away with this with a very large amount of people still praising the game despite these issues, showing immense love for the game that the publishers/developers won't return to its own fans by not fixing these issues.
What this review boils down to is me saying this game shouldn't be supported with the lack of work put in to fix issues that have been present since its launch, despite how good the game might be.

Nier is a game (in)famous for it's multiple endings/playthroughs and Automata seems to follow this trend by having many "multiple endings". The way it felt to me though was just like having a longer game than I originally thought it would be and not like slogging through multiple playthroughs with some minor changes.  What you also should appreciate is that if this were a game made by another dev/studio I could totally see the other endings/playthroughs as being dlc content but instead they are treated as an integral part of the game and dlc is not needed at all to appreciate the length and breadth of NieR:Automata's story. This is simply a great game.

It's really hard to recommend this game at least until they fix the PC port.
One of the most fundamental actions in the game, dodging, is bound to a double tap of a direction key and you're not able to rebind it. This makes timing a dodge extremely difficult for almost no reason.
Whenever a tooltip pops up telling you to press a default key, it's an unintuitve key on the keyboard. For example, "\", the key above ENTER, is bound to 'heavy attack' by default. You're told to press it for a simple attack. Only through trial and error do you realize it's also bound to right mouse button.
The mouse aiming is invisible at times and your character will end up getting confused mid-dash/dodge and turn around if they go past the point of your mouse.
Textures of many things that matter such as characters and faces are amazing. The textures on the floor and walls are incredibly poor. This seems to be a PC-only problem.
The game has a constant problem resizing itself and insisting on playing in Windowed mode.
Also, the Steam trading cards give away some spoilers like the names and existence of major characters.
It's just an overall poor PC port. Game seems enjoyable otherwise, but you're going to have to take some effort modding the game or running gamepad emulation if you want to play normally. Until the developer fixes these issues, it's hard to recommend the game to anybody.

This one is a lot of fun, especially with a group. There are many different game modes that get cycled out but the main objectives are either to hold the point or a combination of holding a point then delivering a payload. Occasionally AI modes come into the mix that are very difficult, providing a new challenge to rage about. There is also ranked, for more competitive play.
There are tons of different champions, and somehow they just keep adding more. There are four classes - Frontline (Tank), Damage (DD), Flank (Assassin), and Support (Healer/Bard). Each class has several different choices to provide different play styles a chance to shine. To further the difference between players there is card system that allows you to customize stats and abilties of the champions you like to play. These are upgradeable and there are many to choose from for each champion.
If you are a fan of cosmetics this game has you covered. There are multiple skins for every champion, and new ones coming out all the time. They run sales on these, and some are common skins that can be obtained from chests. Chests are unlocked as you play, purchased with in game gold, or purchased with real money. Some chests can not be bought with gold, likewise some chests can not currently be bought with cash.
The graphics feel like a slightly improved team fort 2 so performance of the game is great. The maps are detailed yet simple, and the selection is growing just as often as the rest of the game. Sure there are a few bugs, as the game is constantly adding stuff, but they fix most things pretty quickly and they work hard on the game putting content and bug patches out frequently.

I like this controller a lot. In part because I also have a steam link. There are some pros and cons, but overall I like this as much at least as my xbone controller. The ergonomics are a bit weird. It feel really comfy when you first hold it, then when you try to press buttons I find myself reaching a bit. I have smaller hands I suppose, but still to get to the x button I have to move my whole hand. The touch pads are nice, but take a little tweaking and getting used to, not anything serious, just find the right setup for each game and its fine. I personally like the 1:1 mouse mode because thats what im used to. There is a weird mode where it acts like a virtual joystick and it constatly moves when you go in a direction. I did not like that. Even with the haptic feedback I kept going off of the pad. Im sorry valve it isnt like a real thumbstick. The d-pad is also a bit fiddly. I like the set up for fighting games actually. Its not going to give you that fight pad or arcade stick control, but it actually does detect diagonals with the right mode. So like in street fighter just swoop a little 1/4 circle and pound a punch key (not "x") and you got a nice fireball. It actually responds a lot better with fighting than i expected. With menues or things like that where you need a d pad that needs 1 press at a time, this will take some getting used to. Like delibertly pres it, press, quick lift, press. Otherwise it will think you are holding it down. Back buttons, frakking useless. Maybe if I had any game with a lot of commands I didnt want to play with a keyboard they would matter. Most of the time I hit them by accident and they are default bound to either y or x so I randomly like open a menu or relod. I dont like them, they are right on the grip and sometimes I unintentionally grip my controller in tense situations and press these buttons. You can completly disable them though by assigning a funcion that does nothing, like num pad 5 or whatever. Meh to each his own, some people may have more self control and really like them.
Overall this is a cool controller. A little big for my hands, but nothing I cant deal with. I like the pads, which to be honest, is the main feature here. I wouldnt use it for FPS because it is a looooong way off from a mouse. As far as response goes its ok, but when id the last time you used a mouse with only your thumb? Feels like using a laptop to play CS with no mouse. You can do it, but why bother? Nice thing is streaming my desktop with the link. Netflix, music, movies all on my bigger, in front of the couch tv. If I had to give a rating I would say 7/10

This is the best controller on the market, and it will only get better as Valve adds more feature through firmware updates.
Honestly I don't have enough praise for the steam controller.
As of the pros it is comprehensively the best controller you will ever buy.   It has a solid design, feels good in your hand, has nice haptics that aren't too strong, and provide stronger feel on the controls than on the grips (something that is lacking in other controllers.)
The customization options are particularly great.  You can adjust the dead zomes, set the trigger buttons mode-switch on many of the controls, as well as remap everything.  Best yet, Valve plans to continue to add features.
After properly customizing the controls to your liking, the controller has really upped my game on several games.  Being able to change the dead zones and response curve of the analog controls really hightens your ability to play certain games with a controller.  It also makes games that you would traditionally only be able to play reasonably with a keyboard and mouse become playable with a gamepad.
I am still exploring the wealth of features in the setup software, and I've found that for those, such as myself, who love tweaking things this controller is the ultimate toy.
The only real con is that you have to launch games through steam to take full advantage of the controller.  However, that really isn't the biggest deal.  All and all it is by magnatudes better than any controller I've ever used.
