Wow!  I'm majorly impressed by Siralim 2!
I used to play Dragon Warrior Monsters when I was young and have been searching for a game like it in recent years.  This game ticks all of the boxes for me.
-Monster Breeding (very similar to DWM, you get a more powerful monster based on the parents type and stats)
-Fun Dungeons (useful loot everywhere and objectives for each one, the diety system is brilliant and engaging)
-Buffs and Debuffs Matter (contrary to some reviews, this is NOT a press E to win game, it takes careful thought and planning with monsters inherent abilities and the many spells and weapon effects to achieve that kind of gameplay)
-Resource System (meaningful loot and gather system allows you to improve every aspect of your gameplay without feeling grindy)
-Fantastic Soundtrack (usually i play games with a YouTube video or music playlist but not with this title)
-Solid Progression (some of the fights at first seem unfair but when you think about what the game has given you, you can find some fun and diverse ways to overcome those obstacles.  I think their purpose is to push your own limits in the game and not just mash E.  Critical thinking is big here)
-Excellent Performance (no framerate issues, bugs, glitches that I've seen so far)
-Excellent Developer (no bs here, they made a great game and are selling just that, no microtransactions, great customer support, great website FAQ, and interaction all around)
TLDR:
Fantastic game that brings all of the Dragon Quest Monsters nostalgia and more!  The developer deserves a ton of credit for making an honest good game that's too overlooked in a sea of steam microtransactions, asset flips, and hot garbage.
Siralim 2 has restored my faith in modern game developers!  I look forward to many more hours of Siralim 2!
Edit:
There is a minor microtransaction service in the game, but from what I can tell it is purely cosmetic.
I did have a bug that deleted some of my spell gems, one of which was key to my strategy (highest speed creature lost his all enemy curse gem D: it's okay though, I found new strategies to continue on)

Outlandish premises are nothing too new in video games, and even these days you can often find one that makes you tilt your head a bit. But being weird doesn't necessarily mean your game is going to be good. Last Hope's was enough to draw me in, but it didn't take long for me to see the negatives beyond it.
The plot's not described particularly well, but what I gathered was that it's the post-apocalypse, and zombies roam the Earth. An inexplicable, kinda-close-to-being-racist band of Native Americans have survived using their fortified position and jury-rigged weapons. I don't know why the developer decided on them as a focus, or why they'd all revert back to the colonial era in appearance, but it's odd nonetheless. In practice the setting means you have a ton of desert levels to deal with, some neat setpieces, and a whole set of levels where you fight Mad Max style raiders.
Going back to my review of Alien Robot Monsters, I mentioned the game was inspired by Kingdom Rush, but still did its own thing. Last Hope seems like it also is, but just doesn't manage to be as interesting as either of those games. You have blocker towers, poison, anti-air, but not really anything unique. Also, while it might be a personal thing, I also find the game kinda ugly; it looked decent from the store page, but in motion it's not very appealing, and the models seem lower quality than just using sprites. It doesn't help that you spend most of your time in the desert, so there's a lot of brown to look at, but not much else.
The game tries to offer its own spin on things by giving every tower a tech tree you pay to upgrade, but pretty much all the boosts are parts of stuff you'd get normally in a Tower Defense by just upgrading them in levels, and in fact you need to unlock that function for each tower. This would fall into making it a grind, but almost none of what I ran into in my six hours was really challenging. Levels were cheesed easily enough by liberal use of the poison tower, and the first hero unit you get has extreme range and damage, enough to one-shot a lot of enemies. This started being the case after an update, so they may have bugged her. It seems like you can unlock the ability to control up to four heroes later on, but to get most of them you need to pay a large amount of money, and they're not described very well.
Last Hope seems like it has a large amount of content going by the map, and several nodes on it which hide multiple levels, but I can't really work up much desire to play further. It's not really good or bad, just pretty meh. I can't complain too much since I bought it for the early access price of three dollars, and I got it for helping someone out with a trade, but I certainly wouldn't recommend it at ten.

There is something very visceral and personal about Last Hope - Tower Defense.  You aren't facing thousands of monsters... every zombie counts.  Every zombie past the red line means a settler's life lost.
This game breathes freshness into the stale land of tower defense with a unique western setting & storyline combined with fun graphics & entertaining gameplay.
Pros
+ Fun graphics and very different kind of setting -- I like the native American theme with the desert locations.
+ The music is very cool, kind of a rock-western theme that's very atmospheric.
+ Plenty of hotkeys for turrets & your heroes.
+ Indicators let you know which towers can be upgraded, (when you have enough currency & the levels unlocked).
+ Research system allows you to prioritize different attributes of your towers, granting permanent bonuses.
+ Towers have some very cool & funky special upgrades like: an extra flame thrower that can be mounted on the arrow turret, and a golem that spawns from the slowing tower!  (Nice variety of specialized towers, too!)
+ Western/zombie storyline... with a twist! -- very different from typical TD games.
+ Several heroes to choose from, each with their own weapon types & abilities.
+ Several optional side quest lines that have rewards of new heroes, etc., which pose further challenges.
+ Forgiving star system -- 1 or 2 zombies let through don't necessarily negate a 3-star win.
+ Playing maps on different difficulty/modes changes the entrances/goals of each map adding variety and replayability.
+ End-game, Nightmare Mode, definitely adds challenge!
Neutral
~ For each level, pathing has branches, and never know which route mobs will take.  In some cases, this requires a restart of the level, but in general, it just keeps you thinking on your toes.
~ No upgrade preview in-map for what stats will be improved for each tower when upgrading.
Cons
- Cannot build/queue special abilities when paused.  There is a short break between waves however.
- When a zombie crosses the line, the screen shakes and it's quite jarring.
- After finishing the normal campaign, you'll find yourself with many upgrades to buy and heroes to level.  End-game is kinda grindy working toward those things.  However... it took about 16 hours to get to that point, so I am well satisfied with my experience :-)
There are other things that make this game special -- the use of dust blowing across the screen to indicate fast-forward of time, an urgency to gameplay. The story is very fun indeed, and has a cool ending.  (I won't spoil it for you!)
One thing I found slightly frustrating is the tower slots... for a VERY long time, you are only allowed to use 3 towers.  You own all these cool towers, but can only choose up to 3 per map.  Even then, there are occasional desires for one-of's... like a single sentry to pick off the fast guys.  Eventually you can unlock 6 total tower slots, but by that time, you tend to already have your favorites set in stone.
Overall, I have seriously enjoyed this game.  Very unusual & unique.  I highly recommended it: well worth the cost even at full price!

This game doesn't meet the standard I expect in games, and especially not in tower defense. After playing a game like Kingdom Rush, this game falls short in every aspect (while essentially trying to do the same thing). As a tower defense game it doesn't introduce any new elements and feels rushed: you can't see where to place towers unless you click on a construct button - which is unfortunate when you need to place one quickly. The towers are very similar in appearance and if built next to eachother are even hard to click on when you try to select just one (for example if you want to upgrade or sell it). Many towers in the same area looks like a huge mess, especially when additional upgrade icons appear (which they do once you have enough cash for an upgrade) - the icons are the same size as the towers themselves. Towers seem to be exactly the same: can't tell a difference between a tower that shoots single arrows to target one enemy, and a tower that is good against groups. The latter still shoots a single arrow that targets a single enemy. No impact observed graphically.
As a game in general, this falls short in graphics where animations look ugly and really non-smooth, both in cutscenes and the game itself. There is no resolution option. The story is boring, and naive. Can't stand games that drop a few lines just to provide some sort of context. If you do something, at least try to make something of it, or don't do it at all. The game just feels very quickly put together and unfinished.
I think you should instead play Kingdom Rush if you haven't. This game looks like a very cheap copy of it, put in a different context. I guess if you really like tower defense and have finished most of the games that exist in this genre, Last Hope might be sort of enjoyable if you can look past all of its flaws. But I still would rather play Kingdom Rush one more time.

Spending hours progressing just to have it all taken away from you when you come back is really the biggest negative about this game; it doesnt feel rewarding to put the time in.
Me and my friend both bought copies of this game. On our first attempt we built a small house with wooden walls and little defenses. We explored the world, collected food, weapons, clothing, etc. We would occasionally get into skirmishes with other players, since 90% of the players are hostile and shoot on sight (another downside in my opinion). We had several crates full of loot and then decided to log off and get on the next day.
When we got back on all that was left was the foundation to our base and a water collector. This obviously made us feel like we had wasted several hours of time but we werent quite discouraged yet. On our second attempt we decided to make a base that wouldn't get destroyed. We decided to make our base out of three houses; on inside of the other, each bigger than the next. like nesting dolls or something. Then on the outside we built a set a of walls that was much taller than the base for extra protection. Then we built tons of traps around the perimeter. Finally we decided to upgrade the entire base to metal. This took us FOREVER. We easily put 15 to 20 hours into this game on one run. We believed it would be worth it though; we thought it would save our progress and all of the items we collected.
Once we complete the base we got off, but decided to not stay off for long just in case. We took a four hour break and then got back on to see if the base had been tampered with. We we're completely cleared out. We had well over 30 chests full of gear. All of it was gone. We ended up finding a sign inside of our base from some of the admins in the server. They destoryed all of our doors with c4 and took our gear. Well over 15 hours of progress; gone. Of course we decided this game was a waste of time and uninstalled.
We decided to wait until the game was updated to see if they found a way to fix this problem; in short, they havent.
Overall this isnt a terrible game, its fun if you dont go into this game expecting to have a world that will hold your progress. The base building is a waste of time and is arguably a pointless game mechanic. It was most likley added to make the game feel more like "Rust." However a lot of the game is fun; the exploration, the gunplay, most importantly the adventure. As the title might be implying, its much nicer to play this game as a "nomad" just wandering from town to town and ignoring the base building. Since its free to play I at least recommend giving it a try, dont expect a masterpiece though.

Do you ever dream about slaughtering zombies while wearing a banana hammock? If you answered yes, you will love Dead Rising 3.
Warning: Requires a decent PC to play. (My wife's $600 pc runs it fine, but mine couldn't run dead rising 2 and also can't run 3)

Ok, first of all I'm going to talk about the game's performance on my pc. My specs are: Windows 7 professional 64-bit, Intel core I5-3470 3.20GHz quad core, 8 gigs of ram, Nvidia Geforce Gtx 560 ti 2GB Phantom, and a 700 watt huntkey power supply. I read the game's system requirements and saw the insane graphics card requirements. I saw people say they can run it with that card on medium-low settings, so I bought the game. It downloaded, and I launched it. Usually the first thing I do when I install a new game is crank up the graphics as high as they can go and test the performance. I did the same with deadrising 3, and I was very surprised. It ran flawlessly on the maximum graphics settings with my gtx 560 ti 2gb. The pc complained about low memory a few times, so I restarted my pc, and now it's fine. No more low memory complaints from my pc while playing. I can play the game perfectly fine. I made a video of it to show off the awesome performance. Keep in mind the game is locked at 30 fps, that's why my fps didn't go any higher than 32fps. The game runs very smooth and great. Now for the actual review: The game is just like deadrising 2, but with a much bigger map, more crazy weapons and vehicles and psychopaths, more modes to choose from, more stuff to upgrade when leveling up (this time you can pick what you want to level up, it's not like the older ones where the game picked your upgrades for you) They removed gambling and money from the game though, because they also removed pawn shops. You can't buy stuff anymore, but you can make yourself an awesome combo weapon or vehicle easily. Oh yeah, there's no work benches where you combine weapons anymore, instead you can do it anywhere, anytime, as long as you have the blueprint for the weapon or vehicle, and you have the right stuff in your inventory to make something. Oh yeah, you can't make weapons without the blueprints anymore, but it's not so hard anymore to find blueprints. There are about 100 blueprints scattered throughout the game's map. There's also collectibles, like limited edition Frank West statues, annoying speakers to destroy, dead people that died in sad ways to inspect, blueprints for weapons and vehicles to find, survivors to help, and more. There's plenty to do in the game, and there's never a dull moment where you wonder: Hmmm, what do I do now?, because you always have something to do. On top of all that, there's also side-missions. Side-missions randomly pops up, you don't have to find them or anything. When there's a new side mission available, you in-game phone will ring, and you press Z to answer it. Once you answer it, someone on the phone will tell you what you need to do. Of course, you don't have to do the side-missions, but they are fun. They are also timed though, and if you fail to do a side-mission in time, it will fail, and you won't be able to try it again, but don't worry, there are different modes of play to choose from, ranging from completionist, speed run, casual, hardcore, or nightmare mode. I am playing it on completionist. I think completionist gives you the most time. I'm not sure though. On completionist, they give you 7 game days to escape the city. In the older deadrising games it was just 3 days. Oh yeah, there's a lot more combo weapons than in any older deadrising game, and I mean A LOT more. Probably like 100 or so. There are also combo vehicles. You can combine vehicles by parking one vehicle next to another one and holding F while you are standing next to the cars and then left click twice. You can do it anywhere, anytime. Of course there's also co-op, which is fun as always. I have to say the co-op is a lot smoother and less laggy than any previous deadrising game so far. When someone joined my game, I didn't even notice any lag at all. It was super smooth and awesome. I will post the link to my video here when it is uploaded. And now for the final verdict................ 8 out of 10! Summary: Tons of stuff to do, very detailed map and larger than all previous games, fun co-op, less lag, runs very smooth, great graphics, lot's of vehicles and weapons, epic boss fights, and this time there's more than one safehouse! You can unlock safehouses! Some stuff they could improve upon: I would like a sandbox mode with no time limit, like in deadrising 2 off the record, I would like them to fix the slow loading textures, and unlock the framerate. (I known you can do it manually, but I don't want to do it) That pretty much sums up the game. Oh yeah, one more good thing: This time there or no loading screens if you go in certain areas of the map. The whole map is seamless, and you can explore the whole map without a loading screen. Ok, I know this review is long, but I wanted to make a thorough review.

This thing is weird, but in the best way possible.
It allows you to play just about any game provided you have the time and patience. It probably won't let you play competitively, but for just about any single player game, it's the only way I play. It's comfortable to use and it lets me lean back and play.
This thing can emulate an xbox 360 gamepad, keyboard, and a mouse--as well as any combination between them. The first sign that a game will work well with a Steam Controller is usually if it can use a mouse and a gamepad at the same time. One of the few possible issues might be the UI and how it handles that, but in my experience, it's usually negligible or not a problem at all. As for shooters in particular, the track pad has an interesting place. It lets you move the camera really fast, and then you might run into the issue of micro adjustments for aiming. My solution is using the motion controls to turn on when you are holding your aim button and that easily allows me to make those small adjustments while still being able to turn quickly when I need to.
The Steam Controller is insanely customizeable, but has a bit of a curve to it. There's a mountain of options. Different sensitivities, deadzones, toggles, mode shifts, thresholds, whatever. There's a lot. Once you make your first really customized scheme, it feels awesome. Control schemes seem like a very personal thing, which is awesome! No two people play exactly the same, so it's great that there's a controller that can be customized so much.
Seriously recommend to anyone willing to give it a try. The only game genre I can't recommend this for is fighting games, and even then, maybe someone has a control scheme for that.

Basically Fallout with the "Bigger = Better" mindset applied to it. Whether it indeed is better is up for debate, but in my case I'm going to have to fully agree with the side that says it is, because in terms of content this game blows Fallout 1 out of the water.
Although lacking an equally intriguing antagonist, Fallout 2 further builds on the greatness of Fallout 1 and increases the world map at least 3 times, adds many new weapons and perks, adds a fully functional companion management system and more. With a bunch of interesting quests, NPCs/companions and locations this game will keep you going for at least 40 hours the first time through. The first time I completed this game and watched the final cutscene I was left in absolute awe, reminiscing about my adventure-filled journey. What an absolute gem of an RPG that anyone hungry for one should get their hands on.
If you can't get into the "dated" gameplay (read, "if you are severely lacking taste") then I can only feel bad for what you're missing out on.
On a side note, play it with the Restoration Project, it's seriously worth it.

An above average entry in the genre of RPGs where you make numbers go up. Procedurally generated dungeons where you unlock stuff and go deeper.
Although Siralim technically does have a bare bones functional story - in reality it doesn't delude itself into thinking that its a game about progression. Now, there's several different layers of progression - actually learning the mechanics of the game, getting a good feel for creature traits that combo well with eachother, unlocking more creatures, leveling up your existing creatures, getting new artifacts for your creatures which in turn can have a creature trait on them, probably several other things that aren't even coming to mind right now.
Combat is what you make of it. It can get a bit grindy and tedious over the long run, and highly tactical decision making has its place with certain party compositions and against some enemies. But probably, you're going to want to find a party composition where you can safely hold down the attack button and just have all of your creatures cycle through for all non-boss battles - yeah, it sounds pretty lame because it is.
If you can tolerate the amount of grind/tedium that is endemic to the genre, I think there is plenty of complexity that is worth exploring in Siralim 2. If you can't, well, what are you even doing looking around in this genre?

All creatures can be affected by buffs and debuffs; There are several ways to get (de)buffed. For example, spells, creatures' effects, interactive structures/items, consumables, etc...
-*plethera of items*

Fans of older classic games usually have strong opinions on remakes, sequels and prequels. I didn't see why the original Deus Ex was considered to be so perfect and thought of it as an "OK" game. Not great, but enjoyable. Seeing the praising reviews for the prequel, I got interested, as I'm always looking for good RPGs.
The RPG elements in this game are solid. The character clearly becomes stronger towards the end of the game, there are often several approaches to completing tasks and the dialogue is interesting. Common approaches include stealth, hacking security consoles and computers, gunning everything down, finding hidden paths and talking people into agreeing with you. Or some combination of the above.
There are some elements that are a bit weak, though. My main issue is the mid-3rd of the game, when the story progresses very slowly. The player is sent to different places only to be told several times that "the thing you're looking for is not here, but you could find it over there". The game also has a nasty habit of making the player run back and forth by putting objectives at the opposites ends of the same map. This is especially annoying for a stealth character, as they need to sneak past all those guards again. The Missing Lind DLC is the worst example of this. When looking at the plot, The Missing Link DLC is probably the most enjoyable part of the game.
Other issues include boring side quests, generic items and the lack of choices. The side quests are too generic and since the reward is often just some XP and money, it is difficult to get motivated. There are a few unique weapons, probably less than ten, which is too little and removes the anticipation of finding better gear for your character. The armor can be upgraded, but only through experience, not items.
There are some times when the player can make a choice that affects the rest of the game, but these choices seem very insignificant to the main plot.
The graphics are OK, although a bit boring at times, since the yellow-black combination is used too much. The sounds, voice acting and music are much better and fit the game well. Especially the opening theme is great.
Those who wish to find out what happened before the original Deus Ex should definitely pick this one up, as there are several references to the original game. All the gameplay elements, such as shooting and stealth, are well implemented, making the game enjoyable to play. It's the story (or rather the pace of it) and some of the RPG elements that are lacking.
6/10

Ticket to Ride is an adaptation of a popular board game, with the ability to play against AI, or local or online opponents. The board game has a pretty simple rule set that's easy to learn, and it has some good strategic complexity. I haven't been playing it for all that long, but I've definitely enjoyed what I've played so far.
I found the voice acting obnoxious and turned it off immediately. The music grates after a little while, but you can turn that off too. The game controls pretty well and shows a lot of useful information on screen. The menus are a bit clunky, and this actually makes it a little difficult to get in to the online game lobby.
But really, what matters is the gameplay, and Ticket to Ride has great gameplay. I had fun playing against AI and against humans, and there's tons of replay value. This game will definitely be worth it for board game enthusiasts at full price. I'd still recommend it to anyone that can appreciate a strategic, turn-based game. As for the DLC, it allows you to play on different maps, sometimes with different rules. If you like the base game, the expansions will add quite a bit.

Ok, first of all I'm going to talk about the game's performance on my pc. My specs are: Windows 7 professional 64-bit, Intel core I5-3470 3.20GHz quad core, 8 gigs of ram, Nvidia Geforce Gtx 560 ti 2GB Phantom, and a 700 watt huntkey power supply. I read the game's system requirements and saw the insane graphics card requirements. I saw people say they can run it with that card on medium-low settings, so I bought the game. It downloaded, and I launched it. Usually the first thing I do when I install a new game is crank up the graphics as high as they can go and test the performance. I did the same with deadrising 3, and I was very surprised. It ran flawlessly on the maximum graphics settings with my gtx 560 ti 2gb. The pc complained about low memory a few times, so I restarted my pc, and now it's fine. No more low memory complaints from my pc while playing. I can play the game perfectly fine. I made a video of it to show off the awesome performance. Keep in mind the game is locked at 30 fps, that's why my fps didn't go any higher than 32fps. The game runs very smooth and great. Now for the actual review: The game is just like deadrising 2, but with a much bigger map, more crazy weapons and vehicles and psychopaths, more modes to choose from, more stuff to upgrade when leveling up (this time you can pick what you want to level up, it's not like the older ones where the game picked your upgrades for you) They removed gambling and money from the game though, because they also removed pawn shops. You can't buy stuff anymore, but you can make yourself an awesome combo weapon or vehicle easily. Oh yeah, there's no work benches where you combine weapons anymore, instead you can do it anywhere, anytime, as long as you have the blueprint for the weapon or vehicle, and you have the right stuff in your inventory to make something. Oh yeah, you can't make weapons without the blueprints anymore, but it's not so hard anymore to find blueprints. There are about 100 blueprints scattered throughout the game's map. There's also collectibles, like limited edition Frank West statues, annoying speakers to destroy, dead people that died in sad ways to inspect, blueprints for weapons and vehicles to find, survivors to help, and more. There's plenty to do in the game, and there's never a dull moment where you wonder: Hmmm, what do I do now?, because you always have something to do. On top of all that, there's also side-missions. Side-missions randomly pops up, you don't have to find them or anything. When there's a new side mission available, you in-game phone will ring, and you press Z to answer it. Once you answer it, someone on the phone will tell you what you need to do. Of course, you don't have to do the side-missions, but they are fun. They are also timed though, and if you fail to do a side-mission in time, it will fail, and you won't be able to try it again, but don't worry, there are different modes of play to choose from, ranging from completionist, speed run, casual, hardcore, or nightmare mode. I am playing it on completionist. I think completionist gives you the most time. I'm not sure though. On completionist, they give you 7 game days to escape the city. In the older deadrising games it was just 3 days. Oh yeah, there's a lot more combo weapons than in any older deadrising game, and I mean A LOT more. Probably like 100 or so. There are also combo vehicles. You can combine vehicles by parking one vehicle next to another one and holding F while you are standing next to the cars and then left click twice. You can do it anywhere, anytime. Of course there's also co-op, which is fun as always. I have to say the co-op is a lot smoother and less laggy than any previous deadrising game so far. When someone joined my game, I didn't even notice any lag at all. It was super smooth and awesome. I will post the link to my video here when it is uploaded. And now for the final verdict................ 8 out of 10! Summary: Tons of stuff to do, very detailed map and larger than all previous games, fun co-op, less lag, runs very smooth, great graphics, lot's of vehicles and weapons, epic boss fights, and this time there's more than one safehouse! You can unlock safehouses! Some stuff they could improve upon: I would like a sandbox mode with no time limit, like in deadrising 2 off the record, I would like them to fix the slow loading textures, and unlock the framerate. (I known you can do it manually, but I don't want to do it) That pretty much sums up the game. Oh yeah, one more good thing: This time there or no loading screens if you go in certain areas of the map. The whole map is seamless, and you can explore the whole map without a loading screen. Ok, I know this review is long, but I wanted to make a thorough review.

EDIT: As you see below, I've loved the controller. However, I wanted to add that Big Picture Mode is buggy, laggy and the controller does NOT always work as intended because of it. That is a major software issue with amazing hardware.
I honestly have to admit that I was skeptical. And this controller is nowhere NEAR as easy to use as Steam reports to consumers. That being said, the more you use it, the better it gets. You'll just have to get through the hours required to learn the controller.
Never really got the joystick function on the pads to work, but LOVED the trackpad setting. The physical joystick is great as well. The dual-action trigger system is ridiculous. I can't see the functionalitiy in it, and have never used it.
However, the grip-buttons are a godsend to avoid using X and A (by mapping them to the grip), and only using Y and B.
TLDR: Get used to it, and you'll never use anything else. Some functions are more flash than function.

This controller blows all others out of the water. Now, that in mind, it's still not quite as accurate and extensible as a keyboard and mouse combo, but it makes up for this with an extraordinary level of comfort, elevating it to a place where I find myself switching between my K&M and the Steam Controller just simply according to how far back in the chair I want to lean while I play.
At first, the trackpads threw me off my game. I had played with an Xbox 360 wireless controller as a supplement to my keyboard and mouse for years, and it was difficult getting used to the alternate button layout, and the lack of a right thumbstick. However, as I customized my controller profile (for Fallout 4, in particular), I soon found that I was far superseding the abilities of the Xbox controller in terms of accuracy and comfort. By using  a combination of the "mouse joystick" setting for the right pad, and selectively turning on the internal gyroscope whenever I pull the left trigger, I'm at least 90% as accurate with my aiming as I am with a mouse. With my original stick-based controller, this would've never been possible.
The biggest feature of the controller is its ability to almost effortlessly switch between keyboard & mouse emulation and controller input. If I'm playing a game that supports both input methods, I can pick the one that feels the most natural, and even then further customize and tweak it to get all of the controller's responses to a pinpoint degree of responsiveness. Further expanded features like mode switching (wherein you can hold one button/trigger and make others change their functions) and the "hip-fire" stage settings for the triggers allow you to do all sorts of tricks never possible on a conventional controller.
The only mark against the controller, I think, is the difficulty curve in getting it customized. Lots of players have made their own configurations, but for anybody playing a game that's not yet supported and explored on the controller, you're basically left to figure out your own configuration. For me, that's an exhilirating experience, but I could see it being a burden for others. Also, I wouldn't mind if the haptic feedback could closer emulate the "rumble" feature of existing gamepads; it would be nice if force feedback from the game could trigger the haptics and make your thumbpads/thumbstick vibrate, or something (instead of just on input).
Overall though, the Steam Controller does exactly what it advertises: finds a happy middle ground between console controllers and your beloved keyboard and mouse. And, I won't lie: it performs closer to the latter than the former.

My biggest complain with this controller, after using the official Xbox controllers are the extremely small buttons, which are reminiscent to Nintendo DS sized buttons. hard to get comfortable with when you have adult sized hands/fingers. If you've played majority of your steam games over the years with a Xbox controller, then transitioning to this controller will take some getting use to, which may turn some off completely from the controller. If you've been using mouse and keyboard set up, then adjusting to the touch panel to aim will be another major adjustment.
Having gyro controls and adding it to aiming is pretty nice, haven't played with it much but that also takes getting use to. i tried it on a racing game as staring but couldn't get that sweet spot feel, you would get from Wii type gyro/motion controls. Gyroscope control comes in handy the most for mouse users who enjoy those tight precise head shots. I'll honestly say that in certain game types this type of precision is more precise than even mouse at times. I tried this out by playing a game of  Zombie army Trilogy, where i could rack up a ton of head shots without missing much. competing with other players who use mouse though will have them out perform you and beating you to the punch with head shots.
The added of 2 extra buttons on the controller as panels flaps? is a sweet touch. You can hotkey any button to it and for people who like taking pictures you can hotkey your F12 to it and take pictures on the fly, a major plus. The touch panel dpad is a turnoff to me in a way. I see certain games working for it, but others just don't. This controller just isn't fighting game friendly, even with the touch dpad panel. Its pretty much similar to playing a fighting game on your touch screen phone. Personally i think this panel should be a bit smaller but that's just me.
The community for this controller shines a lot for lazy folks such as myself. If you're not into the whole time consuming mapping, you can just boot up a game and find the community part, which has other players who upload maps for the game you are playing and add it to your controller and play the game map/config straight from your controller.
Biggest downside to the controller... You can't use it outside of steam, you can use it to surf the web, but you can't play none steam games with it. The controller doesn't seem to have Xinput nor direct input, which is a major downside. Hopefully steam/valve will address these issues in the future, if not them then maybe a modder will. Also the fact that the only way to take full control of the controller is by booting and playing it in big picture mode. don't dare try to play the game on desktop through steam.
All and all this controller is pretty much worth the investment, if you want to play your games on the Tv screen on a comfy couch, or in my case a comfy bed.

Then I started Steam in Big Picture Mode, as one should. Firmware update. Yes, please.
For a moment I thought my issues were resolved, but I soon noticed that the left pad was still occasionally producing erratic input, and the tracking was so-so.
That
in the controller settings in Big Picture Mode was
from obvious, but I am happy to report that since pressing it, my Steam Controller has been working flawlessly.
I've mainly been playing Euro Truck Simulator 2 with it so far. Setting up a control scheme that works well for me took the better part of an hour, but I dare say that it was worth every minute. The trackpads help a lot with camera movement. I love the way the controller feels, and would not like to go back to the F710 I was using before, at least for this game.

Probably one fo the best stealth shooters I’ve played in the last decade.
I have way more hours logged on this than Steam indicates, with 2 play-throughs on my old console.
It's important to consider that this is not like the original 'Deus Ex', a story-heavy RPG. This is more a stealth action shooter with RPG elements. Decisions you make will influence how you have to go about things but the entire game doesn't rely on it. You will pretty much get to the same points as you would have done, it just about how you get there.
Game-play is a great mix of stealth and action, with a large range of weapons, both lethal and non-lethal. The game offers many strategies you can follow in order to defeat enemies, you can either go in guns-blazing, which wastes really great stealth mechanics which are some of the best aspects of the game, or you can sneak pass or sneak up on enemies. The latter is much more fun, as the game rewards you for dealing with a situation with discretion (e.g. non-lethal, stealth), where as just shooting everyone up can actually prove quite difficult.
The visuals and soundtrack are beyond amazing, it’s so rare now-a-days to find a game with a truly unique style and atmosphere that flows throughout the entire game.
If there is one area where this game falls slightly short, it’s the mechanics. On the whole, there decent, guard move where they are supposed to move, all fine. But the A.I can act a little dodgy, with enemies not noticing quite obvious movements, but it rarely crops up when playing the game and doesn’t tend to affect the stealth system at all. The gun mechanics are also somewhat clunky, but they are fine after you get used to them.
The story is great, following the life of Adam Jensen, Sarif Head of Security, after an incident at their HQ. Jensen is effectively killed in the attack but is “saved” by his boss, David Sarif, by being pumped full of power augments, some necessary to his survival... some not so much. I’ll leave it there so not to spoil anything, but if you’ve played the original Deus Ex games you’ll notice a number of links.
A word of warning though, the Director's Cut Edition which solved perhaps the only real problem with this title, the boss battles, does up the specs and will require a better system than the original. Don't let that put you off though, you can always just drop the graphics a bit when you load up and you should be fine. There have also been a few reports of slight stuttering on the Director's Cut version (which I think steam forces you to buy now) but many fixes are available online, all of which helped me. [EDIT: These issues appear to have been patched out, but again, many fixes also exist online]
If worse comes to worst and you are worried about if this will run on your specs, you can always pick up a hard copy of the original which is still excellent.

The Deus Ex games are first-person shooter RPGs that let you approach your objectives in a way that suits you: direct violence if you enjoy it, stealth if you don’t, and throwing heavy objects around if you like getting caught, beaten and shot.
Considered by me, as the best game ever made.

It's not so much science fiction as it tries to portray a realistic view on humans constantly adding unnatural enhancements. There is a good deal of moral choices and political issues that plague the world. This is a very complete experience as I felt satisfied with everything.
All in all, this is a fantastic game, and I think this is one of my favorite games in the past few years. Though, this is quickly becoming one of my favorite RPGs of all time as I am in love with everything about Deus Ex that this game had portrayed.

Ticket to Ride is a faithful reproduction of the Alan Moon board game of the same name. Unlike most other modern board games that are being ported to tablets and Steam, Ticket to Ride (video game) was developed in-house by the same company that publishes the board game, Age of Wonder.
Age of Wonder is a well-respected game company; their board games are polished and attractive, with lots of "fiddly bits", as board gamers call the detailed pieces of the game. Their attention to detail that is displayed in their board games carries over to the video game versions, as well. The sound, the controls, the in-game tutorials... everything about this game sets you up for success.
Ticket to Ride is very much a game that is well-suited for a video-game version. There are many things to keep track of - cards and pieces on the board - and it plays much faster with a computer doing all the arranging. A game that takes about 45 minutes to play around a table takes about 10 minutes to play in this online version, and is equally satisfying. The video game version also lends itself better to expansions and DLC versions (alternate rules, really). Expansions that cost $25 for the board game because of production and distribution are just a few bucks here. The video game is a great way to try out the expansions before you buy the board game equivalent.
My one  complaint is that it is a bit complicated setting up an (optional) online account with their servers to track your online matches, but if you do, you can track your gameplay on Steam, iOS, Android, wherever. This is a very nice feature, if you are an active player.
I recommend Ticket to Ride if you have and enjoy the board game, or if you enjoy board games in general. Not recommended if this isn't your thing ... if you aren't a board gamer, you probably won't like this much.

I'd like to give Siralim 2 an endorsement just on the sheer volume of content, but it doesn't hold up the experience if the raw act of gameplay isn't enjoyable. It's one thing to take RPG-grinding and build a game around it, another to abandon the conceit of 'fun' to holding down a button to skip thru animations as much as possible. Combat in this game is rote and frustrating because it feels like you never gain access to cool enough stuff to make it worth paying attention to, and when you do, the act of actually outfitting and using your creatures is so frustrating it's not worth it by the you get into battle.
The UI for the various perks and statistics is also less-than-pleasant to navigate--I feel like the same information could be conveyed more efficienctly and in an easier to read fashion as well.
While the variety and different flavours of monsters seem appealing, there's little-to-no reason to go exploring evolution chains when most of the later abilities are weaker than the monsters you start with. I never felt like the game was properly telling me what to do in order to have the best experience, and by the 500th randomly generated floor packed with generic baddies in which I could watch one of many bars increase in value, it became evident the game wasn't going to get much deeper.
Buy Siralim 2 if you have a compulsive need to gain experience in something that doesn't matter at all, AND you also have no need of a story, lore, or engaging combat. Everything is there but enjoyment.

After playing numerous dungeon crawling and pet monster games, this game does not seem to really introduce anything new, the graphics are bland, and the strategy and gameplay seem to be overly simplistic. It seems this game is a step backwards in this genre, and there's nothing in this game that other games doesn't do a lot better.
After trying to play this game, it made me want to close it and play the latest Pokemon game or Etrian Odyssey series that I feel are a lot higher quality. Maybe this is an unfair comparison as Siralim 2 is an indie game, but I feel that indie developers can still push a good game out as they can afford to be more adventurous and innovative.... which this game does not do.
The only reason I would play this is if I did not have access to these other titles as dungeon crawlers are an under-represented genre on the PC platform.

What a brilliant games this is. While it can get grindy at times (especially if you hit a brick wall), there are still other mechanics that make the grinding worthwhile.
PROS:
-Building your team is fun (multiple combinations)
-Boss battles feel like boss battles with unique mechanics
-Varied tileset and side quests to do in each zone
-Great soundtrack
-Good pace of story progression and learning mechanics.
-Great depth for "min-maxers"
-Library menu means no need to constantly Alt-tab or use Steam overlay for wiki
CONS:
-Finger hurts from spamming E button on keyboard (you can hold it to skip animations instead of pressing)
-Can get chaotic with so many effects going off in battles (especially when attempting to figure out how your team died)
Overall this is a fantastic game that has ton of depth past the story progression. Expect 100+ hours into this if you want to get your team as strong as possible.

I picked this up over Christmas vacation. I was completely "unsold" on the idea of the Steam Controller... until I started seeing videos of the Gyro precision, and coming to the realization that the touch pads could also be buttons... I was like... WOW!  Honestly!
So I ordered this with the feeling that.... well if it isn't any good I'll return it.
Well I have to be utterly honest. I have totally and completely fallen in love with this thing!
I have seen many reviewing talking about how hard it is to get used to. I can attest that yes, this can be true. However I have found that on the game I'm just starting with, I have had no issues at all using the Steam Controller. My biggest struggles have been with games that I have already been using a Gamepad for a long time. Like the Batman Games. I have SO many issues trying to adjust to the new controller setup.
So it seems it's just a matter of re-training the old brain. I do love the touch sensitivity, and the gyro for fine tuning that aim.
I love having the right pad setup as a mouse or trackball, the turning is just so much more fluid and natural feeling in 3D games. I had been playing Fallout 4 on an XBox One when visiting family, but on PC, I love the Stream Controller so much more. Makes those zoomed in headshots SO much easier.
For me this is definitely a keeper. Yeah it'll take some adjustment time, but once I'm over the hurdle, I'm sure I'll be playing better than ever.

The good news is that it's literally an electronic version of the board game. Everything works how it should, for the most part. The tutorial is fairly well done and a decent way to teach people how to play the game if you're sick of explaining it, and the AI is passable but not great if you just want to play casually by yourself. More importantly, it supports cross-platform multiplayer between the PC, Mac, web, and iPad versions. It does NOT support playing with the Pocket (read: iPhone) version, which for some reason is the only one which allows asynchronous play, which is kind of lame. It also has no hotseat mode. By far the specialest thing about it is that it installs its own private  (probably non-updated) JVM, which is kind of counter to one of the main points of using something like Java in the first place. It's otherwise functional, even if there are a few weird design decisions.
Awesome boardgame translated faithfully to the electronic medium.

I entered this game with some knowledge of story progression.  Even with that foreknowledge I did not expect to be affected by the story so deeply.  The music is amazing and directed as perfectly as i can imagine, the controls are tight and responsive, and the world is so rich for being so small.
Two issues could be raised, though these are not bad, I want to bring them up.
First, this is solidly a JRPG in both visual and story components.  I liked it greatly, but I understand that is a style others don't.
Secondly, The controls are tight, but fairly unique to this game.  I easily recommend use of a controller over keyboard and mouse, but don't go between this and Dark Souls in the same day.  Both require a lot knowing you're doing the right thing without looking, which is really weird when your dodge button keeps switching.

Go in blind.
I'm serious. Story wise, you want to experience everything for the first time. You will be happier for it.
Therefore, instead of going through pros and cons (everyone else lists these abundantly already), I will simply add my two cents to the more important issues with the game. You have probably heard about a couple of these if you have researched the game somewhat.
Performance issues and lack of updates: I can't really help much there, since I was one of the lucky few who managed to get through the game almost without a hitch. Only hit a crash on one specific area, and it was easily avoidable when I noticed what caused it. However, there are a ton of guides around to help you if you have problems.
Controller/Keyboard&Mouse viability: I used keyboard and mouse. It was not perfect, but is completely doable, even though you can tell certain sections are designed with a controller in mind. For the shmup sections where you feel that the mouse is hindering you in every way: use melee attacks.
There. If either of these two points were the main reason keeping you from buying this amazing game, I hope that you have reconsidered it. If you have, enjoy you new wild ride.

Nier:Automata is probably the best and most inventive game in 2017. The score is among the best I have heard in recent years and the overall story and atmosphere are so refreshingly diffrent than in most games released this year. Espacially the story is so goddam next level that you probably have to watch some Youtubevideos on it to fully understand all the philosophical aspects the game touches and sometimes deeply explores. Many philosophical Concepts found their way into the game, such as Marx and Engels Communism, Nietzsche's existential horror or some of Freud's concepts about moral and so forth. Overall as a game very likely the best 2017, from a technical point of view, this game is disastrous. The Cutscenes are rendered in 30 fps and 720p, the overall graphics are just ugly and the not existent support from Square Enix does not help this game have an easy time. But if you have some bugs to spend, I would recommand this game, if it runs on your PC with the Community Fix, then you can enjoy a hell of a great game, if it does not, just refund it and buy another game.

First off, yes the game needs a patch badly. While the community mod works great, Sqaure Enix needs to support their best game of the year on PC.
With the said, Nier Automata is my game of the year. The game is action packed, story driven, beautfiul to look at, with characters you care about and a plot that you don't know where it is going and are kept in suspense throughout. All of that is to say nothing about the music, because the music is a 11/10 easily. It swells and fades at the perfect times, it sets the mood for areas and encounters perfectly and is memerable throughout and after the game is complete.
So shame of Square Enix for not supporting this game properly but Kudos go to Platinum Games and Yoko Taro for making one of the best games in recent memory for me.

While I certainly haven't had a bad experience with Siralim 2 (I've played 30+ hours, after all) I'm not quite sure I agree with the array of absolutely glowing reviews that I saw when I originally picked up this game. Dragon Warrior Monsters is one of my favorite video games of all time and hearing about a Steam game in the same vein was exciting to me. For sure, this does have a lot of the addicting qualities that you like to see in an RPG of this sort, like the push to continually gain favor with realm gods and build new artifacts for your creatures, along with breeding your creatures to continually be stronger.
Unfortunately, there are some innate issues with the game as well. The magic system is poorly thought out and seems to actively discourage you from using magic a lot of the time, for instance.
And though it doesn't really affect the overall gameplay -- the game is supposed to focus solely on the actual monster collection, kingdom building and battling, after all -- but the game aesthetically is garbage. It looks like an RPG Maker game in all the worst ways. Your "Kingdom" is all inside one building. It will take you less than one hour of gameplay to notice that there are only a relatively small number of actual monsters in the game, with the bulk of the herd being a torrent of recolors of the main "types". Breeding will occasionally make no sense at all, with a life monster as the pedigree having a sorcery-type baby because the secondary parent was sorcery. Wanted a life monster on your team so you could have heals and buffs on your side? Too bad! Now (if you're far enough into the game) you have to waste your time getting into tons of battles so the egg can hatch and you can try to re-breed it into a life-type again.
There's not much in the way of plot either, which I understand is to let the game speak for itself, but I'd still rather a basic plot than the bare-bones explanation you get at the start of the game.
The game has a lot of good moments. The randomly generated maps with their mini-quests and unique gods are interesting to visit and the battle system is interesting and provides a few extra bits of strategy with defending and provoking. If you can get past some of the growth problems that appear in the mid-game which make it a lot more frustrating to play, you'll probably enjoy this game. At its core, it is a fun, if flawed, monster RPG, which is right in my wheelhouse. And if aesthetics of games or a lack of plot doesn't bother you at all, you'll probably be able to binge the heck out of it with no issues. For all of its flaws, it's still a pretty darn good time in the early and late game stages.

This game is the video game equivalent of a choose your own adventure book from back in the 80s and 90s. Good concept, but there's a few issues with the game.
Overall the game is played by telling you a story and then having you choose a response.  Everything in the game is with this system, you normally get a choice to "go on an adventure" and have to choose from 10 or so adventures.  You go on your adventure, get stats and start over.   If there's 10 adventures, and 8 "days" you will go on 80 percent of them.
After your 8 choices, you'll evolve to the next form and continue.  This is the entire gameplay loop, while there's a few stat checks as you go on, if you play well your stats should be high enough that you seem to always succeed.  I got what I believe is the best ending (or at least the ending I wanted) on the first run.    That first run took less than an hour.
And the second playthrough is where the problems really start.
You see, on the second playthrough you get the option of 10 adventures again.  However it doesn't appear these 10 adventures are different, in fact the two I tried on my second playthrough (before putting the game aside for a while) was exactly the same.  This is disappointing, because it really does feel like a choose your own adventure book.  Now I realize that what I'd be asking for would be a ton of work, but for 10 bucks, you get a 30 minute adventure that an achievement hunter will have to play through 14 times if they don't make a mistake.  That's 7 hours of gameplay.  I just don't think it's 7 great hours of gameplay.
But at the end of the day, I realize this is a choose your own adventure book in a video game form.  If that's what you're looking for, this does fit the bill, I just feel there could have been a much better more randomized game where I felt I was going on new adventures each time.
Ultimately, I do recommend this game because the choose your own adventure is a fun take, the writing is excellent, the ability to explore the monster world is fun, and there's good characters in it.  But it is a choose your own adventure that doesn't have a wealth of gameplay or story, and for gamers, that might be a reasonable deal breaker.   But I did enjoy the time and I do look forward to a second play through trying to do something different.  I just wish I wouldn't have had to try so hard to find a new adventure.
I also would probably wait for a sale as 10 bucks is a bit pricy for this, but at the same time, it's what you want to make it.

A very enjoyable and addictive game, if perhaps a little derivative with not much in the way of innovation that I used to expect from this genre. It's interesting that a lot of the criticism that was originally levelled at the first Deus Ex sequel (Invisible War) could also easily be applied to HR, but wasn't. Like Invisible War, HR is essentially a slightly dumbed-down version of the first game, much bigger and shinier granted, but with most of the original's RPG elements simply reduced rather than improved or streamlined. That's not to say it still isn't head-and-shoulders above most of its peers, but when this game first came out developers were chiefly focused on the console versions rather than trying to make a ground-breaking PC game, like the original. And looking at the new version of Thief that's being made, not much has really changed (although I remain cautiously optimistic).
The inclusion of end of level bosses did feel out of sync with the rest of the game, but they weren't a huge departure the original, which also contained similar bosses. Also, it amazes me that although hours and hours of dialogue must have been recorded for the NPCs, they could only come up with two or three basic animations whilst they delivered their lines! I'd rather have more convincing animation from the characters I encounter in an RPG, that actually matches the speech, rather than another bunch of minor side-quests.
The Director's Cut manages to do a good job of integrating The Missing Link, although why they left in the recap cutscene is beyond me, which makes it very obvious when you jump from the original to the DLC, rather than a more seamless join they could have gone for. Other than that I can't say I noticed any other differences from when I played the original. The main difference is that I've upgraded my GPU two or three times since then ;-) The end of level bosses are supposed to have an increased variety of approaches, but none were apparent to me, it seemed like the usual hit-them-with-all-you've-got-whilst-avoiding-getting-killed, to me (apart from the System Shock 2 ending homage, which at least has a method to it).

I can't for the life of me understand all the negative reviews surrounding this controller.  I'm glad I ignored them.  This is probably the best controller I've ever used.  Yes there is a learning curve reaching downward for the ABXY buttons, but you can retrain yourself in a day.
It does all of the things Valve claims.  KB and Mouse oriented games are now playable from the couch and work extremely well.  The trailer shows City Skylines, but it works quite well for RTS games like Dawn of War, and Shooters that support no controller at all like Quake 4.
The inverted angles of the handles help position your thumbs over the trackpads so you can easily use the their entire surface.  Their indented,  have a smooth drag free feel and are very accurate.  All of the buttons feel solid, and the analog stick has a textured non slip rubber coating and rotates smoothly.  The controller uses alot of haptic feedback in the trackpad that I would describe as adding texture to your mousing.  Swiping your thumb across the trackpad makes an audible vibration I would liken to that of a mouse's scroll wheel.  It's helpful in keeping your thumbs from reaching the far edge of each while also providing some slight feedback to what would otherwise be a smooth trackpad.  Don't expect the same kind of rumbling you get from your Xbox 360/One controller though.  As far as I can tell they don't work in that way at all.
As far as accuracy?  No with the trackpad alone you would get owned by experienced players with a mouse.  However the secret is to combine trackpad input with gyro aiming.  The gyro is crazy accurate in the controller and you would be shocked at how easy it is to nail headshot after headshot.  It may even be better then a mouse and I know how crazy that sounds.  Look to the community contributed profiles that's where alot of the potential of this controller is realized.  Pick out a profile with alot of users and start there.  I found that the popular ones had the best ideas that just needed a few tweaks for my personal taste.
The only CON thus far I really have is that I'm not entirely impressed with the range of the wireless receiver.  I have a HTPC/Steam Box under my TV Stand which sits 3 1/2 feet from my couch and the first day it was constantly prompting me during game play that I didn't have a good connection.  Sometimes it would disconnect and reconnect the controller during a Rocket Leauge match for example, and then when it reconnected it swapped my controller with the other players.  There is a coffee table in between me and the receiver, I figured it might be blocking the signal.  I used the included extension and a micro usb cable I had lying around  to lift the height of the receiever over the height of the coffee table and now it works fine.  Seems as though the controller needs direct line of sight for a solid connection.  That, or there was interference with the wireless reciever from my wireless KB/Trackpad which is plugged in close by.
I was torn between purchasing this controller or an Xbox One controller and I ultimately chose this one because Microsoft requires Windows 10 for their $25 wireless adapter, which is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.  Buy one of these controllers and take the time to learn it.  You won't be dissapointed.  Good work Valve!

Hello everyone. So I wrote a review for this game and its DLC a while back when it first came out, and while I've deleted the first one on the actual game (so I could write this one) you can still find my review on the adventure pass on its store page. Now the reason I'm writing this one is because I looked back at my first review and realized I didn't write a fair enough review. I gushed all over about how this was the perfect game and I barely even touched all the problems it has. So, after playing this game for 11 months and thinking it over, I think I'm ready to write an actual proper review for it.
Ok first things first: Do I recommend that you buy this game? That depends on you, the buyer. If you are a fan of Minecraft, you are probably going to love this game and it’s DLC. While it may have a few minor graphical bugs here and there, and the controls may frustrate you at times, you'll probably love this game and play through it multiple times just to see all the outcomes of your decisions.
If you’re a Telltale games fan, you'll also probably like this game, just to a lesser degree. Cause while this is still a fun game, its nothing too new to the gaming industry. You might get invested in the story and characters but you'll probably pick out all the twists and turns in the story. However, you will most likely still have fun with it.
If you are anyone else, who just thought they'd check out the game because it sounded like fun, please realize what you are getting into. Not saying that you’re guaranteed to not have fun with this game, but you may not like the whole "DLC Trap". When you buy the game at first, it will grant you access to the first 5 episodes. However, the game is cut into 2 different sagas out of the 8 episodes and the first saga ends on the 4th episode. While Minecraft fans and die hard telltale fans probably won't mind spending the extra $15.00 to see how the second saga ends, people who just bought the game to see one story, might. And while I still had fun with it, you probably won't be too happy with the "DLC Trap". You also will probably find the errors of the game that I listed above annoying and I haven't even listed the worst ones yet.
Now which type of fan am I? This is important to note since I'm the writing the review, I am a Minecraft fan. Though, I am not afraid to criticize the game in any way.
Ok, so what’s good about this game? Well, its characters and how it keeps you the player, interacted in its quick time events and other types of gameplay. Plus, the story. While it can be cheesy at times, the story is still quite enjoyable even if it is predictable. It also will grant you plenty of playtime as each episode usually ranges to about an hour apiece at the very least.  So again, if you’re a Minecraft or a telltale games fan, you’ll probably enjoy it.

Now onto its bad parts. So as I mentioned before, at times there can be a few graphical errors. Otherwise though, it’s not too bad. However, the control scheme can be excruciatingly annoying. Sometimes you’ll have to press a button quickly or else you’ll fail the quick time event. And while these are usually forgiving, some will make you want to tear your hair out. You will seemingly die no matter how many times you try it, until for some odd reason, it'll work and you can continue on with the story. Most of these seemed to happen in the DLC though, so for the most part, the first 5 episodes shouldn't have these. (Also, side note real fast. If you do end up buying the DLC, watch out for episode 7. While it’s still fun and a good episode in my opinion, the dragging mouse mechanic is REALLY bad, I especially had trouble with one near the end of the episode, where I had to spend 30 minutes of trying and retrying it after watching a 2 minute unskippable cut scene right before it. I finally beat it after I gliched the game where I died and also beat it at the same time.) Now I think the final main complaint I'd like to cover before I move on to a really big personal complaint of mine, is the story. The story as I mentioned before, can be quite nice and pretty funny at times. However, a lot of people complain about it seeming rushed and about how your decisions don’t seem to effect it that much. And beside a couple decisions near the beginning, they're right. The story is okay and is nice, but don't go into this game looking for the best story of a lifetime.
Alright, time for a personal complaint. Now while I don't think this can happen anymore this is still a very big complaint of mine. I was one of the people who decided to buy the DLC for this game cause while I do recognize all the bugs and errors it may have, I still enjoy it and think it’s a really good game. However, I had to update the game in preparation of the new episodes, which I was fine with doing. It wasn't a long update, and I was excited to continue my adventure in the game. So I opened my game, and found that for some reason my main save file had been deleted. What was worse, was that every time I tried to open a new one in that spot, I would get stuck in an endless loop of choosing a character. I eventually found a way to fix this bug thanks to some searching on the steam forums for the game, but my file was still lost. So I had to replay the entire game again just so I could play my newly purchased DLC episodes. To put it simply, I was not happy. Yet I did get over it and like I said, I don't think this can happen to anyone anymore.
Alright, enough blabbing. Let’s get on to my final score. Using Game Informers scoring system, I'd rate this game 7/10. It’s still a good game and there are going to be fans of it (I know I am) and Minecraft and telltale fans will probably love it, but most gamers are just going to want more from its story. So do I recommend this game? Yes, yes I do. Cause it’s still a good game, even if it may fall short at times

I honestly love the core-concept of this game. I'm an enthusiast of FPS games and generally dislike MOBAS, but this game quickly became one of my favourites after playing it for a while. It's everything you could ask for, easy to get into but with a lot of tactical depth that takes a while to master.
This game is esentially a MOBA played in first person with elements of a shooter. It brings together the tactical side of a MOBA and the mechanical skill that an FPS game demands and does it better than any other game I've seen in the class shooter genre.
Unlike most games, which use an "upgradeable skills" system or a "weapon loadout" system, this game uses cards, cards which can totally change the way you play your character while not making it impossible to win without a certain card. It's entirely up to you how you choose to play your character (once you manage to grind for the cards you want, of course, but it's not like Warframe or WoW levels of grinding, you'll actually have fun playing until you have enough currency to get the cards you want).
On the subject of unlockables, most characters need to be unlocked (with the exception of a select few that are free from the start and the other 5 or so that will be randomly selected for weekly rotation), but from my experience, it won't take long to grind for the character that you want given that you're a dedicated player. Any other sort of unlockable is purely cosmetical and won't interfere with gameplay in any other way.
Another thing that needs to be noted is that for your first few games (I think up until level 6 or so, more or less) you'll be going against bots, this is to give you enough time to become familiar with the game mechanics and have at least some type of idea of what you wanna do when you'll start getting into the real multiplayer part of the game.
With all that being said, I hope you'll enjoy your time playing this game! I recommend it to both FPS and MOBA players as it truly is a mixture of both. And obviously, bugs are to be expected as this game is still in beta, but don't let that tought drive you away from trying it out, any game-breaking bugs are usually fixed within a day or two of them being found out.

The below review no longer applies, but leaving it for history:
This game has a lot of potential and I want to like it, but I can't recommend it until the developer gets the PC control scheme fixed.
Some examples of poorly implemented mouse and keyboard UI:
Automatic de-selection of object in focus after every activity (you tell your hero to do something and immediately lose focus, so you have to re-select the hero to adjust orders).  This is completely the opposite of how anyone who has played RTSes or TDs regularly would expect it to behave, leading to lots of frustrating situations.
Extremely awkward way of confirming tower placement (clicking on the tower type assumes you want to click and drag it somewhere rather than just click once to select and click again to place, like every other TD game in existence) and purchasing (double type... wtf?!?).
No standard control conventions seem to be observed even though overall those same commands aren't otherwise being utilized (even simple things like allowing you to select a building and set a rally point using right click)
Escape brings you to pause menu, but doesn't take you back out of it, you have to click the "play" button.
These issues might not be so bad if you could manipulate the game while paused, but fighting with the control scheme in real time quickly becomes aggrivating in situations where you need to react quickly.
There really is no excuse for the reliance on drag-and-drop, double typing, and seemingly forgetting that there are
mouse buttons.

Fast gameplay, acrobatics, and classic game modes such as CTF and TDM are return in this neo-classic shooter. There is one other feature that sets this apart from the rest though, build your own gun! You can change all of the standard pieces of weapons(stock, barrel, clip, scope, etc) but you also have the option of using different ammo types(rockets, scatter, bullets, beam) and ammo property(heal, fire, plasma, etc). You can create something as mundane as a semi-auto sniper rifle using regular bullets to a rapid fire minigun that shoots mini rockets that electrocute everything around them to an auto shotgun that heals allies.

This game is an astonishing work of passion, intelligence, care, and dedication. Thylacine, the tiny indie developer, clearly put incalculable thought into creating this game with all its immense, interlocking, significant, and extraordinarily well balanced systems. Siralim 2 is complex, but never unnecessarily so. Every mechanic contributes to the game; nothing is extraneous despite there being tons and tons of variety.
I think of Siralim 2 as a combination of Dragon Warrior Monsters and Disgaea, dialed up to 11. If you like either of those series, you will love Siralim 2.
From Dragon Warrior Monsters, Siralim 2 draws compelling collection and breeding mechanics, as well as tactical battles where team composition is essential; however, there are a seemingly endless number of unique creatures to collect, and breeding is amazingly complex with creature categories and subcategories, unique creature abilities and statistics, and a "Gene Strength" reminiscent of Disgaea's Transmigration/Reincarnation mechanic, all of which factor in to your decisions about which creatures to collect and breed together to produce your optimal team. A team consists of up to six (!) creatures, all of which participate in each turn-based battle against up to six enemy creatures. Team composition strategy is incredibly deep and there are innumerable combinations that "work", although you will likely have to change your strategy depending on the opponents you expect to face. Obvious and subtle synergies abound, thanks to the huge variety of options available. I haven't even mentioned spell gems, artifacts, runes, or cards, all of which significantly expand your choices.
From Disgaea, Siralim 2 draws the emphasis on "grinding" and replayability that underlies the entire game. Siralim 2's gameplay relies largely on a basic cycle: prepare your creatures in your castle (where the NPCs reside), then venture out into procedurally generated dungeons to progress. Of course, this is a vast simplification, since preparation includes any number of activities such as breeding creatures, upgrading artifacts, visiting merchants, and managing your inventory and your creatures' loadouts; and adventuring includes exploration, battles, mini-quests, and boss levels. What little story there is is not the main focus; instead, you upgrade your character (gaining perks that help you both in and out of battle) and your castle (expanding the NPC services available to you). Nearly everything in Siralim 2 has some sort of progression to it, whether it's improving your artifacts' quality by battling through their inner realms (presumably inspired by Disgaea's Item World) or performing mini-quests for the deity of a realm to improve your relationship so you can unlock various bonuses and rewards. (Each deity has a very distinct and entertaining personality.)
However, as with any grind-heavy game, it's possible to become exhausted by the repetition. Disgaea had obvious "training maps" where you would just level up your characters by performing the same set of actions each time, which very quickly became very boring. Siralim 2 avoids that trap by having procedurally generated levels, but if you are very averse to grinding for progression, you might want to play short sessions and take breaks. In Siralim 2, you mostly have to set your own goals, otherwise progression can feel meaningless; however, it's easy to find goals to aspire to, since the game provides so much to do.
I would also like to commend Siralim 2's transparency of mechanics. It's almost always obvious what something will do, so the player doesn't have to experiment endlessly (or consult a guide) just to figure out basic game mechanics. When something isn't obvious, there is often in-game help to explain it. Many, many games have opaque or hidden mechanics that often cause the player to regret past decisions. (Dark Souls is a particularly notorious example; I would also name Sacred as an offender.)
There is even more in Siralim 2 that I haven't mentioned at all! Note that I haven't even completed the story and I'm sure there is more waiting for me. On top of all of this, Thylacine is still improving and updating the game often, and has already released an expansion for free.
I could go on and on, but Siralim 2 is worth your time and your money. I think lack of exposure is this game's worst problem. It's certainly niche, but it deserves more players. I highly recommend Siralim 2 to anyone interested in an intricate, complex, innovative game that not only embraces the best parts of its inspirations but expands upon those concepts to become a timeless gem that deserves far more acclaim than it has so far received.
