This game is about strategic nuance and figuring out your preferred synergy.  You create yourself a mage, but you are. Ot a front-line troop, you are more like the CEO.  You select your creatures and then command them to do all the heavy lifting for you.  Every creature is unique, even though some appear to be a simple reskin.
CLASS
Every creature belongs to either Life, Death, Sorcery, Nature, or Chaos.  Certain classes are more effective against others, but it does not mean that if you have a party of, say, Death creatures that you will automatically lose against a party of Life enemies.
FAMILY
Creatures also belong to a FAMILY, so you will find Griffons, Ghouls, Yetis, Priests, and many many more.  Each FAMILY has a bias towards certain stats, for example Banshees tend to have decent Intelligence, Defense, and Speed but their Attack is lacking.  Within the family you will find 5 to 6 variations which will each have a unique TRAIT and will have a slight variation to their stat bias, some may have a bit more defense, some may be faster, and so on.
TRAITS
The REAL star of this game is the TRAIT system.  Every creature has its own unique trait and they are very varied.  Here are some just as a taste:
Whenever this creature attacks, the enemy's stats get set to the lowest value.
This creature gives a boost to Defense for every creature from its FAMILY in your party.
Whenever this creature Provokes, your other creatures get an increase to their Attack and Speed.
This creature gives Mend to all your other creatures.
This creature allows all your other creatures to cast Major Healing for 0 Mana.
With Six creatures, you can really have a lot of fun experimenting with different synergies.  I had a party where a creature had a chance to resurrect whenever it hit, another creature that had a chance to resurrect whenever it GOT hit, and another that, whenever a party member dird he got a percentage of their stats as a buff.  I kept the fight going for a very long time, constantly killing and resurrecting my creatures, pumping up my creature to ludicrous levels.  Once I did decide to finally attack he did millions of damage!
Another fun thing is artifacts.  Your creatures can each equip one artifact.  Generally, artifacts just give stat bonuses, however you can also have artifacts with TRAITS on them, which means that in a group of 6 creatures you have a whopping 12 TRAITS to play around with!  The deliciousness of synergies and figuring things out and experimentation is mouth-watering!
SPELLS
Your mage, being the CEO, does not cast any spells himself, but has his creatures do it for him.  A Spell is cast by equipping a creature with a Spell Gem and the Spell Gems themselves are also quite varied.  Spell Gems will have different modifiers on them.  Some use health to cast instead of mana, some will cast on hit, when hit, when defending, when killing, when getting killed, at the start of battle, etc.  You can have two of the same Spell Gem with modifiers on it make the spells work completely differently!  This can lead to some confusion because I was at first thinking "why are my creatures casting a spell???  I did not tell them to!"  And then I looked through and realized that they were casting their spells based on the modifiers.while there isn't a hugely robust tutorial, the game provides you with all the necessary information in the Library.  Take the time to read!  Mich confusion can be averted with a little patience and bookworming.
Truly, there is a lot more to this game!  There are Gods with various favors they bestow upon you, mysterious [REDACTED] Creatures which allow for even MORE customization, Arena battles, customization of just about everything, and lots of Quality of Life things.  Don't like grinding for materials?  Send a party of creatures out to do it for you!  Looking for a specific creature that you have, but need more of?  Create charms that cause myltiples of that creature to appear so that you can get more!  Slow paced combat making grinding a grind?  Turbo Mode!  Boss battles too slow?  There is a punishment that allows Turbo Mode in boss battles!  Too easy?  Punish yourself...there is even a God of Punishment, he enjoys seeing you suffer!  Too hard?  Rethink strategy, grind some lower floors, breed your creatures to make them mich stronger than what their level implies.
To say this game has its hooks in me is an understatement.  I love it, I will be spending mich time on it, and the wonder of discovery is still strong as I am learning new things each time I play!
Criticisms:
Nothing is perfect so I will list some of the things that do not serve to add to my enjoyment here:
Retro-I am kind of sick of NES and SNES graphics, honestly.  Yes I remember growing up with Mario and such, but I am kind of over the charm of 8-bit graphics.  Also, the lack of animation in battles is not pleasing.
Bugs-very few bugs, but I have had a situation twice now where I have grinded out a dungeon and then the evil "program stopped working" thing pops up and forces me to close game.  I did not lose a lot of progress and, honestly, some of it could be due to the fact that I am abusing Synergies to have my creatures with Millions in their stat points and casting a spell that casts three times cast itself....so maybe I just overtaxed the game engine.
Grinding-even with the Quality of Life things, there is still a lot of grinding and repetition of tasks.
Lack of Transparency-in a game so focused on strategic and tactical control, when it comes to actual fights, you cannot view your creature's stats.  So you are getting "+1.2M Attack" messages, but, in combat, you cannot inspect your creature to see how much attack they actually have.
Story-there is bot much of a compelling plot, it is not really the focus of this game, so it is not so much a "story" as it is a "nudge to jeep you moving forward."
To me, these are minor criticisms, not even detracting from my enjoyment enough to give me any pause in recommending this game and looking forward to when I can go, fire up my PC, and continue on my adventure!

To this very day Fallout 2 is one of the best games that I've ever laid hands on. I played it back in school for hundreds of hours and now that you can get it on Steam, I just had to buy it once more. Its graphics might seem quite outdated, but if you're not too much of a superficial gamer, you should give it a shot.
What makes this game so incredibly beautiful is the developers' love for details and a really convincing atmosphere. You get thrown into a post-apocalyptic world full of glorious black humour, knowing only little about your actual main quest. There is barely any hand-holding, which modern RPGs do all too much. In Fallout 2 there are no quest markers, only hints. To solve your missions, you have to listen to what NPCs tell you, instead of mindlessly clicking through dialogues, following a marker on your minimap and shooting a few bandits in the face. As most things in Fallout 2 can be done in a variety of ways, you can solve problems by talking, violence, in favor of your own interests or to help a certain person or faction. And the outcome will always be entirely different. You decide everything.
On your way through the radioactive desert of the American West Coast you will discover tons of secrets, interesting characters, quests and enthralling side stories. Considering its release date, the game's actually huge. I've played Fallout an infinite number of times, but so far I always managed to discover something new – be it a secret area, a new way to solve a certain quest or just another crazy NPC.
As if this wasn't enough cool things to know about Fallout 2 already, there's even more. For example Fallout's unique character creation system. Your avatar will have a truckload of skills, talents, perks and attributes, which have a direct influence on the gameplay and everything else. You want to conquer the wasteland as a highly intelligent scientist and sweet-talker instead of being a violent brute? Want to be a sniper instead of chopping your enemies with a chainsaw knife? Well, just give it a shot. No two playthroughs will ever be the same.
I could go on and worship this game for another 20 minutes, but I think, if you're not convinced by now, you won't ever be. However, if you're into oldschool RPGs, buy this game and experience one of the most superior titles in video gaming history. Period.

I purchased Letter Quest: Grimm's Journey with the remastered version. I decided to play the original first to see what the first game had to offer. I was just expecting a fun word game. For the most part, that was spot-on.
During Letter Quest, you follow Grimm's journey to go get food. There are multiple levels that he works through on the way. In each level, he has to fight one or more monsters. The monsters take damage based on the words the player spells out. Those words must be made based on the titles that are available in the tile grid. The titles can be swapped for others if the player gets stuck. Over the course of the game, the player is able to unlock books, potions, weapons, and other items that help them towards the end. All of those items can be upgraded with in-game currency that is earned when beating monsters and levels.
Pros:
- The graphics are cute and smooth.
- The titles are easy to read, but can be traded out for other options later on.
- There are multiple save slots.
- Family friendly.
- Levels get progressively more challenging.
- Each level offers four different challenges, which players earn stars for when they beat them.
Cons:
- Some grinding might be necessary in the middle of the game, especially for new players.
- Only offers story mode, which makes the game lose it's replayability.
- Upgrading items can take a lot of time.
- Some achievements can be irritating.
People looking for a fun word game will likely have a good time with Letter Quest: Grimm's Journey. But with the remastered version out, it may be better to purchase that, or both versions, instead. The player can then choose which option is more suited for them.

Well, it was fun while it lasted! I got so caught up in the exploration that I almost forgot what I was running around for (stupid pets)!
There's a good challenge on the first playthrough, which you'll inevitably fail because healing is limited, even if enemies don't respawn once killed, and they mostly just run back and forth in extremely limited patterns. Items are limited, though some are re-usable at a cost of gems, which are limited. Backpack space grows quickly, limited to 9 slots. You'll generally have more than enough money to go around, and even money's limited. Items to resurrect dead party members are limited. But there's a shop...limited to only one of each item for sale. Even the initial map is limited!
All the limitations make for good gameplay, though! It forces you to focus on inventory management, particularly only taking what you need instead of trying to load up on everything. The game punishes hoarding pretty harshly when you die. Lots of deaths can also mean not being able to complete a run. In which case you will have start a new game. Once you know your way around, following playthroughs become much more strategic!
Fortunately, each character has their own set of stats, and the gem reduction upgrade you get fairly early on (depending on how murdery you are) makes certain items free to use with certain family members. You can swap party members back at the house whenever you want, so this gives you some reason to not use the boy (occasionally (sometimes(maybe))).
I only had a couple of issues. First and foremost was being unable to change the controls. The gamepad controls are tolerable, but Up to switch items and Down to drop them, particularly when you're forced to use the thumbsticks instead of the D-pad, are not good controls. I dropped items on the ground frequently or found myself set to a random item in my list. Not too terrible, just annoying.
Ladders are also kind of annoying. They stop you from attacking reliably, and you can't jump off the middle so place them wisely. Even attempting to jump off the top is sometimes a gamble.
In the end, it was a pretty good game overall, so go ahead and buy it! It'll scratch that Metroidvania itch for a day or two, at least.

Anyone familiar with the NES classic Legacy of the Wizard should feel an instant familiarity with the setup here: a family of playable characters (each with unique properties), a master inventory of utility items, a sprawling subterranean dungeon divided into a series of biomes to be explored as the player sees fit, and some very cute sprites. I quite appreciate how non-explicit the game is at explaining itself, Weebish Mines rewards experimentation with regard to learning how things work. This might turn some folks off, but anyone seeking a
oldschool exploration platformer should dig it. On the retro modernization front, it must be noted that Weebish Mines throws one particular bone that the often cruel LotW never did and that's no poison potion drops from defeated enemies!
While there may be a few rough edges to Weebish Mines (I really do wish there was a more elegant way of quitting the game rather than resorting to ALT+F4 while not at the family's house), I'm having a great time with it. You couldn't ask for a more attentive and dedicated dev, too. For anyone familiar with the DXF Games catalog, Weebish Mines is a complete no-brainer.

This game is not bad. I can understand why people enjoy it but I had more fun playing Dead Rising 2 than this game. There are many reasons why but it is easier to go over the most glaring issues I have with this game.
1. No experimenting. In Dead Rising 2, it had introduced combo weapons. To me, I loved the combo weapons, no matter how wacky or unimaginable the weapon was but at least you could experiment with it. Dead Rising 3 has the same but it doesn't have as much depth as in Dead Rising 2 because in order to craft combo weapons, you need a blueprint to unlock it rather than experimenting in Dead Rising 2 which unlocks the combo card but you get half of the PP earned while using it.
2. The level up system. In the previous Dead Rising series, it was completely random on what you leveled up. Sometimes it is good and sometimes it is bad but it adds variety and makes you want to level up and gain PP more. In Dead Rising 3, it is very simple and it doesn't motivate me enough to level up. The only skills I did end up leveling was health and item capacity which is a minor issue and can be a tad bit annoying.
3. Blueprint collectables. What is the point of collecting blueprints when they added the option to unlock all of a catagory of blueprints in your level up system. It ruins the point of exploring the open world. Sure you can run around and find other collectables like the Frank West tropies or the Sad Endings, but those only give PP which I never really cared for as much.
4. THE WEAPON LOCKER! Why give us a weapon locker that can spawn insane amounts of items? In fact, why is it in the game? It ruins the point of exploring and creating combo weapons. For those who have not gotten the game yet, essencially, the weapon locker is a locker that can spawn items you have picked-up on during your adventure. It may sound cool but when it allows you to spawn combo weapons, what is the point? All I had to do was craft one combo weapon and went back to the weapon locker to spawn 3 more of it. That kills the combo system that was innovative in Dead Rising 2.
5. Combo Vechicles. Now many of you may wonder why this is a bad thing. "Its a cool thing to have man! A motorcycle combined with a steam roller is awesome!" But here is the thing, it makes the game far too easy. the first 2 combo vechicles you get in the game are easily the best way to kill hordes of zombies. Zombies are nothing more than like annoying piles of paperwork in the office. I know there are other combo vechicles but why use those when I can have a armored car with a shotgun attached to it and blades on the side? Also, you can spawn combo cars from garages as well, making the game even more easy.
6. Boss fights. Now boss fights were the cool things in the Dead Rising series. Seeing a person go mad because of the zombie outbreak and having to fight them was a challenge, but when I can spawn in combo weapons like rabbits spawning kids, then what challenge is there? I fought the first boss only having to drink a orange juice once because of a certain combo weapon that I had spawned 2 more of out. I know in Dead Rising 2, there were some bosses that were hard and unfair but at least it provided a challenge for you to get stronger and get more combo weapons but here, it is pathetic.
7. Co-op. If I am able to beat this game in single player without dying or even getting close to dying, then what is the point of co-op? The game is far too easy and your character becomes a god of death so easily because of the insane combo weapons you can use, which clears zombies and bosses like nothing. So what is the point of co-op to a easy game? There is almost no reason to unless you wanted to play this game with a friend. Sure Dead Rising 2 had co-op but at least the bosses were hard enough for co-op. In fact, I died 5-7 times in Dead Rising 2 because of bosses. Now its just like riding a car with spikes all over it only to try run over a peanut couldn't open.
8. Food combo. Why must I level up and put an attribute to obtain food combos? Why not put blenders around the map like in Dead Rising 2? because food combos are the lifeline to this game. I know that you can make combo weapons now on the go but why food combos too? It makes the game even more easy. Food combos can give you more health squares than a jug of orange juice and it gives you a buff. So why not follow all the other Dead Rising examples and put blenders around the map to craft the food combos? I don't mean like a blender on every corner but like a blender or 2 in each area of the map. That would provide challenge and make the player want to run to it for a huge heal instead, I currently have 7 food combos around me with 6 combo weapons, all of which, I can't carry.
9. Optimization. The optimization and port of this game is a mess. It offers too little and expects players to have powerful rigs. I don't have a powerful computer so I have to try run it at the lowest settings and it still has issues with constant fps drops and random crashing. It is not a very enjoyable experience when ones computer cannot run it so well.
10. THE TIMERS! What happened to the timers from Dead Rising? Why did they disappear for the main story? The timers in Dead Rising gave you pressure if you wanted to complete the story, offering a challenge to do all of the side quest and boss fights in a timely manner. Now, the main story has no time limit and there is no pressure or motivation on the player to even complete the story. Side quest are the only ones with timers but usually it is quite easy to ignore since they only give PP, which is ok but it is also un-motivating to do more when the level up system is quite stupid in my opinion.
11. (last one) The story and characters. The story is very stereotypical and easy to catch on. The plot twist are easy to spot and know and it is quite dull. Characters are not bad but most I didn't care for. Nick Ramos, the main protaginist and player, is a nice guy who is trying to get out alive but is quite bland and is always worried about the number of zombies around him when he can create the most absurd and god-like weaponry I have seen, making me wonder why he is even afraid of zombies when he himself is like a noris god of death. Your co-op partner,♥♥♥♥♥♥ is not very likable and is kind of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who is self-centered. Rhonda can be easily ignored. The only half-decent character is Annie, who you will meet in the start. She has her issues but is more interesting than the others, which is a lot to say for.
Now even with all of these obvious problems, there are some good things for Dead Rising 3.
1. Combo weapons. Even though the combo weapons can be spawned over and over from weapon lockers and are over-powered doesn't make them any less interesting. the combo weapons in Dead Rising 3 are cool to see and hilarous on how they can be crafted. Even though there are less combo weapons in Dead Rising 3 than Dead Rising 2, they are sometimes fun to use.
2. Outfits. Like in all Dead Rising games, you can dress up your character in whatever clothes you want him in and it is no different here. You can have Nick Ramos dress up in ridiculous costumes and outfits from other capcom games like Megaman or in a funny mascot outfit. It also carries over in cutscenes, creating hilarious and funny moments when people talk to Nick calmly while he is in a Banana Hammmock.
3. The map. The map is huge and breath-taking. Even though its not as charming as the mall in Dead Rising 2, it still shows what life is like now in the future and how expansive the map is.
Well, that about sums this review up about Dead Rising 3 for me. Overall, its not bad but it is definately not worth recommending at its price now and it shows how it has taken a bad turn since Dead Rising 2. Here are some pro-tips for beginners I wish I'd known at the start:
1)  In the first dungeon, the Temple of Trials, you're going to be forced to melee.  Everything in here (ants and scorpions) can be kited if you have at least 7 action points.  Punch something (using 3), and move 4 spaces away from it.  It will use all of its action points to close the 4 space gap, and not be able to attack you.  This will save you a lot of trouble.
2)  You can heal yourself using doctor/first aid skills in addition to the powder.  This can only be done successfully three times each though.  (Save your antidotes if poisoned, you'll be able to cure the poison with the use of these skills and/or it will wear off over the course of the time it takes you to attempt to use them)
3)  When you enter the second area, walk slowly forward, one space at a time.  As you notice the raised stone plates, use the traps skill on them.  Even if you skill is low, keep using it.  Eventually, you'll disarm them, for 25 XP each.
4)  You can steal the key from the final guy to avoid fighting him.  You can keep reloading if your steal skill is low.  Alternatively you can talk him out of the fight if you have enough speech skill.
5)  If you level up in the dungeon, don't put points into melee or unarmed. There's a trainer for each in the first village.  If you have less than 55% unarmed skill, you can train to 55%.  There's a guy for melee weapons too, that'll give you +10%.  I'm not sure what the cutoff is.

A while back I posted on this game's forums because it seemed interesting but the screenshots made it look strange to me.  A sort of RPGMaker vibe I guess.  I'm not sure why I didn't buy it sooner, but I always intended to try it.
I have a few other games in this genre and I know of a few others that try way too hard with the nostalgia goggles.  The games always end up feeling forced and the gimmicks wear out their welcome fast.  I keep tricking myself into buying those games too, only to realize that aside from a few (Castle in the Darkness comes to mind as a stellar example of good retro throwbacks) I'm frustrated by the cognitive dissonance that exists between the games-as-advertised and the finished product.
I'm not saying all of the "meh" games in the retro vein deserve to be ragged on.  Far from it.  Personally, I keep buying them hoping that something will capture my attention.  Chronicles of Teddy and Enter the Gungeon come to mind- wonderful throwbacks that offer something new, but unfortunately with my...  Eccentric gaming tastes feel like they're trying way too freaking hard to smash together concepts, both retro and newer-ish, and most of them (to me) feel like I'm playing "Zelda Sandwiched Between Fez and FTL" or some crap like that.
To cut myself off here, Siralim 2 absolutely deserves way more attention and recognition than I've seen it get.  I haven't played a whole lot yet but this developer really, *really* cares about their product.  So much so, that not only do you notice the labor of love immediately upon starting the game for the first time, but rather quickly it sets in, the obvious affirmation that this is a game made by someone who wanted to make something they themselves wanted to play.  To me, that is always a promise that there are still people out there who don't quit- they don't stop working and refining their game until they are happy with it personally.  So yeah, I really appreciate being able to figure those things out so quickly, especially from games that might fall under the radar because it's practically impossible now in CURRENT YEAR to differentiate the good from the ugly side of non-stop game releases.  I admire Thylacine Studios for being indie, having a vision and not once comparing themselves to anything else.
Siralim is actually quite beautiful.  The variety of loot, monsters, and lore are staggering.  I regret not giving it a chance earlier.
Graphics:  Retro stuff you'd expect from a game throwing back to the days of 8-bit RPGs.  Tons of variety in the characters and everything fits together seamlessly, and it's very hard not to admire how much attention to detail was paid.  Smooth framerate and nice, big sprites, without the messy and worthless shader effects that so many of these games think they need because we all know that downgrading our displays with scanlines and horrible curvature, bloom and HDR effects makes us feel so warm and fuzzy.  No, Siralim is proud of it's visual style, and I love it.
Sound:  I haven't heard enough to comment but you don't really need a lot here to be halfway decent.  So far I haven't heard anything that seems out of place.  Siralim is definitely it's own world, it's own game.
Controls:  Playing with a controller worked with no extra effort required by me using DS4Windows on Windows 10 and a wired Dualshock 4 controller.  Pick up and play, no fuss.
Overall:  I intend to sink as much time into this as soon as I get the chance.  This is one of those games where a lot of people will stand tall and say that the asking price is worth it without any questions.  If you like what the description says, if you enjoy quirky RPG's with some mechanics that have meat and depth, there's no reason why you wouldn't enjoy Siralim 2!

I grew up on Dragon Warrior Monsters and Dragon Warrior Monsters 2. This game felt familiar in the best way, in terms of the core mechanics. However, team composition and customization are much deeper than I anticipated - also in a good way. Creatures each have unique traits, which really set them apart from each other and can form distinct roles. It's important to be aware of your enemies' traits - you don't want to let one with a stacking defense buff live for more than a few turns, for example. Conversely, if you can set up your team with the same creature in a way that lets it survive for a few rounds, it might become unkillable by your enemies. I had a ton of fun theorycrafting and putting together a healing-based team focused around two synergistic traits - the first causes any healing on this creature to also be applied to your whole team, and the second causes any healing any of your creatures receive to deal damage to an enemy proportional to the amount healed. Every turn, each of my creatures heals the creature with the first trait, in turn healing all 6 of my creatures, putting out an incredible amount of damage while also maintaining full health. It's not unbeatable - there are plenty of enemy traits that get in the way of this working perfectly, and nothing is stopping my creatures from being one-shot by an overlevelled foe, but it's quite powerful and was very satisfying to put into action.
It's hard to describe exactly how much customization is available to you. The key elements of customization, outside of team composition, are spell gems, equipment, and deity points.
In this game, spells are not restricted to certain creatures. Rather, you can equip any creature with spell gems that enable the castng of the spell they hold. Each creature belongs to a type, sort of an element (life, nature, chaos, death, and sorcery), and a creature can equip any gems of its type. Life spells tend to involve healing or barriers, chaos spells often inflict debuffs - they all have a solid range of effects, though. Each individual spell gem can have a number of traits, such as reduced mana cost, increased damage, increased buff/debuff duration, and even a chance to cast when the creature is hit or attacks another creature. For creatures that are better off attacking than casting, equipping them with on-hit spells can be very effective.
Equipment looks very complex at first, but it isn't hard to work with. There are different types of equipment that enhance health, attack, defense, speed, intelligence, and any combination of these stats. On top of that, a piece can have up to 10 effects on it at max level (equipment levels up as you fight with it equipped). Effects range from flat stat boosts to starting every battle with a specific buff. You can even get a monster's unique trait on a piece of equipment, allowing for some pretty crazy combinations, though each piece can have only one trait. You can unlock an NPC that will let you enchant equipment with certain effects as you desire, provided you have the materials.
Deity points are given when you level up or reach a new level of favor with one of the 15 gods of the game. You can use them to give you and your creatures a very wide range of permanent boosts. I advise investing in the effect that lets you breed creatures of higher gene strength without a ritual, which will let you get stronger creatures faster and without consuming too many resources. The class you choose at the very beginning of the game determines some of the options you have for spending these points. I played a Life mage, which enabled the particular team I discussed earlier with the Overheal trait, allowing my creatures at full health to still receive healing, even if it won't do anything. Don't stress too much over your choices here,  since you can change your class and respec these points eventually, though not for free.
Another nice thing I want to mention is how consistent and useful buffs and debuffs are. The majority of debuffs applied via spell have a 100% success rate, regardless of how powerful your enemies are. Got some annoying spellcasters? Cast a silencing spell without fear that it'll fail and you'll have wasted a turn - unless, of course, one of your enemies has the trait that makes its team immune to silencing effects.

TLDR: Good combat, story (for the first half), substandard companion interaction compared to other Bioware game, beautiful areas and character models, worth a buy
I dont really understand the complaints about the controls, its not that hard to get used to. This game is really good, but it is slightly rough, so I definitely understand why people may not want to give this game a positive review. There's no real character customisation aside from name, its kind of short and ends somewhat abruptly, the pre-rendered cutscenes look abysmal, there is a lot not to like. However, I feel what there is too like outweighs that. This game has one of the most unique and beautiful settings in any game ever, the Jade Empire is such a beautiful place, the Asian mythology is immesnely interesting, the design on the areas still looks good to this day, over a decade post release (at least in my opinion.).  The combat system is a real departure to what Bioware was doing at the time, it was a real time martial arts beatdown compared to the turnbased systems that KOTOR and the Baldurs Gate games had been using. I'm impressed they managed to get that kind of fighting system to work in the KOTOR engine, and its really just a blast to play. The voice acting is fairly good (aside from a few crappy performances), the companions are all voice acted well and designed well, the different models you can choose to play as all have interesting and different designs (Tiger Shen forever).
Honestly, however, one of the games pitfalls is its companions. I love the design and the voice acting, but theres really not too much interaction with them at all. Compared to their Infinity engine games like Baldurs Gate 2, where character interaction is much better. If you come in expecting to interact with characters on the level of say, the Mass Effect Trilogy or the Dragon Age games (not so much the second one, but Origins and Inquisition), you will not be satisified. Not to say that there aren't romances, there are, they are just somewhat rough and seem really rushed. In fact, the last half of the game feels really rushed. The first half immerses you in the story and the setting, and the second half is just a straight sprint to the finish with fight after fight, which is annoying to deal with.
To conclude, despite having some pitfalls, this game is great. I emplore you to purchase it somewhere, whether its here or GOG or Origin, wherever, just pick it up cheap and experience one of the greatest worlds and lore in games. Heres hoping we get Jade Empire 2 sometime in the future.

If ever there was a Bioware game in drastic need of a sequel or successor, it is this one.
Now don't get me wrong... I've sunk a lot of time into the Mass Effect trilogy, I've played through the Dragon Age series plenty too (though Inquisition was downright wretched)... I played Baldur's Gate 2 a lot when I was younger, got through Neverwinter Nights a few times (not so fond of that one), and I played Knights of the Old Republic half to death...
But THIS particular gem is one I never noticed when it first came out. I encountered it by chance while looking around a gaming shop years ago, and noticing the Bioware label I wondered how I'd never seen it before.
And I absolutely loved it.
Admittedly, I'm kinda biased.  I've got a fairly substantial collection of Kung Fu films on DVD. I love anything Wuxia... and this is, first and foremost, a Wuxia RPG... and a pretty well done one at that. Some of the characters are a bit lacking here and there (especially if you want to play a female character, as was a flaw with Bioware games for a long time)...  but the story is very solid and the setting is glorious.
NOW... the downsides.
It is an old game. The PC port of it is notoriously unstable, glitchy, and difficult to get started. I suspect many people will be put off right from the start by the game not starting properly.
If you check the Community Hub, you should find instructions easily enough to get the game to start. The long and the short of it is that you have to go to the game files, remove the "JadeEmpireLauncher.exe" file, rename "JadeEmpire.exe" to "JadeEmpireLauncher.exe" ... then run Steam as Administrator (I'd recommend setting your Steam shortcut to always run as Admin and load Jade Empire from there.
Additionally, if like me you want to stream the game, you'll probably have to run your streaming software (in my case OBS Studio) as Administrator too.
That should get the game running properly...   but then you get into the game, see the start menu, and you'll probably notice that the little cherry blossoms floating down on the screen are stuttering. Or at least I did. It stutters enough to render the game completely unplayable.
BUT that can be fixed too... there is a guide to fix it right here:
Once you're done tweaking whatever settings you need in JadeEmpire.ini and downloading the fix if necessary, the game should then run just fine... and you shouldn't ever have to prat about with this nonsense again (besides running various things as Admin)... and can get on with playing one of the most underrated Bioware RPGs out there.
Enjoy.
COPY AND PASTE steam.dll file from your steam folder to the jade empire game folder, if you get 'Fail to find Steam' error.

I got the remastered edition of this game, which included the original version as well.  Since the remastered version would be bigger and better, I decided to play this version first lest I'd not want to go backwards and ever play it.  After finishing all of the achievements, I can say that I do recommend playing this game.  The fact that they upgraded it and allow you to have both versions without any extra fees says a lot about the developers, who did a solid job making this game.
The gameplay is basically an RPG version of a game like Boggle, where you have a field of letters to work with to spell out various words.  Unlike Boggle the letters don't have to be connected to each other at all.  Each letter has either a single dot, two dots, or three dots on it, which represents the difficulty in using that letter in a word, as well as how much damage it will deal to the enemy.  You go back and forth as they attack you and you hack away at them with what words you spell, with a basic rule of thumb being, the longer the word the more damage you deal.  As you play through the game you will buy upgrades for your character, equipable books that grant various benefits, and selectable weapons that grant a bonus to one aspect of your character.
It's kind of an odd idea on face value, but it gives a bit more purpose and development to what can otherwise be a perpetual routine.  Developing your character and making them stronger gives you more of a reason to keep playing as opposed to an arcade style system where you'd just start all over again each time to earn the high score.  After a bit of a learning curve where you feel like you have to grind for a while, you figure out the right pace for replaying earlier levels at higher difficulties for more gems (currency) without having to keep replaying stages to make any progress.
I think what I enjoyed most about the game as it is designed was the enemies who took damage with multipliers based on certain conditions, such as using letters from a specific part of the board or using certain letters.  It could be a bit annoying sometimes, especially if you weren't given the letter you needed to get the damage multiplier, but there was never a challenge that was too hard to overcome given a bit of grinding or a second attempt with better letter RNG.  For me it just made it so I had to think my moves out a bit more while still trying to get maximal damage, which is far more interesting then only scouring the board for the longest word possible each and every time.
One troubling area for me was how the game replenishes your letters as you spell out different words.  I wouldn't know whether this is true or not, as it would probably require looking at the programming, but it seemed like I got certain combinations of letters more frequently then not.  I'm no Scrabble pro, but my vocabulary isn't half bad and there were several times that the best words I could spell out were the same.  It took away a degree of replayability when the same combinations of letters and words I could spell kept repeating themselves, despite having 15 letters to work with.
A similar issue applies to the final achievement.  This would only apply to those who bother with achievements, but this game's final achievement was quite a grind to earn.  All you have to do is spell out 3,000 words, but by the time you've finished clearing all of the stages you still have 1,000+ words to work on.  There is certainly some range in that aspect as some people might spell out smaller or larger words or have to grind more if they don't get upgrades that dole out more gems, but I doubt my experience was abnormal.  Before I had finished I had fully upgraded every single upgrade possible and was merely going through the motions to get the last achievement.  I don't know if the number of words would carry over if I started a new game on expert mode or not and I didn't want to find out the hard way.
After doing the last achievement it will be some time before I have an interest in going on to the remastered version of this game, but I'm sure I'll enjoy it when my interest returns.  The original version is certainly playable and I would suggest is the better place to start, since now I have something to look forward to moving on.

There are 40 levels in total with a small story to follow, a number of bosses, and various upgrades to help you along the way. The art style is cute but lacking in animations and the small selection of songs can become quite grating, but all of these problems appear to be fixed in the remastered edition.
One issue I found was that not all official Scrabble words can be played here, along with not being able to play two-letter words, which means the game could become difficult when options were tight. My suggestion is to brush up on your knowledge of words beginning with Q without U. If your literacy in English is moderate-high then you'll have no issue playing through Letter Quest.

Pretty simple scrabble-like word game with some basic RPG elements.
It was refreshing to play a word game with a little bit of depth to it.
Gameplay looks like this: you write a word and then you damage the enemy. The longer the word, the more damage you'll deal. Some letters do more damage than others too. A core strategy is to find the longest words with the letters like X, Y, Z, Q, K, H, J in them.
But it would be boring if it was the only approach. Many levels have restrictions. Sometimes you can damage the enemy by writing 4 letter words only, or the words with less than 5 letters. Sometimes you need to finish the word with E to do x7 more damage. There are a lot of these mini restrictions/buffs. It makes the gameplay fun.
You can buy many upgrades with gems (main currency in this game). You can make your weapon do more damage, regenerate life in battle, take less damage from enemy hits, increase your character's HP, get bonus gems at the end of the level and so on and so on.
The first several hours is really fun and quite challenging. But from mid-late game, when you are strong enough to kill everything - it starts to get a bit boring. It gets extra grindy at the end if you are going for the achievements (especially the 3000 words).
Native English speakers should not have any problems with this game and non-native ones will learn some new words ^^
I absolutely loved this game, original and remastered. I found it to be a delightful distraction.
A fun and charmig little letter matching game. It can get intense sometimes, especially in the later levels! I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys games like Text Twist and Scrabble.

TL;DR:  A fun little word puzzle with more than enough to collect for the completionist.  Easily worth the small price tag.
Decent little spelling game.  Mostly, you're just making words from the tiles, though there is occasionally a hangman mini-game mixed in.  Each level can be played in four modes:  regular, timed, special challenge and elite.  Timed was usually the hardest for me (I had to try a few times on some of the levels).  The special challenge and elite really aren't that hard, if for no other reason than that you aren't under time pressure.  If you want to collect and max out all of the toys, you'll be doing a bit of grinding.
Don't expect any deep RPG elements.  There are a few upgrades, gear options, and heroes.  The heroes have different stats, though I never noticed a compelling reason to use one over another.  Character optimization just doesn't seem necessary.  You can carry a few each of two different potions (one heals and one clears tile debuffs).  But you won't be having conversations, nor do you get any choices that affect the story.
The story is told in comics at certain points.  It's fairly lame, doesn't pretend to be anything other than silly, and doesn't get in the way.  I had to go back over the comic while writing this because the story made virtually no impression on me.  Easily forgettable, but similarly forgivable.
The dictionary is fairly good, though it's definitely got gaps.  It didn't recognize heliophobe, for example.
The art style is consistent with the previews.  The music is OK.  It could use more variety, but I've seen far more expensive games with far worse.

Having been a gamer for over 20 years, this controller is one of the best mass produced commercial controllers I have used.  The only downside that I have found so far is that I haven't been able to purchase a 2nd USB dongle so that I can connect the Steam Controller to multiple PC's without taking the dongle with me.  I believe that I understand the decision to use a dongle vs Bluetooth however, it isn't unique for commercial users to operate more than one PC any longer (desktop and laptop?). While I accept the reasoning behind the decision to use a dongle are to reduce support end ensure there are no latency issues, I wish Valve would make the purchase of second dongle an option.  What happens if someone's dog eats their only dongle, do they have to purchase a complete controller?  So if you use this on a single device, I highly recommend it, if you want this on multiple devices wirelessly, I would take this into consideration.

Quite good indeed! I was scared at the beginning thinking that it may not be as suitable as other controllers (ie. Xbox360) or that I will not get used to it.
The truth is all the opposite: I find it much better and comfortable than an Xbox360 controller and it did not take me as long as I thought it would take me to get used to it.
However, be aware, this is not a substitute of keyboard+mouse but something in between it and controller.

Recommended if you love fiddling with hardware & peripherals as much as you love gaming.
Basically, if you want to play mouse games on your couch, this is it.
This is great if you want to play games that don't work with a controller, with a controller. You could use one of the tools floating around to use the analog stick on your XB360 pad as a mouse, but the touchpads are sublime. In slow-paced games like Pillars of Eternity, Sid Meier's Starships, and Civ5, it's amazing, a revaluation. Damn near as good as a mouse.
For non-competitive real-time games like Fallout 4, it's not as good as a mouse, but after a lot of fiddling, it's close- it's as good as you'll currently get without one. I wouldn't recommend it for something like CS:GO, unless you're very, very patient, and not a top-tier player.
With the above said, it takes some tweaking. Some games work great since the dev assigns a default/recommended control scheme, but others flat-out refuse to work because mine was stuck on a combo gamepad/mouse scheme, that would cause games like Rebel Galaxy, Binding of Isaac, and Darkest Dungeon to just not recognize input.
Removing the mouse input from the scheme fixed this, but the deeper issue was that the latest Steam beta I was using wouldn't change control schemes properly. Rolling back fixed this.
I've since got it working great, but the learning curve is there. Your thumbs fall very differently on an otherwise very ergonomic controller, but the touchpads are very alien to begin with. My short time with the controller is yielding fruit, but I'll update this review after I've concreted my opinions.
I play this primarily on my phone, I probably have over 100 hours played.  It's a great game, good enough for me to buy it twice just to be able to play on the go or on the big screen.

Do not under-estimate the power of the Steam Controller. *breathing noises*
Seriously, though.
It looks a little funky, and the touch pads take some getting used to, but that's irrelevant. It really is.
There is no more powerful gaming device on the planet than this controller. There's a deep complexity that borders on alarming. It's like a space sim or driving sim that holds nothing back in terms of customizability and open world game play. The universe is yours to command. Every button, every setting, all touch parameters, the gyroscrope, even down to the haptic response is completely customizable from to its core sensitivites and dead zones to the very behavior of the input device itself.
You can control a mouse cursor with the gyroscope, or use the ABXY cluster as a joystick (you might not necessarily WANT to, but hey, the option is there). You can map any keyboard command, mouse click, scroll or point to any message sending function on the controller, and vice versa.
Will it replace KB&M for first-person shooters? Probably not.
But it does a bang-up job for games you never thought you'd be able to play on a controller, like RTS or point and clicks. It destroys other controllers for games with a controller in mind, because you can really push it to its limits with custom modifiers, key combos and total conversions.
Believe me. This truly is the controller for the PCMR.
In Gaben we trust.

This game was one of my favorites came out. It is still a game that I hold in very high regard and would highly recommend to anyone looking for an RPG to play even with it being an older game. I'll start with the positives about the game and move into how I feel about the port.
The story in this game is fantastic. It really captures the wuxia feel. If you love Chinese martial arts movies, I think it's hard not to love this game. The story almost feels like a Westerner's love letter to wuxia.
Combat is fun. I actually would LOVE to see a Knights of the Old Republic game with a similar fighting style. It just feels way more involved and fluid. With that being said, the game hasn't aged super well in regards to combat in my opinion. Compared to games with similar combat now, it can end up feeling pretty clunky.
This game was beautiful back when it came out, and it holds up pretty well today. The cutscenes are pixel-y on my 1440p monitor, but, overall, there's nothing jarringly bad when looking at the game. It just looks old.
Just like KOTOR, this game does a pretty good job of making you feel like your decisions matter. This is something I feel Bioware has always done particularly well but shines through the best in their games pre-Mass Effect 3. Taking the easy way through problems might reward you sooner, but making the morally right choice will make you feel better or yield a reward later on. In the tutorial, they actually pretty cleverly teach you this with an altar puzzle.
So, overall, I'd rate this game pretty highly and am incredibly sad that it didn't sell well enough to warrant more games being made.
With all that being said, this port just isn't good and is only slightly better if you get the game through Origin. It's difficult to get running. You have to throw the steam.dll into the game's install folder to get it to launch, and, even then or on Origin, you might continue to have problems.
Xbox Controller support is non-existent which is mind boggling considering I first played this game on an original Xbox. Playing with a 360 controller is doable, but I just couldn't get used to turning my character with the triggers outside of combat. I ended up just going back to mouse and keyboard which is doable but feels odd in a game with fighting game style combat. I felt controls were a lose/lose.
I've spent the majority of my time actually playing through the iOS version instead because it just works, and, for $5 cheaper, I'd say just get it on Android or iOS instead. It's a much better way to play this if you don't have or don't want to play on an Xbox.
I am going to recommend the game though as, if you don't have any other way to play it, a bad port is better than nothing.

Monster Loves You is a short game where you shape the story of a monster through your choices from birth to death. What I liked about the game is that the art style is cute and that there are so many endings that you can achieve, whether it's hunting down all of humanity to extinction or being the friendliest critter that connects monsters and humans together. My experience with this game feels like a D&D style board game where you have to make choices and roll dices to break through in critical moments. My only qualm is that the game's replayability sort of diminishes before you finish going through all the endings, mainly because you go through similar processes of "growing up" each time.
Nonetheless, I still liked the game for what it offered. If you like dynamic choice-making, multiple ending, D&D style game (and you love monsters or want to be one) then Monster Loves You is for you. Overall a solid 7/10 enjoyment.

This is a pretty cute and very fun game all about choices.
The writing is clever and the outcome of your choices can be surprising at times.  Each playthrough of the game you get a handful of scenerios to choose from to establish your monster's character and hopefully survive to the next stage.  Because the scenerios offered are randomized, and there are more scenerios offered at each stage than turns you take, every game will play out differently making each playthrough an unique story.  It's not the kind of game where you know how to get the next ending by simply altering one or two choices from one playthrough to the next.

I was always a big fan of those old Choose Your Own Adventure books where pages would end with a choice that would send you off on different plotlines. The whole visual novel genre feels like the perfect place to revive stories like that, but it hasn't really happened in any conspicuous way. Monster Loves You! is like a lot of those little adventures and choices rolled into a big, gooey, adorable ball, which is probably why I found it so engrossing. It's not quite on the level of those literary odysseys of old, but its monstrous heart is in the right place.
The game cold-opens with you being formed in a spawning pool, as all monsters are. Through some initial choices you set the foundations for what kind of monster you'll become, and learn a little about the monster life cycle. From these sticky beginnings you guide your monster though childhood, adolescence, adulthood, and beyond by making decisions during key events in their life. These decisions affect a number of stats which define your monster, and later in life determine what they are capable of and what kind of ending they can achieve.
This might sound a bit heavy so let's dial it back to the part where you're eating garbage and scaring goats. All of these life-altering decisions come in the midst of monsters chewing on each others' heads, pranking each other, and screaming until their ears bleed. The quirky, friendly tone of the writing makes it clear this is a cartoony take on life (as if the vibrant art didn't give it away), and also takes the pressure off of making bad decisions. Nearly everything you do will raise at least one of your stats, though there are rare choices that do nothing or even lower stats a tiny bit.
Your monster is scored by percentage on their Cleverness, Honesty, Bravery, Ferocity, and Kindness. Presented with dilemmas like tricking, scaring, or helping a friend should lead to obvious increases in the corresponding stats. That's actually one thing I want to commend Monster Loves You! for, how clear the results of a choice will be from how it's presented. Other visual novel adventures like Vlad the Impaler don't really give any clues as to how a scene will affect you but all the choices here feel very well telegraphed, enough to easily max more than one stat without any prior knowledge. And once a stat is maxed, it opens up some new options depending on the situation.
Mechanically, there's very little else to the game besides making text choices. Each stage of your life has a number of days to while away, and on each of those you choose an activity. Activities are shown only as icons so you'll never be sure what's going to happen until you've been through them once before, a bit of a contrast from how clear the actual choices are. At the end of the third stage (adulthood) there's a check to see if you can proceed to the final stage, which offers some additional choices and a proper conclusion to the story of the monsters as a whole. It's all quite gratifying to work through, really, given how much thought and detail was put into constructing the monster world and society.
Running though one monster life should only take 30 to 40 minutes, and after that you'll pretty much be chasing endings and achievements. It won't take you long to recognize the same events coming up and start clicking through them madly so don't bank on a ton of replay value here. There is value to be had, though, in the charming writing and visuals that welcome you to the strange and wonderful world of family-friendly monsters. As long as you're not expecting anything sprawling or epic, Monster Loves You! is a fine little diversion that brings back the charm of choosing your own adventures.

Keep in mind: if this were more expensive, this would be a negative review.  That being said, this game is definately good for at least the $1/hour expectation.
However... if you're looking for a good TD that will make you feel challenged, this probably isn't it.
While the hero system has some merit with six different heroes (with a seventh available waaaaay too late to be worth mentioning), with both talents and gear to help you customize your play,,, that works as both an advantage and a disadvantage.  In many cases, you'll have to farm excessive amounts of currency to unlock a hero, then unlock his/her gear, then upgrade said gear... only to THEN have to level up that hero to be useful.  Given how slow leveling is, and how dull farming currency is, that's a monumental task.  Especially given that some heros don't work the way you'd expect them to just reading their stats.
But the real crime here is the towers themselves.
Often times towers will fail to target correctly - either focusing on a slow mob that moved into range first while letting one or more faster ones slip by, or simply not hitting mobs because of strange line-of-sight issues.  For instance, an AoE tower might hit one mob at the back of a pack, but not hit the rest of the pack at all.
Worse still, however, is for the many tens of thousands of currency you might sink into fully upgrading a tower... most of the game can be dominated with two tower types.  And no, they're not the advanced ones.  The most powerful tower seems to be spamming a certain, fully upgraded basic tower... and then adding in an anti-air turret if you have flyers.
For the most part, after about 5-6 hours, the game starts to feel repetitious... and I'm wondering if I have the fortitude to actually finish it.

Update! The devs have promised a patch to overhaul the whole control scheme. As that was my biggest gripe with the game, I'm considering giving it another shot once this patch hits, as I still think some of the ideas on display are interesting. Looking forward to a second chance for this title. I'll reevaluate my opinion on the grind of the game once I can play the levels without control frustration.
Review:
***[Beta PATCH to address CONTROLS ISSUE out, haven't played updated game yet though.]***
There are a lot of things I don't like about this game, but the thing I like the least is that it's a frustratingly poor mobile port. Most things you'd want to "tap twice" to do on a tablet or phone still require two inputs, but it's ridiculous here - double type? Ok... And the control scheme is kinda garbage. There will be moments when you want to respond quickly to changing situations, but can't, because the controls inhibit your intentions.
The awkwardness of the user interface will be most noticeable when you're trying to do anything quickly. You'll be frustrated trying to place towers suddenly when a level's spawn layout changes after no prior warning (which is a mediocre design choice in my opinion, and forces you to build from the red line at the end of the level outward unless you want to get screwed on mobs slipping through your suddenly compromised defenses). The controls also suck when trying to get your hero to target enemies, either for their regular plink damage attacks or for their timed abilities. Also, the timed abilities are a little random in how they deal damage sometimes, which is difficult to square with the "Tower Defense" genre concept in my opinion. Shouldn't be very luck based at all.
There are a lot of things to grind out that make your towers or hero suck a little less, but at least in the early game it's just a grindy slog. Nothing in what I played so far to give you that "oh hell yeah" feeling some other games give you when you unlock a new tower type, no real decisions to make about how to specialize anything - just basic upgrades to basic attributes. I'd love this system if it had more choices in customization, maybe some exclusive choices to specialize a tower more. I dunno, I like that in other games of this kind and feel it might add some legs to the upgrade system to have even just one branching option at the end of an upgrade tree - make a choice, player, and enjoy the rewards.
Why am I bothering to make suggestions for a game I didn't even really like the first time I owned it? Well, the devs responded, and appear to be making a genuine good faith effort to work on areas that I personally found frustrating, and their communication with this review chain has given me some real faith that what we have here isn't a bad mobile port, but the makings of a Good Mobile Port, maybe even something that can find unique excellence on the PC platform if they continue to develop it and continue to pay attention to player response.

NieR: Automata is an action adventure rpg by Platinum Studios and the creative mind of Yoko Taro. The games story takes places in a dystopian future overrun by powerful machine lifeforms which have wiped out all human life on the planet, with last remnants of Human civilization residing on the moon. In their desperation to reclaim their home planet they created a force of android units called the YoRHa which are tasked with taking the battle to the machines and drive them out of the planet.

As for the gameplay side the combat is amazing as you would expect from Platinum, very fast paced and responsive, a spectacle of fluid animations and breathtaking visuals, challenging enemies and boss battles, you can hack into enemies to have them fight their own or take control of them yourself, light rpg elements and a world to explore freely. Had this controller for over 2 months now and I must say, I'm very impressed, it's comfy to hold, feels solid the only thing I dislike is the left and right front shoulder buttons, they emit a loud cheap clicking sound when pressed, but the rest of the buttons are fine. Takes a few days to get used to the controller as it's quite an odd experience, but, eventually the penny drops and you realise the potential this controller unlocks in games which are otherwise tricky to play on keyboard and mouse and those that play very well on keyboard and mouse almost play just as well on the Steam controller. For precision and ease of use, the Steam controller is far better than dual analog controllers, by a long shot.
Gone is the thumb fatigue of constantly pushing the cumbersome anolog stick to try and fine control that camera in-game rather awkwardly as you're constantly jabbing your thumb across the face buttons then moving it to push on the anolog stick as quickly as you can so you can get the camera in position so you can go back to jabbing, but on the Steam controller, you just glide your thumb across the wonderfully accurate and very responsive trackpad ever so gracefully to move or spin that camera around and then back to the buttons, it feels more natural and quicker as you're quickly pressing those buttons then quickly swiping on the trackpad which would otherwise be a much slower process on an anolog stick, playing The Witcher 3 or Dark Souls on the Steam controller is a joy.
The controller UI can be daunting at first, but after a few days you realise you only need to alter maybe half of those options as everything else can be left alone, with plenty of great user config files to download, this becomes less of a thing to worry about.
Valve have added alot of great features to the Steam controller over the past 2 months since I purchased this controller such as Mouse Regions which means I could use it to make my character in an RPG move via the anolog stick rather then click spamming  the mouse pointer to make them move or I can play Legends of Grimrock 2 fairly easily on the controller which would be impossible on a dual anolog controller. Or there's the Touch Menu function allowing you to set upto 16 hotkeys on a trackpad for quick access to in-game menus, functions and hotbars so that even MMORPG's can work very well on the Steam controler which could be a hindrance on a dual anolog controller, it basically adds another 16 buttons to the Steam controller!
A worthy addition for any PC gamer and to replay those gaming greats which you found hard to play on the keyboard and mouse or anolog controller.

There is a lot that I like about this controller.  I really like how customizable it is, especially with respect to the touchpads. I like the touchpads for mouse based tasks and games, thanks to the accuracy and customization options.  I like the underside squeeze-triggers as extra buttons.  I like the Steam-based dynamic profile saving/loading and community profile sharing (which will hopefully improve in the future as more people are using the controller),
I am torn about recommending it wholeheartedly.  The philosophy here is definitely not simplicity, as the "Play any Steam game from the comfort of your couch" slogan seems to imply.  The philosophy is flexibility.
Most of the issues I saw in using the controller, such as the inability to copy your own configurations between different games, can be solved easily through patching.  However, the device's complexity is tied to something that can't be changed: the sheer volume of Steam games out there with vastly diverse control systems.  Games which are designed to have a library of potential actions available to the player, sub-menus and item hotkeys and all kinds of movements and reactions, will require a real time investment to get working.  This controller can be configured to perform in just about any game, but it can involve a lot of trial and error, especially when some of the settings are so hard to parse ("Anti-Deadzone Buffer" comes to mind).
That said, it's true that it's much easier to configure the controller in the middle of a play session when compared to what I'm used to (alt-tabbing, picking up a keyboard, changing settings in another program, then alt-tabbing back in).  It's really awesome to be able to press the Steam button on the controller and be changing the configuration in a few seconds, without ever leaving the game or putting down the controller.  Here, there is simplicity.
I think whether the device will work for you depends both on how patient you are, and on the types of games you play.  The touchpad's accuracy with quick movements over a joystick make it ideal in mouselook or pointer focused games, i.e. FPS or top-down strategy games, and the configuration challenge is mitigated if the game has only a small number of keybindings.  Having only one joystick, it struggles in the area of twin-stick steady directional input, such as 3rd person camera-control focused games such as Tomb Raider or The Witcher, and in games with many keybindings it will require a great deal of fiddling to set up correctly.
I can imagine someone who really likes to dig into a game, set everything up just right, and then spend at least several hours playing will get along well with this device (I imagine this describes a lot folks reading this).  People who spend less time in a wider variety of games and want things to just work immediately are probably not going to be as well served by the Steam Controller, unless the games have simple controls or the community configurations really start to come through.
From my perspective, given how many tasks I prefer to use a gamepad for, this is a highly customizable input device which is unlike most other gamepads available on the market, and it does outperform my previous gamepad solutions in a few critical areas.  It also faces some challenges, but, for its flexibility and unique design, I think it's capable of serving a valuable role in the Steam-junkie's input arsenal.

Letter Quest: Grimm's Journey, developed by Bacon Bandit Games and published by Digerati Distribution is an ingenious little number that basically ties Boggle/Scrabble in with RPG elements.
Little Gimm and Rose set out on a journey to defeat any monster they encounter. Your job is to come along for the ride and use some fancy words to get your way out of difficult situations. Better the vocabulary, better the chance of you winning and sometimes it really isn't as easy as it looks.
Honestly, at first glance it looks like a bit of a childish game due to the animation and bulky look of menus, playable blocks and just the general idea that follows this, but it's honestly perfect for all ages as a casual puzzler to lay back with and get yourself really thinking to try and get passed certain levels.
I enjoy that the difficulty is set in the middle somewhere - Not punishing, and not dead easy. It's pesky in mini-boss fights as well as certain levels (Also hard levels), while not being impossible to get through. It makes winning feel rewarding and for a game to get that right, it has a lot of brownie points from me from the get-go.
Cute, smoothly animated, nicely cartoony, all round really nice.
Don't get me wrong, I really enjoy the soundtrack to the levels, menu etc. However, it does tend to grate a bit after a decent amount of play time as there isn't enough variations to how it sounds. I found myself turning the music down if not nearly completely off after the 3 hour mark hit as that was my limit.
Isn't really much of one, but for what there is of it; it's nicely set-up, easy and simple enough for anyone of any age to navigate around.
Wonderful little blend of RPG and a family favorite (e.g Scrabble/Boggle/etc), It blends together really nicely for a game that can be enjoyed by anyone of any age. It keeps you thinking, possibly even teaches you new words you had no idea even existed while feeling both engaging and rewarding.

Don't let the fact that the game is free-to-play put you off, it is without any shadow of a doubt a lot of fun to play.
While there are the obvious comparisons to be made against Overwatch, that is not to say this is an outright clone or an inferior game. Although this lacks the polish of Blizzard's behemoth I find this game to be far more enjoyable. I admit that it was only after having had a years experience playing Overwatch that I had a greater understanding and appreciation for this type of game after I, like many people, dismissed this as a budget clone.
The characters are varied and challenging to master with a card loadout system to enhance certain attributes depending on your style of play or requirements to better counter an opposing team. There are also a nice selection of cosmetics to work towards, if you're into that type of thing. You can play also train against bots while you learn the ropes, if you so wish, all the while you'll still be able to earn gold (to buy other champions) and gain XP.
It is worth noting there are a variety of flaws with the current OB63 release, namely the new overpowered champion Vivian and bugged daily quests. I'm sure at some point in the near future balancing issues will be fixed and the daily quest bugs sorted but it's important you're aware of the facts as they currently stand if you decide to invest time in this game. Having mentioned this minor criticism I still wholeheartedly recommend giving it a try as you may be pleasantly surprised at what is available on offer here for gratis.

One round, the AI didn't bother with routes and just went for the high-value 5- or 6-piece tracks.
