This is a long and  comprehensive review of how I played and experienced the PC port Saint's Row 2 offered on Steam. Please note this review is my own opinion and not of anyone else. Read if you may, this a single review in a batch of thousands of others.
Like many others I recieved the game. I was happy, for I had not played any game from the series and was looking forward to play it... until I read the reviews. The game is a utterly terrible port. Constant lag, low FPS, unexpected crashing and clunky controls are some of the more serious complaints.
Luckily, a few modders created "Gentlemen of the row" and other mods to put the game into a more playable state. These mods have detailed instructions with the discussion forum for the game along with the community guides to help users put their game into a more playable state.
Without these mods, I was able to get past the first cutscene.
As mentioned above, the port for the game is terrible. I'm suprised that Valve is allowing this game to be sold for money despite being at a near unplayable state. I recommend that you get the console version or Saints Row 3/4. Don't pay full price for this, wait until it's extremely cheap wile on sale or when it's free, like how I and many others got it.
IF you actually do on intending on getting this game and downloading it onto your computer, download "Gentlemen of the row" and other types of mods before playing, this will allow you to bring this game into a PLAYABLE state. Note it will still run like a crippled old person in a 100 meter dash, but,  you can at least still play it.
Expect crashes after playing for lengths of time. Save CONSTANTLY.  DO NOT RELY ON AUTOSAVE.  I recommending saving after and before each mission, side quest, property purchase, unlocked achievement, weapon, vehicle etc. Save often and with mutliple save files if you intend to actually play the game as intended.
I played the game on normal difficulty with a keyboard and mouse. I reccomend on using a controler if you might have one. If you don't, that okay, you can still play it but you will have to adjust to the default controls or personalize your own through settings. One can beat the campaign missions without too much difficulty usuing a keyboard and mouse, however, certain side mission activities such as "fight club", "blazing trails" (flamming quad bike time trials), pleasure activity at the brothel, or certain driving missions will prove to be extremely difficult.
I actually haven't been able to beat the "blazing trails" activities. This isn't due to my ability to drive in game but rather the game itself. Driving isn't as good as Saints Row's counterparts (Mainly GTA and Mafia series games) and how  the vehicle handles is rather clunky. I suspect this is due to the poor port. Couple this with the other issues in this port and you'll have a difficult time beating that damn "blazing trails" activities.
Besides driving, you can also fly planes, helicopters, and drive on boats and jet skiis. There isn't much variety compared to cars and other ground vehicles but you can find different variations of these vehicles when encountered in stores or respective in-game environments. The watercraft preforms well in the game but  can't be customized to your likeing like planes and automobiles. Planes aren't  very usuefull in game and aren't involved in the campaign very much ( i think you have an option to fly a fighter plane in a Brotherhood mission).
Flying and controlling the planes can be iffy on keyboard, but not too bad once you get the hang of flying in-game. You can customize planes like cars but options on customzing are limited. I don't believe you can customize helicopters in-game to my knowledge but the store at the airport has a vairety of helicopters with diefferent paint jobs on sale. There are also a number of planes with different paintjobs available at the store too.
Some Wolverine airplanes are armed with machineguns and rockets (most likely due to the GOTR mod) when bought from the plane store at the airport (tip"check the wings for the gun ports before buying the plane!!!). You can't aim where the bullets and rockets go withoout a reticile and once you are wothin range of a  target, you are to close to the ground or water, rendering them useless in any form of combat. The attack helicopter in the game is much more usueful. It preforms like any other helicopter but has a chain gun and lock-on missiles that can be used agianst air, land, or sea targets. Plus it can fly or hover over any terrain such as cities or mountains with ease, making it an invaluable asset in certain missions and activites. It is also fast compared to other helicopters too.
With costomizing automobiles, you get a wide variety of options on how to do so. You can increase preformance form under the hood of your car or give it a wicked paint job on the outside.  I really enjoy moddifying and customizing the vehicles I get in game - if you can drive it, you can bring it into the shop and bring out your inner automotive stylist that lies within you. Remember to store the vehicle in your garage and save before and after you customize it. I lost a couple custom vehicles due to the game crashing!
Character customization is much like vehicle customization inn a way, there are nearly unlimited possibilities on how to customize your character. Make him or her as you please. This a strong feature within the Saints Row that helps defines
on what the game series is. Besides changing the physical features of your personal character, you can dress him or her up in a wide vairety of clothing offered in game. You can buy many types of clothing or unlock them through missions and activities. You can also create your own outfits using the clothing already within your ownership. Not only can you but many types of clothing but you can customize said clothing too, bringing more possiblities on what you can make your character look like. I believe the GOTR mod allows more freedom when customizing your character and clothing including the removal of the censor bars on your nude character (I would like to state that there are not genitals shown in game, just butts and breast. Nothing fancy or vulgar) if you feel dirty. I made my character paper white, deathly thin, without any sore or hair and abnormal facial features that would make Smeagle from the Lord of the Rings series look ungodly beautiful.
Weapons within the game are okay I guess. The are more weapons unlocked as you progress through the missions and activites in the game. There are multiple classes of weapons : Melee, pistols, smg's. assualt rifles, specials, and thowable explosives. There are are a vairety of weapons within each category and the options to unlock unlimited ammunition (for pistols, smg's, shotguns, and rifles only) for them in certain side activites. I recommend on completing said activities early on in the game to make progressing so much easier. Having unlimited ammuntion for any time of weapon will prove to be useful in boss fights or waves of enemy attacks witin missions. You can dual wield pistols and smg's if you wish while playing, this is extremmly useful as it doubles the amount of lead you thow down range to your target(s) WITHOUT sacrificing accuracy. There are some gag-weapons that are fun to use, they will become available later in the game and can be fun to use, but, their prices in the gun stores are less than desirable.
The game offers 3 unique campign storylines that can be played almost simultaneously. Since rival gangs stick to their respective neighborhoods, you can conquer any gang you like without dealing without the other two. The best part about the campaigns is the lack of overlap inbetween them. You can complete one at time  if you'd please. I killed of the Brotherhood and the Sons of Samedi before taking on the Ronin. I really enjoyed the campaign missions and the storylines within them.

Monster Loves You is a cute little choose your own adventure novel kind of game.  You are a monster goig from birth to death and along the way presented with situations.  You pick the response of your monster.  How you pick will then determine either positively or negatively how it affects your stats.  The stats will determine how successful you are on certain decisions and play a more crucial role at the end.  In the end you will come up with one of 14 different endings.  Each ending has a different achievement both in game and on Steam.  The real goal is to real all 14 different endings.  So you must repeat the process over and over.
The game it cute and whimsical.  It's fairly obvious how to pick your actions to get the desired stat outcome, for the most part.  Some endings are slightly harder to get than others in the beginning.  After you've played it a few times you start to know how each situation will reveal itself and it becomes much easier to navigate the path you desire.
You have to understand, there is a lot of repetition in this to get all the endings.  So if repetition isn't your thing, make this a pass.  If you're willing to keep at it then it's a fun game.  One play through doesn't take too long, but to do them all will eat up some time.  Because you're dealing with the same situations, some of it can become a bit boring after a while as you click through what once was funnny and cute but now is 9 clicks to get on with it.
Overall, I'm glad I got it and am enjoying getting my different endings.  It was on sale so I have no issue with the value.  If you're on a tight budget, then wait for a sale because it is a game that can get stale.

I will start off by saying I'm pretty biased in this games favor since I played many bioware classics such as Knights of the Old Republic and Dragon Age Origins when those games where in their prime. The last time I played this I was pretty young but remember some pretty classic moments such as the first time you meet black whirlwhind, joining the Lotus Assassins, ♥♥♥♥ing up Gao the Lesser and the disguised cannibals at pilgrims rest.
Upon revisiting this game I realized it was still just as amazing as my first playthrough on regular xbox. I laughed pretty hard at the same♥♥♥♥♥♥I did 11 years ago, and moreso upon realizing a lot of the adult humor hidden in some encounters. Combat felt the like the same bare-boned dodge and attack  strategy and suprisingly was still fun despite the dated mechanics. Don't expect a graphical masterpiece, although I did find them refreshing and nostalgic.
The gameplay itself is very linear, quests are easy to complete and have pretty obvious good vs bad outcomes, (In this game you have analogous system to Knights of the Old Republic's light side/ Dark side structure, labeled as the open hand, closed fist system). The thing I love about this game is both routes can benefit you as the evil route can net you money that can buy you techniques, weapons and fighting arts that are not available to the more kindly player, and vice versa. Both are equally entertaining and encouraged, whereas in other Bioware games around this time and even to this day don't seem very balanced.
The fighting styles you pick up are wicked cool and diverse, a personal favorite of mine being a thousand cuts because of the ridiculous speed in which you lay blows down on your enemies. You also gain magical ranged attacks that consume chi in which you can also use to heal yourself mid and post combat. Focus is also a majorly cool addition to the game as it allows you to gain a rather unfair speed bonus over your enemies in combat. Combined with an effective fighting style and you can easily gain the advantage over any enemy in the game. You can also transform into several demon forms you gain from fighting particular enemies.
Let me also talk a moment abou the companions, which I think are some of the best I've ever seen in a bioware game. My personal favorites are Henpecked Hou, who on many occasions tells you stories about his unfortunate marriage and often finding glum "bright sides" to suffering any fate that would give him escape from the married life. Or the careless, half-sober, bloodthirsty Black Whirlwhind who finds violence to be the perfect solution to any situation and as you would expect discloses multiple colorful stories about his past as a mercenary. Or Wild Flower, and the dichotomy between the heaven guardian and the Demon that both reside within her, making the most badass companions to have in combat. As far as Bioware games go, they really made you care for these characters, and the fates they each can, or be prevented from suffering. Don't expect much of a romance betwenn characters, as it pretty much ends up the same way no matter what character you choose.
That being said the controls if you are using a gamepad are pretty annoying to work with. I used an xbox controller and some of the more essential controls would not work, such as switching weapons in the flyer minigame, or targets in combat. It is passable but if you're dedicated to using a controller you may very well use 3rd party software specific to the type of controller you're using. I would suggest using a keyboard if you want a smooth experience without going throuhg the trouble.
If you want to take a break from all the triple A titles and play something brief and amusing without the need to spend hours exploring, this is your game. It's games like these that remind me how far we gaming has come since the days of the '64, original xbox, and Ps2, and not necessarily for the best.

I would definitely recommend this game to friends for at least one playthrough, but there are flaws that would keep me from completing another playthrough.
Story: I don't know of many RPG's that focus on ancient Chinese mythology, so the story seems pretty unique. Although the history of the Jade Empire seems slightly cut and paste, the actual plot seems pretty original. The biggest issue I have with the story, is there doesn't seem to be enough time to truly flesh out the story. Compared to Knights of the Old Republic and Dragon Age Origins, Jade Empire was the shorter game. I feel like if there was more time, it could have been better. Another thing as well, it seemed like a few ideas from Kotor was copy and pasted into this game.
Characters: The characters are a hit and miss for me. Characters directly related to the plot or had a complex side quest seemed better in my opinion. Like with the story, I feel like maybe more time could have been invested to truly flesh out some of the characters.
Moral Meter: I'm not a big fan of moral meters in RPG's. Also, the way of the closed fist seemed too much like Sith Ideology.
Combat: The biggest problem I had with the combat was I wanted it to be more like a fighting game, almost like shenmue kinda. The double tapping for a dodge button didn't always work out. The most effective strategy in the game seemed to be stunlocking enemies to death. There also didn't seem to be a great diversity when it came to character builds, weapons, and fighting styles available to the player character.
Mini-Games: What really surprised me, was the mini-game with fast travel. It was something like galaga and was something I wasn't expecting at all. There was also an interesting mini-game in one of the side quests that seemed pretty interesting and different from the generic fights that it normally invovled.
Bugs: There are two issues that gave me the most problems. The first was the frame rate issue. If I didn't restart my computer before playing, I would get terrible frame rates. Also, there's a bug where the camera would be staring face down at the floor so that you couldn't see anything at all. Reloading the game would fix the issue. I might have came across other issues, but those two were the biggest offenders.
All in all, I thought the game was pretty interesting and is worth at least one playthrough. But just my opinion, there doesn't seem to be a lot of replay value for it.

I've only played about twenty hours at the time of my writing this, but oh MAN those have been an enjoyable twenty hours and they won't be the last.
If you are a fan of monster-raising RPGs--particularly ones like Dragon Warrior Monsters--then PLAY THIS GAME. The best way I can describe this game is that it is Dragon Warrior Monsters ON CRACK. Level your monsters forever, breed them for better and different offspring, craft items for them, enchant said items, teach them spells, dive through roguelike dungeons... and that's still not even everything.
You're also trying to work your way up to gaining favor with all the different gods (who give you abilities and sell you items, and give you points you can use to unlock MORE abilities for you and your creatures), expanding your castle, doing quests, cooking food... I haven't even finished my castle yet and I know there's still things I haven't unlocked yet.
There's a story on the side too, but the main focus is on the gameplay. Even so, the writing is pretty entertaining, and I've laughed quite a few times at things that have happened in the game (as well as raged over the times the game played a joke on me).
Some people complain that the graphics are "outdated" but honestly I think the sprite-based stuff is part of its charm. The monster designs are very nice--they range from your typical weird monsters, to big scary ones, to "cuter" ones (or, well... I use the term "cute" loosely here, but let's just say I was quite satisfied with monsters like the dragons, unicorns, and ravens). No matter what sort of monster you prefer, you'll probably find something you like here. As far as the rest of the graphics go, I do think the smooth text and textboxes are a little jarring alongside the pixelated style of the rest of the game, but I got used to it. Music is nice too, but one or two of the songs don't loop smoothly--otherwise no complaints there.
The monster battles themselves are excellent, of course. They're fairly complex--you'll work your way up to fighting 6v6 monster fights, and they're delightfully chaotic. You can't always just power through them--due to all the different monster abilities and spells, you have to think about what you're doing, and it keeps the battles really interesting. Especially the boss fights, which always have a trick to them. If you're smart, you can turn a monster's ability against it--I had a really satisfying moment defeating one particular boss with one spell that took advantage of the boss's own ability, and basically watched it kill itself. It was amazing.
Catching monsters is simple--while fighting, you can have your monsters attempt to extract a core from one of the eneimes. If you do it successfully, you can go to your castle later and summon a monster with that core (and some materials, which you gather a lot of in the levels you explore). As for breeding, it works basically like it does in Dragon Warrior Monsters... that is, you breed two monsters together, and they leave you with an egg (literally leave--they're not coming back). The egg hatches into a critter that's stronger than its parents, always inheriting the stronger stats. There's different breeding combinations you can do to get different monsters, and as you explore the levels in the game you'll find pages to the in-game breeding compendum, which makes the process a heck of a lot easier.
I think I've rambled enough. As I said before, if you like monster-raising games, you'll like this. It's got a lot more depth than you would expect for a game of this price, so if you're looking for a good monster-raising game, give this one a try.

Wow.  Wasn't expecting much of a game because of the very low early access price tag on this game...
And this is one of the more fun tower defense games I've played.  Very, very impressive!
Here is my "First Play on Launch Day!" Early Access Review Video:
Nice style to the game, the zombies will climb cliffs to avoid your turrets, break through walls, and surprise you in other ways as well!  Pretty standard tower defense style of upgrades and using earned credits to research new weapons and upgrades as you progress through the levels.
I love the art style, the way you can speed things up, and the humorous and witty text found as you play the game.  This is a very fun game, and it shows in the early access score I gave the game, which is heavily lifted because of its very high value score (huge bang for your gaming dollar)!!
My scoring system:
Value:  40 out of 40
Fun: 25 out of 30
Controls & Bugs: 20 out of 20
Graphics & Sound: 8 out of 10
----------------------------------------
My Total Score:  93%     <-  This is a very impressive score for a game that costs less then a fast food burger!
Recommended for most gamers!  For tower defense game fans, I give this game my "MUST BUY" rating!  :-)

Liking most is the focus on the heroes. Assuming this was originally a mobile game it plays well on PC with a clean UI, intuitive control system and
.
Spread across a multitude of zones, higher difficulties and new heroes unlocked once making progress. Basic single line marches quickly turned into enemies taking multiple paths, knocking down walls, climbing up cliffs and spawning from graveyards. Successful missions rewarded gold based on your performance which is then spent on buying and upgrading towers or purchasing new equipment. Heroes have talent trees, skills and equipment slots while towers had upgrade paths. Surprisingly okay story, complete with cut-scenes that added to the overall presentation. Steal at the current price and worth checking out for any TD fan.
Game options are limited (don't seem to do anything, bug?) still provided enough.

I have played through about 5 levels so far and there seems to be a whole lot more(Probably 40+ more) with a second game mode for each level which I am yet to unlock. So far the game seems to have a decent amount of depth with upgrade trees for towers.
I am not a huge Tower Defence fan but this game seems to have a lot of unique features which I haven't seen (Like I said not a huge fan so If some other games you know of have these features then my bad) such as heroes which are also upgradable and help out a lot, each hero has their own unique abilities that make them different. There are a handful in at the moment which should be enough for now.
This appears to have been a mobile game before but it seems put well together for PC as there are keys binded to abilities and such, there are also graphics options but honestly they don't make much difference. There are also NO microtransactions which is a + regardless of whether they were in the Mobile version or not.
--Conclusion--
It's a tower defence game with some unique elements, if you're a fan of TD's then you should check this game out, if not but don't mind them then still check it out. I give the game a 8/10 Mainly because I'm not the biggest fan but I don't see why other people won't enjoy this game if they are a fan since it has a fair bit going for it especially at the price and having no content locked away behind Microtransactions. I'll probably play a fair bit more of the game than I have at the time of the review.

Based on the tabletop boardgame of the same name, Ticket To Ride is a really fun and casual game that is easy to learn and can be played in 20-30 minutes. The starting board is pretty easy and not too hard to win if you're cautious and reasonable. Other boards add new rules and quirks that help keep things from getting stale. It's a very enjoyable game that you can break out when you have a little time and want to play something, but don't have enough time for something more involved. My only issue, and it's a minor one, is that there are no achievements which would encourage different strategies and oft-unseen routes being used.

Well, Ticket to Ride.
It's originally a board game that soon transferred to online play, and it has been controlling my gaming life ever since I have gotten it. Its one of those games you can play when you are bored, and then become immediately joyful and (for a lack of a better word) un-bored. The aim of the game is simple: play trains, connect cities, farm points. The way you play it is entirely up to you. This is how good the game actually is: I was torn between recommending this to those who don't have it, or actually boot up the game and enjoy it all to myself. Unfortunately for me, I chose to recommend it. And now, you should get it for making me waste my precious TTR time writing this.
(NOTE: This game is infinitely more enjoyable with a friend playing with you, and I assure you that there is at least one person who can play with you. But just get the damn game. I'll be waiting in the Lobby.)

First of all I would like to say that this might be one of the hardest thing that I have ever reviewed.  It is really hard to explain this controller in many different aspects.  I will try my best however, but I would suggest reading the entire review, other than just the summary I will put down below, if you can anyway.  Thanks.
This seems to be something a lot of people complained about when reviewing this product.  I however think the build quality is anything but bad or cheap.  The quality of this controller is just as, if not better than a Xbox 360 controller in terms of durability and quality.  All of the buttons felt fine and the plastic was just as good as any other controller I played with.  It feels a bit lighter than the 360 controller, which might factor in why some people thought it was cheap, but it is only a small minor difference, if anything it is practically the same.
I can't believe I have to write a paragraph about the learning curve when using this controller, but honestly it is necessary.  The best way I could describe it is this, imagine when you first used a controller for first person shooters, mainly the duel analog controllers back on the PS2, Original Xbox, or depending on how old you are, the PS3 and Xbox 360.  I remember playing Halo 3 on my Xbox 360, having so much trouble looking around with the camera with analog stick.  I as so used to my mouse that I kept on looking around in circles, moving the camera too much or too little, and getting a bit frustrated with it.  After a while though it just stuck with me, and I was playing Halo 3 just fine, this is what it is exactly like to use this controller.  The touch pads feel so foreign to you, you never really played first person shooters or any games with it, and at first it feels rather odd, frustrating, or confusing, but after a while it just sticks with you, and it works REALLY well.  Sure it takes more tinkering than a standard 2 analog stick controller, but OH MAN, after you get the hang of this controller, it is REALLY amazing.
Hands down, the best controller for customization.  You can change the bindings of each button in Big Picture Mode, choosing between buttons from a Xinput or a Keyboard and Mouse.  This alone is a godsend, some games are IMPOSSIBLE to play with a keyboard and mouse or a controller, but with this I feel like I can play anything.  The fact that you can make the trackpads like a mouse is probably the best part of this controller.  If I want to play a RTS with a controller, I couldn't, but with this, I could EASILY do it.  I LOVE the customization with this controller, it brings so many possibilities and possible new experiences with this controller in any game.  If you hate to tinker around with the controller, you can just pick the most popular template on the steam community and be done with it, or if there is no template but the game supports Xinput, just pick the "Gamepad with High Precision Camera" template and pick trackball mode with the left trackpad.
Some aspects of this are weird, and some are amazing, let me explain.  At first you would think that the right trackpad placement and the analog stick placement are terrible, due it it being the complete opposite of the 360 gamepad, but again I must refer back to using a controller with duel analog for the first time, you will get used to it like I did.  I remember going from a PS2 to Xbox 360, it is weird, yes, but again you will feel right at home after a while.  Next is the back paddles, these are simply amazing.  The fact that I can bind buttons well enough to not even needing to move my thumbs to the ABXY buttons is a welcome edition.  The duel stage triggers also do this as well, in the demo of this controller it showed that you can slightly press down on the trigger to aim down sights, then all the way to fire, I have not used this yet but it seems like a really awesome feature.  Gyro is something I can't really comment on seeing as I never used it, but from what I saw, it is really precise and it will be very useful for precision aiming in games like CSGO.
Overall, this is probably the BEST controller for the PC.  You will need to learn how it works and possibly tinker with the configurations, but it will be worth it.  It is competitively priced with other top brand controllers, and is definitely worth your 50$.  Just don't expect it to be as precise as a Keyboard and Mouse, nothing can be as precise, but expect this controller to give you something new and something better than a traditional gamepad.  It may feel weird at first... but you will get used to it and you will enjoy it, just be patient.  (Also stop making me use BPM please.)

Fallout 2 is a game that went under my games to play radar for far too long, mostly because when it came out I wasn't even   in primary school yet. I'm typically not the biggest fan of this kind of post-apocalyptic setting, in fact this is the only one I like. I owe my discovering this masterpiece entirely to the streamlined fallout experience by Bethesda and later Obsidian.
I found the first dungeon to be ruthless my first playthrough, it took me a reload or two before I managed to survive the initial trial and start the main quest. When I emerged into the wasteland of Fallout 2, I was a bit intimidated, every direction on the map had opened up to me. The main quest giver did point me in the direction of a nearby town, but I wanted to see how far south I could go, maybe discover a cool town or two. Nope, I just ended up with plenty of bullets in my corpse.
I decide to not go south when I reload and instead go to the town that the elder directed me to, this is where I lost interest initially. I ended up not in the mood to read any of the dialogs that would've pointed me in the right direction and instead gave up. A few months pass and on a whim I decide to reload my save and see if I can't make any headway in game. After I did a few side quests I really started to enjoy myself, the battle system I found unforgiving started to feel a little rewarding, and I kept going.
I am a little sad however, I'm nearing the final content of the game and I'm trying my darndest to make my remaining hours on my character, the powerfist wielding warrior Gertrude, last as long as possible.
PROS:
-The game has aged well in my opinion, the graphics may not look as sharp as some people may desire, but the game is  still entirely playable.
-The combat is very fun after the initial slow burn, I'd say about level 5 is where it took off for me.
-The characters have been very fun, I can recall most of the characters I've run into in Fallout 2, the same can't be said of Fallout 3 or New Vegas (granted they each had a few good characters).
-Tons of content, I've spent a good 30-40 hours on my current character and still find new quests.
CONS:
-The game is from the late 90's and has technical limitations because of this (Combat can be very slow when a large number of characters are engaged in battle)
-You cannot reload in combat when it is not your turn to move, this doesn't sound too bad but in large battles where you try to keep your companions alive it can be a little bothersome.
-There is a time limit in game for how long you can play, it's an unfortunate technical issue, however you have about 13 in game years until you are forced to play a new character (my current character is on year 3 near the end of the game)
Final thoughts on the game:
This is honestly the best game I've played in past years, it makes me yearn for games that don't constantly hold my hand. Every mistake I make is punished, every good decision I make is rewarded. The myriad of companions in game really made my experience that much better (barring when Sulik would sit in doorways, blocking my only exit). If I had to give this game a number score it'd probably be an 8 or 9 out of 10. There is no perfect game, and this game certainly has quite  a large number of faults, but this is the most fun I've had with a game since my initial Dark Souls playthrough.

Let me first say that I have been playing significantly more time than it shows here on my phone.

About the graphics. Obviously not amazing, but at the same time, more than functional. Everything is vibrant and easy to interpret. No complaints
About the controls. A gamepad is the way to go, but a keyboard is servicable. Everything can be controlled with one hand.(Insert mastubation joke here). Up and Down Left, Right, A, B, and thats it. (Not even a select, or start. How are we going to enter cheat codes now?).
Don't let the simplicity of the control scheme fool you. There is a lot of depth here. There are a massive number of creatures, combine this with breeding, artifacts, relics, and a host of other options and you have a lot going on in an easy to digest package.
But the true beauty of this game is that you can literally turn away for 30 seconds or 30 minutes  and there is Siralim 2 just waiting for you. It you watch video while you play, listen to podcasts, or otherwise need a distraction from your videogame distraction Siralim 2 is the game for you.
This is in no way a shot at the game or the developers. They are very active and have put together an excellent game. I am very excited about the upcoming DLC. Its just that the main draw for me is the is the casual, approachable (and leavable and returnable) nature of the game, makes it a favorite.
If you want a casual yet surprisingly deep game, give Siralim 2 a try.

Throughout the game you'll receive certain crates dedicated to either dinosaurs or humans now this would be cool if you didn't need these damn keys. Second off each crate takes a certain key which means if you want new dino skins and you get a human key it'll be of little use to you. This whole system is very reminicsance of a free-to-play buissness style which this game isn't and you still have to pay the entry fee.
The next point I want to cover is the horrible and lack of a community. The multiplayer mostly consists of free roam servers which are boring AF and are basicly chat rooms with dinos and if you do anything to make an admin mad say good bye because you'll be instantly kicked by the 12 year old admin. The ranked TDM servers aren't much better as their run by players not Pub Games. Then you get either kicked or banned thus limiting the already small amount of ranked servers you can join. *First Serious Review*
Deus Ex : Human Revolution be it the Director's Cut or not is an amazing game. In this review I plan on examining every important aspect of the game, evaluate it on a 1 - 10 scale, then add up all the results and get the average.
Gameplay - 9/10
The most important part of Video Games. In Deus Ex, gameplay is somewhat similar to generic FPS games, however it adds a realistic touch by adding the cover system. The cover system is almost required to actually stay alive because starting out, (Prologue not included) you can easily be killed in 2 hits (I know by experience).However the cover system can be a bit wonky on the keyboard. Another really cool gameplay element is the ability to add new Augmentations to yourself. Augmentations include the ability to : Find People's Personality, Create a deadly shockwave around you to kill foes, Invisibility cloaking, Badass Shades and many more. Inventory management is like Resident Evil where you have to find ways to fit all your stuff in the right position. In a way, this game can be compared to Dishonored in the Future.
Story - 10/10
The story's output is dependent on which choices you make during conversations, the no. of civilians you saved and what you do in the game in general. Because of this, it is very similar to Dishonored, story-wise as it also sports multiple endings.
This feature truly adds more realism to the game.
Graphics - 8.8/10
This game's graphics are pretty good during the cutscenes, but are pretty lackluster during gameplay unless you play on maxed out settings.
Scenery - 9/10
The game's scenery perfectly fits what you would think the earth would look like when almost everyone wants to become Rex "Power" Colt and the rest who disagree about it rebel. However what you see in this game, is not what you get. Some of the really cool things you see in the game, are just backrounds so that sucks.
Voice Acting - 9/10
This game has great voice acting. Each character's voice is really fitting for them, especially Adam Jensen's. However the character's mouths sometimes lag behind resulting in weird cutscenes.
Final Verdict - 45.8/50 or 9.2/10

This is a reivew based on a playthrough up to level 51 and including all side activities up to that point.
Aura Kingdom is an MMORPG that really follows pretty much all the standard tropes and doesnt bring a whole lot of new things to the table. 90% of the main quest is kill 14 x. Interestingly enough the daily quests, side quests and hidden quests tend to be where something other than kill 14 x happens. You have your standard activities, like collecting flowers, fishing, smithing and mining, however you can only get better at fishing and smithing.
The combat is the usual click on an enemy and let there be skills. You are much more mobile while doing so than in most MMORPGs however, only stopping for a second and not loading up the skill while standing frozen in place.
The class system is one of the unique parts of this game.
Not only is there a lot of different classes but you can actually have 2 classes from lvl 40 on. The second class will be heavyly nerfed compared to it being your first class but you can still use all the skills. Some class combinations grant bonus skills. Now this doesnt seem like much, but there is also the character custumization, masterys, the envo path and all together you can get rather creative. THe best part is that you can reset anything at any time for a small amount of ingame money. So you were a guy that runs around with 2 pistols and occasionaly gets out a sword, that skilled on critical damage and defense and preferred stun abilities etc.? Forget all that you are now a mage that wips out a scythe when he fgeels like it and commands a little demon army. If you get the hangt of it class switching can be a matter of minutes, so basically you are any class at any time throughout the entire game.
The second unique part is the Eidolon system. Eidolons are basically a constant follower and can be upgraded almost as much as yourself. Each comes with its own set of skills, and one liners. You get a small amount from the story of the game, however getting the others involves a LOT of work.
Another interesting thing is how casual the experience is. There is ALWAYS at least one main quest, so you always know where to go and what to do next. And the main quest will also be fitting for your level. Particularly in the early levels the speed at which you level up through main quests is insane. However, as said before it is usually kill 14 x.
The story itself is nothing worth mentioning, sure they wrote a lot and created so many characters and quests and whatever, but they mostly lack uniqueness and feel bland, basically you will find yourself skipping through all the dialogue at some point most likely, because it is so damn boring.
There is no faction system, which can be a good thing, as it doesnt split the playerbase.
The music is just as average as the story.
The graphics are nothing special either. Certain skills can look pretty but thats about it. The anime style of your character and most of the screenshots isnt really all that noticable.
The camera can be a gigantic issue at times when you go full in zoom and cant see anything because the game decided so.
Noticable is also  the small size of each map as well the speed at which you travel between maps. You will NEVER need more than 5 minutes to get anywhere. Quests will never take all that long and neither will dugeons. Alltogether this means that this is the one MMORPG where you can actually just fire it up for 20 mins and leave again and achieve something in the time.
What about p2w? Well obviously I dont know about endgame content but so far there was never even a slight need for money, nor people dominating me because of money, so yeah I'd dare to say no p2w.
Summed up: why did I give a positive rating? Because while it is so god damn average, it uses mechanics that have worked for decades now and is by no means a bad game. Also it is free, and for that price you dont get robbed of your money.

This is not Doom.  It is a generic shooter in a sort of Doom universe.  The multiplayer is ideas stolen from more popular games in the hope that the franchise title will bring in the players.  You have your boost jumps, loadouts, and magic powers.  It is not good.  I got through one and a half matches before hating it.  It is slow and boring.  I tried using the "super shotgun" for my loadout in the second match.  My choice was really choosing to die over and over again.  The "super" part of the "super shotgun" is that it is completely useless.  Shooting someone from right behind them as close as possible resulted in 60 damage.  The enemy player could turn around and blast me to pieces with any weapon while I tried to reload and hopefuly do another 60 damage with a second shot.  After two minutes of this I decided that I hate this game.  Further play resulted in same feelings.  Weapons suck.  I am not putting time into it to possibly get a slightly more useful weapon.  Servers and matchmaking are terrible.  matches would have unbalanced teams (like number of players) or have all players with high latency (red) connections.  I don't understand the magic demons and I don't care.  All I know is that getting a demon is a sure way to win a match.
The campaign also looks great, but is boring and repetitive.  The game wants you to do these stupid melee kills to get health drops.  They are not hard to do because the enemies stand there after you shoot them so you can hit "f" to watch the same "special" melee over and over.  it is boring and unnecessary.  Level design is not great either.  Each level is basically tunnels leading to arenas where you fight a swarm of pathetic enemies before moving through another tunnel to do it all over again.  What fun.

This controller is almost overwhelmingly customizable. Which, I believe, is why so many people seem to have trouble with it.
At the same time, it really *needs* to be as customizable as it is to accommodate the whole "replace a mouse and keyboard with a pad" thing. Which you can totally do, at least for things that don't require lightning-quick movements. Stuff like FTL or HuniePop or anything turn-based is fair game. RTS games are *possible*, but will require quite a bit of practice--and tweaking.
Having said that, the ability to make almost anything on it work to do almost anything you want with as much or as little sensitivity, gyroscopic stuff, touchpad stuff, haptic feedback, basically anything that can possibly be simulated on a controller, that you'd want, is quite nice. There's nothing really like this and never has been, so tweaking this might feel a bit overwhelming. Seriously, it's incredible how much you can tune this controller to basically simulate anything, made much easier by the massive amount of customization options for every input.
It's an excellent controller that deserves credit for being so damned versatile.
Still, at the same time, it's simply too big. Way, way larger than the other supported options, like the Xbox controllers. A lot of people have touched on this, and they're absolutely right, it feels like it's for hands that are just bigger than the normal adult's. It's huge, it really is, and I feel like I'm reaching for some of the buttons on it. Considering how much stuff you may have to reach, it can be uncomfortable. And don't even try fighting games on this thing unless you're ready to train yourself to do it.
It's got its caveats, but damned if it doesn't make up for nearly all of it for how much you can alter on it to fit your needs. Except, you know, the physical size of the thing itself. I get they wanted to fit a lot on here, including what amounts to two mouse touchpads, but...It's just too large.

The controller is packed with features and I like the idea of touchpads but it's not easy to find the sensitivity panel online. This controller would be so much better if trimming was onboard.  Big picture mode complicates things as I am use to the custom resolutions that I have my system set to and the Steam Controller needs to run in big picture mode. Overall, I'm not happy with this controller. Not sure that I will ever use it again. $50 wasted since Game Stop does not refund or exchange opened items. As a whole the Steam controller is a success.
It has three big pros going for it:
1: It's very flexible so firmware updates and community contribution can bring almost anything needed to the table.
2: It is never the worst option for a game input device.
3: It enables controller gaming with games that are not controller compatible, such as amost any point'n click adventure game.
Unfortunately it also has two clear cons:
1: The Y, B, A and X buttons are too far from the right side. And this isn't a matter of me being used to the Xbox controller layout. They really are too far. In fact, they are so far off the side that it can be very difficult for someone with small hands to push X at all. I would've also liked the buttons to be a bit larger.
2:The top of the analog stick is convex instead of concave. I have disliked the convex desing of the sticks ever since PS1. Concave is simply better or as good in every situation so there isn't a reason not to make the top concave.
Edit 11.7.2016
After using the controller for over 6 months I can say that my opinion has not changed. I have seen that there have been negative reviews based on low build quality / part of the controller breaking after only little use. Thankfully I haven't had any such problems.
Edit 17.6.2017
I have now used the controller with about 20 - 30 games (for example yeasterday with Torment: Tides of Numenera) and my opinion has not changed.

Black Isle at their finest.  Game is older than many gamers.  Reviewed ad nauseum, I will take this opportunity to impart an anecdote.
I am currently playing thru this game.  I was getting annoyed at the engine.  Even 17 years ago, the hidden behind walls thing was mad annoying.  I have 1 full playthru, and many partials over that time, the last substantial one I stopped at New Reno.  That was 10 years ago.  I was in a town where there is an important NPC (skeeter) in a building that you can't see inside unless you run behind it.  The doors are on the hidden backside.  I knew as I played before, but was a little frustrated.  I was muttering about how Pillars better have screen rotation.  Then I randomly talked to an npc behind this building a bit.  This one was in view.  I asked about the other guy who is hidden a few steps away, and the NPC says "he's standing right there.  Use your eyes."  Those guys at Black Isle knew full well how frustrating not being able to see an npc standing 10 feet away right in front of you due to an immobile painted background, and put those lines in there.  I bet whoever wrote that bit snickered like I did.  I never read those lines before, in probably 100 hours of varied gameplay.  The nuance and subtlety is what is so great about this game.  The way characters are written, the storylines, and unsanitary reality of what harsh life does to mankind.  The good do indeed die young as even the good ones have some bad in this world.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution was an unexpected pleasure for me. I didn't play the original Deus Ex games, though they'd always been intriguing to me, and I gave Human Revolution a miss on release because I was wary of all the brouhaha surrounding the boss fights. Then along came the Steam Holiday Sale of '13, and the next thing I knew Human Revolution's Director's Cut, with it's "new and improved Boss Fights" and included DLC, had snuck through a credit vent into my library. I fired it up, and what followed was some 80 hours of brilliantly engrossing stealth and exploration, cloaked in a plot of revenge, global conspiracy, and a spectrum of ethically grey corporate interests. And Adam Jensen, one of the coolest protagonists I can recall.
Human Revolution shines as a stealth game, but tends to fall a little flat in the action and shooter departments. That is, the game just doesn't feel like it's open to being played as an gun-toting action romp. The controls come off as too stiff for the quick play needed to be really satisfying for good gunplay. They work well for the slow, methodical stealth movements that made up the majority of my playing though, so that was alright.
Choice is a high point for Human Revolution. There are almost always multiple pathways through a level to an objective, and in the rare case where there aren't, the abilities and skills you gain by upgrading Jensen's "augmentations," the game's role-playing system, will typically open up some alternative path or otherwise provide some other, less obvious means to progress. The levels are also filled with with little nooks and crannies to explore, with plenty lore and story tidbits to discover as well as secret pathways and locations to root out. Added to that, there are often multiple ways to complete most objectives too, be that through dialogue, force, stealth, or something else. You also get to "choose" aspects of Jensen's character and indirectly affect the world through the actions you take, such as whether you choose to go guns-blazing, silent and lethal, or silent and non-lethal, which changes how NPCs react to and interact with you.
That said, during some cut-scenes and unavoidable dialogue it can feel like some of the player's agency is removed and choice isn't available, which can be jarring at times.
Overall, I highly recommend the Director's Cut of Deus Ex: Human Revolution to anyone looking for a very solid stealth game set in an intriguing and nigh-believable future world of corporate espionage and human enhancement.
8.5/10
Pro's: great stealth gameplay; excellent level design with lots to explore; choices everywhere; lengthy campaign; Adam Jensen is a badass
Con's: "stiff" controls don't work well for gunplay; some pointless augmentations; some annoying backtracking through levels; cut-scenes remove player agency

Be warned: the Director's Cut on PC actually has *worse* graphics than the original. the shaders and post processing are completely broken, leading to lack of reflections on car windows, poorly shaded NPCs (a mysterious 'white glow' around them and darkened faces with well-lit mouths spring to mind). There is a Steam thread devoted to comparison shots between the two versions. Plus it's a bit glitchy and ploddy compared to the original as well.
The yellow filter has been removed too, making the game look bland, and somewhat dated (OK, it's three years old now, but still...).
Anyway, positives: boss fights have been fixed, and for a couple of quid it's worth getting if you have the original because the commentary is very interesting, but my advice to anyone that doesn't have the original would be to find an old boxed copy of the non-Director's Cut.
Eidos were supposed to be bringing out a fix, but we've heard nothing from them since October (four months ago), and the promised second-screen functionality has not appeared yet. There's no player's guide either. That was Wii only.
This is a real shame, because the original game is a much loved favourite of mine. It had a great story and was genuinely fun to play, but I simply cannot recommend this version, just get the original and grit your teeth through the boss fights.
This kind of puts me in mind of Lucas buggering up Star Wars with crappy CGI, or the Alan Smithee version of Dune. It's a serious own goal by Eidos Montreal and Squeenix, and the worst thing is we have no idea if it's ever going to be fixed or not.

There are people who know all the ins and outs of the game so well it's ridiculous. Every class has it's strengths and weaknesses, and it all depends on how you play them.
Many people will complain that Humans or Dinos are over powered. I call BS. There are players that can turn the tide for a whole team no matter what side they're on, and it makes it look unfair when really it's just people who know how to play the game well.
This is not a tripple-a sort of experience, but I still enjoy it immensely. The biggest fownfall of the whole series is the fact that they aren't popular. And because they aren't popular people don't buy them, so they don't gain popularity, and the viscious cycle continues.

My siralim review: It's too long to post here. I am very passoniate about Siralim 1 having me exceed the character limit. So just press the full review. I'm just sorry I don't enjoy this game guys.
I'm so sorry Siralim team. I wish I could like this game. But it has way too many gameplay issues.
Firstly, I have to say I was hugely dissapointed when I found out Breeding in this is another word for Fusing in other monster catching games. The reason Fusing works in other monster games is because it's free to summon creatures/Capture/scout creatures. Meaning you will have to grind for Resources in this game. You want to try a combo without using up 2 members of your team? You need to grind for about 20 minutes. And also, no upgrades for resource drops. That makes this a very boring grind. The reason fusing in other games works so well is because it doesn't cost resources to summon creatures. you just Capture and fuse. Making testing and trying things out very fun! But you are limited to how much resources you have. Which makes it a very boring grind.
Secondly, I know a lot of people will say "Oh but Siralim 1 was a huge grind also!" Yes but that leads to my next complaint. Royalty points/Diety Points. In Siralim 1 you would constantly be gaining Royalty points. Giving yourself a large feeling of advancement. In Siralim 2 you gain Diety points by appeasing gods. AKA doing quests in their Realm. For each quest in Siralim 1 you gain 1 Royalty point. Siralim 2 you gain 5/10/15 and so on diety points for gaining enough points from one of the gods. And this feels much more of a boring grind than a feeling of advancement.
Thirdly, abilities getting nerfed. Now I agree some abilities were a bit crazy. But my main issue with this is that the creatures don't really have much of a different function from others. All the abilities are nothing that is really game changing. It's overall just... boring. Seeing that all abilities are mediocre it doesn't really make me want to play and see more. They all feel the same.
I have more but that is all I can think of at this moment. And It's very dissapointing. Trust me it's doesn't feel good to post this! I want to love this game! So much! I love Siralim 1! It's one of my favorite games of all times! And I'm not one of those people who hate grinding in games. I love Siralim 1, Phantom Brave, The Dark Spire! Tons of rpgs that require a huge amount of grinding! The grinding in this game just seems so boring... As I stated on a discussion if they add a new mode where parents don't dissolve after breeding one of my main issues with this game would be solved!
Now don't worry though... This game does have a lot of really good additions. Which is why it's so sad for me to not like it. All the new creatures are really cool and have pretty good abilities for the most part. When they aren't taking nerfed abilities from older creatures. Creatures equipping spells themselves is a really great function. Although if you want to breed a creature from your team you'll have to reequip them to the new creatures. The new realms are nice. And being liked by the gods could be a great function if they didn't limit it to improving your characters and having to grind for a rare drop to try out a breeding combination.
And it's not like I only played for 2 or 3 hours. I've played for 12. And it just doesn't get fun to grind for anything on this game. I'm sorry Siralim team. I wish I could like this game more. And some people may like this game. But I can't recommend it like I've been recommending Siralim 1 to everyone I know.

This game is a mixture of Pokemon and Monster Rancher, with all limitations and petty conerns of reasonable balance thrown out the door. Monster traits include things such as 'Upon dying, 50% chance of reviving with full health.' This can cause crazy interactions and synnergy, and when you include artifact customization (Including the ability to equip an additional one of those crazy character traits) and spell gems, it's insane. But it's balanced because the enemies A) scale infinitely and B) have crazy powerful things too.
However, ultimately this is a game about grinding. Making small goals and progressing to personal benchmarks. If you need tangible story progression in order to have fun, this game is not for you. Otherwise, it will last dozens and dozens of hours. Good stuff.

I didn't think I would enjoy this as much as I did after playing TF2 for as long as I did, but I ended up really enjoying Paladins.
While the last few patches have been rather rough around the edges, and I don't entirely agree with the direction the game is going in right now, these things are to be expected by a game that has been in beta for as long as it has. Paladins has been very experimental with it's characters, balance choices, and takes a fair amount of consideration of the fanbase on the forums when making changes to the game. I don't often feel cheated by mechanics unless they truly needed to be changed, and with most of those mechanics, they were later changed to accomodate for the overall feel of the game. Hi-Rez has done a fantastic job crafting the game thus far, and I can definitely see myself keeping updated on the game's progress until it gets out of beta.
There's the problem though. Keeping up with the game, but not actually playing it.
Paladins is the epitome of what I'll call a burn-out game. A game that you play for a few months or so, then get entirely burnt out on it and never want to play it again.
I have tried to find a reason to want to actually play the game again, but I just CAN'T. I loved it the first few months, and part of me wants to go back and play it, but I've simply hit a wall where the game is not fun anymore.
I recommend the game for someone looking for something to pick up and play, and if they really enjoy it and play it more than a few months, GREAT. That's how a good game like this should be enjoyed.
Maybe I'm just crazy and it's just a personal thing, but I know other people who feel the exact same way about the game who either stopped playing entirely or still force themselves to play it because they have other friends who are just starting to play it or they play on a competetive team.
tl;dr, really good game, unplayable after 3 months. Maybe. Who knows. Play it.

Dead Rising returns to PC with even more addicting zombie killing fun. While most of the features that made Dead Rising 2 such a great game have only been expanded and improved upon, Dead Rising 3 appears to struggle with its own identity with an odd shift in setting and a stronger focus on making a thematic experience. In addition to this identity crisis, the game itself also has some pretty poor optimization work done.
The gameplay in this game is the best in the series without a doubt. Combo weapons from DR2 have been greatly expanded upon in DR3 with a huge repetoire of absolutely insane combinations of common household items. One of my favorites is the "Split-Gun" that basically splits the barrel of an assault rifle into 5, allowing you to completely sweep a street with automatic gunfire and wipe out any zombie in your path with ease. Not only have weapons been improved, but thanks to DR3's much bigger world size, vehicles have been given much more attention. You can now combine two different vehicles together to make a new "combo-vehicle," some of which almost feel TOO powerful. One vehicle, the "Roller-Hog," allows you to cruise straight through thousands of the undead without stopping. Along with all these addicting weapons, the game itself now offers a "combo-meter" that builds up with every consecutive kill. It's a lot of fun to try and beat my own record, especially when you completely use up every weapon in your inventory and are forced to pick up anything you can find just to keep the combo going. Unfortunetly, the game's story missions and side missions are still no fun, despite them no longer forcing you to worry about escorting idiotic AI. The companion AI's are still completely idiotic, but now if you run far enough away from them, they will automatically be returned back to base. In addition to this welcome change, they also made it so that you can complete the story missions at your own pace. At no point did I ever feel pressed for time. If you miss the race against the clock, the game still features a "Nightmare Mode" that reduces the amount of time you are given and increases the difficulty significantly. So the gameplay is far more fun than it's ever been in the series, though it may have made the game a little too easy.
Dead Rising 3 on the technical side isn't as much of an achievement. The game looks good but it's not the best. The game is locked at 30fps unless you modify the game files and unlock the framerate, but doing so can cause some awkward looking, long-distance zombie animations. The game often crashes to desktop for no reason, and the controller support is there, but there are a lot of bugs associated with it. When aiming, the game will continuously zoom in and out, as if the input is being repeated. The same issue happens when trying to hold the inventory button, which can make stressful close-encounters with zombies even more stressful. Hopefully Capcom fixes these issues down the line but let's be realistic... it's Capcom... these problems will stay forever.
The story in Dead Rising 3 is just as completely idiotic and pointless as you might expect. The only good thing about the story is that you can dress up in silly outfits before cutscenes and your character will wear them throughout, which is always good for a laugh. There's also a surprise twist towards the end of the game that I didn't see coming at all and it was a lot of fun to see. But yeah, don't expect anything like "Last of Us" in this game's story. It's all about the stupid gameplay in this game, so you might end up just skipping every cutscene. One thing that bothered me about this game is that they changed the setting from the interior of big, colorful, shopping malls to a boring brown and gray city. You can still explore several different stores and houses, but they aren't as much fun to explore as the casinos in DR2. Not only is the setting not as fun, but the fun, elevator-style music that played a big role in the lightheartedness of the past games has been replaced with fluctiating tense music that icnreases in volume as more zombies surround you. It certainly gives the game more tension, but I feel as though this was the wrong choice and really takes away from the fun in the franchise. There's a few stores that still feature some fun music, but it's not nearly as common as it was in the past games, which I personally feel was the wrong call.
To summarize, Dead Rising 3 is an insanely fun zombie-killing, sandbox game with hundreds of weapons/vehicles to play with that is now and again interrupted by a pointless story and some infrequent crashes to desktop. The modification to the game files will help to improve framerates for most users, but the game overall is optimized very poorly so I wouldn't expect the best performance overall. Pick it up on sale, it's a great game with lots of fun content, but it's clear we're getting "sloppy seconds" with this disaster of a PC port.

So far, I have played this game for 250 hours; I have done a 147 episodes Let's Play of it. I've sat down in front of Final Cut Pro and looked at footage that I've recorded of it for well over 800 hours while editing the whole thing. I've written 293 pages of script about its mechanics, lore, characters, philosophy. I've listened to it's soundtrack countless times, and learned to play some of its songs on the piano.
And yet, somehow, with all of that behind me, I still often find myself thinking "I could be playing Nier: Automata right now".
Screw game of the year. This is my game of the decade.
----
Considering I bothered to post it, I believe I should go ahead and actually try to "review" the game, instead of simply recommending it. Or at least, at the most basic level, justify my affection for it.
Being a game from Platinum, you may be inclined to get it for the combat. You should probably go ahead and NOT to that. It's functional, and I find it very satisfying, but unless you have the patience to tweak it to your liking, which up to a point requires some knowledge of mechanics and a willingness to self impose restrictions, it's probably going to get very easy. Harder difficulty levels exist, but they are, on the other hand, quite difficult, personally I find them kinda boring as it seems to be more about being patient over anything else. Regardless, Dark Souls this is not. If you want a game that is difficult and has rewarding combat mechanics, Bayonetta for sword stuff and Vanquish for shooting stuff. You get Automata for the story.
I won't spoil. No one should spoil it. The story, or perhaps very specifically the story telling, is very interesting. The plot itself is nothing ingenious to be honest, and I find it quite whatever, but the context in which it exists is fantastic. The atmosphere and characterization of the world is mostly well done, though it is still a step down from the original game.
Here is something to consider:
What do you value in your gaming experience? I hear a bunch of people saying that side-quests are all fetch stuff. You "go there and you do a thing". This is, up to a point, a precise and valid complain, however... ALL GAMES are exactly that. It's just a matter of how well they hide it. We are always getting keys to get other keys. Personally, I never noticed this in Automata. Whenever a new side quest popped up I would always go straight towards it because I was curious about what kind of insight it would give me into the world. I was constantly looking forward to these new interaction and the banter that would ensue. If you can't get into this type of mindset, maybe the quests will seem like busy work, but I would also assume that you would be losing a huge part of what makes the game such a compelling experience.
And maybe that's the thing. Automata is an experience. A journey. It has an ending point but it's not really ABOUT that. If that sounds like something you might enjoy, than cool, if not, it's no use getting the game and hoping that it will give you the combat depth of Devil May Cry or Bayonetta, it just won't. It was never meant to. And that's ok.

BUYING THIS GAME WAS ONE OF THE WORST MISTAKES I EVER MADE.
I started this game up expecting to have a good time, as I did with the other Fallout games. I'd played Fallout 1, and I'd heard from almost everyone that Fallout 2 was FAR superior. I throroughly enjoyed Fallout 1, but my main problem with it was that the game was timed, and practically forced you to rush through it. Because of this, I felt as though my experience with the game was cut short. The main thing I was looking for when I started playing Fallout 2 was a lengthier game that would allow me to explore and progress at my own pace.
I got more than I could have ever hoped for.
The game started out slow, much like many other RPGs, and frankly, it was a bit boring for the first few hours. But I knew from my previous experiences that Fallout games only get better as you progress. I made it through the first few areas, and started getting a feel for how things worked, finding plenty of new quests, etc. It was becoming rather enjoyable, then I got the car, which would allow me to carry more things, and explore the wasteland with much more ease. It was very exciting, almost like getting my first car all over again. And at that point I was hooked.
Everything from that point on is a bit of a blur, I remember traveling from city to city, back and forth, looking for every quest I could possibly find. The process of finding better and better gear for my three companions was addicting, the process of ensuring the prosperity of all the settlements was addicting, the atmosphere is addicting, becoming famous for various reasons across the wasteland was addicting, the fact that the game goes into so much detail and lets you influence the way things play out was addicting. EVERYTHING ABOUT THIS GAME IS ADDICTING!
I couldn't help it, hours and hours of my life were being sucked away, and there was nothing I could to about it except keep playing. IT WAS AMAZING.
The final toll was a little over 66 hours for me. And that was all spent on a single playthrough. When I FINALLY beat the game, I felt a feeling of happiness and satisfaction that I haven't felt in YEARS. But most of all, I felt an overwhelming sense of FREEDOM. NO LONGER WAS I SHACKLED BY ITS IMMENSE QUALITY, BY ITS SHEER BEAUTY. I will never play this game for the first time again, that makes me both relieved and depressed. Depressed, because this game is phenomenal, because it is one of the best games I ever played. But relieved, because I will never lose that many hours that quickly ever again.
This game is a true gem. It is an incredible, immersive experience even by today's standards, and in fact, shïts all over most modern RPGs.
That's the problem, though, this game is TOO GOOD. DO NOT PLAY THIS GAME UNLESS YOU HAVE ABSOLUTELY NOTHING TO LOSE.

Possibly the greatest Fallout game of the series. The graphics are obviously worse, but the turn by turn combat has a great feel to it, and the story is beyond anything 3 or New Vegas has to offer.

I got my first taste of Fallout with Fallout 3, and I immediately fell in love. I couldn't think of a better game out there. And then Fallout New Vegas came along. And I'll be honest, I was not a fan. Not in the least. First glance was a desolate land that had more punishing combat and a bizarre ammo system. Fast forward a couple months and I decide to give it another go. For some reason this second foray really opened my eyes and I had a blast with the changed up combat that made you think, and the ammo system that gave you more flexability. And once I started playing I discovered something even more miraculous: the writing. Fallout New Vegas had a more believable environment, better characters, better writing. It simply felt more thought out. And looking into its development I discovered that it had some of the creators of the original Fallouts working on it. So I had to give the originals a try.
So I started with Fallout 1, of course. I bought the pack off of steam and installed it with a gusto. Finally the 5 minute process ended and I delightfully booted up the game, only to have a brilliant rainbow engulf the screen. Great. So I do some quick interneting and download the hi-res pack for Fallout 1 and Killap's Restoration Pack for Fallout 2 in order to plan ahead. Fallout 1 started, and I hit the ground running. My first isometric RPG! Woo-hoo! I immediately fell flat on my face, being killed by rats. I learned my first Fallout lesson: It's okay to run. So after hours of such trial and error I finally completed my game of Fallout 1, and was eager to continue the adventure in Fallout 2.
If you have made it this far, good lord. On to Fallout 2.
Fallout 2, to put it mildly, blew me away. Though the first level was obnoxious as hell. That Temple deserves to burn. Regardless, I pushed forward and entered the world proper. And it was glorious. Everything good from Fallout 1, Fallout 2 has. And then it expands on those. And THEN adds even more. I could do anything here. The world was truely my playground. I could, and did, do anything I wanted. The combat is incredibly punishing, forcing you to make some truely tactical decisions, however it just makes every win that much more satisfying. The dialogue is witty, dark, a tad campy at times, and heartbreaking. The depths of depravity that is portrayed is mindboggling in the modern game sphere. GTA has nothing on this. Additionally I simply love the Enclave. Probably shouldn't, but I do. I really didn't do this game justice at all, did I? When it came down to it I didn't know what to say.
Buy this, install it, download the Restoration Pack, install that, play the game, never stop.

TL;DR: I am recommending this. The Hardware is great, and it works well. The config software & community configs are not the best though.
Full Review:
The Steam Controller is a pretty solid, awesome piece of hardware. I love it. The hardware itself is great, the software is not all that great. But let's get down to brass tacks.
1. The Hardware itself.
You're going to see some folks say "it feels cheap". Well, you have to seriously wonder how they're coming to this determination. It does not feel cheap. It feels perfect for the size. If you compare this to a 360 controller, it will feel different, because a 360 controller is smaller and has more density and heft to it in a smaller footprint. The Steam Controller is solid and durable. With a really good weight distribution. It's well designed, especially if you've bigger hands. The trackpad surfaces are nice to glide over and you can tell that it was designed over time with iteration based on feedback. The important take away here is, if someone has used nothing but a 360 or XBone Controller...and they pick up this device without really holding it and using it for a bit...then yes, their uninformed opinion could easily amount to: it feels cheap. Holding it, gripping it...and using it...you begin to see why it's been designed the way it has been designed. That it's not "cheap" at all...but designed differently, and thus feels different.
They thought of just about everything on the hardware side of things. From the USB receiver, to an extender for the receiver, and right down to the buttons to pop out the AA batteries. It's a solid piece of hardware, well designed and comfortable for long sessions. The plastic is pretty much the same as you'd see with any other device.
2. The software.
Big Picture is required to configure the Steam Controller. This is the biggest and most glaring flaw. Because of the use of Big Picture...you find yourself looking at one of the worst and clunkiest UI's I have used in the last 15 years....and that's saying something. The UI is awful. Terrible. The mitigating factor here is that setting up for a game is a one time cost because your configs are saved on the cloud. Steam needs to have a standard desktop config tool. But even if they never do develop one...I have no doubt that we will see a third party solution here at some point.
It's not that you can't get robust configurations with the software provided. You can, but the UI is a pretty terrible way of having to get where you need to be. Lots of settings, buried behind multiple other areas. It's just terrible. It's not insurmountable though, and as I said it's a one time cost. Because once you get things configured properly...you're done.
3. Community Configs.
These are a double edged sword. First, while you may want to use configs from Woodsie, or others...there is NO search function to find specific community configs. I hope this gets added soon, but Valve has a tendency to ignore common sense suggestions when it comes to the steam client. (See: adding playlists to the music player)
The major problem with community configs happens to be the community itself. A lot of people publish configs and do not describe them in any way. A lot of people simply map directions to the analog stick. (Protip: if you want trackpad directional control for any game, don't even bother trying to find a comm config with this. Just use one that's close and tune it up, changing the control to the left pad, so it's using pad control) The issue is simply one of laziness on the part of a lot of folks. I came away thinking a lot of people who bought the Steam Controller should have stayed with the 360 controller if they love the analog stick so much.
4. Use.
Ive used this in everything from Undertale, to Rocket League to Fallout 4. The pad is a dream. But let's get to the real point of the steam controller: will it do the job of a keyboard and mouse, especially in an FPS?
Yes, it will. If you're willing to do a couple things. First: you have to be willing to setup the controls properly. I used Woodsie's controller setup for Fallout4, made a few modifications for my own comfort....and was ready to go.
The second thing you have to be willing to do is accept that there is a bit of a muscle memory learning curve with this device. It would be impossible to seamlessly translate what your hands do with a keyboard and mouse over to a controller in one swoop. So you need to accept the fact that you're going to have a big of a learning curve with this device. Just like you would with any other new device with a radically different approach to things. Playing Fallout 4 with this takes a bit of getting used to, but it was not only playable...but fun to play with the controller. Despite the fact that Bethesda implemented their controller support in the most idiotic way possible...the SC overcame a lot of that.
5. In closing:
The Steam Controller is a pretty awesome piece of gear. The configuration interface is complete crap though, as are the majority of community configs. I recommend the device, just be prepared and understand that while config can take a bit depending on the game...it's a one time cost. Once you're done, you're done.
