A very fun game, and interesting mix between procedurally generated Dungeon Crawlers, Pokemon and RPG's.
Build up your own base, gather materials, and gather a really huge amount of monsters that each have their own breeding combinations, From the current combinations I have I can see there's atleast 1000+ different monsters in the game.
That said, the game is basically a grindfest. The different dungeons each have their own little differences in enemies, materials and sidequests, but nothing hugely varying, so every time you go out you' still be doing the same thing over and over. I'm still having fun with it though, I'm not really playing hours on end, but I usually play a couple of floors, lasting between 20 - 40 minutes, and continue another time. But again, even though it's grindy, still really fun to play, I love these kinds of RPG's.
The only negative point is the UI and the way you get information. The UI is really oldschool, and in most cases still functions well, but in battles it can be really annoying because you can get a status effect in battles, but you have no way to even know what it does. "Your minion just got Blight!" "Sounds bad, what does it actually do? You can only find that info in the library outside of battle... :V".
It's a bit of a pain to navigate through a lot of menus to actually get the info you want.
That said, fantastic game, definitely a recommendation!

As comsumers we expect a working product for our money but there seems to be increasing cases in the games industry where QA is often not as thorough as it perhaps should be and it is the consumer who ends up with a defective product often waiting for patches that don't fix all performance problems.
Dead rising 3 needs more work in the patch department if it is to see its full potential as a great piece of entertainment.

This is a great little word game that owes a lot to Bookworm Adventures (The devs even give an affectionate nod to this in the game, check out the book salesman). Basically you are given a grid of randomized letters and have to spell words from them to damage monsters and reduce their hitpoints. The longer the word and the more difficult to use the letters are, the more damage it will do. You earn gems for slaying monsters and finishing levels and can spend these to upgrade your characters abilities and buy potions and items to help you in combat. Each level has a set of four challenges, starting at the easy first star and building up the the quite difficult crystal star. Earning stars and crystal stars unlock new things for you to nab in the shop. An addictive little game that is good for coffee break fun or for longer sessions, in fact keep an eye on the clock as its easy to lose track of time.

Monster Loves You!
And I love this game in return. It's a bit of a choose-your-own adventure game, a point-and-click title to be sure, and if that isn't your kind of game, you may not enjoy Monster Loves You!. It's short, too -- you can get through a game pretty quickly, and there's also a ton of reading to be done since the majority of the game is conveyed through text.
But-- that said, this game is still absolutely delightful for what it is, and if this IS your kind of game, you're going to have an amazing time.
Visually, the game is delightful and eye-catching. The art style lends itself very well to the game and the stories that unfold, in my opinion! The music and sound effects are also perfectly on-point, as well, and honestly the main menu music is really good, it's something I listen to by itself because it's so peaceful. The design work that went into Monster Loves You! has not gone unappreciated as far as I'm concerned.
Mechanically, the game works by giving you different actions you can take at various stages of your Monster's life. There are MANY different choices you can make that infleunce your monster's growth, and each one has bearing on not just your stats, but on both your own life and the lives of your fellow monsters. Each time you play, it's a unique experience -- there are so many different events that can happen and choices to make that it keeps things fresh well into multiple playthroughs. Your choices really do have impact and shape how you grow up and how you can later impact the world, and the monster you grow into being will depend entirely on the choices you make. The number of things you can choose to influence the story, the different ways you can ultimately shape the world if you choose -- it's really special.
For those who are interested in them, there are Achievements for completing the game in numerous different ways, and that can incentivize a person to keep playing and to see what more the game has to offer.
At the end of the day, Monster Loves You! isn't a game for everyone. It's a mostly text-based adventure, it doesn't have multiplayer, and it gets repetetive over successive playthroughs.
But it's also a solid game, and it will hold your attention while you play it. It is polished and charming, and even in 2017, the devs are still maintaining and improving it. It is a robust experience for what it is, and even if it's not for everyone -- for those who did take an interest, well, I can at least personally say that I had a ton of fun with this game, and I still pick it up now and again because the world the developers have crafted is nothing if not endearing. It is FUN -- and sometimes that's all a game needs to be. Monster loves you is fun, and well-made, and it's funny and quirky and, at times, poignant, too. It is a well-made experience that puts a smile on your face when you play it, and I think that's a pretty great accomplishment.
And it's for those reasons that I can't recommend this game highly enough. Monster Loves You, and I love this game right back.

f you are looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an Peanut Butter Chocolate Chip Cookies recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
1/2 cup butter,
softened 1/2 cup peanut butter
1 cup packed brown sugar
1/2 cup white sugar
2 eggs
2 tablespoons light corn syrup
2 tablespoons water
2 teaspoons vanilla extract
2 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon baking soda
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 cups chopped semisweet chocolate
Preheat oven to 375 degrees F (190 degrees C).
In a large bowl, cream together the butter, peanut butter, brown sugar, and white sugar until smooth. Beat in the eggs one at a time, then stir in the corn syrup, water, and vanilla. Combine the flour, baking soda, and salt; stir into the peanut butter mixture. Fold in chocolate chunks. Drop by 1/4 cupfuls 3 inches apart onto ungreased baking sheets.
Bake for 12 to 14 minutes in the preheated oven, or until edges are golden. Allow cookies to cool for 1 minute on the cookie sheet before removing to wire racks to cool completely.
And eat it!

Fallout 3 was one of my favorite all-time games. Naturally, I thought at one point, "I've played Fallout 3 and New Vegas, but I've never even heard of Fallout 1 or 2. I wonder what they are like?"
Well my question has since been answered. And my god, Fallout 2 is one of the greatest games made. As most people do, let's go through pros and cons. I'd also like to say that I haven't played this game in a long time, so I'm going off memory.
PROS:
~Story elements. You are The Chosen One, or if you are me, Penguin Johnson. You are the descendant of the Vault Dweller, a member of Vault HMHMHM (woops I can't remember) who saved his/her vault from certain doom by dehydration, when he went out into the wastes to get a Water Purification Chip. Your tribe is dying, brahmin and crops are dying as well. And only one thing can save it. I bet you guessed, "Me!" HAH! DON'T MAKE ME LAUGH! No, a G.E.C.K. In fact, if you were the saviour of the tribe, then they would be doomed because of this games...
~Difficulty. Fallout 3, while I died a few times, wasn't that difficult. However, when you ask this game for help, it flips you off, and says how about you deal with that guy with a machine gun yourself? It then proceeds to laugh as the machine gun guy burst fires and kills you instantly with a critical hit that does 78 damage, and you only had 5 health. You WILL see the death screen a lot if you are new to this game, but that's an element that makes it good.
~So much to explore. This game, has you traversing THE ENTIRETY OF THE UNITED STATES! From San Fransisco, to Klamath. What's that? Never heard of Klamath? Where have you been living, anywhere but in Fallout 2?
~So many weapons! You got your pistols, sub machine guns, assault rifles, snipers, shotguns, knives, blunt weapons, fists, fist weapons, light machine guns, miniguns, plasma weapons, laser weapons, and probably even more. And there are a lot of weapons in each of those categories.
~Characters. Characters are so unique. You have the ghoul from... the ghoul place who makes a joke about what assuming does. (It makes an♥♥♥♥♥out of you and me). Then you got the leader of Vault City, who I shot many times out of pure  annoyance.
NEGATIVES:
-This game, is so broken. I'm not kidding. You know how people say Fallout New Vegas is glitchy? NV is the tip of the iceburg of glitches, and this is the entire thing. Luckily, people have made a total conversion mod which fixes most of the game. It's called Project Purification or something like that. I can't remember.
-SPOILER ALERT! When you get the G.E.C.K. Why? Because SPOILER ALERT AGAIN the Enclave just kills your entire tribe anyway. What was the point? At least I can get revenge on them. Seriously. You have to. It's a main quest to wipe the Enclave out.
So what do I give this game? 7/10. If you didn't have to download a mod this would have been a 9/10 easily, but unfortunately, that's just such a big problem that I can't. But, get that mod, and you will be embarking on a journey, through war. And as they say, war. War never changes. THAT WAS A REFERENCE THANKS FOR COMING!

I started with Fallout 3. I'm not ashamed or anything this game came out before I even knew how to play video games. I still love Fallout 3 and the world Bethesda crafted for it. I've replayed it so much I know it like the back of my hand. Obviously being that there was a number 3 at the end of the title it got in my head to wonder "What were the past games like? Fallout 3 has introduced me to a fantastic world and I want to see where it started!" Opun looking at screenshots I remember thinking "Wow... these games look old and crappy". However as time went on I actually played Half Life 1 for the first time which really open my naive eyes to the idea that "Hey! Just because it's old looking doesn't mean it sucks!" So I looked the games up again and decided on getting Fallout 2 over 1 as it said there was no time limit to 2.
I can now say that I think Fallout 2 (and 1 respectively) is a far superiour game to Fallout 3. It's amazing how a game where many of the character sprites look the same and the world it self is clearly just 2D with an isometric view could get me so immersed. Being able to place plastic explosive at the foot of a door, set a timer, then run like hell to watch it explode is just one of many things that made me fall in love with this game. While the gore and graphics of Fallout 3 are awesome being in a gunfight with raiders in Fallout 2 is even cooler. I've had a raider aim for my head only to miss and hit the other raider coming up behind me.
Fallout 2 is one of the few games that truly made me feel like a Wastleland Vigilante, like Mad Max and Clint Eastwood in one person. I did a mission for a town where I inspected a haunted farm only to find it inhabited by friendly ghouls. When I came back to the town the mayor told me if I didn't find one of their townfolks who had gone missing at the farm they would kill all the ghouls. When I couldn't find him I came back only to find that the mayor had really done it. He really killed all those innocents. So I shot him. I've never been so♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at a fictional character in my life but unlike in a book or a movie I actually got to decide his fate and I decided his time was up.
My hope is that Fallout 4 will look back at some of these games and really try to implement some of the amazing player freedoms that this game allowed. If Fallout 4 ended up being and amazing 3d representation of this game my life would complete.
Edit: Fallout 4 is not a 3D version of this game. Not even close.

When the Steam controller was first available for pre order I decided to go ahead and buy one.  Since I was in the first batch of orders I was in the group that received it a few weeks before the formal launch.  At first I had some issues trying to use it partly because I have not used a game controller very much which in the long run may prove to be advantagious as I do not have a lot of preconceved ideas of how it should work.  The more I have used it the more I have grown to like the unique ways the actuall controlls work and feel.  Along with my gaming PC I purchased a PS 4 in early 2014, this was the first time I had ever used a game controller.  The conclusions that I have drawn from my own personal experience has been that regardless of how good a particular controller may be these devices are just not the best tool for every game type.  This is not an issue with a PC but I feel is a major limitation on a game console and has directly affected my game purchases for my PS 4.  I have only bought 3 games for my PS 4, and the only other games have been the free ones that Sony puts out each month,  At this point the only reason I have not sold my PS 4 is I like using the Netfilx, Amazon Prime Video along with some of the other streaming apps available on the PS 4.  I have pretty much been using my PC for gaming and have large game libraries on Steam as well as GOG.  I built a new small form factor gaming PC last summer that multi boots between Steam OS, Linux Mint (with Steam installed) and Windows 10 and I also have an older gaming PC that is still running Windows 7 Ultimate 64 bit.  I have made it a point to use each of these systems as well as the different installed OS's for gaming and I have experienced the same gaming experience on each of these platforms and there has been no differences in how the Steam controller has pereformed so I would definately give the Steam controller a 5 star rating.  Along with using it for its intended purpose one of my favorite uses has been to control my PC as a HTPC.  I find it very easy to navigate Windows and to use it for selecting what music or videos I want to watch.  I like the controller well enough that I plan on buying a couple more of them and plan on giving one of them to my Son as a gift.  As an after thought, although I have not been keeping close track on battery usage I have only had to replace the batteries once since getting the controller last fall.  At first I was dissapointed that the Steam Controller did not have rechargable batteries in it like the PS 4 and the Nvidia Controllers I have for my Shield Tablet and Shield Android TV box, however due to the long life of the batteries it was a good decision by Valve as it has kept the price for the Steam controller down in compairson to the other controllers that are availabe.

I can't help but feel thisi is an early access version.
But with lots of potential.
What Valve can definitely do to improve this is to set a tool similar to Nvidia's Gaming Experience where a particular game is matched with the best settings against the piece of hardware you own.
So the controller would come up with the best settings for every game you have installed.

This device have a lot of potential but it's really, really hard to truly unleash it.
There is no other controller on the market with the same amount of customable options, you can pretty much play any game any way you want (With a "Mouse&keyboard" in your palms, as a traditional controller or even with gyro controls) BUT you will have to find the combination of settings that works for you. And that will take time. You will tinker A LOT to find what really feels comfortable.
But once that's done, it is a really good experience. Especially for games that would work well with a controller but does not support it (either properly or at all).
That said, it all falls on what kind of person you are. If you are the type that likes to tinker and experiment messing with the settings is almost a game on it's own.
If you are the type that plug the device, select a pre-set from the community cloud and expect it to be flawless, you will end up frustrated. Atleast with the games where it's not that easy.
I recommend giving it a chance overall.

I remember when Bioware made good games. I want you to remember too, so I recommend this game.
Steeped in Eastern myth like a tea made from a lone tree atop a divine mountain, Jade Empire delivers a shining gem of a martial arts-action-rpg experience like an unexpected flying kick to the chest. Choose from many styles and moves, as well as a path of good or evil. The plot and subplots are pretty dope, too.
Be warned, grasshopper: the Steam version might not work on your computer very well. Luckily, refunds are a thing.

Jade Empire was... odd. An action-RPG about martial arts, set in Not-China, with the only "loot" being gems (for improving stats) and techniques (which also improve stats). You wouldn't expect it to be good, and yet, it was. It was also fun.
So, Jade Empire was another Bioware production, very much like Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic. You are the Chosen One, and everyone talks up your destiny, and your talent. The restless dead are haunting the kingdom, and you're out to avenge your people and your master, and along the way you'll be joined by a rag-tag group of companions.
It sounds very boring and by-the-book, but it really, really isn't. The characters are great, the story is told very well, and there is a twist, a genuinely well-done twist. It takes place just as you think that the story is about to end, and it is so amazing. Yes, the game's very old by now, but I'm not going to spoil it.
You have three stats, Body, Mind and Focus (Health, Magic and Special). Body defines your health, Mind gives you Chi, and Focus lets you use weapons and slow down time. Combinations of these give you conversation skills as Persuasion or Intimidation. Increasing one over the other won't gimp you in any way, so you don't need to worry about how to put in your stats. At each level-up, you get points to put into your martial arts, increasing speed, damage and chi. You have weapons-based styles, you have fighting martial arts, supporting martial arts (that don't do a lot of damage, but can be used to disable enemies by slowing them down or knocking them around) and magic skills (like fireballs). It's pretty awesome.
The companion AI is terrible, by the way. You're better off leaving them in support mode (in which they meditate and improve your health or focus regeneration, because they do almost no damage when fighting enemies.
It's a pretty stable game too. The only real bug I've encountered is that sometimes the camera will lock to a top-down view, but if you reload the game it fixes itself.
Jade Empire is highly recommended. It is a console port, but I've always played it with a keyboard and mouse which has worked out okay for me.

Jade Empire is a hidden gem in BioWare's product line. It contains the standard BioWare flourishes: romanceable companions with their own storylines, a breathtaking plot, an alignment system (of sorts). Unlike the Baldur's Gate series or Knights of the Old Republic, this game didn't catch on as strongly (probably to do in part with the Eastern theme). There are even a few twists that you might not expect.
Two of the possible romance targets don't care about your gender. While some think this to be the first step to BioWare's inclusiveness in that regard, Knights of the Old Republic came out two years earlier and had Juhani, who was only interested in female PCs...

It's not going to replace the good 'ol mouse and keyboard in any respect, but holy crap it can go around the world twice before the Xbox pad or DualShock can get their pants on.
With loads of customization options (really, there are too many to wrap your mind around at first), it can be daunting to set up the controller, but if you're not particularly inclined to figure things out for yourself, all Steam games (and a few non-Steam games if you name the file right) have community designed layouts that should be as simple as loading up and testing out. If it doesn't work, don't sweat it, just load up another, or tweak it how you see fit.
Having only used a 360 controller extensively before this, I found that the trackpads were a much smoother and more accurate experience to using thumbsticks. It can take a few minutes to get used to it, but say you're using trackball mode to move the camera, after maybe an hour or two you'll know just how hard and far you need to flick your thumb to do near perfect-to-degree turns. The haptic feedback is really awesome too. It feels like a weak alternative to traditional pad rumble features, but then you realize that it's reacting to what you're doing, and makes this controller come alive.
The face buttons are a tad small and kind of awkwardly placed, but eventually you'll get used to it. The analog thumbstick is kind of the same way. The only thing I really don't like about the thumbstick is that it can be hard to press because of where it is.
The triggers are satisfying, however I wish that the bumpers were a tad easier to push. On the other hand, the grip paddles are really quite marvelous, so I often rebind any bumper actions to these instead and it works out pretty great.
The controller also has a built in gyro, which can take quite a bit to get used to, but it makes first person shooters extremely precise when used with the camera, and it also allowed me to make a pretty good setup for controlling League of Legends.
Overall, I would say that this is the best bang for your buck on the controller market right now. It far outshines the likes of the Xbox and Dualshock controllers, and at $50 and an awesome community making layouts that work with its strengths and around its weaknesses, there is no finer controller for your PC gaming needs.

This is a cute, short, text-based, choose your own adventure story game. I feel people have been a bit harsh about it, so I'm going to give my honest thoughts. Note: I picked this up in the humble bundle, so I didn't pay full price for it (technically).
-Cute art style! Very kid friendly and appealing. It's endearing. I wish there was MORE art to look at though, as most of the game is text based. I could see this being a book series for kids! :)
-Simple and easy to follow, again it's very kid friendly. I didn't have any confusion or difficulty understanding what to do, and the text is written in easy enough terms. However, it's not "too simple."
-More on the story text. It goes into just enough detail to weave together a nice story, without being overly complex. It's all about monsters so it can be a bit "gross" and "cartoonish violence" at times, but it's not disturbing or anything. It has a very whimsical charm to it. I know I've said this already, but it's probably aimed more for 8-12 yr old age range. But as a 25 yr old adult, I still enjoyed it. :)
-Multiple endings and many personal choices. I had fun seeing 2 different endings. It's short enough to run through 2-3 times in one night if you felt like it. So it wouldn't be too much for a kid to handle.
-As I said.... it's for kids. So you might not enjoy it fully as an adult. The dialogue, story, art etc. is all aimed for a younger audience.
-That said, the multiple choice endings are a bit shallow. There's no real point playing more than 2-3 times. I don't see myself grinding for achievements.
-It's more of a visual novel then a game. There's minimal animations, which is a shame because the art style is very charming. It's mostly just point n click, reading text, and using your imagination (which is not so much of a bad thing!)
I'd pick this up on sale, if you have kids, or are new to the whole idea of choice based story games. It's a simple and cute way to get into the genre. I could definitely see myself digging this back when I was a kid too, and I still dig it now!

"The Steam controller is Valve's attempt at cornering the hardware gaming market.
I've owned a lot of controllers in my life. The Steam controller is by far the most different out of any I've used. It's to the point where I'd recommend you suspend your impression of what a controller should feel like when using it.
My first impression of the device was very mixed. The build quality left something to be desired compared to the 360/PS4 controllers, the touchpads were very awkward and I was put off by how some games require configuration before it can be adequately used.
However after using it for a little while I noticed my thought process going into it was the complete opposite of what the controller is geared toward using. It functions like a hybrid of a gamepad and a mouse. When I stopped using the right touchpad like it was supposed to be a joystick, and viewed it more like a series of buttons I moved my thumb over, I noticed my accuracy shot way up. It's a piece of hardware that grows on you very slowly and needs a little patience before it can be used effectively.
It's not a perfect controller, and not one I'd recommend lightly. It takes a lot of getting used to and isn't perfect for all types of games. However it has been an adventure getting used to it and figuring out it's little quirks, and I do salute Valve for trying something new rather than sticking to the current mold."

I started with Fallout 3. I'm not ashamed or anything this game came out before I even knew how to play video games. I still love Fallout 3 and the world Bethesda crafted for it. I've replayed it so much I know it like the back of my hand. Obviously being that there was a number 3 at the end of the title it got in my head to wonder "What were the past games like? Fallout 3 has introduced me to a fantastic world and I want to see where it started!" Opun looking at screenshots I remember thinking "Wow... these games look old and crappy". However as time went on I actually played Half Life 1 for the first time which really open my naive eyes to the idea that "Hey! Just because it's old looking doesn't mean it sucks!" So I looked the games up again and decided on getting Fallout 2 over 1 as it said there was no time limit to 2.
I can now say that I think Fallout 2 (and 1 respectively) is a far superiour game to Fallout 3. It's amazing how a game where many of the character sprites look the same and the world it self is clearly just 2D with an isometric view could get me so immersed. Being able to place plastic explosive at the foot of a door, set a timer, then run like hell to watch it explode is just one of many things that made me fall in love with this game. While the gore and graphics of Fallout 3 are awesome being in a gunfight with raiders in Fallout 2 is even cooler. I've had a raider aim for my head only to miss and hit the other raider coming up behind me.
Fallout 2 is one of the few games that truly made me feel like a Wastleland Vigilante, like Mad Max and Clint Eastwood in one person. I did a mission for a town where I inspected a haunted farm only to find it inhabited by friendly ghouls. When I came back to the town the mayor told me if I didn't find one of their townfolks who had gone missing at the farm they would kill all the ghouls. When I couldn't find him I came back only to find that the mayor had really done it. He really killed all those innocents. So I shot him. I've never been so♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at a fictional character in my life but unlike in a book or a movie I actually got to decide his fate and I decided his time was up.
My hope is that Fallout 4 will look back at some of these games and really try to implement some of the amazing player freedoms that this game allowed. If Fallout 4 ended up being and amazing 3d representation of this game my life would complete.
Edit: Fallout 4 is not a 3D version of this game. Not even close.

f you are looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an Peanut Butter Chocolate Chip Cookies recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
1/2 cup butter,
softened 1/2 cup peanut butter
1 cup packed brown sugar
1/2 cup white sugar
2 eggs
2 tablespoons light corn syrup
2 tablespoons water
2 teaspoons vanilla extract
2 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon baking soda
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 cups chopped semisweet chocolate
Preheat oven to 375 degrees F (190 degrees C).
In a large bowl, cream together the butter, peanut butter, brown sugar, and white sugar until smooth. Beat in the eggs one at a time, then stir in the corn syrup, water, and vanilla. Combine the flour, baking soda, and salt; stir into the peanut butter mixture. Fold in chocolate chunks. Drop by 1/4 cupfuls 3 inches apart onto ungreased baking sheets.
Bake for 12 to 14 minutes in the preheated oven, or until edges are golden. Allow cookies to cool for 1 minute on the cookie sheet before removing to wire racks to cool completely.
And eat it!

So, before I get into anything serious, I need to say that I NEVER leave reviews. Like. this is literally my first. I say this not to cast doubt on what I'm about to say, but instead to enforce how great I think this game has the potential to be.

I played a little of Siralim 1, but only a couple hours' worth. If I'd gotten really into it I might feel worse about Siralim 2, because it seems like it's all the same assets, same main base, same mechanics, but with a bunch of new stuff. More like an expansion than a sequel, I guess. But it would suck to go from having a great hundred-hour team in Siralim 1 to moving over to this objectively-better version where you have to start out all over again.
Regardless, it's a great game. It's the ultimate "keep it in a window and watch a movie or something in another window next to it" game, which I used to use Minecraft for.

If your goal is to explore game systems and experiment with interesting combinations and stat balancing, this is the game for you.  So long as you enjoy (or can stand) the graphics of this game, it is a great pick up for monster trainer lovers.

If you enjoyed Pokemon and Disgaea in your past, and have the time to devote to something equally as big, this is a very solid pick. If you let yourself get into it, the return on investment will be near infinite.
Active updating and supportive devs also doesn't hurt :)
Only complaint I could have is a seeming lack of DirectInput support, but the extremely simple controls make that a rather trivial matter.

A very impressive fusion of the monster-catching and role playing genres, Siralim 2 is quite literally the love child of classics such as Dragon Quest, Magic: The Gathering, and Diablo. What it may lack in visual appeal it makes up for in creativity, strategy, and uniqueness.
At it's core, Siralim 2 is a monster catching game, with you going through a multi-floored randomly generated dungeon, and building an army of monsters to fight with. What seperates this set up apart from others in the genre is that ever monster has a unique special passive ability, such as increasing your party's stats, or counter-attacking in various ways whenever they, or an ally is attacked. Many of these abilities stack, so party building becomes very strategic.
Monsters can equip one piece of gear, and several gems that give them spells (Monsters do not learn skills or spells by leveling up, only by finding and equiping these gems). However, each of these items has a set of randomly generated stats and unique modifiers, exactly like the Diablo series. These stats can be altered and changed for a fee in the player's hub base, so just like party building, this item system adds another layer of depth to how you will play.
All in all, I definately recommend this game to any RPG fan, or fan of similar strategy heavy games (Looking at you, MTG players).

The game is fantastic.  I really enjoy a lot of aspects about the game.  I really enjoy how every decision you make in the game has an outcome, whether it is good or bad. Finally, I like the difficulty of the game.  For my first game, I decided to play on the Medium difficulty, and it's not a walk in the park. My only complaint so far is that sometimes the cut scenes can be laggy, but I believe that is simply that my computer is not in the best shape to be running Deus Ex. Dead Rising 3 has had a mixed reception, in particular because of the day 1 problems it had with many people unable to play. My friend and I were fortunate in that we had none of these problems, so I can only base this review on our experience.
The game itself deviates and evolves the existing formula with a huge city map, and doesn't require the constant need for zombrex. This means you can focus all your gaming skills on surviving, killing, rescuing and dying. We played the game on normal in story mode, so we haven't even touched the DLC yet.
Another thing that's changed is the way you combine items. It used to be that in previous games, you had to combine tape or what have you with certain items. The game has changed this somewhat, to allow you to combine almost anything with anything to create a new weapon or vehicle for the mass destruction of the undead.
When you get to a certain threshold of points, you can add skill points to your attributes, the more you add to a certain attribute the more the skill evolves and adds to your repertoire of skills. It's pretty easy to understand and use, and the variety of skills and options available are good, if not immense.
The negatives of the game, based on the difficulty we played, was that it was a bit easy, except for the last level which was really rather chaotic. The game would have been harder and more fun if some of the side missions were a requirement. The game is also rather short, at 20 hours approximately for the main story, and excluding side missions and psycho missions, it's rather pricey for the hours it provdes. Having said that, it balances this with replayability, with the abillity to redo missions where you failed, and to continue to level up and find all the secrets.
It starts of pretty well, as you take the role of the Mechanic, Nick, but then the game pretty much becomes a free for all to do whatever you want however you want whenever you want. There's a 5 day time line, but since you don't need zombrez, there's no need to reset the time. Furthermore, the game encourages you to explore the vast city, and investigate the nooks and crannies. The city is brilliant, but the number of zombies only escalates the further you go into the game.
Story wise there isn't much of one, though there's a couple of cameo appearnces, but the story is really hammy bad b-movie style. This is intentional and adds to the complete comic nature of the game. You can dress up (or dress down if preferred) in plenty of different outfits. The number of combinations of weapons AND vehicles combines to over a 100. That's pretty good going.
Overall, we had 0 problems with the game, no crashes to speak of, no lock ups or anything. It's a fun ride, with more to do even after you finished the game. To be honest, I think on your own, it's a lonely experience, with two people though, it's an absolute riot.

Letter Quest: Grimm's Journey is a casual word puzzle game with light RPG elements that give the game a unique twist. Whilst the story is almost non-existant, the gameplay is thoroughly satisfying and somewhat addictive, in a way that a lot of casual games tend to be.
You proceed through mulitple stages, coming up against differing enemiesand bosses in a turn based combat system, where your attacks are determined by the words you can create from a random set of letter tiles; essentially Scrabble. Spelling longer and rarer words rewards you with higher damage. RPG elements are thrown in, in the form of upgrades to your character and their abilities, such as increased damage, resistances, critical hit chance, and so on. There are also unlockable weapons, and two further characters with slight attribute differences.
The premise of the game is excellent, though I feel it lacks a little depth at times. I would love to see the RPG elements of the game expanded upon if there was to be a sequel; maybe having a party of characters; being able to cast status effects rather than just attacks all of the time; less linear progression, etc. There is certainly a lot of potential here.
Ultimately, if you were expecting an RPG like experience, you will probably be disappointed by this title. If you enjoy word puzzle games however, this game is a pleasant change and has an interesting core mechanic that will keep you playing for hours.

This overlooked gem is one of Bioware's most unique and risky RPGs yet.  Made in a style similar Knights of the Old Republic, Jade Empire is, at its core, a Bioware RPG.  If you've played them before, you should know the formula.  Tutorial, minor thing goes wrong, first mission, even worse thing happens, and then things open  up where you're given multiple objectives at once and it's up to you to decide what order to do things in.  There's a slew of side quests and different party members to drive your progress forward as you make your way from locale to locale to stop the bad guys (TM).
In spite of following the basic Bioware formula, there is almost nothing like Jade Empire out there.  It's closer to Mass Effect than KOTOR in that the combat is more active and there's not an abundance of stats.  You level up your character by putting points into health, mana or "focus", which is spent to either slow down time or use martial weapons.  Fighting styles level up seperately and are generally made stronger, faster, or cheaper resource-wise.  You can swap styles mid-combat, giving you a number of ways to approach any given combat scenario, though in a realistic scenario you're likely to only have 5 to 6 fully leveled up.  Party members aren't too useful in fights, but you can set them to a passive mode which provides you with buffs or to regenerate one of your stats.  As a result, there's likely one character you'll use most of the game, since you can spend mana to regenerate health as well to fuel your magic powers.
Jade Empire's strength comes from its environment and story.  There are relatively few games that exist in an Eastern Asian setting.  It also has one of the most intriguing villians and pulls off a twist almost as good as the first KOTOR.  There are certainly a few flaws in story telling however, the most obvious being the karma system.  Rather than follow a strict good vs evil system, it's more of an order vs chaos meter.  In practice though, most "chaotic" choices fall under dumb choices that are nonsensical and hurt people for no reason, which is unfortunate since the main villian definitely follows the "order" school of thought but is most certainly a bad guy.  With this karma system poorly thought out, it typically just devolves into good vs bad, and if you're like me, a bad ending just feels like a non-standard game over and tend to be avoided.
Overall, I recommend Jade Empire if you like Bioware's formula, but want to try a different setting.  Expect a lot of interaction with NPCs and a slow start, but there's a lot to enjoy.  Expect your fist playthrough to clock in around 20-25 hours.

Primal Carnage: Extinction seems to slowly improve overtime and can be a lot fun when playing with or against friends. However, the game suffers from constant bugs and glitches after updates, as well as delayed mechanics and some balance issues. So strap yourselves in for the review ride and HOLD ON TO YOUR BUTTS!
Visuals: Primal Carnage: Extinction's visuals are sharp, clean and looks astonishing for an indie title. The game also features many great looking skins that does its very best to enhance the visual experience.
Gameplay: The gameplay of Primal Carnage: Extinction is solid and constantly improving. There are several game modes to choose from such as Team Deathmatch, and Get To The Chopper. Unfortunatly, most of the game's servers are either Free Roam (Team Deathmatch with no time and score) or roleplaying servers that end up defeating the purpose of an online multiplayer battle experience. The game's single player offering is a joke, as there is only Free Roam and Survival. Survival/Horde mode so far only has three maps, and in my opinion is more enjoyable when playing with a group of people instead. Other personal complaints I have are the game's delayed mechanics compaired to the original game such as not being able to control your jumps as a dinosaur and slower crosshair speeds as human. A major complaint in my opinion is the game's balance due serveral classes such as the pathfinder and carnotaurs being very op. The humans could use some improvement on their animations as they feel robotic and lifeless. The new progression and challange system is a great way to get skins but unfortunately is bare bones in its current state. Gameplay can still be fun and enjoyable but Extinction is a bit of a disapointment for those looking for a competittve multiplayer experience.
Community: The community of Primal Carnage: Extinction is in my opinion pretty toxic due to  these types of players: imature gamers , roleplayers (sigh), votekickers (the worst) and admin power abusers. Also the poor devs at Circle 5 are constantly being harassed by frustraited players after each update, and being told to make new dinosaurs. Most of the Free Roam servers are populated by roleplayer types while Team Deathmatch and Get To The Chopper are hardly populated.
The worst kind of players from my experience are the votekickers who abuse the votekick system for their own selfish needs. Votekicking should only be ment to kick players who ignore rules on servers and show disrespect towards fellow players, but any votekick should always be a last resort. But, sometimes there is always that winy stupid person that votekicks players who had done nothing to deserve being kicked are kicked from servers. This had happened to me twice already, one was me not knowing the rules that I cant play as a tyrant and ended up being kicked without warning instead of giving me a chance to change class, and I was automaticly kicked on my second time because there were two friends who were hogging the server. To be honest, just avoid these people in general because they will waste your time and ruin your fun. So how do I have fun then? Simple, I would recommend playing with friends or with people you are farmiliar on a server that is always friendly and welcome as the Primal Carnage community should be.
Primal Carnage: Extinction is still in development and I have faith that the small team of developers will do their best to make Extinction the game that it was ment to be. In conclusion, Primal Carnage: Extinction isn't perfect just as any game isn't. So hey, if your a dinosaur lover like me then this game is for you. I give this game a 7/10.
Pros: Game looks great, Lots of wonderful skins, Game is improveing, Is still fun and enjoyable.
Cons: Balance issues, Delayed mechanics, Too many Freeroam servers.

You like kung-fu nonsense? This game kung-fu nonsense, you buy kung-fu nonsense.
Okay, seriously, Jade Empire is a pretty cool take on a kung-fu fantasy epic as a video game and it still plays fairly nicely on modern systems. The graphics show their age, but asides from a few annoyingly obvious design errors, it is still a fine game that has stood the test of time. Some studio with enough resources really needs to revisit this game concept.
+Proper kung-fu fantasy setting, story and lots of lore
+Interesting and funny support characters
+Almost timeless art style that bravely tries to defy the blurry textures
+Side quests lean more on quality than quantity
+Cool fighting style concepts despite their many flaws
+Enough decision making to make the game worth replaying once at least
+Doesn't try to drag on, first time players should be able to glean around 25-30 hours of content if they do most side quests and such
-Couldn't get the configurator to work at all so had to adjust settings like framerate from ini files
-Fighting styles are very imbalanced and have functional overlaps that make some styles completely redundant
-Some styles actually push the user out of range when executing combos. This means fights with them become an odd jabbing competition where you just walk against enemies and slowly jab them to death to avoid pushing yourself out range
-There is a very limited number of moves associated with every style and upgrading them doesn't introduce new effects or moves but just boringly increases damage by 25%, attack speed by a whopping 5% or makes attacking consume less chi etc.
-Enemies often instantly rotate to track you with their attacks when you dodge and this almost breaks the original dodging mechanic from the Xbox version and leads to absurd situations where enemies hit you even though you're above them in their blind spot and so on
-Enemies can stunlock you to death. Sometimes they even spawn inside you and stunlock you immediately after that
-Hit detection is highly dubious for some attacks: I lost count how many times I saw my staff just go through an enemy with no effect while enemies hit without actually touching you
-Some cheesy boss fights (with large healthpools and infinite regeneration) and other sudden difficulty spikes. Fortunately there's usually some specific cheesy style available you can use as a counter...
-Fights are often irritatingly limited by some invisible boundary to very small areas
-Classic console design cancer: you can't skip many of the cutscenes no matter how many times you've seen them. Sometimes these are right before a fight when you can't save and if you die, you just have to watch them over and over and over...
-Not to be outdone by the cutscenes, in a couple of areas the same enemies respawn infinitely for some reason
-Plenty of outdated prerendered trivial cutscenes that should've been made in-game
(-No borderless window support)

I'll start by saying this is one of the best products I've ever bought. It's not perfect but it's a hell of a good first version of a product. I expect to get even better.
I've had the controller for at least a month now, here are my detailed thoughts.
The controller is familiar, yet foreign, it is unlike other console controllers.
It will take you at least a few hours of playing around with it to start to "get it" and train your brain to use it.  There are many settings, and I would say it is not straight forward to set up your controller.  Once you figure stuff out though, it's easy.
There are many community versions of configurations for popular games.  These make great starting points for your own configurations and save a ton of time.
If a game is unpopular you may have to make your own config from scratch.  Not hard per-se, but you have to learn how to do it.
Games played:
+ Fallout 4
+ Metal Gear Solid V
+ Rocket League
+ Grand Theft Auto V
+ Prison Architect (this game has no controller support by default)
+ Grotesque Tactics (this game has no controller support by default)
Basically you should be able to use the controller on any game outside of the fighting and MOBA genres even if it doesn't support a controller by default.
Pros:
+ Dual stage triggers are awesome, and allow you to do some really neat stuff depending on the game.
+ Battery life is great, I would say I'm getting at least 80 hours on a pair of AA batteries.
+ Very customizable, you should be able to get the controller to feel exactly how you want to.
+ Grips/paddles on the back side add even more configuration.
+ Gyro / Accelerometer support.  Awesome for shooters.
+ Comfortable.  I feel like the controller sits in my hand, rather than me having to hold the controller like the PS4 controller for example.
Cons:
+ Config software is more confusing that it probably should be.
+ Config software has had bugs in the past and probably still does.
+ Config software is still evolving.
+ Learning curve.

It's like Pokemon Go, except it won't lead you across an 8-lane highway. Also, the monsters are better.
Seriously though, I've got some 120 hours in the original Siralim, and the sequel improves on the original in almost every way. If you're not familiar with Siralim, think old-school, 8-bit RPGs like Dragon Warrior and Final Fantasy combined with creature collection and a deep customization/stats system. There are more than 500 creatures to fight or to fight for you once you've obtained them.
The creatures all have unique abilities and they all stack, so half the fun of assembling a squad of creatures is figuring out the best way they can amplify each other's abiltiies. You can forge weapons, enchant them, and upgrade them -- and you decide the bonuses they'll grant based on what works best for a particular creature.
Compared to the first, this game has a better flow, it's more accessible, and there's an abundance of variety right from the get-go -- whereas in the first game you had to complete rituals to unlock new tiers of creatures, in Siralim 2 the creatures get more exotic and strange the further you go into what the game calls "realm depths." (Kind of like levels, but with some big differences.)
The familiar creatures are all back, including favorites like the Fallen Carnage, Unicorn Vivifier and Servant Hunter. The new creatures and creature classes look awesome, and add lots of interesting possibilities for building your team.
There are new realm types, a new pantheon of deities, new types of quests, new upgrades to your castle, a rehauled nether creature system, and even greater customization through runes, gems and the character/creatures/perks point system.
And if you're new to Siralim, you'll feel right at home with the way the game presents itself and operates -- everything feels intuitive, as if Siralim is an RPG gem from the NES era. If you played those early Dragon Warrior and Final Fantasy games you'll pick it up in no time.
Basically, Siralim 2 is the best of the NES and SNES-era classic RPGs with the depth we expect from modern RPGs. It's a nostalgic RPG for adults.
A few caveats:
- The game seemed very easy in the early going, and I'm not sure if that's because I played the original and already knew how to start customizing and enhancing right away, or if the difficulty curve was softened. What I can say is that the game got appreciably more difficult by the 15/16/17+ realm depth.
- As a kid, I could listen to those repetitive 8-bit chip soundtracks for hours-long marathon sessions. As an adult, I have my limits. Even though Siralim 2 has a much wider variety of music, and different tracks for each realm type, the game thankfully allows you to turn the music off while retaining sound effects. Personally, I enjoy listening to podcasts while playing Siralim.
- Especially in the early game, sometimes it's very difficult to whittle creatures' HP down to extract their cores without killing them. If you run into that problem, unequip your artifacts so you can damage early creatures without killing them outright.
- Buddy the Cat should have his own throne! Siralim's dev has a cat named Buddy, and so do I, so I'm partial to little Buddies. Join the campaign to #CrownBuddy!!

If you like collecting and breeding monsters, buy this game.  If you like turnbased fighting, buy this game.  If you like dungeoncrawly grinding, collecting pixel loot, and min-maxing your creatures into little godlets, buy this game.  And if you like randomly generated loot that could be super, game-breakingly awesome, and the occasional randomly generated mob monster that could literally be impossible for you to kill, buy this game.
Also, Siralim 2 is a nice upgrade from Siralim (1).  Upgrade to 2 if you liked 1, but I definitely wouldn't suggest buying Siralim 1 in addition to 2, as they are very similar games, with Siralim 2 having more content and some of 1's rough edges sanded off.  In Siralim 1, what eventually drove me away was the repetition in the dungeon worlds and the odd sameness of the monsters, because they only had like one unique characteristic and limited customization.  Siralim 2 has improved by giving you more realms, more things to do in the realms, and making your creatures, rather than you, cast the spells.  So, your team does a lot more different things, and there's more opportunities for them to be uniquely awesome.  Meanwhile, there's lots of things to collect, upgrade, improve, and loot.
Basically, if you saw the trailer and got little hearts in your retrogamer eyes, buy this game.

As a fan of Bookworm Adventures, I bought this since it looked like quite the same type of RPG/Word-game mashup.
Overall it is pretty fun.  It has the same basic build-words-to-attack mechanic as Bookworm Adventures, but I still feel that that title was more accessible and enjoyable.
The protagonist Grimm here feels quite weak in the beginning, and a few levels into the game the difficulty spikes, requiring upgrades to be purchased to progress further. This is unfortunate, as I feel the game could have added a number of extra quests without much effort to give a feel of constant progress.  Instead it felt like I was constantly retreading old ground on a grind quest to earn gems. This is where it becomes quite obvious that the title was a mobile port (gems = in-app purchases).
Also, as the difficulty increases, the special debuff/damage tiles begin to clutter the board early on.  That gets a bit frustrating to deal with, especially with the quantity thrown onto the board in one turn.  I do believe their presence helps make the game a bit more dynamic, but this could have been tweaked a bit, along with the aforementioned difficulty spike.
Despite those concerns, I still feel the game is easily worth a few bucks and is a good casual game to pass the time. It seems the developers have been cool about updating the game and listening to customer concerns, so that is a plus.
One thing I'd personally suggest to the developers is to fix the fiddly way that the 'Help' button needs to be pressed to find out what a special tile is, or what the current quest is, or stats and other info.  This is where 'tooltips' would be useful.  Hovering the mouse over an item for a second or two could display relevant information somewhere on the screen.  Also, easier navigation with the keyboard would be welcome.
Other than those concerns, I feel this is a pretty nice effort overall.
P.S. The music may get on your nerves after a few loops, so do yourself a favor and lower/mute it in the Options menu!

This is a game in the style of Bookworm Adventures or Word Realms—you have a handful of letter tiles, and you have to spell words to attack various enemies. Longer words and rarer letters make for more damage, and you go back and forth until either you or the enemy falls over. Simple enough. I'm a big fan of that genre (what few games exist for it, anyway), but unfortunately, this game doesn't really do the genre justice.
This game is a lot easier than Bookworm Adventures or Word Realms, though. For one, you have a massive hand of tiles (20 at once!), so it's not at all hard to spell words. Second, enemies rarely do anything especially bad to you—they do sometimes mess with your tiles, but none of the things they do to you are particularly problematic. You can purchase all kinds of numerical upgrades (increased health, increased damage, etc.); some of the challenge missions basically aren't possible until you do this, but that's more due to strange enemy design than due to actual challenge. Also, letters don't have specific point values, but instead are just ranked into three tiers. This makes it easy to spell words that score decently high, but it also means that there isn't much reward for using really obscure letters.
Once you beat a level, you'll have to go back over it three more times, with different rules each time. There's a time trial, which is exactly what it sounds like. There's a challenge level, which either beefs up the enemies or puts restrictions on what kinds of letters you can use. And there's a "crystal star" level, which is where the real gameplay happens; in crystal star levels, different enemies have different attributes that actually affect what words you can or should use against them (one might take extra damage from words beginning with a vowel, and one might be only damaged by words that involve letters from the corner of your grid). Crystal star levels are actually fun, since the different monsters feel different and are more than just blocks of tofu for you to spell words at. (Outside of the crystal star levels, the monsters feel very, very similar—they might do slightly different attacks to you, but they don't feel differentiated from each other at all.)
As far as presentation goes, the game feels half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ The music is awful, the graphics are boring (the monsters are all basically recolors of the same five or six sprites, and they aren't even animated), and while you're not playing this game for a gripping plot, even the paper-thin story is lackluster. This game lives and dies on the gameplay (which isn't really a bad thing, since the gameplay is the most important part of any game, but still), since it doesn't really do anything to make itself pretty.
Overall, this game's only real strength is the price. If you're looking for a word-combat game that actually feels well-made, you're better off playing Word Realms. If you've already beaten Word Realms and Bookworm Adventures and just want something else in the genre, this game will keep you amused for a couple hours, but it won't reinvent your world in any sense. I don't regret the few dollars I spent on it, but neither am I clamoring for a sequel, at least not without some kind of assurance that said sequel would have a lot of improvements to it.

Like it's predecessor, "Fallout 2" is a classic game. That is to say, it comes from a time where men were real men, women were real women, and real, fuzzy things from Alpha Centauri were real, fuzzy things from Alpha Centauri.
My apologies to Douglas Adams.
What I mean is that the experience is born of a time when games demanded a lot from players, and pretty much refused to engage in hand-holding. If your character isn't especially scientific, or stealthy, or good at talking, then you'd better be able to independently figure out combat - or you're out of luck. (A well-rounded character may not be your best bet in this game. That was my approach, but I have a sneaky suspicion that the game is much more rewarding for players who choose to specialize.)
There is one section, very late in the game, which requires you to solve a rather mind-boggling puzzle. If you can't solve it, you can't progress. This isn't like the "Half-Life 2" episodes, where a major design goal was apparently for every player to see the ending. In "Fallout 2," if you can't get through, it's tough cookies.
I cheated. Maybe I'm just a simpleton, but I couldn't get through it without help. I have no idea how anyone figured it out to write the walkthrough, to be frank. (Maybe if I had spend a few hours making detailed notes...maybe.)
Like I said: Games like this are demanding, and do not "suffer fools gladly."
And if you want to know how this kind of RPG gaming got to where it is now, you need to play this classic title.

While Fallout 2's wacky humor and ridiculous references to things like Monty Python and the Holy Grail might not be for absolutely everyone, it does have a much larger world with much more content than Fallout 1 that is, in my opinion at the very least, of equal quality as it's predecessor. The story shares some similarity to the first game, as you play a tribal descendant of the Vault Dweller, sent out to find a device that will save your dying village of Arroyo from famine and disease.
The world, though, feels much larger, showing far more signs of development over the years. Old towns like the LA Boneyard and Junktown have disappeared off the map, replaced with or absorbed into new, more solidly established places like the New California Republic, an evolution of the town of Shady Sands, a San Francisco Chinatown populated by chinese refugees and even New Reno, a city of vice and sin populated by casinos, porn theaters, drug dealers, and gangs of post-nuclear mafiosos all going at each other's throats for control of the city.
Mechanically, Fallout 2 tightens up a lot of stuff from the first game. Most immediately noticeable are things like a "Take All" button in container menus, an option to push NPCs out of the way non-violently should they ever block your path, and an overhaul of the companion system, allowing you to get one extra character in your party for every two points of Charisma, with the limit maxing out at five companions for ten Charisma, and the ability to change every companion's strategic options if you don't want them accidentally mowing you down with a Vindicator Minigun.
Although Fallout 2 was criticized heavily for it's buggy and rushed state of release, with a large chunk of content never seeing the light of day, it has since received support from modders that fix all of these issues. Most notable are sfall, which makes many engine tweaks and quality of life improvements, and Killapp's Unofficial Patch and Restoration Project, which respectively patch out all the major bugs in the game and fully implement all the cut content seamlessly into the game.
All this put together, Fallout 2 is a very large, but tight package with solid mechanics and fun writing, injecting even more personality into the wasteland than the first game. It can miss the mark sometimes, but on the whole it feels like the writers had a fun time, and the game itself is well worth playing even today. Whether or not you're a lover of old-school RPGs, Fallout 2 has a lot on offer, and most of it is pretty superb.

Monster Loves You! is a simple and short Choose Your Own Adventure game. I had the initial impression that it was a point-n-click adventure, but that was very wrong.
The game play revolves around making choices. There are no puzzles of any sort in the game. The gameplay consists of clicking on different icons that start an event that then present different choices for you to pick. The first two thirds of the game incentives building up all your stats as best as you can so that you can eventually become an elder. I failed the first time through and returned to the goo from whence I came to pass on memories to future generations. You can think of those failures as premature endings with little variation depending on your main stat.
My second playthrough was more successful though and I became elder. I decided that I wanted peace between humans and monsters which was easy enough to do since I knew what to do to build up my stats very high all around. The ending variations at this point are much more interesting than the goo type. Unfortunately, while there are some funny or interesting moments, the game’s overall writing wasn’t really compelling. There was hardly a resolution in place for the peaceful ending I acquired which made it feel abrupt.
Replaying the game isn't very attractive since the CYOA aspect is heavily dictated by the desire to max your stats versus making interesting choices. What I mean is, any choice you pick that might seem fun or logical can feel wasted if you could've gained much more by making the "correct" choice. There are plenty of endings to collect for those that don't mind going through the same events over and over. In comparison, I thought Choice of Robots had a more interesting way of making game altering choices from earlier on which kept my engaged for many more playthroughs. I felt satisfied after only two rounds with MLY!.
Monster Loves You! is merely an okay game and does seem geared toward a younger audience. It functioned and didn’t do anything that made it fall into “bad” territory, but didn’t do much to take it past an average, somewhat forgettable experience. If you're interested, I'd recommend waiting until sale season.

If you do decide to go completionist, I imagine you'll quickly get bored at the redundancy and the early charming humor of the game may end up actually becoming an annoying slog to get through.  Just a possible word of warning.
I'm recommending this game enthusiastically (again, I had a great time), but believe it's priced a bit too high for what you actually get (I think it should be a $4.00 game tops).  Definitely pick it up when it's on sale or included as part of a bundle.
I've deliberately not mentioned many details of the game because I feel like the experience is best going in as blind as possible.  Even if you do spend full price for this game, I doubt you'll regret it.

This was pretty much a half-hour long visual novel, but it wasn't anything particularly interesting.  It is a really interesting concept, as you follow a monster from birth to death and help them make decisions in life in a choose-your-own-adventure format, but overall, it fails to deliver much in terms of interesting choices.  If it were on sale for a really low price and you really like visual novel games, then it might not be bad, but for most people, I'd recommend passing on it.

A Kung Fu RPG is an interesting concept with a good story throughout, full of twists and turns. Animations are done really well, being able to change between different martial arts (which are all based on various forms of Kung Fu) attempts to keep the combat fresh, but unfortunately you only have 3 moves in each style (normal, power, area), and as you spend points to level them up, it is inefficient to keep changing and you find yourself using the same moves over and over again. On 17 hours, I've completed the main campaign and done most of the side quests.
On a technical note, the game is a port of the console version and contains many glitches. There is no cursor, yet menus can be controlled via the mouse (you just have to guess where it is, or use the arrow keys). There's an error when you first load, as the game cannot find Steam. This needs to be manually fixed by moving Steam.dll into the Jade Empire directory. It's a good RPG with a nice story, but not without its flaws. I'm surprised they didn't fix some of these obvious issues before charging money for it.

Is Jade Empire a good game? Yes. However, this PC port is honestly atrocious. First off, you need to do a manual fix to even make the game run at all. I am NOT joking. They literally try to sell you something that doesn't work. Luckily, it's a very simple fix, involving copying a file from your Steam Folder into the Jade Empire Folder, but still. I almost refunded it simply since it wouldn't run, before I found the fix and took my refund request back.
As for the port itself? It's a game from the original XBOX, and doesn't even attempt to be taxing on my computer that can run ports of PS3/360 games, yet some areas stutter with single digit framerates for no discernable reason besides the engine crapping itself. At Tien's Landing, literally the second "village" area of the game, the combination of the running water from the river + conversations makes the entire game run at single digit framerates. Again, this is NOT my computer; according to Task Manager, the game is using less memory than even my web browser, it's just that the engine is so poorly optimized that it can't handle it's own game.
(And that's not even getting into the times where the camera would derp out and be hovering 3 feet off the ground and looking straight down, about 10 feet away from my character. It just happens at apparent random after loading screens, and remains until another loading screen (even if you save and load, it loads it with the borked camera) which can be problematic if a scripted event loads you away from a convenient exit.)
IF, however, you're either able to look past all that, or are skilled enough with computers to fix it, can you really go wrong with Bioware's take on the warrior monk theme? It's not their best game, but it's still a Bioware game, and worth playing (if you can find it on console since the PC version is....)

So uh...this PC port does not start off well, basically being a broken product at a first impression. As far as I know you could have the best specs and still start the game unbelievably choppy in this build for whatever reason; yet behind the scenes you are still running at 30fps/60fps when scrolling the menu or seeing the clothes on your character react to the physics... Anyway, it's weird, it's unplayable, but I will tell you to get this game, for its merits of being one of Bioware's classics, and (most importantly) being able to fix this game within this first hour and half of me looking online and fiddling with stuff (which I believe anyone can do, thankfully). You're in your right to be discouraged from this since Steam basically put up an unbroken yet unplayable product, and just leave you there alone to figure it out, but in these easy steps I think you're guaranteed to have the game itself running as it should, and in less time to try and figure it like I had to:
1. Go into your Environment Variables (easy way to pull it up is to search on the start menu and click "edit environment variables", but otherwise it is somewhere in the control panel), you'll see under "User variables for [your username]" there's a variable called "Path" - click on it, then click Edit. On the "variable value:" textbox, go to the very end of it (or hit "End" key), and copy/paste in the path of your Steam folder along with what is already there like this -
;C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam
^it has to be seperated from the rest of the folder-paths starting with a semi-colon, and note this is an example, but usually your Steam folder should be in Program Files (x86) of your hard-drive - this will resolve the "Can't find Steam" error everytime you even try to start this game...
2. The ONLY way to get rid of the chopping performance of the game is to go here -
- and download this zip folder, containing a Readme for instructions, a .dll file and C++ redistributable (vcredist_x86.exe). You simply extract the folder, and put those files in your Jade Empire folder (where your JadeEmpire.exe file is), and if you haven't installed the redistributable already (which usally comes with most games and already installed it for you) then do it again with this one supplied for you just in case. And all of this is verified and was tested on the GOG build of the game they are selling, so it should work for this build being sold by Steam.
3...that's...actually it. You can do this in 2 minutes tops. Run the game from Steam and now it should work for you, from there you just see how it fairs on your computer, but considering it's an old game, the recommeded specs shouldn't be at all daunting. If it's still giving you a bit of trouble, you can right-click on the JadeEmpire.exe, go into Properties - Compatibility, run this in Windows XP compatibility mode, along with checking "Run as an administrator" and click Apply and try to run it again. Aside from that, you'll just have to figure out how your computer fairs with it personally, but the game itself should run properly and not flat-out broken for the customer. Hope everyone sees this at first glance when buying this game and get it running, just thought you might wanna' save some time and get right into playing this gem, or at least know what you're getting into before purchasing.

This game is a love letter to those of us who loved breaking our favorite RPGs.  To those of us who built the perfect teams.  To those of us who found joy in finding that crazy spell combo the developers never thought of.  To everyone who got all the characters to level 100, just to do it.
At a surface level, Siralim 2 seems like the same indie dungeon crawler you've played dozens of times before.  A retro sprite aesthetic, 2D procedurally generated dungeons, and several other seasoned gimmicks many of us remember from your childhood are all here.  What makes Siralim special is that Thylacine Studios took no half measures in crafting a very specific experience.  This is a min-maxxers paradise.
The realms of Siralim 2 are populated with hundreds of monster types to serve as both adversaries and party members.  Each monster has a special ability, and its these often absurdly powerful bonuses that can completely change the way you play the game.  You have things like: heal your whole party for 25% of their HP every turn, lower all your target's stats to be equal to its lowest one on every single creature you attack, give your whole party 30% chance to dodge all attacks, deal damage at the beginning of every enemy's turn, gain huge damage bonuses every time you're attacked, increase your defense by a percentage of your allies', and many many more.
Boring little "+1% passive damage" perks are nowhere to be found here.  There are countless synergies and strategies to exploit, with lots of play and counter-play as a result.  At times, it almost evokes the sense of a collectable card game in how you can cobble together a seemingly invincible combo, only for something else to hard counter it and force you to think on your feet.  There are hundreds of monsters with so much variety, picking just 6 at a time for your party can be torture.  The sheer wealth of meaningful options is hugely liberating in this era of careful moderation in RPGs.
It has to be said that this is a grinder.  You will spend hours clearing dungeon floors, leveling up, getting gear and perfecting your team for the next challenge.  Thylacine Studios recognized their target audience and didn't put in much that distracts from that core appeal.  You're either going to enjoy that endless dungeon crawling gameplay and the many little mechanics that add depth to that experience, or you'll find the repetition tiring and quit early.
This one is for all of you who could never put the controller down after the credits rolled.

This is not a game. This a job you work at to be able to play snippets of a game. You need to grind to unlock breeding, you need to grind to unlock basic features of the game, need to grind for everything. I can handle some grinding but when I have to spend almost two hours to grind to breed a monster is when It goes too far.
I like pokemon, and theory crafting so I thought I would enjoy this game. I was told there would be some grind, but I said to myself " most games have some grind invovled, I can handle it" but I could'nt. I already work during the day, when I come home in the evening spending more time working to unlock content is the last thing I want to do. I won't spend the fifty hours it takes to grind for all the features, breed a few monsters, and beat the storyline.
Sadly the game looks fun and interesting beneth all that grind. It seems to me from what I have seen that most of the monsters are not useless, there are a few which are purely fodder, but most have powerful abilities if used correctly. The aspect of breeding two different monsters to get a third brand new monster is cool as well. The planning invovled with defeating bosses is something I enjoy, the theory crafting of different abilities is something I really enjoyed in card games and pokemon myself. The deveoper seems to think that the insane grind is healthy for the game, which I disagree. I respect myself and my time too much to spend hours to be drip fed content. I don't enjoy being a chinese gold farmer.
If you have don't better things to do than grind, or if you enjoy the theory crafting enough to waste massive portions of your time, or don't work and can spend ten hours a day grinding, then this game is for you.
I think the real problem is how the early game is such a slog, you get no tools and just have to slowly grind your way to unlocking the actual game. I thought I would be able to play through the storyline and experience a portion of what the game has to offer without reptitively killing the same mobs over and over and over, but I was wrong.

Prior to this game, the only game from the Saints Row franchise that I have played is Saints Row IV. I throroughly enjoyed SR4 and when I saw that this game was free I was quick to purchase it.
This was a great choice. I actually enjoyed this game more then Grand Theft Auto V (played it on console) as it does not take it's self seriously meaning that the shenanigans in this game are much more enjoyable.
Saints Row 2 has so far provided me with not only an especially entertaining story, but also a great cast of characters, a wide range of customisation, a ton of side activities and just a ton of fun in general.
This game is fantastic, and even better with the mod called "Gentlemen of the Row", which I highly suggest for bug fixes throughout the game. Personally, this game has ran well for me and I have really had no problems with the port- even the controls are fine. Currently (17.6 hours in) the game has only crashed once, despite others experiencing frequent crashes. This is probably due to my setup which is not fantastic so if you are playing on a low end computer, I don't think crashes will be a problem.
A problem with Saints Row 2 however, is that if you wish to play with a friend it can be quite annoying to set up. If you do wish to play co-op then I suggest you use a software called "Evolve" as I have no issues with it so far.
Graphics wise, the game doesn't necessarily hold up to todays standards, but that is surely to be expected with it coming out 9 years ago (at the time of this review). But, they still look nice and if it really annoys you that much, Gentlemen of the Row provides certain graphical upgrades for the game.
Overall, this game is fantastic and certainly worth the buy if you are interested in games such as GTA.

The art of this game, meaning the story, voice actors, music, designs, concepts, ideas, gameplay devices etc, are all excellent. Fantastic, actually. However, the Director's Cut has a large number of technical problems. There are many bugs and other defects that had already been solved in the original release which are here again in the Director's Cut. If you are thinking of buying this game because it's a great deal, consider the complaints at the Eidos Montreal user forum:
There are problems like bad/jerky framerates, shader and lighting defects, bugs with the non-lethal weapons killing targets, and so on. The game could be a fantastic piece of entertainment, and it does still somewhat shine through despite these defects, but you should be sure about what you're getting into.

The Director's Cut was a different code base, ported back from the Nintendo Wii (?), not the robust PC codebase that was bug fixed.
