Have you ever wanted to play a Batman villain? Wanted to laugh at your antics one minute and then uncomfortably consider the extent of your psychotic sadism the next? Then this is the game for you.
Saints Row 2's appeal doesn't lie soley in its zaniness, but from the way it interplays the underworld rise to power with the wacky nonsense going on when you're playing in the sandbox, making it one of the most effective portrayal of an RPG player character I think I've ever seen. Your character is outright superhuman by the standards of most of the people around them, and seems to be fully aware of it, best demonstrated in the opening missions where five minutes after waking up from a coma, you break out of jail effortlessly and then, upon learning that your best friend is being threatened with the electric chair, storms the courthouse and breaks him free as casually as one would pick up groceries.
The game more or less keeps up that tone throughout, playing up your antics on one hand while never shying away from your brutal disregard for civilization on the other as you tear your way through the three gangs that have taken over the city in your absence before taking out the megacorp hoping to gentrify the city by forcing you out. Your character, which you design but don't really control, is best described as a vengeful hedonist, taking power to satisfy their basic desires of merriment and mayhem while raining down increasingly imaginative hell on whoever crosses them.
The only real criticisms I would put forth are twofold: firstly, the minigames ramp difficulty beyond the point of logic, which creates some hilarious but frustrating scenarios like needing to flee from news vans that can drive at 130 mph and swarm like locusts, often literally boxing you in against a wall if you make the wrong move; and secondly, the ending is a tad weak, and feels more like scraping a final annoyance off your checklist rather than any sort of culmination of your rise to power.
All in all though, Saints Row 2 is a barrel of fun and I absolutely recommend checking it out.

Letter quest is essentially a scrabble game with RPG elements. You spell words based on random letters (ie, like Bookworm) and deal damage to monsters based on the complexity of your words. You earn gems over time that will let you deal more damage, take less damage, or other miscellaneous effects. There is a story, but it is frankly not very good (Grimm is looking for a pizza...).
Normally I am quite critical of free mobile games being ported to PC with a big price bump. Thankfully Letter Quest is very well done and is worth the price. The mobile version is free, but supported with lots of IAP - the PC version is balanced so that you can play normally and get enough gems normally to afford to upgrades that you need. Plus you can directly type in words and such, so in many ways I feel that the PC version is going to be superior for input purposes.
The developers, who are still active (~9 months after the launch of the game), actually support the game and make it quite fun. The game is going to be a challenge for those who don't have a big vocabulary, but if you play enough the power-ups will help you out a lot. I actually learned a bunch of new words by trial and error and I like that it shows the definition for most words that you can spell (apparently the game dictionary is ~190,000 words).
The graphics are repeated a lot but are vibrant and cute. If there is any constructive feedback I can give, it is maybe that a easy mode can be added for kids. Once you are through the first dozen or two stages you really need to be spelling 5-6+ letter words or you are going to be spending forever grinding for potions.
In all a great find and I hope the developers make some other cool games in the future.

4. Other words will make you laugh that they are in game
5. Other other words will make you hungry (see #1)
6. You have a scythe.
7. Did I mention Bacon?

There are only so many ways to implement a word-based game, searching, unscrambling, typing, so standing out of the crowd can be a bit of an issue. Happily Letter Quest has found a winning formula. A combination of humor and tried and true RPG-lite mechanics incentivise and distract from the fact that you're essentially doing primary school English homework.
The aesthetic is decidedly cartoon-ish and crafted with a younger audience in mind but it shouldn't be off-putting to older players. The story is silly, lighthearted, and sparse but is punched up by the amusing and word-play filled enemy descriptions. Finally the sound track is fun and energetic but it only plays one track per level so the looping can get in your head a little if you spend more than a couple minutes on a given level. If you enjoy them though you're in luck as the soundtrack is included with the base game.
Speaking of school work and a younger audience, it was nice to see the developers not pass up the educational opportunity inherent to this genre. Every time you type a valid word you can choose to see the definition and it displays the definitions of every word you actually use. At first this seems pretty useless, for the most part you'll only be typing words you already know, but it's actually a clever bit of forethought by the developers. As anyone who regularly plays word games or does crosswords can tell you, it's very easy to "cheat" at a game like this and use program to come up with the best words given your letter set. By displaying the definitions of all the submitted words it almost makes using an assist like that actually more educational than just typing words you already know. What I'm saying is expand your vocabulary by embracing the urge to cheat.
As far as the RPG mechanics go they've definitely been paired down for both general simplicity and with the intended audience in mind. You can upgrade several aspects of your character (damage, armor, health), apply various passive buffs that are upgraded though an XP system, unlock weapons, buy potions, and even unlock more characters. Another interesting mechanic is the weaknesses that the bosses have. Things like multiplied damage from double letter words or words with both an E and a S, force you to really think about your word selection. Several of the enemies also will restrict your letter choices by poisoning tiles, locking them down for a few turns, or even changing several after every attack. It's a fairly unique mechanic that helps keep what could be very repetitive battles fresh.
Overall, Letter Quest is very well made, especially for a two man team, and can be enjoyed by most any player but will especially be of interest to fans of the spelling genre and those looking for a light educational experience. It doesn't take terribly long to complete the main levels, 4+ hours, but the inclusion of some hard levels, special objectives to complete on each level, and a number of unlocks definitely make the non-sale price point fair.

So what’s the deal?
Well you combine random organized letters which appear on your screen and use those to from words like Minotaur and depending on how many letters you used you deal some damage to the evil creature which dares to stand in your way. Some might take one or two words and others take literally a dozen and you might crush under their bulkiness. One can not always be victorious.
If you beat a stage you’ll notice that you only gained one star. Those stars aren’t your rating on how well you’ve done but just an indication that you’ve beaten this level of the stage. Every stage has four level and the last one is a so called Crystal Star level. I doubt I have to tell you that those are actually very hard.
Every Stage has the same levels. Level one requires you to defeat all monsters, level two is a time trial while level three is a special challenge and well level four is an ultra tough crystal star challenge.
So there’s enough for you to do.
Once you progress through the game you’ll encounter various figures on your way to slay all evil!... with the help of words of course.
Anyway. Those figures will aid you in your battle against the vile creatures of evil!
Well for some gems. Nothing in this world is free. Sadly.
Whether you’re in the need for some more health points or you want a
and therefore stronger scythe, they have exactly what you want.
Besides the obvious health points, armor and weapon upgrades you can also buy certain Books which will give you specific bonuses. One let’s you deal 20% more damage with double letter words like Bubble or Battle. Monster drop 8% more gems with another book. You can also upgrade those books. For every evil creature that you spell to death your current book gains experience points. Sweet ain’t it?
Moreover you can also go ahead and buy a health potion so you can take a beating for some longer.
What would any RPG be without Quests? Well no RPG … I guess.
Letters Quest has a ton of Quests for you. With every Quest you complete you gain a certain amount of gems which you’ll need to upgrade yourself or buy some potions.
Quests require you to do certain things like take 200 damage or use broken tiles twice.
There’s just one thing bugging me … The game’s only playable in english.
So if you’re not fluid with the English Language then I’m afraid you either have to have a Dictionary besides you while playing or you better brush up your English skills.
Well if you’re either a native speaker or rather fluent in English I’d say this game is really worth your time. It’s fun, addictive and can be quite frustrating at times. You’ll feel the pain once you look at the random Letters on your screen and you can’t come up with a specific word in order to kill a ghost which takes only damage from 6-Letter words.
Even if you’re not too fluent in english this game could also be a good exercise to brush up your English. Especially since the loading screen gives you some hints on what to spell with the letter Q for example. Like Qua.
So that’s pretty much it.
Go ahead and use the random Letters on your screen to spell words in order to slay those vile creatures! I’ve said pretty much all that I wanted to say at this point.
... then this game is definitely something for you. I greatly enjoyed the game and despite its rather cute looks it can be rather challenging at times.
Despite all that I highly recommend it. Especially for you spelling bees out there.

*EPISODES 1-5*
The first four episodes of Telltale's Minecraft game are pretty enjoyable. Some episodes are incredibly short, but there's a charm to the story and characters that makes it all enjoyable. But in a strange choice, the main arc of the adventure is wrapped up by the end of Episode 4. It's done well and may actually cause a geniune emotional reaction, but since everything gets more or less resolved, Episode 5 ends up feeling pointless. There's still enjoyment to be had, it just feels tacked on.
As such, I have no real desire to play the other episodes being released as I feel like I already got the complete experience. If you're a fan of Minecraft, then the first four episodes are worth playing through. But if you're skeptical about the whole idea of Minecraft having some kind of story to it, then it's atleast worth checking out at sale price.

Oh boy, here comes the unpopular opinion review. PC gamers be warned, I had to play this in windowed mode, because fullscreen is broken, and at sub 1080 to have a kind of steady 60 frames, which is entirely necessary for this game.  I think this game is okay at best. What you're getting here in this pricey package is a glorified bullet hell with melee combat thrown into the mix and some RPG style elements that hardly matter. It comes along with lackluster visuals and very bland enviorments. Theres maybe two notable scenes in the entire game I can think of off the top of my head that I thought were cool and fresh compared to the decrepit city youll be looking at for about 70% of your play through. Which is about an 8 hour campaign your first go around. The game puts you incharge of an android who is skilled with blades and coupled with esentially what is a mini turrent that floats over your shoulder at all times. The concept initially is pretty cool until you realize how flat the whole experience is and how god awful the camera work is. I've never had to deal with a more trash lock on system in any game prior to this. I could be looking directly at an enemy I intend to be killing and infact had already engaged only to have my lock on decide that it wants to target some other enemy behind me several meters away. Now this would be forgiveable if it was just a fluke every once in a while but its so frequent that It left me hating combat. Unbelievably frustrating after a while. It doesn't help that once the enemy that has been locked onto has been killed it doesn't automatically adjust to another enemy. No, it requires that you manually engage lock on again and hope that its atleast going to focus on an enemy within your view already. This problem is even worse in the "side scrolling" sequences, in which the camera goes into a fixed angle and you engage enemies from either the front or behind you. This part of the game is actually pretty cool and sometimes fun but can also be frustrating due to the camera being too far away to see the cluttered groups of enemies telegraphed attacks so you can attempt to dodge. I really struggled to care about the characters, the story and the overall lore that was being presented to me. It's made even harder to care about when the majority of back stories that explain whats going on and why things are the way they are locked behind futrue playthroughs. Which in my opinion is a shame, because some of the more interesting plot points that could have save the story are missing until you beat the game. I think one of the redeeming qualities in this game are the boss fights. But only about half of them are actually good by design. Initially the first boss you come across as you get officially dropped into the game is found in an amusement park and the overall fight is awesome and really takes advantage of the bullethell concept in this action game. Theres another really solid fight where it requires more timing and dodging to exploit your enemy. But these small moments dont save the game in the long run and leave something to be desired. I can go on and on about all the things I didnt like about this game but I hit the major complaints here. I don't think this game is worth the money, and honestly not worth your time.

People often talk about whether or not video games are capable of being art or not. Roger Ebert once wrote it was impossible because player agency messes with the artistic vision of the director. That's a whole can of worms on its own, but I'm here to say that Nier: Automata has proven Roger Ebert wrong. It has everything to do with the game's director being very aware of what players do when playing video games, and considering as many possible decisions and actions players can make, Nier: Automata accomodates player agency like no other game I've played. Concrete examples are hard to give because it will smash all the surprise, but what I can say is that it is all - for the most part - on the narrative end. And if that's your one concern, then select the game's easy mode and enjoy a huge breath of fresh air in video game development.

My Review of Humble Abode:
Humble Abode is a good start for Venomyth Game Studio's first game. It's not a very long game but it does have some issues that the developer should probably address.
Pros:
-Good attempt at story telling. The game has an aurora of mystery around it (not all of its questions are answered however) so a possible sequel may be in the works.
-The puzzles although simplistic enough do require some forthought. Its not them most challenging puzzles you will ever see though (lots of item searching and such) but the game doesn't overstay its welcome so I can give it a pass.
-Two different ending: One good and the other bad depending on what course of action you take in the end. It doesn't add replayablility but it encourages you to load up your last save and find the other ending.
-The game is a cheap price so you get about two hours of gameplay for a dollar. Not bad!
Cons:
-The game does have some bugs and scripting errors. (Ex. In the guest bedroom, Eddy heres the door open and remarks that the killer may be in the room. After that cutscene, if you do back to that spot the same cutscene will play again even if you already saw it)
-The game lacks a "objective" screen for finding out where to go and what to find. Granted Eddy's home is not very big but that could definetly be a useful thing to add in an update since the game require some code entering to continue in spots.
-Depending on how good or bad you are at puzzles, you could potentially get stuck if puzzle solving isnt your thing.
Overall, if you want a thiller that can last you through the afternoon try this game. It may not be for everyone but its fun while it lasts.

This game proudly proclaims to be an RPG, I disagree with that label, but still enjoyed the game a lot.
Letter Quest is a turn based combat game where attacks are made by forming words from a 3x5 random field of letters. Certain letters are worth more damage, corresponding to their point values in Scrabble actually.
Battles give you gems which allow you to upgrade various aspects of your character (more damage, more life from potions or more specific things like 40% extra damage from words containing double letters), and it's quite a nice little system. Earning plenty of gems and upgrading your character will make the game a lot easier, but at no point totally break it to the point of being too easy.
The "story" goes through a grand total of 40 stages as you follow Grimm's titular Journey to get a pizza. It's utterly forgettable, but cute enough I guess. Do not expect to play this for the story though. Each of the 40 stages has a normal mode, the first star, a time trial mode where you have to be fast, the second star, a challenge mode where enemies have special traits (like not taking damage from 4 letter words). Getting all three stars in a stage unlocks the hard version, which has stronger enemies and another set of special rules (like not having 'A's in there).
All in all there's plenty to do, and the core gameplay is fun enough to last you through it.
It's not the most innovative or deep game in the world, but I'd still recommend it.

It is basically a cross between a form of scrabble, and the free flash game, "The Black Knight" Personally, I wouldn't play something like this unless it were free; However, in the interest of fairness, I do see a very positive use for a game like this: Home Schooled teaching. This would be a great game to get children involved in vocabulary, because the object of the game is to use the scrabble-like pieces to form words. The more complex the words, the more damage you do to your opponent, the more loot drops, the better your score etc. This would be a fun game to get kids involved in learning, without the need for their noses to be stuffed into a book. All in all, I think the concept is neat, the layout is simplistic with no real learning curve, and it was fun. I would recommend it to those who would enjoy this type of game.

Yes! Yeah, I really wholeheartedly recommend it!
For the lovers of word-puzzle games, narrative driven RPG-lights, or for those who played and loved Bookworm Adventures, Letter Quest delivers lots of brain-teasing fun.
Bookworm Adventures (BA) was so much a clear inspiration, one could confuse it as BA's spiritual sequel. It's all there, the stats-enhancing book items, the one-off potions, the funny short dialogues and descriptions. The devs acknowledge the influence in first few levels, but one could argue they nicked truly a lot of it's ideas.
But I think LQ still stands tall on it's own. There's the nice theme of silly macabre grim reaper going for a pizza, the drawings are nice, fluid and distinct, and there's an addition of short semantic explanation of every word you spell. For foreign speakers (like me) and teachers (like - again - me, hope I could play a German version!) it's a godsend fun way of learning more vocabulary.

The best way to describe Siralim 2 is if Dragon Warrior Monsters, Disgaea, and Pokemon Mystery Dungeon were fused into a single game that's greater than the sum of its parts.
I got this game like 30 hours ago and have clocked in nearly 14 hours. I had to sleep and work in that time period as well. Literally all my free time has been spent playing the game, because it's that addicting.
The game slow-rolls you all the increasingly complex systems one at a time, and nothing ever gets old. I haven't encountered anything particularly game-breaking except for a few spelling errors and some awkward controls issues, but it's been overall smooth sailing. I've never felt lost or inundated with information, and the in-game Library is very helpful for the most part, and contains information on pretty much every question I've had so far.
The graphics are generally good, for being pixel art, and the overall aesthetic is really similar to games like the original Dragon Warrior Monsters. The music isn't awful, but the loops are very short so it does get repetitive pretty quickly (spending more than 2 or 3 minutes on a floor means the music will loop eight times or so). Some floors do have great music, though, so it kind of evens out. Since each floor has its own tileset, interactables, and music, each floor does feel very well put together.
The gameplay is solid overall but there are some complaints I could make. Breeding monsters is a blast, and "catching" them (extracting their cores in battle) is generally not particularly difficult. Leveling up creeps to a grind around level 15-20, but luckily dungeon grinding always feels impactful. You're usually not just farming for EXP, you're farming for Power to complete your rituals, resources to hatch eggs or summon monsters from cores or buy items or modify your artifacts. Or favor with a particular God. Or hunting for Artifacts. Or looking to extract Cores. There is just so much to do on every floor! Completing a single floor might only get you part way on all your aforementioned goals, but since it usually generates progress on all of them  it winds up feeling pretty good. Boss battles have been challenging but staggered at just the right pace for me- during the last boss fight I beat him with 2 of my 6 monsters left alive, both pretty low on health and drained of MP. Earlier ones were a bit easier, but that just makes me believe that the NEXT boss will be even more of a challenge.
There are lots of systems to get familiar with- understanding artifacts is a big one. The breeding compendium appears to have thousands of entries so there are tons of opportunities to create new, interesting monsters whenever you get tired of your old ones. There's upgrades to your base that unlock new opportunities for you, from sidequests to vendors to re-rolling stats on your equipment. It seems almost endless, but nothing feels out of place.
This is exactly the type of game I've been dreaming about for years. I've been nostalgic for the original Dragon Warrior Monster games for a long time, and this scratches that same itch tenfold.
What I'm trying to say is, if you think you'd like this game, you'll probably love it. I've already talked two people into buying it and they both are hooked. It's a fantastic game.

If you love min-maxing your team to crush the opposition, and you're willing to look past some odd keyboard mechanics, this game is a must-have. Just as warning: the first time I played , the clunky controls (it's a bit like a console emulator)  really put me off, and I ended up quitting after about 20 minutes, but the creature-breeding and party mechanics drew me back.
When I started playing it again, I just couldn't put it down - and after I while, I barely noticed the interface at all. In other words, the gameplay is more than sufficient to justify looking past its dated interface.
There is a surprising amount of complexity in the stats, spells, creature traits, artifacts, and myriad other game systems, but instead of feeling overwhelming or disjointed, the various pieces integrate nicely. Essentially, each system provides a different set of levers for modifying the core gameplay mechanics. There's also sufficient breadth and balance to allow an incredible variety of viable play-styles.
The pixel art is well done, and the creatures (for the most part) aren't just recolors of the same image. In fact, the handful of bad images are quite jarring next to the rest of them (I'm looking at you, Glutinous Slime). There's a definite NES vibe to the whole thing.
Even if you're on the fence, I'd recommend giving it a try; you'll know whether it's for you *well* before the 2-hour limit on returns.

Executive Summary:
When the engineering of an object makes its use effortless the result is sublime.  The steam controller is exactly this.  If you are willing to game with wireless peripherals or Cherry-MX sounds like a soda flavor, then you should stop reading this, find $50 and buy this controller.  It does take some getting used to (about as long as it took to learn mouse and keyboard movement back in the day).
Pros:
- Haptic feedback
- Everything is configurable
- More buttons than you can shake a joystick at
- Two touch sensitive pads
- Batteries!
Cons:
- My hands seem to sweat more
- Big picture mode is still developing
- Games that support traditional controllers may glitch out when the steam controller sends keyboard and gamepad events
- The controller's emulation of a traditional gamepad isn't that great (the touch pad doesn't emulate a joystick very well, the triggers can be way too sensitive)
The controller felt very light until I put the batteries in, and then the added weight gave it more substance.  The hardware is remarkable. The software needs to catch up.  Some of this can be adressed by Valve, but some of it will be on the game developers as well.  If you're a developer please do your best to support or at least have a recommended configuration for the steam controller.

I got the Steam Controller just before Christmas 2015.
Pros.
Very customizable.
Plays any game compatible with Steam overlay.
Comfortable IMO. Will vary per person.
Haptic feedback can let you know exactly what you are doing.
Cons
Hard to get used to. You will need to take time to adjust.
Most keyboard/mouse games need drastic adjustment to be playable.
Finding a configuration that works for you isn't very easy. Only "most used" tells you what profiles are "rated". You have to actually pick them to see what they are like unless they come with a detailed description in the text box.
For me, the pros vastly outweigh the cons, as I can't properly use a keyboard and mouse for many games. Most people don't have the physical problems I do, but I bet many prefer the feel of a controller. Getting used to the SC will be different for different people. It started to frustrate me at first, but it was worth taking time to get used to. I still need to continue this.
For configs, they just need to update the way the community binds work, and you need to learn how to make your own binds when neccessary. These are not major problems IMO. In fact, they might be too minor to call "cons".
The short version. If you're a hard core competitive gamer, then you'll likely want to stick to keyboard and mouse. If you just want to play all your PC games comfortably, and more accurately, this is your best bet. Just find or make a good config, and make sure you take time to get used to the controller.

I am about 10 days in using my Steam Controller and I love it, but it does have one or two issues.
+ It's well made and to me feels pretty solid
+ The pads are surprisingly easy to use
+ It is customisable - you could spend a whole evening playing with configuration settings.
+ Community submitted configurations, some games have submissions by the developers.
+ Love the two back buttons.
+ Takes some getting used to, but I'm pretty much there. Holding an XBox controller now feels wierd.
+ It works on Windows desktop straight away.
+ The on screen keyboard is the best I've used.
+ Was impressed with how well it worked with a variety of games, including racing, platform, top down shooter and slow paced, turn based strategy games.
- It is well made, but it is bulky. The big downer for me is the X and Y buttons are just a little out of reach, and I don't have small hands.
- I can see the pads getting damaged quite easily, making me permanently paranoid.
- It is customisable - you could spend a whole evening playing with configuration settings :) The configuration is great, the amount of stuff you can do is amazing, but sometimes you just want to jump into a game and go.
- To get the most out of your new Steam Controller, be prepared to start using Big Picture mode. You can understand why Valve did this, but a lot of the features for Steam Controller are only in Big Picture mode.
- haven't tried fast paced, RTS game yet, but i can only imagine my thumb will hurt after an hour.
- The wireless USB reciever that comes with the controller is tiny - make sure you keep it in a safe place (or leave plugged into PC!).
Overall, I think Valve have made a decent controller.

It's not hard to make this game work on Windows 7, so buy  the game while it's on sale. It functions perfectly, and the game is fun to play. It's got good acting, an enjoyable script, fun characters, a higher depth of interaction than many games, and replayability.
Detailed instructions for playing the game on Windows 7 are below (No extra downloads requierd):
-go to C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam
-copy Steam.dll
-go to C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Jade Empire
-paste the Steam.dll
-change the name of the JadeEmpireConfig file to JadeEmpireConfig-original
-make a copy of the JadeEmpire file
-right click and open the properties of the original JadeEmpire file
-click the compatibility tab
-activate the "Run this program in compatibility mode for:" checkbox
-click the dropdown list, and select Windows XP (Service Pack 3)
-click the "OK" button on the bottom left of the Properties window
-change the name of the original JadeEmpire file to JadeEmpireConfig
-To run the game you can: 1) open the file you just altered (JadeEmpireConfig), or 2) while in Steam, launch the game, and when given the option to launch the game, or the Jade Empire Configurations Utility, launch the Jade Empire Configuration Utility.

Dead Rising 3: Apocalypse Edition delivers some gruesome zombie kills, great weapon combos, and provides a unique sense of humor in a genre overflowing with serious tones and dire circumstances that can be a little too much more often than not.
Dead Rising 3 isn’t a new game. In fact, the title was released as an Xbox One launch title last year, and was met with generally favorable reviews. The series has been one that sometimes can struggle to find an identity, and at other times can seem hard to identify with. Dead Rising 3: Apocalypse Edition isn’t immune to these issues from prior games, but does a great job to push the series forward, and provides one of the best experiences yet.
====================================================================================
THE WORLD, STORY, AND QUALTIY OF ‘DEAD RISING’
Dead Rising 3: Apocalypse Edition includes the story from the title that shipped back in November of 2013, which finds our hero Nick Ramos surviving, and eventually thriving, in yet another zombie apocalypse. This time we are put in to the city of Los Perdidos, an interpretation of the City of Angels, but more importantly, a huge open world to explore as much as you’d like. Each little subsection of the map feels somewhat unique, if only because one has a power station, one has a communication tower, and another has its token distinguishing building being a shipyard. The city itself has some stunning skyboxes, and takes advantage of a new engine to make the city seem somewhat realistic. Normally I would grade the city on how “alive” it felt, but you can probably guess that the city didn’t necessarily feel alive. It did, however, feel like a city that has experienced a terrible tragedy.
Buildings are mostly still standing, and there are certainly some interesting buildings, but some of the most interesting places on the map are actually collectibles, called Tragic Endings, the player can interact with and shows some sorrow for the scene that played out. More interesting than the strange shift from slicing and dicing zombies, is the layouts of these scenes. Finding bodies hidden and still cowering inside a crate that is atop a mountain of crates, a family that had a shootout, or stumbling upon a scene with teddy bears and broadswords strewn about puts you in that world, and makes the scenario a bit more real.
The story in Dead Rising 3 does a great job of being cohesive, understandable, and just overall good. I couldn’t think of a better word to describe it. I fully expected after playing for a while for the story to fall off, get too silly, and really lose my interest. That moment did not come. I found myself wanting to get through the story, not just because I had this review to write, but the characters were interesting, the dialogue was solid, and the acting was on point. All of this delivered to me, the best Dead Rising story yet.
None of the other entries in the series really grabbed me the way this one did.
The Untold Stories of Los Perdidos is an add-on that comes in the Apocalypse Edition, and while the stories are in concept a novel idea, they don’t really expand too greatly upon the existing framework. Don’t expect anything earth shattering or brand new mechanics, but they do offer an interesting way to explore other characters within Los Perdidos. Playing new stories like that of a duty driven spec ops team member, or an insane bike gang leader, or member of the survivors. The stories are interesting, the characters fascinating, but the setting, weapons, and skills remain mostly unchanged. Playing these stories following the main campaign will give some intriguing insight and give you a glimpse of the early stages of the outbreak, but also can be a bit easy to breeze through if you’ve leveled up your character, as attributes and abilities are inherited from your main story.
TONAL SHIFTS, GAMEPLAY DISSONANCE, AND SO MUCH SLAUGHTER
The issue Dead Rising has always had has been an identity crisis of sorts. I addressed this in a preview, but what became evident in Dead Rising 3: Apocalypse Edition is that the game doesn’t really have a crisis, it embraces the wacky, insane world they’ve built.
Psycho missions aren’t a new addition to the series, but did seem to be more initially offensive than in previous entries. An obese woman on a scooter farts and vomits her way to, around, and through you on occasion, until you defeat her. During the battle you slip on her vomit, and maybe even wretch yourself at the character. Of course the end of the fight is punctuated by one final burp, or fart, I don’t really know, it was gross. This mission was the turning point for me. I stopped caring that the character was so disgusting, and that prior characters were racial caricatures. I began to understand that these caricatures were actually part of the charm of Dead Rising.
I was impressed that a character in a scooter could make me feel so strongly about her, and more impressed as the character had very few lines of dialogue.
After settling on the fact that Dead Rising was designed to be goofy, insane, and sometimes flat out weird, the game showed itself to be utterly enjoyable. I didn’t care that the story went to some dark places, or that the stereotypical insane general was a bit too gravely and predictable. I enjoyed what the game was doing, and wanted to play more. I particularly enjoyed watching my cutscenes play out while wearing a cheerleader outfit, gimp suit, or Lego-inspired head.
After completing the main campaign and launching the aforementioned Untold Stories, I was having a bit of fun, but realized that a major chunk of the gameplay is fetch styled missions. Someone will come on the radio to tell you to grab something, usually not anywhere close to you, and investigate/clear/pickup what they need. The main story didn’t drag on me with this mechanic, but the DLC stories seemed to just have me trudging through more hordes, and going to do the same things I had done before, just with a different model and cutscenes.
THE FINAL WORLD
Dead Rising 3: Apocalypse Edition represents a few things; a good value, a solid game, and a good time. The story, as mentioned earlier, is one of the best stories in the series (if not the best), fun to play, and only better with a friend. Dead Rising 3’s co-op allows players to jump in and search, collect, and slaughter together, with shared collectible findings so you don’t have to worry about losing progress. I truly enjoyed Dead Rising as a game, and appreciate what it does. While it might not win awards for the best story, or the best anything really, it’s a fantastic game, and deserves your attention.

Please note that for this review, I will be purely reviewing the game itself and not how it performs on PC. However, if you would like to know, it had very bad performance issues and bugs which were fixed after 1-2 weeks after it was released. The game is pretty stable now and should work fine for most users. The game has a 30 FPS cap which can be disabled. However, disabling it causes some bugs (for me, anyway) and most of you will not be able to get a steady 60 fps. The zombie animations are also coded at 30 fps so the game might seem a little fast. Please note that you need a very strong PC to run this game and you need an even stronger PC to run it at a stable 60 FPS as it is poorly optimized but is slightly better now.
Dead Rising 3 is a fun zombie killing games. It isn't a serious zombie killing game and has many absurd and weird combo weapons which can be created and outfits which are equally as funny and weird. The campaign, however, is pretty serious but don't let that stop you from buying this game. I completed it within 2-3 days (around 6-8 hours each day) and there still was a lot of things left to unlock and a lot of combo weapons left to find. If you do not know what combo weapons are, Dead Rising 3 allows you to combine weapons anywhere unlike the previous Dead Rising games and they are stronger than the usual weapons. You can also combine food and vehicles now. The city in Dead Rising 3 is huge and you will definitely miss certain areas of the city after completing the campaign for the first time. The graphics in Dead Rising 3 are okay and they definitely look better than the previous games. Dead Rising 3 also allows a HUGE amount of zombies on screen which increases the fun. Survivors and day and night cycles are still in Dead Rising 3 and survivors now have much more health and won't die as easily. They also do a pretty good job of following you. As for night, zombies still turn stronger and more dangerous when it is night. The timer in Dead Rising 3 is drastically increased and you have PLENTY of time to do the main missions and side missions. For those who would like the old stressful timer back, they can play nightmare mode which decreases the timer by a lot and make the zombies tougher, making you choose wisely on what you should do.  There is a new skills menu in Dead Rising 3 which allows you to unlock special abilities by using attribute points. Attribute points are earned when you level up which requres PP. PP can be earned by killing zombies (especially with combo weapons), doing missions, fighting psychopaths, saving survivors and more. There are many opportunities to earn PP in this game so do not worry about that. However, most of the time, you will not be able to max out all your skills in one playthrough, making you do another. There are seven psychopaths in Dead Rising 3, each one more challenging than the other. Overall, this game is the best Dead Rising game in the series in my opinion and if you are looking for a fun, not serious, zombie killing game, then this is the game for you. Just ensure you meet the minimum specs at least and you should be fine. Dead Rising 3 will keep bringing you back to play more due to its fun experience and many unlockables. I have completed it 2 times on Story Mode, doing my third time now on Nightmare Mode and I think it will be an enjoyable experience for most of you aside from the performance issues which are not as bad now.

Edit: I'm changing my review. I wanted to give Hi-Rez another chance, but there are a few critical errors this game possesses. I will leave my original review so you can see the pros, but the cons:
-Developers seem to care more about money than the gameplay or community (don't even have to take my word for it, watch one of the many videos by pro players)
-Developers have let multiple glitches or game-weakening errors slide while releasing plenty of cash items and cosmetics
-Glitches, plenty of constant subtle glitches (when's the last time YOU recieved a quest?) and random, major (sometimes game-breaking) glitches
-Game is going in a pay-to-win direction
-Matchmaking is absolutely awful. Expect to wait upwards of 5 minutes for a game sometimes. Expect to be a fresh newbie, not even 10 hours into the game, and play against a Diamond or better player (or multiple at once).
-The ranking system is horrible and easily manipulated
-There seem to be only minor repercussions for afking or feeding or being verbally abusive
-(More of an opinion, but: balancing issues. The matches are playable, but plenty of healers have been patched to do less heal and more damage, some damages can burst tanks down as if the tank was a squishy, etc. New characters released are often "broken" and can be nightmarish to play against (the new damage Vivian, for example, has as much health as a tank, a shield, does some of the top damage of the game, has autoaim for an ult)
It's pretty fun until you start getting involved with ranked, testing, keeping track of the development, and community. That, and the potential patches for the future possibly change the game's card system into a grind-driven RNG moneysink. It makes me not want to invest any more time into this.
Old POSITIVE review:
Hi-Rez has had wild success with SMITE so I was excited to give this a chance. This game was swamped with hackers and horrid matchmaking at one point but in the recent past these issues have been attacked and somewhat tackled. It seems like a lot of people have tried it and no longer want to play it because of these factors, but I believe they should come back and give it another chance.
Many fans of Overwatch will find some of the similarities between champions uncanny, but the game enjoyable and distinctly different. You still have to escort the payload and get a spotlight shone on you if you get the best play in the game, but you also have a much less toxic playerbase to deal with, a unique character customization system and you aren't spending a dime to own the game. No, this game is not a clone of OW, and if you do a small amount of digging you'll be able to see for yourself - or maybe just try out the game, lol.
The card system in this game is great and truly allows you to customize each character to fit your playstyle and the team's needs for the match. You place 5 cards of customizable strength that you either earn in a chest or craft into a 'Loadout', which modifies your character's attributes or abilities, and you can choose which to use at the start of the match. You also buy "items" throughout the game and earn credits for defending objectives, pushing payloads, utilizing your character's role (healers get bonuses for healing, tanks for defending, etc). These items are split into 4 categories and offer bonuses like reduced ultimate ability timers, damage negation, quicker reload speeds, etc.
It's fun to play and free to play. Even if you don't spend a dollar, you can still accrue 'VIP' points simply by playing the game, and eventually purchase some of the in-game cosmetics with them. You earn Radiant Chests as you level, and these contain skins or cards. Levelling? So far the highest level I've seen in game is 144, but I've heard you can get up in the 300s. You also earn 'essence' to craft cards, and the real $$$ crystals, and can eventually spend those crystals to buy items you'd normally have to pay cash IRL for. Hi-Rez offers an
, reasonable real $$ bundle that gives you all of the current and future champions and their voice packs. This is a big deal if you don't mind spending a little money, and it's worth every penny. I personally enjoy how you can change the head, body, and weapon of the character and interchange items in skin collections. All characters are incredibly customizable, and you can even earn skin collections for simply playing a character a LOT.
There are a wide variety of characters for you to choose from, and they have an even wider array of distinct abilities and playstyles. It can be hard to stay up-to-date with the meta as it changes, but even characters considered to be low-tier can still terrorize the battlegrounds with careful Loadout selection and itemization.
The team matters, and you can expect to suffer through a LOT of 4v5s and afks when you start playing the game (I noticed these mostly went away after about level 10). Winning any game is possible with determination, however, so never give up. Matchmaking is one of the issues many people have raised in the past, and it is still messy - I'm only a month into playing, unranked, and will at random be paired with or against diamonds or masters - but there is usually some sort of balance.  There doesn't seem to be much punishment for trolls/toxic players, although I haven't come across many if any trolls or outright toxic players yet.
BE PREPARED TO WAIT A GOOD 5 MINUTES IN QUEUE TO JOIN A MATCH... (or 30 seconds, I don't make the rules) this is annoying but a fact of life. It seems like a good 'average' wait time is around 2.5 minutes. If someone doesn't accept, you might have to die of boredom for a few more minutes, but these people get penalized for doing so. At least, if you tab out, you will get a push notification on your computer that gives you a chance to load in.
Glitches can be annoying but thankfully they seldom happen in-game. THESE DAMN THINGS CAN PLAGUE THE MENUS, HOWEVER. Sometimes quests don't reflect the results of games played or come up empty (don't reroll those, you will lose your reroll and still have an empty quest active), or while spectating a player info for their Loadouts or items will be for yours or blank. Sometimes information or characters "dissappear" and the colors and character models (or lack thereof) in the champion select lobby will make you wonder if you're hallucinating. The game also only runs in 32bit, but you can opt into running DX11 in the settings (beta mode)....
After all is said, this is a game in BETA. It has been in beta for a long time, sure, but the glitches don't make it unplayable. The game runs smoothly if you have half-decent internet and computer. It has intense replay value, each character is different enough to present an amusing challenge to master, and it's fast-paced.

Incredible game, very fun and addictive. There's a seemlingly endless amount of content and it never gets boring or tedious. The best part about the game is that it's made by a devoloper that you can tell cares about the gamers. Every system is designed to be as intuitive as possible, and the different mechanics and systems are explained to the player within the game, so that it avoids the problem that many oldschool RPGs like this have which is that they often have obtuse unintuitive and tedious mechanics that you have to learn about through outside tutorials. The game delivers all this content through a very well designed and well organized interface.
The graphics are simple yet beautiful, with brightly colored varied environments and unique monster designs. As simple as the graphics are, they look and feel very polished and lifelike, and avoids the "RPGmaker feel" that indie oldschool RPGs often have. The simple graphics actually help the game because it allows for a greater focus on gameplay, which this game has plently of. The devoloper is also very active within the community, and constantly updates the game with useful features and new content.
Gameplay wise, it's a monster breeding game. You level up monsters, and breed them to make them stronger, or create brand new types of creatures. Each creature has a different trait, and you can combine these traits to make really interesting and powerful combinations. While you're doing this, there's always a goal to be reached. You need to keep your power balance up, get more diety points, build your weapons, finish your rituals, defeat you sigils, micromanage your weapon stats, earn favor with deities, defeat realm bosses, finish your quests and the list goes on and on. This makes the game very addictive because you always feel like you're working towards something. I don't think it's possible to run out of stuff to do in this game, I've played for over 60 hours and I still feel like I haven't scratched the surface of the game.
Highly recommended.

So, after using this to put in 95~ hours on dark souls 2, I feel like I've gotten a pretty nifty feel for the device so far.
TL;DR - Solid controller, uniquely-useful thumbpads. Everything I wanted for a controller, that's actually viable as a replacement for your mouse / keyboard.
Pros - The thumbpads, oh god the thumbpads. The feeling is a little strange to get used to, but there's literally just enough feedback to let your thumbs know when they're being registered (and it's sensitive), without being distracting or easily lost. It's like having two trackballs, in addition to the normal slew of buttons. Takes getting used to, and it'll be a while before I use it to play a shooter of any kind, but the potential is seriously there. On top of that, the buttons are crisp without being annoying or overly stiff; The triggers are satisfying, the bumpers have just the right amount of 'click', and the stick is easy to work. All in all, it fits naturally into the hand, and once I got used to where everything was (the inside two buttons for your ring / pinky had me weirded out for a while), it performed beautifully.
Cons - Only two points, here; First, the D-pad functionality on the left thumbpad is a little wishy-washy feeling; Not because the buttons are bad, but because the markings to let your thumb know where which button is are pretty shallow. I still miss, sometimes, but I get the feeling a bit more acclimation will solve that. Second; My left bumper stopped functioning after 20~ hours of gameplay. Not really a con for the device, as a whole, as I'm sending it in to get a replacement, but definitely a black eye on an otherwise very, very nicely put together package.
Edit: One other point I wanted to make; Uses AA's. I realize that's probably obvious to anyone who did any reading before they bought it, but it caught me by surprise. Means either using the included cord (works beautifully), or investing in 3rd party rechargeables if you want the true wireless. Just kinda struck me as odd, given the sony / microsoft equivalents.

"Monster Loves You!" is literally a Choose Your Own Adventure text game, with some general background drawings. It's not the same as an exploration game where you punch in keywords or try to work your way around somewhere.
The time it takes to complete the actual game is 30 to 40 minutes, depending on how fast you're picking options and reading. Technically, you can fly through it in approximately 15 minutes or less if you know what events and choices you want. Each achievement for the game is completing it with a new ending, and when you replay, the events don't change unless you trigger something specific at the first endgame point.
If you care about getting the achievements, you can reuse saves as some guides explain. It really is not that worthwhile to replay it 14 full times because more than half of those times you'll be choosing the exact same actions.
I thought the game looked a bit interesting in drawing style, hence why I got it. But it turns out that there really aren't that many different graphical screens. And most of the time, they're just shadowed out because of the text boxes, sitting on top of the screen for you to read and decide upon.
Your monster has a set of stats that you can increase as you choose certain events, and the game's ending is determined essentially by those stats, as well as a few other endgame choices. No event until the "final" age event actually triggers the ending. Thus, the game fits an exact carbon-copy mold of the same general things happening over and over, which also adds to your boredom and the game's lack of fun replayability.
Going through the adventure of the game was just really disappointing, as not many of the events are that exciting. The developer's claim of the 900+ choices is quite an exaggeration, since most events don't differ by much at all with their choices. And the fact that it's an extremely short story means that it doesn't require any investment or make you even care about what is happening.
Entertaining choose your own adventure style game. Funny, but short. Definitely worth picking up on sale if you're looking for a casual adventure game.

While this new version of HR goes a long way to solve the original's problems, is essentially a cheap upgrade, and tosses you some DLC to boot, it also adds a few things not listed on the changelog. Namely, a whole host of gitches, bugs and crashes that weren't in the first game.
Despite playing both versions on the same machine, this one had inexplicable FPS drops, graphical bugs, bugs with enemy AI and NPCs not behaving as they should, and worst of all, frequent, unexplained crashes to desktop. Examples follow.
-Throughout Detroit I had some of the worst bugs in the entire game. Frequently my FPS died, despite my system exceeding the game's requirements.
-Detroit was where most of the crashes to desktop were. These were all, save for one, random and unexplained. I would be playing one moment and staring at a black screen the next, my desktop the one after that. I only found one of these bugs to be repeated- stacking a specific two of the barrels in front of Grayson's shop on top of each other caused the game to instantly crash.
-The physics engine would often crash, so be careful when stacking anything.
-
-Thankfully, upon my
All in all, these frequent bugs were eventually squashed, either by the system or by myself figuring out how to ignore them. While it is a shame that what should in all rights be an even better version of DX3 would up so buggy, to the point where I could only avoid losing progress by constantly quick-saving. Yet, these bugs were mostly present in the first area, Detroit, and when I pushed through them all I found what the Director's Cut should have been, one of the best games ever made made even better, lurking beyond them all.
It was one hell of a rough ride, but I would take it again in a heartbeat.

Actual Review
In a nutshell, yes paladins is like overwatch and battleborn or tf2 in some cases. The game is a champion based shooter with 4 different classes, namely, frontline(aka tank), damage, flank and of course the most ignored class, support.
Champions of the Realm
Paladins has a wide range of champions or characters to choose from. There are four classes.
Tank or Frontline- basically the tanky characters that you expect to be in the point but flanks in casual
Flanks- the champions with the best mobility abilities to ambush weak enemies but are frontlines in casual
Damage- your dps in paladins and is the only class that no one messes up even in casual
Support- healers except for pip. The one class everybody ignores in casual but is very important in competitive.
The characters have a decent set of skill each having four main skills and one ultimate that might or might not change the outcome of the game. There are a few unbalanced heroes here and there (ehem vivian ehem) but hirez updates the game frequently.
Game Modes of the Realm
There are three game modes not including competitive.
Onslaught-hold a point to gain points or kill your enemies to gain points.
Payload-escort a payload and the team that escorted it the farthest or the fastest wins. The game kode no one knows how to play decently.
Siege- capture a point to win one point and escort the payload that popsup after capturing the said point to win another point.
These game modes are introduced in massive maps where you ride horses(objectively great i guess, but thats not my cup of tea).
Card System
The best feature that paladins has is the loadout or cardsystem. You can customize your character to play differently than how other people would play that character. This allows great surprises and variety as you play the game and actually offers more strategy unlike other shooters. For example in TF2, if you know how to counter a scout you can counter almost any scout the onlyfactor would be expertise. In paladins legendaey cards would introduce you to different buffs to a characters specific skill. The other great thig about this is that you can copy loadouts from top tier gamers. You can buy cards and legendary cards with essence which are easy to earn.
Skins
Skins are the only thig you have to pay in this gane. While you can buy the founders pack to unlock every champion. I find it easy to earn gold to buy that. I suggest you only invest your money to skins which are great btw.
Overall
This game is great fun and is probably one of the few free to play games that isnt pay to win and doesnt suck. Yes it is comparable to overwatch and battleborn or even tf2 but it has features that seperates this game from them. Great game 8/10

If you enjoy GOOD well put together classic RPGs, you can stop reading this review right now. You should buy this game. You will enjoy it and get your money's worth.
This game is almost exactly like the old Dragon Warrior Monster (and now Joker) games, with several improvements. You can find breeding recipes, so you actually know how to breed up to the rare monsters, every monsters has a unique ability that change how you play, and the strategy actually matters the deeper you get in to the game. I got to level 12 of the dungeon without putting any thought in to how my party interacts with their abilities and got rekt.
The soundtrack is a solid 8/10. I enjoy it a lot, but I find myself tempted to turn it off if a session goes longer than 2 hours. Lots of looping, which you expect from a smaller dev. team.
Some things that took me a second to figure out:
- Getting to breed takes awhile to unlock. I forget what dungeon level it was now, but be patient and just enjoy collecting cores in the mean time.
- To hatch an egg, you have to place it on the hay in the hatchery. (I missed that in the text I guess, and it took me 5 minutes to figure out :/)
Ehhh I guess that's it.
Overall I give this game a 9.5/10. I get that the point isn't to have an amazing plot. But the plot is pretty generic. I think if the developers pushed themselves they could have constructed a more compelling world. But that is just my opinion. This game is still very much a gem in the rough.

An all around fun treat for fans of the franchise. I never managed to play the second one, but this one is certainly strong enough to stand on its own, with minimal knowledge of the existing lore of the game world. Plus, it's just plain fun to run around killing zombies with all manner of crazy weaponry.
You can also (rather easily I might add) finish everything you want without any real fear of the clock ticking out on you. Nightmare mode adds a sense of urgency, but I feel you could still do a decent amount of exploring if you wished.
EDIT: Oh, and any comments about crashing...I personally only ever experienced ONE crash, and that was on exit. I've seen a few bugs (most hilarious and non-game breaking) but on the whole it feels somewhat solid.

Asolutely awesome pixel bashing fun! Haven't enjoyed a 3rd person open world slaughterfest so much in ages. Yes sure there is an issue with the odd crash, tho I have managed to play for hours at a time with no problems.
The graphics are superb, the gameplay has plenty of depth......there are 100's of different objects that can be used as weapons! and so many ways to kill zombies or just have fun with them (like kick a football in their face :-)
On top of this you have a storyline with great cutscenes and voice acting, plus some boss fights that may not be against zombies. It's kinda like a cross between GTA and siphon filter.
Also there is character customisation by way of skill points to increase, and lots of different outfits to find and wear. Try utilising your martial skills in melee zombie slaughter dressed as Bruce Lee, or make a combo weapon with a motorcycle engine with boxing gloves (which gives you attacks like in street fighter) and dress as Ken.

For myself I am happy to have bought it. And show me a game these days that is bug free and doesn't get patched or updated shortly after release (not that I am excusing the lack of optimisation and testing that is commonplace nowdays in the software market).
So I am sure that the bugs will eventually get ironed out. But at least it is not gameplay bugs that i have seen, just the odd crash. However it is still very very playable and just plain great fun!
I give it 8/10. as is.....I would likely increase that after updates and bugfixes.

Dead Rising 3 is another solid instalment in the series, one which is unfortunately marred by performance problems and lacklustre story elements. The essence of what made this franchise good is still there, like the ridiculous combat and comedic game elements, however it just falls short of the “must have” status that the original had. It’s still a blast to play, especially when you unlock some of the more overpowered combos, however there’s probably not enough in there to keep me coming back for untold hours at a time. I'm sure long time fans of the series will find a lot to like in Dead Rising 3 but don’t be fooled into thinking it’s flawless.

This is a good word game. At its core, you look at a bunch of letters, and try to think of words, and that is of course fun.
But this game makes things more interesting by introducing several layers of circumstantial bonuses and restrictions that change over time to keep it fresh. Enemies that can only be hurt by four letter words, books that boost your long word damage (among others), your letter tiles can be subject to status effects that make it very important to either use them immediately or maybe avoid using them for several turns.

First I'd like to say that I played a lot of word games, and this one has got to be the best so far.
- If you're into word games I highly recommend this.
- If you're not that into word games but likes cute graphics with a lot of achievements and replay-ability and challenge, I also recommend this.
- If you hate word games and well hate how the game looks in screenshots then its not for you :(.
The game is seriously great,  you start with a few levels then keeps going on and on.
Every level can be played 4 times, to collect 4 different stars, But unlike all other games that I know you don't need to play it again but faster or better to get the 2nd star, no thats what I like about the game, every star is different.
- First time playing the level = get the first star at the end.
- Click on 2nd star to replay the level but with a timer, You need to finish it before timer runs out.
- 3rd star is a challenge, For an example > Monsters only take damage from words with 4 letters or more, and way more.
- 4th star is same as first but except all monsters are elite and very powerful.
And you got the store, which you can buy upgrades, potions, items and a lot more, you can also unlock new tiles for the letters to spice things up and there are 3 characters in the game, you can get an idea of the store in the 5th screenshot in the steamstore page.
Countless words to spell, Crystal letters that gives power-ups And the monsters can also use negative effects on some of the letters such as poison or spikes or cracks and a lot more, also there are small quests to achieve as you play to get more money.
The game music ... IM SO CRAZY about it in all seriousness I love it I want to buy the soundtrack

OMG The dev replied and apparently the soundtrack is in the game's folder included with the game itself, thats so awesome thanks guys : D
The monsters, level and all designs are totally adorable and the animations are outstanding.
There are a lot of achievements to grind on, And a lot of levels and you can play every level 4 times so yeah that can give you more time to play, I am pretty sure I have around 4+ hours in the game than it shows here but they're all offline mostly and steam does not record that.
THIS might interest many people out there, there is no timer when you're typing the word or thinking it so you can take as much time as you want no need to hurry up and mess up.
A lot of monsters to fight, some with special conditions   EX : only takes damage from words with 2 vowels or more. And moooore that makes the challenge even more crazier than it is.
So summing it all up

1 - Great game, awesome artwork and music.
2 - A lot of levels that are replay-able, great designs on all of them.
3 - A lot of monsters to fight, countless words to spell and special letters.
4 - Kill monsters and finish levels to get crystals to buy upgrades and weapons and more from the store.
5 - Quests to finish as you carry on and you can upgrade yourself and spellbooks.
6 - Up to 40 levels, And after finishing the game you can start new game with expert mode that adds new stuff.

So here is my Review on the Steam Controller.
I have been using this for around 2 weeks now and the first couple of days don't get me wrong were an absoulte headache but it comes down to 2 things.
1ST is myself I am a noob of controller remapping I just like to start a game and go.
2ND Most Recent Steam games do not require remapping but you may find a lot of older titles do and thats where the headaches start.
Now to follow up from the 2ND reason not long after I found you can use community recommened button layouts which take the stress away from going through old titles and configuring just select a recommendation and away you go. And just to add some Game Developers also have their own recommedation layout which is a bonus.
The feel of the controller is great didn't take me long to get use to and believe me I have some strange controllers in the past to play my games on and this one was one of the more comfortable ones, for games that require dual analouge sticks the mouse tracker that is used for the right stick does take some getting use to but back to the remapping you can adjust the sensitivy of it to make it feel a lot better than it is.
I also like the little tones it makes when you first switch it on and when shutting down I know its kinda sad but I like it :) Battery Life is just beyond words it will keep going for ages I have clocked in about 50+ hours and still no sign of it dying.
Along with the Steam Link which I also bought and am pleased That Valve came up with the goods and gave us this nice controller you wont be saying this in the first few days of ownership but trust me as a gamer of 21 years you will love it in the end.

Every time this game goes on sale I wish that more of my friends would pick it up. It's an excellent blend of RPG, stealth, and action in a game that has a compelling and driven story in a dystopian, cyberpunk future setting. Everything about Deus Ex: Human Revolution and the Director's Cut exudes style, and I'd absolutely recommend it to anybody who's even remotely interested in it.

[Small Spoilers]
Deus Ex: Human Revolution - Director's Cut is a solid first person action/stealth game set in a wonderful, cyberpunk future. You play as Adam Jensen, an ex-swat member, who now is the lead security at a massive biotech company. After an accident at the facility, you became badly wounded. Thanks to the power of "augmentatioins" you were rebuilt, and now possess many possible enhancements to help better your stealth, combat, and various other things. You're tasked with finding out what actually happened the day of the attack, why it happened, and who is behind it.
For my playthough I mainly focused on stealth. Other than boss fights, which even after being enhanced in the Director's Cut are still dull, I did not have kill a single individual (which I really like). Exploration, things like finding hidden air vents to crawl through, hacking doors, and hacking into computers, are really satisfying and help set the atmospehere. I encountered a glitch late game that didn't let me progress, but other than that I found few bugs.
Deus Ex: Human Revolution - Director's Cut is a soild game. I highly recomend it, especially if you're a fan of steath.
Gameplay: 9/10 (Focusing primarly on stealth, not gunplay)
World Design: 7/10 (The "hubs" are made of many different levels, because of this it can sometimes be confusing on where exactly you're susposed to go.)
Graphics: 7/10
Voice-Acting: 7/10 (The main characters are voiced very well, but some of the minior characters are absolutly horrible.)
Overall: 7.5/10

Compare and Contrast: Siralim 2 and No Man's Sky
+ They both have procedurally generated levels.
- Only one of the games features actual gameplay in said generated levels.
+ You can acquire monsters in both games.
- You can actually do things with the monsters in only one of them.
+ They both came out on the same day.
- Only one of them is actually in a playable state at launch.
+ They're both considered indie games
- One of them responds to comments and questions almost instantly, going as far as to personally fix someones glitched save via email.
Siralim 2 is a gem. I highly recommend anyone thats a fan of old school rpgs, monster collecting, or completely customizable games to give it a try. It was worth it at full price, it almost feels like stealing when it's at a discount.

Recommended for anyone who ever enjoyed the classic board game Boggle, as this is pretty much a slightly shinier version of it.
You use the letters given to you on a randomized board to spell words.  The longer the word/more valuable the letters used (think Scrabble rules, where using 'Z's, 'X's, etc. nets you more points than 'E's), the more damage done to the monsters.  As you defeat monsters and beat levels, you earn gems, which you can then use to purchase various upgrades.
Each level has four "stars" you can earn: the first is simply for defeating all the monsters on a level, the second is typically a time trial, the third is a unique challenge condition to beat the level, and the fourth is a much harder version of the level.  This adds some replay value, as do the achievements.
The story is almost non-existent, but that's not really the point of playing something like this, so it never bothered me.  Graphics are serviceable, and I did not encounter any bugs.
All in all, fun little word game.  Took me about 8 hours to get all but three achievements, and it never felt tedious replaying levels.

Holy crap. You see games on Steam that cost fifteen bucks that look like they should only cost ten at most, then you play said games, and discover they should have cost five bucks or less at launch. I got this game for $4.79 on sale and it feels like a $10 game of high quality at the very least. There are character upgrades, weapon upgrades, multiple weapons, all the currency is in-game, you can grind if you really want to but probably don't need to, there are special conditions that affect the letters you choose to give them a little bonus (crystals) or a detriment (like whirlwinds, reversal, cloners, etc.), and each of the 40 levels has four variations on how to play it. It's fun, challenging but doable, and just...a damn fine game. I'm ridiculously picky most of the time, and this game is seriously good stuff for the price. I highly recommend this game if you can get if for less than $5.00 on sale, or at full price if you're not a tightwad like me.

Conditional recommendation.
This game itself is very well design and quite fun to play, however, the condition is that you need to either remember a large amount of English words or be willing to do so in a short time. The difficulty of game highly depends on your vocabulary.
Other than the word-spelling part, the mechanism of which is traditional, the game incorporates some RPG elements, such as you battle through various scenes to defeat enemies with different abilities to modify the letter board, you are given quests involving spelling during battles, you can buy upgrades to improve your hero's performances and you can level-up your books to receive bonus under specified circumstances. All these elements and factors are integrated into the game smoothly so that the word-spelling puzzles become very attractive and addictive. Although grinding may be needed at some point, this game is not hard overall. 15-20 hours are needed in order to complete all the stages, achievements and buy all upgrades in the store.
This one is much better than any other word-spelling games on the market, and it might be great game if the producer could bring in more contents (e.g. an intriguing story, NPCs, more weapons, items, foes, etc.).

+ This is a very addicting an cute game for the people who like Scrabble and other similar word games.
- Game can be quite difficult for the people who are not native English speakers. Maybe an easy mode where also the shorter words can make lots of damage would be good.
- Game does not understand all English words so it can be frustrating if you spelled 100% correctly a long word and the game does not approve it.
- Some of the swear words are not approved.
- Word explanations are weird because the game thinks that nearly all words that you made are verbs instead of nouns.
- Sometimes the word explanations can be really far-fetched. If you want to learn new English words from this game then it is probably wise to check all the word meanings from an online dictionary.

Monster Loves You! is a choose-your-own-adventure-esque RPG from Radial Games and Dejobaan Games LLC. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
It’s hard to classify what genre this game should fall into (gameplay wise) as it is very similar to a visual novel, but it does have aspects of an RPG. Whatever it is, it does a good job of being what it is. MLY! has a lot of possible endings and a lot of ways to get to those endings. Naturally, this provides a lot of replay value, which is always a good thing.
The artwork in the game is consistently charming. It is kid friendly (some of the content may be a bit darker for younger audiences. just so you know) and vibrantly colored.
The game as a whole, I think, is very creative. You, as the player, experience the entire lifespan of a monster from spawning to death. What events fill the time in between those two are entirely up to you. Every choice you make in the game not only counts, but very significantly impacts your late and end game.
The Bad
Go ahead and scroll on past this one.
The Meh
If you’re not really a fan of reading, this may not be the game for you.
If you’re looking for a gory, violent game about being a monster, this may not be the game for you.
Verdict: Yea
All in all, Monster Loves You! is a fun, lighthearted game that, I think, anyone can enjoy playing. If you’re looking for something to do around Halloween time and you’ve got some extra cash, take a look at this game. If you have kids and you’re looking for a game for them to play around Halloween, this could just be your game.

Ah... Deus Ex.
I got this game as a gift from my brother, since I bought him a few games as well. It took a while to download (as you'd imagine, 15 GB is a very large game) and I never really got around to playing it. I got bored from WoW and so I decided to play this game.
This game's setting is in 2027 in North America. You are an ex-SWAT member who is a guard at Sarif Industries, where a revolutionary new find equal to that of the Rosetta Stone or Kepler's find is being worked on -- the find of controlled human evolution. This is being made available only to the high-ranked citizens of America (while you hate this find in general, you despise the fact that it is not available to all). This game feels very Mass Effect-y (my favorite game all time), with everything from the music to controlled dialogue to the futuristic aspect. While you are speaking to "your boss", something happens in the labs. I'm not going to say what, because a) I just started playing, and b) I wouldn't wanna spoil it for you all.

I've only had the controller for a few days. I had no idea what to expect, just my imagination and what I've already read. But I gotta say, I feel like this controller is the innovation and change that I believe Nintendo had hoped for when they released the first Wii. At first, I thought that the controller possibly felt cheap, but after using it, that's just because I'm not used to something feeling so thick and durable. To the point, the touch pads are definitely something amazing and there's going to be some great ways to use them if the community has anything to say about it. Each touchpad has only the one click, but the touchpad can use the location of where your thumb is to make that click be a different command. So what I mean is that you can simulate the D-pad on the touch pad. The touchpads definitely take a while to get used to, at least it did for me. I played Portal 2 with it to adjust, and yeah, I fumbled around a bit, but I am really sure that the touchpads will yield greater results than your standard thumbstick controller. I can't say for sure if it'll put you on par with mouse users, but a lot of other people think it will. Functionally, it should give you better reactions results, but using a mouse is more than just flicking your wrist. I described it to my friend as a Ven Diagram where the 2 circles don't even touch. The first circle is the standard thumbstick controller users, the second circle is keyboard and mouse users. I place this controller in the middle as a bridge. You'll be better than standard controller users, but I don't know if you'll be on par with keyboard and mouse users.
All and all, I don't believe this controller is a gimmick. I think it's a fantastic alternative that lets you play games from the couch that you wouldn't think you'd be able to play from the couch. I combined this controller with my steambox pc and have set Big Picture Mode to autostart, so yes, it's equivalent to a console, just an extremely better version of any console. I must warn, a lot of people say it's a 10 hour learning curve to fully adapt. I am one of those that took 10 hours, but others, including maybe you, may adapt in a single round of TF2. Lastly, there are lots of custom control profiles you can get through Big Picture mode and Valve updates the firmware as often as needed. I would definitely recommend this controller.
