Keeps the strengths of the genre - every aspect of the game from party composition to equipment and spell outfitting to individual battle tactics feels like a fresh puzzle to solve. Compared to Siralim 1, it has a lot of nice quality of life improvements.  Combat not taking a year to click through, more monsters, more goals to work towards, etc.  There aren't a bajillion buffs and debuffs to remember any more.  It's got more game to it with less annoying bits.
Its combat is more tactical but less strategic.  In Siralim 1, the majority of your minmaxing time was just spent on figuring out your party of monsters and their layout.  Figuring out complimentary abilities, how to use them, and so on.  Siralim 2 has decreased this to an extent - abilities are harder to build an entire strategy off of.
On the flip side, completely reworking the spellcasting system so that your monsters can cast spells from a replenishing mana pool (versus your wizard casting spells from their non-replenishing mana pool) is an incredible change that adds a LOT of depth.
Considering its price point, if you like this kind of game at all (IE: pokemon) you should get it.

Not Pokemon 2: Electric Boogaloo
Siralim 2 is an oldskool 8bit style RPG reminiscent of Final Fantasy or Pokemon. It has endless creature and realm levels, allowing for potentially infinite play. And contrary to many other procedurally generated games, it's not just infinity for infinity's sake. It's got a staggering amount of content and variety. In fact, the game's still introducing crucial new gameplay elements after dozens of hours playtime.
Compared to the first game, Siralim 2 is a little more reserved in it's approach to levels and scaling. Enemies no longer scale to the player's level, allowing you to farm past realm 30 and beyond even with a suboptimal team. The introduction of gods gives the player more stuff to do and is overall a good move.
The nether creatures take something of a back seat compared to the new breeding system, which is the main way for improving your party aside from levelling. It's also the way through which new monsters are introduced in the wild, which is neat.
All that said, the game is still a little rough around the edges. Strange things occur when you clash together such a staggering amount of variables. Some of these strange things might be intentional (monsters casting spells while silenced via special abilities), others probably aren't (When spell gems should be shared with allies, they're sometimes also shared with the enemy?) and most of it can work in favor of both sides.
Also, the palette swaps are probably unavoidable due to budget concerns I'm still gonna point them out. And the combat can get a little boring eventually, to the point where it eventually becomes the game's weakest feature. An auto resolve option might be problematic to implement, but might also help speed along the game's flow later on.
Verdict: A highly complex game, recommended for anyone who's ever enjoyed a Pokemon or Final Fantasy game. I mean the early Final Fantasy installments ofcourse, not the movie-rpg hybrids that they're making now.

When I first reviewed the Steam controller, I was very positive about it.  After spending a lot more time with it, I have come to the conclusion that the device is almost worthless.  Sure you can play some games like Civ V comfortably from the couch, but that does not outweigh its negatives.
First and foremost, the controller is advertised for being able to control your games from the couch which you will be able to do by streaming your PC to Big Picture using the Steam Link.  Good luck with that because Big Picture is an absolute mess.  You are usually lucky if you can get two hours without it crashing.  If you are not, you will probably crash before you hit the 30 minute mark.  Steam needs to address this immediately.  It should be viewed as a fault with their product.  No, it is broken.  That is that.
Another problem is the controller itself.  It pales next to the common Xbox controller.  It does OK with mouse and keyboard games but flat out sucks if you plan to use it as a replacement for the tried and true gamepad.  It lacks in comfort and precision.  You simply cannot enjoy games that were designed with the XBox controller in mind.  Period.
As I have said before, it is nice to be able to enjoy a game like Civ V from your couch but you have to understand, it is definitely no replacement for a keyboard and mouse.  You can play, but its functionality is pretty mediocre in comparison.  I do give it props for making it possible though.  I do like that.
Sadly, the Steam controller just is not ready for everyday consumers.  Big Picture is a buggy mess.  The controller is awkward.  Little seems to be being done to improve it.  I liked it at first, but it has just been a huge disappointment after giving it a spin with several types of games.

But yeah, I like this controller.

I absolutely recommend this controller to people looking for a decent way to play any [and I mean any] PC game in a couch comfortably.
That being said, prepare to spend quite a bit of time just mapping buttons. If you're cool with that, then you've got the most peculiar and surprisingly functional cross between gamepad comfort and mouse accuracy. It's by no means a replacement for key and mouse, but it certainly works well enough to be a considerable option for you.
PROS:
- Ergonomic design. Real comfy.
- LOTS of very responsive buttons.
- Deeply customizable.
- Dual stage triggers! [comparable to GameCube controller]
- Comes with USB dongle, 4 foot cord for Wired Mode and USB Dock to use with the cord to extend the dongle's reach.
- Battery life of the gods. [I've been playing every day for at least 4 hours a day for a week and the included AA batteries still have not run out]
- Great built-in Gyro sensor.
- Haptic Feedback. [I'm personally not that into it, but it seems like a cool feature to have for immersion.]
- Shareable custom mappings. One person playing a game with Steam Controller can benefit everyone else who does the same in the future. Game specific mappings.
- You can use mappings from certain games in other games.
----------
CONS:
- Aformentioned batteries are non-rechargable.
- Oftentimes awkward face button placement can take some getting used to.
- Adaptive centering stick simulation on mousepads is confusing and never works right.
- Loud, clacky controller. It can feel cheap from it, especially right out of the box with included batteries still not inside.
- Can't configure what the controller defaults to when plugged into non-Steam PC's and systems.
----------
All I can say is that after a while, this deceptively practical controller grew on me. It doesn't work extremely well with every genre of game, but it's an amazing attempt at something truly different and functional. I don't feel like I wasted my money, and that is a lot to say for a company's first attempt at a gaming peripheral.
I give it a 7/10.

As a gaming peripheral, it's performance is superb.
PROS: It's responsive, and the buttons don't feel so mushy that the weight of your thumbs alone can depress them, and it's a lot more confortible to hold than it looks. The trackpads, which are the controller's biggest selling points, perform very well, and very responsively, but they take some time to get used to. And the initial setup is somewhat painful, but such can be expected from such a device this unconventional.
CONS: While it's for the most part solid, it does have some serious flaws. That being valve's choice of input method: the steam controller is essentially seen as a glorified XboX controller by most software rather than as a conventional direct input gamepad, as a result it suffers from lack of compatibility outside of anything made before it aside from your triple-A titles. If valve were to take their time and develop a configurable interpretor for the controller's method of input and output it's analog values without keyboard binding, this limitation would be as good as gone, but until then, the controller suffers this flaw.
All-in-all, it's an awesome controller, but it needs some serious compatibility fixes due to being TOO unconventional. I'd recommend it, but to a very select few gamers out there.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution Director's Cut
There are few games, movies, and others in the entertainment spectrum that have presented a concept or idea in such a way as to evoke an emotional reaction. And then there are those that can actually make you think about their subject matter, long after the experience has ended. Maybe it's just a love of tech, but after playing through Human Revolution, I find myself thinking on things such as the nature of the advancement of humans, and what "being human" means anyway. The world of DE:HR is one exploring the use and impact of advanced prothetics, and the merging of man and machine, either by necessity, by choice, or by being forced. There are many thoughts swirling about, many different approaches, supporters, and defenders. Throw in a competent action RPG (with stealth if you so choose), shadow organizations, and individuals with personal agendas, and you have yourself some good ole fashioned cyberpunk!
I can only hope the real world becomes this exciting, when "augmentation" comes around. Sadly, I don't think we'll have that awesome soundtrack playing in our heads when it does. Here's hoping for a sequel!

Of all the franchises that I never seem to get tired of, Deus Ex stands as one of the most prominent. It doesn't have the overt silly aspects that can be found in some parts of the original game, and takes its philosophy much more seriously, but it is in every way a Deus Ex game.
Handle nearly every situation you come across in any way you choose. Want to shoot everyone? Have at it. Blow them all up? Go crazy. Hack through their computers and take control of their own toys? All yours. Make it from one end of an enemy base to the other, and back again, maybe do a few loops for good measure, and never be seen? All in a day's work.
Serves the story of the game much, much better. If you played DXHR vanilla for its story, you have to get this.

I am writing this review for the Steam Awards badge. this does not make my review any less true, merely horribly overdue.
I nominated Jade Empire for the custom category Hiddem Gem, because it is one. When it was first released it received great reviews, but the sales figures never matched that, probably because it was new and different.
It is set in an Asian setting and draws heavily on eastern mythology. Then it allows you to beat said mythology up with magic, martial arts (including backflips and other acrobatic stunts) and several weapons. Or you can choose to talk it out in true RPG fashion.
It also has a morality system with two sides that are not exactly good or evil, but more like yin and yang. Nobody will really judge you for it either since the way of the Closed Fist and the way of the Open Palm are established philosophies within the game. If you feel bad or uncomfortable making some of the choices then maybe one of those philosophies is just not for you.
I found the story to be ok. It goes on for longer than I expected the first time and if you take the time to look for them it actually has several interesting little tidbits hidden away. This includes the possibility of beating up a "British" person.
Give it a try.

This is quite simply one of the best RPGs I have ever played in my life, and i easily count among the best games  of the genre. Obviously the game looks like a retro, Dragon quest like JRPG (in terms of combat), fairly simple graphics and world desing. But the depth and complexity this game has  in terms of gameplay is sarggering; there's so much to do, from catching and breeding monsters, to a bit of crafting, cooking, and base building to resource management. And none of it is overwhelming or needs micro mangament, And yes the game is endless, and the worlds randomly genrated so I can see myself playing this game for many years to come on the same save.. Well, untill Siralim 3 comes out at least.
So over all  Siralim 2 is awesome, it has everything I've ever wanted in a RPG and many new things I really enjoyed. It's a small download, at a fairly cheap price, with more gameplay, depth, and fun... than most RPGs being made today.

Only an improvement on the first one, Siralim 2 has a much more fleshed out campaign to give you a sense of direction at its start with mechanically interesting and challenging boss fights, and the breeding system makes this game a truly worthy contender for being the Dragon Warrior Monsters of our generation.

Long for the days of yore, when you could belitle your Pokemon playing friends with your mechanically superior Dragon Warrior Monsters? Well tary no more, for Siralim has come to justify your hatred for half hearted creature capture games. This game improves on the original in every way shape and form. The spell gem system is fully fleshed out and makes having a diverse team of creatures a must. The castle quests do a great job of facilitating new players and the realm specific God quests do a fantastic job to keep you busy during the infinite pursuit of the perfect creature. Story is light but entertaining, I especially enjoyed the different Gods and their personalities. Graphics are quite plain and simple, but the varried creature design can be excellent and creative. Re-colors do exist, but are to be expected with the sheer number of creatures available. Each creature has a unique defining trait that changes the party dymanic in interesting ways. Combat is straight forward and enjoyable against the tougher enemies. Sigils are consumable items that will summon a pack of very difficult monsters, which so far have the biggest challange i have found in the game. Siralim 2 is a fantastic creature capture game with solid mechanics in nearly every facet and I highly recommend it. Just be sure this genre is for you. Which it better be... punk

Never done a review before but I must say this game is fantastic. Always been a fan of collecting and training monsters, but never too many games like that in North America. This game scratches that itch perfectly. With 500+ monsters, a bunch of customization, random dungeons you can't go wrong. Do yourself a favor and buy this game.
Solid core mechanics, an obscene amount of content that isn't a pain to grind, and amusing gods.

This is a very mechanical RPG. There's a lot of game systems at work here, but not a lot of story to go with it. However, that does not detract from the experience at all. Summon monsters, level them up, upgrade weapons you find, gear up your monsters. It's a fun game loop that is quite entertaining. The updates and bug fixes are frequent, so problems and issues do not linger.

Siralim 2 is a fantastic successor to the unique monster-collecting/dungeon-crawling/number-incrementing feast that was Siralim 1. Such a great update to the first one that it is both a great starting point for new players and worth the small price for Siralim veterans.
People who love discovery, experimentation, and strategy will be pulled in by all the different gameplay systems Siralim's creators have meshed together. You have a team of six creatures with a variety of combat stats--but it's much deeper than that. Your creature taming character, for one, is one of 5 classes with game-changing abilities. Each creature has spells, which don't necessarily need Mana to cast--some leech off the user's HP or have a % chance to be cast randomly. Each creature has a very unique trait, ranging from Area of Effect attacks to buffing your team's Defense to spitting out a poison cloud when it is attacked. Each creature carries an artifact to specialise its stats and potentially give it an additional trait extracted from other monsters. Siralim 2 is a beautiful and crazy madhouse of potential synergies that just take some critical thinking to achieve. And when you achieve that perfect team--that team that gives the enemy 0 time to react, that team that has a gamebreaking amount of defense, that team that Power Rangers fuses together into one great hound and mauls the enemy--that's what you've worked for for all those hours. But there's always a next step, always something more to perfect.
I do believe that this game has a somewhat niche audience--this is not for people turned off by turn-based combat or repetitive gameplay--but I believe that you wouldn't have even scrolled down this far if that's the case. One thing which might not be too obvious from the previews is the sandboxy nature of the game, which is to say that you make your own goals most of the time. The story will carry you for a while (~20 hours in my case but it could easily be done in less than 10), and afterwards you'll find a multitude of things that can grab your attention. Want to reach floor 100? go for it. Want to collect one of each creature? go for it. Want to start a winning streak at the arena? Finish building all castle expansions? Collect super rare creatures? See how strong you could possibly breed creatures? go for it. Your end-goals are up to you and the game does an outstanding job of inspiring you.
The biggest potential negative of this game is alt+tabbing to desktop and finding that 3 hours have unwittingly flown by. Heartily reccomended if you feel even remotely interested.

Anyway... its a word game with a RPG-like progression system, it combines those 2 really well.
It is a turn based game where you make words that do damage, the better(longer word or harder to use letters) the word the more damage it does. Ever since Bookworm Adventures, I've long been a sucker for the word making adventure game genre. While I've never been able to properly engage in a game of Scrabble, I love the gameplay that this particular genre of game affords.
When I first heard of Letter Quest they were trying to get onto Steam via Greenlight. After much deliberation I picked up a copy of this game via the Humble Store. I fell in love with it instantly.
I didn't have much time to play through this game though, so after playing a while put it aside and waited for Valve to greenlight this. It sure took Valve an inexplicably long wait, but here are the fruits of two men's (and a lot of Greenlight voters') hard work!
As the store page states, it's a combination of Scrabble and RPG. It's a very light-hearted tale of a very hungry Grimm reaper looking for pizza and battling monsters along the way - the story is told through rather whimsical-looking comic strip scenes. Yew spell wards een awder too keel anemees...sorry. Proper words, I mean. None of the words in that terrible sentence (barring the proper homophones) would work. :P
Throughout the level you get gems for killing monsters and finishing levels (breaking gem piles). This is where the RPG aspect comes into play - kill more enemies, finish more levels, and you can use the gems to better upgrade Grimm's books, attributes, etc. in order for him to better survive the trickier stages.
Nearly everything about this game is just perfect. Perfect cartoony visuals. Take a bow,
! Perfect soundtrack. Can't find out who did it, but the chiptune style soundtrack, which you can find in your game files, is gorgeous and fits the game - one of the rare times where it works SO well. Finally, perfect gameplay mechanics. Okay, nearly perfect. While the difficulty scales reasonably well, some of the monsters are rather tough to kill unless you can come up with words that are longer than 4-5 letters consistently!
Otherwise, CTO
has done an incredibly solid job on the coding front. It's rare nowadays for a game to be released on day one with no discernibly game-breaking bugs, and for this game to do so despite being coded by practically one person is a monumental achievement. Integration with Steam features like leaderboards, achievements and even Cloud save are also huge pluses. Not to mention that he (at least I presume it's him) is very active in the Steam forums responding to all sorts of questions, bug reports and suggestions regarding the game, and also pushes out updates as well. Rarely do you ever find developers with this kind of enthusiasm and candour.
This game can stand its own against Bookworm Adventures and the ilk, with its own unique brand of wit and charm. Give yourself a pat on the back, Bacon Bandit Games. You guys deserve it.

If I wanted a "choose your own path" story with a few pictures, I'd purchase a book. It'd be cheaper and I could take it back to the bookstore for credit when I was finished.
On the other hand, however, the story was different and the perspective was fascinating. If you don't mind a game that's almost entirely text-based, by all means, purchase it. There are the foundations for a decent game in Loadout; it's fast-paced, loud, over-the-top warfare, with great stylized visuals and fun gameplay. Even though its unsubtle humour will wear thin quickly, and it does become repetitive before too long, it is still a great way to waste a couple of hours. The most praised part of the game has to be the weaponcrafting, where you can construct a completely unique firearm from hundreds of different pieces, tailoring it to your personal preference and playstyle. You can even test your new weapon on bots, before jumping into a PvP game.
However, there are some major flaws in the game mechanics that can make Loadout a frustrating and unenjoyable experience. Firstly, there's the ridiculous infinite sprinting and jumping. True, this is one of the things that makes the game as fast-paced as it is, but it causes so many problems. There is absolutely nothing stopping you from running from one side of the map to the other. Especially in Capture the Hammer, where the objective is to get to the enemy base, pick up a hammer, and return it to your own base. With infinite sprint, it's very easy to simply ignore the enemy and run past them while carrying the hammer (or any other time), and there isn't even a speed penalty while you are carrying it. Now, you may be thinking, "Surely the enemy team would be able to shoot you before you got anywhere near their base?" - wrong, it's only 4 vs 4, and most of the maps are pretty big.
Also, one of the least-skillful and most used "tactics" I have seen used is because there is infinite sprinting and jumping. Basically, grab a rocket launcher, upgrade it to have six rockets loaded at once, and equip it in both weapon slots of your current loadout. Then, sprint to the nearest enemy, jump, spam the floor with missiles, swap weapon (quicker than reloading) and repeat. Jump, spam, jump, spam, kill, sprint, sprint, sprint, sprint, sprint, jump, spam, jump, spam, kill, etc...
Rocket launchers have one of the longest ranges in the game, which is what they are meant for. At close range, they become unstoppable. And speaking of close range combat...
Melee. It is ridiculous. It completely removes the need for the recently added shotgun. Here's a scenario - You see an enemy coming towards you, and you've just emptied your rifle clip shooting at someone else. Because of the infinite sprint, your enemy is almost on top of you. You decide that you don't have time to reload your high ammo capacity rifle, and change to your shotgun. You can see your enemy has a sniper equipped, and they manage to hit you while mid-jump. They land in front of you - now within range, so you unleash your shotgun pellets at them. Because your enemy instantly jumps again, you only hit them once or twice. You turn around frantically, looking to see where they've gone so you can finish the fight. You see them land behind you, so you fire more of your shotgun shells at them. Their health is now getting extremely low, and you're just about to deliver the killing shot, when suddenly they sprint at you and *BAM!*... you die instantly... but how?
You guessed it, you were defeated in the most humiliating way imaginable. Your enemy pressed "F". They didn't even have to aim, they just pointed their character in the general direction of yours and punched away to their heart's content, reducing your health by almost half with each punch (keep in mind that some of the highest damaging rocket launchers do about this amount of damage). Melee is made even more ridiculous and frustrating by the developers attempts to reduce it being affected by lag, they gave melee an insanely huge range... you can almost snipe people with it...
Now then, the cosmetics. A completely non-compulsory part of the game, you can ignore them all-together. But for people that do choose to buy them, you'll soon find you've burned through your Steam wallet, and only have a virtual T-shirt and a taunt to show for it. It has definitely been said before, but cosmetics are still ridiculously over-priced. The lowest amount of Spacebux (in-game currency) you can buy is 600, and guess how many cosmetic items cost 600 Spacebux in the store? None. 600 Spacebux can only get you ONE of a selection of FOUR avatar pictures... yay.
Ignoring the fact that a single taunt can cost you 8999 Spacebux (which is a little more than €10/£7/$12), let's look at what you can spend your real money on that DOES make a difference to your game (i.e not cosmetics):
1) More weapon slots to store your custom-made firearms. The most you can buy at once is 18, which isn't even all the slots you can buy from the store. This will cost you 30599 Spacebux. (About $47/£26/€37).
2) More Loadout slots to choose from each time you spawn. 9 extra loadouts will cost you 45899 Spacebux (About £39/$71/€56).
3)Experience and Blutes boosts. (Blutes are another in-game currency used to buy gun parts) - these boosts increase how many Blutes and Experience Points you recieve at the end of every game. The boosts are only temporary, and can be only used once. The prices of these vary, a boost of Blutes for 24 hours will cost €1.30/£0.90/$1.60, or a boost for 30 days will cost €15/£11/$19.
So, unlocking this game's full potential of weapon slots and loadout slots is going to set you back at least £65/$118/€93, and that is without any cosmetics or boosts. I know it's a Free 2 Play game, and the developers need to make money somehow, but seriously, the prices are a joke.
Rant over.
Don't get me wrong, I think there is a good game here; but for me, the negatives make the game too unenjoyable.
This review is based on my own personal experience of Loadout, and what I found to be annoying/ridiculous/unbalanced. It may be a different gaming experience for you.

Truly next-gen content, however you must have a relentless PC to experience it to the fullest. My points are relying on my fairly powerful PC, and your experience may differ if yours is too much less.
Pros:
1- "Truly next-gen content." Very great Textures, looks lovely and fairly realistic. The amount of tasks the game performs are great as well--billions of Zombies, each with their assigned missions, whether they are dead, mutilated, roaming or targeting you. as well as a huge number of obstacles, debris, props and any other Classifications for objects.
2- Open-world at it's finest. you've got 4 Islands. each with a different atmosphere, although there is not much classifying differences. Many Freeways and passages to connect each island to the other except for a single pair.
3- After all these years, and the few games that came as sequels to the first game, the game still carries it's light humour, high level of creativity, excellent Open-world making skills and relatable Protagonists. this is unfortunately not the case for many other Games series.
4- Huge Variety for the types of Collectibles as well as their Locations. Not much is needed to be said more than that.
Cons:
1- Very small amount of Options for the Online. I'd hope to see an option that gives random Players to join. instead, you have to choose the style your Co-op mate plays with. And even when I'm in the night, hoping to play with someone who's NOT from this Country (For various reasons), I only find a single person no matter what Game style I choose, who always seems to disconnect.
2- Not many combo vehicles as well as Outfits. Of itself, this may be considered an advantage, because there's more variety. But still, Only 5 considerably cool vehicles, 4 Vehicles, literally, called "Junk" and an extra miscellaneous vehicle. I'd hoped to see so much more. As for Outfits: I like Capcom's Humorous offerings of Clothes. But there's mainly a bunch of Female outfits, Cosplaying outfits and Outfits that look too ordinary. I'd like to see a colour-customizable Tshirt and many more additions.
3- Noisy and reoccuring Protagonist. It is truly annoying hearing this guy going around screaming, shouting, threatening, crying for help and enjoying the massacre. I hoped to see a Protagonist who can see that he can obviously wipe out the Zombie population if he had the motivation. I understand the relatable concept of making these guys, but we've seen that too many times already.
So, the game is actually very good, but I hope to see these cons defected. Vehicles and Outfits have previously already been added to the Game, so that can wipe a few of the flaws. And I need those extra Online options.

Its been a while since I have had so much fun playing a triple A game in a while (Don't count Nintendo, because c'mon it's Nintendo). Now let me tell you the reasons why I enjoyed the game as well as why I think you should play it.
Story: While most people say the story was lacking, I actually thought it was pretty good. While not super top-tier mind f*** territory of a story, I feel like this one fits just right. For anyone who does not know, you need to play this game a couple of times to get the whole story. While I won't anything about the actual story itself (Then why did you make a stor-Shuddup.), I will say that you will play the story as 3 different characters. Not sure if that's a Spoiler but....... sorry if it is.
Gameplay: It is very reminiscent of Bayonetta with the whole hack and slash, with the possibility of even slowing down enemies when you dodge at the right time using Overclock, which is this games version of witch time. Sprinkle in some bullet hell elements and you have another method of combat which you can simultaneously shoot and slash to provide more DPS. You can level up, upgrade weapons, upgrade pods (you'll know what they are when you play), yada yada yada leveling up system in game, WHOO! One thing I really like and find unique about this game is the Chip system. Since you are an android, you can install different chips to boost different stats or even gain new skills (Like Overclock which I mentioned earlier). Now while yes you can just find chips and install them, like any other computer based being, you have a data limit. This limit can be upgraded but even then you will not be able to use all chips since Data caps at 128. Now, each chip can vary in both Level and Storage. So you may have a two +3 Weapon Attack Chips, but one may take 7 Storage while the other might take 14 Storage. You can also fuse two chips of the same level to bump it up to a single chip with a higher level at the cost of more data, but sometimes this is a good way of saving space, it's all up to you. I've never seen another game have a system in which you can boost stats via the character only, not talking about leveling up or getting a god roll on a RNG weapon drop which happens to have stat boosts. Just thought this system/Mechanic was worth mentioning.
TLDR; I think the story was good, gameplay was fun and had a unique mechanic regarding leveling up. Music was unbelieveable (bought the OST), and I had the time of my life playing this game. I give it a 7/10.......... While I would give this game an easy 9, I can't due to the fact that a lot of people, including myself, have had problems running the game. I had a very fortunate solution in which just making the game Fullscreen with Alt+Enter fixed the game for me and I was able to play (For anyone wondering, I was getting a White screen but there was sound). Until this game gets a clear patch which fixes the problems for most people, it'll stay at a 7, but a 9 in my heart. Thanks for reading my review, hope this helped you decide if you want to play this game.

Deus EX: Human Revolution.
Hmm.
How do i even begin this?
From the start, i was interested in the game. Hell, even the name has a certain ring to it that makes it sound so imposing.
I immediately fell in-love with the story.
I love how you have choices about how you'd go about your mission, choices about Adam's augmentations, choices about what weaponry you carry with you and what upgrades you put in it, and choices about what to say.
I loved how even with all the augmentations you have, you'd still be vulnerable and mortal.
I loved how the Side missions unfolded, i loved the not so hidden pieces of lore and secret areas where you find free praxis kits and of course the END of it all.
It accomplishes what it set out to do in my opinion. Tell a gripping story, engage the player and show me what being human truly means when you are now thrust into a world where man becomes half machine. A vision of what might be in the far future and a sort of warning to those with the intellect to make augmentations in the future. Traditional morality and humanity fight a seemingly hopeless battle against the lust for power and the darker side of technological advancement. Absolutely gripping.
I have some qualms about it though:
-The citizens don't seem to feel believeable, its like they're generic NPC's. This disappointed me because of all the technological advances in gaming, they could not make it feel like i was in a techno centric world filled with interesting randomly generated NPC's.
-I keep hearing about harvesters in-game. They apparently take augmentations from people and sell them, literally ripping and harvesting them off people. IT WOULD HAVE BEEN SO EPIC TO FIND AND FIGHT OFF HARVESTERS.
Something like "The more you get aug'd the more they'd come after you" kind of thing.
-For an augmented person, Adam Jensen's movements were quite stiff. Minor issue but an issue nonetheless.
-I feel that this would have been great if you could choose to shift between third person and first person view. WAIT. Hear me out. I know the deus ex games have always been FPS games. Sure. But look at Fallout 3 and New Vegas, the ability to choose makes a lot of difference. I'm the kind of guy who likes to see his character do some cool♥♥♥♥♥♥and sometimes i'm in the mood to see it in first person so i feel truly immersed. To each his own but yeah you get the point.
All in all, this game is something you must play. Period.

Originally released by in 1998, I never really had the chance to play Fallout 2, mostly due to the fact I was too busy being born. Having got wrapped up into the Fallout 3 hype train, I became rather enthralled in the franchise itself. So, several years later, I picked it up and…
...in an attempt to not color my already vibrant opinion of the nearly twenty year old title to nothing but what can be considered felatio, let me just be a bit hypercritical about the game. The most glaring “problem” is what Fallout: New Vegas suffers from, by basically being the same game twice, effectively Fallout 2.0. While it didn’t work to the determent of the more modern entries, it hurts the overall visual experience with the sprites being rather noticeably polarized. Most are ripped straight from the original, built by pixels and with limited frame to frame animation. Then you have the newer 3D rendered sprites with smoother animation, creating an immersion breaking experience.
Thankfully, these sprites don’t really appear in the same cell often, but when they do it is noticeably. Another problem they never fixed was the ♥♥♥♥ING INVENTORY UI! Its clumsy and finicky at best, with the mouse cursor deciding the change sensitivity like a pregnant women. You will work around it eventually, but it just infuriates me how this aspect was never fixed. Its horrid but manages to get the job done.
Getting down on my knees, everything else is, the world, leveling system, character's, weapon variety and quest are, to put it broadly, ♥♥♥♥ING FANTASTIC. While the characters are a tad uninspired and two dimensional, and the story banal, Fallout 2 is possibly one of the best Western RPGs ever made. The leveling system grants satisfaction, managing to maintain this by having “Perks”(effectively permanent stat or combat boosts) that you receive every other level. You can’t help but wanting to progress with the prospect of nearly sawing men in half with not much but as dainty slap.
The world can be summarized as a sour salted candy advertised as extremely so, its daunting at first and WILL kick you♥♥♥♥♥once you pop it in you gob, but will eventually become remarkable sweet. Southern California is huge, being exceptionally difficult during the early game but incredibly rewarding later down the line. The only problem I have with the world is the lack of variety, but I feel the questing can make up for this.
I feel developers can live or die by the hand holding die. Choosing to do so makes the game a breeze, and choosing not to has the potential to make progress come to a screeching halt. Fallout 2 gives you just enough information to get on with the question without some patronizing arrow pointing out where to go. And can even have you thinking about solutions for the rare puzzle here and there. Quest are satisfying and varied to an insane degree.
Fallout 2 might possibly be one of the few games in which you likely won’t see every weapon or outcome. If you ♥♥♥♥ up, you ♥♥♥♥ed up and there is no turning back, with some things being consequently cut off. Prompting actual thought and replay-ability, I love this idea. The weapons on the other hand, are insanely variant. Its not the fact that a quest outcome closes them off from you, it's the fact there are so ♥♥♥♥ing many that you're unlikely to even find them all. Whether this works for the games prosperity or detriment.
Regardless, with its negatives and positives in check, Fallout 2 is one of the greatest title I have ever played. Even with its missteps, no matter how small, they pale to what the game does right. Of fantastic value, Fallout 2 is a must buy title, no matter its age.

Right now, this game isn't very good. It is in early access, being updated frequently, so this game has a chance to become good. But right now i do not recommend it.
Pros=
-potential to be good
-nice mix of unturned (zombie survival elements), minecraft (crafting), and rust (resource collection and base building)
-range of guns and melee weapons to find.
-nice crafting and resource gathering system
-constant updates
Cons=
-a little buggy and a little laggy
-foilage and buildings are not varied. All buildings the same (i would like to see some more types of buildings)
-objects extremely rare everywhere other than the military base. (makes looting anywhere else but the military base almost pointless, making the military base the only place where people really want to go.)
-map isn't very good. (a block for an island, and a couple squares of buildings, i would like to see a more detailed map with a larger variety of towns and other locations, not just three towns, and two military bases.)
-combat isn't smooth. Kind of jerky, consisting of hoping around and quick inaccurate shots.
-graphics and lighting aren't the best, making it hard to see, and annoying to look around.
-no singleplayer. (I think this game would benefit with singleplayer)
Over all this game isn't the best, but the game is still in early access, giving the game potential to become better with the constant updates. I will keep an eye on this game, and i will make sure to update this review according to how the game grows and changes with the updates.

Siralim 2 is a nice turn-based combat and monster breeder game.
The numerous strategical layers and fun boss fights makes this game a true gem of the genre.
The dev has been working non-stop to add even more choices and enjoyable Quality of Life Improvements.
Warning: Huge time sink :)

This game is incredibly deep. As someone who has always appreciated "speccing" in games, Siralim 2 may be the most I've ever been able to sink myself into making creative combos and unusual synergies. I regularly find myself delighted by the fascinating implications of spell gems I come across, or by the innate trait of a newly encountered monster.
Upgrading your Castle continues to open up your options for customization far, FAR into the game.  And the amount of enjoyment I derive from choosing the right enchantments for each creature's artifact is frankly ridiculous.
While the story is beyond thin, the writing is surprisingly entertaining.
When you've developed your team into an effective squad, make sure to have your librarian name those all-stars of yours. They've earned it.
9/10 for gameplay
5/10 for sound
2/10 for visuals

For being a free game, Paladins has gone above and beyond my expectations. Your ability to unlock characters in a timely manner as you play the game, in addition to free characters on "rotation", it seems there is a way to play for everyone. As with most team games, it is best if you play with friends, or with anyone who has communication and cooperation in mind. In-game voice lines allow for fairly complex tactical conversations which are much faster than typing out your responses. Each of the character's abilities in game may be modified via the "card" system, allowing for multiple loadouts for any situation. Each loadout has 5 slots for 5 different cards, and 12 points to disperse among them, allowing for certain cards to have greater effect, most of the time increasing whatever number value the card referes to.
Of course, Paladins being a free game means there are microtransactions for almost everything, including new characters, cards, cosmetic items, and account boosters. The premium currency are "crystals" which can be earned slowly through daily quests and daily login rewards. I must mention that crystals can be used to buy most things, like a character, but are not nessesary to enjoy the game as-is.
Art direction is hit or miss, depending on your prefered style. I feel like Paladins works well with it's cartoony graphics, calling back to the charm of older games like Team Fortress 2. The game seems to lack alot of things in terms of lore. What are the crystals used in most weapons? What does a "paladin" constitute in this setting? Why does a certain character care to fight at all? There are many questions but no answers at this time. As for the personallities of the characters themselves, most seem to fit into predetermined tropes and stereotypes, not really stretching to be original, but certainly portraying the character they are very well. Sound design is fair, most weapons have satisfying sounds for shooting and reloading, and they feel and sound correctly for how powerful a weapon is.
However keep in mind this game is in Early Access, so much of this can change in the coming months/ years. Overall, for a free game in Early Access, I would recommend at least giving this game a try if you enjoy titles like Overwatch, Team Fortress 2, or even MOBAs like DOTA 2 and LoL.

You spell words. You kill monsters. Why? For pizza.
Putting that aside, now for the very long game review.
__________________________
What's there to say when it's basically a word game? As long as you have a good vocabulary you're good to go... but not quite. Throw in the idea of RPGs, and you'll need not only your wits, but strength to overcome this arduous journey. The game itself is like scrabble, but it isn't a crossword puzzle. Consider it boggle, but you don't have to link the letters in a line to form the word. That's freedom, and I like the idea of it. Given a set of 15 letters, you try to form words 3-letters or more.
You think that forming longer words makes you smart and powerful, but I say "That's rubbish." On your quest for pizza, you will find yourself facing some 'smarter' monsters that can only understand certain words you throw at them. If you had the brains but know not how to use it, you will definitely find yourself dead, no matter how much time you spent investing in forming a long word. Naturally, long words do more damage, but would they always? No. Some 'wittier' monsters can only understand baby talk, so insulting them with witty words proves no help in your quest. But I'm sure you are smarter than these monsters guarding pizzas.
By RPG elements inclusion, it isn't you being a hero and saving the day since you're just out hunting for pizza using your trustworthy guide. You equip yourself with books that actually aid you in your journey which automatically writes new experience for itself as you battle your way to the delicacy. You upgrade your stats to aid you in your long battle. You find a new girlfriend and you decide to let her battle for you in the frontline while you take the pizza for yourself. You prove your wits and unlock cool stuff. What more do you want? Oh yes, the pizza.
So let me put my cynical talk aside, the game itself is decent. Difficulty is well balanced, graphics are simple and clean. More importantly, fonts don't hurt your eyes to look at, especially when it's a word game. You will immediately grasp hold of how the game works when new stuff appears which in my view is ideal. Music is alright, and can get repetitive easily but no one said you can't turn it off to play your own songs, so get on with it. As seen in the screenshots, the game plays a campaign story mode, and every stage is the same. Only difference being the difficulty and challenges presented. That much can bore a person with short attention span.
I generally like this game and would definitely recommend it to anyone who likes word games too. Don't forget, it's all for the pizza.

Deus Ex: human revolution - the directors cut is at it's core a cooprate espionage FPS/ RPG. The game really concentrates on story and dialog to pull you through, while at the same time experiencing a brilliantly mastered sneak/ shooter experience all piloted throught the eyes of the modern "6 million dollar man" Adam Jensen. His journey can be experienced in a number of ways thx to the stellar level design which (if you can find them) gives you tons of alternate routes to take to achieve the same goal. This goes for the dialog as well. Options really stand out in this game as it is more or less a linear experience the choices that you make or don't make do affect the game in noticable ways that make it feel.... well, not linear. On top of that it piles on content with an upgrade system that you will have to play through a second time to unlock all of your augmentations (thats right it has a new game plus) and the weapon choices are fairly meaty ranging from the pistol and combat rifle to a crossbow, laser cannon and a custom rocket launcher. All of these weapons can be upgraded wether it's a scilencer or boosting the damage. If all of this wasn't enough the game has an impressive story that draws you in and keeps you guessing for a minium of 30+ hours of "saved" gameplay.
I really don't have any complaints about this game. I bought it on the cheap during the winter sale and I am on my second play through right now on the hardest difficulty and it just keeps getting better. There is just something oh so satisfying about sneaking into the enemies security office, hacking the computer and turning they're own robots and sentry guns against them....pure bliss. I highly recommend Deus Ex: human revolution - the directors cut, it is a MUST BUY!!

For those looking to upgrade from the original:
The advertised boss fight upgrades are good if you want to experiment, but if you've played the game before you'll probably have more praxsis points than you can handle and know the best way to take these bosses down. For those newcomers:
It is a GREAT way for those looking to get into Stealth games.  It is easy to pick up and challenging to master while still not making things EXCLUSIVELY stealth-oriented.  The dialogue battles are also pretty great and tense, and I was amazed to see how they weren't just "do these options in this order".  It does really well at giving you a variety of choices, whether they be diplomatic or aggressive.  The aesthetics are fantastic, the voicework is great (perhaps a few hiccups with the foreign characters), and the overall gameplay is really fun and not repetitive.
A must-buy for all.

Siralim 2 is a brilliant example of everything a true sequel should be - a game that learns from its previous mistakes, and pumps steroids into its previous strengths.
The original Siralim was a compelling game that teemed with promise, but regrettably had some design shortcomings that relegated it to a button mashing grindfest with a frankly bizarre difficulty scaling system. S2, on the other hand, feels big, fresh,thrilling and satisfying from the word go. Here are some of the highlights, with comparisons between the two generations:
CUSTOMIZATION: Damn, Thylacine! So artifacts, spells, passive abilities, rituals, nether orbs and hundreds of different creatures weren't enough? Now, we have God's Favour, Runes, Cards, Multiple Spell Slots, Gems, Meals and who knows what else on the horizon?? That is the sound of an itch being scratched.
The incredible freedom afforded by S2 is palpable. There is a genuine sense as you play that you can try any team comp, any strategy, and you will find a way to make it effective. The game practically screams at you to experiment, and allows a level of creativity that S1 often grazed, but never fully penetrated.
SPELLS: S1's spell system was, in my opinion, dreadful. 99% of the time, spending an entire turn draining your mana into a single spell with a very meh effect essentially removed it as a viable tactical option, given that by the time you had any decent spells, you had invested in your team's abilities so much that you would be mad not to use your turn sending them in to Provoke/Attack. Casting spells felt boring and pointless.
But S2, oh you beauty, you learned well. Now your creatures cast the spells, and by God, do they do it like it ain't no thang. Spells are now gems, equipped onto slots on each creature (which average 3 slots each, meaning you normally have access to no less than 18 different effects in a given round of combat) and these gems can have random situational triggers (such as taking damage). This makes every single round of combat in S2 unique, exciting and meaningful, as a chaotic chain reaction of damage, debuffs and spell triggers can turn the tide of battle at any point!
REALMS: How many were in S1, like seven? S2 says HAVE ALL TEH RAELMS. And Gods, because why not?
THE ONE THING I DON'T LIKE: Those "boss" battles. Very gimmicky. Often frustrating if your team comp is not designed to deal with a particular enemy/effect. Can bottleneck your experience somewhat. Pro tip - INSPECT is your friend.
OVERALL: The game feels much more sandboxy and creative than S1. The battles are geuinely exciting. Things are looking good S2! Keep it up!

Real talk, this is a nerd game for nerds. If you care about HD headshots, go elsewhere.
This game and its predecessor are everything games like Dragon Quest Monsters and Pokemon bring to the table, except with all the complexity and depth being an intentional work of craftsmanship on the part of its (I believe) singular developer, rather than a series of company wide half-flavor, half-We-Have-No-Idea-What-Makes-A-Monster-In-Our-Own-Game-Viable-And-Fun-But-Not-Broken compromises. Which is not to say that every little aspect of the game is perfect (though for an early access game, much of it is functional and very fun), and it isn't to say that every monster is useful (some seem to be tailor made for ridiculously specific situations that are harder and harder to forcibly create the more punishing the game gets, and though I haven't hit that point yet, I can already see it on the horizon), and it isn't even to say that the game systems are so balanced that they cannot be broken (breaking them is part of the fun, you're going to need to to get past the deeper realms). But what there is a kind of ballet to the many, many interlocking game systems as devised by the developer, with an elegance and a real love for the genre. There is so much satisfaction to be had in discovering new monsters, puzzling out new strategies, unlocking new features, and feeling like the game is ready to meet and challenge you on a level that those other games, bless their child friendly hearts, are not.
As a series of final notes, I'll say that in my review for the first game I asked for boss fights and more of a story, and indeed this game delivered these, with me clocking the story's completion at 24 hours (not bad at all for the state of modern RPGs). I'll say this game delivered things I didn't ask for, such as a completely overhauled spell system and a better system for unlocking new monsters, which have brought as much pleasure to me as the angry totem god who called me ugly (more than you think). I'll say this game boasts all I have talked of whilst not even completed and more to come.
So nerds, buy the game.

Siralim 2 reminds me of a dig I read about Skyrim once. Someone said "the game has the breadth of an ocean, but the depth of a puddle."
Siralim 2 is the opposite of that statement; bredth of a puddle, depth of an ocean. There's little story, the castle starts off very small, the graphics are a stylish throwback to the gameboy color, almost everything is locked to keep from overwhelming you. But man, once you start diving into it, you just never hit bottom.
Full disclosure, I was given a copy of this game for free by a volunteer on the project who had a few extra codes. The copy came in exchange for my writing a review, but was mostly an act of goodwill; I'm not exactly IGN over here. That said, I would have bought S2 if I hadn't been given it, I've been waiting for a game like this since Dragon Warrior Monsters came out. The depth in this game is insane without being overwhelming; it reminds me of a tabletop rpg, where you can spend days crafting a finely-tuned character with a novel backstory, or slap a barbarian character sheet down and keep up with him in drinks. It's very liberating.
The progress the series has made from S1 to S2 is quite pleasing as well. I really wanted to like the first one, but it wasn't refined yet. I think this sequel fixes every problem the first had.  There are roughly twice as many realm types as there were before, they're all more interesting than the originals, and they level up linearly; no more doing realm 2 repeatedly because it was always equal to your level, now realm 20 is level 20 (plus some gene strength, a slight boost to enemy stats.) Creature unlocks are gone, now you unlock one monster in the wild from each family as you level / explore, and then as you breed them the resulting offspring are available in the wild as well. Nether creatures as well are supposedly a much more streamlined system, although I haven't reached them yet as I've been busy breeding, 500 creatures to unlock and all. The addition of a bit of story and the gods you have to interact with makes the world feel much more alive as well.
I think this is a must-buy for any who love JRPG's, a focus on progression / complexity, or creature taming games; it's a great mix, but ultimately it's going to be hard for me to sell this to you because I can't say it's better than X. I could say it's better than pokemon, but with the focus on breeding, the equipment, the spell gems, the twelve unique abilities on your team that completely change how a battle plays out? They're really not comparable. Similarly, I could compare it to a JRPG, but the focus is not on the story, it's on your ever changing team, the battle system is deeper than any jrpg I've ever played, etc. It's a very specific kind of game, so niche that aside from a gameboy color game from the nineties I can't think of anything directly comparable.
If Siralim 2 sounds like your type of game, it's got a huge number of positive reviews and is quite stable now, it feels like it should be ready to come out of early access in a few weeks, if I had to guess. You're buying a feature complete game that hasn't crashed on me once in a days worth of playtime. There aren't really any other options in the genre, and if there were I can't think of a single thing I'd want them to add. The game just feels definitive to me, I just can't imagine someone who's at all interested in this sort of thing not owning it. You've probably got fifty shooters and twenty Terraria clones in your steam library, I think it's worth owning something so very unique, an experience not offered by anything else.

Fallout 1 is a great game because of the dozens of ways you can build a character. In fact, it's not that hard to beat the game as a pacifist, relying on skills and such instead of fighting. It offers a true roleplaying experience and rewards creativity. It lets you roleplay the character that you want.
Fallout 2 is the opposite. It is based way too heavily on combat. Even on low difficulties, the fights are really hard. In addition, there are random encounters that happen while fast-traveling, that in addition to be very annoying and repetitive, also contribute to this difficulty problem. You basically get fatally punished for not making a perfect charatcer, and for exploring. The lattter of which defeats the purpose of an open-world game.
Playing a character that is focused around dealing with problems by using things like stealth, speech, or computers is impossible. Only heavily combat oriented characters can survive. But even if you optimize a character for combat, it's still ridiculously hard. I did exactly that (optimizing for combat) and still got 1-hit-killed by a gecko on easy after barely leaving the starting area, so I'm not exactly sure what kind of build is capable of beating this game.
Apparently, you can only play the developer's way rather than playing how you want to play. By not letting you play the ROLE you want, it completely defeats the purpose of ROLE PLAYING. And since it isn't fun and feels more like work, it isn't really a game.
So in conclusion, Fallout 2 neither role playing, nor is it a game.

Bioware took a gamble with a fresh IP that brought not only an unusual setting but also a rather stark departure from conventional RPG combat mechanics. Unfortunately, what starts off as an intriguing world with some real challenge ultimately becomes a tedious and almost entirely linear slog.
After finishing the obligatory tutorial area, the game's world opens up and you're free to indulge in a variety of side quests. While the writing is typical for a Bioware game, you'll encounter interesting scenarios and in some cases make unexpected (if not entirely nuanced) choices. The game uses a binary morality system, similar to Knights of the Old Republic, but the line between good and evil is not always as clear and sometimes it's best to take different routes if only to witness the most interesting results.
Early on, the combat is challenging and you're encouraged to experiment with new styles--at times you're even forced to when facing enemies that are immune to certain types of attacks. It's a little clunky and doesn't hold a candle to proper action titles, but it works and is not really the focus of the game early on.
Unfortunately, the final third of the game eschews this formula almost entirely. You're taken through several sequences of pretty much non-stop fighting, which is where the shortcomings of the combat system really become noticeable. Fights take too long to finish and you will most likely end up exploiting one or two strategies as surefire ways to take care of the onslaughts of enemies. Gone is the element of choice or character development -- you probably won't even feel the need to spend level-up points, given how easy the game becomes with just a few side quests under your belt.
At this point in the game, it becomes very clear that the developers ran out of resources and hastily put together the final segments without much concern for the player. While the momentum had previously been building at a steady and satisfying rate, completing the journey becomes a chore. You're robbed of any real pay off.
The game ran fine for me on Windows 10, barring the occaisional stuttering error, which were usually fixed with system reset. Technically, the game certainly shows its age, but the lackluster final act is what really undoes the whole thing. Unless you really like the idea of awkward real-time martial arts combat in an RPG, give this one a pass. Better games have come since its release.

"Paladins. It's like OverWatch, but with more strategy."
There, now that I've ticked off some fanboys, let's get to the actual review. :D
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Paladins is like Team Fortress 2 and a Moba mixed together, except with loadouts and a simplified 'item store.'
Oddly enough, I had grown out of TF2 AND Mobas (most notably for me, LoL). So what is it about the game that's so great?
The 'carrot on the stick' concept is strong in this one, and in part because it can afford many temptations with the F2P business model. The following things are carrots you can work towards: unlock a character, level up a character, (earn Essence in order to) unlock a legendary card, unlock a (regular loadout) card, and earn a daily login reward. And YES, they are addicting! I fully admit that, and I'm sure the devs would, too.
But before you get upset about the mental games, just remember this IS a free-to-play game, and as such -dare I SAY it- such manipulative practices are forgivable. #
The game is fun. There, I said it. Having powers and abilities that are out of this...realm, yeah, it's cool. And if you don't believe me then -try shooting the fireballs as Drogoz (with Damage-over-Time) or rapid-firing Torvald's Ultimate to shoot someone off the map- and tell me it wasn't a blast after.
Paladins has layers of strategy: team composition, your loadout, which legendary card you pick, and which items you buy throughout the match. (and more, but I won't get into it. got to keep my secrets. ;) )
Okay, you're going to hate me for the comparison here, BUT I'm STILL GOING TO DO IT: OverWatch DOESN'T have all this strategy. Another way to say it is, OW has strategy in different aspects, most notably in the ever-changing team composition.
Personally, I appreciate the locked-in characters, so I -and others- can focus on the other strategies. There is a LOT of customization to HOW you play in Paladins. My Pip might play very differently than your Pip; and I appreciate that. Paladins offers enough choice to let your builds feel personal...yet, not too many choices to where the game would be needlessly complicated or hard to digest. In My Opinion, it's the classic 'easy to learn, difficult to master'.
Like every game, Paladins has its faults. And I KNOW it's "still in beta", but criticisms are still worth mentioning.
It's like a modern day TF2, except it's a Hero Shooter. It's not as polished as it could be, but it's got Progression that feels rewarding, strategy, and the FUN factor.
I recommend. Nine out of 10. no IGN

Normally, I'm one for the epic fantasy RPGs and MMORPGs. The genre of "role playing game" has never crossed my mind as having a potentially educational aspect to it, much less one that could be simultaneously educational AND fun. However, Letter Quest: Grimm's Journey does it very well. The art style is adorable and smooth, the simplistic story is funny and compelling, and the "special conditions" ensure that gameplay is never stale. Small things aren't forgotten by the developers either -- there's comedic blurbs that explain each monster "history" to you on the right when in combat, and on the left there's definitions of the words you're spelling out. If you're a parent trying to get your kids to entertain the idea of entwining education and fun, or if you're like me (a college student killing time), this game is a blast. It's also fun to play with friends! Just gather a couple of friends around the fastest typer in the group and let everyone shout out words.
Now go get that pizza!

I just finished playing Icebound, finally getting the true ending, and I must say that it was amazing. Icebound is definitely one of the best VNs that I have ever played but I suppose I'm getting ahead of myself here. ^^
To begin, Icebound is a visual novel set in a world covered in ice. You take on the role of Dougal, a wandering alchemist who has lost his long-term memories due to a freak accident. Along with his Familiar Isaac, Dougal arrives in the frontier town of Isenbaar and there, he finds out about a challenge specifically designed for alchemists with the promise of a great reward, the Philosopher's Stone. Of course, Dougal decides to participate in the challenge along with three other alchemists, whom he gets to know over the course of his stay in Isenbaar. However, I'll stop summarizing from here since I don't wish to spoil what the rest of the story is about. Suffice it to say that there is a huge mystery going on where there's more than meets the eye. ;)
There are choices which affect what path and ending you get, and there are 3 different endings from what I've found. It's worth it to obtain either the order or chaos path first. Definitely save the other path (where order and chaos are balanced) for last, as I believe that's the true path and it's much better to see it after getting the other paths and endings. In addition to choices, there are alchemy puzzles to complete and they get progressively more difficult. I found them doable for the most part. I only have a minor complaint about the last one but that's only because the graphics for it were changed compared to the other puzzles, which kind of hurt my eyes a bit. But this is more a minor complaint than anything. ^^
The only criticisms I'd give are two. Although there weren't many grammar errors or typos, there were a few so perhaps some proofreading could be in order. Also, even though there were CGs in the game, there was no CG gallery and I would have liked for there to be one in the Extras section of the main menu. Again, these are minor criticisms more than anything.
Overall, I highly recommend Icebound, as it has a great story. I'm surprised it hasn't gotten more attention. It's definitely worth buying and I do love that true ending. I can see that there is potential for there to be a sequel and I'd love if there could be one someday. I'd definitely check it out. :D

Alchemy is more than just a handy skill in the world of Permia. Alchemists are both admired and feared and have the ability to sort out problems and fix what was once broken. I couldn’t get enough of Icebound, by Fastermind Games.
You can read the full review on my website at
, which goes into way more detail.
BUT. I will say that Icebound is easily one of the best visual novels I've played so far. It does so many things right and I had so much trouble putting it down. It's a great game, and definitely worth giving a go.

The story of Icebound revolves around Dougal and Isaac, an alchemist and his familiar who made a terrible mistake, and search for a way to rectify it. Along the way they meet many characters and explore new lands.
The art is decent, there is a variety of art for each character, as well as CG's for important scenes.
This VN does feature some gameplay in the form of Alchemy puzzles. These involve placing colored squares in the right order to fill up a board, these can be quite challenging, and can be a fun break from reading.
The music and sound design is well done, the music compliments the scenes nicely and flows seamlessly with the game.
Players who enjoy fantasy or steampunk novels wil enjoy Icebound, it features a refreshing story with interesting plot points and mystery to keep you interested, and gameplay and puzzles will keep you coming back for more.

Believe the hype. I was skeptical and a bit like "Ehhhh, this sounds like it's just a bunch of fanboys..." too. I didn't even know what Siralim was until I bought this game a couple weeks ago.
If you like this kind of game, you need to buy this game. And if you can't afford it, you need to do whatever it takes to get the $15 to buy this game.

Siralim is a competent game but doesn't do anything special for classic/retro RPGs.
You start off picking one of 5 focuses, like nature or chaos.  I picked nature which so far seems to mean I have a cyclops who hits hard and regenerates a decent amount of  HP every turn.  I also pick up a weaker combat pet that casts a random spell each time it attacks or is attacked.  I'm not sure if everyone gets that pet.  That would maybe be more interesting if I hadn't played Hearthstone which has lots of random spell effects.
The pets have relatively few traits and I can give any spells and equipment to any of them, so not much separates them.
I explore randomly generated 'dungeons' which have settings of desert, jungle, and so on.  The setting makes no gameplay difference.  You go around this basic map collecting loot and fighting monsters.  There's some 'mini-quests' which so far are just fetch quests (pick wood up off the map, bring it to a trader's hut for loot, click on mini-totems for angry totem dude).
Combat is a simple affair.  I can get by just attacking each round and it'll be over after 2-5 rounds.  I have spells I could use that buff/debuff for 5-10 turns, I'm not sure how long until using any of these will be worth it when combat ends so quick.  Lots of the spells require 20-50% of your pet's health to cast which makes them even more inefficient, since each pet does have a mana pool they could use instead.  I assume some could become worthwhile later in the game.  For now I only actively use 1 of my 6 spells (debuffs the targets defense), and one automatically gives an attack buff sometimes when my pet is hit.
I completely explore the first 2 dungeons and at the third dungeon I fight a mini-boss that absolutely devastates my 2 pet party.  I guess this means I'm supposed to repeat the level 2 dungeon to gain levels for awhile.
The game says you need strategy and care to beat these bosses, I imagine this means picking a few spells and equipment that might be a bit better suited for those enemies (although I have not encountered specialized spells/equip yet).  Or you could probably just have a standard gear set up, and use grinding as a solution for most of your woes.
There is a crafting system for components like in Diablo or Grim Dawn, combine basic elements to get something with a beneficial effect.  You also get 'recipes' for evolving your pets, whenever you end up getting those multiple pets to combine into one.
Overall my game time is spent grinding combat and I assume like Diablo and other dungeon crawlers, I'll occasionally consolidate my loot to enhance my powers somewhat.
Overall this is not enough for me.  For a completely pet centric game, I would've lliked to see something more interesting than a 6 party dungeon crawler.  I think of the opening sequence of FF6, which had you using over a dozen moogles to defend a location, or Ogre Battle which does it on a much grander scale, with many parties of 3-6 underlings.
Also i thought I read that this was a rogue-like, when I die my pets just get sent back to base so not sure where rogue-like comes in.
Overall this is an okay game.  It might scratch an itch you have, and depending on what RPGs you've played in the past the experience could be novel and interesting to you.  For someone like myself, who for better or worse has played well over a hundreds of games in the RPG genre over my life, it is not worth 15$ to me for sure, maybe 2-5$.  I've played more ambitious RPGs for free that someone made in RPG maker.
Try it for yourself, and/or support a dev that is making a solid effort.  Here I am just providing a critical review by a veteran and somewhat harddcore rogue-like/rpg gamer.

Really solid monster-collector with randomized levels, very roguelike, but without most of the penalties of roguelikes, like permadeath and such.  I like the game a lot, and as such I have a few suggestions for the devs, from a longtime fan of RPG's and roguelikes.
1) I spent a good chunk of my wet-feet character thinking that the back row was significant.  As far as I can tell, it isn't.  I understand you have to get all the sprites on the screen, but maybe scale back the size some to do a single row, or introduce a guard rating for the monsters in the back if nothing else.  Perhaps allow the PC this option to row their monsters as well.
2) Overhaul the battle interface a little, maybe look at doing a list with HP and MP like FF or something, it's more pleasing to the eye than the bottom row of tiles.  Even if the monsters just flash when they attack and bump forward for a second, it's something I'd encourage you to consider.
3) The map.  I am in love with exploring the different realms, they're fun to uncover, and the style of it really brings me back.  This part of it is nearly flawless, but the map needs some attention, I believe.  Maybe it's meant to be vague to encourage more thorough exploration, but it's nigh unreadable at times.  Maybe a color difference between discovered and undiscovered terrain is what's needed, at the least.
4) Some sort of levelled list of creatures in your stable/in your party.  As it stands I have to check out the character sheet of each creature to determine levels, which evidently are a huge consideration in the game, since you want to construct parties for particular depths/levels.  I also feel like the artifact/equip mechanic needs some love too.  I don't want to have to check out each monster's artifact individually, nor do I want to do the same with spell gems.  It's still in EA so I understand that mechanics are refined further, just suggestions from a fast fan!
All that having been said, I'm having a good time with the game.  Keep up the fantastic work!

If you love old-school RPGs, monster-catching games and/or your played Dragon Warrior Monsters 1 and 2 when you were younger, this is the game for you. A game that literally never ends, Siralim 2 will test your team-building skills with its 537 creatures and traits, 40 runes that alter your skills, about 200 spells to choose from, customizable artifacts, and more. You can also change the way you play by selecting "Punishments" for a personal Siralim 2 experience.
If you're not put off by the old-school graphics, definitely give this game a try.

"I wish Steam would let me filter out Early Access games!"
I've had this thought often as I looked through my discovery queue to see a bunch of copycat, cookiecutter pixel-art roguelikes. I stumbled onto Siralim 2, was ready to dismiss it, and then one of the reviews mentioned Dragon Warrior Monsters. 40+ hours later, I can say that I'm hooked.
Siralim 2 is a fusion of Magic and DWM with a little bit of Disgaea sprinkled in for flavor. You breed creatures and make them stronger, but it's about more than just raw brute force. Each monster species carries a unique trait, and these traits tend to be similar within a family; Spectres focus on reducing enemy stats, Carnages have bonuses activate when they kill enemies, and Storms get bonuses when they're at high HP. Finding the synergies between these is a lot of fun! It's possible to run theme parties as well. Creatures like Hounds, Hordes, and Griffons have bonuses that depend on creatures of the same type.
The developer's quite active as well. The game's already feature-complete, so you're not paying for an alpha! In the 2+ weeks I've had the game, I think there have been 3 major patches updating the UI and balance concerns. A lot of these have come from player feedback as well.
Don't let the early access tab scare you away. This is an example of a dev using Early Access to fine-tune the game so the final product shines. Jump in, have fun, and RIP snowstorm spam.

This game is easily shaping up to be a masterpiece of an RPG. While lacking in the story department, and not the most polished gem on the market, it more than makes up for it in its unique gameplay experience. It feels like a cross between Pokemon, Disgaea, and Dragon Warrior Monsters, with a hint of TCG-esque strategy thrown in.
With infinite levels, over 500 monsters each with their own traits, thousands of collectibles, and an absolutely stunning amount of depth, this game will give you plenty to do and plenty to learn.
For me, it hits all the right spots. Depth without convolution. Grind without monotony. Almost 50 hours in, and - while it's not adrenaline-pumping action - I'm certainly not bored, and I never once find myself asking, where to from here? Punishment for death is low, encouragement to experiment and build multiple parties is high, and the pace of the game is very nice and steady, with discoveries and content fed at a pace that does not overwhelm, but still holds interest.
Plus, the dev gives small updates damned near daily. Dude's a machine. God damn.

Did you enjoy Pokémon as a kid? You might find this game brings back very fond memories. Yes, there are some admitted flaws and crashes, but the consistent patching is truly excellent in finding and correcting them. If you are a patient gamer, with an interest in developing and testing teams/skills/gems ideas this game is for you.

Everyone is comparing this to Dragon Warrior Monsters. There's a good reason for that: it FEELS like Dragon Warrior Monsters, but with layers and layers of added complexity.
Every monster has a special trait that makes it unique. This is not hyperbole; literally every one of the 500+ monsters has a special effect, like poisoning all enemies when it gets hit, or absorbing the stats of enemy monsters it kills. This makes team building incredibly satisfying; whatever sort of synergy you want, there's a monster combo that does it.
Add to that artifacts your monsters can equip, and which can be customized with materials you'll find while exploring, so you can tailor THOSE to whatever style you want.
Bolster that sort of combo-crafting with runes YOU, the player, equip, and spell gems for your monsters, which not only grant spells, but also can have special effects that trigger randomly. . . and there are at least a half-dozen systems this review doesn't even cover! Gods, cooking, sigils, and don't even get me started on the awesomeness that is the breeding system.
I've gotten more hours out of this than I have out of AAA titles I payed four times as much for, and there's still so much content I've barely touched! I cannot recommend this game enough; get it immediately!
