If you think it was difficult growing up as a human, just consider how it would have been growing up as a monster. Your life starts in a tank of slime and while growing up you gain different amounts of personality traits (bravery, cleverness, ferocity, honesty, and kindness) and the respect from other monsters based on the desicions you make as monsterling, adolescent and fully grown monster. If you are sufficiently respected you may continue your monster career as an elder, or you get recycled in the tank. You may even go on to achieve great accomplishments in the diplomatic interactions between monsters and men. You can write monster history!
Monster Loves You! is a cute little game, or rather a cute little interactive story, where the choices you make matters. It is very nice in small doses, but after a couple of lifetimes the little adventures you experience starts getting a bit repetitive. The same can be said about the music. It is interesting that the way some choices influence the personality are not immediately obvious, but that they start to make sense after a while when more is learnt about monster life. The storyline is inventive and clever and the monsters are cute to look at. Monster Loves You! offers a relaxed escape from the human reality.

Simple, but deceptively replayable. It's a choose-your-own-adventure type of game, starting you as a monsterling that was just born. This is simple but, again, rather adictive. After 6 hours and about 8 (?) playthroughs I'm still getting newer and newer stories as I go along, which adds the replay value of the game (besides the fact that it possesses 14(!!) ending, to my knowledge).
Graphically it's just multiple backgrounds with no real animations (unless you click your monster avatar, which will make him jump and say weird♥♥♥♥♥♥xD), so to review graphics, I'd really review one thing:
Nothing short of great. Buttons are clear, with something indicating what the story behind each clickable button may consist of. A scared monster face may lead to a story about investigating a human house, for example. Nothing more to say, really, informative, simple and slick, the UI excells in this adventure game unlike for of its genre.
With no voice acting, that leads the music which is kind of a few tracks that repeat themselves. They are pretty good and chilling, suiting the happy and cute atmosphere the game transmits.

[Note: The game time logged on Steam does not reflect the time I spent playing Fallout to date. I bought it back in 1997 on CD-ROM and have owned a couple of other bundles which included it since, and have completed Fallout 2 at least a dozen of times since first release.]
This is definitely a worthy successor to the first game.  It's bigger, better and it follows the original story line of the "lone wanderer." You're in search for the G.E.C.K., thar Garden Of Eden Creation Kit to save your village.
The recipe is the same as in Fallout 1, just improved. It's one of the best RPGs I've played and it thankfully gives you a different setting than the typical fantasy, elven and dwarf infested dungeons. Not that I have anything against that, but this is refreshing!
In addition, there is the community developed "Fallout 2 Restoration Project" which adds A LOT of content, fixes and tweaks to the game, that were never added properly, were buggy, or missing. Even if you have completed this game a number of times before (I would hope at least once!), then this adds a tremendous replay value.
The cast members of the previous game resume their high quality performances again and all I can say is: Go play. For the love of the lone wanderer, play this game!

Drawing from its inspiration, it features a breeding system and randomly generated dungeons that can be infinitely explored. The game also features its own innovative twists in the form of spell gems, artifacts that can grant traits, and a deity reputation system.

Cons:
Overall, Siralim 2 is a great game with stunning amounts of content. As far as I know, it's pretty much one of a kind in term of the market niche it fills. Highly recommended.

The first was great, and this is a big improvement. More monsters, more customization, more unique abilities. If you've never heard of it, think of it like an infinite pokemon like. I was hesitant to give a good review, since the game has many flaws, but the recent content and balance patches are amazing, so here you go. I recommend Siralim 2.
Positives:
- That pokemon feel
- Insane amount of content (castle building, monster breeding, gods, cooking, artifact enchanting, spells, etc...)
- It is grindy, but you always unlock some new shiny stuff in some areas while you grind on other areas (you grind for materials, favors, to unlock new combo breedings, to finish large enchantments, etc...)
- You can combo monster powers and artifact powers in unexpected and clever ways
- Developer constantly improves the game, it is really going to the right direction
Negatives:
- Low gfx and other production values. Pixel art is nice, but meh. Music is rather annoying, sound effects are average at best.
- It really can get grindy. The new turbo mode helps a lot though.
- Some things work quite mysteriously. I still don't know what the DOT damages (poison, burn, etc) are based on, for example.

This game reminds me of the older monster raising games I used to play on the gameboy. Mainly Dragon Quest Monsters. Which is fantastic because I've missed that series since the DQM 2 remake doesn't seem to be heading out of Japan. This game scratches that itch for a more robust monster RPG with the same kind of randomly generated dungeon diving that was in Tara/Coby's Journey. The grinding feels more meaningful as well since you work towards earning favor with the various gods. I do have a fairly minor issue with the game though. Mainly with the creature designs themselves. There are MANY monsters in this game and they have unique abilities buuuut...there are a lot of creatures that are recolors or simply have something added to them. One that made me laugh was a sphinx monster with the big change from the original being an axe laying up against it. Not wielding it or anything...its just there. I'm not too deep into the game though and I do like the creatures. I just wish that the differences between the various base creatures was larger. Give that Gorgon Witch a sick hat. Aside from that I've really enjoyed what I've played and if you're looking for an rpg you can sink tons of time into I say go for it.

This game is freaking GREAT. Honestly, I tried the portable version of Siralim 1 and liked it. Decided to try Siralim 2 and, even in early access, it is improved in many ways. The combat is a bit more complex (your creatures can all learn spells, the way traits and stuff works is a little more transparent now, creatures have powers that synergize in more interesting ways) and still super fun.
The graphics turned me off at first, I'll admit it. And the fact that there are no flashy attack animations didn't help my initial thoughts of the game. Really everything about the visual aspect of the game is fairly unimpressive. HOWEVER, the game is REALLY fun. I've actually come to enjoy the graphics and I like that the attacks don't have animations. Why? Because there is so much complexity to how you play the game. Building a team is more than picking an attacker, a tank, a healer etc. that you usually see in video games. Each creature has a special trait that makes them unique. One starter creature gains 40% defense after every successful attack, for example. Another creature has a 50% chance to revive a random party member on attack. And there are even creature types that synergize with the same creature type. If you've played Magic The Gathering and you've seen Sliver cards you'll know what I'm talking about.
I've only scratched the surface of the game but I had to pull myself away to keep from playing all night long. I haven't touched the breeding, gene boosting, nether creatures, enchanting, advanced crafting, cooking etc. and STILL think this game is awesome.
Must have. Buy now.

Much has been improved since the prior game, especially the spell system as each creature can now equip gems to cast spells based on their element type. This makes party configuration and customization miles better than the previous entry. Additionally, the reputation based systems add a compelling reason to revisit the different realm types, of which there are quite a ton. That, coupled with the new breeding system grants almost endless playability, as you can increase the "gene strength" of offspring giving them greater possible stats with each new generation. There are also many combinations that cause new "evolved" type creatures to be formed which combine two creature types.
In terms of criticism that could be leveraged against the game, I would say that the art and map generation are a bit lacking. The game reuses most (maybe all) the creature graphics from Siralim, but there are new ones included as well. This, I don't mind so much as it only means more content. However, I would have liked to see a change of tileset for Siralim, as the layout is more dynamic this time which is great, but the textures/feel of the city are the same as the previous game.
The game (as of now) is still only at version 0.1 in early access so much may change, but for those who haven't played the first game I would recommend to pick this game up as the content included already surpasses the first game and overall I find it way more fun to play than the first game.

Nomad is a mix of Minecraft and DayZ, taking the worst of both games and making it something totally not unique and mindlessly boring.
You are put into a world where zombies have somehow destroyed society as we know it and you have to survive. Waking up at a beach with nothing but a rock and the distinct feeling that something is lacking, you have to gather resources like wood, stone, metal and especially food and water. There are towns scattered across the map which have some resources, but also zombies that appear randomly and attack and most likely kill you. The lack of any explanation or tutorial will be the worst enemy within your first few hours.
Within the first minutes of this game it becomes painfully obvious that this is not only a very early alpha game, but also that the developers have absolutely no clue on game design whatsoever. The interface is a good candidate for the worst interface ever made in gaming history, and leaves you clueless every other second. In fact I spent my first few minutes in this game trying to figure out how to close the inventory screen, because it opens if you access anything with E, but close by hitting Tab. This "intuitive" UI continues through everything. You cannot drag&drop items (obviously too hard for the devs to implement), you click on every single item, then on either use, scrap or drop at the bottom. And what happens on "use" often is a mystery, if anything happens at all.
You can carry 2 tools (weapons, pickaxe, stick) in your hands, and 8 items in your inventory. And since items don't stack ever (except for ammunition), the very first thing you need to build is a backpack. This requires you to scrap your clothes to get cloth, so you will run around naked for basically the rest of the game, because cloth is just to valuable to wear it. You can gather wood and stone with the rock you woke up with, but only on specific mining nodes. Trees are obvious, but while rock is everywhere around you, just special rocks actually drop stone. Yet another hint on how unintuitive the game is.
Since it is very easy to build houses, you in fact can make on within the first 10 minutes of the game, just with your lovely rock, the world is filled with abandoned player-houses. The game's towns don't look any better though, most of them are blind copies of the exact same house with the exact same rooms over and over. Also almost all of them are empty and contain no loot, so most of the time is spent on walking through abandoned houses, which all look exactly the same, hoping for a bottle of water before you die from thirst. so you can eventually progress in the crafting tree.
It is very easy to die in this game, may it be because hunger and thirst drains faster than you can replenish it, or because zombies - while being easily dispatched - will make you bleed, and - we all know how the body works - bleeding never stops. Unless you apply bandages, but those require cloth, which is required for several other crucial tools as well. Effectively gathering resources is a nightmare, and it soon becomes clear why there are so many "no zombie" server variants are out there.
Graphically this game is worse than Minecraft. While it claims to have a "retro" look, it is actually just badly designed and thrown together crap, that makes you wonder if they have any designers at all. Not only do the town buildings look all the same, they even use the same bad textures all over the place, which will also make your house look really bad. But they spent time on creating masks for your character as head wear, so you can run around naked with a pig mask. However the only thing this gives you is the distinct feeling that the developers are just making this game for the lols, and that it will never turn into something even remotely fun.
The only thing positive I can say about this game is, that it is free. Although you can spent money to become a premium member, but my strong advice: don't ever do that, this game is not ever worth a since cent.

Before You Buy:
What's in the Box?
1x USB Wireless Dongle
1x Dongle "Dock"
1x Micro USB Extension Cable
2x AA Batteries
1x Steam Controller
Misc. Pamhplets/Instructions/etc.
Review:
I bought this yesterday actually, and I have to say that I was impressed. The build quality was excellent, the functionality was there, and the overall presentation of the product was really nice. The only downsides to it are the possibility that you get a defective USB dongle (which I did when I bought it yesterday [I returned it this morning and got a replacement at GameStop]), the learning curve that comes with the controller, and the overall button layout. It functions well in games such as Batman: Arkham Knight (if you can run it), The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, Tomb Raider, Hitman: Absolution, etc. as well as other titles by utilizing pre-established game profiles. For the games that don't have their own controller profiles, you can set your own or choose from a number of templates. There is also a customizable desktop-friendly mode that utilizes the trackpads to use as a mouse and scroll wheel and the bumpers as mouse buttons. This is all changeable of course. Personally, I think that the X,Y, B, A Buttons are a bit too close to one another and awkward to reach from the Right Control Pad (I find myself pressing the B Button instead of A pretty often) and the Steam Button and accompanying buttons are too far from everything else on the controller. Overall, I think that the quality of tjhe controller itself coupled with it's customizability and versatility make it a real keeper. It is taking some time to get used to it, but I can see it becoming a regular thing that I use to game. As a side note, it is very good for the price. Other controllers like the Xbox One Controller go for about $10 more and the dongles alone set you back almost 40 bucks. All of this is provided by Steam/Valve "free of charge" (worked into the price of the controller).
I hope this was helpful and educational to anyone that is thinking about/hestitating to get a Steam Controller!

The DLC expierience has been phenomenal, just like the game. The DLC adds four new chapters, along with characters, weapons, and new automobiles. Overall, Capcom managed to redeem this games high quality by fixing practically every reported problem. This game is one to buy at the 35-40$ mark if you have a high end PC and could run great graphics, if not, 20$ is a good deal for this game that boasts unique features like no other.

Story/Gameplay:
I love Dead Rising and bought a Xbox 360 specifically for the first Dead Rising. Dead Rising 2 was also a great game and expanded with even more things. The first two games I believe had some great stories and psychopaths. Dead Rising 3 introduced Nick Ramos, who I found to be just as likeable as the other two protagonist from the first two games. Maybe it's just me, but I found the psychopaths a bit more believable in the first two games. Then again this is Dead Rising and things are a bit over the top. This game takes place 10 years after part 2 and If you have played all the games *including case west* then you will be suprised to see all the references from previous games. I did not play case west, but I don't believe it mattered that much as far as the story goes.
With that being said, I don't think you're supposed to focus too much on Dead Rising's story. It's really not that hard to follow and the game sums up a lot too. The gameplay portion is what you would expect from Dead Rising. Thousands of zombies on screen and multiple ways to kill them. The introduction of combo vehicles makes things fun and interesting. The map can be a bit tricky to get around at first, but eventually you should learn how to navigate it quickly.
Closing:
I initially started playing on a keyboard and mouse, but quickly switched over to a controller. Don't get me wrong, it is playable, but I found it a lot more enjoyable and easier to play on a controller. I will say that I strongly believe this game needs a FOV option though. There were times where I would have much appreciated the ability to zoom out a little further from the default camera position. I strongly recommend removing the 30FPS lock as well. The game runs a lot better... well it did for me.
If you're a Dead Rising fan, I would suggest trying this out. It's definitely a worthy sequel and is fun. With the recent release of patches, Capcom has improved stability a little bit more for me. I would assume that things can only get better from here.

Did you ever read one of those choose-your-own adventure books as a child? This is essentially that, but as a videogame, with a visible character for you to be. You evolve with your actions, leveling your personality and form depending on your choices. It is a highly fun game, with plenty of replay value--though I do warn you should always click on whatever new adventure you have possible to avoid repetition. It's definitely more akin to a book then a game, so don't hop in expecting a average 'point and click adventure'. Another slight warning; This game is very child-friendly from what I've played so far, but does depict death and the 'natural cycle of life'. I feel as if it covered the topic wonderfully (Especially if you choose to 'delay' near the end, and talk with the monsterling.), which may actually be a plus for parent's who aren't quite sure how to explain such complicated matters to children. An average playthrough is roughly one-hour long, but the game is definitely replayable for at least two more times (possibly not in the same day, however.) In the end, I highly reccomend it for both it's nostalgic feeling, and general entertainment.

This is a game that expects you to replay earlier levels for more currency to unlock new items every once in a while, and maybe return to them to unlock new paths on "Hard Stages". If you just play the "required" levels, the game actually ends quite early, and there's a bonus world at the end which is sort of an HP sponge slog.
I will also admit I dislike this game's dictionary - it feels incredibly limited, which is ill-suited for a game wherein you need to create words it recognizes as such to play. Letter Quest is a pretty fun word game with light RPG mechanics. Essentially, you're a grim reaper-looking dude who's on a quest to get pizza - a much more relatable story than many other games I can think of. On the way, he has to fight monsters, such as ghosts, snakes and giant rabbits - just like going to the corner pizza place in real life. You defeat monsters by spelling words on a Boggle-like board, doing more damage for longer words or words with less common letters. Then you earn points that you can use to buy upgrades.
The game does get a tad repetitive after a while, but it's a fun thing to play for a little while here and there. My only serious complaint is that the game is a mobile port - not a problem in itself, but there are a few cases here and there where it really shows, with instructions to "tap" a button, for example - just little things not exactly meaningful when you're playing on a PC instead of a tablet or some such.

If you love Scrabble (like any healthy, well-adjusted adult should) and you love RPGs (because you aren't a soulless monster/Nazi/piece of human waste), then you'll love Letter Quest.

Here you are born in a tribal village in the wasteland of america,  your home where your ancestor known as the vault dweller of V13 was exiled from his overseer due to the fear of spreading diseases and radiation inside the vault towards the pure dwellers, your ancestor did nothing wrong but saved his people from being forced out of the vault into the cruel wasteland due to a dying water supply and being raided by monsterous mutants of the Master's army, he walked north and north to find a tribal village on the wasteland... in present time, you discover your home village is dying.. brahmin are dying, children sick with diseases. everything was starting to fall apart slowly, but you the decendant of the v13 dweller have been chosen by the village's elder to go out the wasteland explored by your ancestor to find the mighty G.E.C.K to fix all this hell happening.. and that is where your journey begins.
Now with some quick tips before you first time play this game:
I reccomend reading this guide to help you get started playing, trust me its worth to read than being torn to shreds by a small Enclave patrol or getting shotgunned in the face when you try to fight with melee in a random encounter. small spoilers because the guide also brings up the details with all the quests available in this game

You can also choose to do what ever you want. Killing before asking/chatting, turning the tables of the side quest (i.e giving the brahmin you were meant to guard to the twins when you trick your dumb tribal friend into running away)
you can't slaughter the villagers in your home cus otherwise the game will be over insta.
There are also Companions that you can take with you on your travels, based on my experience I will give you the details of the companions I had with me.
Vic This man may be your second/first companion you can bring along, he's good for ranged weapons, be sure to collect his rifle at his shack in the first town you go to, but he's often slow and bad for melee combat.
Lenny A ghoul, he's not great with combat and carrys a knife with him but he is a decent doctor, have him as your field medic and sort. Also he cannot run.
Marcus this guy has a talking head voice acted too, but if you want this big hulk with you, its best you either take his mini-gun away and give him a plasma rifle, or have him as your only companion because he will freaking kill every single thing in his line of fire no matter who's infront when you're in combat, his mini-gun often has a unaccurate shot hitting mutiple targets in a burst of fire which means he can instantly kill you or his fellow companion by accident.
K9 this cyber dog is simliar to the famous dog-meat but he can talk and is cool, you can find him inside a lab at the navvarro Enclave base, its best you get in there with the highwayman car otherwise you will have a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥experience getting killed by enclave patrols in 1 turn every time.
Goris this DEATHCLAW is quite a badass, except he can only fight with his claws in melee so he can sometimes get in your line of fire including marcus's and his animation with his jedi cloak gets repeative.
The story also has multiple endings on every town and faction you have met along in your travels, your actions towards them will bring them a future, for example if you slaughter the slavers at the Den and free the slaves, the town will flourish and sort, and if you screw up modac its gonna die because you made a mistake on your decision.

Oh wow, where to start.
This is my first forray into the Deus Ex universe.  Funny story behind that fact is I have an Deus Ex 1 CD I received in a bundle from an old computer I bought from Alienware when I was a spoiled little kid who didn't know how to build a PC yet, nor was it really mainstream to do so.  (Oh the horror of my parent's wallet!  But I will say it was a dream come true.  Thanks Mom.)    Anyway, I believe at the time I was too young to appreciate the story-driven action game like Deus Ex.  In other words - the game required not only a bit of intelligence, but patience.  You mean I can't just shoot everyone?!   Maybe you can, but not in the opening dock scene for Deus sake!  I'm rambling, the undiagnosed ADHD explains it all, back on track now:
Graphics:  I think they're nice and up-to-date.  I actually like the way the faces and animations look over games like Metro 2033.    Do those game have technically superior graphics?  Maybe so, but Deus Ex: HR captured the atmosphere and the characters feel real to me; their eyes seem more alive, and their movements with purpose.  I think well done on all levels.  Some may argue the proportions aren't exactly realistic, but from the commentary I think they exaggerated certain features on purpose and again I think it works great.
Sound:   The voice acting is supurb.  All the guns make their appropriate rattle, boom, and pop.  Even the stun gun has a charming buzz.
Augmentations are especially cool.  I don't want to spoil them or what each one does.  The sound of  The music is cool and fittting.  It kinda reminds me of Mass Effect a bit, and that's certainly a pro in my book.  All digital, just like the world Adam Jensen - the main protagonist - lives in.
Story:   The amount of detail and love put into this story is what really sold me on this game and made it the game I wish I'd picked up years ago.   The only bonus to waiting so long was I got it on sale for $5 bucks, and the extra polish.  The director commentary was enjoyable, and gave you a feel of the dev team - obviously a cool and talented group of devs.  I almost feel like it was a steal, but I paid in full when I went out like a fanboi and bought the companion book, Deus Ex: 'The Icarus Effect.'  (So far, also a good read, and compliments the game as much as it is a stand alone story worthy of becoming an expansion pack - I wish.)
I won't give the full story away since I'm lazy, but in short, you're Adam Jensen.  You're a pretty cool guy and you have awesome taste in beards and sun glasses.  You're also a bad♥♥♥♥♥security contractor for Sarif industries, a large biotechnology corporation.   Sound cool?  Good.
You wake up from a brutal attack on the laboratory for whatever nefarious reasons.  The love of your life is gone alongside her team of scientists.  Where the heck did they go?  We don't know ...
Not yet.
6 months later . . .  You're back at work . . . you've got work to do, but all you can think about is what happened and figuring out whose behind it.  Your boss tells you to hurry up, you would rather snoop on Pritchard's computer to find his dirt.  He must know more than he lets off!    He's literally speaking through a bio-chip in your head!  Damn you Pritchard.  I missed you, you pony tailed smart♥♥♥♥♥ thanks for fixing my augmented eye balls.   (OK on a tangent, sorry.)
The story unfolds, the plot thickens, you hide, you shoot;  remember your choices influence game dialogue and events!   I really don't want to give it away!  Let's just stick with biotechnology, corporations, illuminati, and cool sun glasses.
Also as a side note - apparently everyone in the future still smokes too much.
Gameplay:
The gun play is miles ahead of the original Deus Ex.  The physics seem decent, the bullets and damage system is rather realistic.  I like the way you shot a gun and it feels right.  They obviously did their homework on this, even though the game is aimed to utilize stealth over force IMHO.
If you don't like guns and hurting people is wrong - you can always go on the stealth approach and literally not kill a single person in the game, spare the bosses.  I like options!
The augmentations are done nicely.  The one everyone loves is The Icarus landing system as an example.  Basically, you can jump from any height and electromagnetic energy or something discharges before you hit the ground and saves you from going to the ER.  Not to mention it doubles as a shock-wave like weapon to all surrounding enemies.  Then of course you have hacking and the many passive augmentations, such as the rebreather we all know and love.
It's not exactly open world, but there are some interesting paths to take - at least you always have a duct to crawl through - some might say this a con - and even the developers admit they may have overused to duct crawling.
I question the AI like most games, but for the most part, in a game like this where it's a mostly linear path to take - they get it right for the most part spare some path finding issues when the AI is startled or "Oh my God I heard something, but I can't open this door to find out what it is, etc."   There's challenge to be had, but you can certainly exploit the game in ways to make it easier.  Nothing game breaking though.
I find the quiet, stealthy approach to be the most authentic experience to be had in the game.  But don't forget to shoot off a .38 with explosive rounds - now that's fun.  That's what save games are for dummy!
Of my few complaints is I find that heavy weapons are cool, but cumbersome and not really worth the inventory space they take up; they are rarely useful unless you like blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up and reloading.  (Guilty as charged.)  I also question the usefulness of some of the augmentations.   Some augmentations are WAY more useful than others, such as hacking or arm upgrades/strength for inventory space and smashing walls..  I swear I can't imagine going through this game without having the hacking augmentation to read the dirty e-mail coorespondences, or the ability to smash through a wall - it's almost necessary to enjoy the game, and I think that makes sense if you're head of security and your best friend is Pritchard.
You best know how to h4x.
Anyway.  I give it a 9/10.  Loses a point for ending, and some minor things.  10/10 games don't really exist anyway!  But let's assume I'm forgiving I'd have no problem saying 10/10.   Needless to say I installed the original Deus Ex from a CD (Yes a CD-Rom people, remember those?  I don't miss them much though!)
Just buy it.  Or go back in time and buy it.  Either way, 5 or 10 bucks - worth every penny if you call yourself a PC gamer!

Writing this after finishing my first play through, having only played this version, the Director's Cut.
I'm also somewhat disappointed after missing out on the Pacifist achievement.  I think i know where i went wrong, but now I don't have the motivation to play through again just to get it, as i'd be doing everything practically the same way again even if i also went for the 'Foxiest of the Hounds' achievement.
And thats really the big appeal of the Deux Ex games where you receive a set of tools and a sandbox to go try them out and see what happens.  There's always more than one way to accomplish your goal and crucially HR retains the same feel from the original game.
I still quite vividly remember the iconic first level and tooling about trying different things, messing with the AI, turning on taps and piling up random bits of junk for no reason.  Fortunately the same feelings of freedom and rewarded ingenuity are present again and once I got my first mission after the tutorial it was like being back on Liberty Island again.  I was hooked and I knew this was a game i'd be finishing.
I want to mention the voice acting as its some of the best i've heard in a while.  Although i can't really say it for Jensen himself who seems to have a rather one note delivery, but both the supporting cast and the dialogue were great. The dialogue options synced up nicely too and avoided the ambiguity that Bioware's often suffers from where what you say wasn't exactly what you expected.
Actually there's so many good things about this game its easy to take them as a given.  The story, background and world building, level design, pacing, feedback, augmentation choices are all top notch.   Graphically its merely functional.  Its not pretty, infact its downright ugly in places.
The boss battles are probably the weakest part of the game.  There are multiple ways to succeed in them, but it becomes basically a case of keep trying things and dying until you find the thing that cheeses it in the cheapest way.  It should feel rewarding like the rest of the game does but instead, all i feel is relief that i'm done with it.
The Missing Link DLC comes with the Director's Cut.  Its quite a significant addition to the story and playthrough time.  The whole thing's taken me 32 hours to finish.  So there's a lot of bang for your buck there. The game certainly wants you to play it through multiple times with different story endings and mission outcomes, a new game+ and non-lethal / shooty-bang bang game play choices.  So there is potentially hundreds of hours of fun to be had here.
In conclusion if you loved the original Deus Ex back in the day, and you've been even slower than me to pick this up or get around to playing it from your ever expanding library of unplayed Steam sale purchases, then you should, because its definitely still Deux Ex, and that's definitely still a good thing.

hell yes this game! get it! like it says: there are over 500 monsters to collect through various means (capturing their cores from similar monsters in the field, breeding 2 different monsters to make a new, more powerful monster from their genes, or gaining the support of the various members of the pantheon of gods/goddesses in the game.), there are hundreds of spells to use and all the monsters and spells fall into one of several categories-each with their own strengths and weaknesses against each other (like how the life and death monsters/spells interact with each other). i've played for 12 hours so far and haven't even met all the gods yet. i think i have yet to run into 2 of them. i've reached level 25 and have already come across enough monsters and breeding recipes (the game provides a complete list of all combinations of breedable monsters and their outcomes [i'm assuming this because i keep finding pages of the breeding list and some are numbered as low as 34 and some go as high as 1002-so i imagine there are at least 1000 combinations] to produce 2 eggs (when you breed 2 monsters together, they leave your stable-essentially you sacrifice those 2 monsters to make the new one). i haven't hatched them yet but i'm excited to try them out. many of the monsters can have different traits that provide a boost one way or another (like boosting stats, or providing a regen effect to the whole party) and when you breed monsters with different traits, you can get a new, more powerful trait (although i'm not sure if that happens every time). there's a ton of depth to the game and it looks like it'll live up to it's claim of endless content with no level caps for the most part. no level cap to the game is definitely a plus in my opinion. there's a relationship levelling system with each of the gods that not only provides unique monsters to summon and fight with, but they also give you something called divine points that you use for your player character to do things like provide permanent boosts to your creatures or increase the resources you get from battle or provide xp to monsters in the stable so they continue to level up even when not being used( there's also one that allows your eggs to retain a percentage of the xp from each of its parents and one that adds a percentage of your creatures' speed value to their attack value-as well as stats that will let you increase your damage output and reduce the damage you take). with so many things you can level up in and put divine points in, i'm excited to see how my creatures increase in power as i progress through the game.
on top of all of that, there is a slew of 'artifacts' that your monsters can equip. as of right now, they can only have one equipped at a time, but i'm hoping that number increases to 2 or even 3 (but no more-that'd be insane) in the future. you can make all the different types of artifacts at the blacksmith you can upgrade your castle with or you can buy some from the merchant square you can also build. there are axes, maces, swords, staves, and other weapons that boost your monsters' attack and often another stat as well depending on the type of weapon. (staffs seem to increase attack and intelligence, whereas axes seem to increase attack and speed) there are also gloves, shields, and other armors that boost your defense and other resistances and there are even ribbons and necklaces and other accessories that boost intelligence or speed and other stats like that. all of the artifacts will endlessly (i think it's endless-i have some at level 1 and some as high as level 9) level up while equipped to a monster. as your rack up kills, you level up the artifacts.
this game is something i can see myself playing forever. an endless amount on endlessness. i wish i could more than recommend it.

This, together with "Zelda: Ocarina of Time" and "Vampire: Bloodlines" is one of my favorite games of all times.
Strange mix, I know, but the thing connecting them is great storytelling.
The world is very charming, inspired by chinese fairy tales and wisdom. With the ways of the Open Palm and the Closed Fist it has some interesting philosophies built into it and tries not to fall into the good/evil trap. I think this was very successful. the philosophies seemed a little bit over the top, but all in all believable (and for something that was made up for a single video game this is a lot).
The graphics have aged well and are nice to look at (I mean yeah, the number of NPCs walking around is very low and thus the same model repeats).
I loved the combat system. It is a mix between RPG (acquiring and levelling skills) and Beat 'em up games. I found this very intriguing. In fights you can switch between different styles and each style has several different attacks. You can transform into all kinds of creatures to gain their skills. You can use weapon styles for massive damage, but using up your focus (which you can also use to slow down time). You can use your Chi and magic styles for different styles of spellcasting (but you can also use your Chi for healing or empowering your strikes).
And there are several support styles allowing you, for example, stuns or stealing enemie's Chi.
It is fairly easy to abuse. As soon as you have access to a few key styles you can win every combat with just those.
But it is still fun. You still have to position yourself and to wait for the right moment to strike.
And even though this game is mostly linear (linear main plot with plenty of optional side quests) I do love playing this game again and again (my playtime here is not correct, I used to have a non steam version before). It really managed to give you a sense of wonder and immerse into this world. You will meet fox spirits and cannibals, demons and golems. And you have a big group of followers, all with (somewhat) complex relationships and their own motivations.
So I would completely suggest trying out this game (but I think it might be free on other platforms).

I would recommend this on sale for about a dollar.

As simple as the game sounds, it actually is enjoyable. The short stories where you make your choices are all pretty amusing, and each choice gives you very different results. Unfortunately if you're going for all of the achievements, you will start repeating these stories. There are enough stories for a playthrough or two (maybe three), but the achievements take 14 playthroughs. Fourteen. By the time I reached the last few I wasn't even reading the stories because I had memorised their symbols.
Other than that, I did really enjoy the game, and if you remember reading those old choose-your-own-adventure books and liking them, then you'll probably enjoy this too.
I reccomend it if it's on sale and you just want something to relax to between games. One play through takes about 50 mins. Several achievements to unlock and the stories are pretty clever.

Monster Loves You is a casual choose-your-own-adventure type game with some mild RPG elements. The game consists of many small storylets which you can choose a respone to, and are then rewarded with stat points corresponding to that response. These stat points make up the “personality” of your monster, and later may determine how much other monsters respect you, and ultimately your ending.
I generally like things like raising sims and CYOA games, so I was kind of surprised by how little I enjoyed this game. Overall, I see two major issues with it: it lacks meaningful choices, and it’s too long for what it is. Most of the storylets described rather mundane events (i.e. should I save my friend from bullies, or join in on beating him up), so seeing alternative resolutions to those wasn’t especially interesting. And there doesn’t appear to be any real consequence to raising a ferocious monster versus a kind monster, aside from gathering achievements.
CYOA-type stat building games can be fun if they don’t overstay their welcome (for example, The YAWHG), but I found myself getting pretty bored by about the halfway point of each playthrough of this game.

Optimization:
So, I was fortunate enough to not run into any crashing problems like most people are having. The game starts up and runs fine. I have only experienced it freeze once, but other than that... no problems. FPS on the other hand is a little unstable. Now, i'm not running this maxed out, but pretty damn close to it and at 1080P. There are times where my game runs pretty damn smooth, but it is not consistant. I believe i'm averaging around 40-50 FPS most of the time, but there are certain sections of the map where my FPS dips. Now, it's definitely not unplayable, but there are times when you can tell i'm hitting around 30FPS or so. This usually occurs in the sunset hills entrance where there are two buses with all the football player zombies.
Story/Gameplay:
I love Dead Rising and bought a Xbox 360 specifically for the first Dead Rising. Dead Rising 2 was also a great game and expanded with even more things. The first two games I believe had some great stories and psychopaths. Dead Rising 3 introduced Nick Ramos, who I found to be just as likeable as the other two protagonist from the first two games. Maybe it's just me, but I found the psychopaths a bit more believable in the first two games. Then again this is Dead Rising and things are a bit over the top. This game takes place 10 years after part 2 and If you have played all the games *including case west* then you will be suprised to see all the references from previous games. I did not play case west, but I don't believe it mattered that much as far as the story goes.
With that being said, I don't think you're supposed to focus too much on Dead Rising's story. It's really not that hard to follow and the game sums up a lot too. The gameplay portion is what you would expect from Dead Rising. Thousands of zombies on screen and multiple ways to kill them. The introduction of combo vehicles makes things fun and interesting. The map can be a bit tricky to get around at first, but eventually you should learn how to navigate it quickly.
Closing:
I initially started playing on a keyboard and mouse, but quickly switched over to a controller. Don't get me wrong, it is playable, but I found it a lot more enjoyable and easier to play on a controller. I will say that I strongly believe this game needs a FOV option though. There were times where I would have much appreciated the ability to zoom out a little further from the default camera position. I strongly recommend removing the 30FPS lock as well. The game runs a lot better... well it did for me.
If you're a Dead Rising fan, I would suggest trying this out. It's definitely a worthy sequel and is fun. With the recent release of patches, Capcom has improved stability a little bit more for me. I would assume that things can only get better from here.

The enjoyment of the Steam controller hardware depends on how much someone wants to tinker with the settings. While I did enjoy playing games like X:COM with it, I constantly was reminded I was playing on an emulator controller. Want to throw a grendade correctly? Use the touchpad. Can't remember what Shift+L do in the tutorial? Look at your controller settings in the Big Picture Menu. Controller would then freeze, forcing a restart on Steam Link.  Sometimes I had to actually load a game up with a mouse in certain instances, which defeats the purpose of using this controller in the first place.
Honestly this controller has a lot of potential for the PC market, and I am a big fan of the Steam Link. But the way its marketed is that "it is a passport that will bring thousands of games previously only playable with a keyboard and mouse". When you still need a mouse and keyboard to access basic functions like starting a game, then no it doesn't work as advertised.

I set out to play some games to give this controller a decent run-out, yet I still have absolutely no idea if this is a decent controller or not - on account of every single game uses it differently and to varying degrees. There's no consistency, no way (I can see) to adjust the controllers mapping inside the game, and some games just don't even register the input at all (despite suggesting they support it). You'll spend *far* longer maapping the controller out than actually playing the game. It feels wonderful in the Steam Big Picture UI though.
Leave it alone for now, let them fix it. Come back and see if the second revision is any better.

Letter Quest: Grimm's Journey is a solid title that has plenty of unlockables, enemies waiting to be defeated by your ability to construct words, a story that might make you hungry, an experience appropriate for your children, and an expert mode once you progress far enough in the game.
The gameplay consists of spelling words and utilizing beneficial tiles while avoiding the bad ones as much as possible. The protagonists in the game has different base stats that determine evasion, hp, critical chance, and more. These affect the battles in significant ways and are able to be upgraded in the in-game shop. There are also hangman sections where you guess the word to get the treasure in the chest and merchant sections that allow you to buy items in between battles. It's been quite the bug-free experience too.
The game recognizes a fair amount of words. You can spell slurs, but the game will not recognize them unless they have a non-vulgar definition. Every now and then, an odd definition might pop up (definitions are provided for your perusal after spelling and submitting a word).
This game favors people that are familiar with English. For non-native speakers, I suggest using some aids due to a possible "grindy" nature the game can take on if you can't spell 4-8 letter words regularly. Keep the "ings" and "eds" in mind for increasing word length like winged and winging or touched and touching.
The art style is clean, clear, crisp, and cute. And maybe another c word. Clover? Anyway, some of the special tile sets that you can use vary in their readability. I like the default one and the transparent style. The Word With Friends style made my eyes water when trying to decipher the font. I suppose I'll never play Words With Friends.
I had a good amount of fun with this title as I do enjoy words. If you like spelling and enjoy Scrabble (this is a single player game with some leaderboards, I believe), then feel free to pick it up. You'll get hours of enjoyment and challenge for a fair price. If you ever see this game on sale, then you can definitely pick it up without doubts.
P.S.
It's far superior to its mobile version. It's always a wonder to see triple A ports that can't even support proper resolutions.

Without a doubt, this game is easily going to absorb and satisfy you for a solid 50+ hours of powerfully deep, and utterly mind-blowing, awesome. Whether you are a fan of japanese action/platformer (rpg) games, or a returning fan of Yoko Taro, this game will satisfy everyone who gives it a chance. I HIGHLY recommend this game to all.

It's not helpful to say that you should give this game a try without knowing much (or, ideally, anything) about it. But you've never played anything quite like it.
Fans of Yoko Taro's work often refer to this as his first/only good game. It functions, you see. (And it's got Platinum on board! You know the boffing will be solid.) It doesn't fight you as you try to play it. It's 100% Certified Non-Kusoge.
But it does mess with your expectations in just about every other way a game can. It's weirder than it first appears, and darker, and more thoughtful, and more honest.
I finished this game months ago, and I still think about it at least once a day.
Do consider just playing it.

Great game that does a fairly good job balancing stealth, action, dialogue, and character progression. Also does a nice good job of making multiple approaches viable. For example, in an early mission, you have to infiltrate a police station that's off limits to non-officers. The first time I did the mission, I sneaked into some sewers nearby and hacked a computer panel that opened a door into the station; the second time, I just walked in and did a persuasion mini-game to convince the security doorman to let me in.
The level design's also pretty good and really rewards exploration. The missions are linear in the sense that you have to get from Point A to Point B, but there are multiple routes to Point B, each with computers to hack and rooms full of goodies like ammo and candy bars.
However, the game does become really easy towards the end even on the highest difficulty setting, as you'll easily be able to obtain almost all the augmentation upgrades by the end of the game. As such, it starts to become less "take the route that works for you" and more "take one route, then go back to explore all the others for ammo and candy bars."
Overall, pretty fun game. Also, since it's a prequel, you won't need to play the original Deus Ex to understand it.

This is one of the few early access games I would recommend. Daily updates. A dev who chats with the players during early access. Great music. And all the monster collecting you could want. Now lest talk about gameplay. On its surface this is a basic monster collecting and breeding game. You start off selecting your favorite critter from five choices. Each one is specialized in it own way, be it offense, defense, spellcasting, debuffing, or support. You will find all kinds of playstyles to choose from. Then you are sent off on your first quest; to kill some powerful monster summoned by a BBEG. Well along the way you will find more critters than you can shake a stick at and you will eventally fill your party with them. You can have up to 6 in your party at once and like I said before, each has its own thing that its good at, which can be further customized by equipping spells and artifacts. You want a tank that taunts enemies and every time he gets hit he places a DoT on the entire enemy team? go for it. Want a ninja that can dodge lightning and summons meteors every time he swings his sword? yep, you can do that too. Ok, ok, what about a dragon that resurrects allies whenever a spell is cast? you know it.
Unlike other capture and breeding games in the genre, this time you can only evolve critters by breeding. You will come across breeding recipes along your journey. The downside is every time you breed or aquire a new type of monster, that creature can also show up in random battles. So while filling out your codex, the enemy list gets larger. At first you only fight about 8 types, but this list will quickly grow. There will be some where your party composition take easily and some not so much.
TL;DR this is a mildly interesting game in early access. devs are receptive to their userbase. and the game should be checked out if you like the genre.

I'm slightly torn on my desicion to recommend the game, but at the end of the day I feel I have to. Right up front, it should be noted that the game lacks a bit of polish; the gunplay is rough, collision doesn't always function right, things like that. Overall, however, it is a fun game. My two biggest issues are simply this; Number of players and the unlock system.
At least in my region, there are only about six servers with anyone in them at any given time. They are always the same servers with the same game modes. About three are so called "Chill or Kill" servers, in which killing has more restrictions than an inmate in super max, which generally just leads to a bunch of dinos standing around while people have unrelated arguments over chat. The other two are roleplaying, which, hey, if that's what you want, go for it. But these are non kill, no action servers in which people make up stories over chat. The remaining server is team death match, which can be fun depending on map and participants. The total player count between all of these servers is only about sixty or so people.
As for my issues with the unlock system, the game seems to take somewhat of a free to play model while not being free to play. There are boxes that drop which require a key to open. You must purchase these keys. While not all drops are boxes, this is nonetheless a frustrating concept. While some games have managed to get away with this (cough Overwatch cough) my complaint is that, 1. I simply disagree with paying for a game and then paying to unlock drops, and 2. This game is no triple A title. I honestly think a move to free to play format would help with player numbers and result in a more profitable game, but that's me.
All that being said, the game is fun if you're willing to just enjoy it. The concept is solid, the core gameplay, when it hits it's stride, is a blast, and at the end of the day, you get to be a dinosaur. While the art isn't perfect, as an animator in the software development field, I'd like to point out the high quality dinosaur animations and, in most cases at least, skins.

Well what can i say, the wait was very much worth it, not for the story as much this time as there really isnt much of that until the end chapter, but what this game makes up for in the lack of storytelling, is an EXCELLENT free-roam experience in a city size area with the MOST zombies i have ever seen before, this game definitely pushes next-gen to it's limits and unleashes constant hordes of zombies around your area.
I have seen over 2000 zombies on the screen at once when PC enemy draw-distance (LOD) settings are set to maximum, and even if youre driving around in a car, they spawn rapidly, so there's no way to outrun them, you gotta go through them. The shear amount of them will constant make your jaw drop, you have to see this in 1080p.
Online Co-Op is only 2 players but even though the devs stated they had network issues when trying 3-4 players, they have stated that in the future they may be able to do it (please do! plzplzplzplz!!!), as stated by Mike Jones "But yeah, I'm a big versus player, I love that stuff, so I think in the future we're definitely going to explore how we can get more players in there."
!!!  DO IT  DO IT  DO IT  DO IT
Idea for solution:  Divide the zombies if you have to between 4 players, its not like there isnt enough of them already for 2 players, theres plenty for 2, and surely there must be enough to divide for 4.
This game is a load of fun, even though the story is short, there is plenty of things to do and explore afterwards.
---In Depth Section---
Graphics: 9/10
Pushes next gen hardware to extreme heights, be advised if youre buying this on PC, you need a very powerful machine. Draw distance, shear amount of zombies, animation/zombie detail and amount of junk in the world to play with, ammounts for a game so pleasant to the eyes that you always feel overwhelmed.
There is however, very few graphics options, it would be a lot of help to people if some more were included to help lighter machines cope with the game, for example Shadows can be set to low or high, but you cant turn them off. A point is lost due to this, and that there is also a lack of weather, every day is a perfect sunny day.
Gameplay: 8/10   (9/10 if you have a controller plugged into your PC)
The game feels super fluent with it's animations and with it's amazing Craft-Anywhere system, the biggest word here is FUN, and there's lots of it, especially if you play with a friend. If your friend happens to talk to you on his microphone, it actually attracts the zombies, so sshhh quit yelling! :D A couple of points are lost here due to 2 things which severly impact your game. Problem 1: The Safehouses give you as many Miniguns/best-weapons as you can carry from the beginning of the game, which basicly makes the game super easy even on nightmare mode, it's too easy to stock up on Godlike weapons which turn the entire game into a breezy scenario, these shouldnt be accessible until you complete the game in my opinion. Problem 2: The very few psychopath bosses in the game are soo easy, you can just play with them, there is a large outcry from many forums stating this a lot, the bosses in the game have no difficulty whatsoever, you can defeat them all
, very very easily. The community strongly suggest a massive difficulty increase to Psychopaths.
Thankfully those dont take too much out of the game, however another point is lost because the PC controls are very finger-twisty and a lot of the weapons in the game dont behave the same as others just like it, making you very confused on how to operate some weapons completely, especially if they have multiple modes.
Sound/Music: 9/10
The music is amazing, including Dubstep, Heavy metal, Rock, Irish Dance, Punk, Dance/Club, Chiptunes, you name it! there's tonnes of music around as you walk about and explore, however a point is lost here, because whilst there's good music all around you, there's no interactive in-car radio or walk-around radio, the tracks you hear are just for ambience, or apart of boss/cutscene music. It would be nice if you could listen to them on the fly! There's no way to enjoy this games fantastic soundtrack line-up. Weapons all sound great, you really feel the oomph! in your guns and melee weapon sounds are just brutal, Capcom really has it mastered here. The voice acting isnt the best, but it IS great, iv lost count of how many times Nick grunts in the game, it almost gets anoying :P  Oof! Ah!, Rrf!, ooh!, Gasp!, *heavy panting!*   A bit too much, but overall, no complaints, it makes the characters feel more alive.
Overall: 9/10
So long as you have the hardware, this beast of a game will give you more than your moneys worth of fun, theres much to do and collect as part of side missions and the storymode on first play will easily take you over 12 hours to go through (took me 23 hours, casually playing the storyline). Although the main storyline is a little lackluster and without proper climax, it's the ability to freeroam in any chapter of your choosing (later chapters have more special zombies). Finally there is free-roam, and Online co-op free-roaming seals this game as a permanent classic that is very easy to come back to. Dont be surprised if this becomes game of the year.

This is a fun and clever game for people who like word puzzles. After finishing both Bookworm Adventures and Bookworm Adventures 2 I knew I that the full depth of the RPG word game genre had not yet been discovered. I knew that there needed to be greater challenges, more powers, more wordcrafting and more stats. Grimm's Journey a firm addition to that genre and delivers on all of the above.
PROS: This game takes most of the core elements that made Bookworm Adventures great and expounds on them.
There is a lot of content: Each individual level has 3 more challenges to add both depth and varied game play. So each"level" is really 4 as you attempt to collect all 4 stars. The first star is always a standard play-through, the second is usually a time challenge, the third is a run-through where each monster has special restrictions or weaknesses, and the fourth is hard mode where the monsters are high-powered. This provides a decent amount of extra playtime and provides more choices on what type of game play you are feeling during any session.
Stats are awesome: The game stats that are tracked are comprehensive. Max damage with and without bonuses, palindromes spelled, the number of times you have used each letter, how many times have you spelled bacon...that is just a few. The list of tracked data is huge and is lots of fun to look over.
CONS:  I really wish there were still even more powers. The "books" that you can equip can help both form a strategy or just generally make your character more powerful. I feel like more options in this category should have focused more on that strategy element
It is difficult to craft a strategic run during a given level because they are mostly short (2-5 enemies) and a decent number of enemies have powers that can change tiles or prevent you from using certain tiles. In bookworm adventures 1 you could carefully spell short words using left over letters as you purposefully work toward collecting the necessary letters to spell "Nonproliferation". A mode or "book" that protects your tiles from alteration or lockdown would go a long way toward empowering the overly calculating player.
OVERALL:  This is an awesome game that exands the niche RPG, word-game genre. This game is worth every penny and has been a great addition to my "regularly played" game collection.

This game is like the roided baby of Pokemon and Monster Rancher.
You start the game by choosing one of 5 classes and are given two starting creatures. You use these creatures to travel through 15 different types of procedurally generated realms beating up other creatures and stealing their cores. You use these corse to summon creatures of your own so you can grow your team of six creatures and even mate them to discover new varieties and increase their strength. The game has a bit of story but the core of gameplay is about mixing and matching your team of creatures to overcome your opponents.
Here is what you can do to customize your play:
You have 6 creatures who each have a unique talent.
Each creature can equip an artifact which boosts their stats, give buffs, and can even give access to another unique talent.
Each creature can equip 3-5 spell gems giving them access to spells they can cast in battle or effects that trigger when they attack or are hit.
You can equip 5 runes which change aspects of play. (For instance, creatures who are sleeping might stay asleep even after taking damage).
If you like infinite dungeons, capturing monsters, breeding monsters, collecting loot, and min / maxing then this game is for you.

If you like either Pokemon Mystery Dungeon, Dragon Warrior monsters, or Dragon Warrior Mystery dungeon, or all of the above, you will most likely enjoy this game. You build a team of 6 monsters with tons of very interesting abilities to choose from. Then dive into a mystery dungeon where loots are monsters are randomly generated. You level yourself and your monster, unlock more spells, items, and more monsters. Combine all of those to create a kickass team.
At the time of the review the game is still in early access with partial features but I'm already enjoying it, a lot.

This is hands down the single best game Bioware has ever made. Even above Mass Effect 1 for me. My only regret for it is that Bioware did not move development over to the Xbox 360 during development (which was on the table,) since it was lost in the shuffle from one generation to the other.
That aside, this game is just a joy to play. It being an action RPG, especially after all those years of more turn based, segmented fare from their studio, was such a joy to experience when I first played it. The fighting system is varied, there are several avenues to suceed, all of them entertaining. It is for this reason that, though the system can be abused, it just adds to the charm. In every moment, in every piece of it, you can see a real love for this property. It being Bioware's first in house IP is a large part of that, but it is also the source material. It turns out that the folks over at Bioware are big Wuxia fans, and if you aren't by the end of this game, you may not have a heart.
My favorite element of the game though, is the morality system (though I will admit it is more of a de jure love than de facto.) Where in Knights of the Old Republic you have Dark Side and Light Side choices, in Jade Empire, you have the Way of the Open Palm and the Way of the Closed Fist. The best way to describe the difference is for me to say that one is a personal choice, but the other is a personal philosophy - either path can be misrepresented, and there are no right answers. At least, in theory. In practice, having come right off of Kotor, and being originally for the OG Xbox, concessions had to be made. As it is practiced by the player, it too often comes across as little more than the Dark/Light Side heavy handed choices. This just serves to make those occasions where it does work extra special, and they really shine. I don't know whether it was a hardware or design limitation. If Bioware ever does make a Jade Empire 2 which could realize the system as it is described is as exciting an idea as I can imagine.
Alas, it was lost in the shuffle for better hardware, and though it is made by one of the most famous developers in the business right after one of their biggest hits and right before their biggest hit, there are seemingly few who have played or even heard of Jade Empire. That is the biggest shame of all. I exhort all who are on the fence to buy this game immediately (also, play with a gamepad. It works brilliantly.) You won't be sorry.

The way Jesse (the MC) can influence the story feels a little underdramatic, as you will be constantly be told that "X will remember that." There are a few moral choices to make within the game which I won't spoil though.
The world itself is colourful and very Minecraft-esque. Telltale did a wonderful job trying to give that Minecraft feeling into the game. I can definitely get that Minecraft vibe from it (how could you not?). I'll refrain from going into much depth, as there are way better curators that can deliver way better reviews than I can.
Overall, the game and storyline itself is perfectly fine. I like it. It's not the best in the world, but I like it. If you're a Minecraft fan (and there are a lot of them), then go ahead and give it a try. If you don't have the money or are unsure, maybe go watch some videos on it. It's not an extremely moving game to me, but you can definitely become immersed in it while playing it as seems to be the case with Telltale games.

I've had this thing for a few days now, and it's been an interesting experience. I've owned an xbox 360 controller in the past, and not much else.
The customization on this thing is insane, pretty much anything can be tweaked to your liking. If you don't want to spend the time, you can grab someone else's config from steam community.
If you miss the 2nd joystick (like I did at first), you can make the touchpad act like a normal thumbstick if you want. But be warned that it does feel awkward at first.
The haptic feedback is also pretty neat. Depending on how you configure it, the touchpads vibrate when you use them, and it makes it feel really responsive.
But the highlight on this gadget is the gyroscope. Almost none of the video reviews that I saw talks about this, and it's probably one of the coolest features that the controller has to offer.
It's insanely accurate! You rotate the controller - roll, pitch, or yaw, again depending on the config - to provide mouse input. You can tweak the sensitivity on it as well.
The touchpad + gyro motion sensor combination makes first/third-person shooter games more than just playable, it really tickles your brain and it's a lot of fun to use. My favorite configuration is to have it turn on when the left bumper is pressed (iron sights) so that it physically emulates aiming.
I haven't tried it yet, but racing games are probably a ton of fun to play with this thing, since you can configure it to act like a physical steering wheel.
There are a few downsides:
1) If you have small hands, this controller's going to be really hard to use.
2) The ABXY buttons need to be bigger. They're much too small at the moment, which I presume was done in order to make room for the two trackpads.
3) You need to put in two AA batteries to use it wirelessly (There's a pair included in the box). Otherwise, you're gonna have to hook it up using the microUSB cable to your computer. Thankfully, it appears to have a really long battery life, but I would have still liked to see Li-ion batteries so that I can recharge it easily.
4) You really need to be aware of how you're holding it -- avoid bending your thumbs too much when using the touchpad or else it's gonna be uncomfortable. Think of it as fixing bad posture for your back, but for your fingers instead.
5) Big picture mode. At the moment, you need to run this to configure the controller. This program feels like it's still in Beta. It works half the time, and the other half it behaves weirdly especially if you're in-game.
6) Certain games (BETHESDA, PLS) don't play nicely with the controller. Skyrim, for example, doesn't allow hybrid keyboard/mouse + gamepad configurations, so you have to choose from one or the other. Most configs that you'll find on steam are keyboard/mouse, which was good enough for me but if you configure it incorrectly it won't recognize any inputs.
If you're on the fence about buying the Steam controller due to bad reviews:
If/when you decide to get this, you should play it safe and think of it as more of an interactive toy that interfaces with the games that you already own, rather than a replacement for your xbox controller. That way, you'll get more out of it and know what to expect.
Overall, I really like the controller. I could see myself using this for a long time and possibly even replacing the keyboard+mouse for certain kinds of games.

NOTE: I might add to this review as I try different games, which will be added at the bottom.
Other people have made some really good in-depth reviews, so I am just going to highlight a few features. First of all I am a PC gamer, I own/have owned several Xboxes and Playstations and have played with both controllers. I know personal preferences differ but between Xbox and Playstation controllers I prefer the Xbox ones. That said, now that I have the Steam controller, I prefer the Steam one. You can tell it's made with the PC in mind.
I am still going through a period of adjustment as, due to muscle memory, I am used to the 4 buttons on the right hand side to be where the right trackpad is. So I often wind up pressing the B button when I mean to press the A button at the bottom. This is not an issue with the Steam controller, it's just a matter of being used to other controllers.
I don't play shooters with controllers. I play other stuff with controllers, but not shooters. I will always play shooters with mouse and keyboard until someone gives me a VR gun at which point I will be swapping to that. However I decided to give a couple of shooters a try with the Steam Controller to see how well the trackpads would work. I tried with Deus Ex Human Revolution and Warframe.
First thing I noticed is just how much more precise the trackpads are and I love that. I was still pretty bad even with the Steam Controller, but I could still appreciate the difference. I am not such a bad shot with a mouse, honest. Anyway, the precision with the Steam Controller comes at a cost, as you have to remember not to rest your thumb on the trackpad, or remember not to move it unnecessarily as that will move your view. With a stick you could move your thumb around and rest it on the stick itself without actually moving the stick. That's easily solved by moving your thumb elsewhere but I am trying to give you the idea from someone who is making a transition from other interfaces.
The second thing I noticed is that, because I am not using a stick for my view, I am not having the weird inverted axis problem I have with other controllers. I know those who have been using the controllers for shooters for years don't have that issue but I do, i.e., my brain sometimes likes inverted axis, sometimes it doesn't. So sometimes I will want to move the stick up to look up, sometimes I will want to move it down. With the trackpad on the Steam Controller I don't get any of this, I just slide my thumb up when I want to look up or slide it down when I want to look down, that's it.
I tried a couple of other games, one was Injustice: Gods Among Us and the other was Strider. Aside from the issue I already mentioned where I expect the buttons to be higher, there was absolutely no transition, I could just use the controller, it was crisp, it was responsive, absolutely loved it. But those are the kind of games where I lay the mouse and keyboard to rest.
The extra buttons at grip level are welcome, although sometimes you might wind up squeezing them by mistake. Yet, it really hasn't happened after I got used to holding the controller.
I don't have the biggest hands (damn dem girls, you'll say, always complaining!) so I find that if I want to have the index fingers on the bumpers and the middle fingers on the triggers I am more likely to squeeze the grip buttons because of how I have to turn the grip, so I find I move the index fingers in between - but it depends on the combination of buttons I am pressing. I have to do that with the Playstation controllers as well (actually I have it worse with those), while the Xbox wins on this one, I can easily use four fingers for those four buttons rather than two. That said, as I am getting used to the controller, I am learning not to squeeze it to death and this problem is vanishing with time.
Wifi dongle worked just fine, installing the controller was painless. You just plug it in, start Steam and if there is an update Steam will install it, controller just works without you needing to do anything.
There are modes, it will emulate traditional controllers if it needs to or it can also emulate keyboard and mouse, no need to get a third party program to map it for you anymore.
I find the ability to type with the controller while in Big Picture a nice touch. Steam borrowed from the mobile era on this one. You get a virtual keyboard which is split in two, one side for each hand (a bit like a Windows 10 tablet keyboard), and you can use both trackpads to move two cursors (again one for each side) on top of the letters. My slight beef with it is that because the trackpads are so sensitive, sometimes when you then press on the letter you want it winds up moving to the next one. But if you type a few sentences you start getting used to it.
Because the movement with the right thumb is different from both mouse and traditional controllers, some people might need a bit of time to adjust in order for the muscle memory to kick in and being able to aim that cursor as you want it.
I love the haptic feedback on this controller. On the Xbox controller sometimes I have to dial it down a notch because it sends vibration down my wrist and I find that uncomfortable. It isn't very easy to explain the Steam's experience in words, since the best way to experience it is through touch, but it doesn't shake the whole controller and it gives a nice textured feeling when it happens; not once have I had the urge to go find the settings to change it.
TL;DR - If you have never used a controller before, a lot of these things might not even be a factor for you. You will just get used to this controller and be done with it. If you have used others, you might find you need to settle in. Regardless, I am already thinking of selling my Xbox controller because I just outright prefer the Steam one.

A cute game that is best described as a light RPG using mechanics from popular word games.
Progress through zones and defeat monsters using a Scrabble type system of creating words from letter jumbles, enjoyable if you like the idea of a single player Scrabble and taking your time. Additional challenges are condition based such as time limits or letter limit caps which serves to increase variety and challenge difficulty.
The role playing aspects are fairly light. Clearing a zone or additional challenges in each zone yield gems which are used to purchase both cosmetic and equipment upgrades, increasing your stats or limited use buffs. Chests that may appear in each zone are solved using a system analogous to the popular word game Hangman.
Overall the art style is cute and well designed, and serves as a strong word based puzzle game. Grinding might be an issue for some as some challenges are gated by equipment and your stats. A great addition is the inclusion of word definitions after playing a word, though at present some definitions need some tidying up, something the developers seem keen to do. I can certainly see the potential for this to be used as a useful educational tool after tightening the definitions, but it is equably just as enjoyable as a casual game for those that enjoy word puzzles and word challenges.

The RPG elements allows you to customize your character and allow for a natural progression since the challenges become tougher as the game progresses.
Not being a native English speaker, I consider the game the provide a decent challenge while not pushing me away. It actually has that "just one more" quality that will have you engulf many hours in it without really noticing. A real word aficionado might find the regular mode on the easy side but will certainly enjoy the more challenging expert mode. It took me about 10 hours to complete the main quest and roughly 75% of the overall challenges. Depending on your level of vocabulary, you can probably complete the whole thing (including achievements) on normal in 10 to 15 hours.
Overall a really enjoyable game that's easy to pick up and play for a quick session or to really dive into for hours at a time. I suggest you give the demo a try even if you're not usually a fan of word games.
