This is a borderline positive recommendation, for a number of reasons.
The story as a whole is good, but dissapointing. It is a very predictable story. You are a student to a great, but unknown master with a dark past that wants to keep you safe until the hand of destiny itself sets you on a path to restore balance in the empire. There is a twist that feels telegraphed and a bit of mystery surrounding one of the characters that gives itself away before you're even two hourse in, if you're paying attention. It is short, but in this case it's a good thing, as the story is so generic it would feel like wading through a pool of undried cement. At just about 25 hours, give or take, it paces itself rather well and is coherent, but for a game with conversation options, it's extremely linear, especially once you enter the fortress. The biggest let down is the conversations. Each conversation you are given a number of lines you can choose which amount to nothing unless it's an obvious good vs. evil type of choice. Each character you speak to reacts almost the same way and says the same things regardless of your answer, with some exceptions with the three romance options (two per gender). Also, every important character that you encounter more often than once will repeat themselves almost endlessly. In one conversation I had with the Water Dragon, she told me the same thing no less than seven times, to the detriment of my already dying brain.
The combat is, well, annoying. On one hand it's dynamic, keeping you involved in every fight, which is a good thing. On the other hand it's repetitive and even outright annoying. Your attacks have this bothersome ability of knocking back the enemy you are attacking just out of reach of your next attack, unless you pin them to the edge of the fight zone. Fast styles are almost hands down superior to any slower style because each attack interrupts your enemy (unless they are a massive enemy like the toad or elephant demons or the jade golems). The mechanics of each enemy, while interesting at first become a nuisance the further you go into the story, especially ghosts.
There is one mini game (thankfully) in the game, but I won't go into it as you can effectively skip all of it unless you want to finish a character's quest line. The other ones are useless, or next to.
The redeeming quality is the game's companion characters. For a short game they are rather one dimensional but interesting enough to last you the first half of the game after which you won't get anything more than remarks out of them, with the exception of your romance option. They will comment as you adventure and then when you all group up again will act like they were just then hearing about what was happening for the first time. However, they are colorful and fit very well within their one dimension, fleshing it out very well.
I understand that the review seems rather negative, but I rather enjoyed the game, with some glaring exceptions. Jade Empire is akin to that somewhat annoying dinner guest, who is pleasant enough company but you can't quite wait for them to leave, as much as you might wish to feel otherwise.
Overall this is a game that, in my opinion, desperately needs a sequel to redeem itself. I recommend it, but only barely. The Steam Controller
There are a few things that I want to say before I review it.
1. This is the first controller that I have used to a great extent. I used a crappy controller and an xbox 360 controller previously, but not very much.
2. I beat Portal 2 and played a lot of Rocket League using the Steam Controller.
3. I have medium sized hands.
________________________________________________________________The Steam Controller was an attempt to make games that are best played with a keyboard and mouse be possible with a controller, and to allow players to play on their couch. I believe that this was a huge step in the right direction.
The main feature of the Steam Controller, obviously, is the 2 trackpads. These actually do very well, and feel good to run your fingers over. I found Portal 2 easy to run through.
Another major feature is the ridiculous amount of customization with the buttons and sensitivity. Each button can be bound to any key on the keyboard/mouse, the trackpads' sensitivity and use can be changed drastically, and there are 2 buttons at the back of the controller that can also be used and customized to your liking.
The only thing I did not like about it was the fact that I could not play GTA 5, of all things, easily while using the Steam Controller. I reccomend, if you play that as your main game, or others similar to it, buying or using an xbox or xbone controller.
Rocket League is very easy to play with the Steam Controller. Arials are pretty easy to pull off and you have easier control over moving your car. The Xbox controllers would preform similarly to the Steam Controller.
8/10. All in all, i'm very impressed with the Steam Controller and I hope Valve continues to work on this and make a master-race controller.

As a forewarning, if you have Xbox/DS layouts engraved into your fingers, you might not take well to this. I've used about every Nintendo console, 360 and PS3 so I've never gotten attached to any one design.
I took well to the Steam Controller, but your results may vary.
So far, this is doing very nicely. I can't say it runs everything I can throw at it, as it's terrible for Project Diva (rhythm game), but I have consoles for that regardless.
The dual stage triggers are great for Dolphin, and in other cases make things very easy to work with if you're willing to put in the time. They can be either two inputs depending on how fast you pull the trigger, or a two stage mechanism (such as aim/fire).
The touchpads are definitely better to work with than a laptop's, but aren't as good as a proper mouse. Considering the intended use is to play such games sufficiently, rather than be outright better, this is fine. I like using them for general browsing, though the keyboard isn't great (though enough for small text boxes like naming things, I wouldn't write a review with it). Using a touchpad as a d-pad is something I haven't gotten down yet, but I wouldn't give up on it either. What's really fun for me is the "touch menu", where you can set up anywhere from 2-16 actions on areas of the pad that are all readily usable. Assuming use as camera movement, it's pretty nice. If you're just navigating around or have all the time in the world to aim (Portal) then it's great on its own. If you need precision with time, you can either set it up in tandem with another input (like one stage of a trigger) for more fine movement, or enable the gyroscope for some really interesting times.
The buttons are a bit small and mushy, they're fine for controlling actions but as stated already, not good for rhythm. Their placement may also bring back the "X controller engraved to your fingers" issue if you have muscle memory for button presses. "X" and "A" may also be semi-difficult to press, but if you're already playing a controller game you can make up for that with...
The handle bumpers are pretty glorious. They're either two free buttons to use with your remaining fingers or a button to hold for mode shift (changing the normal actions of other buttons/sticks/pads). So far I use them to access what the face buttons would be doing, and if all four are important (not all games need them for gameplay) I leave the other two on "Y" and "B" as those are easily reached.
Overall, I'd say it's worth giving a shot if you're not allergic to plastic and either don't have or are willing to unlearn muscle memory. It's a pretty handy tool to have.

The only (well, actually not the only, but more on that later) real problem is, that as unique as this game is, it more or less tries to do the same unique things like its predecessor did, thus robbing itself of most of the surprise of novelty for people who played the first Nier (Gestalt or Replicant). The gameplay is pretty fun, although the balancing of the difficulty levels remains opaque, everything above "medium" is punishing, and "medium difficulty" itself not that much challenging, making it possible to mow through most of the game without fiddling around with the way you equip your skills and buffs (the "Chip" system) all that much, if at all.
Where it gets problematic is the abysmal technical quality of the port. They really outdid themselves this time, quality-wise. You have to rely on mods to get this game running properly- mods of whose existence you are most likely to be completely oblivious of. In 2017 I shouldn't have to run an overlay to get a game to scale to full-screen, and that's just the tip of the iceberg. The whole engine is a mess, though a pretty fixable one, as the modding community proved once again. But it shouldn't be their job to fix these things (Very much appreciated that they do, but it's basically unpaid labor).
I still recommend this game, but again, in 2017, this kind of performance is a HUGE caveat.

Just over a decade ago, life was simpler and more frivolous, so every fictional discovery was fascinating and entertaining. It was in that simple, mid-teenage life, that I dug Fallout 2 out of a fortunate coincidence. A disc copy of the game, in a modest gaming magazine, to whose cover it was poorly attached. It seemed interesting enough, and with little knowledge of cRPGs or English, I went home and gave it a try. Boy, was I enthralled by this game. A game which would, about ten years later, still be the most cherished piece of gaming I have ever experienced.
Fallout 2 ventures deep into the dark territories of humour and morbidity. Not many have the grit for its atmosphere, inauspicious and heavy as it is, its dense soundtrack that evinces feelings of gloomy solitude and decadence; exactly the vibe you have got to be in when playing any Fallout title, for that matter. Back when I first tried it, I would engage in conflicts between the curiosity to explore its narrative and the uneasiness caused by that very atmosphere, even after having previously and briefly tried Planescape: Torment - an equally dense game. Fortunately for me, I got past that.
Provided that you can also overcome such uneasiness, you've got an unparallelled RPG challenge ahead of you. Fallout 2, very much like its predecessor, is beautifully written, and cleverly designed in a way that connects your actions to the realities and contextual changes of Northern California as you go. The turn-based combat is typical late-90s cRPG gold. The S.P.E.C.I.A.L role-playing system, a jewel derived from Gurps, offers you that edge of character construction and skill management that makes a bonafide RPG pleasurable. The post-apocalyptic setting and aesthetics, built on the famous premise of the Divergence - the historical fragmentation in which the fictional linearity of the game took a different course from that of our world in the heat of the Cold War, leaving the former with that futuristic-50s style -, renders Fallout's identity unique and typically dark humoured. Its characters are deeply unpredictable and credible, especially the companions, much more mature than those of the previous installment (with all due respect to the likes of Ian and Dogmeat). The game leaves that bitter feeling of longing should they pass away or have to be left behind for some reason. Each companion adds to the player's enterprise, each has their own story, each has their own passions and motivations. And flaws.
Fallout 2 appeals to multiple audiences. Those looking for an RPG; those looking for a post-apocalyptic piece; those looking for a story-driven game; those looking for open-world dynamic narratives; those looking for a demi-horror title; and so forth. While it may not touch some of these categories in depth, it is a game that brings them all to a perfect harmony. Be ready for a challenge, an unforgiving gameplay, but be also ready for enriching rewards that will open your mind to new spheres of role-playing gaming.

text: Deus Ex: Human Revolution - Director's Cut is certainly a game that I would recommend to everyone, fans or not, as it simply an intuitive, perfectly done sequel for the Deus Ex series. Human Revolution by itself I believe must of been brilliant in its own aspect but I never played the original, the Director's Cut that I went through truly was incredible, whether it be the graphics, gameplay or its mind-boggling story it truly is a pleasure that I would give 9/10 simply because 10/10 doesn't exist.

I really wanted to down vote this game as it appears to be a blatant mobile app port, but after playing through three times I can’t. The game is strangely addictive and I find myself wanting to see all the endings.
The UI looks and feels like a mobile app. It consists of large, easy to press, buttons on a simple background. The buttons come in two different types, pictures which are somehow related to an action, and dialogue for different choices and tests.
The game play is simple, you click a button, read some text, and see how your choices modify your stats. You go through several development phases, starting as a baby slime and moving up through full fledged elder monster. If you make it to the end, you can decide the fate of monsters and humans.
The choices and options can get repetitive over multiple playthroughs. This is particularly frustrating since auto-saving means you you need to start from the beginning each time you attempt to get a new ending. As there are 14 different endings, I really wish there was some sort of save or rewind functionality so that you could skip the earlier phases.
As long as you don’t mind eating children or kittens it's a good game to kill some time.

Human Revolution captures the spirit and themes of the original Deus Ex, and turns it into a fun-to-play modern game. This is perhaps the only 'stealth' game I've truly enjoyed playing, and yet the player who prefers to go in all-guns-blazing is rewarded with a satisfying arsenal of weaponry. Sneaking around the docks triggered a lot of nostalgia for the NSF airfield of the original game; Human Revolution definitely feels like a Deux Ex!
I was a bit worried that the Director's Cut version of game was verging on overly-long (with the addition of the extensive 'Missing Link' chapter before the finale of the main game); but the inclusion of this chapter paid off for me at the end of the main game, where the reveal sent shivers down my spine in a way it didn't when I first played through this without the DLC.

This is a great RPG from BioWare that fuses beat-em-up elements and the RPG-style gameplay you've seen from other BioWare titles. While it might feel a little clunky if you're coming off the heels of a Mass Effect or Dragon Age title, it still holds up well. It also happens to be the last game BioWare made before selling their souls to EA (who I guess never had any interest in this IP, given that it never did get a sequel), so if you want to see how things have changed it could certainly serve as a little case study.
One big problem is that the PC port (which was done by a company called LTI Grey Matter, which I can't find any info about online at all) is rather sloppy. Playing in widescreen stretches the UI out and I had some issues getting it to run at more than slideshow framerates on my GTX 960 (a perfectly capable card for a game like this). There's also some issues that seem to be particular to the Steam edition of the game, but you can find a few guides around to mess with the files necessary to fix that. The game has full controller support though, being that it was on the Xbox at first, so that's cool. I would actually recommend using a controller if possible, since the mouse camera movement is way too fast for me even on the lowest sensitivity, but maybe that's just me.

Contrary to plenty of other controllers, if used with a PC, this controller allows the user to control their entire computer and not only the games they play. It allows one to move the mouse, click on things, pause videos, go back to previous webpages (and forward, as well), etc. However, it, if not already self explanatory, does not type. When it was announced long time ago I was very exited to see how it will become. First previews looked great, then the prototype which got rid of some things people thought might be great, and then the final one, which came more close to the classical gamepads we all know.
I waited for a while after it got released to everyone before I bought one in a local store (great that they partnered with retailers to make that work, saving me the shipping costs and the waiting time).
It immediately got a firmware upgrade after plugin, and another one some days later when I decided to switch to Steam Beta since I have read that some of maybe pending issues are already fixed there.
For me it feels comfortable to hold it, it feels slightly bigger than my 360 pad, feedback it provides it also nice.
A whole lot of buttons, but when you think about the games that are supposed to be played using a keyboard, that's required, since they normally do have many functions to be assigned. Configuration options are huge, and community profiles are a great time saver. I like that you cannot only assign keys, but also a 'description' to them, so that you easily know when quickly checking in the overlay what ingame action the button will do.
So far I tried:
In Steam BP itself it works just like any other gamepad. Integration is nice though, means it tells about the existence of the controller, easily updates firmware, saves profiles, also the screenshot and steam overlay functionality is good to have.
When you write text you have this split keyboard, where both touchpads and shoulder triggers work for half of the keys each so you basically type with two(four) fingers (but you can also fallback to using the stick and A button as in the past, which ever way you like). New feeling, but works pretty quick.
A small but also - since the 360 pad does not do this - very nice fact is that once the PC shuts down, it turns itself off immediately, instead of waiting for many minutes until it realizes that connection is lost. Very good detail.
Overall I think it's a great replacement for separate keyboard/mouse in the living room, which as per my understanding is what it is meant to be. There surely are things I prefer using my 360 pad, and there are others I will never ever play on a TV, regardless the input device, but for all the games that do not bring gamepad support it's a very nice experience what this thing can do.
I can fully recommend it to everyone who does not (yet) expect it to work in a plug and play mode without the need for personalization. I think PC gamers are used to custom keyboard settings, and everyone who is will be more than happy with this device.

IMO, This is a great series, And I've enjoyed it thoroughly. I thought at first that it might end up being too angled towards younger players to have much appeal for me as an adult, but my concerns were quickly put to rest. The story is captivating, I love the characters and the enemies, (the wither storm was fackin' cool) and there's humor and action abound. This may well be my favorite telltale game.
People Complaining about having to pay more to access episodes 6-8 really need to dial it back a little. There was definitely no promise of a limitless stream of episodes when you purchased the game. episodes 1-4 are the first season arc, and 5 was a lead into the next "season", the way i'm looking at it. You're not paying more money so you can finish the game you bought before, you're paying more money for another game that follows the first but doesn't have it's own package. If I remember correctly, it was sold originally as a 4 or 5 episode series, not an eight episode series. I feel like people are enraged basically cause they didn't package the adventure pack as a seperate "Minecraft story mode, season 2", but that's basically what the adventure pack is, in my eyes.
If you've ever played any of the other telltale games, you know that this is how it works. you don't pay one flat rate and then get to follow the story indefinitely, you pay for episodes either in bundles (sometimes seasons) or one at a time as they come out. I see nothing wrong with this. If you buy any other game, they don't give you sequels for free just because you want to know how the story turns out. the fact that this game is episodic in nature doesn't mean that mechanic stops, they need to make money to make more episodes just like games that come out in big long packages need to charge money for a sequel game, it's the same process, just chopped up into smaller, cheaper, more frequent packages.
Even if you don't agree with me, at the very least, it's not as bad as games that make you pay not for more game, but for little add-on features that usually should've been in the game from the start. (I'm looking at you, Total War)
All that aside, i really can't recommend this series enough if you enjoy this sort of game. I'll be buying episodes 6-8 first thing when i get paid tomorrow.

I never once looked forward to playing Jade Empire after the first time booting it.  Sure, it was serviceable enough of an RPG to keep me coming back until its conclusion but the game's flaws are too numerous and damaging to make it truely enjoyable or worthy of recommendation.  From its exposition-choked opening hours to its final moments which can be replayed quickly to achieve all possible endings, thus cheapening the experience, Jade Empire just feels weak and overwrought.  Dialogue is so ridiculously heavy and voice acting sometimes so poor that it had me angrily jamming my finger into the LMB repeatedly within ten minutes of starting the game.  Despite the game's insistence that I use various martial styles to deal with different combat situations, I rarely needed to do more than equip my longsword and spam the LMB in order to win fights.  Meh.  Jade Empire is clearly the result of a young Bioware biting off more than it can chew.  Add to this the fact that Bioware and Valve released a broken and unplayable version of this game onto Steam, requiring the consumer to do the necessary legwork to get it working and the result is a very resounding NO.

Well, this will be interesting.
The Steam Controller is perhaps a interesting sort of gaming controller. What makes this one unique, is the fact that as mentioned: It has haptics and dual touchpads as the primary means of controlling. This differs from conventional controllers in that, instead of using a analog thumbstick pair, you are using the touchpads. The controller is slightly larger than the Xbox 360 Controller and weighs about the same without batteries installed.
Let me first start by saying the first 3 days using the Steam Controller, were actually nothing great. The controller to me, is awkward because of the layout. Instead of the A,B,X,Y buttons being in the upper right corner of the controller, they are where the thumbstick would normally be. This meant that I had to keep reminding myself, that the touchpad was above my thumb and not to the side. Above this, I was simply not used to the touchpads. The concave geometry of the touchpads (very slight concave at that), feel a little awkward; but in the long run are designed to give you a sense of where the center point is on the touchpad.
The biggest complaint that I had in the first 3 days was the fact that the touchpads were making me aim really poorly. In most FPS and TPS games I played, I found myself aiming at everything except the targets I was trying to kill. This is because not all games have a developer submitted profile, thus you need to use a template or a community added profile. This being mentioned, I found myself fine-tuning the touchpads to my own liking; which in some games it would take me up to 10 - 15 minutes of minute adjustments to perfect. However, once you perfect the touchpad to your liking; everything gets better.
The sheer amount of customization you get for all the buttons and the touchpads, is what sold this controller for me. Unlike a conventional controller, your touchpads can be adjusted in many ways. I found myself changing the horizontal line (left to right aim) at a steeper angle to accompany my natural thumb radius. This was such a good thing, because it allowed me to fit the controller perfectly. The downside is, every game you play; you will need to create a profile (or at least fine tune). I find that the most profiles or templates by default are not great for my needs. The community has a bunch of custom profiles for each game; but the lack of having a "universal" profile which can be choosed is a little disappointing.
Needless to say, after 4 - 5 days of daily use; I found myself adapting to the controller quite well. One such example is Saint's Row IV, where I was initially struggling to shoot anything; whereas now I am able to perform well. The neuroplasticity of the brain has helped greatly in this venture, but also the very intuitive customization of the touchpads had also been a great help. I have also been getting used to the difference in the A,B,X,Y location, so I am not constantly confusing myself in heated fights.
The shape of the controller is also another thing worth mentioning. The geometry of the controller's handles are much better than Playstation and Xbox 360 controller handles, because it gets fatter at the bottom. This keeps the controller in your hands, so that it doesn't slip out after lengths of play. Even in one sitting (3 hours of Saints Row IV), my fingers did not get soar, because the controller was not moving out of my hands. Also, the edges of the handles have an upwards bank that make your thumb tendon rest on it, allowing your thumbs to arc down at a comfortable angle. The controller does not have any vibrators; but I think that is ok because if there were vibrators, people would lose their aim pretty fast when the controller shakes in their hand. Bad idea to implement rumbling with touchpads.
So here is a breakdown:
Positive:
+Superior ergonomics compared to Xbox 360 Controller.
+Highly customizable controller, every single input can be changed.
+Haptics are included in the thumbstick and pads.
+You can use it wireless or wired, you don't need to buy separate controllers or parts.
+Thumbstick is convex, making it harder for your thumb to slip off it.
+Has a gyroscope, making it a good candidate for racing games.
Mixed:
=Takes days to get used to it, but once you adapt it is great.
Negative:
-Lack of game-independent profiles for the touchpads.
-Left and Right bumpers require slightly too much effort to press.
Overall, I think this is a worthwhile device for anyone who likes to use controllers. I will be using this more in many games to play, but I sure hope the negatives get ironed out.

This game is amazing. It is an episodic adventure where you you make choices on whsat you want to say. I'll talk about the gameplay and characters, then go into six quick reviews about the six current episodes so, spoiler warning, I guess!
Gameplay:
You play as Jesse, a gender-determinant character with the appearence selected from six options, three per gender. In this game, it's not exactly Minecraft, where you can explore and build forevermore. That's great. I didn't sign up for a discount Minecraft. In this game, you watch the other characters interact and talk with you while you select what you want to say. At other times, you move around in a certain area, getting to select the people you wish to talk to, what ou want to interact with, or have to solve some semi-complicated puzzles. (Puzzles aren't that diffucult, but aren't so easy that you get bored with them) You have multiple quick-time event during the chat sessions in the "story-mode" of the game, though the game gives you time to do them if you're caught off-guard and if you fail, sometimes you dont' die, other time you do but are only taken back a little so you don't have to restart upon death. (You don't really even die, it's like you went back in time)
Characters: *Places spoiler tag*
These characters are amazing. Here's the main group: Jesse, Lukas, Reuben (Formerly), Ivor (Tag-along), Petra, Axel, and Olivia. Lukas is just so likeable and lovable, it pains me in a jerk run to insult him because he tries to deny the fact you're being a jerk. Reuben the pig was an adorable little piggy that was yours and everything! Ivor was played as the villian in the beginning, but his motivs were revealed and now I don't want him gone. Petra is a warrior with a heart of gold or something. Axel is really strong and funny, and it's enjoyable to have him aroun.d. Olivia is Jesse's supportive friend though Jesse does often have to help her with inner problems. The people in this game seem so much like real people in personality, I stopped seeing them as digital images and when some of them died it hurt.
Overveiw:
This game has gotten complaints it's not a telltale game. Well, sorry, kid, but I wasn't looking for one in the first place! This is the only TellTale game I own, and my life isn't over or anything. I have Minecraft, if I wanna play it, I'll go there. This isn't a beg for money, it's something I'd always invest in for more. The Minecraft tag drew my attention, and research made me realize this was something more than Minecraft. It is truly Minecraft: Story Mode. A gamemode.

Let's start by saying this... "Monster Loves You!", despite graphic, is pretty much a text-based game. We are playing as newborn monster. Our decisions will shape his personality, that has five main categories - Bravery, Cleverness, Ferocity, Honesty, Kindness. This stats will then affect our later decisions. Depends on how high they are, we may either be successful or fail miserably choosing our fate. There are three main endings and each of them have few variants, that usually depends on which of our trait is the dominant one.
Game is pleasant, but a tad short. Main con is rather low number of situations when our traits are truly put to the test. Also, sometimes options are ambiguous, so when you choose one of them with clear intention in mind, you may find out that it lead to something entirely different - which may be consider good thing and bad thing at the same time.
It's a cute game that didn't reach it's full potential. Better buy it as a part of a bundle or during sale.

I completed the original edition and have started the Director's Cut again.  So far, I'd say that this game is a must for fans of the first Deus Ex - nearly as good, which is high praise.
For people who have the original Human Revolution game, I can't really see why you'd bother with this update, unless you do want to replay the whole game.  It really should have been put out as a patch.  That said the original was heavily patched.  Even then it needed a powerful PC to run smoothly.  Initially it was unplayable, due to stuttering.  On my new beast it's very smooth.
The game... Like the first DE game, this is science ficiton with a conscience - a thoughtful and interesting projection of how unfettered science might take us down a very dark path.  It's a role playing game with high production values.  The Director's Cut introduces more ways to accomplish missions, which is more in tune with the first game.  Graphics are stylised, but I got used to them. I also got used to and came to like the cover system.
The plot is rich and the character well developed and well acted.  Sadly though the closing segments are rushed (as they were with the first Deus Ex) and there are loose ends around what happens between you and the key characters that are entirely ignored when you choose your ending.  That's a real shame.  I would have liked to have suitable final words with David Sarif, Megan and Faridah Malik.  Compared to the end of Half Life 2, episode 2, this is a glaring let down.
Ultimately I gave the first DE game a 10 and the Human Revolution take an 8.  The Invisble War version, for reference, I rated a 6.  Why "only" an 8 for HR?  Well it is ultimately a remake and I'm not that wild about remakes.  But it's a very good one and 8/10 is a very good score.  A stronger ending could have clinched a 9.

Hi there,
My Steam Controller Rating = 2/5
(in comparison: I would rate the xbox controller 4.5/5)
I bought the steam controller just for fun and wanted to try something new. I normally try to play with xbox 360 controller whenever I can, since I enjoy playing from the couch. I sit 8-10 hours on a desk, so I try to avoid doing the same at home playing games.
My opinion of the steam controller:
pro:
- playing games on my couch, which would require a keyboard/mouse are finally enjoyable with this controller thanks to the thumb pad
- good customizablility of each and every button, etc. (configuration), overlay buttons, etc.
- you can load configurations made by other gamers (so you dont have to invent the wheel again)
- feedback through click sounds and vibration for analog and touch pads
neutral:
- haptics is ok. Though it is bigger and heavier than the xbox controller. Thus I prefer the haptics of the xbox over the steam controller.
cons:
- click sound of buttons (thumb pad, d-pad and rear buttons) is way to loud. It is really annoying. This makes the controller "look" really cheap - I dont know why they designed it that way, but this is the biggest flaw in the controller in my opinion.
- not an alternative for the xbox controller
- really bad for twin stick games (shooter, etc.)
- needs big picture mode
- steam exclusive for now (no software available to configure it for your none-steam-games)
Concusion:
I like this controller for games, which are normally not playable with the xbox controller. For example I really liked playing Valhalla hills and other strategy games with it, fps are ok as well, if they are not already customized for xbox controller.
BUT, twin stick shooters or other twin stick games are imo unplayable with this controller. The thumb pad is not on the same level as an analog stick in terms of precision, feedback, fast change in direction and easy handling. The thumb pad is more like a laptop touch pad.
Therefore, if you are looking for another controller to switch to in order to play keyboard/mouse games, look no further. If you want to play all your games only with this controller, I suggest you get at least an xbox controller as well.
I thought about returning the controller because of the annoying click sounds and to be honest I havent made up my mind yet. But for strategy games only a few buttons are required and therefore the clicks are down to a minimum.
Hope this helped.

It's no secret that I absolutely loved Mystic Hospital for it's great writing, creepy atmosphere and unique premise.  It set such a high bar for me that in some ways Cinderstone Orphanage had a hard time reaching it.  That's not to say the sequel is bad, because it's a very solid hidden object puzzle adventure in its own right, and certainly one of the better examples of the genre.  But, despite being the first game in the series to implement the ability to collect and use powers in its puzzle solving, the very paint-by-numbers feel of the rest of the story and gameplay left me wanting more.
Once again, the agency's top agent has been tasked with investigating yet another perplexing incident, this time at the Cinderstone Orphanage, home for children with paranormal abilities.  An unexplained Christmas Eve explosion has left the building in shambles and its children and mentor missing, body and all.  It's up to The Agent to get to bottom of the things and rescue the vanished orphans and their caretaker.  I can't say the story had me as intrigued this time around, but anywhere The Agent goes, I go.
I've always been fond of a more realistic art style in HOGs, and Cinderstone Orphanage falls into that category with its gorgeous painted scenery.  Unlike most modern-day titles in which bright blues, reds and purples feature prominently, Cinderstone's color palette is subdued with the images all having a softly classical feel to them.  As I explored the orphanage, there were areas that I'd sit admiring the breathtaking view for several minutes, especially rooms barely touched by the explosion.  If only I'd been able to behold its beauty before the conflagration overtook it.
Gameplay is fairly standard HOPA fare, save for the addition of acquiring special powers that are used in puzzle solving and further exploration of the game areas.  Looking through walls, moving items with your mind and bringing drawn pictures to life all have a distinct charm to them, though I would have preferred a little more challenge in their use.  Items and areas that are to be manipulated glow the respective ability's color, which makes little sense to me since you have no way of choosing which ability to use as the game does it for you.  Not a huge complaint, just something I'd prefer to have been more game-y than it is.
Story-wise, this entry is the weakest in the series.  I understand that a majority of HOG players are women (although that seems to be changing), so plots that appeal to the maternal instinct tend to crop up quite a bit; and while it's nice to see The Agent concerned for the children's welfare, having him outwit freaks and monstrosities gives his adventures some edge.  The writing is more sparse as well with about half the number of journal entries as Mystic Hospital and less character-building mouse over text, something I sorely missed.  What's there seems to be more to the point without as much of The Agent's sarcastic flare that I so love.  Alas.
Fortunately, the bonus chapter nicely fills in missing story details, adds on to the series' over-arcing plotline, and gives us a hint as to where The Agent will be going next. Theater freaks you say?  YES!  The gameplay is also enjoyable with The Agent exploring a handful of newly uncovered areas, new puzzles (and old ones with added difficulty), and just enough hidden object scenes to keep you busy, but not totally inundated as they were in Mystic Hospital.
Having said all that, would I recommend Cinderstone Orphanage?  Absolutely!  As a continuation of The Agency of Anomalies storyline, it's a worthy entry to the series with solid HOPA gameplay and a gorgeous world to explore.  I'd say most of my disappointments are based on personal taste, and while I'd have liked a creepier atmosphere to the game, others may find the story and themes fully entertaining.  So yes, definitely grab this along with Mystic Hospital when you get the chance.  Here's looking forward to The Last Performance.

First of all, I have never played any Dead Rising game before, Always saw it, never got it. not on Xbox not on 360, not even on Xbone or PC as it was locked for my region (god knows why).
Always heard it was a great game, so I took my chance and bought this one. and am really glad I did!.
At the beginning, the game started crashing every 10 - 30 mins of gameplay, it was a mistake from nvidia drivers for my case as i rolled back to 335.xx and worked fine till they released their fix on 344.xx. after that its smooth sailing (at least for me).
When I first started the game, I didnt expect much, as I bought it for the co op with my friends. but soon I got hooked up pretty bad. the game had its own charm of sucking you in, and you just want to keep  on playing, finding weapons/vehicles blueprints, making them and smash zombies with them. its so satisfying to no end. I beat the story with alot of time being spent with my friend co oping. now we are on our second play through to level up our characters and finding all weapons/vehicle blueprints as well as collecting the various statues etc.
Gameplay:-
The gameplay is very much unique at least for me. I loved how you are free to roam around do whatever you want and just Keep on killing zombies with whatever you can find. from a hammer to kitchen knife. anything you can find.. it can be used!. Free roaming got us really hooked that we forget about the story. luckily they put a timer for you to remind you of the story. Its not a type of timer that gets you worried as you have enough time to roam around,, do side quests, extra missions and complete the story with at least 24 hours left on the clock (we have done that).. Best thing about that. you can do all that while wearing your BEST outfit!. you can combine whatever you want, or just have fun with pre made. from disco dancing cloths to megaman costume ( you get that once you complete the story). and you can wear women cloths if thats your cup of tea ;). Fun to  no end!. all the combination of combos with different weapons. its just very fun to roam around the zombies and just combo their asses.
Graphics/Animation:-
Deadrising 3 has pretty much good graphics. the amount of zombies being rendered around you is ridiculous. soo many you just want to stop in the middle. and just Keep on KILLING. never saw that much NPC roaming around you in one scene in a game before.
Story:-
Story was fine. as I did not play the first nor the second one, I felt missed out. but they did some explaining toward the end. didnt really catch it as my friend was talking over the  mic and I didnt hear anything :P. but It was fine. It got my hooked up till the end. thats rare...
Complaints:-
The game has 30fps locked. even though thats not really an issue for some, but it is for me, I hate 30 fps. Dead Rising 3 is the third in a series of games that pretty much lowered the value of a zombie as a horrirfying enemy. No longer are zombies scary, but instead cannon fodder that even a casual little kid can destroy in the thousands. Since I beat the game 100% along with all achievements, I think my opinion matters more than most. Ignore all the fools who rank this game low because their rig was not powerful enough to handle it on max settings. I ran the game just fine maxed out. Yes, I had the game locked at 30 FPS, but big deal. If that is their complaint, they must have terrible eyesight, because I see everything just fine. Stop being a nitpicking crybaby and learn to play. Dead Rising 3 is a good game, but nowhere near as good as the amazing Dead Rising 1 and Dead Rising 2. They severely dumbed it down to make it accessible for the casuals, non gamers, and new gamers. It's main problem is that it has absolutely no challenge. They turned the standard mode from the past DR games into "Nightmare mode", which is no nightmare. It's a joke. All it is, is story mode with a timer. That timer combined with the escorting of survivors is what gave the classic DR games their challenge. There is no escorting survivors back to the safe room like in the old DR games. Very horrible idea. One of my favorite parts in the old DR games was gathering up survivors and managing a group to get them back to the safe room within the time limit. It gave the game challenge and replayability. It always felt different each time I played. On DR3 everything feels too static and linear. You get a posse of survivors to follow you, but they act more like AI teammates than survivors. AI teammates are not needed anyways since the game is so easy you can do it without them. I didn't once bother getting a AI team set up. All they would do is slow you down anyways. At least having to escort survivors would give a legitimate challenge and stay true to the original. The game is not bad just because it is simplified compared to the last DR games, it's just lacking the gameplay features that made me love the series to begin with. Graphically, the game is great looking with realistic looking characters. They are not quite next gen, but with the amount of zombies on screen at once, it is obvious why this game was not possible on the last generation of consoles. If you thought there were tons of zombies on screen at once on DR1 and 2, you have not seen anything yet. In the early chapters, the amount of zombies is on par with the last two DR games, but when you get to the later chapters, the city is practically a sea of zombies. The map design is alright. Not as great as DR1's Willamette Mall and DR2's Fortune City, but it gets the job done. The amount of weapons are awesome. I especially liked how you could craft stuff out of anything. If they would have kept crafting tables instead of crafting stuff out of thin air, it would have gave the game some much needed challenge. The music is terrible. I didn't really care for the soundtrack. Sounded bland and cheesy. The last 2 DR games had good soundtracks, especially DR1. Controls are fine, and feel pretty much the same as the past two DR games. One major problem though, is that there are barely any unarmed moves. Frank West and Chuck Greene had a bigger variety of moves to use on zombies. This is a good game, just not a classic, which is disappointing to me since DR1 and DR2 are two of the few games from last gen that I would put up there with some of my favorite games of all time.

Despite the old graphics and occasional clunkiness, I think this is one of my newest favorite games. I was surprised by how well it stands up against the newer titles. If anything, the fact that this came before many of Bioware's other titles elevates it to a higher status for my regard.
The rundown:
Graphics:
This is an old game, and as such, will have old graphics. Textures aren't particularly high, faces can be a touch blobby, and clothing moves like awkward paper. I also found the cutscenes, while also marked with the usual low quality of the time, also had a strange film grain effect. This may be removable, but I never found it so pressing as to search for the option. Some of the cutscenes that involved content of a more gory/violent/disturbing nature did not appear so, though one's imagination can fill in the gaps (this may be a pro or con). Overall, I found the graphics acceptable for serving their task.
Audio:
I enjoyed the musical score, particularly the swells that appeared during the more intense moments in the game. I'll probably go see if I can hunt down the OST (EDIT: found the OST. It's still great). As for the dialog, I found the majority of major characters to have intriguing voices, and rarely felt the need to read the subtitles and skip when speaking with them. This was not always the case with the minor characters. I suspect the voices themselves are more than decent, but the lack of camera movement during a conversation could become a little stale (a flaw of the time, I would think).
Characters:
Unsurprisingly, this is where the high quality really shone through. Although there weren't as many opportunities as I would have liked to interact and speak with the companions (though to be fair, that's always my complaint), I found their backstories interesting and genuinely wished to know more about them throughout the game. I wouldn't have minded a few more side quests, or the ability to take more than one companion along, as I found myself taking the same two out. This just means further playthroughs are needed for the future.
Story:
What I liked about it was its seeming simplicity. It began in a rather straight forward manner, following some of the usual tropes. However, as the story progressed, I enjoyed seeing the new twists, and I wish to give particular commendation to some of the aspects in the ending. Unlike some of Bioware's more recent titles, I really wasn't certain if I'd made the 'right' choice (assuming there had been others - I've only played through once, following the Open Hand path). This ambiguity was very appreciated, and it's something I'm still thinking about. Some form of sequal would have really been fantastic, as I would have loved to see what my impact on the Jade Empire ultimately ended up being.
In short, despite the aging, I found the game to be extremely entertaining, and possibly a necessary staple to anyone curious about playing more Bioware games. I can definitely see myself replaying it. For information purposes, my playtime ended up being 23 hours.
One last note: The steam edition of Jade Empire had this issue where upon startup, it would tell it 'couldn't find steam' or some such drivel, and then promptly close. The fix was relatively easy. Exit steam entirely, and then run it as administrator, and then start Jade Empire. That should allow the configuration paths to form correctly (I believe that was where the issue lay, but I can't be certain. Regardless, the game worked normally for me then on out).

If I buy a game, I'll almost always complete it. So I'm thankful I jumped in and bought Deus Ex, otherwise I would never have seen the greatness it (eventually) has to offer. Had I been able to play the first hour or so, I would probably have resolved never to play the whole game, clunky as it was. The gameplay, graphics and writing seem very slipshod at first, but gradually more and more moments of greatness piled up until I realised the truth: I love this game.
Does it feel dated for a 2011 release? Yes it does, and mostly in good ways. Deus Ex reminded me of the feeling of playing games like Half Life and Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory for the first time, and I realised how much I'd missed those games. It's not just a nostalgia trip either. There is sophistication here that I haven't seen performed so well anywhere else. There's a moment where your character, Adam, and another major character appear to part ways permanently, and in any other game that would simply be the way the story goes; no matter how hard you'd fight, [x] minutes into a major battle you'd get [event y] and nothing about how you fought it could change that. Not in Deus Ex, however; you really can alter that course. When a go-between tells you that you've got a hard choice between saving the scientist who'll be your star witness in a prosecution case or saving the lives of dozens of other people, but you can't save both... in any other game you'd assume that this is a strictly A or B situation. Deus Ex will surprise you when you discover there really is a third way. The results of your earlier actions carry really nicely from  the past to the future, sometimes in small ways such as the script and sometimes to a much more significant degree. You will not see my game, and I did not see yours.
So, yes, it was 2011 and yet that low-res skybox does appear to be a 16-colour bitmap. Yeah, the animations often look like something from ten years ago. No, your enemies cannot climb ladders or follow you into the vents. But so what, when it does so many things brilliantly? I took 43 hours to beat this game ONCE, partly as a result of hunting all the little secrets and also because I found so many things to do that are fun but slow. The first time I unlocked the ability to hack security turrets to make them hunt guards, I carried that thing around with me for the rest of the mission. Later on, I'd be punching a hole through the wall of my enemies' HQ, dumping a hacked turret in their reception area, and walking out nonchalantly through the hole I'd made while bullets and screams echoed behind me and achievements for great marksmanship flashed up on the screen. Wonderful.

Whether you will enjoy this controller seems to depend a great deal on what sort of gamer you are, so let me say that I'm the sort of gamer that plays mouse-and-keyboard PC games the overwhelming majority of the time, and will always, always go to the "options" menu to rebind keys as the very first thing I do in a new game.  Steam controller is made for people who enjoy experimenting with new control schemes.
I, for example, have never liked WASD, and use W for right, S for left, E for up, and D for down because that leaves my pinky and index finger free to roam for other keys, which is much more efficient than the industry standard.  I also am not averse to "dual-wielding", and playing with a  controller in the left hand, and the mouse in the right, and this configuration actually works
with this controller.
If you can't be bothered to learn, there are pretty much always a set of custom controls from the userbase that seem pretty popular, although I personally always prefer my own homebrew to the local favorites, so I can't comment on how well that works out for people.
The Pros:
* Mode switching.  I love this feature.  Sort of like making shift-Q do something different from just Q alone, you can sacrifice one button to double the functions of another.  With the extra two "grip" buttons on the back, You can use one as a "shift key" and basically have twice as many buttons as your normal controllers. (Granted, with Joy2Key, you could already map contoller buttons to shift keys and the like, although this promises to update automatically.)
* There are multiple modes for the touchpads and stick.  You can set the d-pad-looking touchpad on the left to be nine buttons depending on where on the pad you click, for example.  Mode shifted, these can even be different, so un-mode-shifted left touchpad might be menu navigation, while mode-shifted, it pops up different windows.
* Touchpads can be "click" or "tap".  You can calibrate the sensitivity of your trigger buttons, and set two functions to trigger buttons depending on sensitivity settings.
* "Dual wield" with a mouse in the right hand, and the controller in the left.  It gives you analogue touchpad or stick controls instead of just WASD. With mode shifting, you can generally use the left half of a controller the way that you used the keyboard, and if you don't mind a few grip-shifts (brace the controller against your leg) for less-used controls, you can reach over for the face buttons one-handed, and have more keys at your fingertips than I am comfortable reaching on a keyboard.  (Yes, I can reach the U button on a keyboard with my left hand, but I tend to lose the homekeys when I try.)
* No matter how badly the game's options are lacking, (or worse, nonexistant in a bad port,) you can rebind keys however you want.  This means I can play games with hideous control schemes even when the game's designer never even deigned allow us mere players to rebind keys outside of trying to look for an .ini file.
The Cons:
*
- You currently have to go into Big Picture Mode to change controls for some inexplicable reason.  Rumor has it Valve is working on a stand-alone contoller-profiling app, and I believe it because it would be idiocy not to have such an app, but for now, this means that I have to constantly close the game, then go into BPM, then rebind the keys (possibly having to write down what I wanted them to be), and then close BPM, and relaunch the game.
* BPM is also unreliable.  Sometimes, I find my control scheme is something from two expermental setups ago, and I have to close the game right after starting it, launch BPM, reload my keybinds, close BPM, relaunch the game.  It gets annoying when this happens enough times.
* You can only have one set of mode-switched keys, unless Valve decides to add more.
*
The Steam Logo light never turns off, and is rather bright and distracting.
* It takes more force than I like to click the shoulder/"bumper" buttons and touchpads.
* The analogue stick's grippy bumps are only on the sides of the stick, not the top, and that tends to irritate my thumbs along where the transition occurs.
* I'd like it if the USB cable were longer.  It comes with disposable batteries, but why would you want something that needs constant replacement or can leak acid into your controller?!  I scraped enough leaky acid out of my gamebricks and TV remote controls to never want to see a AA battery again.
* I'd have preferred a true d-pad, replaced the analogue stick, instead, and shoved that touchpad down where the analogue stick actually sits.  Reaching the top-right area of the left touchpad requires shifting my grip.
* The "trackball mode" the recommend for navigating desktop is hypersensitive to what skin cell leaves the pad surface last, which basically means that the cursor/camera is going to go God-knows-where the instant your thumb leaves the pad. Turn trackball mode off immediately, and use Mouse Region mode or Mouse with no trackball and where it keeps seeking when you hold your thumb off the edge.  Basically, the defaults are bad, so make sure you enjoy experimenting with custom layouts.
PRESUMING Valve fixes the first couple cons, (and they're banking too heavily on the controller working for them not to,) I can pretty strongly reccommend this controller over any standard game controller, at the very least.  Prefering a controller over a mouse and keyboard for day-to-day computing is still a lousy joke, but pitting it head-to-head against my old game controllers just for gaming, this costs the same money for more features and more flexibility, so yeah, get it.

Nier Automata left me speechless.
It wasn't love at first sight, I had to learn how to love this game.
And when I did, when it finally clicked, I was hooked.
SPOILERS
Nier Automata really begins near the end of Route A. That's when things start to get interesting, and it keeps getting better and better from that point on.
The plot may be the strongest point of this game, but gameplay-wise it is so customizable that you can craft the experience to your own liking.
Want it to be easy? You can do that. Want it to be hard as hell? You can chose to do so.
Want to focus on melee combat? Go ahead. Want to turn it in a TPS? Your choice.
The soundtrack is perfect. It build the atmosphere perfectly, it's very nice to listen to, every track is just amazing and left me speechless.
Graphically, it's not a masterpiece, it's not your typical AAA-looking game, but damn, does it look beautiful. It may not reach the technical levels of Uncharted 4, but the art-style makes up for it and goes well beyond that.
I recommend this game, maybe one of the best that 2017 had to offer.

Monster Loves You is a charming little choose your own adventure game in which you develop a monster from birth to death, or even beyond when it's death should have come, if you play your cards right. The whole story is played through reading little vignettes about moments in your monster's life then deciding what it's going to do at that moment. When it's still a baby your choices will mostly just effect its own personality, but as it gets older the things you decide will also come to determine how much other monsters respect it and eventually how well their tribe gets along with their closest neighbors.
The game contains much more replay value than you might expect; you never get enough turns in a stage of life to pick every story to read through and it's also randomly (as far as I can tell) chosen what stories will be available for you in each new game, so if you start a new playthrough you'll find plenty of new scenarios to play through as well as being able to make different choices in ones you've drawn before.
I would definitely recommend it to anyone who wants something light and fun to kill a couple hours.

Certainly not the next step in storytelling games. I guess it is a fun read on the first two playthroughs, though.

This is only a reveiw for the current state of the game.
When I first booted it up, it seemed pretty interesting. It looked like something I could get into. The game is a sort of Depth/TF2 type deal, typically with one team being dinos and the other being humans. There's a bunch of servers, but it seems mnone of them are exactly "official servers" meaning all you're getting is community-run madness most of the time. A few too many RP servers for my taste, honestly.
Also, if you thought you were going to escape all that by plaing the single-player mode, well good luck, because there basically isn't one. If you think you can entertain yourself with solo horde mode that ends the second you die, then I applaud you. As for me, this is much less than enough.
Finally, the killing blow for me, personally, was the steam market glitch. After finding a server that I rather liked, I decided to buy a number of skins from the steam marketplace so I could use the in-game. Of the 15+ skins I bought (coming out to around $6.93) i started up the game and entered the customization screen. Once there, I was immediately met with a bug. This bug spawned after a recent steam update and prevents any skins you have in your steam inventory from showing up in the game. It turns out i'm not the only one who has had this problem. there are many discussion threads about this, not of which have managed to bring a full resolution to this particular problem. After a number of attempts, several suggested fixes, skimming both the threads and several websites and forums, I was no closer to fixing the issue than when i had started. I've tried EVERYTHING, so before you suggest anything else that you think might work, don't.
I have made up my mind, I am walking away from this game until it has been fixed. At the current point in time, I suggest you do NOT buy the game, and wait until this nigh-invincible bug has been purged from the system.

DXHR Director's cut is an interesting upgrade. In my opinion the most important change is the ability to handle boss fights differently. In the original release of the game, player choice was always emphasized to such a great extent, that it was always a little jarring when, after sneaking around a level avoiding killing and being seen, you suddenly were forced to use brute force to defeat an enemy. The update is not a vast improvement, but does allow for a greater number of options when playing against these final bosses and do feel a little bit more integrated with a stealthy play style. Speaking of the player choice, this feature is what sets apart DXHR. The ability to go through the vast majority of the game without firing a shot leads to some amazing gaming experiences. It can be extremely frustrating when trying a non-lethal stealthy playthrough, to have to go through and play an area multiple times, but the feeling of mastering an area is extremely gratifying. The game's story, while being forumulaic in a few places, is really quite good, and engaging enough to drive me forward to resolve the various story arcs. The best part of this game is its world, with the ability to both traverse it in many different manners in which the player sees fit, but also to make both storyline and gameplay decisions, that affect the world around you. The  game's environs, though not graphically cutting edge, do serve, along with the rather strong color palette, to really bring the game to life and in conjunction with the soundtrack and story, can be very immersive. The game is not without its flaws, the most glaring, in my opinion, being the lack of ability to track, from start to finish, whether or not both a non-lethal and completely undetected stealth playthrough has been completed. When I was first playing DXHR, I inadvertently killed an enemy somewhere and when I finished the game believing I had completed a non-lethal playthough, I was not awarded with the achievement. If there was some way of tracking campaign-spanning achievements, that would be extremely helpful. Secondly, the game's voice acting was extremely hit or miss, and in places even groan-worthy, but this could be looked past in the grand scheme of the story. All in all, frustrations aside, this game is easily of my top five games, with the graphics, soundtrack, rich story, and especially gameplay combining for an immersive, rewarding and fun experience from start to finish that has a very high replay potential.

So I saw this was available for a free weekend, and I'd been curious about it for some time. After taking this opportunity to play the game, I bought it in a heartbeat.
For all of its bizarre visuals and eerie music (Which I admittedly turned down in favour of playing my own music while golfing, sorry devs!), as well as its silly golf-cart physics and other shenanigans, buried deep beneath all of that is a surprisingly good golf game.
In particular, the game's advertisement of having "A swing mechanic designed to be satisfying" is actually spot on the mark - For a simple mechanic based on using your mouse to imitate the swing of the club, the game does a really good job of helping you feel the 'weight' of the club, and the guide ruler helps you angle your shot just right. I've had a lot of fantastically satisfying moments where I've chipped a ball into the hole from off the green, and it feels perfect.
My only complaint, one that is shared with other players currently, is that there's only one 9-hole course available at the moment, but honestly for the price (55 cents a hole when it's not on sale!) I'd say it's worth it.

Nier Automata is a strange game in many ways. It's hard to nail it down. It starts as a good old fashioned shmup, then transitions to a dual stick shooter, then it's a 3rd person rpg. You keep playing and you get the first ending and you ask yourself "Wait, that's the end?" but it's not. You start again, and after the third 'ending' you get the title card.
You read that right, this game doesn't really even start on the story it's trying to tell until you beat it three times. That's what kind of game Nier Automata is. The music is haunting, melancholy, and beautiful. The world is a strange mix of dull emptiness and vibrant life. It's this strange amalgam of a million things that shouldn't work together, but do. And at the end of it all it'll leave you breathless.
The care and attention that has been put into this game astonishes me. I can point to the exact moment I knew I was playing something different. There's a part of the game where you're told "This will be recorded" while you're interacting with a menu screen, setting your brightness and such. I assumed this was a throwaway line to add realism.
No. You later play through that exact situation again from a different perspective and the menu literally plays back everything you did. I have no idea why that was considered an important story element. I don't really think it was that noticeable to many players. But it still blows my mind that a developer took the time.

I've heard Jade Empire described as BioWare's awkward teenage phase, and I'm inclined to agree.  Jade Empire is basically KOTOR as filtered through the wuxia genre. While the setting is a refreshing shift from the space-opera-or-European-fantasy split of most BioWare RPGs, the story is the exact same one they're always telling and this experimental phase leads to a lot of stumbles.
After NWN and KOTOR's simplistic Good/Evil dichotomy, but before Mass Effect's Idealistic Good/Ruthless Good dichotomy, Jade Empire experimented with the notion of Open Palm vs. Closed Fist, which in theory was a more interesting philosophy of "help people to the point of coddling" vs. "be self serving so people don't become dependent on you." In practice, however, Open Palm was still White Hat and Closed Fist was still Black Hat, which is shown best just before the climax where you press the Big Bad's right hand man into your service, and your only possible responses to your party's objections to that are "let your new minion go" or "mindrape everyone who disagrees."
As with most of BioWare's works, the story is filled with these false dichotomies, where you're allowed no middle ground between all-loving saint and sadistic bully. The writers seem to have some sort of outright contempt towards the notion of neutrality, a point that seemed to be poorly parodied in KOTOR II, but that's neither here nor there.
All of this would probably only warrant Jade Empire my usual unenthusiastic recommendation I give for most of BioWare's more mediocre titles, but the gameplay mechanics solidly push this game into the "can't recommend" bin. Jade Empire entirely does away with BioWare's usual RPG standbys, starting you off with a selection of predesigned character models that never change, and the only equipment you ever accrue are either combat styles - which each level independantly as if you were taking a dozen different prestige classes - and gemstones, which provide extremely minor stat boosts, with extra slots opening up as you progress through the plot. None of this is BAD per se - certainly less interesting, to the point where I kind of wonder why they even bothered with the gems instead of focusing entirely on honing your martial arts skills - but the problem just boils down to the fact that combat is clunky and not really fun.
Combat basically boils down to four things; punching your enemy in the face, using a heavy attack when they block,
healing when you're injured, and using the Spirit Thief style when you're low on chi. Unfortunately, some enemies (demons, mostly) are immune to Spirit Thief, and chi only restores from certain spirit fonts or by using the Spirit Thief ability. The biggest annoyance though, is the recurring issue with your attacks slowly knocking your opponent back at a rate slightly faster than you can walk (which is obscenely slow in combat, as if your character had a ball and chain on each ankle). So every few strikes, you'd be forced to awkwardly hobble your way back into melee range before continuing, often leaving yourself open to blows in the meantime.
It's not a dealbreaker, as the combat ultimately proved so easy for the most part that I barreled through almost every single threat in the game with very little effort. But "easy" does not necessarily equate to "fun," and while manageable every fight in the game felt like swimming through jelly. The fact that your allies are almost entirely useless may be justified by the ease with which you can solo everything, but that begs the question of why they're even there other than a few moderately interesting character designes to piddle about in the background of your fights half-heartedly holding aggro for one or two of your opponents.

I loved this game when I played it on the original Xbox. Now I can't imagine why. It has possibly the worst combat and camera controls of any game I've ever played.
During combat, some button presses are often delayed by a few seconds. If you begin a combo and then try to dodge, it will complete the combo before dodging. Often so much time has passed between when you press the dodge button and when you actually dodge that you may no longer want to dodge. But you will. Oh yes, you will. The same goes for if any enemy is hitting you. You will wait for the enemy to finish THEIR combo before you dodge/attack. Basically, the combat is very stilted and unresponsive.
The camera is perhaps even worse. It's understandable given the age of the game and the hardware it was developed on that the camera would be somewhat limited. You can only tilt the camera up, not down, and the camera movement is very imprecise. That's all forgiveable. What is not forgiveable is how the camera behaves in combat. If you are fighting near a wall the camera will tilt at odd angles preventing you from seeing what is going on. This becomes especially annoying when you are fighting in a small room. You may be fighting blind 75% of the time.
There are other issues with the game, as well, such as the invisible barriers that surround you during battles, the stilted dialogue, the overly simplistic RPG elements (there are only three attributes), and the fuzzy cutscenes.
I just can't recommend this game, which is a pity. I really did love it on Xbox. Kind of makes me question the judgment of past me.

I decided to play Jade Empire after having played the KOTOR games multiple times, Mass Effect 2 and 3, and Dragon Age: Origins. I was on a BioWare binge, and needed more of what made those games so special.
: The graphics are a highlight of the game, even if somewhat dated today. The worlds are rich and colorful, the game has its own unique art style, and it's fun to see the different special powers and items in play.
: For those of you familiar with KOTOR, the level design will remind you at times of certain worlds in that series. BioWare is very good at creating an atmosphere or "feel" with their level designs and this is no exception. However, there aren't all that many worlds to explore in comparison to BioWare's other games. KOTOR II, which was released a year before this game, contained over 7-8 different worlds, not including shorter stages. Jade Empire barely has 5, and not even the supposedly grand Imperial City is quite as large or expansive as Nar Shaddaa. (It comes across as more of a small village than anything.) I could compare it to watching an older Hollywood film - one can often tell that the sets are as large as the view of the camera; one step to the right and you're in a studio. Similarly, the limited nature of some of these areas makes them feel less authentic.
: The music is enjoyable enough and fits the artistic theme of the game. However, it is mostly forgettable, with one notable exception - the Imperial Palace theme ("Anthem of a Tyrant"), which invokes a bit of a Darth Vader or Don Fanucci vibe. The voice acting is decent (albeit a little cartoony at times), and I had no complaints about the sound effects.
: I did not find either the story or the characters particularly original or compelling. However, that is not to say that there are no highlights; Hou has some smirk-worthy moments as a repressed husband and Silk Fox leads an interesting dual life. But other characters are defined by single traits: Dawn Star, for instance, is the generic good-hearted heroine with no flaws, and the Black Whirlwind is drunk and roguish. Things get especially cringe-inducing when the game tries to shoehorn a backstory into the latter. Unlike Dragon Age, which contains multi-layered characters, or Mass Effect, which explores personal changes through the game's arc, the characters here are fairly static and uninteresting.
Plot-wise, the game borrows a critical element from KOTOR II without coming up with many creative plot ideas, so hardcore BioWare fans won't be too thrilled with the game's writing. Unfortunately, hardcore BioWare fans are the group most likely to try this game.
: The gameplay heavily revolves around combat, which heavily revolves around melee attacks, which heavily revolve around incessant clicking of the mouse. There are moments when strategy is involved, usually when facing off against multiple strong enemies. In addition, the PC can learn a couple of ranged attacks and possess weapons, but the selection is disappointingly limited and you'll find yourself resorting to the same two or three fighting styles over and over. Not to mention, almost every conflict in the game is resolved through combat, which grows tiresome. The enemies often take twenty hits to go down, which tests not one's skills but one's patience. Furthermore, some levels contain dozens of battles with groups of the same kind of enemy (often respawning!). However, there are a few battles in the game that require more creativity to fight, and although they do not dominate most of the game's combat, brawling with these foes can be very enjoyable.
I think that the game in general relied too much on combat, while devoting little attention to gameplay through dialogue/choices, strategy, etc. In addition, the combat itself was not varied enough for me to forego this issue - I found myself terribly bored throughout the third act in the game, simply tolerating each battle just to get to the end.
The game does implement an alignment system, but it seems to matter a lot less than in other BioWare titles. At the end of the day, combat is Jade Empire's main feature, and it's not as fun as one might expect or hope.
:
- The combat is often repetitive, some characters are flat, and the game feels disappointingly short and lacking in an engaging plot. However, despite these flaws, there are some well-designed environments, and the originality of the artwork and setting is a strong point. If there's a Jade Empire 2, BioWare needs to recognize this one's limitations. Jade Empire had the potential to be a great title, but given the drawbacks outlined above, I can only call it decent. I would recommend it to dedicated BioWare fans, but not really anyone else.
Oh, and the flyer levels - really, Bioware? You thought it was a good idea to implement scrolling shooter stages?

I have over 100 games on Steam, and yet this little game is probably the one I'm playing most on Steam (for Linux) at the moment. So I felt I should review it to let the devs know. They aren't making their fortunes on it after all. So buy it now, it's a lot more fun than many much higher priced games.
It's a very simple but nicely balanced space invaders clone that has you jumping straight back in for another game when you die. It differs from old school space invaders in that the aliens don't approach, just slide side-to-side and shoot (though they do get a bit faster as you progress). You have infinite ammo and just hold down fire for a generous stream of bullets (though there could be some smarter strategy I'm missing). Once you kill one wave of aliens (four rows, each with one of seven or eight types) the next wave immediately pours in. You get a short-lived powerup weapon by shooting the spaceship alien that appears in the middle of the top row about half the time, and there's a nice slo-mo as you get it which can be used tactically. Waves can be shot as they arrive, which rewards planning when to get powerups.
Once you get good at dodging, the skill is in choosing how to distribute your fire and keeping your score multiplier up by ensuring you don't get stuck on the wrong side of a hail of bullets (it rises as you shoot aliens but resets back to 1 if you don't shoot one for too long). The game feels fair, and it's quite relaxing when things are going well.
The only very slight annoyance is that it slows down over time (noticeable after about an hour on my low-powered Linux box), maybe due to memory leaks (I have 8GB, but haven't checked the usage). But restarting is quick so it's not a big deal.
So thanks for a fun game, devs. Now I'm off to beat my highscore.
