*This is a mixed review, read on to find out why*
At first glance, I added this to my wishlist instantly when I saw it. What more could one want than a modern Retro styled Arcade Machine like Space Invaders on Steam? However, upon finally buying it, I found out quickly that it lacks expected features beyond bare bones Space Invaders. With that said here is what I thought of it:
Pros:
♦ Retro Arcade Machine feel
♦ Decent Retro Graphics
♦ Great Space Invader feel
♦ Sound/Music was decent
♦ Keyboard controls worked (You can only use keyboard, see cons for more)
♦ Great for killing time (If you have nothing to do or little time, this will suit you)
♦ Multiplayer is cool (Take turns playing on the same pc to see who can get the better highscore, really good if you want to settle a bet or something)
Cons:
♦ Doesn’t add anything new to Space Invaders
♦ Needs local and global highscores for each game mode (Adding this will give you a reason to play as people love competing against others)
♦ No Achievements & Steam Cards (This game would be much better off with achievements to give people something to aim towards when playing)
♦ Doesn't tell you the number of waves you have cleared (I'd personally like this out of own preference)
♦ Claims to be intense retro space shooter but has no difficulty progression (There are no bosses, waves don't seem to get more difficult due to being randomly generated and enemies don't change in variety. Therefore, difficulty relies on the five or so randomly generated variants of enemies to how difficult a wave is, which isn't really that difficult)
♦ Enemies that give powerups are randomly generated (You can get them on any wave and don't have to do anything to get them. I would have expected hitting x score, clearing x waves or killing x units etc would trigger one, but you get them randomly which makes them pointless)
♦ No ingame options (Can't change controls, graphics, sound levels from within the game)
♦ Lack of enemie variants (Seems to be about five different enemies and that's it)
♦ Can only use keyboard (Can't use controller, mouse or anything else)
♦ Lack of Steam Features (Such as achievements, cards, highscores etc)
Overall, despite the large number of cons over pros, this is a game I'd give a mixed review to if I could. It's not terrible but it's not good. You will get your monies worth if you like the basic bare bones Retro Arcade styled Space Invaders. However, it lacks anything more than that and doesn't add anything new to the Space Invaders game which you can play for free on almost any flash game site. Also, it has nothing other than the game score to keep you playing and lacks any sign of Steam Features. Lastly, for the price and what it is, you'll get a bare bones Retro Arcade Machine styled Space Invaders and nothing else. Therefore, if you like Space Invaders you'll get your monies worth and this is for you. However, if you don't then this isn't for you as you'll be disappointed with the lack of features.

Monster Loves You! is short and solid.
It's a choose-your-own-adventure style game with a very high density of choices to be made crammed into a small package. The result is that everything you do feels important, and with too much to do in a single play-thru the replayability factor is somewhat high. However, the game isn't long and multiple play-thrus--once you understand the format--can be accomplished in rapid succession and the game peters out.
Still, it has lovely graphics and makes for a few really fun rounds in a notably unique monster world and culture. While not being expansive it is highly detailed and definitely worth a look if you enjoy the pick-your-consequences genre.

The puzzles are good, but sometimes it's not clear at all what you should be looking for. And this in a bad way, like it feels as if they forgot to put a clue in the dialogue when they should have. But you run into that problem in most, if not all point&click adventures, when the player's and the protagonist's (or writer's) logic sometimes become "out of sync"...
The atmosphere, graphics, animation, characters, dialogue and humour are all great.
There were some unexpected 4th wall breaking jokes which were a pleasant surprise. I can't imagine how fresh that must have been back when the game first came out. There are enough jokes to justify a second playthrough if you don't get them all the first time.
Even though it looks like a wild cartoon, it's still charming with well designed characters and good dialogues that you can connect with. Guybrush is a great character and I felt with him throughout his adventure.
I really enjoyed the music, voice acting and sound effects. I played with the "ultimate talkie edition" mod to get the old graphics with the new sound. If you play the game without this mod you can't have the new sound when you choose to play with the old style graphics unfortunately. I don't really like the new designs although some things do look cool.
To be honest I did expect this "legend" among adventure games to be bigger, longer, more complex, ... But in the end I like it the way it is. Short, simple, not too many locations, not too difficult puzzles, no complicated story, just a good time and a few laughs. I have of course already been spoiled with newer games like Broken Sword or Syberia. In it's time this must have been really something.

The series has prided itself as having a large and diverse number of ways to complete mission objectives, and this one proudly carries this tradition on, having sprawling levels with hundreds of different paths to completion based on the player's choice and their abilities on hand. It accomadates a large number of playstyles with an opened ended leveling system to provide an extremely replayable experience that takes numerous playthroughs to get old. Alright, confession time: I'm using a Mac, and have a wrapper that is making the game run at all. I did buy this game legitimately though (3 times to be precise)
Confession over.
Now then, do I like this game? Yes. would I recommend it to my friends? Yes. But the best way to describe this game is that it's akin to an uncut gem; still beautiful to look at, sure, but there is so much potential that's not quite realized. The game was clearly made as an "in between game," something that can keep the developers busy while the think-tank works on the next big project.
That said, this game is one of my favorites, and I have a short list of favorites. My most love aspect is the combat, as it's not the "choose an action" type from KotOR 1, but neither is it the "Pause and command" type from Mass Effect. It's more free flowing and it gives me the feeling of being a wushu master, or in this case, the Spirit Monk, and I love how each style can flow so smoothly into each other. Some better than others, but finding the best combo for you is part of the fun.
One major gripe for me though is that, for the sake of time, the story was made FAR to predictable. Granted, I still felt the happiness and sadness that I was supposed to feel, but there was always that underlying thought that I knew it was going to happen...but then it makes up for it somewhat with the unpredictable side quests, so it's a little for given.
Overall, I love the game, and if anyone that has a Mac wants to play this, here's what you do.
1. Buy the game. Doesn't mater from where, but this is Steam, so lets say from here ;)
2. Go to
, and find the games wrapper. No, you can't buy from him.
3. Fallow his instructions. He outlines what to do on the page, and with a youtube video, so both should help.
4. Download Direct X 9 when prompted. The game MUST have this or IT WILL NOT RUN! Other games need this to, so it's no real loss anyway.
5. Make sure to use a two button mouse. I know from experience that the Apple Magic Mouse will work with the game, but the right mouse function does not work, and trust me, I was able to make the game a lot easier by just switching mouses. (mice?)
6.1 You may need to turn down the graphics a bit, but I've found that just turing the shadows off is enough for the overworld if you still want to have some nice looking polygons.
6.2 To play the SHMUP portions of the game more effectually, but still have some nice graphics , just turn down the graphics during those sections to zero and it'll play like butter-nice and smooth. I would definitively recommend this game, it starts slowly but as I progressed in the story I appreciated it more and more, despice some flaws in the gameplay and the annoying bioware "black & white" morality system.
Technics:
win 7 + xbox controller, no problems , nothing to complain about.
Gameplay:
The controlls are a bit rusty and at times ungainly, it doesn't respond as well as it should, making it at time very difficult to resolve a fight. The advanced combat style system, while a good idea could do with some streamlining, there are almost too many styles (something between 15 and 20) but you end up using only a couple of them exclusively.
The combat in itself can range from very difficult (even with a controller) to smash a button simple. Bioware should have remembered they are first and foremost a RPG company, action is not their fortes.
Still when you get the hang of it, the fights are usually fun and very kung-fu likes , I only wished it had been a bit simpler and more responsive.
The RPG part is working nicely, although it sometimes feel like we could do with a little less dialogue, but like in many bioware games we feel obliged to go though everything a character has to say just in case something interessting is hiding in the choices.
Graphics and sounds
For a game this age I'm agreably surprised with the nice graphics. The background landscapes are beautifully rendered with a lot of colour , the music and sounds goes nicely with it giving it a distinctively fantasy oriental feeling. Yes it's dated but at anno 2015 I didn't have any problem with it, and as the game went on, I was actually more and more impressed about the nice backgrounds and objects put in the game. The characters look quite nice , maybe a bit boring but nothing too serious. The attention to the details is maybe what impressed me most, everything feel very oriental, from the design of GUI to the music or the decorations, very nice.
Plot
At first it doesn't really engage, but after an hour of two the game become more and more exciting, the characters who start at bit bland become more fleshed out and interesting and the quests and surroundings get better and better. In fact the game get really interessting 1\3 into the story when you reach the capital. In short it might seem a bit boring at first but things get better with time, give it a chance.
Toward the end it get really amazing and I have to say it's one of the most engaging RPG I have played for a long time. The story is much better than NWN2 (expensions included) and the ending is much better than masseffect and even KOTOR 1. The Bioware "morality" system however annoyed me with it's very basic evil and good choices. It's very black and white and counterintuitive , bioware doesn't manage to give us clear motivations to behave like a "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" , most people will naturally choice the "good-guy" choices especially when being a bad guy doesn't give you any clear advantages. This is not a new problem for bioware RPG however and it's something most of us have learned to live with in those games. Still a bit annoying.
The story start a bit tame, but it very soon become a lot more exciting. In fact towad the end I was really engrossed in it and the game amazed me more and more as I progressed. The story is one of the best I've experienced in a RPG for quite some times and it's very refreshing.
Conclusions
The game has its flaws, but mostly it's great  especially if you like a great and engrossing story. The beginning is a bit tame, and take some time to familiarise yourself with the controlls which can feel cluncky at time. But as a whole the great story and interessant characters make it worth your time, I definitively recommend this game.

Jade Empire is a good game (though not a great one) that is worth playing if you are either:
A) A fan of Bioware games and want to know how they got from KOTOR to Dragon Age, or
B) Looking for an interesting RPG set in a faux-Chinese fantasy setting (as opposed to most RPGs, which are set in faux-European fantasy settings).
This is clearly a Bioware RPG.  The overall framework.  The way you gather and interact with your party.  The interface.  The dialogue choices and morality system.  All are very typical Bioware.  If you like those things, great.  If not, be warned.  If you've never played a Bioware game, then I'd probably recomed that you start with either Knights of the Old Republic, Dragon Age, or Mass Effect, all of which are better games (over all), than Jade Empire.
Jade Empire excels over other Bioware games, in my opinion, in three areas.  First, the combat system is above average for a Bioware RPG.  Similar to, but much smoother than, KOTOR.  Less tactical, but also less frustrating, than Dragon Age.  In fact, I think this is what they were going for with Dragon Age II, they just didn't get it quite right (given that Dragon Age II was rushed out the door, this is not surprising).  Combat is fun and fluid, and yet still tactically interesting.
The other area, is that the basic mini-game (a bullet hell, bomber-run style airplane game), works better than most Bioware mini-games.  Admittedly, this is a low bar.
Finally, the setting here is easily the most original that Bioware has ever done.  I really hope that they readdress it.  We don't see a lot of respectful, well-crafted, Asian-inspired fantasy settings in North American produced RPGs--and certainly not ones where all of the characters look Asian and have Asian-sounding names.  Yes, it's a hodge-podge of Chinese art, archetecture, and fantasy traditions--but Dragon Age is a hodge-podge of European-inspired art, archetecture, and fantasy traditions.  This is a great world, and I hope that they come back to it.
So what's the down side?
The minor complaint is that a few of the fights (less than 5) are wildly imbalanced.  As in, everything else will be trivially easy, and suddenly you will hit a fight that feels almost impossible.
The more serious complaint is that the game is really short, for a Bioware RPG.  My first playthrough of most Bioware RPGs takes between 40 and 70 hours.  My first playthrough of Jade Empire took less than 20 hours.  The game just felt TOO streamlined.  For example:
- Large sections of the Empire were mentioned, but the player was never allowed to visit them.
- Only 1 party member has a side quest.
- The romance (whichever option you take) feels very rushed, because of a general lack of interaction.
- One playthrough is not enough time to explore the corners of the combat system, but the storyline is too linear and the game too lacking in side-areas to explore, to encourage much replayability.
If anyone else had made Jade Empire, it would be a very good RPG.  Heck, it's still a very good RPG.  But for a Bioware game, it's a bit disapointing--which is sad, because it has a tremendous amount of potential.

Dead Rising 3 is the next latest installment in the Dead Rising franchise. It has everything from the older games and has some much needed improvments.
However much to my disapointment the story in this Dead Rising is terrible. Everything was very predictable, the main character is essentially a blank slate in contrats to the older games where Chuck was a pun making badass who wishes to clear his name and take care of his daughter, and Frank who is a reporter and will do anything to uncover the truth. But the character Nick in this game is just terrible. There is no badassery here and he seems only interested in the girl in the story dispite the fact the city is going to be blown up within 7 days. The love story was entirely pointless and it didnt even add anything. It was just there. Some of the characters were pretty good though such as♥♥♥♥♥♥whom the player gets to play in coop mode but sadly he is rarely in cutscenes and doesnt comment on the situation much.
Again with the Psychopaths in this game there was some disapointment. In the previous game the psychopaths in the main story had at least some sense of dignity and were all a big part of the story however that is not the case in DR3. One of them just constantly grabs her boobs and makes sex jokes....and shes the commander of some military squad...it made no sense at all. Now were she a side quest psychopath it would be understandable but having an over the top psychopath as part of the main story was quite upsetting.
It feels like the strayed from what their main stories were about. There was some well written humor in the main story which was quite believable but there was also terrible humor aswell.
Side quest psychopaths were done extremely well and each one has their own weakness however this is made pointless as the character can level up to becoming overpowered so fast that it just ruins the boss battle. You can literally kill the first psychopath within 1 minute....
All that aside the game is a lot of fun! and the improvement to level up your own stats when and how you want was awesome. If you level up certain stats and ignore others you can make the game much harder on yourself and thus turn it into a real dead rising game where the bosses are hard and the military is actually a threat (just like in the previous games)
Nightmare mode is pointless. It makes the game a tiny bit harder and gives you less time. Nightmare is supposed to make the game feel more like a dead rising game however it felt it did the opposite for me. You have less time sure but by less time they really mean that time has been sped up a great deal leaving you not able to complete all the side quests before the story ends unlike in the previous games where this was possible but with some effoty.
All in all a great game. Tons of fun but if you are looking for a challenege (and I mean even a tiny challenge) either stay away from the game or only level up stats that do not make your character overpowered.

[note: I have used this device for less than a week. This review is based on initial impressions]
This thing is a great, *great* idea, and a wonderful addition to my couch-based gaming. The integrated configuration, and community of configuration sharing, makes it hands down much better than other software. The touchpads are a great interface, and when properly configured, are a really nice way to control things.
However: 90% of what makes this product great is the software. The only reason the software is tied to the controllers is because there's no way anyone would buy a controller if they could get this functionality via software alone (in a less-cynical view, I think that the software uploads the bindings to the controller itself, for input efficiency). The ability to save configurations per-game, and share them with the community, is the killer feature of this product.
The configurations, so far, appear to be entirely per-game. I haven't spotted a way to save my own "template", for example. Inputting these configurations is also tedious, one button at a time. There is no "partial template", or similar (eg: "make this pad act like arrow keys")
Interestingly, under Ubuntu at the time of this writing, attempting to configure the controller at all results in steam immediately crashing. I don't hold that against the controller itself, as I suspect this will be fixed soon.
On to the hardware itself. Firstly, when you take it out of the package, you're going to notice: AA-batteries. What the crap? My instinct was to put this thing away and never touch it again when I saw these. These should use rechargeable batteries as standard. There is no excuse these days for using a disposable battery. Add to that, there is no obvious way to turn off the controller when not in use (other than via Steam itself),
And finally, my main complaint: While the touchpads are a joy to use, they have both a "touch only" and a "click" action. The click *feels* horrible, and *sounds* worse. This product would be greatly improved by not having a click integrated into the touchpads. The "grip" buttons similarly have a loud and clunky "click" associated with them, which again feel horrible and sound even worse. The grip controls seem like a natural place for mode changes, and there are some neat tricks you can do with mode changes to make "hard press" on the touchpad a different action from "soft press", but silent pressure-sensitive controls have existed for a long time, and I really would prefer this thing not have the option at all, over this loud and clunky implementation.
The best configurations I've seen have been "light touch" ones, which make use of the touchpads exclusively. Even with these, you will still *accidentally* click, often, which makes the whole controller feel worse.
This is very clearly an "initial version" of the product. I would strongly recommend avoiding this controller completely until they make one that doesn't constantly sound like a stapler. Software problems will be fixed over time, I assume, but I'll be living with these buttons for a long while.

The 2009 special edition of the 1990 classic 2D adventure game is a proper remaster: it preserves the original story and quirky characters, while vastly improving the audiovisuals. Witty and charming as ever; beautifully looking and sounding as never before. Not much to shiver me timbers about, but deserves a jolly yo-ho-ho and a bottle of rum.
As with many LucasArts adventure video games, I played the MS-DOS original around the turn of the century on my first home PC and it still holds a special place in my heart.
(+) the main story following the early exploits of a young pirate wannabe, Guybrush Threepwood, as he tries to prove his mettle on Mêlée Island™ and discover the eponymous secret of Monkey Island™ in a fictitious Caribbean setting
(+) a skeleton crew of unforgettable characters, with the crafty love interest Elaine Marley and the nefarious Ghost Pirate LeChuck aboard
(+) helmed by the legendary Ron Gilbert, co-written and –designed with his protégés Tim Schafer and David Grossman, loaded deck-to-deck with their unique brand of wacky hijinks and comedic dialogue
(+) the original text-only script fully voice-acted by a professional cast, including Dominic Armato as Guybrush, Alexandra Boyd as Elaine and Earl Boen as LeChuck who all voiced originally their respective characters in the later entries of the Monkey Island series (
of and
)
(+) the original heavily pixelated VGA 256-colour graphics, designed by the team under Steve Purcell, fully reimagined  with high-resolution 2D hand-drawn visuals, a lot of background details and modern effects added, preserving the original concepts and making the art direction possibly timeless
(+) the original MIDI soundtrack by Michael Land and others completely re-orchestrated and expanded to its fullest Caribbean-flavoured glory with ambient sound effects that perfectly match the pirate theme
(+) the original point-and-click controls modernized, with the verb commands assigned collectively to a separate menu and individually to hotkeys, and the inventory relegated to a separate window
(+) the original and remastered versions can be seamlessly switched back and forth at a press of a button
(+) the dialogue tree, default click actions and (almost complete) lack of failstates or dead-ends were innovative in the genre at the time, a trail-blazing example followed since to this day
(+) the puzzles are usually logically sound: the only challenge comes down to finding the required items, figuring out the right sequence or (rarely) struggling with the controls
(+) the insult-and-retort swashbuckling mechanics, reminiscent of the taunt-heavy duels between Inigo Montoya and Dread Pirate Roberts in the 1987 cult classic
or the Errol Flynn black-and-white movies, feel as fresh and creative as ever
(+) the hint system with gradually more detailed suggestions introduced in the special edition offsets the minimal degree of hand-holding for the novices of the genre
(+) perfectly playable with a mouse and keyboard, though analogue controllers are also supported
(+) English, French, German, Italian and Spanish subtitles and interface to choose from, but the audio is English only
(−) noticeably shorter than many adventure games to follow its original release
(−) the point-and-click controls with the separate menus for verb commands and inventory items are not very intuitive by today’s standards
(−) no concept art gallery nor developers’ commentary, which would be a real booty for the fans, arrr!
(−) a frequent and annoying bug wherein the menu keeps popping up when the protagonist has been left idling for too long, even during long non-interactive sequences
(−) unskippable end credits
(−) no way to change the language in-game after the initial selection screen other than manually editing the settings file
(−) the achievements added to the Xbox version are conspicuously missing on Steam

A gem of an Old Bioware game! I had no idea before I actually tried it. I have no idea any longer why I hadn't tried it and I can only wonder why it hasn't meritted more attention as an intellectual property.
The story, pacing, and other such plot elements are, to my taste, legit in comparison to other Old Bioware titles like Knights of the Old Republic and Baldur's Gates. Happily, it was one of those RPG stories I was not expecting to get caught up in and which I was memorably rapt and engaged to explore my first playthrough. Several of the side characters are memorable, the rest being amply adequate, and the romance subplots are nice enough. Appreciable world building polishes like an original language are interesting and, in my opinion, respectable artistic investments. For RPG completionists, there is to be divined (I have done so) a long enough but not too long set of missable items, etc.,  to hunt up. Certainly the character customization and development available here is nothing to Neverwinter Nights (and the same are far and away the most attractive aspects of NWN) and the martial arts dynamics are (presumably) little match for actual fighting games. But I found both highly satisfying in their simplicity. It's a sweetly elegant and intuitive simplicity, not an underwhelming simplicity, in my opinion, and to the extent that I reckon it a major asset of the design.
Overall, I've continually considered Jade Empire an unique and highly pleasant flavor to occasionally crave.

If you enjoyed the first release of Deus Ex: HR, or have been looking for a reason to pick it up, the Director's Cut is a good deal. In addition to placing the Missing Link chapter in proper continuity, it makes improvements to the boss fights and smooths out a few rough edges in the graphics. And, for those of you who already own the original game and/or the Missing Link, you get a nice discount. I like seeing companies continuing to support their games and make them better, and offering a modest bargain for those who have already purchased the game is a nice gesture.
The Director's Cut retained everything I enjoyed, beefed up the overall game, and was at least partially successful at improving the notorious boss fights. It's worth it if you feel like giving the game another run, or want to pick it up for the first time.

Let's get straight to the point. These are my first impressions as I haven't spent that much time in the game, but these are the things I noted right off the bat:
Pros-
-Runs well on  low-end systems (obviously)
-Shows lots of promise
-Great dark, post-apocalyptic atmosphere
-Tense Player-Versus-Player action
-Attentive developer who listens to the community, and seeks to improve the game.
Cons-
-(Formerly too little loot, but that has been thankfully resolved by the developer, who has upped the spawn rates of items in the 1/12/2016 patch, kudos to him.)
-Melee combat against zombies is questionable. Fighting the few ones that you find with a melee weapon is guaranteed to get yourself bitten, there is no way to avoid it. At least in similar games, such as Unturned by Nelson Saxton, it is possible to whack a zombie over the head with an axe without getting yourself chomped on before the undead thing finally dies. (I would recommend to the developer to allow the player to walk backwards a bit faster, as well as give them a longer attack reach than the zombie. Therefore, a player can engage a zombie with their rock, and possibly not get themselves bitten up in the process.
-Zombie pathfinding can be made a bit better... But I haven't really had enough encounters with them to tell whether or not that is nescesary.
Conclusion:
This game is enjoyable, and compared to other blocky zombie apocalypse survival games of it's kind, it may be lacking in content, but definitely preforms better  in terms of atmosphere as well as delivering a more delapitated, wastlandish aesthetic. I'd recommend this to anyone who has played such games before, (such as Unturned) but desires a darker, grittier experience.

Easily one of the best games of all time. I have had it for years on my Xbox 360 and played it from start to end several times. I love the ability to play your way from start to finish.
I have had files where i run around with a rifle spraying and killing everyone, files where i sneak around and beat down everyone, and files where i sneak past everyone avoiding fighting.
The two issues i had with the game where 1) the boss battles where areas where you couldn't do it your way and had to just fight them head on, and 2) after all the effort i put in to it in each file i had to start each new game from scratch so it felt like my effort was for nothing.
The directors cut fixes these issues (mostly). The boss battles have been totally revamped so that you can use a stealth approach, or a hacking approach, rather then just a head on fight. You still have to kill the bosses so a pacifist approach isn't allowed but its still great. As for the issue of having to restart from scratch, they added a New Game +. It is not a complete NG+, and only brings back your augments (Character Upgrades) but not your guns, ammo, or money, but it does make it much better as the augments are the biggest part of the game. You could go through the entire game without firing one bullet (I have several times), but it is nearly impossible to play without upgrading your augments (And impossible to do it without using any augments that you start with).
I recommend that you get this if you can afford it. I recommend that you get it if you can't. Get it no matter what. ONE OF THE BEST GAMES OF ALL TIME.

I did not know Deus Ex before i saw it on Steam. I purchased this game because it was on sale, cost only $4.99. I watch some trailers and reviews reckoned i could give it a shot. And gladly its worth the money.
For starters, this game is somewhat like Mass effect + Dishonored hybrid, assuming you know both these games. You might not agree, anyways its just my opinion. But be warned, to me this isint quite a shooter game. It's an FPS, it has got a handful of guns and you can shoot things as shown in the trailer but most of the times you'll be doing lots of stealth, hiding behind covers trying to sneak past enemies. Sounds pretty familiar? (Hitman). Well if you dont like the stealth approach, you could go gun blazing, but i dont think this is the way this game is meant to be played, especially during the first half of the story which is after llike 10+ hours of gameplay (for me) mainly because you could be easily outgunned. Of course you could jump right infront of the enemies and shoot them in the face tough later in the game prior to sufficent upgrade of your carecter.
So..... If you are looking for fast-paced shooter like COD, your wont get it. Its a slow-paced game involved lots of thinking as in how do i get past this, how do i access that, something like that. If you're in it for the story telling and RPG experience then i recommend you to grab it. The voice acting might not be fantastic but it works and it surely gave me a somewhat unique experience that not many games could offer.

"Monster Loves You!" is a fun, short game in the style of a "choose your own adventure" novel. While fun and interesting at first, this game quickly becomes repetetive and is easily completed in less than half an hour if you read fast. I've played the game about an hour or so total, and I've beaten it at least three times. Once you've beaten the game once, you can play through it again rather quickly, as many of the options are the same throughout the game and once you've read them the first time, there's no real reason to read them again. All in all, it's a fun time waster, but with limited replay value. I recommend it if you can find it on sale and want a VERY light visual novel to play around with. It's a lot of fun and there are some good humorous bits, but overall it's a pretty ordinary game.

Monster Loves You! is a casual, text based, Create-Your-Own adventure game.
You are a monster, living in a monster town. You begin as a tiny monsterling, and grow as the game progresses. Through childhood, into adulthood, and possibly even as a monster elder, you must make choices. Each choice alters your monster in some way, and lead up to several different endings based on how you choose to play. The writing is humorous at times, with you having to decide between truth or lies, fight or flight, and occasionally whether to help someone out...or just eat them and be done with it. The art style is something out of a toddler's story book, which fits surprisingly well with the game's design; and the story itself isn't very long, which makes it a great time filler.
The game is simple, easy to pick up, and family friendly. However if you don't enjoy point and click games, or the Create-Your-Own adventure style, then this probably isn't the game for you.

A good game even without the nostalgia value, although the nostalgia’s lens helps.
This is one of the very first games of its genre. I would recommend it just for the historic experience, so you can later appreciate how far we have gone and how much we owe to the first “graphic adventure” games. However, with the right mind frame you can enjoy the game by itself despite its age.
Good puzzles with a hint system. Actual puzzles, better than some of the more recent games.
Decent voice work and subtitles (always a plus if English is not your first language).
There is a certain naivety to it that I find charming.
Completed it in under seven hours.
Although the art has been updated, the engine has not. I missed having the option to double-click so Guybrush would move faster (it is available on the map view, though).
The game is more about fun and puzzles than about any historical accuracy or engaging story telling. We know nothing about Guybrush and his motivations. He simply arrives to Melee Island wishing to become a pirate and you are supposed to care about it. At some point you will find electric lights, a stapler, and a pair of wax lips. These elements can subtract some enjoyment because they are so out of place; but I prefer to take the game as the make-believe of a child so the details or the story’s logic don’t matter as much as having fun.
If you like to solve puzzles this game is a must. One of the best mind twisting adventure games ever.

Takes some getting used to, but it has a nice feel and adds some nice buttons on the grips. Being able to customize your controls is awesome and its a fairly easy system to handle. Its still not up to par with a mouse in terms of precision but that could just be me still getting used to it. And set up is insanely easy, and being able to play games from the couch is awesome. And the streaming quality is just wonderful.

Played Rocket League with the Steam Controller and it is incredible. In some cases the developers will make their own configs for you to use, and the one that Psyonix made is very good. I found it's a great replacement for the staple controllers normally used. In terms of other games where a controller is recommended, the controller is just as good as other gamepads but made even better with the ability to change "keybindings" on the controller itself. You can make the A button move forward if you want.
The support from Steam for adding features and config options are abundant but the many options can be overwhelming. I tried to play a game that heavily uses the mouse (Starbound) and I'm confident that with practice and the right configuration I could play it like a pro. FPS games are a step up from other gamepads but without practice you would be better off with a keyboard and mouse because the trackpad is better than a joystick but less precise than a mouse. Again, this is all based off how much practice you get.
Ergonomically, it hits all the marks. The "backwards" handles have a surprisingly good grip and your fingers can use all the buttons at the resting position. The trackpads are comfortable under your thumbs.  The only awkward part on the controller is the bumpers only because you need to move your fingers farther than you are used to with an Xbox controller.
ADDENDUM: Since it's release, the controller has been massively updated like the additions of action sets and new games like XCOM 2 and Dark Souls III come with native support which means that the controller is breaking ground with the mainstream and getting even more attention.
As a quick summary, it excels as a replacment for your typical controllers and can be the same for FPS and mouse heavy games with the right practice. It's heavily configureable and even if you don't know how the community has dozens of configs to pick from.

This is a casual, interactive novel, not an actual game, you play as a newly spawned monster and through your actions decide what kind of monster you will become, which also affects your reputation and how much the other monsters will respect you.
The game play consists of choice and consequence but in a lighthearted way (except towards the end if you become an  elder). There are several "quests" or choices that come up which vary with each playthrough and are specific to the life stage of your monster, and the game has multiple endings.
On the whole this is a cute, fun and at times funny game, but if you are trying to get all the endings I'd recommend leaving the game awhile inbetween each playthrough. The reason is that even though you don't always get the same quests, after awhile they do start to repeat...so after the first couple of playthroughs it gets a bit, well, repetitive .
Not only that but there is no save feature, meaning that to get every ending you have to play through the entire game each time.
Otherwise this is a quirky and enjoyable choose your own adventure and definitely worth a look, especially if you can catch it on sale.

The Good:
Cute graphics
Decently priced
Decisions affect your stats that in turn gain access to new decisions
Children-friendly
Casual
Excellent if you liked Choose Your Own Adventure books
The Bad:
Most choices don't really matter
Sometimes you will not be offered an option you like
Not for those who like intricate stories that have several endings
I recommend this game for children who enjoy fantasy and adults who like a casual storybook game.  Monster Loves You is a "choose your own adventure" version of the entire life cycle of a monster, from spawn to death or glory.  The game poses many situations you must choose from a list of options to solve, each of which usually change one or more of your stats such as bravery, cleverness, or honesty.  You also have an ongoing respect stat that affects how your monsterkind treat you and how likely they are to follow under your leadership.  As a monster you undergo many phases of life all culminating with a large conflictual theme in the end that you must resolve.
Choose your own adventure, monster-style.

!!! DEUS EX !!!
Fortunately, the massive hype surrounding 2011’s “Deus Ex: Human Revolution” was matched by an equally outstanding game. With its beautifully-realized cyberpunk world; stealth gameplay that rivaled top-shelf espionage titles; enough conspiracy theories to shake a tin foil hat at; and, best of all, its return to the “play how you want” formula that made the first game so good, “Human Revolution” was a success.

Despite its brilliance, “Human Revolution” was far from perfect, bogged down by unfairly difficult boss battles that were skewed towards specific play styles, the occasional bland texture, and sometimes wonky enemy A.I. The Updated Version of this game "Director's Cut" has solved these problems and polished the game so much more.
The main complaint of the game, to date, is its color choice while looking through Adam Jensen's augmented visor. A hew of yellow coats the screen. Acourse this can easily be solved with any one of the many many graphic mods for this game revealing it's true colors. The color choice, for me, was never an issue.
With its flowing, open approach to mission structure, thoroughly engrossing story and gorgeous visuals, this is the kind of game that all others should strive to be. While there are some elements that don't feel quite as developed as they should have been, and augmentation is more Hobson's choice than true choice, Human Revolution provides a level of quality that only the most adamant cynic could fail to be impressed by. More importantly, it is everything a fan of Deus Ex could want in a game.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who loves Si-fi worlds and rpg based games. A "Must Play" game for sure.

+ The gaming mods are really clever, sometimes you have to collect a glass bottles after you kill someone to gain points for your teams, if the bottle is stolen from you by enemy player, the points are saved for them. In some other mod you have to steal a big hammer and bring it to your base. You have one hammer in your base too and you have to defend it. The hammer is really allmighty weapon. Capture the flag mods with either three points you have to control the most time or one point spawning in random places and you have to reach it first.
What I dislike on this game:
- The costume customization could be bought only with real money, so there are only about 4 different guys running in the game. I get it is the only way how the game earns money, but it´s a little bit boring. The game could learn from Team Fortress 2 or Dota 2 where the cash is earned from the different items with different quality when some items are dropping in the game.
- The gaming mods are fun to play, but the teamwork is really necessary in all of them. So it´s fun to play with friends, but it could get really annoying playing it with other players, that for example don´t understand, that it is necessary to collect a glass bottle after enemy is killed...
- The experience from shooting is not good because the game is not a first person shooter. You can see your hero and it´s fun to see him, but by shooting it´s kinda weird.
- Sometimes you can meet on the public servers guys with a lot better weapons than you have and it could be frustrating too. If you´re reaching for Jackhammer, noone is around and suddenly you notice there is a shooting tower made by some of the enemies next to it. Simply, there is some disadvantage for new players or low-level-players in the game, but if you like the customization of guns, you just have to count with that. Reassurance yould be for you, that not every customization option brings the advantages to the gun ;)

Telltale has created something special here. They took a well-known setting, added an epic adventure on top of it and what I enjoyed most about this was that they "made you care". People think they are entitled to receive all of whats currently only available in the adventurer pass for free as they have bought the base game, but what people don't realise or appreciate enough is the quality at which these episodes are delivered. I mean, just look at the intros at the beginning of every episode... Telltale deserves to make good money off of good work and if getting another 3 episodes of this amazing gaming experience means paying another 15 bucks, then that's a win for me. Not because I love throwing out money, but because it gives people the opportunity to get extra content for a game they love and enjoy. And if people can't live with this it is also ok, everyone is entitled to their own opinion, just please don't rate this game down because you can't live with the business practices of the publisher, rate the experience you got within it.

Time and time again I had found myself getting back into the game, and then quitting for a lack of content and very repetitive XP grinding from daily quests and dungeon runs, then going back to Aura Kingfom and repeat the process. For a game made in 2012 or 2013, the game is quickly nailing itself into the coffin. Not many players occupy servers like they did a few years ago.
Pros
+ Several classes with their own playstyle from wielding a Holy Sword to casting heals with a harp to shooting a hand cannon (with the ability to build a minature turret for 30 secs).
+ You can sink hundreds of hours in this game if you're a first timer.
Cons
- Combat is repetitive. Since the game has no mana bar to cast spells, all combat is spamming skills until someone is dead.
- The campaign requires a lot of grinding. The story stops at Lv 60, restarts at Lv 62 until a certain level before you guessed right, grind more XP to continue with the main quest.
- Lag occures very frequently and it's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to deal with, especially at the log in screen when lag interferes you from imputting your PIN correctly.
- The game developers do nothing about the bots which take your quest kills, annoy you with spam mail and persuading you to buy in-game currency for real life money. They even place scamming messages in the Party Finder textbox on your HUD
- The game is massively based around Play-to-win. Need a costume? Need a new Eidolon (summoned creature)? Need a new and faster mount? Buy AP (Aeria Points) with your real life money and trade them for new gear.
- The game developers are not confident in updating their servers with new things, ways to improve gameplay or fix something that everyone in the Aura Kingdom community suffers from.
- Crafting your gear is so expensive (especially for lower levels) so begging, saving a lot of coins or buying items with AP and selling bought gear for gold is the way to get crafting done.
Verdict: 4/10

2. The controller could also use a storage slot for the small USB wireless connection.
3. Button spacing could be better designed.

Multiplayer was my favorite aspect of the few Star Fox games I've played, and Super Sky Arena captures and tweaks the concept extremely well. The maps are tight, but not crowded; the gameplay fast, but not too difficult for new players pick up and have fun. There are ample options to outwit your opponent and various pickup items that require skill to deploy.
It's still in early access as of this writing, but it's very polished. I've never seen a glitch or crash mid-game. The maps are varied and contain obstacles and designs that give strategic advantages to skilled fliers. The characters have fun little voices that announce things based on who's winning the match. Very little about it feels unfinished or unbalanced for casual play.
If you're looking for a great local/online multiplayer game, it's definitely worth the buy--despite the Early Access state it's been in for a rather extended period of time (as of this review).

Jade Empire is like your second playthrough of Knighs of the Old Republic, where you purposefully make all the bad choices just to be 100% evil, except they did it with design choices instead, and the result was a game that is 100% poop.
------------------------------ORIGINAL REVIEW:
I was really excited to play this game, since it gets unreal praise from everyone.  Too bad it's terrible.
Combat:  This game has the most unintuitive, unengaging, clunky, button-mashing-dependant, wtf-was-that-unfair combat system I've ever seen in any game.  The combat system is built for 1-on-1 fights, but the game constantly pits you against 6 people at once, some of which will invariably be wielding weapons.  Since there are no area or sweeping attacks, and you're forced to damage one enemy at a time, this means you'll get surrouncded and stun-locked to death.  Oh, and wielding weapons depletes your "Focus" bar - when it gets empty, you are restricted from using weapons, a limit not placed on your enemies.
Dodging: In the game options, you can change the dodge controls - you can have your character dodge when you double tap in a direction, or when you move in a direction while holding down "Block".  Choosing double-tap means your character will dodge forward whenever you change directions mid-run outside of combat - only forward, though, that's the only direction you're allowed to doge in outside of combat.  Needless to say, this gets very aggravating very quickly.
Camera:  All the game's problems are exacerbated by the game's camera, which hovers right behind your character, but low enough that you can't see your hands.  This basically makes it impossible to judge how far away you are from an enemy, and whether you're close enough for your attack to hit.  It's a crap-shoot.  Easily fixable if you could angle the camera to one side, but it resets right away.
Maybe it's a bad port to PC, and that's the reason for all these problems?  I can't belive this game came out 2 years after KOTOR, which had none of the issues above.  I can count on one hand how many games I've willingly abandoned, and now Jade Empire is part of that list, right next to Fable 3.  Maybe the story becomes AMAZING a few more hours in, but this game is absolute agony to play through - not worth it to me.

Jade Empire is a solid BioWare adventure game with an enjoyable world and storyline, complemented by a frustrating combat system and stripped-down RPG mechanics. It probably won’t be your favourite action game of all time, but you definitely won’t regret playing it.
Jade Empire was created between the releases of two highly successful titles, which later overshadowed its existence, although not without reasons. At its core Jade Empire is nothing more than an attempt to recreate the success of Knights of the Old Republic with a new world based on a highly fictional version of early Imperial China. For the most part, it works well… just don’t expect much historical accuracy, especially on the shoot-em-up stages against the ancient Chinese Luftwaffe. Yes, you read this correctly.
An RPG usually is as good as its story, and the game won’t let you down in this regard. The plot is solid with a few good twists, the characters are memorable enough, and the mandatory romance subplot doesn’t feel as forced as in most games. But it’s hard not to notice that most quests are recycled from KotOR and Neverwinter Nights.
So, why is Jade Empire so obscure and forgotten? For two reasons. The first is the lack of actual role-playing elements, and the second being the combat system.
This was the first title where BioWare tried real-time player-controled action instead of random-based mechanics, and it’s not working too well. Fighting is just mindless button mashing and the hit detection is beyond horrendous; using hand-to-hand styles almost equals a death sentence. As you can imagine, this creates
issues in a Kung Fu game.
Still, Jade Empire is a solid title, and highly recommended for those who like BioWare’s KotOR era. Set the difficulty to easy or medium to avoid the frustration over the combat system, and enjoy this little piece of uniqueness.

A link between Knights of the Old Republic and Mass Effect. A rather simple and quick ARPG, Jade Emprie satisfies mainly on its story and setting. The fighting system is very run-of-the-mill button mashing, and the skill system is not very interesting. However, for fans of BioWare and RPGs, there is enough here to satisfy.

I volunteer at animal shelters and I've done some work at vetrinary clinics, and the simple exposition style effectively brings to mind images of actual suffering I've seen.
(Minor spoilers)
There are several instances of unavoidable cat murder and abuse. I've got a bleeding heart, and I know it, but It was hard to enjoy the story knowing that just one decision ago I had broke a window with a live kitten, or that I had torn a live cat (which had been mewling and purring just a dialog ago) in half to appease two of my monster friends.

So... this game.
Do I recommend it?
Short answer: Oh heck no. Don't buy it, it's not worth the 23€. Or even the 38€ for the DLC and the game itself.
Now, where shall I start...
This game, first of all, the subtitles often don't match the stuff that is really said. I understand english well enough, so I don't need them, but the german subtitles often look like they were made with Google Translate.
Also, the camera position and the controls are not really great. Especially the moving of the cursor in the quicktime events is really bad, and it's really hard to hit the targets with the xBox 360 controller. But the quicktime events with the keyboard and mouse work kinda well.
Another thing are the puzzles. They are so easy, everybody can solve them in three seconds. I know this game was made for younger people in the first place, but maybe then the difficulty should be adjustable or something.
One of my biggest issues with this game, is the lack of time you play it. I have not bought or played the DLC, and I needed around 5 hours for the first 5 episodes. In my opinion, 23€ for 5 hours is way too much. Like, WAY too much.
Take The Witcher 3 as an example. You pay 50€ for like 200 hours of gameplay. You pay 30€ for DLC of another 200 hours. Telltale, please, take an example from those guys.
To the story:
The descisions don't feel like they do ANY impact, other than a few lines of dialouge. Yes, there are those that do a big impact, like what character you save or so (I hope this did not really spoil anything.), but those are the only ones that do any impact.
The characters aren't really interresting, and full of clichés.
You have the kinda shy guy that gets pushed into the role of the hero, you have the smart girl, and you have the ignorant big guy with strength.
Are there any good points to this game?
Umm.. the music is pretty nice and the artstyle fits Minecraft. And that was it.
Don't buy this game.
Go buy the real Minecraft.
You're gonna have way more fun with that one.
Thanks for reading this, and thanks for understanding that this is my opinion, and you may find that this game is great. I don't. But if you think so, hey, I'm cool with that.

In this game, you can shoot a dinosaur in the face until it dies; the death animation being ragdolling to the ground like this is an indie browser shooter. And on the other end of the coin, you can grab a human in your dino jowls and watch it's character model struggle to stay in sync with the mouth, hilariously.
This isn't a hate-review, I really enjoyed this game. The graphical quality of the game is absolutely breathtaking; assuming you've got the specs for it. I know this is the norm for every UE game, but it's always a plus to have environments of such quality. The concept is good, I loved the idea of being able to deathmatch as a dinosaur or human; and it wasn't tedious or boring to switch between the two. The classes were enjoyable despite not being very broad (though honestly to be expected.) Each of them look and play very well. But I DO wish there was a sort of skill bar that reflected your kills; like I don't know, maybe a raptor could have more varied attacks on a bar rather than flailing it's arms and jaw around like a short-bus dinosaur.
The gameplay is genuinely fun, the maps are small, obviously; but still an adventure to go through. The game is exciting to play and addictive in my experience. The dinos look good, the humans look generic but that's to be expected... The skins are not that exciting or worthwhile at all, but that doesn't really matter to me.
One complaint I see on other reviews are the lack of balance in classes, and when you have a game that's animals vs humans that's supposed to be pretty obvious. In these kinds of games, there's COUNTLESS human characters. People obviously want to be dinos more; and now they have that opportunity. I don't think there's much you can do about that balance without using dictation.
Overall, I found this game a good way to spend time; and a fun and addicitve way. I would reccomend it to people looking for something new to play. Because, yeah... you can be a ♥♥♥♥ing dinosaur!

Jade Empire is without a doubt a very good game. It stands, however, very firmly, as a mid-point between Bioware's other landmark titles: Knights of the Old Republic and Mass Effect. It is very recognisable as a spiritual successor to the gameplay style of Knights of the Old Republic. On the other hand, you can see much that would go into Mass Effect being developed in Jade Empire. It says more than anything about Jade Empire that I could not write a paragraph in review without mentioning Bioware's other two excellent titles.
The characters and their development, the storyline, and quite frankly the world developed around them, simply doesn't live up to the heights generated by the other series mentioned herein. It perhaps helps with immersion that I was a Star Wars fan prior to playing Knights of the Old Republic; but Mass Effect's dramatic introduction of an entirely new universe was simply amazing and Jade Empire achieves nothing of the sort. It is a nice world, more densely populated than Knights of the Old Republic which makes it feel more immersive. But unfortunately it just does not stand out. It is not particularly memorable, and there is virtually no reason at all for the game to be open-world (when it does open up). If you are thorough, there is literally no reason to return to places you have visited in the past in Jade Empire, and that is rather unfortunate.
It is an aging game, so the graphics look a little dated at this point but you can still see that for their time they were quite pretty and it does not in any way impact the enjoyability of this title. The gameplay is also quite interesting, very fast-paced and there are a really wonderful array of fighting-styles that your character can learn. Slightly unfortunate, however, is the loss of the ability to play as other characters at will, which was a welcome feature included in Knights of the Old Republic.
All in all, this game is definitely worth looking into, especially for fans of Bioware's other excellent RPG titles. I have been rather critical in this review but it is only because Bioware has soared so much higher in other outings and with so much potential it is rather unfortunate that Jade Empire failed to achieve these expectations. Nonetheless, I still consider it one of the better RPG games I have played and would recommend giving it a shot. 8/10.

:MAY INCLUDE SPOILERS:
This game is very unique. The art and soundtrack are charming, the story is intriguing, and it's very replayable. There isn't really much for gameplay, being that the game is mostly decision making, which is by no means a bad thing. It'll take you at least a while to get all the endings, and even then there is just a bunch of different things that can happen. The writing is very humorous and clever, and the whole style of the game is charming.
There are 5 different stages in this game: Morsel, Kid, Adolescent, Adult, and then Elder. Each of them have some differences. The 1st stage is very short, and will also determine a large part of what happens later in the game. The second stage doesn't have any major twists, although your traits (kindness, cleverness, honesty, etc.) will develop much more rapidly, which makes this a good chance to get a headstart on what traits you want more of. The third stage is much like the previous, but the story is more open, because you aren't in the brood cave the whole time like you were in the second stage. This stage takes a few more days and you become a little bit less impressionable, as well as it being much more likely to lose parts of your traits as well as gain them. There is a few chances of respect being earned in this stage, but it will not be majorly used until adulthood and elder. Similar to the other stages, the fourth stage takes the longer than any of the other ones. This stage is more free because you can decide whether to socialize with other monsters, or go out and adventure. During this stage you will be much less impressionable, and your traits will probably stay mostly the same. You will also rack up respect. Respect is very important as in most cases, it will determine your fate. Once adulthood is over, you will start to realize that your life is coming to an end and you have to make a few decisions, if you want to try to live, if you will dissolve, if you will ascend, etc. Once you go back to the spawning vat you will be confronted by elders. You can dissolve, or try to ascend into an elder. This part is kind of complicated, so I'll just sum it up. If you dissolve you will end your game right there, but if you try to become an elder you will have a chance to be tested. If you fail the test or dissolve, you will dissolve, but if you complete the test you will move onto being an elder. Once you become an elder, it's up to you to determine whether to fight the humans, make peace, etc. (Or become a neurosurgen.) This stage is probably the most unique for a few reasons. It adds two new factors, Humans opinion on monsters and vice versa. By the end of the stage the percentages and a few last decisions will determine how the game ends. Besides that, most decisions will require a trait. So you will have a better chance to complete something that requires more ferocity if you have 90% compared to 30%, adding a more rpgish aspect into the game, making the elder stage even more interesting.
Sorry if this was more a guide than it was a review, but I hope it helps. This game is great, and I really love a lot about it. Of course there are downsides to a few things, like not as much character establishment, and things like that. Another thing about the game is that the story is VERY open-ended, almost everything is determined through your choices, which might explain why there's not as much character development. Other then that, this is a very unique concept and was very well executed. The game is charming, funny, replayable, and even at some times heartwrenching. And I would love to see a sequel to this game, because it really deserves it. It's definitely worth the money, so buy it and give it a try.

The nice thing about Monster Loves You! is that it's not for you as a seasoned gamer, but for your children (with or without your help).
You start your journey in a pool of goo, and from that slimy craddle to your comfy grave, you're confronted to numerous adventurous situations, in which you'll have to decide how you will react. Depending on your choices (presented as text options) you'll progress into branched mini-stories, receiving or losing points in a serie of traits like Bravery, Cleverness, Cruelty, Kindness and so forth.
From an adult perspective, the game might seem unchallenging and you'll really enjoy the last part, dedicated to politics and community management. But from a child perspective, the game offers alot of behaviors to explore, and to learn that choices have consequences - both in short and long term. And it's possible to be really really mean too - you're a monster after all and nobody will punish you for that.
The art is cartoony and childish (of course), and the langage proper to the young audience. Even if the total play time for a character's life is short (about an hour), it's possible to come back once in a while to have fun guiding another creature in the path you've chosen.

Ok, ok, 'The Secret of Monkey Island' is one of the best adventure games of all times. But I have to give a negative review anyway. Why? Because this special edition seems to be only a sloppy modernisation to generate a quick buck riding on the famous name.
The modern graphics are decent and the English voiceover is of decent quality too. Problem is, the voiceover is only in
English. I wanted to play this with my kids, which don't understand English and also can't read yet.
Alas, that would not be a reason to write a negative review. But the interface is just horrible. You can't play with just the mouse. The remake of the game with the revolutionary mouse only SCUMM system, won't give you access to the inventory without the keyboard. That is insane. Also, for most advanced interactions you have to slowly scroll through 9 unintuive icons (come on, a steering wheel for 'use'?) with the mouse wheel, before you find the one you need (or use the keyboard again). Main menu navigation also relies on keyboard for going back from submenus.

I also had problems with an apparently missing mouse cursor graphic (mostly during dialog), which resulted in clicks not registering where the mouse cursor was pointing at.
TL. DR.: All in all not recommended because the user interface makes this really great game almost unplayable.

The next installment of the Red Orchestra/Rising Storm series! A realistic shooter similar to its predecessor, it still uses the dated Unreal Engine 3, but it seeks to impress the audience with new dazzling graphics and the
inducing experiences of the Vietnam War.
Cons:
- Repetitive game play (Play relatively same 3 maps because thats what people vote for)
- No multiplayer campaign map mode (As Red Orchestra 2 has)
- No incentive for teamwork (Players run off solo and do whatever they want, getting kills for a higher score is all that matters to them)
- Few custom map servers (Plenty of custom maps, but only some servers employ any at all)
- Removed cover system/shooting blindly from behind cover (As in Red Orchestra 2)
- Removed bots from multiplayer (Good because now you know your playing against human players, bad for low pop servers)
- Cannot use joystick to fly helicopters (You need 3rd party software like JoyToKey to avoid using mouse & keyboard)
- No TrackIr or VR support (Use your mouse to turn your head when flying)
- No server queue (You need to use Steam server browser queue or spam the connect button on full servers)
- SDK is buggy/unstable and frequently crashes
Pros:
+ Added Helicopters (With a fair damage model)
+ Added Character customizations (Not everyone is identical)
+ No weapon unlocks (Leveling up is purely for prestige/cosmetic purposes, all weapons come unlocked at lvl 1)
+ Slightly upgraded graphics and uses Wwise sound engine now
+ Added new squad system (Squad leader is no longer a class role, anyone can take it)
+ 3D proximity voice chat (Good for talking to someone near you, also used for micspamming)
+ Wide variety of weapons/variants/attachments (Bayonets, Folding stocks, traps/mines/grenades)
+ Variety of call-in support abilities (Napalm strike, Canberra bomber, Artillery, Ambush Respawn)
+ Vietnamese can use existing in-map underground tunnels and climb up certain obstacles
(nit picking)
- Still uses Unreal Engine 3 in 2017
- Several game crashing bugs
- Characters speak loudly when near the enemy (Detrimental when trying to remain hidden)
- Dead bodies despawn in 5 seconds
- Minimal gore (Not as frequent as Red Orchestra 2 dismemberment/blood)
- No singleplayer
- Idle players are not auto-kicked (Server specific issue, but people can idle and take up player slots without anyone noticing (even in spectator mode))
- No other drivable vehicles besides Helicopters (No APC's, Tanks, or Patrol boats)
- 64 players max per server
- Rare, but hacks are
.
+ Can zero weapon sights (Rarely do you use this except for the RPG)
+ Can use bi-pods and surfaces to stabilize your weapon
+ SDK for creating custom content (maps/mods)
+ Realistic load-outs
+ Developer created tutorial
+ Can spot targets manually
+ Can shoot through certain materials
+ Freeplay mode (Shooting range to test weapons and learn to fly helicopters)
+ Can vote for maps
+ First person game-play only

Though I only have a few hours in the PC version thus far, I played this game twice back to back on the PS4 around release and since then it has become my favorite game of all time. Yoko Taro is an absolute madman and takes you on a ride full of action, tragedy, and lots of dead machines. I'll avoid spoilers by just saying that the story of this game is beautifully told and executed. If you're used to any of Taro's other works you know what you're getting into, if not then strap in and get ready for a wild ride. The gameplay is fairly typical Platinum fare so if you like slashing up huge groups of baddies then you're gonna feel right at home. I might add that it is quite satisfying to watch some of the move executions and crazy attacks that you can do with the various weapons in the game.
Music and sound design is the other part of the game that really stands out. Keiichi Okabe and his studio, Monaca, have been working with Taro for quite some time now. Nier's soundtrack was incredibly composed and made such a huge impact in game at many points throughout the story. Automata is very much like this. There's so many techniques and influences throughout the OST that really make it feel like it is interwoven with the story and gameplay seamlessly. I'm infinitely impressed at how well all the elements meld together to create the masterpiece that is this glorious game.
On a side note, I haven't noticed many issues for this port in the hours that I've played. There was a tad of studder at first but after turning off AA and keeping ambient occlusion on it runs perfectly on my rig. A patch would be very much appreciated though

Sure it may look weird, Fells different. But i like the approach Valve took to this. It's aweosme when you try it, trust me I know what you're probably thinking about this controller. I thought the same until I tried it.
So the Layout is quite simple.
It comes with the classical D-pad on the left of the controller, D-pad Works great for me, No problems yet. It feels good and is very easy to use.
Then comes the new circle thing. I call it the swipe pad. In a game I found out you litteraly swipe the pad and the game changes it camera towards the direction you swiped in. It is failr simple to use and really great for FPS Games.
Then their's the bumpers and triggers you're familiar with. (If you tried ps and xbox, if not, well I don't know if you're familiar with it)
Then the analog stick comes to move the video game characters. Fairly staright foward and simple, and really easy to use.
It has the same deafult button layout as Xbox and Nintendo. ABXY, Located rigt under neath the Swipe pad. Depending on the game you're going to get different controls with it. If you're smart you'd know that. If you didn't know that well ta da, now you do. Really smooth design and I like it.
Then it has the star menus, The Steam logo button gets you back to steam, sorta like SHIFT-TAB In Game. Farily wuick to do if you're looking for a guide or ect... The one pointing to the left does something while the does somethiong as well, depending on the game you use it's different.
It then has a smooth design to it whilst being unique and cool. Overall the controller looks and functions well. I have not had a single problem with it.
The Steam controllers also makes it much easier for me to play my games. It is waaaaaaaaaaaay easier to play the controller than a keyboard in Oulat, Lego Worlds ect...
Overall I highly reccomend.

This game needs a lot of work, there are optimisation issues all over the place, You will need quite a beefy computer just to play this at a stable framerate, it's more taxing than it should be.
I've only had the game crash once but I've had tons and tons of issues ingame, I've had specific dialogue become muted such as my own characters voice, with everyone else and all other audio playing fine, I've had all audio cut out for 30+ seconds as well.
I've also experienced a lot of very delayed pop in on textures, models and various other aspects of the game world, at one time the game wouldn't load in a part of the map I was in for a good minute, just showing a very low texture placeholder.
Cutscenes have bugged out on me on several occasions forcing me to skip them and refer to elsewhere (youtube etc) to view them instead because I missed a fair bit of the ending.
My game would also hang in place for usually over a minute at a time, this would always fix itself eventually but took me entirely out of the game, this happened at least a dozen times in my playthrough - sometimes minimising fixed this but it also made steam freeze until it sorted itself out.
One of the bosses completely bugged physics wise on me and was jittering all over the place, I recorded this because it was so bizarre to me:

Visual spoilers for seeing a boss fight but no characters/plot elements are shown in the video.
I have beaten the story of the game and when it worked I did have fun, I honestly enjoyed off the record more but the various glitches I've experienced have certainly tainted my view of this game.
Glitches aside, the game is a fun continuation of dead rising with plenty to do and explore, various gameplay changes have been made arguably some better than others, for example being able to choose what to spend your level ups on is a very welcome change to me but the books have been reduced in amount and effect, limiting you to only having one stat boosting book on you at a time (until you hit level 50 and get an appropriate skill to enable all but there are still only 9 books)
Weapons are fun to find and make, some combos seem much more useful than others for example the freedom bear now has about 6 or more variations to it which are all seperate combo blueprints which I only used once then went back to combining scythes and katanas because that was a better use of my time in almost every way, some weapons certainly outshine others balance wise, you'll find one you love and then keep making more or spawning a ton from a safe house weapon locker which is also a thing, you can now spawn in any weapon you've ever picked up at least once from any safe house locker which feels too easy.
while still regarding difficulty the game introduces "nightmare mode" or rather it made easy mode then called the regular dead rising experience nightmare mode, nightmare is the difficulty players of previous games will be more used to while this games "normal" difficulty is made easier in several ways, my first play on normal I found myself just tanking most damage from bosses as we dps raced for a minute, it didn't feel like there was any threat and I beat the game with no deaths. If you're a fan of dead rising games I would suggest just jumping into nightmare right away and ignoring that normal even exists.
Another change I found odd was the survivors, you'll find random survivors in the open world usually with the objective "clear the zombies around X survivor" and upon doing so they thank you then run behind a corner to disappear, again with most actual side missions you get calls for there is almost no escorting, instead you are mostly given fetch quests for bizarre reasons such as "I lost my tarot cards, please find all 5 scattered around the town and then ill come with you" it feels like busywork, making the game feel longer than it actually is, again half of these will run off and some will become followers which you can summon but the AI isn't fantastic, they sometimes have trouble pathfinding and there didnt seem to be a way to tell them to go to the safe house unless you got in a car without them and left them behind.
In earlier dead rising games you had to do the story when it was available, as is the case in DR1 with: "The next case will be available at 5pm" etc, here however you have one big time limit to do the whole thing, in normal mode it felt very generous as I was barely over half my alloted time when I was finished and as far as I know I only missed one side mission when I got to the point of no return in the story.
There is no infinite mode or free roam but you can exploit a section in the final level to get infinite time, look this up yourself as it may contain story related spoilers. You can however replay any story chapter you like but not everything is saved, you keep stats, kills, weapons etc, but all safehouses will need to be cleared again and doors unlocked from side missions will be locked again making it difficult to get all the collectibles if going for 100% as you will need to do the side mission again for that area to be available.
my specs for reference:
Windows 7 64bit, AMD FX-8350 CPU, 16gb DDR3 RAM 800mhz, two 2gb geforce GTX 760's
FINAL WORD:
If the game worked at a better standard with less glitches and better optimisation, I would recommend it but as it stands I cannot, I'd advise against buying unless significant patching has been done since this review, but as always your mileage on the glitches will vary, you may have less/more/none of the issues I had, buy at your own risk.
