Foreword: For those saying this game crashes for everyone, this game does not crash for me. For me it runs fine. I am not sure what issue most people are having but I am here to say the game works for me. Worst problems I had: frame stuttering/drops (mainly when there are thousands of zombies on screen). Put over 30-40 hours into the game so far and I have not had 1 single crash. I have even streamed the game and used background programs running which would increase CPU usage. I already played through it and beat the game, got S ending and am already level 50! Would recommend to all Dead Rising fans.
Gameplay review: Gameplay is standard Dead Rising fare. They have improved on the movement, animations, driving, crafting, skillsets and almost everything else in the game. Graphics seem to be a slight improvement as well. Some of the main differences between the past two DR games, some survivors are saved by you and then leave the area to go on their own. The survivor mechanic is also changed, whereas the first two games you would save people and take them back to a safe zone, this one you save people and they join your team, either staying till they die or they are dismissed back to your safehouse. The game is also more openworld than the last two games, the first game being in a mall and the second being in a Las Vegas type strip. Dead Rising 3 is in an open city where you can drive around and travel from area to area (i.e. downtown, down by a marina area, the industrial area, the hills where people live in mansions and, and more). The zombie count has also been significantly increased, there are many more zombies in the game than the first two. It was easy to get 10,000 zombie kills within a weekend of playing the game. The new fighting moves are awesome, and you now have special kills with most all weapons, for example running up and cutting a zombies head off with a big knife, or sticking a chainsaw attached to an AA-12 shotgun into a zombie, revving the chainsaw and then blasting them to bits with the auto-shotgun. Moves like that are pretty cool. The minibosses are still there, and the overall feel feels the same. There is also a twist at the ending which is pretty cool. Overall I'd say this is a hit for Dead Rising fans.
Bottom line: If you like Dead Rising, get this! It rocks. Make sure you got a good PC too. If you aren't a Dead Rising fan, or not a fan of Capcom, or if you don't have a good PC and/or aren't well-versed with tinkering on your PC to get the game to work, or you refuse to contact Capcom for support if your game doesn't work, I would not recommend this game for you. The game does seem to suffer some minor technical issues, but the 30 framerate cap can be easily overridden with a text file created in the games main directory, and I have not been suffering the crashing problems that many others seem to be suffering.
Everyone else though, I would recommend!

Hey there all. First off, I've had my experience with Starfox games since I was 4 with Starfox64 being my first, to playing all others eventually including the unreleased Starfox 2(snes). With this game being multiplayer focused, I was at utmost happy with a game like this coming into existence. I've played multiplayer modes of all starfox games as well with friends over the years and had a blast playing them all(with the probable exception of SF64's multiplayer which SF64 3D improved on).
Onto Game Review
(Based off playing some local multiplayer with friends, playing with devs online, and playing with a couple friends online)
~Controller functionality~
I like the responsiveness on controls. Quickly pointing out however that the game at its current state does not have button mapping nor have support for D-Input controllers either it seems, only for X-input controllers at the moment. I'm sure this is something that will be dealt with in a future update.
~Gameplay customization~
Something I'm really glad was implemented that seems to be extending to what SF Assault and SF64 3D offered as far as game customization. It makes you feel like your setting up a game of Smash in your own way.
Time, Lives, and Points. These are your gamemode options very identical to how SF Assault had those choices. Your able to also choose if the dual lasers item should be a thing or not on the map(thank you) as well as choosing how items are on the map as well.
~Gameplay Balance~(in current version when this was written, may or may not be addressed in the future)
Lasers: My immediate beef with this is the weird recoil it causes that slows you down for that brief moment you shoot, it's not something I was as comfortable dealing with as the other SF games didn't have this kinda behavior with the lasers. Damage seems perfectly fair enough but what discourages me(and a couple of my friends) from optimally using the laser over the charge shot is that it's not as accurate enough and it doesn't have that rapid behavior that SF64(3D) and SF Assault did.
Charge shot laser: This one is kinda funny to talk about. It's balanced, just not in the most normal way. This shot can literally go through walls and ground which can be abused. What does hold it back however is that it takes so long to charge compared to other SF games. Speaking of which, I visually get thrown off by thinking my laser is fully charged with the reticle changing right as you begin charging as opposed to it changing right as it becomes charged similar to how it does in SF64(3D) and Assault. Another issue is if you make a collision that would otherwise bounce you to the side or backwards with or without being stunned, the charge goes away, which is normally acceptable, except that idea that you'd generally still be holding the laser button while having done so, in result it doesn't actually restart the charge even if you are still holding the button after collision.
~Mobility~
I once again have mixed feelings about this one. Going into a complete stop with your ship is something foreign to the other SF game's arwings with the only pseudo exception being the Arwing in SF Assault which using the "Brakes" allows for a close to halted movement, which however was limited by a meter. In this game you can basically just sit still if you wanted to with your ship which kinda worries me cause there were sometimes where I purposely abused this to achieve some kills, in thus can promote a campy play style. I don't dislike the idea of having ships go into a complete stop, but in my opinion I feel like there should be a carry off to this to avoid benefiting from camping.
Speed: I know there are pickups that allow you to go faster, but at default I feel the ships movement speed doesn't feel as natural without having to constantly use the infinite amount of boost you have which I feel right now is the only ideal way to even move to begin with.
Barrel Roll: They don't reflect laser bullets :v ... but that aside, I did like what they did with it essentially being a strafe tool.
Looping: Something interesting they did with this one. Going for a U-turn or a Somersault? Same button. When you press it, it starts to curve you upward in a loop, manually pressing it again in the middle of it will cancel the loop phase, meaning you can use it to create a U-Turn maneuver or you can cancel it immediately if you feel it seems like a bad idea. It's really flexible and it was something I didn't even expect to think about when it comes to a SF like game. My only issue is that it doesn't feel as fast as SF64(3D)'s somersaults, the difference is kinda little but with the amount of SF64(3D) I played and it's multiplayers, I really feel the frames matter.
~Visuals~
Pretty...
Um maybe with the exception of Molten Core which was sometimes hard to see where you were going in the caverns, I don't think the lighting was very friendly with that and it was something that was talked about me and my friends.
Otherwise the use of color is very different compared to the SF games though I do feel like it's going for a more brighter and colorful SNES(referring to SF and SF2) style. The idea is really neat.
~Online~
Having playing with the devs online with their location being in Europe with me located in the West Coast of the US, and pinging at around 130-160. The game is surprisingly still playable with some hiccups of here and there telling the game where a player is really at sometimes, but it's not as irritating as I'd come to expect of oversea online play.
Currently the only way of playing online is either joining or hosting a server in a form of server codes loaded as symbols(e.g. Volcano-Moon-Tree) along with choosing a region. So basically it's either find some friends you know to play with or play the guessing game. I would assume this will change in the future.
[POSSIBLE BUG]: when a friend of mine and I were doing 1v1s, whoever hosted had won in a game, it would cause the client player to not load the countdown at all for the next time a game was loaded and also not showing up as a player on the left side of the screen to the host either, while leaving the other player awkwardly free roaming. In result we would have to restart the server room when this happens
~Local multiplayer~
It works :v
only thing that bugs me is that it's a forced 4 screen split even if you are playing with 2 or 3 players.
~Conclusion~
I'm having fun so far. I have hopes for this game seeing a future and if the devs are reading this, thanks for having me play with you guys. :)
p.s. (add more competitive options in the future maybe? :3 )

For any newcomers interested in this title, unless you're willing to take a chance and have some decent PC skills, try and give it a shot, but only if the game is dirt cheap on sale. For everyone else, I've been told the GOG version of Jade Empire runs fine without any problems, so you may want to check them out instead. Steam really needs to pay more attention to the games it offers its customers.

Those with a taste for Wuxia film will enjoy the authenticity of kicking martial butt through BioWare's rich world of (mostly) traditional Chinese fantasy, but this title is not without it's fair share of problems.
Nearly a decade after first release, it would be unrealistic to expect Jade Empire to represent the pinnacle of modern gaming experience; but if you get past the idea that 2005 brought only the meteoric rise of WoW - and a sequel to Battlefield - there is still plenty of entertainment to be had.
For the most part, bags of kung-pow action, offbeat one-liners and a colourful cast including John Cleese (yes, that John Cleese) distract from the game's more serious shortcomings; and although far from perfect, the story is strong enough to carry you most of the way with tongue planted firmly in cheek.
Combat is the clear focus for much of the title, and while hardcore gamers will probably be disappointed at the simplicity of A-buttoning your opponent(s) to a meaty pulp, there are a number of different fighting styles to switch between that help to keep the beatings somewhat fresh.
Taking nothing away from many other reviewers who could not get this title to run at all, somewhat surprisingly, Jade Empire fired up first time on my own modest system (Win7, 32 bit). Aside from one story-halting bug about half way through - fixed with a simple patch in my case - the title ran without hitch. Judging by other reviews however, I'd be wary of purchasing this title for a Windows 8 system.
Despite the age of this title, the occasional bug, and it's clunky, badly dated interface, I'd still recommend this to those with a love of Wuxia, or just looking for something a little different.

Of all the amazing RPG's that BioWare has made over its many many years, Jade Empire is the weakest entry. That is not to speak of it negatively, however, as it still possesses an engaging story with a creative mythos to play with. Gameplay is pretty mediocre, and the characters are not as memorable this time around. Yet still, the game will probably keep the hardcore RPG fan entertained long enough to complete its 20-30 hour experience. Not recommended to most gamers.

I played The Secret of Monkey Island as a kid on windows 98. If you have any interest in point and click adventure games from the 90s, this is a must have to your collection.
I would highly suggest anyone playing it for the first time to play it in it's original pixelated state. It has a lot of charm to it and the visuals are more 'realistic' than the cartoony modern day graphics. For the time, this was one of the easier games. The built-in tip system is too much of a tease for me and i have a hard time with it when it's so accessible.
In my humble opinion, the internet killed the adventure game series, along with advances in technology. Back in the 90s, it was more viable to make adventure games because there weren't very good alternatives.
Nowadays, you can just google the answer to a puzzle in the game and there are (for the average person) more engaging games out there. but the charm, humour and style of this game still entertains me to this day.
Not a lot of replay value, beyond nostalgia, for me. Once you've beat the game, that's it. Some of the puzzles can be more tedious that entertaining, as well.
But it's definitely worth picking up if you've never had the chance to play it before.

The Secret of Monkey Island is one of the best point and click adventure games ever made. In fact, I've found myself replaying this game along with Monkey Island 2 (which is even better in my opinion) many times, which is something I don't usually do with point and click adventures. A huge point of contention for this re-mastered version of the game was the visual overhaul; let me say that I have never understood this criticism as the vibrantly colorful and cartoonish visuals seem to fit the mood of the game perfectly, and are reminiscent of the also excellent Curse of Monkey Island. Speaking of which, the voice actors from that game make a return here, and they bring life to the characters in such a way that I can't imagine anyone else doing their voices. The music has similarly been updated, and it is nothing short of spectacular; hearing the main theme of the game in such high quality is a dream come true for fans of this series, and the rest of the tracks are equally beautiful. Now, as for the puzzles...most do make fairly logical sense if you can see how things might make sense given the context of the game, but there are several genuine head-scratchers that might have you screaming "moon logic!" Stick with it and don't give up though, this is a game that everyone should play just for the experience. This game, along with the next two games in the series, is nothing short of a work of art, and you owe it to yourself to see if it can mean as much to you as it does to some many other people.

The gyroscope feature of this controller makes it perfect for first person or 3rd person shooter type games.  When I first got the controller, I was disappointed with how difficult it was to aim with the trackpad - a track pad can never be as articulate to aim with compared to a mouse.  I recently found a video from a Valve developer demonstrating how to combine the gyroscope feature with the track pad to aim in FPS/TPS games and after tweaking the sensitivity and acceleration of both track pad and gyroscope I was amazed.  Aiming with the gyroscope feels second nature and took no practice at all to get dead on accurate with.  Its important to adjust the sensitivity and acceleration until you find settings that work for you.  This part can feel frustrating but stick with it.
For competitive FPS gaming, I feel that the mouse will still reigh supreme though with lots of practice on the steam controller it could work.  I mostly play single-player games and this works perfectly.  Sharing some tips below that worked for me:
* Track pad mode - mouse
* Track pad sensitivity - around 50% or more
* Track pad acceleration - Low
* Track pad track ball mode enabled with Medium friction
* Gyroscope mode - mouse
* Gyrosocope sensitivity - around 30%
* Gyroscope acceleration - Disabled
* Gyroscope track ball mode disabled
* In-game sensitivity (X and Y axis) - this is game dependent and the guidance is to set it as low as possible (I'd say around 10-20% for games I've tried like hitman absolution and MGS5)
Valve have truly innovated here and after decades of PC gaming we can finally play games twitchy FPS games from the couch.

Dead Rising 3 is a departure from the other games, but one that I actually ended up enjoying more in many ways. Full disclosure before we begin. I always enjoyed the Dead Rising series in concept, but struggled with some of the gameplay systems. I think the second hit it off with me far better that the first, but the interesting things about the game for me were unpolished, and the parts that frustrated me were a focal point. Extremely difficult boss battles, cool weapons being very restricted, no mode that wasn’t time restricted to let me mess around in the world, and the game feeling like it was always encouraging me to grind and restart rather than just play through - all problems I had while playing. I think the timer was the bit that I did understand though. It was what the game was all about, and not just a tacked on idea. I just wished I could run around in the world and explore freely without the restrictions. There was always a strange innate anxiety that I wanted a break from while playing the game.
Dead Rising 3 making the decision to essentially cut the player loose from the time restrictions by slowing it down to essentially 1/10th the speed should sound like a great idea to me then right? The answer is that I’m not so sure. I really love having the open world and side missions to play in, but I feel like, in this case, that should be a mode apart from the story. If you are a player who still wants that pure experience there’s still “nightmare mode” which feels much closer to the older games in difficulty and restriction. It brings the timer back to an urgent level and increases the damage done by enemies. I ended up only giving the game a playthrough on Nightmare mode after I completed the game. This essentially meant I was almost max level, and it still felt very difficult. I recommend it to anyone who enjoyed the series prior.
When speaking in terms of scale Dead Rising 3 is bigger than Dead Rising 2, but not as much as I initially thought. There are almost always more zombies on screen at one time by an order of magnitude, but the environments play a few tricks. It feels like the environments are bigger to allow for more room for driving, traversal, and open platform. However, most of the buildings are completely closed. As I was running down streets, through always, and through storefronts out the backdoor I realized that while there might not actually be that many more buildings to run through than the second game, I felt more exhilarated dealing with the large hords of zombies. At least until I started unlocking weapon blueprints, to which there are many extraordinarily powerful ones. Honestly though, that’s what this game really feels about.
Weapon blueprints are found in the environment, normally after a bit of platforming. The “supercombo” blueprints always spawn in the same places, but sometimes don’t spawn. This slows the power creep down a little bit, but even some of the basic combo weapons are extremely proficient at killing hundreds of zombies before breaking. The weapon power coupled with the ability to craft weapons using part categories after investing just a few skillpoints means that the player has ready access in the field to some of the most powerful weapons in the game half way through a story run. There’s also lockers at safehouses that you can pull any item you’ve picked up, or any weapon you’ve crafted out of. It is restricted a bit so you can only pull four combo weapons out, or two supercombo weapons. After making a few supercombo weapons and visiting a safehouse it felt like any mission in the game was relatively easy, especially boss battles. I ended up having more fun collecting all the blueprints and collectibles than I did playing through the missions usually.
Killing zombies is extremely fun for me and didn’t get old until most of the way into my second playthrough for me. The gore is impressive. The sounds design often put me on edge when difficulty couldn’t. My only issue with the visuals was the overall artstyle. I don’t think I’ve seen a more brown game in recent times. When put up against its predecessors the color scheme of this game is something that’s really easy to start cringing at. The weapon effects including ice, fire, lighting, and fireworks all help bring the tone up enough that it doesn’t get too depressing to just run around. The weapons are fun to use and some are far more satisfying than others to use. Melee combat is the focus, but some of the ranged weapons are absolutely overpowered for bosses. It ends up leading to an interesting balance in how weapons are used, but because of how powerful everything ends up being the differences are less important later in the game.
Difficulty, at least in the normal mode, ended up being extremely low. I did die a few times, but in almost all cases that was because I purposefully underpowered myself to test the my limits traversing the streets. Boss patters were easy to learn and there are several simple blueprints that I got early on that made the boss battles all absolutely trivial, and in some cases unintentionally funny. I rarely felt like I was having much of hard fight in boss battles. I think I would have had more of a fun challenge if there were more human combative enemies, but that weren’t complete bullet sponges. Men with guns are few and far between, and every single one of them can take quite a few hits before going down. Combat is straight forward and awkward with them more often than not though.
The missions find themselves in favor of a more traditional openworld game. There are clearly marked miniboss battle objectives. Quite a few people can be found who won’t budge until you go fetch something for them. There are a few creative and fun side missions that were very clearly given a lot more though and love. These sidemissions end up normally giving survivors that can tag along even in missions. The survivors actually hold up pretty well against zombies in the day, and Nick ends up capable of running with a posse of half a dozen survivors all armed to the teeth with unlimited ammo combo guns. The story missions are fun to play generally, but the story really doesn’t hold up too well.
The protagonist Nick is bland at best. He is a really ‘nice guy’ and actually has a story reason for being important in this game, but as the game progresses he started grating on my nerves more and more. Some of the support characters made me downright fist pump sometimes though, while others left me rubbing my eyes and forehead. The story has a lot of parts that feel like they should have never made it past the idea stage, but they would have made it into most Hollywood action movies. Overall the story wasn’t for me, but the voice acting, character emotional expression, and cutscene camera work all ended up making it a very enjoyable ride. Just don’t expect to be blown away by any twists or presented with any profound questions.
While it has a lot of problems, they often feel like it was a choice between “challenge” and “wacky fun” and that’s a compromise I’m willing to go along with for the ride. It might have been easy, but I haven’t had as much fun killing zombies in a long time.

****WARNING: PLEASE READ BEFORE PURCHASE****
*TWO GAME BREAK BUGS PREVENT PLAY ON WINDOWS 7/8, FIXES BELOW*
This is an EXCELLENT game, an ancient chinese mythology version of KOTOR. However, this steam version WILL NOT launch on Windows 7 and 8 without a few back end tweeks. Lots of google investigation returned a lot of confusion. But I found the proper way to get this game running. Do the following semi-easy fixes depending on the errors you receive:
"FAILED TO FIND STEAM" BUG
This is because this game was made for older OSes, where steam is typically located in C: Programs, not C: Programs(x86). In order to fix this do the following:
1. In your Jade Empire folder change the file "JadeEmpireLauncher.exe" to "JadeEmpireLauncher_Backup"
2. In the same folder rename JadeEmpire.exe to JadeEmpireLauncher.exe
3. Right click My Computer(Called This PC in windows 8.1) and go to properties, then click Advanced System Settings, under the adavanced tab, click Enviroment Variables. Look for the "Path" variable, high light it and the edit button. A window will pop up. Put your cursor in the "Path Variable", it will be a Path to your Program(x86) folder. Go to the very end of the path already in there and add a ; a SEMI-COLON, NOT a : colon. This is going to seperate the first path from the new one.
4. After that semi colon, simply put in the past to steam that you use such as: C:\Program Files (x86)\steam. Hit Okay.
5. Please, REBOOT YOUR COMPUTER <- THIS IS IMPORTANT For some reason this game won't register this change unless you reboot.
"IN GAME STUTTERING" BUG
GREAT! You made it into the game. But it's running with this horrendous unplayable stutter even though you are running at a solid 30-60 FPS. Here is how you fix it:
1. Go to Jade Empire folder.
2. Open the JadeEmpire.ini file with notepad.
3. Find the entry ClampFPS=1 and change the 1 to a 0.
4*. (If you are only running one video card, skip to 5)  If you are on a gaming laptop that runs a high performance video card alongside an intergrated one, this game almost ALWAYS will naturally try to run off the integrated card instead of the good card. Go into Your card's control panel and under 3d settings, click Add Program, select Jade Empire, then change it from Integrated to High Performance Card.
5. Turn off the steam overlay by selecting Steam->Settings->In-Game->Uncheck Enable Steam overlay.
6.And as always after doing this, REBOOT YOUR COMPUTER. The game WILL NOT recognize it if you don't.
This is a GREAT game and a lot of fun. But it wasn't updated for newer systems. These fixes aren't as hard as they found, Give them a shot.

I really feel like I should bother to write a review for this game.
Back in the days, I used to play this game quite a lot on my Xbox, so I was really excited when I realized that this game was also getting released on Steam.
First off, let me address all the people saying that they could not get this game to run on Win7 and above. I myself also use Win7 and have played it multiple times
. The game runs just as smoothly as it did on my console, if not even smoother.
And if you had sacrificed a mere two minutes of your lives searching for a solution to the infamous "Steam not found"-error you would be able to enjoy this game in its entirety as well.
For those too thick-headed to look it up themselves:
a) Either replace the JadeLauncher.exe with the JadeEmpire.exe or
b) add your Steam directory as a path in Win7 (and above).
It really is not that hard, guys.
But enough with the whining. I came here to write a review about the game and this is what I will do.
I'd really like to compose some kind of list of the pros and cons of the game but unfortunately, I cannot think of anything that'd fall into the latter category.
Even though this game might not be up to the modern-day graphics standard (also meaning that there is no HD remake ... yet), the game makes up for it with an intense and engaging story, an entertaining combat system and a wide variety of different combat styles and techniques.
The choice, as with many Bioware titles, is complely up to you:
Whether you prefer the classic martial arts, like the brute force of a wide arsenal of different melee and (one...) ranged weapons, fancy being a ranged spellcaster or even prefer to transform into a various amount of demons to squish your foes in an instant, the game does offer you every single one of these possibilities.
The choices you make on your way to your ultimate goal do, of course, affect how the story develops and how the people react to you. There are the two big classic sides of good (the so-called Way of the Open Palm) and bad (The Closed Fist). Depending on those you gain different trinkets and skills and shape the climax of the game.
But you don't have to travel alone. The game helps you out with several companions, each one with an interesting back story and unique abilities. Don't like dragging someone along the whole time who is only getting in the way? It's not a problem! Almost every companion has two different ways to aid you in combat: Attack and support.
But I do have to say that most of the compnions fancy you being the nice guy, so you might have a hard time dealing with them when walking the dark path.
Unfortunately, there are some techniques in the game that cannot be accessed and learnt during the game (and of course, these are mostly only the cool ones). Nevertheless, some talented modder thought of a solution to this problem and released the best and most popular mod for Jade Empire: Jade in Style. If you already know the game and are looking for a little more variation in styles you should certainly check out this mod.
The world of Jade Empire seems somewhat like a mashup of many different clichés of medival Asia but it really doesn't matter after the first few minutes of gameplay.
Sadly, you cannot explore most areas - the game basically tells you where to go and the progression through the different areas is rather linear, especially when entering a dungeon.
I'd really like to talk about its main feature - the story.
But I won't because I do not want to spoil anything and I am not quite sure I would be able to say something different than "OMG, it's so epic!!" (you get the gist).
Let me just say that the game contained the most WTF plot twist of my childhood.
So, in conclusion, I'd like to say that I highly recommend this game. I have by far not talked about all the features this game offers because I feel that some things should be yours to discover.
Once you get it to run, the whole experience is at least as good as it was "in the olden days". It even offers full (Xbox) controller support, but is just easy to play with a mouse and a keyboard (it's what I did).
I hope that a few of you will not be deterred by the vast amount of negative reviews regarding the PC adaption because it really is a very good game.
But go and see for yourselves!

Cute, but underwhelming, and lacking in both content and cohesion.  All things considered, mediocre at best.
This short, light hearted narritave driven game aims to tell a notably different story every playthrough based on your actions.  Unfortunately, the story is broken up into tens of small, fairly mundane story arcs, which are generally kept very separate.  One's actions have little effect on future story arcs, with only the occasional action which benefits from high stats in certain areas.  Additionally, the overarching plot is weak.  It lacks substance.  Very little that happens in the tiny sub-arcs actually seem related to the main story-line at all, and the climax of the game seems to have little to no build up.  It just suddenly happens after you've complete the requisite amount of missions.  Every aspect of the game I can think to name lacks depth:  the interactive elements, the characters, the story, the visuals (there are only a few images used the entire game).  Further, despite the attempt to make a story that is adaptive to the player's choices, the lack of content makes the replay value extremely low, so expect to only get a couple hours out of this game.  It only says I have 10 hours because I accidentally left it on over night.
TL;DR:
Highly lacking in content, with a surprisingly bland story.  Mediocre at best.

I really love this game.  In fact, I can't really think of a single bad thing to say about it.
- The premise is cute and funny.
- The cartoony artwork perfectly matches the tone of the game, and the randomly generated character designs help keep each playthrough fresh.
- The music is relaxing, yet upbeat.
- The gameplay is simple, revolving entirely around text trees, but it effectively facilitates a successful choose-your-own adventure.
- There are a huge array of quests programmed into the game, and you will get a slightly different mix of options each time you play.  I have run through the game 15 times, and have yet to explore every scenario, let alone every dialogue option of every scenario.
- The humour is great.  It can be a bit crass or gross at times, but you *are* playing as a monster.
- I like that you can mold your character's personality as you go, so if you don't want to be a mean monster you don't have to be.
- Each game takes just 15-60 minutes (depending on how fast you are clicking through the text), so it doesn't feel like a slog to keep trying for new endings.  Also, it is great to play as a virtual palate cleanser in between other games.

So I have had this game for a while, and the total amount of hours I have invested in it is actually a bit higher than the number my steam shows. Either way, despite all the hate this game has been getting, I am absolutely in love with it. One more thing, I have not experienced most of the problems people are complaining about, so honestly my review is based on my personal exp.
There are two things that are painfully obvious about this game. First of all, it's an older game already (the engine) and it's definitely an indie game (the game organization, etc.). It's a game that has some problems that other indie games of this type have, but for me they were never gamebreaking.
The game in itself looks amazing. Even though they are using an older engine, I am in love with the graphics here. The dinosaurs look amazing, fluent animation and the landscape is beautiful. The density can really make it difficult to navigate sometimes (especially when playing as a huge tyrant) due to all the trees, bushes and grass.
I only wish that the humans were done better. They look a lot more outdated and far less detailed and smooth than the dinos, which is kinda to be expected I guess (i mean the main stars are the dinos), but considering that you play with humans equally as you play with dinosaurs, I think it is necessary for them too look just as good.
The game offers several different modes, the top ones being Team Deathmatch and Get to the Chopper. There are also Survival mode, Dino Deathmatch and Free Roaming. For my personal taste the top ones are really the best ones. I kinda wish Dino Deathmatch was more popular, cause everybody gets to play as a dino, but still, team deathmatch is enough if nothing else.
Now, I am not gonna lie, there are a lot of empty servers, there are a lot of free roaming servers, but I never have problems finding a  Deathmatch game. There is always at least one (there is 2 or 3 servers) server that has more than 20 players playing at the time. I mostly play on this one Hybrid server, which mixes Team Deathmatch and Get to the Chopper. It's really fun. Another one is a random server which I only know has a max of 250 kills ( I am sorry for not knowing the real names of the servers lol). There is also one more, but I use it less than the other two, not sure of the name at all. EIther way, I really never have to wait more than a minute to join a populated server.
The community. Now this is one thing that people keep complaining about the most I think, and I am not sure why. In all this time playing the game, I have never had issues with any admins, I have never been banned from a server, and I have never been butthurt by anyone. Most likely because I just play. That's what I came to do. I don't bother joking or talking in the chat, because it's distracting and people tend to♥♥♥♥♥♥too much, but if you don;'t pay attention to it, you won't get butthurt and won't push yourself into a possible ban. Just play the fugging game and enjoy killing each other.
The bugs are there, the lag is there, but it's not too big of a deal. I have a powerful system and a decent internet connection, so I am not hit by these very often. And when I do, it rarely results in me dying in the game.
The market is solid. There are tons of skins that you can get for free just by playing, or you can invest a bit into crates and keys to open them. Now in my case, I actually use the Steam market to get skins for cheap a lot. Either way, spending money is not necessary for you to enjoy the game.
All in all, I recommend this game. I think it's fun, for a couple of hours a day, to just mess around and kill people or dinos. It has some flaws, but I don't think they are that bad for your not to give it a try. If nothing else, the game is not that expensive, and if it's too big of a price, just wait for sales. I got it for around 6 euros. And for that amount, you are getting your money's worth.

I must be lucky, I've had zero crashes even after unlocking the frame rate and have been loving the game to death since launch. It could still use a lot of optimisation, but for the most part performance has bounced between "a little juddery" to "perfectly playable". with thankfully much more of the latter than the former.
DR3 is easily the best Dead Rising yet when it's running smoothly. I love the new setting, the story feels like a worthy addition to the series' lore and the characters are, as I expected from a DR game, very over the top. There's also a VERY cool twist at the end that I didn't see coming that tickled me pink.
I don't love the new graphics and atmosphere, though - DR2's women were somehow so much more beautiful (remember the perfection that was Rebecca Chang and those psycho twins?) and I'm not a huge fan of how serious and gritty DR3 is. Still, the game has to evolve so whatever, plus I still got to slaughter zombies wearing a sombrero, a trucker mustache, a banana hammock and go go boots so the cheese is there, it's just a little less obvious.
The new open world and drivability of the levels is a nice change, but I hate how so many streets are permanently blocked off with no option to un-block them. I love the incredibly detailed zombies and the creative ways they can be sliced, diced, burned and blown to bits, and the combo vehicles are sooo useful and fun to drive.
And the weapons... holy crap these guys put a lot of them into the game, and the combinations are INSANE! I love the Ultimate Grim Reaper the best; that thing alone levelled me from 45 to 50 in less than an hour.
I'm really pleased how the devs addressed so many of DR2's problems in DR3. Hate feeling time pressure? Cruise through Story Mode at your leisure. Story mode not pressured enough? Switch to Nightmare Mode and enjoy less time to do stuff, more aggressive zombies and no automatic save points - it's toilets only for you.
Ally AI is so much better than before and survivors and companions are actually genuinely useful this time around. The psychopaths are as pleasantly oblivious to the apocalypse happening around them and are hilariously unhinged for the most part. The actual psychopath battles, though, are too easy even without combo weapons and the final boss battle is just pathetic. Dark Souls this isn't.
I also felt the game was a bit short - I played in Story Mode and beat it in under 20 hours and that was with a *lot* of screwing around. Happily, I had so much fun I *want* to play it again in co-op and Nightmare modes, so make of that what you will.
Overall I'd say DR3 is a clever and well-done evolution of the concepts seen in DR1 and 2, and I consider it money well spent. If you like Dead Rising at all, you should totally play this one.

Jade Empire is an immersive 3rd person game with an emphasis on story and martial arts - themed combat. JE was published and developed by BioWare, which many may recognize as the company under EA which is known to deliver on immersive, story rich games which often include innovative gameplay mechanics, such as the Mass Effect or Dragon Age series. Jade Empire is no exception, as the fighting is very rewarding and, surprisingly, does not get repetitive nearly as fast as you might expect it to. Different martial arts styles are very distinctive from one another, although certain martial arts and weapon styles outshine others, which means most players may opt out of changing styles due to the success they have with a certain one. Decision-making is a pivotal part of the game. The decisions you make will branch the story out to a certain extent, affect how characters react to you and also affect the ending too.
Jade Empire's story is long and immersive. You take the role of a student in a martial arts school lead by your mentor, Master Li. You can choose your character from a selection of different toons, either going with a pre-selected loadout (Starting styles and stats, like in many MMORPGs) or making your own loadout. Your own character isn't voice acted, which is a shame, but it's not that big of a deal.
Jade Empire is quite a long game and it takes you through various cities, villages and wildernesses throughout China. The game has a companion system, which lets you be accompanied by one character out of many others who you meet on your journey. You can switch out companions at nearly any time you wish, as they all follow you during your journey in the background. (Appearing in a camp when not selected). The story takes many turns and if you are into Chinese mythology or history, you will definitely enjoy Jade Empire. The game is a bit old, but it is not it's fault and I still warmly recommend it to anyone. It requires some patience from the player to listen to the narrative and get immersed in the story, as all BioWare games do anyway. In my opinion, the combat is very fun and rewarding, as for some bosses and enemies you really have to plan ahead and switch styles during the fight in order to survive.
The characters and the plot are what shine in the game the most for me. Some provide comic relief, some provide moral guidance for the decisions you must make during your journey, and some work to intrigue you and astonish you. My favorite character is hands down is Henpecked Hou, an awkward chef who acts as comic relief by complaining about how he will get beat up by his wife and who also provides a unique drunken martial style by throwing wine bottles at you during combat. A great guy indeed.
All in all, there is only one thing that I can think of that Jade Empire really, really needs. A sequel. Seriously. The game has a great story as long as you have the patience to play through it. The game is great and the main factor that makes it great is that there aren't many games like it out here in Steam.

Jade Empire is an action roleplaying game which puts you in the role of a young martial artist on a quest to free his/her master from the grasp of the sinister order of the Lotus Assassins while slowly discovering the history and the machinations behind the titular Jade Empire. The game heavily borrows from the Chinese tradition and mythical lore for its setting and characters.
The main beef of the gameplay are the martial style you can use in combat: some of them are about using a weapon like a sword or a staff, others allow you to cast spells or incapacitate your enemies. You can equip four of them at a time and learn to use them in tandem, manage their mana cost (or better said, chi or focus cost depending on the style used) and upgrade their stats carefully. Enemies respond differently to the various style, forcing you to switch between them during each battle. Other novelities from Jade Empire, gameplay-wise, are about the techniques, permanent stats bonus you can collect for your character from quests, and gems, which provide some bonuses when equipped.
Jade Empire remains a classic BioWare videogame at its core, with plenty of companions you'll learn to know better during your journey, interesting secondary characters and a pletore of either funny or interesting sidequests. There is even a karma meter (which judges your action through a "good" and "evil" scheme of some sort) and the possibility to change the later story drastically depending on your allignment and previous choices. In the end, you can even romance a character of your choice.
It's worth mentioning however that Jade Empire is somehow scarce when it comes to explorable locations and, at least on normal difficulty, the game can become rather easy really quickly (namely, some styles are very unbalanced and, generally, using a stunning style in tandem with an heavy damaging one is sure to make most enemies encounter a breeze).
The Special Edition of Jade Empire adss content that once belonged only to the Xbox version and its collector's edition. Also, starting up this Steam version could require some workaround.
All in all, Jade Empire is a classic RPG from the golden age of BioWare: you should totally buy it if you enjoy the other games made by this studio, but be also warned that not everyone could find the Eastern theme going in Jade Empire that appealing

This has always been one of the most adventure-inspiring games out there. With a large open world and tons of content to explore, an open class system that's brilliant before its years, Dungeon Siege tends to receive far less praise than it deserves. Particularly because of the unnecessary tinkering that has been done with it get it on Steam. Multiplayer, in the days that it was available, was a masterstroke and a great feature of the game, and although you cannot import an entire party into a multiplayer game (that you can none the less play on your own), it's recommended to employ the work-around to do this because it just adds to the hours of replay-value and the challenge involved.
RPGs of this day and age are of course technically superior in every way to this game. Look at its successor: Dungeon Siege 2, that improves upon virtually every aspect of the game. You can tell, however, that Dungeon Siege was a developers team's dream brought to life and they are very proud of it, despite the monetary adversity they faced during its production (The Chris Taylor interview about Dungeon Siege, particularly the bit about Apple as an investor is definitely worth a listen).
Despite its aging geometry, low-resolution textures and poor UI scaling to high resolutions when applied to this day and age, and despite the alternative games that I play just as well, I keep coming back to this title at least once every two years for a full playthrough of the story.
Its and old game but so much fun.

However, the game is not without flaws. However, these flaws are mostly caused by Steam and Gamespy rather than the game itself. One of these is the game not including Legends Of Aranna, the expansion for the game, but if you look online, you can probably find a way to integrate it into the game (If not, feel free to add and message me, as I have the files available.) Another problem is that the multiplayer ran on Gamespy, so to play multiplayer, you need to find an alternative method (Check online or steam guides for Dungeon Siege for help). Overall, I would reccomend definitely at least trying the game out when its on sale.

As someone who grew up with the 1997 sequel, it was fantastic to finally come back and experience the original Monkey Island's story. The writing and style is just what I wanted. I do have a few gripes with the game itself. The beginning act drags on for a very long time, though thankfully you can complete the tasks in almost any order (completing Thievery last will, however, cheat you out of a story-important cutscene, which seems like an oversight). Complaints have already been made about the Special Edition artwork, which was not painted in tandem with the original game's creators and have become highly controversial, but besides that, some of the backgrounds (noticeably the area around the monkey head and some of the forest paintovers) are patchy and show pixels. The addition of a large full moon in one background becomes an obvious oversight during a cutscene with a shooting star. However, none of these are game-breaking or make the experience unpleasant. The puzzles are both difficult and fun and the special edition, if you choose to play in that format, gives you a little help by limiting options when you're stuck. The music is excellent and the original game is fully intact for nostalgia players. I feel it's appropriate that this special edition feels a little young and awkward, because that's what the original game was. All of the problems you could have, old and new, will be fixed in the sequel, so I almost recommend playing that one OVER this, but if you do, you'll miss out on the jokes, the puzzles, and the environments this first one has to offer. I'll always be a huge fan of both.

As the write up states - it's a choose your own adventure.
The game have basically five phases (birth, child, adolescent, adult, elder).   Each phase has "mini adventures" from which to choose and then options within the adventures.  The choices drive your "personality"
Good - the little adventures are amusing and there's a semi randomness to what gets offered as a selection in each phase that lends to some replayability.  There are 14 possible outcomes for the end game.  It takes about 10-15 hours of game play to achieve all 14 outcomes.
My criticism is with the choices lacking materiality on the final outcome.  The choices cause the trait percentages to vary. Basically you get about 30 or so choices and find they lead to one final choice yielding your outcome - you could choose the same 30 adventures/same choices every play through, get to 80% in every trait and about 70% in respect.  (not that you'd do that, but you could and it would not restrict final outcome overly much at all other than neurosurgeon and modest legacy).
Basically the choices at birth/child/teen just arent material enough.  They should cause the final outcomes to be far more restrictve and potentially open up new content.  Instead  all forks in the path lead to what is effectively a common point.
My second criticism would be the elder phase -  the choices are mundane - one choice will pretty much cause How monsters/humans view one another to go up and the other cause it to go down.  The phase is akin to clicking "help" or "sabotage" buttons 15 times in a row.  The adventures themselves were creative but the choice selections and how they cause ""your own adventure" to evolve in my view lacked creativity.
Summary - The mini adventures are quite amusing but other aspects of the game are lacking.
For 2-3$ and the replayability of seeing how each choice affects your traits it gets a borderline thumbs up.

To say it simply, I'm a huge fan of a controller. Specifically the Steam Controler. I don't know what they smoked to get the inspiration for this thing but the whole controler just feels "right."
When I picked it up the first time the contours of the face threw me off. The fingertip buttons underneath were odd. The touchpads felt rough and odd. I launched Fallout 4 with mixed expectations. I had to adjust tracking speed twice but once I got it right everything started to fall into place.
Within 5 minutes I was warming up to it and getting used to the new control interface.
Within 10 minutes I was enjoying it.
Within 20 minutes I was hopelessly in love with it.
For years I've sat up ridgidly, one hand on the keyboard, the other on a mouse. As I used the Steam Controller I found myself leaning back, sliding back off the edge of my seat, relaxing. When I got done playing it wasn't over either. Sure I needed the keyboard to type, but that was it.
The Steam Controller has not only changed the way I game, but the way I compute. I can now sit back and relax as I browse the web, read articles, load videos to watch, etc.
No other controller for the PC has had this effect on me. I've tried the XBox, Playstation, Logitech, and a couple others and none feel right. I went back to my PS3 to watch a Blu-ray and the controller just felt wrong. Steam has me sold. I'll be buying a Link as soon as I can.

For a game that has the style and scale of a Battlefield game and the realism of something akin to Arma 3 I figured I would LOVE this game. Well I can say every all 4.4 hours of me playing this game have literally been the worst time ive had playing a game in years.
The general quality of the game is fantastic, its a great looking game. The issues I have are gameplay. A few of them being: Bipods are clunky and hard to use. Sometimes you can deploy them, others you cant. It depolys automatically, meaning I have no clue when what or where it will work. The most I can say is it seem sto work without fail on sandbags.
My next issue is the HUD. If your going to go without an HUD, have an alternative way to learn the information. The problem here is that the game doesnt know if it wants to have an HUD or not. When you spawn in, you see pretty much everything. Capture point locations, friendly units, their enemy marks, your compass, all of that. While the compass can be left on via a setting in the menu, the rest can not. Instead if your looking at a friendly unit it will SOMETIMES dispaly an IFF arrow over their head. This system leads to a LOT of friendly fire and deaths as you dont know who the hell your aiming at and dont want to be kicked for shooting a friendly.
Finally all I can say is that the first person view in generally feels clunky and blocky. Weapons are far to large in your view, sucking up a lot of your view which you already cant increase via a FOV slider or something. Secondly when your turning or looking around with a weapon it kind of swings in that direction but just stays there. makes aiming from the hip or aiming in general a bit of a pain.
Basicly this game is a example, gameplay wise, of what games like Battlefield and such should be. You die in 2 or so shots. Makes the firefights short and brutal and makes weapon selection more enjoyable. Instead of the Call of Duty style looking for the exploit gun you use whatever your most comfortable with or personally prefer.
That being said you will spend 99% of your time staring at empty land or dying in 30 seconds. A lot of the staring ends in a bullet to the head as well. For whatever reason I didnt not enjoy a single second of playing this game. It was a chore. Anytime I died I felt cheated, any time I got a kill I didnt care at all. I didnt feel acheived whatso ever.
My advice? Just buy Arma 3. At least they know how to balance out realism and practicality.

Jade Empire is an essential Bioware roleplaying experience.  I prefer it to earlier offerings like Baldur's Gate because their creative team realized their own fantasy world from the ground up.  It sucessfully blends the tropes and conventions of classic wire flying films and asian folktales in what feels like a love letter to the genre.
As I write this the JE is almost ten years old and examining it reveals a prototype for the story driven/ action rpgs like DA and ME that would follow.  It is a sweeping tale that that places the player in the familiar role of the "chosen one" whose actions will shape the course of the entire world as they chart their own personal destiny.  If this were a tabletop rpg I would hate this contrived convention but it works quite well in a single player video game.
My only complaint is that the PC version seems to respond more sluggishly to controller input than the console version that I played when it relased in 04.

I first played Dungeon Siege back when it was first released. I had never gotten further than an hour into it, and as the years went on, I lost the chance to play it to completion (my laptop being too advanced for it.)
Steam has now given me that sense of closure I've yearned for all these years, and uh, yeah, the game kinda sucks the ding-dong.
DS is a Diablo clone through and through. You point, you click, things happen. Said things can be: attack enemy until one you dies, collect items, open doors, or use switch. And that's the game. The story is generic high fantasy albeit a rather bad incarnation. It's forgettable, spread woefully thin, and the names are stupid. There are no characters of note, your party members have as much personality as dry oatmeal, and I honestly forgot the name of the kingdom I was even in.
But how does it play? In a word, poorly. Imagine having an entire party to control as you play your Diablo clone! Imagine clicking on the wrong thing every 10 seconds in the heat of a hectic battle because character portraits with their respective inventory icons take up the whole left corner of the screen! Imagine watching your characters do absolutely nothing as hordes of enemies wreck them! Imagine trodding through boring, empty levels as you swear every 30 seconds as you realize members of your party decided to give up on life and just stand around doing nothing!
I watched two of my party members literally - L I T E R A L L Y - pivot in place and stare at a group of attacking enemies rather than attack them. Those members died. Your party has virtually no soul: no unique skill trees, no various classes, nothing. Just boring stat growth with no appeal. You know what did this game in for me? Trying to fit my entire party onto a moving platform only to realize that it was A) impossible, B) frustrating, and C) poor level design.
I only beat this game because I learned about the God Mode cheat, disbanding my entire party, and just running through the game. No shame, it wasn't really worth it in the end. Which, oh yeah, the Steam version of this goes boom-boom in its pants and kicks you to the main menu so you can't see the ending.
Play Titan Quest instead. Play Torchlight instead. Or just play Diablo again for the 30th time instead.

The Secret of Monkey Island(TM). Once, when I was much younger, I tried it. I was too impatient to figure out the at-times difficult puzzles and work my way around the lengthier segments of the game.
Now, having revisited it with a more positive and patient mindset, I found myself wrapped in a humorous adventure filled with references, and reasonably challenging puzzles; ones that aren't ridiculous, and always have a degree of logic to them.
Your standard point-n'-click adventure, where you walk around locations, click on stuff, pick it up, push and pull things more than is probably necessary, and try to combine
in your inventory. Fun, but I had some problems with the Special Edition's hitboxes. I had to aim
below everything I wanted to click on to do everything with, and I found the scrolling options for use/push/pull annoying so I just used CTRL to bring up the quick list. Faster than scrolling! If you don't mind doing a bit of fiddling with the controls, and remembering to save in different slots so that the glitches that the Special Edition has don't ruin your game like it almost did for me, it's an enjoyable game.
"My name is Guybrush Threepwood, and I want to be a pirate!"
You play the aforementioned Guybrush Threepwood, and his 'humble' quest to become a man of ill repute (pirate) soon spirals into a quest to find and defeat the evil Ghost Pirate LeChuck and his crew of undead sailors! (Who can certainly play the violin pretty well). I wouldn't want to ruin any more for you. Just soak in the world, and make sure to talk to everyone!
The new graphics of the Special Edition, while a little unsettling at times, (Guybrush's hair looks a little strange), are mostly spot on. Of course, if you're an old school player or you just want to experience the game how it used to be, old music and all, just hit F10 and you'll be immersed in old-school Monkey Island(TM)! Seamless, too, so you can do it at anytime, and it's nice and smooth. I enjoyed seeing the attention to detail from the new artists, capturing and improving on the aspects of the old graphics, capturing it all pretty much perfectly (Guybrush's hair!).
The atmosphere is excellent, really immersing you in the strange locales of Melee Island(TM) and Monkey Island(TM)! It just does a wonderful job of making you feel like Mr Thriftweed- I mean, Threepwood. Yes.
The sounds are even better, the voice actors doing a wonderful job of bringing the characters to life. The music is also excellent, a sort of reggae style pirate beat, with both the old and the new versions being really good. I enjoy the map music of Monkey Island(TM) and the catchy violin song that the pirates play the most.
The Secret of Monkey Island(TM): Special Edition does a masterful job of portraying a crazy haven for pirates and immersing you in a truly humorous story about Monkey Island and it's inhabitants. Highly recommended, though there are a few bugs, so save often!
Just remember...
"Woof, woof, arf, bark, a-roof wuf, LeChuck!"

This game may not have the most impacting choices, but the story line is amazing and rich with emotion. The aesthetic in the world design is top-notch, and the character designs betray quite a bit about their individual thoughts and beliefs. Nier: Automata is an outstanding game for people looking to delve into a world without much introduction to the previously established universe (From Drakengard to Nier) and those who want to continue to develop their understanding if they've played the previous games. The combat is more bullet hell than anything, but the story mode keeps the style of the game fresh by changing the orientation of both your camera and your fighting style based on location, as well as introducing unique weapons and character abilities.
Nier: Automata is not a game to pass up and should be picked up by any RPG fan. It is lengthy, but it is rewarding to both find the true ending (out of 5) and to take on the toughest challenge the game has to offer.

Think Star Wars (Especially since this came out around the same time as they were working on the Knights Of The Old Republic games), the 'Open-Palm' path is basically the Jedi to the more Sith-like 'Closed-Fist'.
I may be slightly biased due to my love of martial arts and mythology, but this game is rich with both, so I don't care, it's great.
It's basically like being the major protagonist of a fantasy, kung-fu, cult-classic movie, for 20+ hours. There are demons, spirits, gods, ghosts, assassins, pirates, heavenly plains, and so many other things that I can't mention without spoilers.
There are a lot of comments and reviews and whatnot for this game saying that it's not playable, or it's broken, and that it's all Steam's fault everyone is awful wah I'm a big whiny man-baby.
It's not broken. If you're not an idiot. This game is nearly a decade old. It needs a little help to be able to run on newer computers.
If you're on Windows 7, you will need to go into the game files, right-click on the "Jade Empire" application, go into the compatibility settings and set to run with Windows XP compatibility. There, I fixed it, now stop complaining.

Unfortunately this version is extremely difficult to get working on a 64bit OS. I have tried to install it on windows 7 and windows 8.1 and it failed to work on either without quite a bit of surfing forum posts for solutions, most of which didn't help in the slightest as every OS seems to have a range of problems running this game and finding the solution for my particular problem "Application Error: Steam failed to start" (despite steam running at the time) was difficult to say the least. Eventually I got it working by copying the Steam.dll from the main Steam folder ( C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam  - on my system) and replacing the Steam.dll file in the game folder ( C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\SteamApps\common\Jade Empire - on my system) with it.
There is no guarantee that this fix will work for anyone else but it seems so ridiculously simple a fix that its just appalling the publisher hasn't bothered to fix it themselves. In addition the configuration utility, that you are forced to use, is simply broken on windows 7 and 8 but the game tries to force you to use it anyway. This requiredme to rename JadeEmpireLauncher.exe to something else (e.g. JadeEmpireLauncher_BACKUP.exe) and rename JadeEmpire.exe to JadeEmpireLauncher.exe.
If you're happy to mess around with this like I did then the game itself is good, but for the amount of effort put in over two separate OS's and no guarantee that it will function on a third I can't really recommend buying it from steam until these problems are fixed (and seeing as these problems have been around for years and the developer is now owned by a different publisher its almost certain that they will never be fixed).

I usually do not leave negative reviews for anything and try to see something positive in every product I buy. But with this game, I can't help it.
The game tries to be a "party-based Diablo", but it fails miserably at it. The combat is very simplistic (left-click, wait for the enemies to die, move on) and makes Diablo feel like a game of chess. The leveling system is one of the most boring ones I've ever seen: your 3 stats and 4 skills grow naturally as you fight or cast spells, and all they do is allow you to use new spells and slightly increase your chance to hit - no active abilities, no auras, nothing. The level design is atrocious: you are going to fight the same copy-pasted groups of enemies for an hour in a long location consisting of copy-pasted corridors, then move to another similar location, and so on. The story is nearly non-existent, the lore entries are very scarce and don't give you much information about the world. All the characters are very forgettable, and the companions never say anything beyond the few lines the first time you meet them.
Overall, this game feels like a tech-demo for a decent engine that was sloppily put together by a bunch of programmers under extremely strict time constraints. It is probably the most generic and forgettable game I've ever played.
I will give the game credit for its visuals (pretty good for its time), music and certain technological innovations. Jeremy Soule did an amazing job, as always, and you will recognize the musical style from Morrowind, Neverwinter Nights, KotoR, etc. I, however, don't think music and visuals can make up for the lack of... well, game.

It really pains me to say this, but this really is just for those with a big package of nostalgia behind them. Like me, yes. But replaying this after over 15 years or so, it's just such a drag that it's unbearable to play for me.
Diablo 1 is better. Torchlight is better. Dungeon Siege II is better, iirc. Why?
The best thing about this game is that you can have a huge party. That's really cool. Now, you don't *need* to, but this game really empathizes this feature through """""""""""""""balancing""""""""""""".
It has no loading screen after the initial one, which is quite impressive for such an old title. And the maps aren't small, either. It's quite a journey!
It's a very simple Hack&Slash, which isn't bad per se. Your guys level up automatically, you influence their stats slightly by equipping them with the appropriate means of attacking, like bows for dexterity, swords for strength and spells for intelligence.
------------
Now then, the worst thing that makes this game a drag aside from the low-budget execution (sound-design is something they almost could have used PC-speakers for. Those from the good old days. But that's not too bad, it's just lacking in every aspect sound-wise)
You wanna know what the real kicker is?
The loot is set. It's set in stone. The devs chose the loot you get whenever and whereever you find it. It's not randomized at all. At all.
And 95% of it sucks absolute hyper♥♥♥♥♥ It's almost funny. You have I believe 8 guys, all specialized in something. And sometimes, there is a chapter with barely anything to equip your party with.
That essentially means that all you do is set your party to aggressive, navigate them around a bit and let them do ***EVERYTHING*** else including healing. Then you press a key for the entire party to tell them to loot everything in sight. Which is cool, don't get me wrong. But all they're collecting will be absolute
.
So you barely do anything in this game. You can pretend to do some quests, but 90% (really!) of them mean to simply get to the next chapter quest-hub and talk to people and on the
linear way, you clear out some dens or something. Quest completed.
Again, this all wouldn't be such an issue if this would feel rewarding in a sense like in the good ol skinner boxes you expect from a dungeon crawler. But the loot is absolute ♥♥♥♥ing garbage most of the time - BY DESIGN!!!
By the way, there is an awesome community for this game with great modders and... hackers? who will restore the cut expansion from the Steam version for you. You guys rock, by the way. Putting honestly so much effort in such trash. I really can't wrap my head around why my child-me could put up with this in a monthly basis for a year or so. I remember being amazed by the graphics a bit. Well, that's over now.

I am doing a complete re-review of this game, since I'm finally able to actually play it now. My views haven't changed much, I still don't recommend the game.
Despite getting absolutely no support from AeriaGames for oh, I'd say about four months now, I fixed the graphics bugs I've been getting and am now ready to play Aura Kingdom. It's fun...ish. Not many games I play give me something to do aside from the main quests when I'm a lower level, so that's a plus.
The gameplay I did like, a little more free-form than most MMORPGs where you're literally standing in a single place waiting on cooldowns 100% of the time. With Aura Kingdom you have a little more wiggle room to move around, I don't think you're supposed to be up against one monster at a time. However as you level up you're gonna be confused about what stats you might want for your character. I say want, but at later levels your wants will be heavily outweighed by your needs and if you messed up early on, you're gonna pay for it.
Community...I really wish I could give this a pass because the community is actually there, only problem is they make you feel like a social outcast. I can't count on my hands and feet the number of groups and single people I approached asking about the game (what build I should go for, help with quests, a simple 2-minute dungeon run...) and was either told to bugger off or was just plain ignored. This includes whenever I'd ask a question on map chats, no answer even though there are numerous other people talking amongst themselves for everyone in the area to watch.
The customer service is where this really gets me...I used to be a huge fan of AeriaGames. Played almost all their games, played competitively, worked towards getting all the achievements...lately however it seems that AeriaGames just simply doesn't care anymore and waits for their paycheck at the end of each day. I keep hearing that once you buy something from them and don't buy anything the following month you get banned. Now I also know that you can email them asking to lift it and they usually will but that's just poor practice to begin with. As I stated earlier, when I tried this game in December I was having major graphical bugs in the tutorial zone where I couldn't see anything on my screen other than the background (sky) image and flame effects. I tried getting support from it and after some time, I still had nothing for it.
Aura Kingdom has some ups and some downs, I'm actually playing it despite my negative review because I want to get to end-game to see the rest of the game. I mean, it isn't a BAD game...that's what bothers me, whenever I play games like this I always say "it isn't a bad game" but that doesn't really mean it's a good game either. If you enjoy MMORPGs where you're left to figure out most of the game's inner workings on your own then play Aura Kingdom. If you'd rather play games for the social aspect and immediate helping hand, stay away.
Overall no paid to win. only paid for cosmetic.

The original has been praised time and time again, and I feel no need to go into it but I will say this; Deus Ex was one of the most influential games of all time, both from a story perspective but also in regards to the gameplay. With this being said, there is a lot for a prequel to live up to and with my expectations already set much higher than I assumed possible, Human Revolution easily rests aside its older brother.
The original wasn't much to look at in comparison to todays graphics, but you could easily look past that thanks to it's incredible story and gameplay and the same can be said for Human Revolution with one small difference. The art direction and execution is simply wonderful. I constantly had to explore and gaze in awe at some of the locations and little surprises it had in store for me. When you visit Belltower's headquarters, you realize very quickly that a lot of thought and effort has gone into making the visuals fit together with the feel.
Corporate espionage has never felt and looked this good. This coupled with the fantastic music score and sound effects makes for a great experience for old and new fans alike, the same goes for the special effects and CGI. That's not to say the graphics are the most impressive I've ever seen but they definitely live up to what can be expected.
Admittedly, some of the scenes door get a little repetitive and if you look closely enough at the animations you can see some idle poses that get reused often but it's nothing that comes close to putting you off playing. The variety in animations is fairly impressive, each time you take someone down lethally or not you'll sit back and say; "Wow, that was pretty damn cool." especially when you're able to take on two enemies at a time.
One of the most important things to me while playing a game is player involvement and immersion. Feeling like you're really arguing with David Sarif regarding security loopholes really feels natural and the seamless binding of conversations with superb voice acting seals the deal.
There isn't as many side objectives as the original, but they're well written and often force you to once again become rapidly involved in the politics and moral conundrums that make us human, a strong tie in to one of the three points of view explored in the game itself. With this being said, multiple endings tend to encompass differing points of view that one person may entirely agree with while another detests.
The freedom to choose your play-style, and then experience the consequences they bring really make you feel as though you're making a difference. A funny example would be if you stumble into the ladies bathroom while in Sarif Headquarters, Pritchard will make a remark essentially telling you what Manderly would in the original; "Stay out of the ladies bathroom, you idiot." Little things a long the way tie the game in with the universe perfectly and often you'll hear songs re-mastered that, if you're a returning player will send a little shiver down your spine. This being said, there are multiple references to key plots in the original too, Page Industries marks just one of many.
Another feature worth noting is your choice, lethal or non lethal. A stealthy player who silent hacking, knockouts and gas grenades isn't punished by forcing them into an environment where they simply cannot win; the same goes for an aggressive shoot-first ask questions later sort of guy. The bosses have been reworked to allow greater flexibility and more variety instead of forcing people to pull out the big guns that they may or may not even have. Another key element is the incorporation of the missing link DLC pack which should have been execution like this much before the directors cut was released.
If you still need a reason to buy this game, the achievements are worthwhile and actually feel like accomplishments, and truly the only way to play is on the hardest difficulty. There is countless hours of fun and replay value if you want with many sections of the game offering interesting and often humor filled emails, pocket secretaries and conversations. If you need something more, there is a debug mod available which allows you to essentially cheat or modify the game in many ways similar to what Shifter or the console in the original did, as well as modify the inventory to allow for greater stacks and more room to store an arsenal of weapons to solve any situation.
Some advice would be to save often and don’t rely solely on the quick save function, especially if you're trying for some of the harder achievements. A whole game can be ruined by one accidental alarm or a bug you encounter so tread lightly and be sure to make backups of your files before you go using mods. Always read the instructions and remember, your mileage may vary.
After your first play through, starting a new game with all the augmentations, maxed out weapons and infinite possibilities really makes for a great run. On my third play through I decided to read every email and ebook as well as exploring everywhere on the map. Every time you play you'll find something new, a new path you didn't know existed, a new ammo drop or an upgrade.
In summation, a great game worthy of your time if you like stealth or combat, or if you just cant get enough of Deus Ex's universe. Get it while it's on sale, or get it when it's not. I couldn't recommend it more. The poor support for SLI and occasional frame rate jitters can be fixed with relative ease, but unfortunately the controller support is subpar. I play using a keyboard and mouse and I found it to be no less difficult than any modern first person shooter to date.

To be clear: I do not like this controller for gaming.
There is a lot this controller does that other controllers do not, and it is innovate. I tip my hat to valve for taking the "controller standard" and turning it in to their own thing. Gyroscopes, dual touch pads, rear buttons, long lasting battery life, half-press trigger buttons... This should be the new standard, and for my part I hope Valve have patented the design and technology they have put in to this.
Unfortunately this controller is not really for me. As a dedicated PC gamer, all games I prefer to play with a mouse and keyboard, and the one or two games which are horribly ported and require a controller, I still prefer to use the 360 controller, for the reason that sometimes too much change at once isn't always a good thing. The new features are so different to anything we have used before that it takes too much getting used to. If I use a controller, I use it casually as a one off thing - I don't want to learn an entirely new button layout.
I got the Steam Controller with the Steam Link, which is another innovate and well made piece of kit. However to use a Steam Link fully with desktop streaming, as well as gaming, you need either a wireless mouse/keyboard, OR; A Steam Controller... So that I don't have to get up and go to the PC when a game innevitably crashes.
for £40, I have a very very decent mouse and keyboard substitute, for much cheaper. That, in all honesty, is the only reason I have the Steam Controller at this stage.
You may ask why this isn't a negative review if it doesn't work for it's intended use. The reason is simple: I believe the technology and effort that Valve has put in to this deserves a high place in our future - but as a direct replacement to a 360 controller, I just think it could use a bit of work in terms of build quality and button placement.
