The good, the bad and the ugly for Fallout 2.
Fallout is one of those game franchises that gives me he warm-tingly feeling just thinking about the games and while Bethesda has made some great sequels with Fallout 3 and New Vegas, by far one of my favorite games of all time has to be this instalment.
Now, just to save time the review of this game could be applied to the original Fallout game with one major difference; there’s no annoying time limit. Now, sure the lack of that time limit may affect some’s perspective of realism but I think the freedom to explore and do side-quests makes the game more enjoyable but that’s just my opinion.
The good:
Grittiness of stories, environments, and characters has been something that’s been fairly popular in today’s gaming culture but nothing that’s come out recently could hold a candle to this game. Throughout the game you’re subjected to a very harsh environment where even the most civilized towns seems to have a dark streak that plays into the general feeling that the world is, in fact, completely screwed up and it’s up to you (ironically titled “the chosen one”) to save not only your village but the whole region from various forms of corruption and evil.
Or you know… not… that’s what’s so great about this game! It gives you real choices on how you want to address problems you come across. Do you want to kill the slavers holding onto a mission critical NPC? Or do you want to trade in a companion and join them? Do you want to work towards putting a stop to the growing chem addicts in the region? Or ensure the chems keep flowing freely? Sorry, I kind of got off topic there. Bottom line, this game’s dark themes and choices give this game a level of depth that makes replays all the more enjoyable.
The Bad:
Some of the problems that gripped old PC games like this is they are often under-developed. It’s hard to tell if they just ran out of time on some things or in the case of things like the child-killer perk they were just WAY too controversial to be put in at release. Some of the things they took out though honestly would have made the game more enjoyable. If you have the time, do some research and take the time to get a good unofficial patch to restore some of these missing pieces.
The ugly:
The learning curve… Look, this game is not for the meek. You’re going to die and you’re going to die a lot. It falls under the category of old-school rpgs where even the easiest difficulties can be brutal for those who don’t know what to expect playing a game like this. In fact, if you don’t know what you’re getting into playing this game I’d warn you that you will probably restart a few times until you can get a character build that works for you (I recommend custom builds) and just like with all old games like these SAVE OFTEN.

I absolutely love this game, it is very fun and hilarious. However, there are a few mods I would highly reccomend installing if you plan on playing it with the remastered graphics:
- The "Graphics and Performance Booster" mod, which just polishes how it looks, smooths those annoying rough edges, and just generally makes everything look better. (But also note that occasionally when LeChuck comes on screen, his particle effects will glitch around. Just pause and alt+tab to fix it.)
- The "Guybrush Hair Patch" mod, which gets rid of Guybrush (the main character)'s terrible new haircut and gives him his classic messy wavy hair back. It's really down to personal preference, but that's how he was supposed to look originally and it's better in my opinion.
Other than that, the game is amazing. The hint key is something every point n' click game should have, it comes in handy and removes the need for walkthroughs (usually). I could go on and on about how this game is great, but you should just buy it and experience it for yourself.

It was fun! ...For the first run or two.
Well that was upsetting. Monster Loves You! is a text, choose-your-own-adventure game where you start your life out as a newborn baby monster and you live your life up until your return to the slime vat pool or until you finish the game as an elder who transcended above death to decide what ulitimately happens between the humans and monsters when the inevitable conflict happens.
You have 5 personality traits, Bravery, Cleverness, Ferocity, Honesty, and Kindness. You gain and use your traits to your advantage in situations that require them. This would be awesome if there was actually more situations that required that. Because more or less everything you do it a sure thing. It's pretty obvious if you're going to lose something or gain something from most interactions. I'll continue that shortly.
You use these personality traits to your advantage to gain respect from other elders and monsters so you may be respected enough as an individual to transcend into becoming an elder on the day you are supposed to die. Then once you are an Elder, you must work to either build or sabotage human and monster relations in the coming days before the conflict of humans and monsters. It is this point I believe the story ends with the effort you put into this before the conflict.
Everything about this game was really cool except that this game doesn't vary or switch up the story at all. By my second playthrough I already knew pathes and things I needed to say to reap the most (xyz) out of that "adventure" So I could get my stats high or close to maxed out as possible while getting tons of respect from the elders. I was hoping that after each death it'd be like a new life with new characters and new adventures. But I kept seeing the same thing over and over again already and it got really tedious and simply not fun. It immediately became apparent that i'd just start grinding to get medals for achievements. I don't care so much about the medals. It's nice to see new endings. But that's not the point of a game like Monster Love You! or at least shouldn't be circled around what the ending is going to be. The meat and soul of the game which is the time spent in each life stage is where you're spending most and pretty much all of your time as opposed to the scripted age-transistion stages. It was like I had a really amazing, fan-friggin-tastic sandwich, and in two playthroughs I felt like I was eating the same sandwich for months. I was so sick of it.
Contining on that point is that you get really familiar with each adventure pretty easily, they're very distinct and memorable most of them. And the options listed make it very obvious which choice is going to get you the most points and the good stuff.
I was investing in honesty and kindness to achieve renown for honesty and kindness in the game, but I knew the choices in the game so well and understood where I could get off chalk-free in two playthroughs I already knew where I could build ferocity without consequence. I had kindness and cleverness maxed, I had honesty about 86% up there and I had roughly 69% ferocity. I shouldn't be able to get my ferocity stat so high while striving to get honesty and kindness. Cleverness was just so easy to pick up. It made it super-easy to bend the end game to my will because I had such high stats overall I could make the story anything I wanted it to be. Therefore there was really no reason to keep playing the game. Because in two playthroughs I could understand the routes I need to take to get the most (xyz) and how to get the medals and other things.
It as a really fun game my first two runs. After that, it just simply wasn't fun. Definitely wasn't worth the money I paid for it, I expected much more out of it after reading such nice reviews.
Also continuing, from what i've heard in the game, sounds like the game has only 3 soundtracks in it. And that's just a big no-no. The art directive is okay. They could've worked harder in a lot of areas, but whatever. The humor in this game is great. But it's not funny after you read it the first time.
Regardless, Monster Loves You! is a nice and funny and enjoyable game. But after the second playthrough or third, you realize you're just doing the same thing again and it's not fun. I was really hoping that my deaths in the game would have an influence on my next life (which I read this in a review, this was a lie or a fabrication of their beliefs of what's going on in the game) But it doesn't and that's when I realized I was going to just be doing the same thing over and over again.
Overall, this game wasn't worth the money I paid for it, I bought it for about 4 dollars and I personally just wouldn't really recommend it at all to be honest. As I said, it's fun and it's nice. But I personally think you should keep that money for something nicer that pops up on the steam store or in a steam sale that you'd rather grab.
Anyway, thank you for reading my review. I hope it helped you in your decision to purchase this game or not, have a good day.

This game was released back in 2011, and only last year have I decided to play it (first on consoles). Deus Ex: Human Revolution stays true to the stealth genre. In fact, the combat system is quite unfair; this is not your shooter where you run and gun anything you see, because if you do that, you'll become good friends with the Game Over screen. The game encourages stealth, and you are awarded experience for finishing objectives by not engaging/fighting/seeing enemies.
The system requirements are quite fair in the sense that you wont need a big gaming rig to play on max setting and retain a solid framerate. However, with the recent Director's Cut ugprade, in order to fully utilize the features in this re-release, you'll need a second monitor with touch-screen support, which I can't really comment on personally, but I will assume that it's similar to the Wii-U. A great feature in the Director's Cut is the addition of New Game+ and reworked bosses. In New Game+, your augmentations/upgrades/skills carry over. The boss difficulty has been rebalanced, and in addition, there are different methods to kill or incapacitate (or have a turret kill them for you). My favorite addition with the Director's Cut is that by default, you can have two energy-cells recharge, instead of just one1.
1. In the original Deus Ex: HR, if you did a takedown, you had to wait a minute (without any augmentations) for your energy to recharge, and only one energy-cell would charge. You had to have a lot of stockpiles of cyberboost energy kits to restore your energy.
If you're into stealth games, then I'd recommend Deus Ex: HR. You'll probably spend a lot of hours playing, and there are tons of story-decisions to choose from, which alone offer enough replay value.

This is a classic staple in the Action/RPG genre. In my mind, it may be more basic than Diablo or Baldur's Gate, but it has unique qualities about it that make it stand out in my mind. It may be old, it may have a lacking story, but overall it is a fun experience that anyone who considers themselves a fan of RPGs should pick up and kill time playing.

First: go into the file directory and change the compatability mode to Windows XP
I loved this game when it was new (before I had Steam) and continue to play it from time to time.  I admit I prefer the Cat Mansion mod, but even without that it's a very good example of the genre.
Automated attack allows a casual aspect and control of up to 6 characters allows for playing around with character development.  The story is pretty straight forward and there's not much descision making, but, if one were suficiently dedicated, there is an editor that could be used to create whatever plot line and world archetcture desired.
The game is dated and doesn't always run on modern systems (thus the compatibility mode suggestion) and it barrowed heavily from Diablo for equipment style.  That said, it was a great game in it's time.  Fully modable, seamless area transitions, multiple characters, side quests, network play; the game had LOTs of potential.
It has its flaws.  It easily could have been more dynamic with both story and NPC interaction.  The lack of a more open world or re-spawning monsters made progression limited, but again, the editor allowed for all of that.  I suppose the game itself could have been more fully developed by the developer, but at the time the focus was on encouraging an active modding community (which was a true novelty when the game was released).
Ultimately it's the casual control style that keeps me coming back to this one.  This game is fun to play.

One of the hardest large scale FPS games there is.  The learning curve is pretty high and TTK (Time to Kill) is usually just a shot or two with most weapons.  This game is the for tactically motivated, hardcore, stealthy and/ or flanking inclined gamers.
For all of the FNGs (F-- New Guys)  out there, be aware that it's going to be rough the first few hours.  You are going to die A LOT until you learn the routes and places that you should be safe and where enemy combatants will likely be.
You are likely not going to get the class that you want.  You'll have to be there at the very beginning of the game to stand a chance of getting something other than "grunt" aka. the standard infantry unit.
If you have patience to understand the flow of the battle and the abilities of your class then you should be able to make the best out of supporting your team to victory and/or being a productive member of your squad. It's absolutely enthralling when you get to a level where... everything fits and you feel that the rush of battle hitting the shots on moving targets or ambushing 5 unaware enemy players.
...
For those that are apprehensive due to lack of content, be aware that there are custom map servers out there that do a very good job of making modded maps that work well for each faction's abilities.   TWI is also running contests on a regular basis so you'll see new maps to fight every so often.
Community is a bit strange. Many try to roleplay like they are really in 'Nam  but whatever, take that with a grain of salt.
Graphics aren't the best but that's because the battlefields are huge so textures need to be lower in order to not break memory (RAM) limits. They are good enough that players can still hit targets from at least 250 meters away without a scope.

On paper, it is kind of weird to have blindfolded androids fighting chubby machines in an apocalypse settings. However, once invested into the story, the game becomes a war of two factions without their creators. The story aspect is filled with twists and foreshadowing, which tells the purpose of the war between androids and machines. It has multiple endings and a true ending that will be unlocked once Ending A,B,C, and D is unlocked. In my opinion, the emotional peak of this story lie in its true ending which is an innovative way to use the game as a storytelling medium. I am truly stunned by the reveal in true ending.
On the gameplay aspect, the quality of action combat is assured as it is developed by Platinum Games. Fighting animations are polished and make the battle feels smooth and stylish. The mixture of bullet hell elements within a 3D fighting space adds an extra layer of challenge. However, there is sequence where you are forced to re-do story parts in a different character that has a hacking gameplay in exchange of less combat moves. I personally thinks the hacking gameplay is pretty boring and ruins the pace of the action, thus leading to boring gameplay whenever the story requires you to control said character.
In conclusion, I think it is a great game. Its offers a gaming experience that I will always remembered. I recommend everyone to try it out when given the chance because it will worth the money and time spent.

The controller of the future is here!  Got one of these for Christmas and have only been using it for a couple days now but I already love it!  I was skeptical how well the gyro controls would work but they are amazing.  I also really like how you can use the touchpad like a trackball to throw the cursor with some momentum.  The haptic feedback felt a little strange at first because it's very dissimilar from the rumble and shake of other controllers, it has clicks and buzzes I was unaccustomed to.  The extra shoulder buttons on the back of the controller are nice, and the ability to add shift modes and button combinations in the config really opens up the control customization options.  Using the controller for texting has a clever interface and was surprisingly intuitive.  It does take a little getting used to because there really is nothing else quite like this controller, but I got the hang of it pretty quickly.  It also does require a little setup time with each game to fine tune and adjust the controls and sensitivities, although being able to access other profiles from the Steam community cuts down on this configuration time greatly.  I tried this controller to play Descent Underground and was amazed how intuitive and simple the controls became, when I used to rely on a complicated HOTAS configuration for this type of game.  I forsee myself using this controller for most of my games in the future, including games I previously preferred a mouse and keyboard or even a joystick for.

If you like Bioware-style RPGs, definitely consider getting this game--especially if it's on sale. A lot of folks have been complaining about being unable to run the game, but there are a number of fixes for the issue listed online. I initially had the same problem, but after running the game as an administrator and fiddling around with a few of the game's settings, I was able to get the game working and haven't had any problems since.
As far as the game goes, the level design is impressive--many of the areas still look nice, despite the outdated graphics. The dialogue can be hokey at times, and it's important to keep in mind that the game is not at all an accurate representation of Chinese culture and narrative. The levelling and customization system is not as deep as other RPG's, but overall combat is fun and more oriented toward the Action RPG genre than KOTOR. There's a really excellent mod called Jade Empire In Style that adds a lot more depth to the game's combat and customization system if players feel like the vanilla version isn't satisfying enough. The story, while far from perfect and full of cliches, is good enough to keep the player engaged and interested in what will happen next. My biggest complaint about the game mechanics is the morality system--it is apparent that Bioware was attempting to make a morality system that was less about good vs. evil, and more about whether or not the ends justify the means. If this system were to have been implemented correctly, it would be possible to take the path of the "closed fist" without being an evil jerk. Unfortunately, despite a fair amount of dialogue in the game about how neither "path" is inherently evil, it's not really possible to follow the way of the closed fist without being a really terrible excuse for a human being.
Right now I'm far from beating the game, so I can't comment on the ending, but despite it's flaws it's been a very enjoyable RPG.

If you are a fan of Fable or Knights of the Old Republic, you will definitely enjoy this game.
For starters, the combat has a very Fable Like feel. Same as the non-open world aspect of it, which I personally enjoy. It's easy to know where you've explored and what you've accomplished. Also, the map markers which indicate where you need to go or where the individual you must seek out are very easy to understand.
The dialogue is exactly how Knights of the Old Republic works. The main story is very well done and it keeps you wanting more, the downside is your companions. I didn't feel as connected or as interested in them as I did with the Old Republic. I felt Bioware let us down very much in that aspect. There are few times were you can really even talk to each individual member. Also, the fact you only get one companion at a time adds to that. Romancing, also. I enjoyed that quite a bit in Old Repulic because I felt a deeper connection between the characters. Word of advice, be VERY careful of what you say. I said one wrong thing early in the game and ruined my chances completely. Overall, if you're looking for a deeper connection towards the individual characters, you will not, imo, be as concerned with these guys as in KotOR. That being said, it is good on it's own merits.
Dialogue, some of the dialogue is very tedious and made me lose interest. It didn't have to much to do with the story at times and the lore was subpar. The documents and scrolls which you read are the main highlights in opinion. Very well written and nicely done.
The combat is awesome. It takes a bit to get used too, but once you do it's a breeze. Multiple styles to learn make it quite an enjoyable experience. Also, leveling is a lot simpler as well. I simply balanced every time I leveled and all the gems I received by the end of the game made it a cake walk.
The lack of changing armor was a bit dissapointing and really lacked customization. Also weapons, though there are an abundant of fighting styles. Weapons are almost next to non-existent. That is one thing you have to look out for when leveling, your skill points. If you waste the few you get throughout the game on a weapon you won't use much later, you will have quite a bit of trouble.
Now the story. It consists of 7 chapters. The first 4 chapters are very thoroughly done and constists of an abundant amount of side quests, which in all reality, aren't too important. They mainly give you pointless gems that are much too weak. It's even worse if you are Open Palm, because you're not taking any rewards. After 4, all side quests drop immedietaly. They are very rushed and seemed to cram all the story into those last 3, so it kind of feels like you are being jipped out of content. Again comparing it to the Old Republic, the worlds on that game were huge and provided quite a bit of content. There are only 3 villages you visit in this game, and almost no one to talk to beside quest givers.
Overall, for what it is, it's wonderful. The Old Republic scaled down with a different way of combat, much like Fable. The story has it's twists and turns but feels rushed towards the end. The lack of connection I felt to the characters was a bit upsetting but the wonderful graphics of it's time and smooth gameplay, especially during fights make up for it. It's a good 15-25 hour game and replay value is great especially if you want to go Open Palm or Closed Fist.

I loved videogames as a kid and my favorites were the action and rpg games where I played the hero with the sword slaying my enemies.  Naturally I was pumped as I put my max strength character into this world, heroically exterminating giant ants with my spear.  And after that earned me the title of 'Chosen One' nothing could stop me.
So weapon in hand I search for injustice in the closest town and find a slavers guild.  There is no room for this evil in my world!  I charge right through the front door and skewer the boss twice with my trusty spear of justice...   at which point six heavily armored guards blast my head and arms off with submachine guns, as my 11 year old eyes stare in shock at my blood sputtering corpse on the floor.
I would forever remember this day as when I TRULY understood why guns are better than swords.
Fallout 1 and 2 are both artifacts from a time when there was no mainstream gaming.  Big companies all made indie games, and this is a result when that money isn't restricted by demographics and overprotective mother influenced censorship.  No indie game can match the beauty that comes from collaboration and detail this game has in both its gameplay and art.
For truly shocking me into the reality of a world that no HD game has done since, Fallout 2 gets 10/10.

Monster Loves you is a choose your own adventure style story.
The main backbone of the story follows your life, as a monster, from the moment you are born in the "spawning vat".  As you progress through the story, at certain points in your life you are given adventures to go on. The choices you make in these adventures determine the course of your life, and the overall outcome of the story. There are a wide array of adventures available at each section.
You might think that this is simply a game for kids, but while kids will enjoy this, it does have some aspects where an adult might understand the more mature themes. It is worth noting however, that the overall playtime for the game is quite low, but trying to get the possible endings & exploring all of the available adventures will bump that time up somewhat.
The graphics in this game are very nice. Although they are not the most important part. That falls to the text. The story is written in a very nice way, that makes it easy to enage in.
The game is controlled via a mouse although if you can stream to or play the game on a tablet, it will work much better.
The music in this game is very nice. It's not too obtrusive and compliments the storylike nature of the game.
Something I do feel that this game would really benefit from is if there were some way of making user-generated adventures. After several play throughs, you will come accross all of the adventures and end up repeating yourself.
All in all, ths is a very nice choose your own adventure game which is definitely worth buying. Although, If you don't like reading, then don't buy the game.

Venice is a puzzle game from casual game company PopCap.  While the company is very familiar to many people, this game is not.  It's a hidden gem on the PC platform, and it has a harsh difficulty curve.
The game centers around Venice, Italy sinking into the waves, and it's up to you, as a random small-ish gondola, to save the treasures of Venice before all is lost.  It's a better story than Bejeweled, but not exactly AAA writing.  But, for what it needs to do, it sets the game up perfectly.
If you've ever played Luxor or Zuma, the game controls essentially like that.  Your objective is to match all of the shapes without letting any fall into the water below.  This is where the game can and will screw you over multiple times, by placing nearly impossible trick shots that rely on pin-point timing and accuracy.  It can get frustrating, but you feel a good sense of accomplishment after completing the level.
The music is up to PopCap standards, as it fits the gameplay very well, and adds to the atmosphere.  The visuals do the job, but show their age.  Not too much to the point of looking bad, but enough to notice.  I have a reoccuring problem with many of PopCap's games.  It doesn't detect that my graphics card supports hardware acceleration, even though it does.  I'm sporting an AMD Radeon HD 8240, and my old iBook G4 from 2005 supports hardware acceleration.  I don't get it, but the game looks nice even without accelerated graphics.
Overall, I give this game my Seal of Reccomendation.  Pick it up if you want an obscure classic.  I'm not responsible for any hardware-related damage you may inflict upon your system.

The controller of the future is here!  Got one of these for Christmas and have only been using it for a couple days now but I already love it!  I was skeptical how well the gyro controls would work but they are amazing.  I also really like how you can use the touchpad like a trackball to throw the cursor with some momentum.  The haptic feedback felt a little strange at first because it's very dissimilar from the rumble and shake of other controllers, it has clicks and buzzes I was unaccustomed to.  The extra shoulder buttons on the back of the controller are nice, and the ability to add shift modes and button combinations in the config really opens up the control customization options.  Using the controller for texting has a clever interface and was surprisingly intuitive.  It does take a little getting used to because there really is nothing else quite like this controller, but I got the hang of it pretty quickly.  It also does require a little setup time with each game to fine tune and adjust the controls and sensitivities, although being able to access other profiles from the Steam community cuts down on this configuration time greatly.  I tried this controller to play Descent Underground and was amazed how intuitive and simple the controls became, when I used to rely on a complicated HOTAS configuration for this type of game.  I forsee myself using this controller for most of my games in the future, including games I previously preferred a mouse and keyboard or even a joystick for.

This controller is absolutely awesome. Where do I start?
Valve has created what I think most have been looking for, and that is a controller that bridges mouse and controller.
Right out of the box I was very impressed that Valve did not even skimp out on the batteries, the controller came with two Duracell AA batteries, not some off-brand garbage.
All of the controls and design feel very well made and it fits naturally in your hands. It helps that it looks very sharp, and the Steam button that lights up when the controller is powered on is very cool.
Setup was very simple and painless, and it didn't take long for me to catch on to how it all worked. It is highly customizable and can play any game in your Steam library, even the ones that have partial or no official controller support.
Sure you will probably want to make some modifications, but for the most part you should be up and running with either your own tweaks or one of the community's configurations.
Also, I know this is a little insignificant feature overall, but you can customize the sound the controller makes when it powers on and off, and I personally found that really cool.
This thing absolutely rocks. Since I've gotten it, I've been trying out playing my games with just the controller. I must say, I'm impressed.
Thanks to its limitless customization, I had no issues playing my favorite games without having to sit over a keyboard. You can even interact with your desktop normally as if you were using a mouse, definitely handy.
It did take a small amount of getting used to, but there are certain games that I would prefer playing on the controller much more now, such as the Euro Truck Simulator games and Cities: Skylines to name a couple.
If you are looking for a good controller to play PC games with, I highly recommend this.
There isn't the hassle of opening developer consoles in games and downloading other programs, it's very simple and easy to use and it works very well.
All in all, this controller is definitely worth the asking price.

Jade Empire won my heart several years ago, when I first played it on the original XBOX. For those of you who are familiar with BioWare products, it will come as no surprise that Jade Empire lives up to being a quality role-playing game. Clearly inspired by ancient Chinese mythology and folklore, this game is both alluring and enticing to players who can appreciate compelling storytelling combined with a refreshing cast of characters. While this particular title has a relatively simple design in comparison to many of BioWare's other creations, I would still encourage you to pick it up and check it out - Particularly if you are interested in refreshingly original environments, and parables.
While I recommend the game itself to anyone, I must ADVISE CAUTION TO THOSE SEEKING TO BUY IT ON STEAM. For some, the game will not operate smoothly (if at all) without downloading and installing an additional file. For those of you still needing help, there are many thread discussions regarding this error inside the community forums.
Alternatively, you can download and install the two files that I used (they worked for me) from:
For reference, I believe this is the thread where I originally found the solution:
Jade Empire follows an orphaned martial arts student, initially training under Master Li, who is unaware of his/her full potential... Or for that matter, the road that lies ahead of them. Little does the protagonist know that every step of the journey will be a test of character, which might or might not conflict with their martial skills. While facing other-worldly creatures, in a unique combat system, the student will grow to master his/her ability -  and only then can they face the dark power growing in the Jade Empire. This game does feature multiple endings based on the players path and decisions throughout the game.
The story is absolutely gripping, and is divided into 7 chapters, each featuring their own set of sub-quests.  Some quests are entirely optional, such as the option to form a romantic relationship with a NPC team member. I was honestly very impressed by some of the same-sex options, considering the release date of Jade Empire. This might actually be one of the first games that provided this option to the player. Throughout the game, the player will be able to make decisions for their character, which can in fact impact the ending. Furthermore, some of these decisions can also be used to influence your party members into following different paths as well.
There are two major philosophies that seem crucial to the game as well: The Way of the Open Palm, and the Way of the Closed Fist. These two opposing philosophies can easily compare to Yin and Yang (or the Dark Side and the Light Side from Star Wars). However, it is important to recognize that just because someone practices the Way of the Closed Fist does not actually mark them as evil... Likewise, a follower of the Open Palm is not automatically good either. Followers of the Open Palm believe that maintaining harmony is important, whereas the followers of the Closed Fist believe that one should become self-reliant. Whether or not an individual is good or evil boils down to the context surrounding the event, so Jade Empire strays from painting a black and white world. That in itself, is a noteworthy mention, all too rare in video games.
Another brilliant feature implemented in Jade Empire are the mini-games. I really really really enjoyed the Raiden-inspired Dragonfly mini-game. Seriously, just go check it out on YouTube or something, you could spend hours doing this alone. It is sooo fun!
I might have been lucky, but I didn't have any problems with the controls in this game. They were pretty straightforward, and the game is compatible with a XBOX360 controller. On the other hand, a friend of mine confirmed that Jade Empire is not compatible with the PS3 controller. Otherwise, the controls work perfectly fine for me, as to be expected. The combat system is a bit more complex than other games I've played, but the innovative style is addicting, I promise.
The first thing to consider is that this game came out in 2005. As a result, the graphics might be considered outdated by many of you. However, I do not feel like the graphics are so outdated that they become a distraction. The visual aesthetic of the game may not be the best, but it's definitely not the worst.  I rather enjoy the art style of this game, however I cannot say that the graphics are the highlight of Jade Empire either... And yes, you will get stuck in weird camera angles until you reload it sometimes. There are glitches. Do not panic.
I think the language might be made up, but it sounds decent to me. The voice acting wasn't horribly obnoxious, and some of the music in this game is enjoyable to listen to. The audio surrounding this game meets par, as there isn't a lot to nit-pick.
Honestly, Jade Empire doesn't get old to me. I found the experience to be extremely enjoyable, and have since beaten the game several times since my first playthrough in 2005. Definitely worth playing twice!

Fallout 2: A Post Nuclear Role Playing Game. I have many fond memories of this game, it is one of my all time favorites and even after all these years, after all the hours and hours and hours I have put into the game across several different computers; I can still play it shamelessly for hours and never get bored. Its like a great film that you never tire of. I bought Fallout 2 back in '99, as a teen and could not stop playing it. I ended up becoming so engrossed in the game, that I took to the internet and found myself at the No Mutants Allowed forums where I started a long running RP called Fallout: Systematic Annihilation (My name was TRAG on those boards.) The RP was a little hit on the website, and we had quite a few fans that read it regularly and even joined in the fun. But, I didn't stop there- Chris Avellone started releasing a little document called- The Fallout Bible. I was pulled in yet again. I have read that Bible more than once- I even have a digital copy on my cell phone for my reading pleasure. Yeah, this game started an obsession. Thankfully, it never got bad enough to where restraining orders were necessary (This is a joke of course, but there are those out there that have gone that far).
So, you have read how this game has touched my life, and inspired my imagination. Now, you are probably wondering- where is the review!?!
Fallout 2 is an isometric post apocalyptic role playing game with turn-based combat. That being said, this is not just any isometric RPG, this is one of the most well written, deep, open world rpgs ever crafted. Your choices here carry real weight within the world- Want to be a Slaver? A rough, hard living slave catcher/seller. All you have to do is get a tattoo on your forehead that the world can see and you can be one. The only problem is that people really do see it and their reactions to you will reflect that. Needless to say, Slavers aren't exactly welcome in many places in the wasteland. You may wish to rethink that life choice.
But, this game is not just about career choice, this is a game with a deep strategic combat system that will challenge even the most hardened RPG gamer. The game does not hold your hand and more than likely you will die a lot. Saving often is the best tool in your arsenal, and you will be relieved when you can reload your game only a few moments before you told that Super Mutant and his pals to shove it up his you know what, and instead he shoved it up yours...Lets move on.
This is a CRPG in every sense of the word, so if you get the feel that there is a feeling that you could be playing this on a table with some friends and a cashe of multicolored dice, you probably could. In fact- There is a Pen and Paper version of the S.P.E.C.I.A.L. system (the rules system the game is powered by.) on the internet and you can find it at No Mutants Allowed (the most well known Fallout fan site, find them here
.)
There is so much that I can say about this game, but I won't, because I believe that you owe it to yourself to see it with your own eyes.
Fallout 2 is considered one of the greatest RPGs of all time for a reason: It lives up to the previous statement. It really is one of the greatest RPGs of all time. The writing is top notch, the sheer amount of choice and freedom. The methodical and satisfying development of your main character from an upstart, inexperienced tribal into a wasteland killing machine who is feared throughout the region, or a hero reveared by the struggling wasteland people. The choice is yours and your actions and decisions will determine the man/woman you become in this harsh and unforgiving post apocalyptic wasteland. You will need all the help you can get, and companions are there to meet and join your quest to restore your village and save its inhabitants from starvation, disease, and destruction.
This game is so detailed for its time, that even today I am finding things I have never seen in the game before; and I have been playing it since 1999, a year after it was released! If that doesn't give you an idea of the replayability factor I don't know what will.
If you purchase this game, you will come back to it year after year. And if you are a fan of pen and paper RPGS, CRPGS, or old school RPGs, then Fallout 2 is a godsend. Bigger and crazier than its predecessor Fallout (Which itself is an AMAZING game.) Fallout 2 takes you to the future that everyone hopes will never happen and lets you either wallow in it, or conquor it.
I HIGHLY recommend this game for any RPG fan. It will ensnare you, it will inspire you!!

So, I found this game today on the store because I received a coupon for it. With 75% off, I figured why not? I didn't pay much attention to the reviews and just gave it a go.
What you have here is a cute and charming choose your own adventure game, with pretty backgrounds and nice ambient music. However the entire gameplay consists of essentially multiple choice answers to various situations. You go through each stage of a monster's life, from being born, an adolesencent, an adult, and then you either dissolve and die or become an elder. When you're an elder you decide the fate of the monsters versus humans.
Depending on your choices you gain points in personality traits, which you need for other decisions later in the game. Based on your personality and your choices you can get one of 14 endings. An average play should take about 40 minutes, as it did with me.
It's a very charming little title, and if you know what you're getting, go ahead and buy it. But if you're looking for something beyond "click click click" for forty minutes, your attention is best placed elsewhere.

An overall good quality Choose Your Own Adventure-esque game. The game does require reading, so an adequate level of English and patience is required. It will require multiple playthroughs if you want to get all the achievements, which may become tedious if you do not have the patience to go through the same game multiple times. There are many choices which you can make within the game, which all eventually affects the type of ending you will get. If you enjoyed reading Choose Your Own Adventure books in your childhood, then you will certainly enjoy this game. If you didn't enjoy those books or you don't even know what I'm talking about, still buy this game because I guarantee you will enjoy it!

Dungeon Siege was the game of my childhood.
As a classic hack-and-slash rpg released in 2002, it built the foundation for modern rgp today. Elements taken from  Dungeons and Dragons were lovingly brought to life with early game engines, while clever Easter eggs were hidden throughout the game for only the most dedicated of players to find.
This Steam version, however, is not complete and Steam is preventing players from providing guides to fix this. What was availaible previously with purchase, the expansion and mod packs, has been stripped from accounts while guides to revert this have been taken down because Steam isn't making money off of them.
The game is from 2002: it's buggy, the graphics are fairly poor, and the mechanics are rudimentary. The community playing this are people who grew up with it, and Steam isn't going to entice new players to play an old game if they won't even allow that community to fully enjoy it.
